structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The Virginia Association for Home Care and Hospice and the West Virginia Council for Home Care and Hospice represent skilled home health, Medicaid personal care, Hospices and private duty health care providers.
*   Our mission is to advocate on the behalf of our members, ensure the delivery of high-quality care and educate the community.
*   We are providing the following items for deregulation, believing they are redundant, burdensome, costly, and serve little to no value for the overall health care system.
    *   In some cases, these regulations have a negative impact taking clinical staff away from patient care.
*   Reduction Audits
    *   Medicare skilled home care and hospice are highly regulated.
    *   Oversight by Medicare and state licensure organizations on the delivery of care is comprehensive.
    *   Over time, the Center for Medicaid and Medicare (CMS) has added many additional reporting requirements.
        *   These requirements are redundant in nature and have little to no impact on the delivery of care.
        *   Non-compliance with most of these requirements has subjected the industry to a variety of “audits” that result in retraction of payments.
            *   These retractions have little to do with patient care as they are simple documentation errors.
            *   They do not drive improved outcomes or care.
            *   They are a paper chase that is time-consuming and costly to the provider of care.
    *   We propose a reduction to the numbers and types of audits Medicare organizations are subjected to.
        *   The variety and number of audits is time-consuming, often taking nurses away from the provision of direct care to patients.
        *   It is a costly paper chase and time-consuming with a focus on paperwork compliance and not actual patient care.
*   Occupational Therapy
    *   We believe that occupational therapists should be allowed to admit home health patients to care if this is the sole service being delivered.
    *   Under the current situation, a registered nurse or physical therapist are the only disciplines that can open a case.
    *   This practice is a misuse of precious health care workers.
    *   Many patients with Alzheimer’s and dementia do not need to receive skilled nursing care or physical therapy.
        *   They do need occupational therapy and aide services.
*   Managed Care Organizations
    *   Managed Care Organizations are not required to follow the standards set for home care or hospice providers that have been established by CMS.
    *   Each plan sets its own unique standards of care, authorizations, audit processes, and payment schedules.
    *   We believe that lack of CMS oversight of managed care practices makes all patients at risk for poor care and potentially the cost of care if payment is denied.
    *   Managed care organizations should not be allowed to deny care that has been ordered by a licensed health care provider practicing within their scope of practice.
    *   Furthermore, they should not be allowed to deny payment for services that they have preauthorized nor should they be allowed to down code claims.
    *   We believe that there should be focused audits on Managed Care Organizations that change CMS mandated assessment answers and coding to conventions.
        *   Managed Care companies intentionally down code patient records in their internal review process without ever seeing the patient receiving care.
        *   This allows the Managed Care companies to pay the provider a lower rate and increase their revenue.
    *   Medicare Advantage, Medicare Administrative Contractors, Recovery Audit Contracts, and CMS should provide standardized guidelines to billing and audit procedures.
        *   As opposed to publishing standard “success with medical records request” type publications, we should not have to deal with differing sets of criteria based on the payer and/or entity administering the audit.
*   Reduce Documentation and Reporting Requirements
    *   Over time, CMS has established increasing documentation and reporting requirements for the provision of care.
    *   Many of the requirements are redundant and do not properly reflect the delivery of care needs.
    *   These requirements continue to grow in a feeble attempt to reduce “fraud, waste, and abuse”.
    *   We have provided a small list of the most egregious documentation requirements:
        *   Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) is a reporting requirement implemented by CMS as little more than a feeble attempt to stop fraud, waste, and abuse.
            *   Under this rule all staff must use a system that captures time and location information.
            *   Eliminate the current requirements for Electronic Visit Verification.
            *   Current technology has created a number of issues with connectivity among systems.
            *   There is little to no consistency between vendors of electronic visit verification systems.
            *   This has been a costly process for both states and providers.
            *   Nothing is being done with the data collected.
        *   The submission of a Home Health Notice of Admission (NOA) requirement is completely redundant and adds no value to the delivery of care.
            *   The requirements associated with the documentation are the same as those found in the Start of Care and Care Plan documentation.
            *   In addition, this notice is confusing for patients.
            *   If this document is not complete or deviates from the requirement, the home health agency’s claim will be rejected even though care was delivered.
        *   We believe that the face-to-face requirements for an admission to Medicare home health can be significantly simplified.
            *   A simple order from the physician authorizing services should be sufficient.
            *   The current requirements are constantly being revised by CMS which causes additional confusion for both physicians and home care organizations.
        *   Home health is perfectly positioned to provide a robust chronic disease management program to Medicare beneficiaries.
            *   Many times, beneficiaries do not meet the current homebound requirement for Medicare home health services.
            *   We propose the elimination of this requirement.
            *   This would improve access to care for more people and potentially reduce hospital readmissions.
            *   By expanding eligibility beyond individuals confined to their homes, more people could receive in-home support, potentially improving their overall health and well-being.
            *   Home health services can play a crucial role in managing chronic conditions, preventing hospitalizations, and improving quality of life.
            *   By expanding access to these services, more people could benefit from the individualized care and support they need to maintain their health at home.
            *   Studies have shown that home health care can help prevent hospital readmissions by providing ongoing care and support after a hospital stay.
            *   Expanding eligibility for home health services could lead to fewer unnecessary hospitalizations and a more efficient healthcare system.
            *   The current homebound requirement limits who can access home health services, even if they need support to manage their health conditions.
            *   Removing this restriction would allow more individuals, including those who can leave home for certain activities but still need help with daily tasks, to benefit from in-home care.
            *   The current homebound requirement can place a significant burden on family caregivers who may not be able to provide all the necessary support for their loved ones.
            *   By expanding access to home health services, families can receive much-needed respite and support, reducing stress and improving their well-being.
        *   The OASIS data collection requirements are a burden to patients and clinicians.
            *   The initial OASIS takes in excess of 90 minutes to complete.
            *   It has many internal requirements that are prescriptive in nature.
            *   For example, clinicians cannot use symptoms such as muscle weakness, gait instability; they must be much more quantitative and descriptive.
            *   These types of requirements do not improve care.
        *   Current arbitrary time frames are a burden to providers and have no direct impact on the delivery of care.
            *   Admission assessment is required to be completed by RN if nursing services are ordered.
            *   Under current regulations, the initial assessment must be completed within 48 hours from referral or discharge date.
            *   Resumption assessment must be completed within 48 hours from discharge date.
            *   HHA supervisory visits must be done every 14 days.
            *   Arbitrary timelines ignore agency staffing considerations and can easily be adjusted to two business days without harm to patients.
        *   CMS claims that documentation is a cornerstone of the start of care assessment process, serving as a record of the patient’s initial evaluation.
            *   This requirement is in addition to the OASIS documentation mentioned above.
            *   We would suggest that the care plan be the primary document capturing all relevant patient information, assessment findings, completed in a timely manner.
            *   Furthermore, the care plan documentation serves as a tool for continuity of care, providing subsequent caregivers with a comprehensive understanding of the patient’s health status and needs, promoting a seamless transition in care delivery.
            *   In the event of audits or quality reviews, thorough and accurate documentation can demonstrate compliance with agency protocols and regulatory requirements.
            *   While we agree that documentation is a cornerstone of care, CMS has created redundant requirements.
            *   The Start of Care assessment process is yet one more example; similar to other requirements, its elements include the patient’s medical history, current medications, allergies, and any pertinent social determinants of health.
            *   Additionally, the nurse should record findings from the physical assessment and any specific needs identified during the evaluation.
        *   Home health clinicians work in diverse and sometimes unpredictable environments.
            *   Visiting patients in their homes means encountering a wide range of living conditions, which can affect the assessment process.
            *   Another challenge is the variability in patients’ health literacy levels.
        *   The primary obstacle faced by clinicians is the time constraints due to the multitude of different documentation requirements.
            *   Clinicians frequently juggle multiple patients and administrative responsibilities, which can limit the time available for thorough assessments.
            *   This can lead to incomplete evaluations, overlooking vital information that may impact patient care.
            *   All of these requirements put patients at unnecessary risk.
*   The current regulatory requirements for an Emergency Preparedness Plan are excessively burdensome.
    *   Among requirements are evaluation of staff risks, patient risks, community risk, risk assessment, training, reporting, and table-top exercise.
    *   Home care organizations have no authority to force a patient to comply with any of their emergency preparedness strategies.
    *   In addition, there is nothing in this regulatory requirement that benefits or improves the quality of care given to the patient.
*   The Ensuring Access to Medicaid Services final rule (Access final rule) was issued in April 2024.
    *   The rule mandated a number of changes for Medicaid Home and Community Based programs.
    *   Many of the requirements of this rule are redundant to what state Medicaid programs already have in place.
    *   One of the most troublesome aspects of this rule is its mandate regarding what percentage of Medicaid reimbursement must be paid directly to personal care aides.
        *   As written, the rule fails to recognize many costs of providing this type of care.
        *   It ignores the requirements of registered nursing oversight, administrative support, technology, malpractice insurance, and many other costs associated with this type of business.
*   The current Patient Driven Grouping Model is exceedingly complex.
    *   It adds a significant burden to the provision of care.
    *   It forces clinicians to justify in great detail the need for care that has been prescribed by physicians.
*   Commercial insurers should not be included in CMS payor mix calculations or determinations.
    *   In general, those persons receiving care paid for by a commercial insurer are younger and have fewer health care issues.
*   Home care providers continue to have significant issues with low reimbursement from Medicare Advantage plans.
    *   Often reimbursement is less than 25% of the actual cost of sending a nurse to a patient’s home.
*   No Managed Care company should be allowed to deny a claim if it has been preauthorized by the managed care company.
*   No preauthorization should be required to treat a patient discharged from a hospital.
    *   This requirement only slows down the treatment of care which has been ordered by a physician.
*   End-of-life care is a challenging time.
    *   We believe that any barriers to Hospice care should be eliminated.
    *   Nurse Practitioners and Physician Assistants should be allowed to certify terminal illness for Hospice patients.
    *   Under current regulation, there is a cumbersome payment process that Hospice and Nursing Facilities face when the patient is a long-term care resident of a nursing facility.
        *   It is called the “room and board pass through”.
        *   It requires the Hospice to pay the nursing facility for each day a patient uses a bed.
        *   The Hospice in turn bills CMS for the nursing facility bed use.
        *   This payment requirement is cumbersome for both nursing facilities and hospices.
        *   This requirement should be eliminated.
    *   We believe that the Hospice Outcomes and Patient Evaluation (HOPE) assessment is unnecessary.
        *   CMS developed this new patient assessment tool to replace the Hospice data set.
        *   HOPE is a new requirement to further standardize data collection to provide clinical data that could inform future payment refinements.
        *   The use of the HOPE assessment will take nursing staff away from patient care.
    *   To certify a patient's terminal illness under Medicare hospice benefits, a physician must be enrolled in or validly opted-out of Medicare.
        *   There are many physicians that are not enrolled or validly opted out of Medicare.
        *   This requirement has resulted in eligible patients not receiving Hospice care.
        *   This requirement serves no benefit to patients or Medicare and is redundant to other long-standing practice standards.
    *   These requirements serve no real purpose other than a paper compliance standard.
    *   They are of great burden to Hospices.
    *   They consume staff resources and have no impact on the quality of care.
    *   Recently, CMS suspended the Hospice Special Focus Program.
        *   The program was intended to identify poor performing hospices.
        *   An evaluation of the program noted a number of methodological faults.
        *   The current survey and certification process is an adequate tool for rooting out poor performing organizations and should be used as such.
*   Our final issue is with regulatory changes made to the Fair Labor Standards Act.
    *   Under the Obama administration, the Department of Labor changed long-standing regulations that allowed personal care aides to work an unlimited number of hours not subject to overtime.
    *   The nature of personal care is a good amount of companionship care involving little to no skills.
        *   This includes things such as watching television, taking a person to a doctor appointment, playing games, reading, etc.
    *   The requirement of overtime pay came as a detriment to the person receiving care.
    *   State Medicaid programs made no accommodation for overtime pay, forcing agencies to only allow aides to work 40 hours or less.
    *   Personal care aides were forced to work multiple agencies to make ends meet.
    *   Patients suffered from a loss of care continuity as more personal care aides were necessary to provide the same amount of care.
    *   We believe this rule change in itself has done nothing but exacerbate the shortage of in-home aide care.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: Representing home care and hospice providers in Virginia and West Virginia, these associations advocate for deregulation by identifying numerous redundant, burdensome, and costly CMS and MCO requirements that detract from patient care and restrict access to essential services.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Virginia Association for Home Care and Hospice and West Virginia Council for Home Care and Hospice
- **Type:** Trade Association
- **Role/Expertise:** Advocates for members (skilled home health, Medicaid personal care, hospices, and private duty health care providers), ensures high-quality care, and educates the community.
- **Geographic Scope:** State (Virginia and West Virginia)
- **Stake in Issue:** Direct providers of home health and hospice services, seeking to reduce regulatory burdens, costs, and improve patient access and quality of care.
structuredSections.corePosition: We believe that many current regulations imposed by CMS and Managed Care Organizations are redundant, burdensome, costly, and provide little value to the healthcare system, often negatively impacting patient care by diverting clinical staff to paperwork. We advocate for deregulation and streamlined processes to improve care delivery and access.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Reduce the numbers and types of audits Medicare organizations are subjected to.
- Allow occupational therapists to admit home health patients to care if it is the sole service being delivered.
- Implement CMS oversight of Managed Care Organizations' standards of care, authorizations, audit processes, and payment schedules.
- Prohibit Managed Care Organizations from denying care ordered by a licensed health care provider.
- Prohibit Managed Care Organizations from denying payment for preauthorized services.
- Prohibit Managed Care Organizations from downcoding claims.
- Conduct focused audits on Managed Care Organizations that change CMS mandated assessment answers and coding.
- Standardize billing and audit guidelines provided by Medicare Advantage, Medicare Administrative Contractors, Recovery Audit Contracts, and CMS.
- Eliminate the current requirements for Electronic Visit Verification.
- Eliminate the Home Health Notice of Admission (NOA) requirement.
- Significantly simplify the face-to-face requirements for an admission to Medicare home health, making a simple physician order sufficient.
- Eliminate the homebound requirement for Medicare home health services.
- Establish the care plan as the primary document capturing all relevant patient information and assessment findings, eliminating redundant Start of Care assessment requirements.
- Eliminate the excessively burdensome regulatory requirements for an Emergency Preparedness Plan for home care organizations.
- Re-evaluate the mandate in the Ensuring Access to Medicaid Services final rule regarding the percentage of Medicaid reimbursement paid directly to personal care aides, recognizing all costs of providing care.
- Exclude commercial insurers from CMS payor mix calculations or determinations.
- Prohibit Managed Care companies from denying claims if they have been preauthorized.
- Eliminate preauthorization requirements for patients discharged from a hospital.
- Eliminate all barriers to Hospice care.
- Allow Nurse Practitioners and Physician Assistants to certify terminal illness for Hospice patients.
- Eliminate the "room and board pass through" payment requirement for Hospice and Nursing Facilities.
- Eliminate the Hospice Outcomes and Patient Evaluation (HOPE) assessment.
- Remove the requirement that a physician must be enrolled in or validly opted-out of Medicare to certify a patient's terminal illness for hospice benefits.
- Re-evaluate the regulatory changes made to the Fair Labor Standards Act under the Obama administration that subject personal care aides to overtime, allowing them to work unlimited hours not subject to overtime.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- Medicare audits are redundant, focus on documentation errors, lead to payment retractions unrelated to patient care, are time-consuming and costly, and take nurses away from direct patient care.
- Current home health admission rules prevent occupational therapists from opening cases even when OT is the sole needed service, leading to misuse of healthcare workers and inadequate care for patients (e.g., those with Alzheimer’s and dementia).
- Lack of CMS oversight allows Managed Care Organizations to operate with inconsistent, unique standards, authorizations, and payment schedules, placing patients at risk for poor care and denied payments.
- Managed Care Organizations intentionally downcode patient records to pay providers lower rates and increase their revenue, without ever seeing the patient.
- Increasing CMS documentation and reporting requirements are redundant, don't reflect care needs, are ineffective at reducing "fraud, waste, and abuse," and consume excessive clinical time.
  - Electronic Visit Verification (EVV) causes connectivity issues, lacks consistency between vendors, is costly for states and providers, and the collected data is not utilized.
  - The Home Health Notice of Admission (NOA) requirement is redundant, confusing for patients, and causes claim rejections for minor deviations even when care is delivered.
  - Constantly revised face-to-face requirements for home health admissions cause confusion for physicians and home care organizations.
  - The homebound requirement severely limits access to home health services for many Medicare beneficiaries who could benefit from chronic disease management, preventing hospitalizations, and reducing caregiver burden.
  - OASIS data collection is burdensome (takes over 90 minutes), prescriptive (requiring quantitative descriptions rather than clinical observations), and does not improve care quality.
  - Arbitrary regulatory timeframes for assessments (e.g., 48 hours for initial/resumption) and supervisory visits (e.g., every 14 days) are burdensome, ignore staffing considerations, and put patients at risk due to time constraints on clinicians.
  - The Start of Care assessment process creates redundant documentation requirements on top of OASIS, contributing to clinician time constraints and incomplete evaluations.
- The current Emergency Preparedness Plan requirements are excessively burdensome, do not benefit or improve patient care quality, and home care organizations lack authority to enforce patient compliance with these strategies.
- The Ensuring Access to Medicaid Services final rule's mandate on direct payment to personal care aides ignores critical operational costs for providers, such as nursing oversight, administrative support, technology, and malpractice insurance.
- The Patient Driven Grouping Model is exceedingly complex and burdens clinicians by forcing them to provide excessive justification for physician-prescribed care.
- Home care providers experience significant financial issues due to low reimbursement from Medicare Advantage plans, often receiving less than 25% of the actual cost of providing care.
- Preauthorization requirements for patients discharged from a hospital unnecessarily slow down the initiation of physician-ordered care.
- Cumbersome hospice regulations, such as the "room and board pass through" payment process for nursing facility residents and the new HOPE assessment, are burdensome, consume staff resources, and do not improve quality of care.
- The requirement that a physician must be Medicare enrolled or opted-out to certify terminal illness for hospice results in eligible patients not receiving care, serving no benefit to patients or Medicare.
- Changes to the Fair Labor Standards Act regarding overtime for personal care aides have led to detrimental consequences, forcing aides to work multiple agencies and causing a loss of care continuity for patients, exacerbating the in-home aide shortage.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The detailed explanation of how the Fair Labor Standards Act changes for personal care aides, specifically the introduction of overtime pay, negatively impacted both aides (forcing them to work multiple agencies) and patients (loss of care continuity and exacerbating aide shortages), directly linking a policy change to real-world detrimental outcomes.
- The striking statistic that home care providers often receive "less than 25% of the actual cost of sending a nurse to a patient’s home" from Medicare Advantage plans, vividly illustrating the financial unsustainability faced by providers.
- The insight that OASIS data collection forces clinicians to use overly quantitative and descriptive language, prohibiting the use of simpler, clinically relevant terms like "muscle weakness" or "gait instability," which highlights a disconnect between burdensome documentation requirements and actual improvement in patient care.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "They are a paper chase that is time consuming and costly to the provider of care."
- "Managed Care companies intentionally down code patient records in their internal review process without ever seeing the patient receiving care. This allows the Managed Care companies to pay the provider a lower rate and increase their revenue."
- "We believe this rule change in itself has done nothing but exacerbate the shortage of in-home aide care."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- If pursuing deregulation in the healthcare space to improve value to the consumer, the first thing that should be targeted is the asymmetric payment systems that Congress created decades ago.
  - Hospitals are paid more for the same service compared to physicians in private practice.
- Children's and Cancer hospitals were exempt from this and have cost-plus pricing applied.
- This system does not abide by free market principles and further consolidates the market.
  - The physician fee schedule does not keep up with inflation.
- Private practices, where care is less expensive, close or sell to private equity or hospitals.
- Meanwhile, hospitals are paid more for the same service and are kept afloat.
  - They are given the excess capital to buy those private practices.
- This leads to healthcare consolidation and higher prices.
- It induces bottlenecks and decreases the negotiating power of physicians, as they are beholden to fewer employers.
- The current administration needs to continue its excellent efforts on price transparency.
- The administration also needs to make payments site-neutral with no exceptions for Children's or Cancer hospitals.
- The physician fee schedule also needs to be reformed and needs to keep up with inflation.
- Physician private contracts are often linked to Medicare rates, so commercial rates follow the physician fee schedule payments.
- This construct will see the elimination of private practice and higher healthcare costs if nothing is done about this.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An individual advocates for healthcare deregulation through site-neutral payments without exceptions and physician fee schedule reform to counter market consolidation, preserve private practices, and control rising costs.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Andrew Tompkins
- **Type:** Individual
- **Role/Expertise:** Implies deep understanding of healthcare payment systems, market dynamics, and the challenges faced by private practices.
- **Geographic Scope:** National
- **Stake in Issue:** An individual concerned about the structure of healthcare payments and their impact on market competition, physician autonomy, and consumer costs, potentially with a professional connection to private practice healthcare.
structuredSections.corePosition: If we are truly pursuing deregulation in healthcare to improve consumer value, the immediate focus must be on reforming the asymmetric payment systems established by Congress decades ago. The current structure, which favors hospitals over private practices and fails to adjust physician payments for inflation, is directly causing market consolidation, driving up healthcare costs, and diminishing physician negotiating power.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Continue current efforts on price transparency.
- Make payments site-neutral with no exceptions for Children's or Cancer hospitals.
- Reform the physician fee schedule to ensure it keeps up with inflation.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- Asymmetric payment systems created by Congress lead to hospitals being paid more than private practice physicians for the same service, which violates free market principles.
- The physician fee schedule does not keep up with inflation, causing financial strain on private practices.
- Less expensive private practices are forced to close or sell to private equity or hospitals due to the economic disadvantages created by current payment structures.
- Hospitals receive excess capital due to higher payments, which enables them to acquire private practices, leading to healthcare consolidation and higher prices.
- Market consolidation induces bottlenecks in care delivery and decreases the negotiating power of physicians by limiting employer options.
- Inaction will lead to the elimination of private practices and a sustained increase in overall healthcare costs.
- Physician private contracts are often linked to Medicare rates, meaning an inadequate physician fee schedule negatively impacts commercial rates as well.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The historical exemption of Children's and Cancer hospitals from site-neutral payments, operating on a cost-plus pricing model, is highlighted as a specific structural issue contributing to market distortion.
- Insight that physician private contracts are frequently tied to Medicare rates, illustrating how an inadequate federal physician fee schedule cascades to affect commercial rates and the financial viability of private practices.
- A clear articulation of how the current payment construct directly contributes to healthcare market consolidation, increased prices, and reduced physician autonomy.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "If you are pursuing deregulation in the healthcare space to improve value to the consumer the first thing that you should take aim at is the asymmetric payment systems that Congress created decades ago, whereby hospitals will be paid more for the same service as physicians in private practice."
- "This construct will see the elimination of private practice and higher healthcare costs if you do nothing about this."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   NNPEN (National Nurse Practitioner Entrepreneur Network) is a national network of Nurse Practitioners (NPs) who own and are employed within nurse-led clinical practices.
    *   These NPs are included within MACRA’s QPP definition of “eligible clinician” and CPC+’s definition of “practitioner.”
*   NNPEN believes that replacing a legislative/prescriptive definition of scope of practice with one that defers to the education and training of the designated practitioner’s license is a good thing.
*   Comments relate to the effect of recent Executive Orders and how CMS, guided by healthy healthcare competition policy, can take the lead with other payers in constructing infrastructure that facilitates the quickest uptake of, and access to, advanced practitioners into the Medicare provider network.
    *   This would increase competitors and competition.
*   NNPEN restricts comments to preparing NPs to be informed risk-takers in Value Based Payment (VBP) risk programs that can sustain small, nimble group practices.
*   NP Scope of Practice (SOP) success is a pyrrhic victory and will not reduce harmful barriers to healthy competition without NP access to VBP arrangements.
    *   These arrangements can reliably reward NP outcomes that flow from the Nursing Process.
    *   Recent executive orders give new and significant urgency to the conversation about NP risk-taking skills required to succeed in VBP programs.

#1—Preserve/extend the low cost and high quality benefits of the Nursing Process
*   Uncontroverted literature of >100 peer-reviewed studies finds that NPs produce quality and cost outcomes as good or better than those of physician PCPs.
    *   This is attributed to the integrated view of the patient that is the backbone of the Nursing Process.
    *   This patient-facing, hard-wired Nursing Process also explains why nurses are consistently viewed as the most trusted profession and the group most trusted to “fix” health care.
*   Yet, the Nursing Process is "desecrated" by the dominant medical model pressure to “see” 25-30 patients per day, squeezing patient office visits into 15-minute segments.
*   NP-owned practices are typically small and community-based by design.
    *   They struggle to find Small Business Administration (SBA) lenders that appreciate their creditworthiness.
*   To preserve the benefits of nurse-led care, NP practices need many more sustainable independent practice options that give consumers access to healthcare and preserve the benefits of the Nursing Process in all fifty states.
    *   Recent Executive Orders do not do that.
    *   CMMI has stood up only one model, the REACH ACO, as “NP friendly” because it recognizes the physician and NP PCP’s network eligibility and payment options as equivalent.
    *   CMMI’s dominant Medicare Shared Savings ACO model does not offer this equivalence.
*   Even Original Medicare, which does not reflect the anti-NP bias of private insurers built into managed Medicare, punishes the NP PCP by paying NPs only 85% of the physician fee schedule for the same work.
    *   It adds insult to injury by perpetuating an “Incident to” billing policy that recognizes the billing provider (deemed to be the physician in most institutional settings), not the treating provider (who would be paid only 85% of the physician’s charges).
    *   MedPac’s recommendation to abandon incident-to billing has not prevailed.
*   Given these VBP program limitations, the SBA needs much more encouragement to create a robust lender safety net for NP practices, which form the healthcare safety net in underserved communities.

#2—Full Practice Authority (aka Independent Scope of Practice) will generate a much-needed NP primary care outcomes database that supports pricing based on competition
*   As long as the NP is not the independent Primary Care Provider, no performance data is being separately attributed to the NP.
    *   This syphons NP value off to benefit the billing physician and allows payers to resist exploration of VBP with NPs for “lack of credible data.”
*   CMS terminating the practice of "incident-to" billing would support collection of the longitudinal data that is essential to measuring and documenting the NP’s (and all other PCPs’) management of population health risk.
*   The metaphor “when Medicare sneezes everyone gets a cold” is trite but true here, comparable to the government funding technology development in early years by supplying expensive hardware.

#3---Payer barriers limit ready access to NPs by their beneficiaries.
*   NPs report insurers deny empaneling them, noting their panels are full.
*   Insurance companies do not keep their directories up to date, creating a false perception of the number of available providers in geographic areas.
*   Holding insurance companies accountable to maintain their directories with accurate provider listings ensures availability of providers to care in areas, especially in provider shortage areas.
*   Insurers must stop discriminating against NPs and provide access to their panels—both medical and psychiatric mental health panels.

#4--Credentialing Barriers.
*   When new NPs are hired and the practice is credentialing them, insurers allow physicians to submit claims under the credentialed physician’s NPI ("incident to") pending the approval of the new hire.
*   NPs are not afforded that same privilege, which creates a financial hardship for the NP business owner who hires a new NP and must wait 3-6 months for the credentialing process to be completed.
*   Streamlining the credentialing process is sorely needed to reduce practice burden.

#5---Financial Support.
*   A national NP education loan program is needed that parallels the medical education loan program.
    *   This program should be administered by community-based DNP schools of nursing.
    *   It should fund NP student preceptors and the infrastructure necessary to administer the preceptor program.
    *   Supporting attachments on physician shortage and physician funding were AI-generated on October 7, 2024.

#6--Without NPs delivering primary care access across the nation, CMS will fail to meet its Quadruple Aim Goals
*   The U.S. is losing primary care physicians at an unprecedented rate across the U.S., especially in rural areas where needs are extremely high and opioid addiction/deaths are skyrocketing.
*   Many doctors are moving to "concierge" care models which leave out the poorest/sickest in the U.S.
*   NPs are the fastest growing health care professional group by a significant margin.
    *   The American Association of Nurse Practitioners’ website reports there are 385,000 NPs in America in 2024.
    *   According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, overall employment of physicians and surgeons is projected to grow 4 percent from 2023 to 2033 with 23,600 openings annually.

#7—NPs are a growing workforce trained in primary care and are obscenely underfunded.
*   As the number of Nurse Practitioners (NPs) continues to grow, it is essential to allocate funds to nursing education.
    *   This funding should aim to attract highly qualified educators.
    *   It should also provide incentives for preceptors who dedicate their time to training the next generation of nurses and NPs.
*   Additionally, financial support is needed for business training and for small businesses run by NPs.
*   Pilot programs through CMS (Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services) should also be funded to support NP practices that care for Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries.

*   Empowered by the current administration’s libertarian leanings, and reinforced (but never enforced) by ACA Section 2706 prohibiting insurer discrimination on the basis of license, DOJ and CMS have the power and gravitas with a top-of-license SOP vision to overcome the staunch payer resistance and physician stonewalling that still confounds SOP progress in more than half of U.S. states.
*   The marketplace and the workforce are ready for SOP change that is refreshingly bipartisan. The time is now!
*   NNPEN applauds President Trump for his recognition that advanced practice providers, specifically Nurse Practitioners that can practice independently, are the market disruptors his administration needs to break down the barriers to healthy primary care access.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The National Nurse Practitioner Entrepreneur Network (NNPEN) urges HHS and CMS to eliminate discriminatory barriers to full practice authority, ensure equitable value-based payment access, and provide financial support for Nurse Practitioners, arguing that these changes are essential to expand primary care access, particularly in underserved communities, and achieve healthcare competition goals.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   As a professional working in long-term care (LTC), I respectfully implore CMS and related agencies to reevaluate the current reporting requirements for COVID-19 and other respiratory infections by facilities through the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN).
*   The mandatory reporting requirements served a critical purpose during the height of the pandemic, allowing public health agencies to:
    *   Monitor the spread of COVID-19.
    *   Apportion resources.
    *   Implement emergency response strategies.
*   However, with the end of the declared public health emergency and infection patterns stabilizing, the perpetual requirement for routine NHSN reporting has become a substantial administrative burden for LTC staff.
    *   LTC staff are already facing workforce shortages and high operational demands.
*   Facilities have fully developed their internal infection prevention practices and now have the tools and protocols to monitor and manage infectious disease trends without federal reporting mandates.
*   The duplicative nature of data entry across systems takes away from direct resident care.
    *   This is especially true in facilities with limited staffing resources.
*   I support CMS’s efforts to reduce regulatory burden and refocus facility resources on quality care and staff retention.
*   Voluntary reporting, targeted surveillance, or periodic audits could still provide valuable data without placing undue pressure on frontline staff.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: A long-term care professional urges CMS to reevaluate mandatory NHSN reporting for respiratory infections, arguing it's an administrative burden post-PHE that diverts resources from direct resident care, suggesting voluntary methods instead.

-   I am advocating for Head Start children.
-   I appreciate the energy and focus of Robert F Kennedy Jr.
-   Healthier children is a must!!!
-   A necessary change is to the CACFP and what foods are considered reimbursement and the amount of food distributed to young children.
    -   The cost return our program receives from CACFP is extremely low, and it puts our children in a vulnerable state.
    -   Children need protein in the morning, high energy foods for lunch, and healthy snacks.
    -   At Family Forum, Inc. we make our food from scratch and only provide quality, which costs our program.
    -   When reimbursement from one program is low and the cost of food is high, then other areas in our program suffer, such as wages for qualified staff and classroom supplies (diapers etc).
-   Children's behavior happens all day.
    -   The children in Head Start are dealing with difficult family home situations, and our staff work with both the child and parents.
    -   One gratifying way we can begin to support the child's nutritional development is to start with the meals being served.
    -   Mr. Kennedy has spoken loudly about Autism and other concerns of children, and we need to honor this work by providing quality food for our youngest children.
-   Head Start needs Federal Funding increase for 2025 and the future.
    -   It costs money to invest in children and make a difference.
    -   Invest in one large, successful program and you will see healthier communities, stronger families, and a growing economy.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)
    *   Subject: Regulatory Improvements to Promote Innovation and Reduce Costs
*   As a concerned citizen and advocate for evidence-based, compassionate care, I urge HHS to embrace regulatory reforms that integrate innovative, plant-based, and psychedelic-assisted therapies into the broader health care framework.
*   We are at a pivotal moment where innovation can intersect with compassion and science.
    *   Alternative therapies such as medical cannabis, psilocybin, ketamine, and ibogaine have demonstrated promising results in treating conditions such as PTSD, depression, chronic pain, and substance use disorders.
    *   When supported by sound data and clinical oversight, these therapies offer cost-effective and outcome-driven solutions compared to many conventional treatments.
*   We can start with our veterans, many of whom are suffering silently.
    *   Increasingly, veterans are traveling outside the United States—particularly to Mexico for ibogaine therapy—because they cannot access the help they need here at home.
    *   These are our heroes. We owe them better.
    *   HHS should prioritize domestic research, clinical access, and regulatory frameworks that bring these treatments within reach of our veteran community—without forcing them to leave the country in search of healing.
*   Additionally, patients facing terminal illness should be fully supported through expanded application of the Right to Try Act.
    *   Individuals at the end of life deserve the dignity and freedom to explore all potentially beneficial treatments, including psychedelic and plant-based options, when traditional approaches have failed.
    *   Regulatory flexibility and moral clarity must guide our policies in these cases.
*   To further support this innovation-based health care transformation, I recommend that HHS:
    *   Remove regulatory barriers to research and clinical trials involving plant-based and psychedelic medicines.
    *   Develop CMS-backed pilot programs for employer-sponsored health plans that incorporate these treatments.
    *   Ensure data transparency by allowing self-insured employers access to health claims and utilization data to evaluate alternative care models.
    *   Collaborate with the VA and other federal partners to develop and monitor treatment pathways specifically for veterans using these emerging therapies.
    *   Expand access to compassionate use and early intervention programs through the Right to Try pathway.
*   Ultimately, innovation in health care must not only reduce costs but restore hope and healing—especially for those who have served and those facing the end of life.
*   The United States has an opportunity to lead ethically, scientifically, and economically in this next frontier of care.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: A concerned citizen and advocate urges HHS to reform regulations to integrate innovative plant-based and psychedelic therapies into healthcare, specifically to benefit veterans and terminally ill patients through expanded access, research, and data transparency.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- There have been various moves to deregulate various agencies under the federal government, including education, research, and health.
  - These strategic agencies have suffered from the current President’s aspiration to deregulate in the name of cutting down spending.
- One such agency affected is Planned Parenthood.
  - Defunding Planned Parenthood could have significant consequences for public health, particularly for low-income and underserved communities.
- Planned Parenthood provides essential services.
  - These include cancer screenings, STI testing, and contraception.
  - Without funding, many clinics may close, leaving patients without affordable healthcare options.
- Patient reliance on Medicaid is high.
  - Over half of Planned Parenthood’s patients rely on Medicaid.
  - If defunding efforts succeed, these individuals may struggle to find alternative providers that offer the same level of care.
- Clinic closures are already occurring due to financial strain.
  - At least 20 Planned Parenthood clinics have already shut down this year.
  - If funding is further restricted, up to 200 clinics could close, affecting millions of patients.
- Defunding Planned Parenthood may increase healthcare costs.
  - The Congressional Budget Office has estimated that defunding Planned Parenthood could increase government healthcare costs by hundreds of millions of dollars.
  - This increase would be due to higher rates of unintended pregnancies and untreated health conditions.
- Defunding may have disproportionate effects on rural areas.
  - Many Planned Parenthood clinics serve rural communities where healthcare options are limited.
  - Losing these clinics could force patients to travel long distances for care or go without necessary medical services.
- It is essential that the federal government takes a second look at some of the agencies they are deregulating and defunding.
  - The consequences may be dire if care is not taken.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An individual warns that defunding Planned Parenthood, as part of a broader federal deregulation trend, will severely harm public health, particularly for vulnerable populations, by closing clinics, increasing healthcare costs, and disproportionately affecting rural areas.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The Next Generation Pet Food Manufacturers Association (NGPFMA) requests that HHS leaders rescind the FDA’s enforcement of the zero-tolerance policy regarding Salmonella in raw pet food products, as outlined in Compliance Policy Guide Sec. 690.800.
    *   While we fully support science-based efforts to ensure pet food safety, the FDA’s current approach—treating any and all Salmonella presence in raw pet food as adulteration—is not supported by sound science, consistent legal reasoning, or practical understanding of how food is handled in real-world settings.
    *   More concerning, this policy results in redundant government oversight that places undue financial and operational strain on manufacturers without delivering proportionate public health benefits.
*   Duplication of Government Oversight
    *   A critical yet often overlooked issue is redundancy in the federal food inspection process.
    *   Many raw pet food products are made from meat that has already passed USDA inspection and been deemed high-quality and fit for human consumption, meaning the USDA has certified it meets rigorous safety standards for people.
    *   However, once this same food is processed and packaged for pets, it undergoes a second evaluation by the FDA, which deems the product unacceptable for animal consumption solely based on Salmonella presence, regardless of the strain’s pathogenicity or risk.
    *   This dual-agency oversight, often reaching contradictory conclusions about the same product, effectively doubles inspection costs to U.S. taxpayers.
    *   It also creates a climate of regulatory uncertainty for manufacturers, discouraging innovation and driving up prices for consumers.
    *   A reevaluation of this redundant and inefficient framework is warranted.
*   Legal and Scientific Concerns
    *   Federal case law—including Supreme Beef Processors v. USDA and APHA v. Butz—has clarified that Salmonella's presence in raw meat does not inherently render the product harmful, particularly when it is not intended for human consumption as the bacteria is inherent in the meat.
    *   Under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA), food is considered adulterated only if it contains a harmful "added substance" or if an inherent substance is found in quantities likely to cause injury to the intended consumer.
    *   Furthermore, the FDA’s own Compliance Policy Guide is non-binding and does not confer legally enforceable authority.
    *   Enforcement actions should be based on actual evidence of risk—such as insanitary production conditions, misuse, or illness—not mere detection of non-pathogenic bacteria in otherwise clean facilities.
    *   Inconsistently, the FDA permits Salmonella presence in raw meat, poultry, and livestock feed, provided it does not pose a threat to the intended species.
    *   Yet when it comes to raw pet food, the agency applies a blanket zero-tolerance standard without regard for context, science, or relative risk to the products’ intended consumer - pets.
*   Scientific Inconsistencies
    *   The FDA’s zero-tolerance stance on Salmonella in raw pet food is inconsistent with its treatment of other food categories.
    *   For livestock feed and human foods such as raw poultry, eggs, and flour, the presence of non-pathogenic Salmonella is not automatically considered a basis for recall.
    *   FDA policy does not consider poultry feed to be adulterated unless the Salmonella strain is pathogenic to the animal for which it is intended.
    *   The same principle should apply to pet food.
    *   Dogs and cats are far less susceptible to Salmonella-related illness than humans, and most documented illnesses in pets from Salmonella are rare or unverified.
    *   None exist in the CDC database to link human illness to handling of raw pet food.
    *   There is no justification for singling out raw pet food when other raw products, with equal or greater risks of cross-contamination, are treated with a more balanced, risk-based regulatory approach.
*   Human Health Concerns: Risk vs. Responsibility
    *   We understand that the FDA justifies its zero-tolerance policy as a means to protect human handlers from secondary infection; however, this reasoning is flawed.
    *   Consumers interact daily with raw meats, eggs, and produce that can harbor pathogens, yet those products are not banned or recalled solely on theoretical risks of mishandling.
    *   Public education, hygiene guidelines, and proper labeling—not punitive enforcement—have long been the FDA’s response to these situations.
    *   There is no compelling evidence to support a unique risk profile for raw pet food that would justify regulatory discrimination.
    *   If a consumer mishandles raw pet food—despite warnings and handling instructions—the resulting risk is no greater, and often much less, than from preparing raw chicken or baking with flour.
    *   The rationale that raw pet food poses a unique risk to human handlers is not supported by comparative data.
    *   The risk of transmission from properly labeled and handled raw pet food is minimal—particularly when the product has already passed USDA inspection.
*   Our Request
    *   We respectfully request that the HHS:
        *   Rescind the FDA's the zero-tolerance policy on Salmonella in raw pet food, especially where there is no evidence of injury, pathogenicity, or insanitary production conditions – CPG 690.800.
        *   Acknowledge the redundancy and inefficiency of dual-agency inspection and explore inter-agency collaboration to reduce regulatory overlap.
        *   Initiate a public rulemaking process to adopt a science-based, risk-informed standard for Salmonella in pet food, aligned with those applied to other food categories.
        *   Engage with industry stakeholders, including manufacturers, veterinarians, and scientists, to craft fair, practical, and evidence-based regulations.
    *   We are fully committed to producing safe, high-quality pet foods and ask that federal policy reflect that same commitment—balancing safety, legal clarity, scientific rigor, and economic responsibility.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   In response to HHS’s request for information (RFI) concerning suggestions for deregulation, I write to suggest steps by the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) in relation to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA).
    *   A. Prepare for waivers of HIPAA provisions during public health emergencies.
    *   B. Review in light of current priorities proposals included in OCR’s Proposed Modifications to the HIPAA Privacy Rule To Support, and Remove Barriers to, Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement (Dec. 21, 2021; Docket No.: HHS-OCR-0945-AA00).
*   A. Prepare for waivers of HIPAA provisions during public health emergencies:
    *   Two authors have advised that “HHS prepare for future health emergencies with advance planning for HIPAA waiver practices.”
    *   They also advised “that the National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics be tasked with the fact-finding and policy work needed to develop legislative and administrative recommendations for HIPAA waivers permitted under Section 1135 of the Social Security Act.”
    *   Discussions about HIPAA waivers should involve all relevant stakeholders.
    *   Ultimately, their report suggests “that the US Congress reform the statutory HIPAA waiver rules.”
    *   However, pending these changes, the authors also suggest that OCR could draft in advance of emergencies with stakeholders ‘shelf waivers’ that would then be implemented during emergencies or assess changes that could be made through regulation rather than statutory changes.
    *   These waivers could include consideration of certain issues such as telehealth and the duration of these flexibilities.
    *   It is worth noting that such waivers now potentially may impact other rules that cross-reference the Security, Privacy and Breach Notification requirements, such as 42 CFR Part 2 (Confidentiality of Substance Use Disorder Patient Records) and state regulatory provisions.
*   B. Review in light of current priorities proposals included in OCR’s Proposed Modifications to the HIPAA Privacy Rule To Support, and Remove Barriers to, Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement:
    *   In 2018, HHS issued a request for information as part of its Regulatory Sprint to Coordinated Care.
    *   HHS at that time solicited input on topics such as the accounting of disclosures requirement.
    *   It also sought input on “Encouraging covered entities, particularly providers, to share treatment information with parents, loved ones, and caregivers of adults facing health emergencies, with a particular focus on the opioid crisis.”
    *   Eventually, HHS issued in 2021 a proposed rule discussing several possible changes to HIPAA: Proposed Modifications to the HIPAA Privacy Rule To Support, and Remove Barriers to, Coordinated Care and Individual Engagement (Jan. 21, 2021, Docket No.: HHS-OCR-0945-AA00).
        *   This proposed rule included discussion of potential changes to the Accounting of Disclosures requirement (45 C.F.R. § 164.528).
            *   In 2011, OCR published a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) on accounting of disclosures under the HIPAA Privacy Rule.
            *   This was in part to implement the statutory requirement under the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act (“the HITECH Act”) to require covered entities and business associates to account for disclosures of protected health information to carry out treatment, payment, and health care operations if such disclosures are through an electronic health record [EHR].
            *   However, this requirement has never been finalized.
            *   HHS in 2018 and 2021 expressly discussed withdrawing the 2011 Accounting of Disclosures NPRM and starting from scratch.
            *   As HHS has moved to align HIPAA and 42 CFR Part 2 (Confidentiality of Substance Use Disorder Patient Records) regulations, similar accounting of disclosure requirements now reside within Part 2 as well.
        *   In addition to discussing the Accounting of Disclosures provisions, HHS in 2021 discussed several potential/unfinalized changes concerning mental health and substance use that it could reconsider (e.g., use good faith vs. professional judgment standards in certain provisions).
        *   The need for additional subregulatory guidance on some of these topics also was noted in the 2021 proposed rule and elsewhere.
    *   This current RFI provides an opportunity to review 2018 docket comments and 2021 proposals given current priorities.
*   The views expressed are solely my own and should not be imputed to other individuals nor to any public/private entity.

structuredSections.corePosition: I suggest that the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) take two crucial steps regarding HIPAA: first, proactively prepare for waivers of HIPAA provisions during public health emergencies, and second, review and potentially finalize previously proposed modifications to the HIPAA Privacy Rule aimed at supporting coordinated care and individual engagement. structuredSections.keyRecommendations:

  - HHS should undertake advance planning for HIPAA waiver practices for future health emergencies.

  - Discussions about HIPAA waivers should involve all relevant stakeholders.
  - Pending statutory changes, OCR could draft "shelf waivers" in advance with stakeholders for implementation during emergencies, or assess changes that could be made through regulation rather than statutory changes.
  - These waivers should consider issues such as telehealth and their duration.

  - This current Request for Information (RFI) provides an opportunity to revisit 2018 docket comments and 2021 proposals in light of current priorities.
  - Specifically, reconsider potential changes to the Accounting of Disclosures requirement (45 C.F.R. § 164.528), which has never been finalized despite a 2011 NPRM.
  - Revisit potential and unfinalized changes concerning mental health and substance use, such as using good faith versus professional judgment standards in certain provisions.
  - Address the noted need for additional subregulatory guidance on some of these topics.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Radiology Business Management Association (RBMA) submits comments regarding Virtual Direct Supervision.
*   Response to HHS RFI on Deregulatory Plans
    *   Request to Make Permanent Virtual Direct Supervision for Diagnostic Imaging Studies with Contrast
*   On behalf of the Radiology Business Management Association (RBMA), we respectfully urge the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to direct the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) to make permanent the policy allowing virtual direct supervision via real-time audio/video communication technology for contrasted imaging studies.
*   Established in 1968, RBMA is a professional association consisting of nearly 2,000 radiology practice business leaders who represent over 1,200 radiology practices in all 50 states.
    *   This includes diagnostic radiology, interventional radiology, nuclear medicine, Independent Diagnostic Testing Facilities (IDTFs), and radiation oncology.
*   RBMA is the trusted partner of radiology professionals, advancing the industry and broadening our members’ capacity to provide superior patient experiences.
*   On May 14, 2025, the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) issued a request for information (RFI) seeking input from the American public on how to deregulate across all areas the Department touches.
    *   HHS’s goal is to “address regulations that are unnecessary, inconsistent with the law, overly burdensome, outdated, out of alignment with current executive orders, or otherwise unsound.”
*   The RFI poses questions and asks respondents to describe how their issue would lead to cost savings, address regulations that impose undue burden on small business and private enterprise, impede access to delivery or care of services, are obsolete and/or interfere with the public or private sector’s ability to address chronic health conditions or otherwise promote the health and wellbeing of Americans.
*   RBMA addresses questions 3 & 4 in this comment letter:
    *   3. What regulations should be reconsidered, that relate to E.O. 14192?
    *   4. What alternative approaches could be taken to achieve or accomplish the same goal with a lesser burden? What would the impact on cost and savings be?
*   Background:
    *   During the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency (PHE), CMS revised Title 42 of the Code of Federal Regulations Section 410.32 (b)(3)(ii).
    *   This revision allowed the supervising physician or non-physician practitioner of Level 2 diagnostic tests to be “immediately available” through virtual presence using real-time audio/visual communication technology.
    *   This policy is currently extended through December 31, 2025, and has proven to be both safe and effective.
*   Issue:
    *   During the past four years, outpatient hospital departments, physician offices, and freestanding independent diagnostic testing facilities have safely and effectively implemented virtual direct supervision models.
    *   They have shown that deploying virtual direct supervision is an excellent innovation that drives patient access while at the same time improving patient safety without a threat to program integrity or overutilization.
    *   In deploying virtual direct supervision models, imaging providers must ensure that appropriate protocols are in place to train qualified persons on-site as well as the physician providing virtual direct supervision in an emergency response.
    *   RBMA members report that they are better prepared to respond to contrast reactions by maintaining crash carts, evaluating patients, and diagnosing and differentiating different types of adverse reactions to contrast material.
    *   Evidence continues to demonstrate that virtual supervision has not compromised patient safety.
    *   Radiologists, while highly trained in diagnostic interpretation, do not receive specialized training in managing contrast reactions.
    *   The radiology field is currently facing a severe workforce shortage.
    *   Virtual supervision has become a critical tool that enables practices to meet the growing demand for imaging services while maintaining high standards of care.
    *   Eliminating this flexibility would significantly reduce outpatient imaging capacity.
        *   This shift would force many patients to seek services in hospital-based settings.
        *   This shift would not only increase healthcare costs but also reduce access and convenience for patients.
    *   Additionally, allowing remote supervision of contrast studies is necessary for those practices that deliver care to rural or underserved areas where challenges to access to care persist.
*   Conclusion:
    *   We strongly believe that making virtual direct supervision a permanent option is essential to sustaining access to timely, high-quality outpatient imaging services.
*   We welcome the opportunity to discuss this further and provide any additional information that may assist in your decision-making.

*   In response to HHS’s request for information (RFI) concerning suggestions for deregulation, I suggest that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) consider developing new coding within Medicare and Medicaid.
    *   This new coding would permit reimbursement for group and individual behavioral health therapy provided by pastoral counselors and lay counselors.
*   As this is a complex area, one way for CMS to begin this process is:
    *   By including a request for information/comment on these issues within one of its upcoming payment rules.
    *   Or by issuing a separate RFI/RFC on workforce topics and barriers to including these types of providers in its payment programs.
*   Including additional provider types may in part help mitigate the significant shortage of mental health and substance use professionals that exists within many areas of the United States.
*   Affordability, providers not being within health plan networks, and stigma/discrimination are among key barriers for those seeking behavioral health treatment.
*   Definitions vary, but pastoral counselors may range from "ordained religious figures like priests, chaplains, and rabbis to practicing psychotherapists who provide what some call pastoral psychotherapy."
*   States typically provide exemptions for clergy counseling within their own church/institution/ministry.
*   However, pastoral counselors seeking to provide care outside these settings may face reimbursement and other barriers.
    *   A pastoral counselor who also meets requirements to be licensed as another type of provider, such as a social worker or marriage and family therapist, presumably could qualify for reimbursement by public and private insurers.
    *   But those with degrees and experience solely in divinity, pastoral counseling, or theological studies alone likely would not qualify in many cases for reimbursement under Medicaid, Medicare, or private insurance absent additional on-the-job and/or academic training.
*   Few states seem to have reimbursement specifically for pastoral counselors absent their having additional background or licensure.
    *   Though some states (e.g., Indiana, Tennessee) do appear to include pastoral counseling within the scope of their Medicaid programs.
*   The Veterans Administration and Medicare typically do not cover pastoral counseling, but Tricare may, subject to physician supervision.
*   The number of pastoral counselors is likely fairly low (about 200 graduates per year and perhaps about 1940 in total as of 2014).
    *   However, clearer reimbursement pathways could help bolster the field.
*   As with other types of professionals in the behavioral health world, pastoral counselors could not treat all patients or conditions.
*   These professionals also may be subject to unique ethical and legal considerations given their role as clergy or an affiliation with a religious institution (though some pastoral counselors may not fall within these categories).
*   Large numbers of Americans continue to adhere to a wide variety of religious traditions.
*   Providing an additional option for those who wish to seek it could:
    *   Support some behavioral health patients.
    *   Serve as one more tool in overcoming the shortage of behavioral health professionals.
    *   Perhaps meet the needs of some patients and families.
*   This would be one step in supporting faith-based entities and providers in meeting the needs of their adherents and parishioners.
*   For similar reasons, I urge CMS to explore the potential of reimbursement for lay counselors.
*   Lay counselors include:
    *   Those who lack academic background and experience.
    *   Those who already are certified or licensed as health professionals but not specifically trained to provide behavioral health services.
*   Lay counselors may include front office staff, clergy, community health workers; some, but certainly not all, may be religiously affiliated.
*   Lay counselors may receive additional behavioral health training from specialized or academic programs but generally are not considered behavioral health providers for reimbursement purposes.
*   Some lay counselors may be considered peers or people with lived experience of mental health or substance use.
*   As one author observes, "There are thousands, perhaps tens of thousands, of people who, in the context of a rigorous, supportive, collaborative learning community can provide safe, compassionate, high quality mental health care to those who are still suffering.”
*   There is no reason to tie reimbursement solely and in all circumstances to one’s license or certification, though concurrent efforts to bolster the formally trained and licensed behavioral health workforce remain vital.
*   Accordingly, I urge CMS to further explore the possibility of reimbursing lay programs or counselors whether directly or when acting under the supervision of licensed professionals.
*   The views expressed are solely those of the author and should not be imputed to other individuals nor to any public/private entity.
*   Citations should not be construed as endorsement of any product, service, or religious viewpoint.

structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   A significant shortage of mental health and substance use professionals exists within many areas of the United States.
-   Key barriers for those seeking behavioral health treatment include affordability, providers not being within health plan networks, and stigma/discrimination.
-   Pastoral counselors seeking to provide care outside traditional church/institution settings face reimbursement barriers, as those with solely divinity or theological degrees typically do not qualify for reimbursement under public or private insurance without additional training or licensure.

structuredSections.notableExperiences:
-   Challenges the conventional view that only traditionally licensed professionals can provide high-quality behavioral health care, advocating for the inclusion of pastoral and lay counselors as a viable expansion of the workforce.
-   Highlights the nuanced definitions and roles of pastoral counselors, acknowledging their range from ordained clergy to practicing psychotherapists, and detailing specific reimbursement hurdles they face when operating outside religious institutional contexts.
-   Introduces the concept of "lay counselors" as a largely untapped resource, including individuals with lived experience, arguing for their significant potential to deliver safe, compassionate care.
-   Suggests that the currently low number of pastoral counselors could be significantly increased by establishing clearer and more accessible reimbursement pathways.
