- Allow providers within integrated delivery models to bill and receive payment for Part D medications in inpatient settings directly through Part D, not the inpatient prospective payment system.
    - Allow outpatient pharmacies to bill Medicare D for oral cancer therapies during Medicare A covered stays.
    - Add all NCI-designated cancer centers to the PPS-Exempt list.
    - Expand SNF consolidated billing chemotherapy exclusion to include oral cancer medications billed through Medicare D.
- Change 42 CFR 423.100 to allow coverage of off-label prescriptions under Part D for a medically accepted indication.
- Allow payment for all services when a patient receives multiple services from physicians in the same specialty within a group practice on the same day.
- Provide flexibility under EMTALA to allow hospitals to transfer stable patients from an emergency department to another hospital within the same health system for appropriate care based on acuity and complexity.
- Work with Congress on enacting a statutory change to permanently eliminate the requirement that a Medicare beneficiary’s home is not an eligible originating site for telehealth services (42 CFR 410.78(b)(3)).
- Work with Congress on enacting a statutory change to permanently eliminate the requirement that telehealth originating sites must be located in a health professional shortage area and outside a metropolitan statistical area (42 CFR 410.78(b)(4)).
- Issue public notice that MA plans must comply with the SNF Coverage Presumption under 42 CFR 409.30.
- Allow Advanced Practice Providers (APPs) to satisfy a hospital's on-call obligations (42 CFR 489.20).
- Streamline medical documentation requirements for prior authorization of clinical laboratory tests.
- Remove “date of service” roadblocks to prior approval and payment for laboratory testing services.
- Strike language in the NCCI Medicare Policy Manual that results in conflicting coding guidance and inappropriate denials of medically necessary services.
- Modify 42 CFR §418.22(b)(3)(iii) to require hospice providers to document medically necessary support for hospice services based on professional clinical judgment, removing prescriptive structural requirements for documentation.
- Work with Congress to remove the statutory 3-day inpatient stay requirement for SNF benefits (42 CFR 409.30).
- Eliminate 42 CFR 424.57(f) prohibiting CPAP payment to suppliers affiliated with sleep test providers, or at least revise the "affiliate" definition to remove ownership language.
- Modify 42 CFR 482.41(c)(4) to permit greater flexibility in the physical environment to match acuity level, rather than tying reimbursement to physical location.
- Work with FDA to increase resourcing and survey stakeholders to modernize the approval and reimbursement processes for emerging therapies and technologies (T Codes), aligning with advancements in AI and flexible care delivery.
- Transition all current CMS Innovation Center mandatory models to voluntary and refrain from implementing any future mandatory models.
- Consider solutions to promote enhanced access across state lines for telemedicine (42 CFR 410.20(b)), including:
    - Establishing a standard that interprets place of care as the location of the provider.
    - Creating a federal exemption for duplicative state requirements for specialists.
    - Permanently recognizing therapists (PT, OT, PTA, OTA, SLP) as providers of telehealth, regardless of setting.
- Allow services provided “incident to” in a free-standing clinic setting to be rendered under “general” supervision where patient safety is ensured (42 CFR 410.26).
- Improve clarity and consistency in supervision requirements across settings (42 CFR 410.27) and provide consistent telehealth coverage under both the Physician Fee Schedule (PFS) and Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS).
- Harmonize supervision for services provided by residents in teaching settings (42 CFR 415.172(a)(2)(ii)) with the incident to standard (42 CFR 410.26) to permit audio-visual supervision to the same degree as for clinical staff.
- Reconsider mandatory use of the THA/TKA PRO-PM measure under current CMS quality programs and support voluntary adoption.
- Suspend mandatory reporting for the Excessive Radiation Dose or Inadequate Image Quality for Diagnostic CT in Adults (CMS-1206v2) measure until further refinement.
- Redesign the Severe Sepsis and Septic Shock Management Bundle (SEP-1) measure for partial scoring and allow clinical exceptions.
- Take immediate steps to address underlying flaws with the Medicare Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (CLFS) payment system.
- Permanently remove CMS provider enrollment requirements for home addresses when working remotely (42 CFR 424.516).
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Administrative Burden:**
    - New transfer protocol and emergency services training requirements are duplicative and overly burdensome.
    - Routine respiratory illness reporting is burdensome and data is not meaningfully used.
    - The 60-day "look back" validation survey process is volatile and burdensome, resulting in additional findings.
    - Interpreting sub-regulatory guidance as regulation creates inappropriate expectations and potential overinterpretation, lacking opportunity for stakeholder input.
    - Outdated nursing care plan requirements consume time without improving care quality, failing to adapt to EHRs and multidisciplinary care.
    - Facility-specific provider agreements limit healthcare systems from operating efficiently system-wide.
    - Requirements for ink signatures on laboratory test orders create unnecessary clerical work and delay testing.
    - HAI reporting for non-specific infections (CAUTI) or low prevalence procedures (abdominal hysterectomy), and vaccination data, are administratively burdensome without meaningful federal action.
    - The complex logic of the OAS CAHPS survey makes implementation, maintenance, and data improvement very difficult, and patient-level data sharing restrictions limit its usefulness.
    - Duplicative complaint investigations by both state survey agencies and accrediting organizations are unpredictable, punitive, and time-consuming, with no standardized process or communication.
    - Medical documentation requirements for prior authorization for laboratory tests are inefficient and burdensome.
    - "Date of service" requirements for laboratory tests create roadblocks to prior approval and payment.
    - The all-or-nothing scoring, abstraction, and documentation burden of the SEP-1 measure are problematic.
    - The THA/TKA PRO-PM measure's small sample size (due to shift to outpatient settings) leads to statistical volatility and magnified impact of missing data, resulting in financial distortion and unfair accountability.
- **Access and Clinical Practice Barriers:**
    - Hospitals are burdened with managing patient discharge when community resources are lacking, leading to longer stays and overcrowded EDs.
    - Conflicting state and federal Life Safety Code versions (2012 vs. 2021) risk noncompliance for hospitals.
    - Narrow temperature parameters for operating rooms in current Life Safety Code add administrative burden through case-by-case documentation.
    - Medicare Part A bundled reimbursement often fails to cover costly oral Part D medications in inpatient settings, leading to patients being unable to continue cancer treatment.
    - Exclusion of off-label medications from Medicare Part D reimbursement creates access barriers for hematology/oncology patients and conflicts with standard medical practice.
    - Current payment policy allowing only one E&M visit per specialty per date of service disadvantages patients and efficient physician practice, hindering patient-centric care by sub-subspecialists.
    - EMTALA regulations limit health systems' ability to triage patients based on acuity across facilities, leading to inefficient use of complex care capacity.
    - Restrictions on Medicare telehealth originating sites (e.g., beneficiary's home, rural areas only) severely limit access, especially for urban beneficiaries.
    - Medicare Advantage plans requiring prior authorization for SNF placement after a 3-day qualifying stay, despite existing presumption of coverage, create discharge delays and deny access to skilled care.
    - Requirement for physician-only on-call lists limits availability of specialty services, particularly with physician shortages.
    - Conflicting NCCI coding guidance results in inappropriate denials of medically necessary services.
    - Strict interpretation of physician signature placement for hospice benefit certification leads to retrospective denials and recoupment of payment for medically necessary services.
    - The 3-day inpatient stay requirement for SNF benefits presents a clinical and operational barrier to appropriate patient care.
    - CPAP payment prohibition when suppliers are affiliated with sleep test providers disrupts continuity of care and limits patient choice, especially in rural areas.
- **Innovation Barriers:**
    - Facility-specific provider agreements restrict healthcare systems from adopting system-wide approaches, hindering innovation.
    - Physical environment requirements tied to outdated reimbursement models prevent flexibility in patient care settings and implementation of advanced care delivery modes.
    - CMS and FDA reimbursement policies cannot keep pace with emerging therapies and technologies (T codes), limiting adoption of AI, flexible care models, and virtual tools.
    - Mandatory CMS Innovation Center models may be misaligned with provider operations, fail to recognize patient complexity, use inappropriate measures, and inadvertently reduce reimbursement, creating barriers to innovation.
    - Disparate state licensure requirements for telemedicine and federal deference reduce access, create burden, and challenge continuity of care, inhibiting modern multi-modal care models.
    - "Direct supervision" requirements for "incident to" services (42 CFR 410.26) and differing supervision rules across settings create administrative burden and limit fluid site-of-care models.
    - Inconsistent telehealth coverage (PFS vs. OPPS) results in access challenges and financial burden for patients receiving home-based services.
    - The expiring flexibility for audio-visual supervision of graduate medical trainees hinders development of their capability in using these tools.
- **Measure Distortion and Fairness:**
    - The THA/TKA PRO-PM measure's small sample size (due to care shift to outpatient) leads to statistical volatility and financial distortion in quality programs.
    - The CT radiation dose measure uses proprietary logic and non-peer-reviewed standards, raising concerns about its accuracy.
    - The SEP-1 sepsis measure's "all-or-nothing" scoring and abstraction burden make it problematic for fair assessment.
- **Reimbursement Complexities:**
    - Oral Part D medications in inpatient settings are not sufficiently covered by DRG reimbursement.
    - Prior authorization and date of service requirements create reimbursement complexities for laboratory testing services.
    - Conflicting NCCI guidance leads to inappropriate denials.
    - Strict interpretation of hospice certification documentation results in denials and recoupment.
    - The Medicare Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (CLFS) payment system is outdated and problematic, being the only one based on commercial payer rates.
- **Workforce Considerations:**
    - The requirement for providers to enroll their home addresses when working remotely raises privacy concerns and limits remote work flexibility.
    - Physician shortages are exacerbated by the inability to allow APPs to satisfy on-call obligations.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Modernizing E-Signature Requirements
    *   Subject: A Submission to HHS Request for Information on Deregulatory Plan
    *   Docket: AHRQ-2025-0001
*   Executive Summary
    *   Vial is a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company that develops drugs and conducts clinical trials in-house, using modern technology to streamline operations and accelerate drug development.
    *   We have firsthand experience with the regulatory burdens of outdated e-signature requirements that impede efficiency and innovation in clinical research.
    *   This submission supports HHS Secretary Kennedy's "10-to-1" deregulatory initiative by identifying specific regulatory barriers that force healthcare providers to focus on paperwork rather than patient care.
*   Current Regulatory Burden: 21 CFR § 11.200
    *   Outdated Dual Authentication Requirements
        *   The FDA's current e-signature regulation, established in 1997, requires at least two distinct identification components for non-biometric electronic signatures.
        *   This dual authentication requirement forces clinical-stage biopharma companies like Vial to use specialized, Part 11-compliant e-signature systems that are far more expensive and complex than mainstream solutions.
        *   CMS requires only one distinct identification component for electronic signatures conducted by physicians in clinical practice.
    *   Barriers to Innovation and Patient Access
        *   The current FDA requirements create several critical barriers:
            *   Regulatory Burden Increases Cost and Delays Timelines of New Therapies:
                *   Complex administration requirements are a burden on physicians conducting trials.
                *   This increases the cost of trials, delays trials, and reduces the number of physicians that engage in clinical research.
                *   This creates pressure to move research overseas.
            *   Delayed Modernization of Clinical Trial Modernization:
                *   Technology investments to modernize clinical trials are not made due to the high regulatory burden.
                *   This increases the cost of trials and reduces the competitiveness of American biotechnology.
*   Comparative Analysis: HHS Agency Inconsistencies
    *   More Practical Approaches Within HHS
        *   Other HHS agencies, other than FDA, maintain security while reducing burden through more practical e-signature standards:
            *   Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS): Accepts single-factor authentication e-signatures with secure authentication, audit trails, and legibility requirements.
            *   National Institutes of Health (NIH): Requires electronic signatures through mainstream tools like DocuSign, explicitly prohibiting wet or typed signatures.
    *   International Standards and Global Competitiveness
        *   The FDA's dual authentication requirement conflicts with international standards like the European Union's eIDAS Regulation, which accepts single-factor authentication with appropriate security measures.
        *   This misalignment forces sponsors to maintain different systems across regions, increasing costs and complexity.
*   Vial's Experience: In-House Clinical Trial Operations
    *   Our In-House/Innovative Clinical Trial Model
        *   Vial is vertically integrated with both in-house clinical trial operations and an in-house technology platform that operates trials end-to-end.
        *   Vial’s experience building a modern technology platform to operate clinical trials as efficiently as possible has highlighted the challenges in adhering to outdated FDA regulations on technology platforms.
    *   Barriers to Further Innovation
        *   FDA's dual authentication requirements prevent Vial from building greater efficiency into the platform.
        *   Doctors on the Vial platform complain of inefficient electronic signature processes that are time consuming.
        *   Vial brings this recommendation to HHS to support the modernization of clinical trial infrastructure, which will result in cost and speed improvements that lead to a more competitive U.S. biotechnology ecosystem.
*   Policy Recommendation
    *   Proposed Change: Remove 21 CFR § 11.200 to permit single-factor authentication for electronic signatures when combined with robust audit trails, secure user authentication, proper record retention, and non-repudiation capabilities.
    *   Rationale: This change would align FDA with CMS’s electronic signature standards and align with international standards (EMA).
*   Alignment with RFI & Administration Goals
    *   Strengthen Biotech in America:
        *   Modernizing e-signature regulations to enable secure single-factor authentication will streamline clinical research operations, lower costs, and accelerate the development of new therapies.
        *   This directly supports domestic biotechnology innovation.
    *   Lowering Healthcare Costs:
        *   Modernizing e-signature requirements would create significant clinical trial cost savings resulting in greater pharmaceutical innovation leading to reduced costs for American consumers.
    *   Empowering Healthcare Providers:
        *   Current requirements are time consuming for health care providers and delay much needed American biotechnology innovation.
*   Economic Impact Analysis
    *   Cost-Benefit Calculation
        *   Based on Vial's clinical trials and projections:
            *   Current Costs: Part 11-compliant electronic signature systems cost 3–5 times more than traditional electronic signature solutions as a result of the added regulatory burden.
            *   Time Savings: Document processing time reduction of 80–90%.
            *   Scalability Benefits: With lower regulatory burden, technology systems will scale much more efficiently.
    *   Industry-Wide Savings
        *   If implemented across the clinical research industry:
            *   Direct Savings: Estimated $100–200+ million annually in reduced e-signature system costs.
            *   Indirect Savings: Faster trials will lower the cost of developing new drugs and improve competition in the pharmaceutical sector, reducing costs for American consumers.
            *   Innovation Benefits: Reduced costs will lead to greater American R&D competitiveness leading to new breakthrough innovations that improve the quality of life for Americans.
*   Conclusion
    *   Vial strongly supports HHS's deregulatory initiative and submits this proposal for striking FDA e-signature requirements under 21 CFR § 11.200.
    *   This targeted reform would reduce bureaucratic barriers, lower costs, and enable healthcare providers to focus on patient care rather than paperwork compliance.
    *   Our experience as a clinical-stage biopharma company shows that maintaining security and data integrity doesn't require burdensome dual authentication.
    *   By aligning FDA requirements with other HHS agencies and mainstream technology standards, this reform would accelerate clinical trials, reduce costs, and expedite innovative therapies to patients.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- Executive Summary
    - Vial, a clinical-stage biopharmaceutical company, develops drugs and conducts clinical trials in-house, using modern technology to streamline operations and accelerate drug development.
    - We urge HHS to eliminate the outdated software validation requirements in 21 CFR Part 11 that are actively hindering American medical innovation.
    - These 28-year-old regulations, which represent a clear example of a good idea that has gradually deteriorated, impose unnecessary costs on drug developers, delay trials, and provide no measurable benefit to patient safety or data integrity.
    - By removing these requirements, HHS can quickly advance innovation and strengthen America's competitive edge in the global pharmaceutical industry, while maintaining robust safeguards through modern quality systems that exceed the effectiveness of traditional validation.
- The Burden of 21 CFR Part 11 Software Validation Requirements
    - Outdated and Overly Prescriptive Regulation
        - Since its introduction in 1997, 21 CFR Part 11 has required that all software used for electronic records and signatures be validated for accuracy, reliability, consistent intended performance, and the ability to discern invalid or altered records (§11.10(a)).
        - In practice, companies must undertake extensive documentation, testing, and review for all software systems, regardless of their risk profile or intended use.
        - By contrast, neither the EU nor the FDA prescribe detailed software validation requirements for clinical trial systems.
            - The EU has no explicit validation mandate.
            - ICH GCP and FDA regulations simply state that sponsors must ensure validated systems are used, without specifying how validation should be performed or its rigor.
            - The FDA's own guidance only calls for documented requirements, a test plan, and test results, criteria already met by standard quality practices and the other requirements of 21 CFR § 11.10 (b–k).
    - Disproportionate Costs and Delays
        - Resource Drain: Validation projects routinely consume 20–25% of software development budgets for pharmaceutical companies, with smaller organizations disproportionately affected due to limited resources.
        - Implementation Delays: The need for exhaustive validation documentation and testing significantly delays the deployment of new, potentially beneficial digital tools in clinical trials and drug development.
        - Barrier to Modernization: The high cost and complexity of validation discourage the adoption of modern, cloud-based, and AI-driven technologies that could improve trial efficiency and data quality.
    - No Demonstrable Increase in Data Integrity or Patient Safety
        - Despite these extensive requirements, there is little evidence that the current validation regime meaningfully improves data integrity or patient safety compared to a risk-based or quality-focused approach.
        - Most data breaches and errors in clinical research stem from process failures or user error, not software defects that would have been caught by traditional validation.
- Benefits of Removing Validation Requirements
    - Cost Savings
        - Direct Savings: Eliminating validation requirements would substantially reduce software development project costs, freeing capital for R&D and patient care.
        - Indirect Savings: Faster implementation of digital tools would reduce trial timelines, leading to earlier access to new therapies for patients and lower overall drug development costs.
    - Increased Innovation and Competitiveness
        - Faster Adoption: Removing validation barriers would enable rapid adoption of cutting-edge technology, including eSource, decentralized trial platforms, and advanced analytics.
        - Level Playing Field: Smaller sponsors and startups would be able to compete more effectively, fostering a more dynamic and innovative biotech ecosystem.
    - Maintained Oversight Through Modern Quality Systems
        - Quality Management: Modern quality management systems (QMS) and vendor qualification processes are sufficient to ensure software reliability and data integrity.
        - Audit Trails and Access Controls: These features, now standard in commercial software, provide robust protection against data loss or tampering without the need for burdensome validation documentation.
- Policy Recommendation
    - Remove 21 CFR § 11.10(a) and all associated software validation requirements from Part 11.
    - Sponsors and regulated entities should continue to ensure that software used is "fit for intended use" and maintain appropriate quality management and security controls without the need for exhaustive validation documentation.
    - This approach would align US regulations with global standards.
- Alignment with HHS Deregulatory Goals
    - Reduces Unnecessary Regulatory Burden: Directly supports the "10-to-1" deregulatory initiative by eliminating a major source of inefficiency.
    - Lowers Healthcare Costs: Reduces the cost of drug development, ultimately benefiting patients and payers.
    - Accelerates Innovation: Enables rapid adoption of technology, improving the speed and quality of clinical research in the United States.
- Conclusion
    - Vial strongly supports the removal of software validation requirements in 21 CFR Part 11.
    - These requirements are no longer justified in the context of modern technology and quality management practices.
    - Their elimination will lower costs, accelerate innovation, and maintain high standards of data integrity and patient safety.
    - We urge HHS to act decisively to modernize clinical research regulation and ensure the U.S. remains a global leader in life sciences innovation.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- I am a patient under active evaluation for dysautonomia (mixed POTS/vasovagal profile).
- During routine IV access, I consistently detect a pronounced saline or metallic taste within seconds of a standard 0.9 % NaCl flush.
- I experience a strong bitter/chemical flavor if an IV-form medication (e.g., dexamethasone) is given orally.
- This sensory response appears to correlate with my periods of positional tachycardia, elevated diastolic pressure when supine, and other autonomic “flare” symptoms.
- The underlying pathway is plausibly vagus- or glossopharyngeal-mediated, as vascular-borne ions or volatiles can reach retronasal olfactory fibers and trigger central autonomic circuits.
- Key advantages:
  - Passive, non-invasive, and zero-cost — requires only one intake question: “Do you taste saline when your IV is flushed?”
  - May flag heightened vagal sensitivity and help clinicians identify patients who merit early autonomic testing (tilt-table, HRV, catecholamines) before years of misdiagnosis.
  - Aligns with AHRQ goals of reducing diagnostic delay and improving patient safety through simple, low-burden innovations.
- In patient forums and dysautonomia support groups, many individuals report this same phenomenon, often preceding or paralleling formal diagnoses.
  - This informal consensus suggests it is more than coincidence and may reflect underlying autonomic hypersensitivity.
- While anecdotal at present, the consistency and specificity of this sensory sign warrant prospective study.
- Collecting it during intake or IV placement would cost nothing and could quickly build a dataset linking saline-taste sensitivity to autonomic metrics.
- I encourage AHRQ and partner institutions to consider adding this question to existing dysautonomia or syncope research protocols.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
-   VIP Kinder College is a network of licensed early childhood programs in Indiana.
    -   It serves nearly 100 children across multiple sites.
    -   Programs are Paths to QUALITY Level 4 and nationally accredited.
    -   Has been proudly serving families for over a decade.
-   Strongly urges HHS to retain the current CCDBG federal regulations.
    -   These regulations safeguard children’s health and safety.
    -   They support stability and fairness for both providers and families.
-   Many children cared for at VIP Kinder College have families who rely on child care subsidies.
-   The recent regulations requiring prospective payments and enrollment-based payment practices have been transformative for operations.
    -   Timely, predictable payments allow for:
        -   Planning staffing.
        -   Purchasing materials.
        -   Meeting daily needs.
        -   All without disruption to the quality of care provided.
    -   These changes have made it easier to accept families who use subsidies.
        -   Increased both access and equity.
-   Paying based on enrollment rather than attendance acknowledges the reality of fixed costs in child care.
    -   Whether a child is present or not on a given day, staffing levels, classrooms, and meals must still be maintained.
    -   These regulations help programs remain financially stable.
    -   They allow parents peace of mind.
-   Strongly supports maintaining the requirement for states to use grants and contracts to expand access.
    -   Especially for infants, toddlers, children with disabilities, and those in underserved areas.
    -   These populations are the hardest to serve without financial support and planning tools.
    -   VIP Kinder College programs have used these strategies to open infant classrooms and expand availability to those most in need.
-   Removing these safeguards would not only harm programs like ours.
    -   It would reduce the supply of child care.
    -   It would force small providers out of business.
    -   It would undermine quality for thousands of children.
-   The families in our community depend on CCDBG and the fair policies currently in place.
-   Asks that HHS continue using the public comment process before implementing any regulatory or deregulatory changes.
    -   Appreciates this opportunity to provide input.
    -   Believes ongoing transparency and collaboration with providers is essential to meaningful and effective reform.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: Vip Kinder College, an Indiana-based network of nationally accredited early childhood programs, strongly urges HHS to retain current CCDBG regulations, particularly those mandating prospective and enrollment-based payments and state grants for access expansion, asserting their vital role in ensuring financial stability, equitable access, and high-quality care.

- I am an early childhood educator, currently working in an administrative position.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   In alignment with the President’s Deregulatory Initiatives and the Department of Government Efficiency Deregulatory Agenda (Executive Orders 14192 and 14219), this brief outlines recommendations to modernize and reduce regulatory burdens within the Head Start program administered by the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), an agency of HHS.
*   These recommendations target regulations that impose unnecessary paperwork, administrative complexity, and outdated service delivery models—particularly those that impede workforce retention and technological innovation—while continuing to protect the health, education, and well-being of low-income families and children.
*   Relevant Executive Order Criteria Addressed:
    *   Regulations that impose significant costs upon private parties that are not outweighed by public benefits.
    *   Regulations that harm the national interest by significantly and unjustifiably impeding technological innovation, infrastructure development, and economic development.
    *   Regulations that impose undue burdens on small business and impede private enterprise and entrepreneurship.
*   Key Recommendations for Deregulation and Modernization
    *   Eliminate the 90-Minute Minimum Requirement for Home-Based Services
        *   Current Requirement: All home visits in Early Head Start must last a minimum of 90 minutes.
        *   Issue: This rigid requirement impedes flexibility, limits family access, and restricts innovative hybrid or virtual models.
        *   Proposed Action: Rescind the 90-minute minimum and allow programs to tailor visit durations based on child and family needs.
        *   Expected Savings: Reduces staff burnout and time inefficiencies, improves service reach without compromising quality.
        *   Statutory Authority: Not explicitly mandated by the Head Start Act; modification can be accomplished through changes to program performance standards.
    *   Streamline Health Documentation Requirements
        *   Current Requirement: Manual verification of immunization, health insurance, and physical exams.
        *   Issue: These requirements duplicate existing public health systems (e.g., ACA, Medicaid, state registries).
        *   Proposed Action: Authorize automated verification via state databases and CAIR (California Immunization Registry).
        *   Expected Savings: Estimated savings of 8–10 hours per child per year in documentation time across thousands of enrollees.
        *   Statutory Authority: Head Start Act allows flexibility in health requirements based on availability and community needs.
    *   Expand Qualified Mental Health Consultant Categories
        *   Current Requirement: Onsite services must be delivered or supervised by licensed psychologists.
        *   Issue: This inflates costs and restricts access in rural and low-income areas.
        *   Proposed Action: Permit LCSWs, LMFTs, and certified behavioral health consultants as eligible providers under federal rules.
        *   Expected Savings: 30–40% reduction in mental health consultant contracting costs.
    *   Workforce Burden Reduction Through Technology
        *   Issue: Head Start teachers spend excessive time on manual documentation of DRDP, GOLD, and observations.
        *   Proposed Action: Permit voice-to-text tools, AI-supported observation apps, and predictive assessment scoring.
        *   Technology-Based Deregulatory Actions:
            *   Accept AI-tagged observations as official documentation.
            *   Allow integrated lesson plan tools to fulfill both planning and DRDP evidence.
            *   Enable asynchronous parent communications to satisfy engagement requirements.
        *   Expected Savings: 10–15 hours per month per teaching staff; projected national savings in the tens of millions annually.
    *   Reduce Redundant Monitoring and Reporting for High-Performing Grantees
        *   Issue: Equal monitoring burden is applied regardless of risk level.
        *   Proposed Action: Implement performance-based monitoring waivers for programs with demonstrated compliance.
        *   Expected Savings: Reduces staff time on audit preparation and report submissions by 30–50% annually.
    *   Simplify Procurement and Budget Authority Rules
        *   Issue: Federal thresholds (e.g., $5,000 equipment limit) and strict procurement protocols delay essential improvements.
        *   Proposed Action: Raise micro-purchase threshold and authorize cooperative contract usage.
        *   Expected Savings: Expedites facility and technology upgrades without formal bidding delays; reduces administrative time.
    *   Eligibility Alignment and Automated Benefit Verification
        *   Issue: Families are required to submit duplicative eligibility documents for Head Start despite being enrolled in SNAP, Medicaid, or WIC.
        *   Proposed Action: Enable cross-agency data use to auto-confirm eligibility.
        *   Expected Savings: Reduces family burden and accelerates enrollment timelines.
*   Why Deregulation is Urgent: Workforce Impacts and Shortages
    *   California alone reports over 10,000 vacant teacher positions, with preschool and early childhood roles hardest hit.
    *   20% of Head Start and Early Head Start classrooms remain closed nationally due to workforce vacancies.
    *   Retirements surged 26% post-pandemic, and burnout has accelerated exits from the field.
    *   Deregulatory relief would retain more educators, reduce unnecessary paperwork, and support the mental health and sustainability of this critical workforce.
*   Conclusion
    *   In accordance with Executive Orders 14192 and 14219, the Department of Health and Human Services is urged to adopt these deregulatory reforms to promote efficiency, leverage modern technology, and remove burdensome barriers to family service delivery.
    *   These proposals align with lawful statutory authority, reduce federal spending, and expand access to services without compromising quality.
    *   This submission represents one of potentially many areas within HHS where substantive, outcome-based deregulatory reform is not only possible—but imperative.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   We feel strongly that the home and community-based services (HCBS) payment adequacy mandate (i.e., 80/20 rule) and associated reporting requirements should be removed.
    *   These regulations, codified at 42 C.F.R. § 441.302(k) and § 441.311(e), mandate that at least 80% of all Medicaid payments for homemaker, home health aide, and personal care services be spent on compensation to direct care workers.
    *   They also include expanded compensation reporting requirements for these services and habilitation services.
    *   While the HCBS payment adequacy mandate was intended to alleviate recruitment and retention challenges facing HCBS providers, it instead risks further disruption and diminished access to an already fragile system of supports and services for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD).
*   Home and Community-Based Services for People with I/DD
    *   Due to decades of insufficient Medicaid funding, access to HCBS is fragile, and regulations impacting the HCBS service delivery system must be approached cautiously and with confidence that such regulations will strengthen the system.
    *   When a regulation increases the cost of service delivery, there must be commensurate and simultaneous funding available to achieve the underlying intent of the rule.
    *   As Medicaid payment rates continue to stagnate, providers are often forced to make impossible decisions to shutter programs when well-intended policy initiatives are undermined by inadequate funding and a lack of stakeholder engagement to fully understand the impacts of the rulemaking.
    *   Long-term underinvestment in HCBS, together with insufficient reimbursement rates, have further hampered the ability of community providers to offer direct support professionals (DSPs) competitive wages and benefits.
        *   DSPs are the workforce delivering crucial supports that enable people with I/DD to live full and independent lives in their homes and communities.
        *   This has led to an exodus of qualified workers from the field, and the resulting workforce crisis has had a profound impact on the ability of community providers to deliver essential programs and adequately support people with I/DD in our communities.
    *   During the pandemic, we had to close 3 of our homes because we were unable to recruit and retain enough qualified staff members to support our clients.
        *   Relying on reserves, we increased our wages by 65%, without receiving any increase in our payment rates.
        *   While we have since received small increases in our payment rates, they do not cover the increases we needed to give to retain our staff members.
        *   While we are now better able to recruit and retain staff members, we are still in the process of reopening the homes that were closed.
        *   We have a waiting list of dozens of people who are looking for support.
        *   Without consistent staffing, we are unable to respond to those people and that waiting list.
    *   Our nurses are making more than our administrators.
    *   Hiring accounting staff, particularly CFOs, took 2 years.
*   HCBS Payment Adequacy Mandate
    *   We urge HHS to rescind the existing HCBS payment adequacy mandate and replace it with rulemaking that addresses the root cause of the workforce crisis: stagnant and insufficient Medicaid payment rates that do not provide sufficient funding for competitive wages.
    *   When initially proposed, CMS requested comment on whether the HCBS payment adequacy mandate should be expanded to residential habilitation services, day habilitation services, and home-based habilitation services for people with I/DD.
        *   Hundreds of community providers submitted comments responding with a resounding “no”.
        *   While CMS ultimately did not expand the 80% threshold requirement to habilitation services, it did impose HCBS payment adequacy reporting requirements on habilitation services.
        *   CMS simultaneously failed to provide adequate guidance to states in differentiating habilitation services for people with I/DD from other services.
        *   This failure to address the foundational issue of Medicaid payment adequacy risks misclassification of habilitation services and dangerous application beyond the rule’s intent.
    *   Standardized formulas interpreted by people who read the rules and do not understand how services are implemented can mean that services such as nursing and behavior analysis are not considered direct support, and are not a part of the 80%.
        *   These kinds of services are critical to supporting our clients, as are the supervisors who manage the housing we provide.
    *   Additionally, as we provide affordable housing for the majority of our clients, we must receive adequate reimbursement to manage rising housing costs: food, utilities, maintenance, and the like.
    *   We also provide transportation and must manage the realities of rising costs in this area.
    *   All of these costs must be managed with 20% of our woefully inadequate reimbursement.
    *   We have not identified costs for administering our programs, which we are also required to provide.
        *   This includes critical services like billing, accounts payable, payroll and HR, and managing programs to meet the countless rules and regulations.
    *   For the reasons stated above, we urge CMS to rescind 42 C.F.R. §441.302(k) and §441.311(e).
*   Payment Rates
    *   In order to address the workforce shortage, CMS should instead consider rulemaking that provides oversight of stagnant and insufficient Medicaid payment rates that do not include adequate funding for competitive wages.
    *   The source of the direct support workforce crisis is state-determined payment rates left unadjusted for rising costs, inflation, and increased service expectations for decades at a time.
    *   Regular review of payment rates which adjust for inflation and include a competitive wage within the underlying payment rate model would better effectuate the rule’s intent to address the direct care workforce crisis and increase access to HCBS.
    *   In Minnesota, we received rate adjustments in 2023 which would have made a small adjustment in the inadequacy of our payment rates.
    *   However, in the 2025 legislative session, many of the ongoing mechanisms to address rate inadequacy were removed because they were deemed to be creating the state’s forecasted budget deficit.
    *   For all the reasons stated above, we urge OMB and CMS to rescind § 441.302(k) and § 441.311(e) and replace them with rulemaking that ensures the provision of adequate Medicaid payment rates.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
-   The attached report to HHS recommends targeted deregulation of certain Medicaid Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) rules.
    -   The focus is on improving access, promoting individual choice, and ensuring the long-term sustainability of service providers supporting individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD).
    -   The HCBS Settings Rule and the Medicaid Access Rule, as currently written, are creating unintended barriers to services and innovation.
    -   Providers across Florida report that these rules are limiting access and flexibility for individuals with I/DD.
    -   The recommendations support reforming or rescinding key provisions, while still upholding civil rights and service quality.
    -   The recommendations given are specific in the report.
-   Recommendations:
    -   Amending the Settings Rule to explicitly affirm that "intentional communities" can be valid HCBS settings and/or eliminate the Settings Rule altogether.
    -   Clarifying that individuals participating in Adult Day Training (ADT) programs can earn wages while receiving HCBS.
    -   Repealing the 80/20 Rule under the Medicaid Access Rule, which currently mandates that 80% of specific HCBS funding be allocated to direct care worker wages—posing serious financial challenges for providers and/or eliminate the Access Rule altogether.
-   These recommendations aim to protect personal choice, enhance employment opportunities, and prevent provider closures that would otherwise limit critical services to individuals with developmental disabilities.
-   States are interpreting the Settings Rule and the Access Rule as they seem fit.
    -   This is wrong and is based on philosophical viewpoints and not real data.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   On behalf of IARF, thanks for the opportunity to assist the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) in identifying regulations for rescission or replacement.
*   IARF is Illinois’ largest trade association representing community-based providers serving and supporting children and adults with intellectual/developmental disabilities (I/DD) and serious mental illnesses.
    *   Our members provide services in over 900 locations throughout Illinois.
*   We strongly believe that the home and community-based services (HCBS) payment adequacy mandate (i.e., 80/20 rule) and associated reporting requirements should be removed.
    *   This mandate is codified at 42 C.F.R. § 441.302(k) and § 441.311(e).
    *   It requires that at least 80% of all Medicaid payments for homemaker, home health aide, and personal care services be spent on compensation to direct care workers.
    *   It also includes expanded compensation reporting requirements for these services and habilitation services.
    *   While intended to alleviate recruitment and retention challenges for HCBS providers, it instead risks further disruption and diminished access to an already fragile system of supports and services for people with I/DD.
*   Home and Community-Based Services for People with I/DD
    *   Access to HCBS is fragile due to decades of insufficient Medicaid funding.
    *   Regulations impacting the HCBS service delivery system must be approached cautiously and with confidence that they will strengthen the system.
    *   When a regulation increases the cost of service delivery, there must be commensurate and simultaneous funding available to achieve its underlying intent.
    *   Illinois has made significant headway in investing in I/DD services and supports since 2018, but we must remain mindful of well-intended federal policy initiatives and their impact on direct service delivery.
    *   Prior to 2018, Illinois’ I/DD service array experienced a ten-year drought of investment in services and supports.
        *   This occurred simultaneously with a mandated increase to the state minimum wage, which increased service costs with no commensurate rate increase.
    *   Since 2018, Illinois has made deliberate and focused investments in the I/DD workforce.
        *   Our Direct Support Professional (DSP) wage rates will reach 142% of the minimum wage by January 1, 2026.
        *   While this represents significant investment and has largely stabilized our DSP workforce, similar requirements, such as state-level "passthroughs," have ignored rate model intentions and removed needed flexibility from provider organizations in meeting local workforce and service needs.
*   HCBS Payment Adequacy Mandate (Federal)
    *   We urge HHS to rescind the existing HCBS payment adequacy mandate and replace it with rulemaking that addresses the root cause of the workforce crisis: stagnant and insufficient Medicaid payment rates that do not provide sufficient funding for competitive wages.
    *   When initially proposed, CMS requested comment on whether the HCBS payment adequacy mandate should be expanded to residential habilitation services, day habilitation services, and home-based habilitation services for people with I/DD.
        *   Hundreds of community providers responded with a resounding “no.”
    *   While CMS ultimately did not expand the 80% threshold requirement to habilitation services, it did impose HCBS payment adequacy reporting requirements on habilitation services.
        *   Simultaneously, it failed to provide adequate guidance to states in differentiating habilitation services for people with I/DD from other services.
    *   This failure to address the foundational issue of Medicaid payment adequacy risks misclassification of habilitation services and dangerous application beyond the rule’s intent.
    *   Illinois has established rate methodologies for services outlined in our adults with developmental disabilities HCBS waiver.
        *   These methodologies, particularly in our community-integrated living arrangement (CILA) residential service model, build in assumptions about how rate components are used by contracting provider organizations to deliver services.
        *   The DSP wage rate component, for example, is an ‘average rate’ that includes components intended to cover costs in addition to wages and benefits for a DSP.
        *   However, recent increases in Illinois’ DSP wage rate have included ‘pass through’ requirements that have ignored the original intention of the DSP wage rate, impacting the ability of provider organizations to address costs such as overtime.
        *   Additionally, these requirements negatively impact the ability of provider organizations to address recruitment and retention needs by mandating how DSP wage rate increases can be spent.
    *   We fear maintaining the federal payment adequacy mandate across HCBS services will further exacerbate this situation by ignoring how states have set rate methodologies.
    *   For these reasons, we urge CMS to rescind 42 C.F.R. §441.302(k) and §441.311(e).
*   Payment Rates (Proposed Alternative)
    *   To address the nationwide workforce shortage and reinforce federal commitments to effectively supporting children and adults with I/DD, CMS should instead consider rulemaking that provides oversight of stagnant and insufficient Medicaid payment rates that do not include adequate funding for competitive wages.
    *   The source of the direct support workforce crisis is state-determined payment rates left unadjusted for rising costs, inflation, and increased service expectations for decades.
    *   Regular review of payment rates which adjust for inflation and include a competitive wage within the underlying payment rate model would better effectuate the rule’s intent to address the direct care workforce crisis and increase access to HCBS.
    *   In Illinois, we have seen significant investments in rates and reimbursements since 2018.
        *   This came as a result of compliance issues with our Olmstead Consent Decree, a rate study, significant advocacy from individuals, parents, and provider organizations, as well as leadership by our Administration and legislature.
    *   We know firsthand that establishing mechanisms for regular rate increases impacts the health of the service array.
        *   For example, our adults with developmental disabilities HCBS waiver ensures some specific rates for service are tied to U.S. Department of Labor Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) indicators, which ensures rates can compensate for inflationary pressures.
        *   However, other important rates, such as our DSP wage rate, have not been tied to such indicators.
    *   We believe CMS has an important role to play to ensure states are meeting requirements they’ve outlined under their waivers by ensuring state payment rates meet adequacy measures.
    *   For all the reasons stated above, we urge OMB and CMS to rescind § 441.302(k) and § 441.311(e) and replace them with rulemaking that ensures the provision of adequate Medicaid payment rates.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: IARF, Illinois' largest trade association for I/DD and mental illness providers, urges HHS to rescind the HCBS 80/20 payment adequacy mandate and replace it with rulemaking that ensures adequate Medicaid payment rates, arguing the current rule harms access and flexibility without addressing the root cause of workforce issues.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** IARF (Illinois Association of Rehabilitation Facilities)
- **Type:** Trade Association
- **Role/Expertise:** President & CEO, representing community-based providers serving children and adults with intellectual/developmental disabilities and serious mental illnesses.
- **Geographic Scope:** State (Illinois)
- **Stake in Issue:** Members are direct providers of home and community-based services (HCBS) whose operations, financial stability, and ability to provide care are directly impacted by Medicaid payment rates and related federal mandates like the 80/20 rule.
structuredSections.corePosition: We feel strongly that the home and community-based services (HCBS) payment adequacy mandate (i.e. 80/20 rule) and associated reporting requirements should be removed. While the HCBS payment adequacy mandate was intended to alleviate recruitment and retention challenges facing HCBS providers, it instead risks further disruption and diminished access to an already fragile system of supports and services for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD).
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Rescind the existing HCBS payment adequacy mandate (42 C.F.R. § 441.302(k) and § 441.311(e)).
- Replace it with new rulemaking that addresses the root cause of the workforce crisis by providing oversight of stagnant and insufficient Medicaid payment rates.
    - This rulemaking should ensure that payment rates include adequate funding for competitive wages and are regularly reviewed to adjust for inflation and rising costs.
- CMS should play an important role in ensuring states meet waiver requirements by ensuring state payment rates meet adequacy measures.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- The HCBS 80/20 payment adequacy mandate, despite its intent, risks further disruption and diminished access to already fragile HCBS for people with I/DD.
- Regulations that increase service delivery costs without commensurate and simultaneous funding will weaken the system.
- The mandate ignores the foundational issue of Medicaid payment inadequacy, which is the root cause of the workforce crisis.
- The mandate (and similar state-level "passthrough" requirements) ignores established state rate methodologies, which build in assumptions about how rate components are used by providers.
    - This impacts providers' ability to cover costs like overtime and address recruitment/retention needs by mandating how wage rate increases are spent.
- CMS failed to provide adequate guidance to states in differentiating habilitation services, which risks misclassification and dangerous application of reporting requirements beyond the rule’s intent.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- Illinois experienced a ten-year drought of investment in I/DD services prior to 2018, coinciding with mandated state minimum wage increases that raised costs without corresponding rate increases.
- Despite significant state investments since 2018 (including DSP wage rates reaching 142% of minimum wage by 2026, which largely stabilized the workforce), state-level "passthrough" requirements have already negatively impacted providers' flexibility by ignoring rate model intentions and restricting how wage increases can be spent.
- Illinois' improvements in rates and reimbursements since 2018 resulted from compliance issues with an Olmstead Consent Decree, a rate study, significant advocacy, and state leadership, demonstrating the positive impact of focused investment.
- The insight that tying some waiver rates to U.S. Department of Labor Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) indicators has helped compensate for inflationary pressures, though other important rates (like DSP wage rates) are not similarly protected.
- The core insight that the actual source of the direct support workforce crisis is stagnant and insufficient state-determined Medicaid payment rates, left unadjusted for rising costs, inflation, and increased service expectations for decades.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "When a regulation increases the cost of service delivery, there must be commensurate and simultaneous funding available to achieve the underlying intent of the rule."
- "We urge HHS to rescind the existing HCBS payment adequacy mandate and replace it with rulemaking that addresses the root cause of the workforce crisis: stagnant and insufficient Medicaid payment rates that do not provide sufficient funding for competitive wages."
- "The source of the direct support workforce crisis is state-determined payment rates left unadjusted for rising costs, inflation, and increased service expectations for decades at a time."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   HCBS Settings Rule – 42 CFR 441.301(c)(1)(vi) - Conflict Of Interest (COI) requirements should be modified:
    *   While the intent of the rule is theoretically good, its application will impose undue burdens on small rural providers in Kansas.
    *   These providers will be required to divest parts of their organizations without the ability to replace the service revenue.
    *   This will eliminate functions currently provided by case managers that lead to efficient and effective whole person services honoring choice of community provider.
    *   60% of a case manager’s time is spent in billable TCM services.
        *   Inadequate rates and administrative tasks morphed the TCM service into “service coordination,” which was subsidized by agencies who found value in these service coordination parts.
    *   The other 40% is spent on service coordination tasks best suited for a case manager to provide, bringing continuity to all services an individual receives.
    *   Case managers are in fact quality monitors for other services in the organizations they work.
    *   Billable TCM services are only a part of the overall tasks a case manager performs for individuals in Kansas.
    *   However, without a revenue stream to support these “other” tasks, even partially, it will be difficult for providers to continue them.
    *   There will be no public benefit to dismantling service providers in Kansas through implementation of COI language.
        *   While on the surface the idea of separation seems necessary, individual/family input reveals recipients don’t see the need.
        *   The relationship with their case manager is too important to them.
    *   The “only provider exception” would be difficult and confusing in Kansas.
        *   Individuals would be put in a position to make changes to providers without choice.
        *   New providers might form then dissolve due to lack of revenue to sustain the business.
        *   It would take only one other provider in the area to disallow this option and force individuals to change providers against their choice, even if the only option is not a desirable option.
        *   When larger state-wide companies move into the State or area, service/support tends to be surface level, leaving small providers to “pick up the pieces” when supports are immediately needed.
        *   Independent case managers will complete the limited allowable paid functions under the TCM service code.
    *   The COI regulations for HCBS Settings will also impede delivery of care or services.
        *   Individuals will not receive the same quality of coordinated care they are receiving now.
        *   Stripping the functions of case management away from other HCBS services will lead to inefficient and ineffective whole person services and supports.
        *   This will lead to increased costs in medical and health care when supports are fragmented.
        *   Independent case management organizations cannot sustain the comprehensive nature of the current functions case managers attached to HCBS providers complete.
        *   Fragmented services lead to cumbersome delayed communications for individual and families also.
    *   Removing case management from service providers will impede delivery of care in health care situations through more complicated and cumbersome communication with multiple providers for health care providers.
        *   Due to the complexity of support needed to ensure quality of care and decrease the likelihood of hospitalizations, readmits or exacerbation of chronic health conditions prevalent in the I/DD population, health care coordination for individuals with I/DD requires designated time and attention from staff outside of current HCBS service definitions without additional reimbursement.
*   Alternate approaches to allow current provider organizations to continue to provide service coordination/case management and HCBS services:
    *   1. An exemption for small rural providers with less than 150 service recipients could be added to the current regulations.
    *   2. A requirement for robust safeguards to ensure HCBS service recipients’ choices are being obtained and honored while still allowing TCM and HCBS service to coexist within the same provider.
        *   In Kansas, the State, CDDO (who currently complete the assessment for HCBS eligibility) and MCOs (who currently develop the person center service plan and determine what services the individual is eligible for), provide multiple layers of oversight available to develop a comprehensive system ensuring assessments for funding and service choice remain conflict free.
    *   This change would not have any effect on the other intents of the rule – to ensure people live in settings that are integrated in the community and have rights to privacy, dignity and autonomy.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: Christa Jones, an individual, urges modification of the HCBS Settings Rule's Conflict of Interest requirements, arguing they create undue burdens for small rural Kansas providers, fragment essential case management services, and ultimately harm individuals' access to quality, coordinated care.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Christa Jones
- **Type:** Individual
- **Role/Expertise:** Professional/Advocate experienced in rural HCBS delivery and case management.
- **Geographic Scope:** State (Kansas), Rural
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly concerned about the negative impact of COI requirements on small rural HCBS providers, case management services, and individuals with I/DD in Kansas.
structuredSections.corePosition: The HCBS Settings Rule's Conflict of Interest (COI) requirements (42 CFR 441.301(c)(1)(vi)) should be modified because their application will impose undue burdens on small rural providers in Kansas, forcing them to divest essential case management services, thereby fragmenting care, increasing costs, and diminishing quality for individuals with intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD).
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Add an exemption for small rural providers with less than 150 service recipients to the current COI regulations.
- Implement a requirement for robust safeguards to ensure HCBS service recipients’ choices are being obtained and honored while still allowing Targeted Case Management (TCM) and HCBS services to coexist within the same provider.
  - Leverage existing oversight layers in Kansas, including the State, CDDOs (who assess HCBS eligibility), and MCOs (who develop person-centered service plans), to ensure conflict-free assessments for funding and service choice.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- The COI requirements will impose undue burdens on small rural providers in Kansas, forcing them to divest parts of their organizations.
- Providers will lose essential service revenue and the ability to perform crucial case management functions.
- The rule's application will dismantle service providers in Kansas, despite lack of perceived need from individuals/families.
- The "only provider exception" would be difficult and confusing, potentially forcing individuals to change providers against their choice, even if new options are undesirable or unsustainable.
- The COI regulations will impede the delivery of care and services, leading to a decline in quality of coordinated care.
- Stripping case management functions from HCBS services will result in inefficient and ineffective whole person services and supports.
- Fragmented services will lead to increased costs in medical and health care, as well as cumbersome and delayed communications for individuals and families.
- Independent case management organizations may not be able to sustain the comprehensive nature of current case management functions without integrated revenue streams.
- Health care coordination for individuals with I/DD, which requires designated time and attention, will become more complicated and cumbersome due to communication with multiple, separate providers.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- Case managers spend 60% of their time on billable TCM services, but inadequate rates and administrative tasks have transformed TCM into a "service coordination" function often subsidized by agencies, with the remaining 40% dedicated to crucial, unbilled coordination tasks that ensure continuity of care.
- Individual and family input indicates that recipients do not see the need for the separation of services, emphasizing the importance of their relationship with their case manager.
- Larger state-wide companies entering areas tend to provide "surface level" service/support, often leaving smaller local providers to address immediate, complex needs.
- The complexity of support needed for the I/DD population (to prevent hospitalizations, readmissions, or chronic condition exacerbations) requires dedicated time and attention for health care coordination that falls outside current HCBS service definitions and lacks additional reimbursement.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "There will be no public benefit to dismantling service providers in Kansas through implementation of COI language."
- "While on the surface the idea of separation seems necessary, individual/family input reveals recipients don’t see the need. The relationship with their case manager is too important to them."
- "Stripping the functions of case management away from other HCBS services will lead to inefficient and ineffective whole person services and supports."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- I am a small business owner who runs an early childhood center.
- I am reaching out to make the plea- that prospective and enrollment-based payments and grants and contracts are important regulations to keep;
  - they help expand supply and choice for parents receiving subsidies.
- CCDBG minimum health and safety standards are important regulations to keep to protect children’s health and safety in child care supported by public dollars.
- These federal child care regulations shouldn’t be eliminated.
- Prospective child care payments will make it easier for us to serve families with child care subsidies;
  - it can be hard to find child care and federal regulations should require states to use fair and timely payments to child care providers.
- Thank you for engaging the public in this RFI process, and I ask that you commit to continuing to do so through the established notice and comment process before enacting any new regulatory, or deregulatory reforms.
  - This process, while not perfect, gives impacted stakeholders an opportunity to share their own expertise and supports more transparent and effective rulemaking.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An early childhood center owner urges the preservation of federal child care regulations, particularly prospective and enrollment-based payments and CCDBG health and safety standards, to support providers, expand choices for subsidized families, and ensure fair state payments, while advocating for continued public engagement in rulemaking.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Tammy Dant
- **Type:** Individual
- **Role/Expertise:** Small business owner, runs an early childhood center.
- **Geographic Scope:** National
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly impacted as an early childhood center operator serving families with child care subsidies and subject to federal child care regulations.
structuredSections.corePosition: I strongly advocate for the retention of current federal child care regulations, particularly those related to prospective and enrollment-based payments, grants, contracts, and CCDBG minimum health and safety standards. These regulations are crucial for expanding child care supply and choice for families using subsidies, and for protecting children's well-being.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Keep prospective and enrollment-based payments, grants, and contracts regulations.
  - These help expand supply and choice for parents receiving subsidies.
- Keep CCDBG minimum health and safety standards regulations.
  - These protect children’s health and safety in child care supported by public dollars.
- Do not eliminate federal child care regulations.
- Federal regulations should require states to use fair and timely payments to child care providers.
- Commit to continuing public engagement through the established notice and comment process before enacting any new regulatory or deregulatory reforms.
  - This process allows impacted stakeholders to share expertise.
  - Supports more transparent and effective rulemaking.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- The potential elimination of current federal child care regulations, especially those regarding prospective and enrollment-based payments and CCDBG health and safety standards.
- The difficulty for child care centers to serve families with subsidies without prospective payments.
  - This directly contributes to the challenge families face in finding child care.
- The lack of fair and timely payments from states to child care providers.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The insight that prospective child care payments are essential for centers to effectively serve families receiving child care subsidies, directly linking payment structure to service accessibility for children and families.
- The perspective that the existing notice and comment process, despite its imperfections, is a vital mechanism for incorporating stakeholder expertise and fostering transparent and effective rulemaking.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "prospective and enrollment-based payments and grants and contracts are important regulations to keep; they help expand supply and choice for parents receiving subsidies."
- "Prospective child care payments will make it easier for us to serve families with child care subsidies; it can be hard to find child care and federal regulations should require states to use fair and timely payments to child care providers."
