    - Only 17% of patients currently receive these preps without cost-sharing.
- PBM practices limit patient choice and steer patients away from effective, FDA-approved preparations.
    - PBMs direct patients and providers toward outdated, high-volume preps or non-FDA-approved over-the-counter (OTC) regimens.
    - A study showed only 26% of patients used low-volume prep, while 52% used OTC and 23% high-volume, despite low-volume being more effective and tolerated.
- Inadequate bowel preparation, often a result of PBM practices, severely impacts the quality and effectiveness of colonoscopies.
    - Inadequate prep occurs in 15-35% of colonoscopies.
    - It impairs Adenoma Detection Rate (ADR) and cecal intubation rates.
    - Leads to longer procedure times, higher healthcare costs, and worse outcomes.
    - Older/OTC preps do not consistently meet the 90% adequacy threshold set by Tri-Societies.
- Patient hesitancy and non-completion of bowel prep are significant barriers to colonoscopy.
    - 86% of patients identified bowel prep as the worst part of the colonoscopy.
    - 49% cited inability to complete prep as their greatest challenge.
    - 75% of patients were not offered a choice of preparation options from their provider.
- PBM-imposed utilization management tactics create substantial administrative burdens for providers.
    - Practices spend an average of 13 hours per week per physician dealing with prior authorization.
    - 94% of physicians report delays in necessary care due to prior authorization.
    - This diverts clinical resources, increases overhead, and contributes to clinician burnout.
- Delays or reductions in CRC screening due to cost-sharing or formulary restrictions lead to higher long-term healthcare costs.
    - Treating late-stage CRC is more than twice as expensive as early-stage treatment.
    - An 8% reduction in screening could result in a 5.1% increase in CRC incidence and a 9.1% increase in CRC mortality, along with significant cost increases.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- CMS Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz's personal experience with an inadequate bowel prep, which necessitated an early repeat colonoscopy, is cited as a real-world example of the policy's impact.
- A 2024 Colon Cancer Coalition survey revealed striking patient perspectives on bowel preparation: 86% identified it as the "worst part" of the colonoscopy, and nearly half (49%) cited the inability to complete the prep as their greatest challenge, surpassing other concerns like results or time off work.
- The same survey highlighted a significant patient choice issue, noting that 75% of patients were not offered a choice of preparation options, despite taste and volume being major drivers of hesitancy.
- Data from a large real-world dataset (33 million patient encounters) showed that despite low-volume preps being more effective and better tolerated, only 26% of patients used them, while over 75% were directed towards less effective or less tolerable high-volume or OTC options.
- The comment emphasizes the direct link between PBM practices and major quality metrics, showing how PBM restrictions lead to lower Adenoma Detection Rates (ADR) and contribute to preventable cancers, beyond just patient inconvenience.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "This modest yet impactful update would eliminate ambiguity in existing policy that Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) have used to impose inappropriate cost-sharing on patients, undermining screening rates and increasing downstream healthcare costs."
- "However, the effectiveness of this life-saving tool is heavily dependent on adequate bowel preparation. Without a properly cleansed colon, polyps can be missed, leading to higher CRC incidence, delayed diagnoses, repeat procedures, and significantly increased healthcare costs."
- "According to a 2024 Colon Cancer Coalition survey, 86% of patients identified the bowel prep as the worst part of the colonoscopy, and nearly half (49%) cited the inability to complete the prep as their greatest challenge, more than concerns about the results, time off work or transportation."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- I work in human resources, so I’m used to navigating systems and procedures.
- But nothing prepared me for how broken and dehumanizing the ADHD treatment system is.
- I wasn’t diagnosed until my mid-30s, after years of being labeled “disorganized,” “too emotional,” or “a poor planner.”
- In truth, I was exhausted.
  - I couldn’t keep my focus at work, would leave meetings unsure of what just happened, and constantly stayed late just to catch up.
  - At home, it was the same:
    - I’d forget to pick up prescriptions, miss deadlines for bills, or zone out while my kids were talking.
  - The guilt was constant.
- The worst part was the insomnia.
  - It wasn’t just not falling asleep—it was this endless cycle of anxiety.
  - I’d lie there going over every task I forgot, every interaction I fumbled.
  - I’d wake up more tired than when I went to bed.
- Starting stimulant medication changed everything.
  - My focus improved, my work performance stabilized, and my sleep became manageable.
- But staying on treatment? That’s a different battle entirely.
- First, I couldn’t find a single psychiatrist in my area accepting adult ADHD patients.
- My primary care doctor wasn’t comfortable prescribing stimulants, so I had to go the telehealth route.
- That helped—until the pharmacy issues started.
  - Every month feels like Russian roulette.
  - Is the medication in stock?
  - Will it be a new manufacturer that throws off my response?
  - Can I get the prescription filled on time, or will I have to miss work because my brain isn’t functioning right?
- The Schedule II classification is the core of the problem.
  - It treats ADHD medications the same as fentanyl and methadone—while Xanax, which is far more addictive, is a Schedule IV drug.
  - There’s no scientific rationale for this.
  - The DSM-5 removed amphetamine addiction as a diagnosis.
  - These medications have been used since World War II.
  - If they were that dangerous, wouldn’t we have seen a crisis by now?
  - Instead, we’ve created a crisis of access.
- I’m asking for two things: make telehealth access permanent, and reclassify ADHD medications to Schedule III or lower.
- People with ADHD didn’t ask for this condition.
- We’re not seeking a shortcut or an edge.
- We’re seeking stability, dignity, and the right to treatment that’s safe, effective, and accessible.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An individual working in human resources with personal experience of ADHD describes the broken and dehumanizing treatment system, advocating for permanent telehealth access and the reclassification of ADHD medications due to unscientific Schedule II restrictions that create an access crisis.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Anonymous Anonymous
- **Type:** Individual
- **Role/Expertise:** Works in human resources; personal experience navigating the healthcare system for ADHD treatment
- **Geographic Scope:** National (implied by reliance on telehealth for access)
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly impacted by the challenges in accessing and maintaining ADHD medication due to current regulations and system failures.
structuredSections.corePosition: The ADHD treatment system is fundamentally broken and dehumanizing, largely due to unscientific Schedule II classification of medications which creates severe access barriers and causes significant distress for patients. I believe these medications should be reclassified to Schedule III or lower, and telehealth access should be made permanent, to ensure safe, effective, and accessible treatment for those with ADHD.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Make telehealth access permanent.
- Reclassify ADHD medications to Schedule III or lower.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- Difficulty in finding psychiatrists who accept adult ADHD patients.
- Significant and ongoing challenges with pharmacies regarding ADHD medication:
  - Uncertainty about medication stock availability.
  - Inconsistency with different manufacturers, impacting treatment response.
  - Difficulty in getting prescriptions filled on time, leading to missed work or impaired functioning.
- The Schedule II classification of ADHD medications is baseless and problematic:
  - It equates ADHD medications with highly addictive substances like fentanyl and methadone, while less addictive drugs like Xanax are Schedule IV.
  - There is no scientific rationale for this classification.
  - The DSM-5 no longer includes amphetamine addiction as a diagnosis.
  - Medications have been safely used since World War II without a crisis, indicating their safety profile is misrepresented.
  - The classification has created an "access crisis" for legitimate patients.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- Experienced a late diagnosis of ADHD in their mid-30s, after years of being mislabeled and experiencing significant professional and personal struggles including chronic exhaustion, focus issues at work, missed deadlines, and debilitating insomnia rooted in anxiety over forgotten tasks.
- Described the experience of monthly medication refills as "Russian roulette" due to unpredictable stock, manufacturer changes, and timing issues at pharmacies.
- Provided a specific critique of the Schedule II classification, contrasting ADHD medications with Xanax and citing the DSM-5's removal of amphetamine addiction as a diagnosis and the historical safe use of these medications since World War II.
- Detailed the significant positive impact stimulant medication had on their life, improving focus, work performance, and sleep.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "But nothing prepared me for how broken and dehumanizing the ADHD treatment system is."
- "Every month feels like Russian roulette."
- "The Schedule II classification is the core of the problem. It treats ADHD medications the same as fentanyl and methadone—while Xanax, which is far more addictive, is a Schedule IV drug. There’s no scientific rationale for this."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The American Nurses Association (ANA) submits comments in response to the United States Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS’) and the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA’s) Request for Information (RFI) on eliminating outdated or unnecessary regulations to lower costs and empower providers.
*   The nursing profession has been constricted by undue regulations that hinder the profession and create unnecessary barriers for nurses and patients across healthcare settings.
*   ANA appreciates the opportunity to detail the concerns of both registered nurses (RNs) and advanced practice registered nurses (APRNs) to HHS and FDA and seeks collaboration to remove these barriers.
*   ANA is the premier organization representing the interests of the nation’s over 5 million RNs through its state and constituent member associations, organizational affiliates, and individual members.
*   ANA advances the nursing profession by fostering high standards of nursing practice, promoting a safe and ethical work environment, bolstering the health and wellness of nurses, and advocating on healthcare issues that affect nurses and the public.
*   ANA members include the four APRN roles: nurse practitioners (NPs), clinical nurse specialists (CNSs), certiﬁed nurse-midwives (CNMs), and certiﬁed registered nurse anesthetists (CRNAs).
*   RNs serve in multiple direct care, care coordination, administrative, and leadership roles across the full spectrum of healthcare settings.
    *   RNs provide and coordinate patient care, educate patients and the public about various health conditions, including essential self-care, and provide advice and emotional support to patients and their family members.
*   Nurses are critical to a robust healthcare delivery system, meeting the needs of all patients and providing quality care that leads to better health outcomes.
    *   Nurses are critical to coordinated care approaches for patients in all care settings.
    *   Patient-centered care coordination is a core professional standard for all RNs and central to nurses’ longtime practice of providing holistic care to patients.
*   There are persistent regulatory barriers that constrain RN and APRN nursing practice.
*   While ANA understands that HHS can remove many of these regulatory barriers, it acknowledges that additional barriers to nursing fall under the scope of other federal agencies and encourages HHS to work with and encourage other applicable federal agencies to remove these barriers.
*   1) HHS Must Allow APRNs to Practice at the Top of Their License.
    *   APRNs are highly trained medical practitioners, but many states still do not allow them to practice medicine to the full extent of their license.
    *   Full Practice Authority (FPA) allows APRNs to practice at the top of their license, but only 24 to 28 states (depending on the APRN practice area) currently provide FPA.
    *   ANA agrees that APRNs and physicians are trained in different ways and have different roles in treating patients.
    *   FPA does not change APRN scope of practice (SOP) but simply allows these clinicians to practice advanced practice nursing in the way they are educated and trained.
    *   Due to regulatory barriers, APRNs, including NPs, CNSs, CNMs, and CRNAs, face real barriers to practicing medicine at the top of their license due to outdated regulations.
    *   HHS has the authority to provide FPA to patients who receive healthcare through federal programs, such as Medicare, by creating a program similar to the Veteran Affairs’ (VA’s) National Standards of Practice.
        *   The HHS program should include both RNs and CRNAs, who are not yet included in the VA’s National Standards of Practice.
        *   Requiring national standards in other care settings, such as facilities that accept Medicare or Medicaid, would allow APRNs to practice at the top of their license while seeing patients covered by federal insurance programs.
        *   These standards would only cover patients covered by federal insurance programs and would not require other payers to follow federal rules.
    *   The care provided by APRNs to Medicare beneﬁciaries is comparable to the care provided by physicians.
    *   There is also legislation introduced in Congress that would remove many of these barriers, but ANA strongly encourages HHS and its subagencies, such as Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), to remove these barriers on its own, instead of waiting for Congressional action.
    *   Physician organizations oppose many of these changes, viewing the practice of medicine as their exclusive domain.
        *   Modern medicine is built on interprofessional healthcare delivery, and patients should be able to choose which type of healthcare provider they want to see.
        *   Recognizing the important role that non-physician providers play in our healthcare system is increasingly important as the healthcare delivery system faces real shortages in clinicians, particularly in primary care, mental and behavioral health, and in rural/underserved areas.
        *   The physician shortage is only expected to grow, and APRNs are trained and ready to ﬁll care delivery gaps to ensure patients have access to the care they need.
        *   Outdated SOP laws do not allow APRNs to practice in the settings and manners in which they are needed the most.
        *   Realizing a shortage of physicians, physician groups have informally ceded full practice authority to APRNs and other non-physician providers, but there is pushback whenever this is formalized by either states or the federal government.
    *   It is past time for APRNs to have the needed regulations that deﬁnitively allow them to practice at the top of their license, which they are trained and highly qualiﬁed to do.
    *   Allowing APRNs to practice at the top of their license is particularly needed in rural areas.
        *   People who live in rural areas face greater barriers accessing care, leading to delayed care, which allows diseases to progress and become more expensive to treat.
        *   Removing APRN practice barriers will help make timely care more accessible in rural areas and help address the chronic disease epidemic, aligning with the priorities outlined in the Executive Order Establishing the President’s Make America Healthy Again Commission.
    *   Providing full practice authority to APRNs is an excellent way to ensure that APRNs can practice at the top of their license.
    *   ANA urges HHS to remove all barriers that prevent nurses from practicing at the top of their license and ensure that patients have access to care from trusted nurse clinicians in their communities.
*   2) HHS Must End Collaborative Agreements.
    *   Collaborative agreements fulﬁll a regulatory requirement placed by many states on APRN practice, requiring an agreement between a physician and an APRN for either a limited period (transition to practice) or granting permission to practice.
    *   Many of these requirements were relaxed during the COVID-19 public health emergency (PHE) with no negative effect on patient care.
    *   ANA believes that the ﬂexibilities provided during the pandemic should be made permanent.
    *   These collaborative agreements do not relate to the APRNs' SOP, and there is no evidence to suggest that they protect patients.
    *   Additionally, these transition-to-practice requirements are becoming increasingly difficult to initiate and maintain as primary care physicians and psychiatrists increasingly decline to offer them.
    *   Mergers and acquisitions also prevent physicians from signing agreements with APRNs who are not employed by the parent organization, creating additional barriers to practice.
    *   Physicians and APRNs collaborate to meet patient and community needs without the need for collaborative agreements.
    *   ANA urges HHS to end unnecessary and overly burdensome collaborative agreements.
*   3) HHS Must End Unnecessary Supervision Requirements.
    *   Supervision requirements, similar to collaborative agreements, generally require a physician to sign off on an APRN’s work.
    *   Many states allow APRN practice without unnecessary supervision requirements (NPs in 39 states, CNSs and CNMs in 28 states, CRNAs in 27 states).
    *   During the COVID-19 PHE, the Trump Administration relaxed these supervision requirements without any difference in patient care.
    *   Part of the reasoning behind supervision requirements is to prevent APRNs from exceeding their scope of practice.
    *   Supervision requirements pose an increased burden on practitioners and facilities in rural areas due to unique challenges.
        *   Often APRNs and other clinicians must travel to where patients are, and direct supervision requirements add to the already-lengthy time and distance needed to provide prompt, appropriate care to patients.
    *   APRNs wish to practice at the top of their license within their education, training, and expertise, and are not interested in providing services for which they have not been trained.
    *   ANA maintains that these reconﬁgured supervision requirements should become permanent and urges HHS to formally remove them.
    *   a) HHS Must Remove Overly Burdensome Supervision Requirements for CRNAs.
        *   Federal requirements regarding supervision requirements for CRNAs continue to be overly burdensome.
        *   While there is no federal statutory language requiring supervision requirements, states currently must individually request permission from CMS to remove them.
        *   The federal government was right to rescind supervision requirements in a final rule in 2001, but that rule was withdrawn and replaced with the current bureaucratic opt-out process.
        *   This process places an extra burden on states.
        *   Only 25 states and one territory have completed the opt-out process of federal supervision requirements for CRNAs.
        *   These overly burdensome requirements can be easily removed by amending 42 CFR § 482.52(a)(4), 485.639 (c)(2), 416.42 (b)(2), and 485.524 (d)(3)(ii) and eliminating 42 CFR § 482.52(c), 485.639 (e), 416.42 (c), and 485.524 (d)(5).
        *   HHS should rescind physician supervision requirements from the conditions for coverage for ambulatory surgical centers and the conditions of participation for hospitals, rural emergency hospitals, and critical access hospitals.
*   4) HHS Must Remove “Incident to” Billing from Medicare Reimbursement.
    *   “Incident to” billing occurs when an APRN bills payors under a physician or provider National Provider Identiﬁer (NPI) and is then reimbursed at 100 percent of Medicare rate instead of at 85 percent.
    *   This is a massive roadblock for APRNs looking to start their own business, as they would be reimbursed less for the same work.
    *   This is another reason why Section 2706 nondiscrimination regulations are essential for APRNs.
    *   Currently, private payers set their rates and can choose to reimburse APRNs at a lower rate than physicians.
    *   This system reflects an earlier era, before APRNs received the advanced training and clinical experience they have today.
    *   “Incident to” billing has very strict oversight parameters and places the physician at the forefront of the medical team, which may have been true in the past but is not necessarily true today.
    *   Care coordination and other interdisciplinary care models are becoming increasingly commonplace, and APRNs are often leading these efforts within their scope of practice.
    *   “Incident to” billing also has a direct impact on RN care, as the care they provide is only captured under the physician NPI.
    *   RN work is essential in many aspects of modern medicine, including remote patient monitoring and ambulatory care, but that work is hard to see as Medicare, and most other payors, only reimburse under the physician NPI and not under the RN NPI.
    *   Medicare beneﬁciaries have become increasingly reliant on APRNs, leading the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) to recommend eliminating “incident to” billing.
    *   MedPAC has veriﬁed that eliminating “incident to” billing will not change the quality of care or how it is delivered.
    *   Additionally, “incident to” billing creates inﬂated claims, crediting physicians in instances when APRNs have often conducted the bulk of the work.
    *   Ending “incident to” billing will, therefore, help CMS reach its goal of eliminating waste, fraud, and abuse in the Medicare program.
    *   ANA strongly opposes the use of “incident to” billing and believes it should be removed from the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) (42 CFR §410.26) to create an equal playing ﬁeld among all practitioners.
*   5) HHS Must Standardize Terms in Regulations.
    *   The CFR refers to medical practitioners by different terms depending on where the service is provided and under which federal program the patient is receiving healthcare coverage.
    *   This leads to confusion for both practitioners and administrative staff as it forces practitioners to know not only where the patient is located, but also which program is providing coverage, before they can provide treatment.
    *   In the calendar year 2024 Physician Fee Schedule proposed rule, CMS declared that it would use the term “practitioner” for anyone who provides care to patients, instead of using different terms for physicians or APRNs.
        *   ANA strongly supports this proposal and was pleased to see it incorporated into the ﬁnal rule.
        *   Yet, this change has only been accepted by CMS and is not standard practice across all HHS agencies or the larger federal government.
        *   As a result, there are different rules and regulations depending on which federal department is funding or regulating care.
    *   These variations in terms cause confusion and make it more difficult for practitioners to know what regulations apply before they can administer care to patients.
    *   Standardizing terms would remove unnecessary regulatory barriers and allow practitioners to practice medicine without worrying about what program the patient is covered by and what federal regulations apply.
    *   ANA supports the standardization of terms across the federal government, and the term “practitioner” should be used for all healthcare providers.
*   6) HHS Must Allow Continued Use of Telehealth.
    *   Prior to the COVID-19 PHE, telehealth was a very small part of Medicare and was only used in very speciﬁc situations.
    *   One of the few upsides from the COVID-19 PHE was allowing for the expanded use of telehealth, which led to greater access to care.
    *   Telehealth was shown to be a safe, efficient, cost-effective way to treat patients for many chronic conditions and for carrying out varying forms of healthcare visits, such as primary care screenings, postoperative visits, and acute stroke care.
    *   Telehealth use during the COVID-19 PHE was found to be associated with fewer emergency department visits, reduced inpatient admissions, and lower overall medical costs.
    *   If beneﬁciaries do not have access to telehealth, they will often be forced to use the emergency room, which is the most expensive point of care.
    *   The end of the COVID-19 PHE returned some of the telehealth rules to their pre-pandemic status, but Congress has fortunately continued to extend telehealth ﬂexibilities through the end of this year.
    *   ANA has long advocated for HHS’ subagency, CMS, to take the position that they have the regulatory authority to make some ﬂexibilities permanent, but CMS has continued to maintain that only Congress has that authority.
    *   42 CFR §410.78(b) provides practitioners with the general rules for telehealth, and while there are limitations, there are many services that can be provided on a permanent basis without waiting for Congressional action.
    *   Relying on this section of the law would reduce the need for waivers and provide practitioners with more tools that they can use to treat their patients on a permanent basis.
    *   Making the ﬂexibilities permanent would permit many patients in rural areas to visit the practitioner of their choice.
        *   Currently, many rural areas have a shortage of nurses and other healthcare professionals, which telehealth would help improve.
    *   Many patients who beneﬁt from telehealth would not otherwise be able to see their practitioner or would rather be forced to seek care through more costly emergency services.
        *   This may be because they have limited mobility, cannot afford transportation, or do not have paid time off from their jobs.
    *   Telehealth has allowed many patients to see their practitioners from locations other than the practitioner’s office, resulting in better health maintenance and follow-up, which can ultimately lead to a healthier public.
    *   There are shortages of physicians and other healthcare practitioners in many rural areas, and APRNs are critical to ensure patients do not face gaps in needed care.
    *   Continuing to allow telehealth access will make Americans healthier by allowing patients to receive more timely care, have needed follow-up visits, and obtain preventative care, especially in rural communities or areas with provider shortages—therefore, aligning with the Administration’s vision to Make America Healthy Again.
    *   ANA urges HHS to make telehealth ﬂexibilities permanent.
*   7) HHS Must Interpret the Rural Emergency Hospital Provisions Correctly.
    *   Congress recently created a new class of hospital called the “rural emergency hospital” (REH).
    *   REHs were created as a way for rural hospitals to survive in a time when hospitals are closing at alarmingly high rates in rural areas nationwide (146 rural hospitals closed or stopped providing inpatient services from 2005 to 2023).
    *   REHs receive a higher Medicare reimbursement rate under federal regulations than non-REHs, but an ambiguity in the authorizing statute has been an obstacle to many hospitals that requested REH designation.
    *   HHS has interpreted the REH authorizing statute as forbidding REHs from receiving Medicaid payments in most cases.
        *   This becomes an issue because while REHs do receive a higher Medicare reimbursement rate, many of these hospitals are in regions where a large percentage of the patient population also receives health insurance coverage through the Medicaid program.
        *   The loss of Medicaid reimbursement would be a death knell for these hospitals, and, as a result, they are not seeking to change their status to an REH.
        *   This only serves to compound existing ﬁnancial challenges faced by these hospitals as they struggle to remain open.
    *   This interpretation is likely not Congress’ intent, as Congress would not have intentionally put hospitals in this impossible position of having to choose between Medicare or Medicaid payments.
    *   Having the ability to accept beneﬁciaries covered by Medicaid and Medicare is crucial, as the nurses in these hospitals know the impact on patients when they do not have access to care.
    *   In line with the Executive Order to Make America Healthy Again, ensuring access to healthcare services in rural areas is paramount to keeping communities healthy.
    *   HHS must clarify that REHs may participate in the Medicaid program without unnecessary limitations, as it would allow hospitals to fulﬁll Congressional intent and become REHs.
*   8) HHS Must Work with the VA to Finalize the VA National Standards of Practice for All RNs.
    *   ANA encourages HHS to work with the VA to ﬁnalize their National Standards of Practice for VA employees, speciﬁcally for RNs and CRNAs.
    *   The VA has been slowly creating national standards for years, but they have yet to propose or promulgate national standards for RNs.
    *   These standards are not an overreach, as they do not override state law and would only apply to nurses while they are working at VA facilities as the existing standards for other professionals do now.
    *   The VA, like other hospitals across the country, is faced with a shortage of nurses, which hinders the ability of patients to receive needed care.
    *   A lack of a national standard hinders the ability of nurses to easily transfer to VA facilities to address nursing shortages in states where they are not licensed to practice medicine.
    *   Like RNs, CRNAs face similar barriers at the VA.
        *   While the three other APRN specialties (CNSs, CNMs, and NPs) received national standards of practice in 2016 (38 CFR §17.415), CRNAs were not granted the same privileges that other APRNs receive.
        *   The lack of a CRNA national standard is especially egregious; in some states, CRNAs are the only providers for anesthesia services in nearly all rural hospitals.
        *   As many anesthesiologists refuse to leave their urban hospitals, CRNAs—like many other APRNs—have been ready and willing to move to areas with shortages.
        *   Without a national standard of practice, it would be extremely time-consuming for CRNAs to receive the state licensing necessary when switching facilities to address anesthesiology shortages at VA facilities in other states.
    *   These national standards are long overdue to address this burdensome regulatory barrier that only serves to hinder veterans’ access to care.
    *   ANA strongly supports the implementation of national standards for all nurses in VA facilities so that these clinicians are able to practice where they are needed without unnecessary barriers.
    *   Although these National Standards of Practice fall under VA jurisdiction, HHS must use its inﬂuence to encourage the VA to ﬁnalize them.
*   9) HHS Should Work with Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) to Repromulgate Proposed Rules on Special Registration.
    *   In the final week of the Biden Administration, DEA released a long overdue proposed rule on special registration for telehealth prescribers of certain controlled substances.
    *   While ANA appreciated that DEA issued this statutory mandated rule, the proposal contains many provisions that create new regulatory barriers for nurses and patients.
    *   One example where the proposed rule may have unintended consequences is requiring at least 50 percent of prescriptions in a calendar month not to be Schedule II narcotics.
        *   DEA does not offer any reason for this number, and it is illogical.
        *   Prescribers may have a different patient mix in a given month, or they may have other reasons for not issuing speciﬁc prescriptions which could cause them to run afoul of the regulations.
    *   Another proposal that creates an unnecessary burden to practice is requiring that patients and practitioners be physically located within the same state.
        *   While ANA understands the intention of this provision, it recognizes that there are areas of the country where it is very common for residents to cross state lines for work, healthcare, and other daily activities due to geographic proximity.
        *   Often, in these cases, a patient would be unnecessarily barred from continuing to receive care from their established and trusted provider simply because their residence is over the state line.
        *   Moreover, the rule allows for no exception, even when the provider is licensed in both the state where they are physically located and the state where the patient is located.
    *   ANA urges HHS to work with DEA to explicitly allow for telehealth prescribing across state lines, provided that the practitioner is licensed to practice in both states where the practitioner and the patient are physically located.
    *   Although these rules fall under DEA’s and the United States Department of Justice’s jurisdictions, both HHS and FDA have vast expertise and sway in the ﬁelds of healthcare access and drug regulation—two barriers posed by these proposed rules.
    *   Telehealth prescribers are already operating under a waiver that allows patient access; therefore, it would not be detrimental to telehealth prescribers or consumers to continue operating under the current waiver until a revised proposed rule can be published.
    *   ANA believes that HHS and FDA must use their inﬂuence and work with the DEA to get rulemaking that does not create new and unnecessary regulatory barriers or burdens.
*   10) HHS Must Direct CMS to Reform the CPT/RUC Process.
    *   Reimbursement for all practitioners is determined through the Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) and the Relative Value Scale Update Committee (RUC) systems.
    *   These were created, and are still run, by the American Medical Association (AMA).
    *   The AMA has a contract with CMS to determine Medicare payments, and most, if not all, private payers use the CPT system as well to set reimbursement rates.
    *   ANA is proud to be the only nursing organization that has advisors representing nursing in both the CPT code development and RUC code valuation processes.
    *   While nursing is represented in this process, they are not heard equally.
    *   Since CPT and RUC are driven by the AMA, often non-physician provider perspectives are overlooked, resulting in a general perception that the payment system is biased towards physicians.
    *   CMS has sought comment on rulemaking on the CPT/RUC process and whether it should be replaced with a different payment system.
    *   While ANA does not believe that the CPT/RUC process should be replaced with a different payment system, reform is needed.
        *   A complete overhaul may create havoc in the healthcare delivery system since the current reimbursement determinations are ingrained into both public and private payment systems.
    *   ANA believes that the current system must be reformed to better reﬂect the critical role of non-physicians in the healthcare delivery system in payment decision-making.
    *   CMS should reconsider the current contract with AMA and demand that changes be made to make the CPT and RUC systems more inclusive of non-physicians, such as through having a better balance of physicians to non-physicians on each of the RUC and CPT panels.
    *   ANA believes that CMS should use its regulatory authority and require that the AMA provide more seats and input into the process for non-physicians.
        *   This is particularly important as nurse practitioners continue to meet more and more of the nation’s primary care needs.
    *   The elevation of non-physician perspectives in this process is critical to creating more transparency in how payments are determined and ensuring payment rates appropriately reﬂect how care is provided to patients.
    *   ANA urges HHS to direct CMS to institute real reforms to the CPT/RUC process to better reﬂect the provision of healthcare by all clinicians.
*   11) HHS Must End Outside Regulation of Nursing.
    *   Healthcare, and non-healthcare, professions generally regulate themselves; however, there is one glaring example where this is not true: nursing.
    *   Nurses are the only healthcare professionals who do not regulate their own profession, as there are states that require physician representation on nursing boards.
        *   This is patently unfair and is not a matter of education; generally, the reasoning is to give objectivity to the nursing board.
    *   Nurse licensure must be run by nurses as they are the only ones who understand the education and training needed to become a nurse.
    *   ANA ﬁrmly believes that healthcare professions should regulate their respective professions, and that other healthcare professions must not be primary in regulating the nursing profession.
    *   Removing requirements to have physicians sit on nursing boards is simply a common-sense reform that would put nursing on par with other healthcare professionals.
    *   ANA strongly urges HHS to end all outside regulation of nursing practice.
*   12) HHS Must Ban the Use of Non-Compete Agreements for Nurses in Medicare and Medicaid Facilities.
    *   ANA strongly believes that non-compete agreements are harmful to frontline nurses.
    *   ANA understands that non-compete agreements may have some utility in business and ﬁnance, especially among management and design personnel as they have access to corporate secrets.
    *   Nurses, especially frontline nurses, do not have access to corporate secrets.
    *   Therefore, the only reason for nurses to sign non-compete agreements would be to force them to stay in their current job and limit their employment opportunities.
        *   This takes nurses out of the free market and artiﬁcially caps salaries.
    *   Banning non-compete agreements for nurses would raise salaries by increasing competition for nurses who are in demand without decreasing the supply of nurses in the marketplace.
    *   Higher salaries and greater employment opportunities would likely draw more people into the profession and could help alleviate the current nursing shortage.
    *   Unlike non-compete agreements, a combination of Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and non-disclosure agreements can protect patient and business information without imposing additional restrictions on job mobility.
    *   Some of the non-compete agreements that ANA is aware of are extreme.
        *   One member mentioned that their office had a non-compete that forbade them from working as a nurse for a speciﬁed period of time within 7,500 miles of their current workplace.
        *   That covered the nurse’s employment not only in New York state but also the entirety of the contiguous 48 states, Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico, and Guam.
        *   Such agreements are not intended to protect business interests other than tethering nurses to speciﬁc roles, reducing their employment prospects and exacerbating workforce shortages.
    *   Distance is not the only unfair element in non-compete agreements.
        *   Sometimes these restrictive agreements can last for years, leading nurses to feel that they are either stuck in their current position or they must be retrained in another nursing specialty in order to seek other employment—which takes both time and money.
    *   ANA urges HHS to ban non-compete agreements in facilities that accept Medicare and Medicaid.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The American Nurses Association urges HHS and FDA to eliminate outdated regulations that restrict nursing practice, including full practice authority for APRNs, by ending collaborative agreements and supervision requirements, reforming billing and terminology, making telehealth permanent, clarifying rural hospital payments, finalizing VA standards, revising DEA controlled substance rules, reforming payment processes, ending outside nursing regulation, and banning nurse non-compete agreements.

- **Name/Organization:** American Nurses Association
- **Type:** Organization
- **Role/Expertise:** Premier organization representing the interests of over 5 million registered nurses (RNs) and advanced practice registered nurses (APRNs) in the nation, advancing nursing practice standards, promoting safe work environments, bolstering nurse wellness, and advocating on healthcare issues affecting nurses and the public.
- **Geographic Scope:** National
- **Stake in Issue:** Direct impact on the ability of their members (RNs and APRNs) to practice at the full extent of their education and training, affecting patient access to care, healthcare costs, and the professional autonomy and economic well-being of the nursing workforce.
structuredSections.corePosition: The American Nurses Association (ANA) believes that the nursing profession has been unduly constricted by outdated and unnecessary federal regulations that hinder nurses' ability to practice, create barriers for patients to access care, and increase healthcare costs. We urge HHS and FDA to collaborate with us and other federal agencies to remove these persistent regulatory barriers, empowering nurses to practice at the top of their license and ensuring patients receive the quality care they need.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Allow Advanced Practice Registered Nurses (APRNs) to practice at the top of their license by providing Full Practice Authority (FPA) in federal programs, similar to the VA's National Standards of Practice, explicitly including RNs and CRNAs.
- End unnecessary and overly burdensome collaborative agreements between physicians and APRNs.
- End unnecessary supervision requirements for nurses, making permanent the flexibilities granted during the COVID-19 Public Health Emergency.
    - Specifically, remove overly burdensome federal supervision requirements for Certified Registered Nurse Anesthetists (CRNAs) by amending and eliminating specific sections of 42 CFR (§ 482.52(a)(4), 485.639 (c)(2), 416.42 (b)(2), 485.524 (d)(3)(ii) and 42 CFR § 482.52(c), 485.639 (e), 416.42 (c), 485.524 (d)(5)).
- Remove “incident to” billing from Medicare reimbursement (42 CFR §410.26) to create an equal playing field for all practitioners.
- Standardize terms across the federal government, specifically using "practitioner" for all healthcare providers to reduce confusion.
- Make telehealth flexibilities permanent by utilizing HHS's existing regulatory authority (42 CFR §410.78(b)) without waiting for Congressional action.
- Correctly interpret the Rural Emergency Hospital (REH) provisions to clarify that REHs may participate in the Medicaid program without unnecessary limitations.
- Work with the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to finalize National Standards of Practice for all RNs and CRNAs in VA facilities.
- Work with the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) to repromulgate proposed rules on special registration for telehealth prescribers of controlled substances, ensuring they do not create new regulatory barriers.
    - Explicitly allow for telehealth prescribing across state lines when the practitioner is licensed in both states.
- Direct CMS to institute real reforms to the Current Procedural Terminology (CPT)/Relative Value Scale Update Committee (RUC) process.
    - Reconsider the current contract with the American Medical Association (AMA) and demand changes for more inclusive representation of non-physicians on CPT and RUC panels.
- End all outside regulation of nursing, specifically removing requirements for physicians to sit on nursing boards.
- Ban the use of non-compete agreements for nurses in facilities that accept Medicare and Medicaid.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Regulatory Burden on Nursing Practice:** Undue regulations hinder the nursing profession and create unnecessary barriers for nurses and patients across healthcare settings.
- **Limited Practice Authority for APRNs:** Many states and federal programs do not allow APRNs to practice to the full extent of their license (Full Practice Authority), despite their advanced training and ability to fill care gaps, especially in underserved areas.
- **Opposition from Physician Organizations:** Physician groups often oppose changes that would formalize full practice authority for APRNs, viewing medicine as their exclusive domain, despite the informal ceding of authority and the need for interprofessional healthcare delivery.
- **Clinician Shortages:** The healthcare system faces real shortages in clinicians, particularly in primary care, mental and behavioral health, and rural/underserved areas, which outdated regulations exacerbate by limiting APRNs' ability to practice where needed.
- **Burdensome Collaborative Agreements and Supervision Requirements:** These requirements are unnecessary, lack evidence of patient protection, are difficult to initiate and maintain, and prevent APRNs from practicing efficiently, especially in rural areas.
    - Specific concern for CRNAs due to the bureaucratic opt-out process for federal supervision requirements.
- **"Incident to" Billing System:** This system:
    - Reimburses APRNs at a lower rate (85% vs. 100%) for the same work, creating a roadblock for APRNs starting their own businesses.
    - Reflects an outdated model where physicians are always at the forefront, ignoring modern interdisciplinary care models.
    - Causes RN care to be captured under physician NPIs, obscuring the essential work of RNs in areas like remote patient monitoring.
    - Creates inflated claims by crediting physicians for work largely performed by APRNs.
- **Inconsistent Regulatory Terminology:** Different terms for medical practitioners across federal regulations cause confusion for providers and administrative staff, requiring them to know a patient's location and coverage program before providing treatment.
- **Uncertainty of Telehealth Flexibilities:** The return of some telehealth rules to pre-pandemic status limits access to care, particularly for patients in rural areas, those with limited mobility, transportation issues, or inability to take time off work, leading to more costly emergency room visits.
- **Misinterpretation of Rural Emergency Hospital (REH) Statute:** HHS's interpretation forbids REHs from receiving Medicaid payments in most cases, creating an impossible choice for rural hospitals between Medicare and Medicaid payments, threatening their financial viability and access to care in rural communities.
- **Delay in VA National Standards of Practice:** The VA has not finalized national standards for RNs and CRNAs, hindering nurses' ability to easily transfer to VA facilities across state lines to address critical nursing shortages and limiting veterans' access to care.
- **New Regulatory Barriers from DEA Proposed Rules:** The DEA's proposed rule on special registration for telehealth prescribers of controlled substances introduces new burdens, such as an illogical 50% Schedule II narcotic limit and a requirement for patients and practitioners to be in the same state, even if the provider is licensed in both.
- **Bias in CPT/RUC Reimbursement Process:** The AMA-run CPT/RUC process is perceived as biased towards physicians, overlooking non-physician provider perspectives, leading to non-representative payment rates.
- **Outside Regulation of Nursing:** Nursing is uniquely regulated by other healthcare professions (e.g., physicians on nursing boards), which ANA views as unfair and hindering the profession's ability to self-regulate based on specific nursing education and training.
- **Harmful Non-Compete Agreements for Nurses:** These agreements are considered harmful to frontline nurses, limiting employment opportunities, artificially capping salaries, hindering job mobility, and exacerbating nursing shortages, with some examples involving extreme geographical and temporal restrictions.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The relaxation of collaborative agreements and supervision requirements during the COVID-19 public health emergency demonstrated no negative effect on patient care, suggesting these barriers are truly unnecessary.
- Despite physician organizations informally ceding full practice authority to APRNs due to clinician shortages, they often push back when this authority is formalized by states or the federal government.
- The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) has verified that eliminating "incident to" billing would not change the quality of care or how it is delivered, yet it would help eliminate inflated claims and better reflect who provides the care.
- Telehealth use during the COVID-19 pandemic was associated with fewer emergency department visits, reduced inpatient admissions, and lower overall medical costs, highlighting its efficiency and cost-effectiveness.
- One member shared an extreme example of a non-compete agreement that forbade them from working as a nurse for a specified period of time within 7,500 miles of their current workplace, covering virtually the entire United States and its territories, illustrating the punitive and restrictive nature of these agreements.

- "ANA knows that the nursing profession has been constricted by undue regulations."
- "The care provided by APRNs to Medicare beneﬁciaries is comparable to the care provided by physicians."
- "One member mentioned that their office had a non-compete that forbade them from working as a nurse for a speciﬁed period of time within 7,500 miles of their current workplace."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I am commenting on the U.S Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
*   The years of pregnancy to age three set the foundation for a baby’s development, learning and relationships.
    *   Babies rely entirely on the adults around them—parents, caregivers, and early childhood professionals—to provide safe, nurturing care.
    *   When babies or their caregivers face reduced support or program quality, babies can end up facing long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences.
    *   When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health.
*   Regulations matter.
    *   HHS, as the leading Federal agency tasked with enhancing the health and well-being of all Americans, plays a critical role in ensuring that babies, families, and the professionals who care for little ones have access to the resources, protections, and supports they need.
    *   In considering changes to regulations, HHS must preserve regulations that:
        *   Keep young children safe and healthy.
        *   Enable the adults in their lives to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
*   For example, regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings are needed to keep babies safe and developmentally on track.
*   Regulations that keep children and those who care for them healthy, like those that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care, must be maintained.
    *   This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe.
*   HHS rules reach far beyond just Medicaid and early learning, with many HHS programs laying the foundation of quality care and critical support that babies need.
*   Any changes to regulations must be:
    *   Transparent.
    *   Grounded in evidence.
    *   Focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
*   Because each regulation is different, HHS must continue to give the public—including families and early childhood professionals like me—ample time and opportunity to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes.
    *   We need a robust public process to make sure that the rules work for babies and those who care for them.
*   To keep America’s babies healthy, HHS must maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services.
*   Please uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
*   I would also like to add that I am a product of Head Start Services.
    *   I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career.
    *   I have a Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma.
    *   I have been a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for the past twenty-three years servicing the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles.
    *   It gives great pleasure to give back to my community.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An experienced early childhood education professional and Head Start alumna urges HHS to maintain and strengthen regulations that ensure the safety, health, and development of young children, advocating for transparent, evidence-based changes and robust public input.

structuredSections.keyRecommendations:

-   Preserve regulations that enable adults to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
    -   Specifically, maintain regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings.
    -   Maintain regulations that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care.
-   Ensure any changes to regulations are transparent, grounded in evidence, and focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
-   Provide ample time and opportunity for the public, including families and early childhood professionals, to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes through a robust public process.
-   Maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services for babies.
-   Uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   Reduced support or program quality for babies and caregivers could lead to long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences for children.
-   Regulatory changes that are not transparent, evidence-based, or child-focused could negatively impact the well-being and safety of children, families, and their service providers.
-   Inadequate public involvement in the regulatory process may result in rules that do not effectively serve the needs of babies and their caregivers.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I've had ADHD all my life but didn’t know what it was until my late 30s.
    *   I always just thought I was “bad with details” or “easily distracted.”
    *   Turns out, that’s not a personality quirk - it’s a medical condition.
    *   Not knowing that cost me years of job hopping, financial instability, and a divorce that I still feel guilty about.
        *   My ex used to say I never listened, or that I forgot everything she said.
        *   And she wasn’t wrong - I just didn’t know why.
*   I work as a welder, and being in that trade saved me from unemployment.
    *   Even that’s hard without treatment.
    *   When my ADHD is unmanaged, I forget safety steps, misplace tools, or miss critical details.
        *   It’s dangerous.
    *   When I don’t sleep, which happens a lot, the mistakes multiply.
        *   I lie awake thinking about bills I forgot to pay or texts I didn’t answer.
        *   The anxiety snowballs.
*   Once I finally got diagnosed and put on meds, things got better.
    *   I’m safer at work.
    *   More present with my kid.
    *   I sleep better.
    *   But access is always at risk.
        *   Doctors around here don’t want to prescribe Schedule II drugs.
        *   My PCP sent me to a telehealth clinic, and that’s been a lifeline.
        *   If those flexibilities go away, I don’t know what I’ll do.
*   The Schedule II status is killing people’s stability.
    *   You can’t fill early, even when you know the pharmacy won’t have it in time.
        *   And most of the time they don’t.
    *   Or it’s a new generic that feels off.
    *   The DEA still treats this like meth, even though there’s no data to support that.
    *   No one’s out here abusing their ADHD meds - we’re just trying to function.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An individual with ADHD, who works as a welder, urges the agency to maintain telehealth flexibilities and reclassify ADHD medications to Schedule III or IV due to the dangers and instability caused by current Schedule II restrictions and access issues.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Anonymous
- **Type:** Individual
- **Role/Expertise:** Welder; individual living with ADHD
- **Geographic Scope:** Local/State (indicated by "Doctors around here")
- **Stake in Issue:** Direct personal stake in access to ADHD medication and treatment, which significantly impacts job performance, safety, financial stability, and family life.
structuredSections.corePosition: I am urging the agency to maintain telehealth flexibilities for ADHD medication prescriptions and to reclassify ADHD medications from Schedule II to Schedule III or IV. The current Schedule II status creates significant barriers to accessing necessary treatment, leading to instability, safety concerns, and unnecessary anxiety for individuals like me who rely on these medications to function daily.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Keep telehealth flexibilities for prescribing ADHD medications.
- Move ADHD medications to Schedule III or IV.
- Make the system match the reality of what these drugs actually are.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- Undiagnosed ADHD severely impacted personal life, leading to job hopping, financial instability, and divorce.
- Unmanaged ADHD poses significant safety risks in the workplace (e.g., forgetting safety steps, misplacing tools, missing critical details).
- Lack of sleep due to ADHD-related anxiety exacerbates mistakes and anxiety.
- Access to ADHD medication is at risk due to doctors' reluctance to prescribe Schedule II drugs.
- Current Schedule II status creates instability for patients:
    - Inability to fill prescriptions early, even when pharmacies have stock issues.
    - Frequent pharmacy stock shortages.
    - Inconsistent efficacy with different generic versions of medication.
- The DEA's classification of ADHD medications as Schedule II is perceived as inappropriate, akin to treating them like illicit drugs, despite lack of data supporting widespread abuse among users.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The personal cost of undiagnosed ADHD included years of job hopping, financial instability, and a divorce, highlighting the profound, long-term impact of untreated neurodevelopmental conditions.
- Specific examples of workplace dangers as a welder due to unmanaged ADHD (forgetting safety steps, misplacing tools, missing critical details) illustrate the severe real-world consequences beyond personal discomfort.
- Reliance on telehealth as a "lifeline" due to local doctors' reluctance to prescribe Schedule II drugs showcases the critical role of these flexibilities in accessing care.
- The unique insight that "No one’s out here abusing their ADHD meds - we’re just trying to function" challenges common misconceptions about these medications and their users.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "The Schedule II status is killing people’s stability."
- "No one’s out here abusing their ADHD meds - we’re just trying to function."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- I spent two decades trying to hold a career together as a high school teacher.
  - I loved the students.
  - I loved the subject matter.
  - But I could never stay on top of grading, lesson planning, or even remembering which emails I’d responded to.
  - I lived in a constant state of mental triage.
  - I thought I had anxiety and burnout - turns out it was untreated ADHD the entire time.
- I was diagnosed at 47, after losing my job, my marriage, and my health.
  - My ex-wife had tolerated my forgetfulness and disorganization for years, but when I forgot to pay our mortgage three months in a row, that was the final straw.
  - I don’t blame her.
  - Our lives were chaos.
  - I couldn’t focus, couldn’t sleep, and I was constantly overwhelmed.
  - I applied for disability after I had a breakdown and couldn’t finish a single task for weeks.
  - That’s what untreated ADHD does.
- Medication helped tremendously.
  - I could finally prioritize tasks and follow through.
- But just as I began recovering, the system started to push back.
  - I couldn’t find any psychiatrist accepting new ADHD patients.
  - My primary care doctor wouldn’t prescribe stimulants because they’re schedule 2.
  - I found a telehealth provider - and it saved my life.
  - But now I worry every day that these flexibilities will be revoked.
  - Losing access to that care would mean starting over again from the bottom.
- Filling my prescription is another uphill battle.
  - The pharmacy runs out.
  - They swap brands without warning.
  - And because it’s a controlled substance, there’s no room for error - no early fills, no workarounds.
  - And I ask: why is Adderall regulated like fentanyl while benzodiazepines are schedule 4?
  - Why are we still operating with science from 1970s?
  - The DSM doesn’t even list amphetamine addiction anymore.
  - The only people harmed by these restrictions are those who actually need these medications.
- I’ve lost a marriage and a career to undiagnosed ADHD.
- Please don’t let bad policy steal my recovery, too.
- Make telehealth permanent.
- Reclassify these medications.
- And start treating ADHD like the lifelong disability it truly is.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: A former teacher, diagnosed with ADHD at 47 after significant personal losses, advocates for permanent telehealth access and reclassification of ADHD medications, arguing that current regulations are outdated and harmful to those who need treatment.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- Thank you for taking the initiative to seek public comment identifying unnecessary, unlawful, unduly burdensome, and unsound regulations.
- Trust that your analysis will include not only final rules but also proposed rules that are burdensome in unforeseen ways, fail to benefit the American public, and stifle American businesses.
- Please consider withdrawing the following Proposed Rule:
  - Docket No. : FDA-2007-N-0363 Electronic Distribution of Prescribing Information for Human Prescription Drugs Including Biological Products.
  - This FDA Proposed Rule, published in the Federal Register of December 18, 2014, would end the long-established, U.S. Food Drug and Cosmetic Act required, communication of critical information via printed labeling (known as Prescribing Information (PI)) which currently accompanies all prescription drug products.
  - It would replace printed PI with a digital repository from which health care professionals would need to retrieve the PI.
  - FDA-2007-N-0363 is unnecessary, unduly burdensome on community pharmacies, unsound due to unintended consequences on patient safety and healthcare professionals, and arguably unlawful under current labeling requirements of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
  - The FDA Proposed Rule was not sound regulation in 2014 when it was proposed, nor is it sound today.

- Background
  - FDA published data indicates pharmacists utilize printed PI as a reference for critical clinical information more than 75 million times per year.
  - 96% of all comments submitted to the FDA opposed the elimination of printed PI.
  - 93% of comments submitted to the FDA by health professionals opposed the elimination of printed PI.
  - A 2013 GAO report (GAO-13-592, July 2013) stated that “…there are disadvantages that could offset advantages gained from relying on electronic drug labeling as a complete substitute for printed labeling.”
  - Studies show 82% of community pharmacists referred to the printed PI in the last month.
  - Studies show that 82% of community pharmacies have experienced a loss of internet connection due to natural disasters or technical problems.
  - Community pharmacy databases are HIPAA compliant with restricted access to internet searches for electronic PI.
  - Under the COVID Emergency Use Authorization, FDA suspended the requirement for a printed PI for new drugs or new indications for COVID, thereby limiting the transparency of key clinical data and risks.
  - The pharmaceutical industry sponsored the proposed rule, which represents a significant unsafe shift in responsibility for providing patient safety information from the drug manufacturer to other less reliable and less accessible sources.

- Patient Safety
  - FDA-published data indicates pharmacists utilize printed PI more than 75 million times per year as a reference for critical clinical information.
  - Community pharmacists rely on the printed PI that accompanies all prescription drug products for critical clinical information on dosage and administration, drug-drug interactions, contraindications, warnings, side effects, and route of elimination challenges for patients with impaired renal or kidney function.
  - A 2013 GAO report found that:
    - “Relying on electronic labeling as a complete substitute for paper labeling could adversely impact public health by limiting the availability of drug labeling for some physicians, pharmacists, and patients by requiring them to access drug labeling through a medium with which they might be uncomfortable, that they might find inconvenient, or that might be unavailable.”
    - Pharmacists said they “are familiar with using paper labeling” and they find it “easier, when counseling patients, to take the paper version of the labeling directly from the packaging and show it to the patient at the counter rather than searching for the labeling on a computer and then showing the patient the computer monitor or printing the labeling.”
    - A study from The Annals of Pharmacotherapy, noted by GAO, found that if “pharmacists’ workflow is disrupted because they need to print drug labeling for patients, it could reduce the time available for patient consultations.”
    - GAO referenced an Institute of Medicine report that showed “interruptions to pharmacists’ workflow have been shown to increase the risk of errors made when dispensing a drug.”

- Unduly Burdensome
  - The cost burden to pharmacists would further accelerate pharmacy closings, especially in rural areas.
  - According to a study by GoodRx, more than 40% of U.S. counties are currently pharmacy deserts.
  - When the Proposed Rule was published in 2014, the FDA projected an annualized cost burden to pharmacies of $47 million to $89 million.
  - That cost in 2025 dollars would be devastating to community pharmacies.
  - The Proposed Rule has lingered on the Unified Agenda for over twelve years, negatively impacting access to capital and expansion of production at United States based producers of printed PI that support the pharmaceutical industry and American health care system.

- Unlawful
  - FDA lacks the authority to promulgate a rule that permits such a complete replacement of required paper labeling in favor of electronic information.
  - The FDA’s enabling statute, the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA), requires that such required labeling be printed information that physically accompanies the drug product from the manufacturer.
  - FDA promulgated the current Physician Labeling Rule in 2006 (71 Fed Reg at 3963; January 24, 2006).
  - Such labeling is a compilation of the core information about the product as approved by the FDA based on the agency’s analysis of the new drug application or biologic license application.
  - It contains the critical information necessary for safe and effective use.
  - It is written for the healthcare practitioner because prescription drugs, under 21 USC 353(b), require professional supervision of a practitioner licensed by law to prescribe and administer the drug.
  - Therefore, the PI is “required labeling” for virtually all prescription drug and biologic products.
  - Under 21 USC §§321(k) and (m), the prescription drug label must be “written, printed, or graphic matter” and it should also be “upon the immediate container of any article.”
  - The term “labeling” means all labels and other written, printed, or graphic matter upon any article or any of its containers or wrappers, or accompanying such article.
  - The FDCA states that a drug or a device product is misbranded unless its labeling bears adequate directions for use and adequate warnings.
  - Moreover, the provision exempting material judged to be “labeling” for prescription drugs from the misbranding provision applicable to “all advertisements and other descriptive printed matter” specifically identifies labeling as printed matter, i.e., “This paragraph shall not be applicable to any printed matter which the Secretary determines to be labeling as defined in section 201(m) of this Act.” (21 USC 352(n))

- U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Action Requested
  - The Proposed Rule has not been finalized but remains a threat to public health.
  - Please formally withdraw FDA-2007-N-0363, Electronic Distribution of Prescribing Information for Human Prescription Drugs Including Biological Products.

structuredSections.corePosition: We believe the FDA's Proposed Rule FDA-2007-N-0363, which would eliminate printed prescribing information (PI) in favor of a digital-only repository, is unsound regulation that is unnecessary, unduly burdensome on community pharmacies, poses significant risks to patient safety, and is arguably unlawful under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. We urge the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services to formally withdraw this Proposed Rule.

structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Patient Safety Risks:**
  - Reliance on digital-only PI would limit availability for some healthcare professionals and patients who may be uncomfortable with, find inconvenient, or lack access to electronic media.
  - Disruptions to pharmacists' workflow from needing to search or print digital PI could reduce time for patient consultations.
  - Workflow interruptions are shown to increase the risk of dispensing errors.
  - Shifting responsibility for providing patient safety information from manufacturers to less reliable/accessible digital sources is unsafe.
  - During COVID, the suspension of printed PI for new drugs/indications limited transparency of key clinical data and risks.
- **Undue Burden on Community Pharmacies:**
  - The proposed rule's projected annualized cost burden ($47-$89 million in 2014, significantly higher in 2025) would be devastating to community pharmacies.
  - This cost would accelerate pharmacy closings, exacerbating the problem of "pharmacy deserts" (over 40% of US counties are pharmacy deserts).
  - Community pharmacies regularly experience internet outages due to natural disasters or technical problems, making digital access unreliable.
  - HIPAA compliance restricts general internet searches for electronic PI in pharmacy databases.
- **Unlawful Under Current Statute:**
  - FDA lacks authority to fully replace required paper labeling with electronic information because the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) mandates that required labeling be printed and physically accompany the drug product.
  - FDCA defines "label" as "written, printed, or graphic matter" upon the immediate container, and "labeling" includes all "written, printed, or graphic matter" accompanying the article.
  - The FDCA specifically identifies "labeling" for prescription drugs as "printed matter."
- **Negative Impact on US-Based Producers:**
  - The Proposed Rule's prolonged unfinalized status (over twelve years) negatively impacts access to capital and expansion of production for US-based producers of printed PI.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- Pharmacists utilize printed PI as a reference for critical clinical information more than 75 million times per year, with 82% of community pharmacists referring to it monthly.
- A significant majority (96%) of all comments and 93% of health professional comments previously submitted to the FDA opposed the elimination of printed PI.

- The rule's projected cost burden on pharmacies (tens of millions annually) is presented in the context of over 40% of US counties already being "pharmacy deserts."
- Pharmacists find it easier and more efficient to use paper labeling directly from packaging when counseling patients compared to searching and printing from a computer.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:

- "Studies show that 82% of community pharmacies have experienced a loss of internet connection due to natural disasters or technical problems."
- "The cost burden to pharmacists would further accelerate pharmacy closings, especially in rural areas. According to a study by GoodRx, more than 40% of U.S. counties are currently pharmacy deserts."
