-   "Re-regulation offers a chance to repair harm, reimagine care, and ground federal standards in justice, wellness, and sustainability."
-   "We urge this administration to reimagine efficiency—not as reduction, but as reinvestment in care, equity, and community sustainability."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   America's Blood Centers (ABC) is the national organization representing community-based, independent blood centers.
    *   Our member organizations operate more than 700 blood collection sites in over 1,100 communities.
    *   We provide close to 60 percent of the U.S., and a quarter of the Canadian, blood supply.
    *   These blood centers serve over 150 million people and provide blood products and services to more than 3,500 hospitals and healthcare facilities across North America.
    *   All ABC U.S. members are licensed and regulated by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA).
*   HHS is seeking information on ways to deregulate the federal government, including identifying regulations and guidance that impose undue burdens and significant costs on private parties not outweighed by public benefits.
*   ABC appreciates the opportunity to provide comments and recommendations regarding unnecessary regulation that pose undue burdens on both FDA and blood centers.
*   Unnecessary regulation has at times decreased the availability of blood products while increasing costs without any commensurate increase in safety.
*   Unnecessary and outdated regulations add operational complexity, limit innovation, or otherwise fail to enhance the safety and adequacy of the blood supply.
*   Additionally, unnecessary regulation poses a significant burden on the FDA, ultimately generating unnecessary work for the agency.
*   We encourage HHS to evaluate current and future regulations and have provided recommendations on regulations and guidance that should be modified or repealed.

*   Priority I: ABC Recommends Reducing Undue Burdens Imposed on Both FDA and Blood Centers by Amending FDA Guidance for Industry Regarding Licensing Requirements for Blood Centers
    *   Background
        *   Every two seconds, someone in America requires a blood transfusion, and each day, over 42,000 units of red blood cells, platelets, and plasma are used by patients.
        *   Blood centers frequently open additional sites to meet demand and ensure a safe and available blood supply.
        *   However, government regulations impose unnecessary and burdensome barriers to a safe and available blood supply when blood centers adapt.
        *   Outdated regulations currently govern the collection of automated (apheresis) blood products at new donation sites.
        *   FDA regulations (21 CFR 601.12) require licensed establishments to report changes to their approved biologics license applications (BLA).
        *   FDA’s Guidance for Industry and FDA Review Staff: Collection of Platelets by Automated Methods and FDA’s Guidance for Industry: Recommendations for Collecting Red Blood Cells by Automated Apheresis Methods state that implementing automated collection is a change with "substantial potential to have an adverse effect" on product quality.
        *   This requires submission of a supplement to the blood center’s BLA and receipt of approval by FDA prior to interstate distribution (21 CFR 601.12(b)).
        *   As a result, each time a new donation site is opened, a blood center must go through an extensive licensure process, which can take more than a year.
        *   This delay occurs despite the new site using the same Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), devices, and standardized staff training as their primary licensed facility.
        *   Additionally, blood centers must provide two months of quality control data as part of this process.
        *   This data is duplicative, unnecessary, and burdensome because medical device manufacturers already perform mandatory validation testing for 510K clearance, and blood centers also conduct full validation of the collection process.
        *   The substantial manufacturing steps (infectious disease/bacterial testing, product modification, final labeling, storage) all occur at the manufacturing site, typically holding the BLA for all products.
        *   This unnecessarily delays blood availability and largely duplicates FDA review.
        *   While these requirements may have been reasonable for new technology, they are no longer necessary given the safety history of automated (apheresis) devices at new fixed and mobile sites.
    *   Recommendation to Reduce Undue Burden and Significant Costs
        *   Minimizing duplicative data and allowing immediate implementation of all apheresis product collections at new fixed sites would ensure a safe and available blood supply and minimize FDA administrative burdens.
    *   Proposed Changes to FDA Guidance for Industry
        *   Amend the FDA Guidance for Industry: Recommendations for Collecting Red Blood Cells by Automated Apheresis Methods:
            *   Section VI. Registration and licensing procedures for the manufacture of red blood cells collected by automated methods (p. 7): Insert language stating that if the primary facility is already approved for the automated apheresis product, implementation at new fixed sites is a minor change requiring only an annual report description (21 CFR 601.12(d)), not prior approval.
        *   Amend the FDA Guidance for Industry: Collection of Platelets by Automated Methods:
            *   Section X. Reporting changes to an approved biologics license application (BLA). A. Prior Approval Supplement (PAS) (p. 23), second bullet: Insert language stating that if the primary facility is already approved for the automated apheresis product, manufacture of Platelets, Pheresis at new fixed sites is a minor change requiring only an annual report description (21 CFR 601.12(d)), not prior approval.

*   Priority II: ABC Recommends Eliminating the Surface Antigen Testing Requirement for Hepatitis B.
    *   Background
        *   FDA should apply evidence-based decision making to its testing requirements to ensure justification by commensurate increases in safety.
        *   Hepatitis B is a liver infection caused by HBV, spread through bodily fluids.
        *   U.S. began testing for HBsAg in 1970; anti-HBc testing was mandated in 1991; HBV NAT (nucleic acid testing) was finalized in October 2012.
        *   Current, more sensitive and specific assays (HBV NAT and anti-HBc) provide superior detection capabilities, rendering HBsAg testing duplicative and unnecessary.
        *   The continued inclusion of the HBsAg test does not further increase safety.
        *   HBV NAT testing can detect infection up to 11 days sooner.
        *   Residual risk of HBV transfusion-transmission has dropped from ~1 in 200,000 units (pre-NAT) to ~1 in 3 million units (current).
        *   Studies (Stramer et al. 2013, Dodd et al. 2018, van de Laar et al. Netherlands) demonstrated no confirmed HBV-infectious units with HBsAg would be missed by HBV-NAT and anti-HBc alone, with a negligible increased risk of less than 1 per 4 million donations.
        *   Estimated cost of HBsAg test is $1.00 to $1.50 per test, representing $15MM to $22.5MM annually.
    *   Recommendation to Reduce Undue Burden and Significant Costs
        *   The HBsAg testing requirement for whole blood and blood components should be removed.
        *   FDA was poised to eliminate this in 2020, but the meeting was postponed and did not address it.
        *   HBsAg testing is outdated, incurs significant costs, and does not increase transfusion safety, as other methods are highly effective.
        *   ABC recommends discontinuing HBsAg testing, retaining NAT and anti-HBc.
    *   Proposed Changes to FDA Guidance for Industry
        *   Reissue the Guidance for Industry: Use of Nucleic Acid Tests on Pooled and Individual Samples from Donors of Whole Blood and Blood Components, Including Source Plasma, to Reduce the Risk of Transmission of Hepatitis B Virus, with the removal of the HBsAg testing requirement.

*   Priority III: ABC Recommends the Alteration of HTLV-I/II Testing to One-Time Testing for Donors of Whole Blood and Blood Components Intended for Transfusion in the U.S.
    *   Background
        *   Human T-lymphotropic virus types I and II (HTLV-I/II) are retroviruses transmitted from mother to child, sexually, through intravenous drug use, and other blood exposure.
        *   HTLV-I/II can be transmitted via transfusion of cellular blood components but not by plasma.
        *   Leukoreduction is highly efficient at preventing transmission from cellular blood components containing residual lymphocytes.
        *   Pathogen reduction technology (PRT) is used for platelet components.
        *   Transmission is markedly reduced or eliminated following refrigerated storage for approximately 10 days.
        *   ABC submitted a joint comment letter to FDA on March 25, 2025, requesting this change, with additional studies and international experience.
    *   Recommendation to Reduce Undue Burden and Significant Costs
        *   The HTLV-I/II antibody testing requirement at each donation should be revised based on:
            *   Declining prevalence of HTLV-I/II infection in U.S. blood donors.
            *   Low incidence observed among U.S. repeat blood donors.
            *   Low likelihood of infection and disease in recipients of HTLV-I/II antibody-reactive Whole Blood and components.
            *   Efficacy of leukoreduction in reducing infectivity.
            *   Use of effective PRT for some platelets.
    *   Proposed Changes to FDA Guidance for Industry
        *   Reissue the FDA Guidance for Industry: Use of Serological Tests to Reduce the Risk of Transfusion-Transmitted Human T-Lymphotropic Virus Types I and II (HTLV-I/II).
        *   Require one-time donor testing for antibodies to HTLV-I/II coupled with effective leukoreduction.

*   Priority IV: ABC Recommends FDA Withdraw the Malaria Draft Guidance and Ensure there are no Requirements for Malaria Testing of Blood Donations at this Time.
    *   Background
        *   FDA published the Draft Guidance for Industry: Recommendations to Reduce the Risk of Transfusion-Transmitted Malaria in January 2025.
        *   ABC submitted a joint comment on March 13, 2025, stating:
            *   Real-world modeling studies (including malaria-endemic locations and semi-immune donor populations) are needed to determine test sensitivity and justify testing burden.
            *   An option to continue the present TTM risk reduction questioning without testing is necessary to ensure any testing burden is justified by commensurate safety increase.
            *   The current deferral policy is extremely effective.
            *   Testing requirements add significant financial costs without a significant increase in safety.
            *   Only one malaria test is currently approved for blood supply screening.
            *   Supply chain challenges could adversely impact blood availability without an alternative test.
            *   Multiple tests should be available prior to creating any new testing requirements.
    *   Recommendation to Reduce Undue Burden and Significant Costs
        *   To prevent undue burden and significant costs, FDA should withdraw the draft guidance.
    *   Proposed Withdrawal of FDA Draft Guidance for Industry
        *   FDA should withdraw the malaria draft guidance and ensure no requirements for malaria testing of blood donations at this time.

*   Priority V: ABC Recommends Lowering the U.S. Platelet Content Requirement (PCR)
    *   Background
        *   To reduce unnecessary regulation, support innovation and availability, and increase platelet availability, FDA should lower the U.S. PCR, the minimum number of platelets per unit.
        *   Platelets are cells that form clots, used for cancer patients, surgery, and trauma victims.
        *   The current minimum PCR of 3 x 10^11 platelets per unit, set in 1972, was not derived from clinical effectiveness studies but from the average total number in a pool of six whole blood donations.
        *   The U.S. minimum PCR is higher than Canada and most European Union (EU) nations (2.0 to 2.5 x 10^11 platelets).
        *   Harmonization with EU minimum PCR will increase platelet units without negatively impacting patient care.
        *   A lower PCR generally does not correlate with a patient needing more platelet transfusions.
        *   Clinical trials in the U.S. (including PLADO) and elsewhere demonstrated acceptable clinical effectiveness of a lower PCR for preventing bleeding in thrombocytopenic hematology-oncology patients.
        *   One apheresis platelet donation, if large enough, can be split into multiple units; reducing the PCR will allow blood facilities to increase the number of platelet units produced.
        *   An analysis of two large blood center databases suggested a 21 to 23 percent increase in platelet units without collection procedure changes.
        *   Donor impact: A lower PCR could reduce collected platelets from some donors, allow shorter collection times, reduce donor adverse events (AE), and increase donor satisfaction and retention.
        *   Patient impact: Contemporary platelet pools (four to six units, 2.2 to 3.0 x 10^11 platelets) show no appreciated impact on clinical efficacy; no differences in transfusion reaction rates.
        *   Reducing the minimum PCR to 2.5 x 10^11 is a conservative approach, increasing availability without compromising patient safety.
    *   Recommendation to Reduce Undue Burden and Significant Costs
        *   FDA should reduce the minimum PCR from 3 x 10^11/unit to 2.5 x 10^11/unit to expand platelet supply availability and align with international standards.
    *   Proposed Changes to FDA Guidance for Industry
        *   Amend the FDA Guidance for Industry: Collection of Platelets by Automated Methods:
            *   Section VI.D. "Actual platelet yield" bullet (p. 10): Change "≥ 3.0 x 10^11" to "2.5 x 10^11".
            *   Table 1 (p. 13), row 2: Replace "≥ 3.0 x 10^11" with "2.5 x 10^11".
            *   Section VII.A.2. "Labeling" bullet (p. 16): Change "> 3.0 x 10^11" to "2.5 x 10^11" and "< 3.0 x 10^11" to "< 2.5 x 10^11".
            *   Section VII.C.2. "Transfusable Platelets, Pheresis components" bullet (p. 20): Change "≥ 3.0 x 10^11" to "2.5 x 10^11".
            *   Section IX. Second bullet (p. 22): Change "< 3.0 x 10^11" to "< 2.5 x 10^11".

*   Priority VI: ABC Recommends Allowing Blood Centers to Convert Plasma from Transfusable to Further Manufacture Without Requiring Expiration
    *   Background
        *   FDA should allow blood centers to convert recovered plasma collected through apheresis from transfusable to further manufacture, without requiring expiration, for more effective blood inventory management and to avoid product wastage.
        *   Both whole blood and apheresis methods employ identical donor screening and produce plasma for patient transfusion.
        *   Plasma derived from whole blood not needed for transfusion may be acquired by fractionators to create essential products (Factor VIII concentrate, immunoglobulin, albumin).
        *   Apheresis plasma is identical to whole blood plasma, yet FDA requires apheresis plasma not transfused to expire (one year from collection) before it can be used for fractionation into protein therapy products; instead, it may only be used for diagnostic products after expiration.
        *   Blood centers are experts in managing inventory, but cannot always perfectly meet demand, leading to some excess.
        *   Donors intend their blood to be used for saving lives or reducing suffering; every component should be used before it expires.
        *   Using all components from one donor is the most cost-effective method.
        *   Plasma fractionators need excess plasma, which should not be wasted if there is a surplus of transfusable plasma.
    *   Recommendation to Reduce Undue Burden and Significant Costs
        *   FDA should allow blood centers to convert plasma collected through apheresis from transfusable to recovered plasma for further manufacturing, without requiring expiration.
    *   Proposed Changes to FDA Requirements
        *   ABC recommends that FDA eliminate the current expiration requirement and allow blood centers to convert apheresis plasma from transfusable to recovered plasma for further manufacturing.

*   Priority VII: ABC Recommends that FDA Allow Blood to be Held for Up to 24 Hours at Room Temperature Prior to Processing into Components
    *   Background
        *   FDA should allow blood to be held at room temperature for up to 24 hours prior to processing into components, aligning with current evidence and international standards.
        *   Currently, FDA requires platelet concentrate separation from whole blood within 4 hours of collection, or up to 8 hours with clearance.
        *   Europe and Canada allow a 24-hour hold without refrigeration.
        *   Studies show no significant issue with overnight hold of whole blood.
        *   The 8-hour hold often does not allow enough time to separate platelets from whole blood, particularly for mobile collection sites.
        *   A 24-hour room temperature hold would provide more time, increasing platelet inventory for patients.
        *   The 8-hour requirement creates staffing issues (night staff processing evening collections); a 24-hour hold would allow daytime staff processing.
    *   Recommendation to Reduce Undue Burden and Significant Costs
        *   FDA should allow blood to be held at room temperature for up to 24 hours prior to processing into components to reduce refrigeration burdens, allow more platelet products, and increase inventory.
    *   Proposed Changes to FDA Regulations
        *   Amend 21 CFR 640.24(b): Change "The platelet concentrate shall be separated within 4 [four] hours" to "The platelet concentrate shall be separated within 24 hours".

*   Priority VIII. ABC Recommends that FDA Allow Source Plasma to be Held for Up to 24 Hours After Collection at Room Temperature Prior to Freezing
    *   Background
        *   Current regulations (21 CFR 640.69(b)) require plasma intended for injectable products to be stored at a temperature not warmer than -20 °C "immediately after filling."
        *   This requirement is burdensome and unnecessary.
        *   The European standard allows source plasma to be frozen within 24 hours of collection.
    *   Recommendation to Reduce Undue Burden and Significant Costs
        *   FDA should allow source plasma to be held at room temperature for up to 24 hours prior to freezing, aligning with international standards.
        *   A 24-hour hold offers more flexibility for blood centers (e.g., batch freezing) and more effective inventory management.
    *   Proposed Changes to FDA Regulations
        *   Amend 21 CFR 640.69(b): Change "Immediately after filling" to "Within 24 hours of filling".

*   Priority IX: ABC Urges FDA to Modify the Criteria for Use of Cold-Stored Platelets (CSP)
    *   Background
        *   FDA Guidance (2023): Alternative Procedures for Cold-Stored Platelets allowed extended use from 3 to 14 days for active bleeding when conventional platelets are unavailable or impractical.
        *   With newly available CHIlled Platelet Study (CHIPS data), the criteria for CSP use should be updated.
    *   Recommendation to Reduce Undue Burden and Significant Costs
        *   Allowing CSP to be used for any purpose, or at the discretion of the transfusing physician, would significantly reduce waste, decrease costs associated with product movement, and ensure platelet availability, especially in rural areas.
    *   Proposal to Modify Criteria for Use of CSP
        *   ABC urges FDA to quickly modify the criteria for CSP use based on data obtained from CHIPS, which has completed data collection and is expected to be published soon.

*   Priority X. ABC Recommends Reducing Undue Burdens Imposed on Blood Centers by Amending FDA Regulations to Allow a Physician’s Designee to Perform Donor Physical Assessments for Blood Pressure and Pulse
    *   Background
        *   FDA regulation 21 CFR 630.10(f)(2) states that if a donor's blood pressure is outside specified limits (90-180 mmHg systolic, 50-100 mmHg diastolic), donation is only permitted when the responsible physician examines and documents that donation would not adversely affect donor health.
        *   Similarly, 21 CFR 630.10(f)(4) requires a responsible physician's determination and documentation for donors with pulse outside 50-100 beats per minute or an irregular pulse.
    *   Recommendation to Reduce Undue Burden and Significant Costs
        *   FDA should allow a qualified physician’s designee to perform donor physical assessments and documentation for blood pressure and pulse deviations.
        *   This would maintain donor health while allowing physicians to perform other essential clinical and medical functions.
        *   It is unnecessary to call a physician for otherwise healthy donors with minor deviations.
        *   Current requirements result in wasted donor and staff time and preventable loss of valuable blood products.
    *   Recommended Changes to FDA Regulations
        *   Amend 21 CFR 630.10(f)(2) and 21 CFR 630.10(f)(4): Insert "or a qualified individual designated by the responsible physician" where physician examination is currently required.

*   Priority XI. ABC Recommends Reducing Undue Burdens Imposed on Both FDA and Blood Centers by Developing a Pre-Approved Variance Process for Operational Changes at Blood Centers
    *   Background
        *   FDA processes for variances are lengthy and burdensome, even for minor modifications, under current alternative procedure regulations (21 CFR 640.120(a)).
    *   Recommendation to Reduce Undue Burden and Significant Costs
        *   A pre-approved variance process would remove unnecessary administrative burdens for both blood centers and FDA.
    *   Recommendation to Develop a Pre-Approved Variance Process
        *   ABC recommends that FDA develop a pre-approved framework for commonly requested variances or alternative procedures to expedite innovation and pilot testing.

*   Priority XII. ABC Recommends that FDA Allow the Determination of Donor Eligibility within 24 Hours Before Collection
    *   Background
        *   FDA regulation 21 CFR 630.10(c) requires donor eligibility determination "on the day of donation."
        *   This allows a donor to fill out a questionnaire at 1:00 a.m. and donate at 11:00 p.m. the same day, but not at 11:00 p.m. for a 6:00 a.m. donation the next day.
        *   There is no reason for this distinction.
        *   Current requirements prevent full utilization of internet computer-assisted self-interview (C-ASI) processes, resulting in product loss and wasted donor and staff time.
    *   Recommendation to Reduce Undue Burden and Significant Costs
        *   FDA should allow the determination of donor eligibility within 24 hours before collection.
    *   Recommended Changes to FDA Regulations
        *   Amend 21 CFR 630.10(c): Change "on the day of donation" to "on the day of donation, and within 24 hours before collection."
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: America's Blood Centers urges the Department of Health and Human Services to deregulate and modernize FDA guidances and regulations concerning blood collection, testing, and processing to reduce undue burdens, lower costs, and enhance the availability and efficiency of the U.S. blood supply without compromising safety.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** America's Blood Centers
- **Type:** Organization
- **Role/Expertise:** National organization representing community-based, independent blood centers; operates over 700 collection sites, provides close to 60% of the U.S. and a quarter of the Canadian blood supply, and serves over 150 million people and 3,500+ hospitals. All U.S. members are licensed and regulated by the FDA.
- **Geographic Scope:** National (U.S.) and International (Canada).
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly involved in the collection, processing, and distribution of blood products; seeks to streamline regulations to ensure a safe, adequate, and cost-effective blood supply for patients while reducing operational burdens and costs for blood centers.
structuredSections.corePosition: We believe unnecessary regulation has at times decreased the availability of blood products while increasing costs without any commensurate increase in safety. These outdated regulations add operational complexity, limit innovation, and burden both blood centers and the FDA. We encourage HHS to evaluate current and future regulations, proposing modifications or repeals to ensure a safe and available blood supply.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Amend FDA guidance to allow the implementation of all types of apheresis product collections at new fixed sites as a minor change, requiring only a description in the blood center’s annual report, provided the primary facility is already approved for that product.
- Eliminate the Hepatitis B Surface Antigen (HBsAg) testing requirement for whole blood and blood components intended for transfusion, retaining HBV NAT and anti-HBc.
- Require one-time donor testing for antibodies to HTLV-I/II coupled with effective leukoreduction in donations of whole blood and blood components intended for transfusion.
- Withdraw the FDA Draft Guidance for Industry: Recommendations to Reduce the Risk of Transfusion-Transmitted Malaria and ensure no current requirements for malaria testing of blood donations.
- Lower the U.S. Platelet Content Requirement (PCR) from 3 x 10^11/unit to 2.5 x 10^11/unit to expand platelet supply availability and align with international standards.
- Allow blood centers to convert plasma collected through apheresis from transfusable to recovered plasma for further manufacturing, without requiring it to first expire.
- Allow whole blood to be held at room temperature for up to 24 hours prior to processing into components, aligning with current evidence and international standards.
- Allow source plasma to be held at room temperature for up to 24 hours after collection prior to freezing, aligning with international standards.
- Modify the criteria for use of Cold-Stored Platelets (CSP) to allow for any use, or at the discretion of the transfusing physician, based on new CHIPS data.
- Amend FDA regulations to allow a qualified physician’s designee to perform donor physical assessments and documentation for blood pressure and pulse when measurements fall outside normal limits.
- Develop a pre-approved framework for commonly requested variances or alternative procedures to expedite innovation and pilot testing for operational changes at blood centers.
- Amend FDA regulations to allow the determination of donor eligibility within 24 hours before collection, rather than strictly "on the day of donation."
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- Current regulations for licensing new apheresis donation sites are extensive (over a year for approval) and duplicative, requiring unnecessary data submissions and delaying blood availability.
- Existing hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) testing is outdated, duplicative of more advanced tests (HBV NAT, anti-HBc), and incurs significant costs ($15MM-$22.5MM annually) without increasing transfusion safety.
- Requirement for HTLV-I/II antibody testing at each donation is an undue burden given declining prevalence, low incidence in repeat donors, and effectiveness of leukoreduction and pathogen reduction technology.
- The proposed malaria testing guidance would impose significant financial costs without a substantial increase in safety, and the lack of multiple approved tests poses supply chain risks.
- The U.S. minimum platelet content requirement (PCR) is higher than international standards, unnecessarily limiting platelet supply and potentially increasing donor collection times.
- FDA rules requiring apheresis plasma to expire before it can be converted for further manufacturing into life-saving protein therapies lead to unnecessary product wastage.
- Restrictive 8-hour hold times for whole blood prior to processing for platelets are impractical, especially for mobile collections, and create staffing issues, unlike international 24-hour standards.
- The "immediately after filling" requirement for freezing source plasma is burdensome and less flexible than international 24-hour standards.
- Current limitations on the use of cold-stored platelets (CSP) restrict their availability for broader patient needs, despite new evidence supporting wider application.
- Regulations requiring a responsible physician to personally assess donors with minor blood pressure or pulse deviations cause wasted donor and staff time and preventable loss of blood products.
- FDA's lengthy and burdensome variance processes for even minor operational changes impede innovation and efficiency at blood centers.
- The "on the day of donation" rule for donor eligibility prevents efficient use of modern pre-screening technologies, leading to product loss and wasted time.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The critical and continuous demand for blood products, with over 42,000 units of red blood cells, platelets, and plasma used daily and someone in America requiring a transfusion every two seconds.
- The paradox of new apheresis donation sites taking over a year to license despite using identical procedures and equipment as already-approved primary facilities, highlighting regulatory inefficiency.
- The insight that an outdated HBsAg test, while once cutting-edge, now costs the industry $15-22.5 million annually without adding safety benefit due to more advanced HBV NAT and anti-HBc testing.
- The U.S. platelet content requirement (PCR) of 3 x 10^11 was established in 1972 based on historical pooling methods, not clinical effectiveness, and is out of step with lower international standards.
- Data suggesting that lowering the PCR could increase platelet unit production by 21-23% from existing donations, offering a significant boost to supply without changing collection procedures.
- The frustration that identical apheresis plasma intended for transfusion must expire before it can be used for life-saving fractionation products, leading to unnecessary waste despite donor intent.
- The practical challenge posed by the 8-hour whole blood hold time, especially for mobile collection sites, leading to staffing issues and missed opportunities to create platelet products, contrasting with safe 24-hour holds in Europe and Canada.
- The seemingly arbitrary nature of donor eligibility rules that allow same-day pre-screening for 22 hours but disallow it for 7 hours into the next day, hindering the use of modern online questionnaires.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "Unnecessary regulation has at times decreased the availability of blood products while increasing costs without any commensurate increase in safety."
- "The continued inclusion of the HBsAg test does not further increase safety over the two remaining HBV tests and should be eliminated."
- "Donors intend their blood to be used to save a life or reduce the pain and suffering of others. Every blood component should be used for this purpose before it expires."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I am commenting on the U.S Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
*   The years of pregnancy to age three set the foundation for a baby’s development, learning and relationships.
    *   Babies rely entirely on the adults around them—parents, caregivers, and early childhood professionals—to provide safe, nurturing care.
    *   When babies or their caregivers face reduced support or program quality, babies can end up facing long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences.
    *   When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health.
*   Regulations matter.
    *   HHS, as the leading Federal agency tasked with enhancing the health and well-being of all Americans, plays a critical role in ensuring that babies, families, and the professionals who care for little ones have access to the resources, protections, and supports they need.
    *   In considering changes to regulations, HHS must preserve regulations that:
        *   Keep young children safe and healthy.
        *   Enable the adults in their lives to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
*   For example, regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings are needed to keep babies safe and developmentally on track.
*   Regulations that keep children and those who care for them healthy, like those that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care, must be maintained.
    *   This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe.
*   HHS rules reach far beyond just Medicaid and early learning, with many HHS programs laying the foundation of quality care and critical support that babies need.
*   Any changes to regulations must be:
    *   Transparent.
    *   Grounded in evidence.
    *   Focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
*   Because each regulation is different, HHS must continue to give the public—including families and early childhood professionals like me—ample time and opportunity to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes.
    *   We need a robust public process to make sure that the rules work for babies and those who care for them.
*   To keep America’s babies healthy, HHS must maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services.
*   Please uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
*   I would also like to add that I am a product of Head Start Services.
    *   I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career.
    *   I have a Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma.
    *   I have been a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for the past twenty-three years servicing the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles.
    *   It gives great pleasure to give back to my community.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An experienced early childhood education professional and Head Start alumna urges HHS to maintain and strengthen regulations that ensure the safety, health, and development of young children, advocating for transparent, evidence-based changes and robust public input.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
-   **Name/Organization:** Elizabeth Villanueva
-   **Type:** Individual
-   **Role/Expertise:** Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma; 23 years as a vendor for the state of California Early Start system; former Head Start recipient.
-   **Geographic Scope:** Local (South Central Los Angeles, San Pedro, CA) / State (California)
-   **Stake in Issue:** As an early childhood professional directly involved in providing services to vulnerable children and a beneficiary of early childhood programs, she has a direct interest in regulations that ensure quality care and support for young children and their caregivers.
structuredSections.corePosition: I strongly believe that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) must preserve and uphold regulations that safeguard the health, safety, and development of young children from pregnancy to age three. These foundational years dictate lifelong well-being, and effective regulations, grounded in evidence and developed transparently with public input, are crucial for ensuring access to quality care and services.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   Preserve regulations that keep young children safe and healthy.
-   Preserve regulations that enable adults to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
    -   Specifically, maintain regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings.
    -   Maintain regulations that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care.
-   Ensure any changes to regulations are transparent, grounded in evidence, and focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
-   Provide ample time and opportunity for the public, including families and early childhood professionals, to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes through a robust public process.
-   Maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services for babies.
-   Uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   Reduced support or program quality for babies and caregivers could lead to long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences for children.
-   Regulatory changes that are not transparent, evidence-based, or child-focused could negatively impact the well-being and safety of children, families, and their service providers.
-   Inadequate public involvement in the regulatory process may result in rules that do not effectively serve the needs of babies and their caregivers.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
-   Personal testimony as a "product of Head Start Services," attributing her education and career advantages to the program.
-   Extensive professional experience as a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for 23 years, specifically servicing "the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles."
-   Expresses deep personal satisfaction and commitment to her work, stating "It gives great pleasure to give back to my community."
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
-   "When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health."
-   "This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe."
-   "I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Zocdoc appreciates the opportunity to comment on regulations that raise the highest barriers to competition and the Administration’s focus on unleashing American innovation.
    *   As a healthcare technology organization, we’ve spent nearly the last two decades bringing market forces to healthcare to address rising costs, diminishing quality, and to increase access across the United States.
    *   We’ve built the nation’s leading patient-centered marketplace that allows users to search, compare, and instantly schedule the care they need with the providers of their choice.
    *   In doing so, we empower patients, bring efficiency to providers, and save time, money, and resources for the healthcare system in aggregate.
    *   Our goal is to build the connective tissue of healthcare, by stitching together the patchwork of incumbent players so that they can work together for the betterment of all Americans.
    *   This requires the ability to be nimble, which is often inhibited by unnecessary regulation and bureaucracy.
    *   Our hope is that this deregulatory initiative can help remediate these issues and empower the digital health industry to innovate at the pace needed to truly serve patients.
*   About Zocdoc
    *   Zocdoc was founded in 2007 with a mission to give power to the patient.
    *   We offer an online marketplace that enables millions of Americans each month to independently find in-network doctors, see their real-time availability, and instantly book appointments online for in-person or telehealth visits.
    *   By building a true marketplace, we are bringing choice, competition and transparency to the largest and most important consumer service in our country: healthcare.
    *   We make it easy for users to find and book in-network care.
    *   Users can intuitively research options based on what is most important to them (insurance, reviews, location, availability, etc.), independently select the provider who best suits their needs, and instantly book online.
    *   Zocdoc hopes to continue to leverage technology to empower patients seeking care across the country.
    *   However, regulatory ambiguity prevents Zocdoc from utilizing technology to rapidly innovate and expedite access to care.
        *   For example, the Anti-Kickback Statute (AKS) was written in 1972—decades before today’s prevailing digital technology.
        *   It governs improper payments for referrals and offers an important set of measures to prevent fraud and abuse.
        *   The AKS serves an important purpose, yet, when applied too broadly, it hampers innovation and, in doing so, can obstruct or delay care.
    *   Healthcare providers typically provide compensation to market their practices via online platforms like Zocdoc, which can implicate the AKS when those practices serve federal health beneficiaries.
    *   Under current law, there is no distinction between illicit referral practices that incentivize fraud and waste and marketing and scheduling services that add efficiencies to the market by simplifying access to necessary and appropriate care.
    *   We were grateful to receive a favorable Advisory Opinion in 2019 from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Office of the Inspector General (OIG), which allowed us to grow exponentially and unlock care in important and underserved areas across the US—importantly, outside the major metropolitan areas.
    *   We have since provided up-to-date information on our business practices in order to receive an additional favorable Advisory Opinion in 2023, certifying that Zocdoc continues to not run afoul of the outdated statute.
    *   While we recognize the importance of preserving the AKS, the Advisory Opinion process is lengthy, and delays Zocdoc’s ability to implement consumer friendly changes to our platform.
    *   Additionally, while we appreciate the engagement and feedback we’ve received thus far, we fundamentally believe this process is not the best use of the OIG’s time and resources.
    *   The OIG should not have to serve as a product manager to innovative health-tech organizations.
    *   Rather, the OIG should focus their efforts on their chief mission, to route out fraud, waste, and abuse in the system.
*   Health Information Services Safe Harbor
    *   The AKS is extremely broad in its applicability.
    *   As a result, it has been necessary over the half-century since its enactment to add dozens of safe harbors and for the HHS-OIG to issue hundreds of Advisory Opinions, which clarify that typical business practices that encourage efficiency and do not present risk of fraud and abuse are permissible under Federal law.
    *   Health information service providers (including online appointment booking platforms) perform one such business practice that leverages technology to provide a crucial link between patients and providers and ensure seamless access to healthcare.
    *   A health information services safe harbor would provide clear guidelines to modernize this decades-old regulation and remove the ambiguity that exists for American healthcare innovators.
    *   This would allow patients and providers to use digital tools to make healthcare more accessible and efficient, and in doing so help hospitals, health systems, community clinics, and independent practitioners improve access to care.
    *   The Health ACCESS Alliance represents a growing list of 30+ organizations, which include hospitals, health systems, FQHCs, health tech innovators, patient advocacy orgs, trade associations and more.
    *   Zocdoc has joined the Health ACCESS Alliance to advocate for common sense modernization through their support for the Health ACCESS (Accelerating Consumer’s Care by Expediting Self-Scheduling) Act, which is a bipartisan, bicameral bill that would create such a safe harbor.
    *   This would allow health information services to help Americans, including federally funded beneficiaries, find care more easily, without unnecessary legal uncertainty.
    *   The HHS-OIG should add a safe harbor to the AKS that states the applicable legal framework for hospitals, health systems and other provider organizations to partner with online health information services, which surface capacity within a constrained healthcare workforce through a scheduling platform.
    *   Roughly 20% to 30% of a provider’s time goes to waste due to last-minute reschedules or cancellations.
    *   By leveraging scheduling technology to surface providers’ real-time appointment availability, patients can book a near-term, in-network doctor visit in an ambulatory setting rather than go to the ER, which will save billions for American taxpayers.
    *   This also allows care organizations to optimize the use of their most valuable asset: providers’ time.
    *   Long healthcare provider wait times exacerbate morbidity and mortality for patients with preventable or treatable conditions.
    *   Long wait times also force patients into unnecessary emergency room visits, which are on average 12 times more costly than treatment in an office setting.
    *   The following safe harbor addition is recommended:
        *   Through the statutory authority found in Section 1128B(b) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. § 1320a-7b(b)), we recommend achieving the desired deregulatory relief by adding the following new subparagraph:
            *   “(M) any remuneration paid by a provider of services (as defined in section 1861(u)) or a supplier (as defined in section 1861(d)) to an information service provider (as defined in paragraph (5)), if—
                *   (i) such information service provider does not—
                    *   (I) steer or lead a consumer to select a particular provider of services or supplier based on the amount a provider of services or supplier pays or may pay the information service provider;
                    *   (II) provide, or represent itself as providing, any medical items or services, diagnostic or counseling services or assessments of illness or injury, or make any promises of cure or guarantees of treatment;
                    *   (III) provide contact information regarding a consumer (as defined in paragraph (5)) to providers of services or suppliers, except to the specific provider of services or supplier selected by the consumer;
                    *   (IV) provide or arrange for transportation of an individual to, or from, the location of a supplier; care program beneficiary other than the inherent convenience of the information service or as permitted pursuant to the nominal value guidance; or
                    *   (VI) engage in targeted marketing of a particular provider or supplier through phone calls or text messages, with respect to consumers or potential consumers who have not previously interacted with the information service provider or who have opted out;
                *   (ii) the methodology for determining compensation paid to the information service provider by a provider of services or supplier is set in advance in writing, and the compensation: (I) does not exceed fair market value; (II) is for services, specified in writing; and (III) does not take into account the value of any items or services payable in whole or in part by a Federal health care program that result from recommendations by the information service provider for the provider of services or supplier;
                *   (iii) such information service provider clearly discloses the financial arrangement between it and the providers of services or suppliers participating in such service to consumers;
                *   (iv) such information service provider furnishes provider- and supplier-specific information to consumers based only on objective, consumer-centric criteria;
                *   (v) such information service provider develops objective criteria for participation in such information service and does not exclude any providers of services or suppliers who meet such criteria from participating therein; and
                *   (vi) such information service provider meets such other conditions as may be determined appropriate by the Secretary.'';
        *   and adding:
            *   “(5) Definition of Consumer; Information Service Provider.—For purposes of paragraph (3)(M):
                *   (A) Consumer.--The term `consumer' means an individual who uses a web-based platform operated by an information service provider for the purpose of searching providers of services or suppliers.
                *   (B) Information service provider.--The term `information service provider' means any individual or entity operating a web-based platform that makes information regarding providers of services or suppliers available to consumers.''.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I am commenting on the U.S Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
*   The years of pregnancy to age three set the foundation for a baby’s development, learning and relationships.
    *   Babies rely entirely on the adults around them—parents, caregivers, and early childhood professionals—to provide safe, nurturing care.
    *   When babies or their caregivers face reduced support or program quality, babies can end up facing long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences.
    *   When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health.
*   Regulations matter.
    *   HHS, as the leading Federal agency tasked with enhancing the health and well-being of all Americans, plays a critical role in ensuring that babies, families, and the professionals who care for little ones have access to the resources, protections, and supports they need.
    *   In considering changes to regulations, HHS must preserve regulations that:
        *   Keep young children safe and healthy.
        *   Enable the adults in their lives to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
*   For example, regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings are needed to keep babies safe and developmentally on track.
*   Regulations that keep children and those who care for them healthy, like those that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care, must be maintained.
    *   This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe.
*   HHS rules reach far beyond just Medicaid and early learning, with many HHS programs laying the foundation of quality care and critical support that babies need.
*   Any changes to regulations must be:
    *   Transparent.
    *   Grounded in evidence.
    *   Focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
*   Because each regulation is different, HHS must continue to give the public—including families and early childhood professionals like me—ample time and opportunity to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes.
    *   We need a robust public process to make sure that the rules work for babies and those who care for them.
*   To keep America’s babies healthy, HHS must maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services.
*   Please uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
*   I would also like to add that I am a product of Head Start Services.
    *   I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career.
    *   I have a Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma.
    *   I have been a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for the past twenty-three years servicing the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles.
    *   It gives great pleasure to give back to my community.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An experienced early childhood education professional and Head Start alumna urges HHS to maintain and strengthen regulations that ensure the safety, health, and development of young children, advocating for transparent, evidence-based changes and robust public input.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
-   **Name/Organization:** Elizabeth Villanueva
-   **Type:** Individual
-   **Role/Expertise:** Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma; 23 years as a vendor for the state of California Early Start system; former Head Start recipient.
-   **Geographic Scope:** Local (South Central Los Angeles, San Pedro, CA) / State (California)
-   **Stake in Issue:** As an early childhood professional directly involved in providing services to vulnerable children and a beneficiary of early childhood programs, she has a direct interest in regulations that ensure quality care and support for young children and their caregivers.
structuredSections.corePosition: I strongly believe that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) must preserve and uphold regulations that safeguard the health, safety, and development of young children from pregnancy to age three. These foundational years dictate lifelong well-being, and effective regulations, grounded in evidence and developed transparently with public input, are crucial for ensuring access to quality care and services.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   Preserve regulations that keep young children safe and healthy.
-   Preserve regulations that enable adults to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
    -   Specifically, maintain regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings.
    -   Maintain regulations that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care.
-   Ensure any changes to regulations are transparent, grounded in evidence, and focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
-   Provide ample time and opportunity for the public, including families and early childhood professionals, to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes through a robust public process.
-   Maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services for babies.
-   Uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   Reduced support or program quality for babies and caregivers could lead to long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences for children.
-   Regulatory changes that are not transparent, evidence-based, or child-focused could negatively impact the well-being and safety of children, families, and their service providers.
-   Inadequate public involvement in the regulatory process may result in rules that do not effectively serve the needs of babies and their caregivers.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
-   Personal testimony as a "product of Head Start Services," attributing her education and career advantages to the program.
-   Extensive professional experience as a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for 23 years, specifically servicing "the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles."
-   Expresses deep personal satisfaction and commitment to her work, stating "It gives great pleasure to give back to my community."
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
-   "When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health."
-   "This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe."
-   "I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The American Medical Association (AMA) thanks the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for the opportunity to provide comments on the Request for Information (RFI) titled “Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation to Make American Healthy Again.”
*   We welcome the opportunity to work alongside the Agency to identify rules that can be streamlined or rescinded and to propose practical, data-driven strategies that maximize administrative efficiency while protecting patient safety and program integrity.
*   The comments respond to each question in the notice and offer concrete recommendations for achieving these shared goals.
    *   **1. What HHS regulations and/or guidance meet one or more of the following seven criteria identified in E.O. 14219? Should they be modified or repealed? What would be the impact of this change, especially the costs and savings?**
        *   The Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS)
            *   Since its implementation in 2017, MIPS has failed to demonstrate improvements in health outcomes or reductions in avoidable spending.
            *   It continues to impose significant compliance costs on physician practices.
                *   In 2021, a JAMA Health Forum study found physician practices spent $12,800 and 202 hours per year to comply with MIPS.
                *   CMS estimated the total burden for calendar year 2025 reporting requirements to be 586,877 hours and $70,166,672.
            *   The program disproportionately harms small and rural practices, which are small businesses, by cutting their Medicare reimbursement up to -9 percent.
                *   This is despite being “approximately as effective as chance in terms of identifying high versus low quality performance,” according to a JAMA study.
            *   The regulations governing MIPS are not based on the best reading of the underlying statutory authority as established by the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act (MACRA) of 2015.
                *   MACRA streamlined three historic precedents to MIPS into one to reduce burden.
                *   MACRA required the Agency to share timely data, including claims data, with physicians.
                *   MACRA encouraged reporting via qualified clinical data registries (QCDRs).
                *   Despite these statutory requirements, the Agency left in place many legacy elements of the three predecessors, limited the effectiveness of QCDRs, and failed to share timely data with physicians.
            *   The AMA provides detailed recommendations and accompanying statutory authority to make urgently needed improvements to reform MIPS regulatory deficits and reduce burden, allowing physicians more time for patient care.
                *   Award multi-category credit and ensure that MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs) are clinically relevant so patients can compare quality and cost across physician practices.
                    *   Provide multi-category credit for aligned measures across MIPS categories.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: MACRA recognizes conceptual overlap between categories. CMS has previously used this overlap (e.g., bonus points for end-to-end electronic reporting). MACRA does not prohibit multi-category credit; CMS has broad discretion in methodology.
                    *   Develop clinically relevant MVPs based on patient condition, episode of care, and clinical priority areas, not by specialty.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: Statute is silent regarding measure focus/weights. Section 1848(q)(2) provides broad authority. Section 1848(q)(10) requires consultation with stakeholders.
                    *   To incentivize participation in MVPs, reduce the burden of MVPs.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: Statute is silent regarding measure focus/weights. Section 1848(q)(2) provides broad authority. Section 1848(q)(3) provides broad authority for performance standards.
                    *   Remove or tailor population health quality measures, which CMS has added as a foundational MVP requirement and new category.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: Statute is silent regarding measure focus/weights. Section 1848(q)(2) provides broad authority. Section 1848(q)(3) provides broad authority for performance standards.
                    *   MVPs should remain voluntary.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: MACRA expressly provided a phase-in of MIPS requirements with gradual increase of downside financial risk. Requiring a substantial shift in requirements when financial risk is -9% conflicts with this phased approach. Statute encourages group participation via TINs, not subgroups. Section 1848(q)(1)(D) requires CMS to establish group assessment processes.
                *   Reduce unnecessary quality measure reporting burden and eliminate arbitrary scoring rules that drive up the cost of compliance with MIPS.
                    *   Lower the quality data completeness requirement to 60 percent of eligible patients.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: Section 1848(q)(3) provides broad authority to modify performance standards.
                    *   Eliminate the scoring cap on all topped-out measures and measures without a benchmark.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: 1848(q)(2)(D)(i)(II)(aa) directs the Secretary to establish an annual final list of quality measures, but does not specify a timeline for removal or mandate treatment of identified measures for scoring/reporting. Secretary has discretion. Section 1848(q)(3)(B) directs consideration of historical performance, improvement, and opportunity for improvement, but does not define terms, allowing for consideration of other factors.
                    *   Explore a new methodology for scoring measures.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: Section 1848(q)(3) provides broad authority to establish performance standards. The 10-decile benchmark methodology was created by regulation and can be modified.
                *   Fix the long-standing inaccuracies with the MIPS cost measures and nullify their negative impact on Medicare physician practice payment and patient access to care until these issues can be properly addressed.
                    *   Remove the Total Per Capita Cost (TPCC) and Medicare Spending Per Beneficiary (MSPB) Clinician measures.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: CMS can propose removal. Unlike 2020, there are now 33 episode-based MIPS cost measures, many addressing primary care, accounting for 33.4% of Medicare Parts A and B spending.
                    *   Resolve the problems with the cost measures (e.g., specialists hurt, misattribution).
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: Section 1848(r) and 1848(q)(10) require stakeholder consultation and incorporation of expert comments. 42 CFR 414.1380(b)(2)(v)(A) allows exclusion if data leads to misleading/inaccurate results.
                    *   Reweight the Cost Performance Category to zero percent of MIPS final scores to nullify the negative impact of the problematic measures.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: Section 1848(q)(5)(F) directs reweighting if "not sufficient measures... applicable and available." 42 CFR 414.1380(c)(2)(i)(A)(2) clarifies "not sufficient measures" includes when CMS cannot reliably calculate a score that adequately reflects performance.
                *   Share timely, critical MIPS performance data and Medicare claims data with physician practices to facilitate better quality and lower costs.
                    *   Make Medicare claims data and meaningful MIPS attribution, measure, and performance data available on a rolling or, at a minimum, quarterly basis during the performance period.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: MACRA requires timely (e.g., quarterly) confidential feedback (Section 1848(q)(12)(A)(i)). MACRA allows use of prior/rolling data for illustrative calculations (Section 1848(q)(12)(A)(iii)). MACRA requires sharing information on services furnished by other suppliers/providers (Section 1848(q)(12)(B)(i) and (ii)).
                    *   Correct inconsistencies in the MIPS public use data files as soon as possible, particularly regarding missing national provider identifiers (NPIs).
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: Section 1848(q)(9)(D) requires periodic posting of aggregate MIPS information. While not requiring specialty info, ensuring data accuracy is essential for public information and research.
                    *   Clarify the number of unique clinicians participating in MIPS in future Quality Payment Program (QPP) Experience Reports and include a breakdown of different scores unique clinicians receive through multiple groups or Alternative Payment Models (APMs).
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: Section 1848(q)(9)(D) supports posting aggregate information.
                    *   Expand QPP Experience Reports to include detailed data from both QPP and claims data sources to inform opportunities to improve quality, reduce costs, and develop MVPs and APMs.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: Section 1848(q)(9)(D) supports posting aggregate information.
                *   Maximize usage of electronic health records (EHRs) and other emerging technologies while minimizing wasteful “check the box” reporting exercises.
                    *   All Promoting Interoperability (PI) measure reporting should be done through “yes/no” attestations.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: HITECH Act specifies attestation as a way to satisfy meaningful EHR use (Section 1848(o)(2)(C)) and permits "other means specified by the Secretary."
                    *   Reverse mandatory reporting of PI data for all Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) participants (regardless of Qualified APM Participant (QP) status), which started in 2025.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: MACRA states MIPS-eligible professional does not include QPs (Section 1848(q)(1)(C)(ii)). Previous CMS guidance states QPs are excluded from MIPS reporting. MACRA only says "certified EHR technology is used" for QPs (Section 1833(z)(2)(B) and (C)), implying attestation is sufficient.
                    *   Restore 75% CEHRT utilization threshold for Advanced APM participants.
                        *   Reasoning/CMS Authority: MACRA only says "certified EHR technology is used" for QPs (Section 1833(z)(2)(B) and (C)). This broad definition was intentional to minimize burden and incentivize APM participation.
        *   Physician-Owned Hospitals (POHs)
            *   The AMA urges the Agency to reinstate flexibilities from the 2021 Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment (OPPS) final rule and rescind regulatory barriers from the Biden Administration that impede expansion of POHs serving more Medicaid patients.
            *   These regulations conflict with the best reading of the statute and impede competition and innovation.
            *   POHs provide high quality care and needed competition, stimulating innovation and improving care, lowering costs, and expanding access.
            *   The Biden Administration revoked flexibilities and further limited the exception process for existing POHs to expand.
                *   Regulations set discretionary factors for application review.
                *   Rules reinstated limitations on high Medicaid facilities (200% increase limitation, main-campus limitation) equivalent to those for applicable hospitals.
                *   Included high Medicaid facilities in community input and a two-year limitation on new applications.
                *   This is inconsistent with plain language of the statute and Congressional recognition of two POH types (applicable and high Medicaid facilities).
                *   Including high Medicaid facilities in community input and moratorium creates barriers disproportionately affecting hospitals serving vulnerable populations.
        *   Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System Code G2211
            *   The AMA urges the Agency to revisit and revise its utilization assumption for code G2211 (Office/Outpatient Evaluation and Management (E/M) Visit Complexity Add-On) based on actual 2024 Medicare claims data.
            *   During 2021 rulemaking, CMS estimated G2211 would be reported with 90 percent of visits, then revised to 38 percent for 2024.
            *   An AMA analysis of the first three quarters of 2024 Medicare claims shows G2211 was reported with only 10.5 percent of office visits, stabilizing around 13 percent, with a projected year-end utilization of 11.4 percent.
            *   The consequences of the misestimate are substantial because G2211 was implemented in a budget-neutral manner, triggering a disproportionately large downward adjustment to the Medicare conversion factor.
            *   Actual allowed charges for G2211 totaled approximately $395 million, far below CMS’ projected $1.3 billion, a nearly $1 billion discrepancy leading to an avoidable across-the-board cut in physician payment.
            *   In the forthcoming Calendar Year 2026 Medicare Physician Fee Schedule proposed rule, the Agency should prospectively correct the G2211 utilization assumption and apply an upward adjustment to the 2026 conversion factor to restore balance.
        *   Info Blocking – Rescind the Biden Administration’s Information-Blocking Provider Disincentive Rule
            *   The AMA urges the Agency to rescind its July 2024 final rule establishing payment disincentives for alleged information blocking by physicians.
            *   This rule is a duplicative, counter-productive mandate that should be revoked.
            *   Creates Redundant and Conflicting Enforcement Layers
                *   Overlaps existing Federal authority: The 21st Century Cures Act already assigns OIG and ASTP/ONC power to investigate, and OCR to sanction, information blocking. CMS’ new payment cuts punish the same conduct a second time, often through multiple programs (MIPS, PI, MSSP, IPPS, CAH).
                *   Constitutes impermissible double jeopardy, paralyzing providers with concerns about being penalized regardless of action.
                *   Adds no value beyond HIPAA and state access laws: Patients have enforceable rights under OCR-HIPAA and state statutes; extra Medicare penalties provide no incremental consumer protection.
                *   Complicates private-payer compliance: Physicians must meet diverse insurer interoperability rules; CMS disincentives multiply national policy.
            *   Fails the Statutory Test of “Appropriate” Disincentives
                *   No education–first pathway: Unlike other HHS compliance regimes, it moves directly to financial punishment, even though rules are new, complex, and poorly understood.
                *   Penalties divorced from conduct severity: Dollar impact depends on provider type and Medicare revenue, not intent, frequency, or harm, producing arbitrary outcomes.
                *   Insufficient due process: Payment reductions begin before clinicians can contest OIG findings; appeal rights differ by program, leaving many without a meaningful pre-penalty hearing.
            *   Practical Harm to Beneficiaries, Value-Based and Chronic Health Care
                *   Threatens access: Indiscriminate financial penalties compound inadequate physician payments, imperiling small, solo, and rural practices, and undermining capacity to tackle chronic disease.
                *   Chills participation in quality and alternative payment models: A single disputed record request can erase an ACO’s shared savings, zero-out PI points, and crater a group’s MIPS score.
                *   Penalizes the innocent: Group-level sanctions mean one physician’s lapse can slash revenue for every clinician under the same tax ID, undermining encouraged team-based reporting.
            *   AMA Recommendation: Education, Correction, Proportionality
                *   Rescind CMS’ disincentive rule and rely on existing OIG/ONC investigative and OCR corrective-action tools.
                *   Launch a unified HHS “Interoperability Assistance Hub” to provide authoritative guidance, technical help, and standardized interpretation.
                *   Adopt a notice-and-cure framework: Deliver written findings, allow at least 45 days for remediation, impose penalties only if egregious conduct persists.
                *   Calibrate any future sanctions to proven misconduct, tying the amount to intent, scope, and patient impact, not gross Medicare reimbursement.
                *   Guarantee uniform, timely appeal rights, suspending penalties until final adjudication.
        *   Stark Law Restrictions for Rural Physician Practices
            *   The AMA recommends a “rural exemption” to Stark Law’s Site-of-Service requirements and the In-Office Ancillary Services Exception.
            *   Current restrictions have forced many specialists to discontinue satellite office operations in rural communities, where access to specialty care is already limited.
            *   Previously, physicians had satellite offices leasing space for a few days/half-days a month, often using referring physician’s equipment, which did not meet the 8-hours/week statutory requirement and were found to violate Stark Law.
            *   This forces patients to drive long distances to see specialists.
            *   Restoring flexibility would improve access in underserved areas and remove unnecessary administrative barriers.
        *   Independent Dispute Resolution Process Under the No Surprises Act
            *   The AMA urges the Administration to finalize updates to existing regulations to streamline the Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process that was proposed but never implemented.
            *   Specifically, require Claim Adjustment Reason Codes and Remittance Advice Remark Codes on initial payments or notices of denial.
            *   Revisit unnecessarily restrictive batching and bundling requirements.
            *   Limit the 90-day cooling off period for batched claims.
            *   The AMA looks forward to continued engagement to streamline No Surprises Act claims processing to reduce backlog and burden while protecting patients, fairly settling disputes, and encouraging fair contracting.
            *   The AMA also urges stronger enforcement of existing rules, citing reports of repeated payer noncompliance (disregarding timeframes, "ghost claims") with minimal ramifications.
        *   No Statutory Authority to Mandate Payment Model Participation
            *   Creating APMs such as the Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM) with mandatory participation is not based on the best reading of the Agency’s statutory authority.
            *   Congress did not intend for the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI) to employ mandatory participation in experimental models.
            *   The statute does not expressly require models to be voluntary, but it does not authorize CMMI to mandate participation.
            *   The Agency’s interpretation is overly broad; statistical necessity for "testing" does not grant sweeping authority for nationwide payment and delivery reform.
            *   Congress's use of "participate" and "participant" reinforces intent for informed, voluntary decisions.
            *   The argument that Medicare program participation is voluntary, thus mandatory model participation is "technically still voluntary," is rejected; CMMI lacks authority to make Medicare participation more burdensome than Congress intended.
    *   **2. What regulations should we reconsider as we look to achieve some of the policy objectives outlined in Executive Order 14212, “Establishing the President’s Make America Healthy Again Commission,” to focus on reversing chronic disease?**
        *   For over a decade, the AMA has undertaken large-scale initiatives to prevent cardiovascular disease and Type 2 diabetes and improve health outcomes.
        *   We welcome opportunities to work with the Administration on reversing chronic disease through deregulation and other avenues.
        *   Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program (MDPP)
            *   Enrollment for MDPP was just 9,015 Medicare beneficiaries at the end of March 2024, compared to over half a million in the CDC’s National Diabetes Prevention Program (NDPP).
            *   A major reason for this discrepancy is that MDPP limits suppliers to in-person programs, preventing virtual participation available in NDPP.
            *   We urge the Agency to align NDPP and MDPP supplier regulatory requirements by removing the in-person presence stipulation.
            *   We similarly urge the Agency to remove the per lifetime cap on MDPP benefits, which does not exist in NDPP and unnecessarily restricts participation.
            *   MDPP requirements are different and harder to implement than NDPP, causing lack of alignment and requiring differing internal accounting/reporting systems.
            *   HHS should streamline requirements to the National DPP standard:
                *   Align MDDP with NDPP metrics (weight-reduction, physical activity minutes, hemoglobin A1C reduction).
                *   Allow participants to report weight via digital apps or scales.
                *   Remove the once-per-lifetime cap on MDPP services.
        *   Diabetes Self-Management Training Services (DSMT)
            *   DSMT is a proven intervention, but current regulations place unnecessarily rigid requirements on Medicare DSMT services.
            *   HHS should:
                *   Remove the requirement that the majority of initial DSMT be given in a group setting in a building and allow virtual or asynchronous video delivery.
                *   Remove the arbitrary one-day waiting period and allow DSMT and medical nutrition therapy on the same day.
                *   Remove overly restrictive caps on hours (initial: up to 10 hours/12 months; subsequent: up to 2 hours) for additional flexibility.
                *   Streamline referral orders to reduce paperwork burden and barriers to access, allowing but not requiring referring provider to include specific session details or attest to their exact role.
        *   Hospital Readmission Reduction Program (HRRP) and Readmission Measures
            *   We urge the Agency to sunset HRRP and all readmission measures in CMS’ various quality programs, including MIPS.
