structuredSections.detailedContent:
- We are writing in response to the U. S. Department of Health and Human Services’ request for input from people living with chronic disease, and their family members, on HHS regulations and/or guidance that impede access to, or delivery of, care or services.
- The FDA’s proposed ban on electrical stimulation devices to treat severe self-injury and aggression should be withdrawn.
  - This withdrawal should be consistent with the Trump Administration’s deregulatory initiatives.
  - It would better promote the health and well-being of individuals, like our son, who have developmental disabilities and engage in chronic, treatment-resistant, dangerous, and life-threatening self-injurious (SIB) and aggressive (AB) behaviors.
- My husband and I are the parents of a 58-year-old son, Peter John Biscardi (P.J.), who is a client at the Judge Rotenberg Center (JRC) in Canton, Massachusetts.
  - JRC is the only school in the country that uses the graduated electronic decelerator (GED).
  - P. J. has benefited immensely from the use of the GED as part of his therapy.
- Our son P. J. has been a client at JRC since 1978 when he was eleven years old.
  - He was on the GED for many years.
- Our son was diagnosed with autism when he was three years old, and later diagnosed with mental retardation.
  - He is severely afflicted with these conditions and was very violent and dangerously self-abusive when he was young.
  - He is also basically non-verbal.
- Prior to entering JRC, he attended several day programs that had successfully served other children with autism and intellectual disabilities, but were unsuccessful in treating P. J.
  - Despite these other schools' efforts to control and teach him, and the use of medication to treat his violence, his condition continuously deteriorated, and he became more violent and self-abusive.
- The last school that P. J. attended, prior to attending JRC, treated his hyperactivity with amphetamines.
  - While these medications did calm him down somewhat, they also depleted his appetite to the point that he lost weight, becoming very thin, and he stopped growing for more than two years.
- Examples of the types of dangerous and life-threatening behaviors he exhibited before he went to JRC include:
  - Put Drano into his mouth, receiving severe chemical burns in his mouth as well as on his hands and legs.
  - Drank shampoo.
  - Tipped over large pieces of furniture.
  - Ran full-force into walls, causing one wall in our house to crack.
  - Ran into busy streets.
  - Violently banged his head with his fists many times a day.
  - Intensely bit his hands and wrists many times a day.
  - Despite our locking all the cabinets and drawers, occasionally, one of us would forget to secure the lock, and P. J. found a razor, started playing with it, and accidentally sliced his arms and legs.
- P. J. developed large callouses on his hands and wrists as a result of him biting himself.
  - These callouses would sometimes crack and bleed causing him pain.
- When he was living at home, our other children (a girl one year older and a boy three-and-a-half years younger) were constantly in danger from his violence and destructive behaviors.
  - He managed to knock the top bunk off his bunk bed while his younger brother was sleeping on it.
  - He knocked over a large chest of drawers onto his brother.
- My husband and I were also in danger from his violence.
  - At one time, when my husband leaned over to tie his shoe, P.J. grabbed a chunk of my husband's hair, ripped it out, and dropped it, bloodied, to the ground.
- The positive reinforcement that my husband and I used did help somewhat to curtail these dangerous behaviors, but did not stop them.
  - As he grew, he continually became a more severe threat to his own safety and to that of others.
  - None of the treatments used by other schools stopped his violence.
- Since he has been at the JRC, and received a combination of reward and punishment therapy, including the use of the GED, he has improved drastically.
  - He no longer runs into traffic, but instead, walks with us and follows directions.
  - He no longer has any desire to "taste" foreign substances.
  - The calluses on his hands and wrists have healed.
  - He does not show any aggression toward his roommates or classmates.
  - His teachers and roommates are safe when they are with him.
  - When he comes home to visit once a month, he is calm, relaxed, and happy.
  - He can go on field trips into the community.
  - Most importantly, he is happy and healthy.
- The use of the GED has always required court approval in Massachusetts for each and every client for whom it is recommended.
  - The proposed ban on the GED would ban a court-approved treatment that has saved the lives of many.
  - This brief two-second skin shock is a small price to pay to alleviate the self-mutilation, self-poisoning, self-abuse, violence and aggression that he previously exhibited.
- P.J. has exhibited no side effects from the GED, as he had previously experienced from drugs that were prescribed for him to try to control his behaviors.
  - Since attending JRC, P. J. has not been treated with any drugs to control his behavior.
- Our son P. J. is no longer on the GED, because it worked!
  - P. J. was taken off the GED for the last time in the Spring of 2014 and continues to thrive.
- I think of the GED as more of an emancipator than a punisher.
  - The program at JRC and the GED have not only saved his life, but have given him the high quality of life that is extremely rewarding.
- Although P.J. is now off the GED, we are concerned that if the GED is banned, other students with violent behaviors will have to be suddenly taken off the GED.
  - This raises extreme worry for the safety of our son, both at school and in transit, as well as the safety of other students and staff.
- Please direct the FDA to withdraw the proposed ban and leave the treatment planning to us (his parents), his treating physicians, and the courts.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: Parents of a 58-year-old son with severe developmental disabilities urge the FDA to withdraw its proposed ban on electrical stimulation devices (GED), citing their son's life-saving and transformative experience with the treatment at the Judge Rotenberg Center.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Peter and Maureen Biscardi
- **Type:** Individual
- **Role/Expertise:** Parents of a 58-year-old son with autism and mental retardation who exhibited severe, life-threatening self-injurious and aggressive behaviors.
- **Geographic Scope:** Local/State (Woburn, Massachusetts)
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly impacts the availability of a treatment (GED) that they credit with saving their son's life and vastly improving his quality of life, and raises concerns about the safety of other individuals who currently benefit from the treatment.
structuredSections.corePosition: We believe the FDA's proposed ban on electrical stimulation devices should be withdrawn, consistent with deregulatory initiatives and to better promote the health and well-being of individuals with developmental disabilities who engage in chronic, treatment-resistant, dangerous, and life-threatening self-injurious and aggressive behaviors. Our son's experience demonstrates that the graduated electronic decelerator (GED) is a life-saving and emancipating treatment when other methods have failed.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Direct the FDA to withdraw the proposed ban on electrical stimulation devices for self-injurious or aggressive behavior.
- Leave treatment planning for individuals with severe developmental disabilities to their parents, treating physicians, and the courts.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- The proposed ban would eliminate a court-approved treatment that has demonstrably saved lives and significantly improved the quality of life for individuals with severe self-injurious and aggressive behaviors.
- A ban raises extreme worry for the safety of current students at facilities like the Judge Rotenberg Center if they are suddenly taken off the GED.
  - This concern extends to the safety of other students and staff at the school, as well as the safety of their own son during visits or in transit, even though he is no longer on the GED.
- Previous alternative treatments, including medication, were ineffective and/or caused severe negative side effects for their son.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- Their son exhibited extremely dangerous and life-threatening behaviors prior to JRC, including ingesting Drano and shampoo, running into walls and busy streets, severely biting himself, and physically endangering family members.
- Previous pharmacological treatments for their son's hyperactivity caused significant negative side effects, such as severe weight loss and inhibited growth for over two years.
- The graduated electronic decelerator (GED) is described as an "emancipator" rather than a punisher, having not only saved their son's life but also given him a high quality of life.
- Their son was able to be taken off the GED in 2014 and continues to thrive, demonstrating the long-term effectiveness of the treatment in modifying behavior.
- The use of the GED in Massachusetts always requires court approval for each client, indicating a level of judicial oversight for this treatment.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "This brief two-second skin shock is a small price to pay to alleviate the self-mutilation, self-poisoning, self-abuse, violence and aggression that he previously exhibited."
- "Our son P. J. is no longer on the GED, because it worked!"
- "I think of the GED as more of an emancipator than a punisher."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Abbott Laboratories (Abbott) appreciates the opportunity to provide input related to the May 14, 2025 Request for Information (RFI) published in the Federal Register at 90 FR 20478.
*   Abbott, headquartered in the US, is committed to helping people live their best possible life through the power of health.
    *   For over 130 years, we’ve introduced new products and technologies in nutrition, diagnostics, medical devices, and branded generic pharmaceuticals.
    *   In the United States, Abbott provides a broad portfolio of advanced cardiovascular and neuromodulation technologies, diabetes care products, nutritional products, and diagnostic tests.
*   As a company dedicated to building life-changing health technology, Abbott believes the best health care product is one that helps the people who need it most.
    *   We are dedicated to helping people live more fully by designing access and affordability into our life-changing technologies and products.
*   At times, well-intentioned regulations can create unforeseen bureaucracy, ultimately impacting the ability to provide health care products to the people who need them most.
    *   In our comments, we’ve identified a cross-section of regulatory areas where recission will improve patient access and utilization of agency resources.
*   Of note are several areas of FDA and CMS regulations that increase the burden to bringing innovative diagnostics used in certificate of waiver laboratories and point of care settings.
    *   Access to tests in these near-patient settings benefits patients in rural and other health care settings, where access to health care services has diminished over the years.
    *   Many of these regulatory areas, such as the FDA point of care exemption limitations and the certificate of waiver by application process, have been in place for decades.
        *   This was when near-patient testing was novel, before much of the population learned to use at-home tests during the COVID-19 pandemic, and before technological advances automating elements of the testing process.
    *   Because of these changes, this is the time to reassess these areas and ensure appropriate regulatory pathways for diagnostics used in near-patient settings.

*   **Specific Recommendations for Recission:**

    *   **1. FDA – 21 CFR § 878.9; 21 CFR § 882.9; 21 CFR § 862.9; 21 CFR § 864.9; 21 CFR § 874.9; 21 CFR § 866.9; 21 CFR § 880.9; 21 CFR § 884.9; 21 CFR § 868.9; 21 CFR § 872.9; 21 CFR § 888.9; 21 CFR § 870.9; 21 CFR § 876.9; 21 CFR § 886.9; 21 CFR § 890.9; 21 CFR § 892.9.25**
        *   We recommend FDA rescind the portion of these regulations that require manufacturers to submit a premarket notification to FDA for in vitro devices intended for point of care (POC) or near-patient testing.
        *   Congress intended for FDA to exempt low-risk Class I and II medical devices, including in vitro diagnostics, from premarket notification with limited exceptions (FD&C Act §§ 510(l) and 510(m)) because general controls (e.g., quality system regulations and postmarket regulations) provide sufficient regulation.
        *   When implementing this new authority over two decades ago, the agency promulgated blanket limitations applying to in vitro diagnostics, which disproportionately impact point-of-care (POC) diagnostics (referred to as near-patient testing) used at or near the patient.
        *   Despite significant technological advancements, these limitations remain and continue to stifle POC innovation by imposing a higher bar to market for POC IVDs as opposed to IVDs for centralized testing.
        *   The value of POC in vitro diagnostic testing, including those tests intended for use in a doctor’s office, school, workplace, rural settings, or even the home, was demonstrated during the COVID-19 pandemic and continues to grow today.
        *   Significant regulatory hurdles make it extremely difficult for developers of POC tests to succeed.
        *   Throughout Title 21, identical limiting language appears, requiring a test that would otherwise be low-risk—and could therefore be available by adhering to FDA general controls without additional premarket FDA review—to go through FDA premarket review for the sole reason that the test is intended for the POC setting (e.g., 21 C.F.R. § 862.9(c)(9)).
        *   Over two decades have passed since the promulgation of these outdated regulations, and modernizing the treatment of POC or near-patient testing in a risk-based manner would benefit all patients.
        *   Categorically limiting a device simply because it is POC no longer makes sense; it does not support public health in today’s health care environment and creates unnecessary regulatory hurdles that stifle innovation.
    *   **2. FDA – 21 CFR Part 11 (Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures)**
        *   In August 2003, FDA issued guidance narrowing the scope and application of regulation 21 CFR Part 11 and announced its intent to re-examine the regulation.
        *   Underlying predicate rules and the significant resource expenditures associated with Part 11 were identified as reasons for enforcement discretion.
        *   However, nearly twenty-two years later, Part 11 remains in the Code of Federal Regulations.
        *   Since the regulations were promulgated, the common use of electronic systems has greatly expanded.
        *   We, therefore, recommend, as part of deregulatory actions, to reassess the need for 21 CFR Part 11 (along with associated Part 11 guidance).
    *   **3. FDA – Final guidance Commercially Distributed Analyte Specific Reagents (ASRs): Frequently Asked Questions; Guidance for Industry and FDA Staff September 2007**
        *   ASRs are defined in regulation as “antibodies, both polyclonal and monoclonal, specific receptor proteins, ligands, nucleic acid sequences, and similar reagents which, through specific binding or chemical reactions with substances in a specimen, are intended for use in a diagnostic application for identification and quantification of an individual chemical substance or ligand in biological specimens" (21 CFR § 864.4020(a)).
        *   We recommend withdrawal of this final guidance.
        *   The guidance unnecessarily sets forth a narrower interpretation of the definition of an analyte specific reagent than contained in the regulation.
        *   Withdrawal of the guidance will reduce confusion.
    *   **4. FDA/CMS – CLIA Waiver by Application**
        *   While clearance or approval is the standard to market medical devices in the US, a subset of in vitro diagnostic medical devices requires a second submission, called CLIA Waiver by application or dual submission when combined within a 510(k) or PMA submission (collectively “CLIA Waiver”).
        *   In vitro diagnostic devices used in certain professional settings (CLIA-waived laboratories), such as a physician’s office, are subject to this additional requirement, which does not apply to any other type of IVD, including those for use in the home.
        *   We recommend re-assessing how the standard for CLIA Waiver has been implemented.
        *   We believe the statutory language and legislative history support an interpretation of a study design based on a demonstration of accuracy—to mean the test performs the same in the hands of waived users and laboratory professionals—without incorporation of the concept of total allowable error, which, although not specifically stated in implementing guidance, has been implemented in practice as part of the current standard.
        *   The above understanding of a demonstration of accuracy is supported by legislation associated with the CLIA Waiver standard, including the addition of “by the user” codified at 42 U.S.C. §263a(d)(3) and the accompanying House Committee Report (H.R. Rep. No.105-310, Sec. 21).
            *   The report explains that the criteria for waiver should focus on test performance “by the user” and the potential for operator error, and that interpretations of “erroneous results” and “accurate” should not include inherent clinical sensitivity/specificity, which are parameters properly reviewed for product approval/clearance.
        *   Subsequent legislation further clarified the standard in relation to the CLIA Waiver guidance to require the guidance to address “the appropriate use of comparable performance between waived user and a moderately complex laboratory user to demonstrate accuracy” (section 3057 of the 21st Century Cures Act, P.L. 114-255).
        *   A re-assessment of the statute and legislative history in relation to how the CLIA waiver standard has been implemented, which would include removal of the concept of total allowable error, provides an opportunity to realign review resources, support healthcare accessibility, and remove barriers to innovative diagnostic tests reaching patients in the CLIA-waived laboratory setting.
    *   **5. FDA – Best Practices for Selecting a Predicate Device to Support a Premarket Notification [510(k)] Submission: Draft Guidance for Industry and Food and Drug Administration Staff; Evidentiary Expectations for 510(k) Implant Devices: Draft Guidance for Industry and Food and Drug Administration Staff; Use of Clinical Data in Premarket Notification [510(k)] Submissions: Draft Guidance for Industry and Food and Drug Administration Staff**
        *   We recommend rescinding the following three 510(k) draft guidance documents issued by the FDA in 2023 because they each include recommendations that are not supported by existing statutes and regulations and are inconsistent with longstanding regulatory practice.
        *   Use of guidance documents to establish new and/or changed requirements for an established submission pathway, 510(k), creates unpredictable regulatory expectations, increases FDA resources to review additional information, and is not in the best interest of the public health.
        *   Illustrative examples from each of these draft guidance documents support our recommendations:
            *   **(1) Best Practices for Selecting a Predicate Device to Support a Premarket Notification [510(k)] Submission: Draft Guidance for Industry and Food and Drug Administration Staff**
                *   This draft guidance document establishes specified characteristics for selecting a predicate device that are not found in statute.
                *   It also recommends manufacturers disclose information regarding their predicate device selection process in a public-facing 510(k) summary; however, this information is not a required element per 21 CFR 807.92, it is irrelevant to the determination of a substantial equivalence determination, and may inadvertently result in disclosure of proprietary information.
            *   **(2) Evidentiary Expectations for 510(k) Implant Devices: Draft Guidance for Industry and Food and Drug Administration Staff**
                *   This draft guidance document appears to change the definition of an implanted medical device as defined in 21 CFR 860.3(d).
                *   It also includes blanket recommendations that do not consider the risk of the device, which is inconsistent with FDA’s longstanding statutory benefit-risk and “least burdensome” principles.
            *   **(3) Use of Clinical Data in Premarket Notification [510(k)] Submissions: Draft Guidance for Industry and Food and Drug Administration Staff**
                *   The examples and recommendations included in this draft guidance document related to the use of clinical data in 510(k) submission suggest a deviation from the statutory standard to demonstrate equivalence and a shift towards a premarket approval (“PMA”)-like demonstration of safety and effectiveness.
    *   **6. FDA – “Evaluation of Thermal Effects of Medical Devices that Produce Tissue Heating and/or Cooling.”**
        *   We recommend withdrawal of the draft guidance.
        *   The guidance is overly broad in scope as it widely applies to many device types and well beyond the guidance it is intended to supersede, which was limited in scope.
        *   We are concerned this broadly encompassing guidance that includes within its scope all premarket submissions, including IDE Applications—without any delineation across the product lifecycle—will impede device discovery and development as it is inconsistent with the criteria for IDE applications and a least burdensome approach.
        *   Further, the guidance has created much confusion because it conflicts with FDA established policies and FDA-recognized consensus standards.
    *   **7. FDA – Proposed Rule introduced in the Federal Register in December 2022 (87 FR 75536), Docket No. FDA-2019-N-2650 titled “Investigational New Drug Applications; Exemptions for Clinical Investigations to Evaluate a Drug Use of a Product Lawfully Marketed as a Conventional Food, Dietary Supplement or Cosmetic); Industry Guidance titled “Investigational New Drug Applications (INDs) – Determining Whether Human Research Studies Can Be Conducted Without an IND”**
        *   We recommend withdrawal of this proposed rule and accompanying guidance document.
        *   The Investigational New Drug (IND) application framework was established to ensure the safe conduct of human research involving drugs, such as studies with the intent to pursue FDA approval of a new drug, studies for a new use of an existing drug, and studies to support a change in a drug’s labeling or advertising.
        *   This proposed rule and guidance document establish criteria and processes to submit nutrition or food research protocols for an evaluation to determine if such protocols are exempt from an IND.
        *   Food is carved out of the statutory definition of drug (see FD&C Act 201(g)(1)(C)).
        *   Additionally, the commercial intent of bringing food to market is not to treat, mitigate, prevent, or cure disease, which is the commercial intent of a drug (see 201(g)(1)(B)).
        *   Subjecting nutrition research to a process to determine if drug regulations apply is counterproductive and will unnecessarily delay important research with the potential to improve population health by improved nutrition.
        *   The proposed rule indicates that some nutrition research would require an IND and other nutrition research would require FDA to grant an exemption from the IND (i.e., submission and review of a nutrition study protocol by FDA).
        *   Implementation of this process would significantly increase FDA time and cost because this activity is not supported by current staff levels.
        *   It's unclear what problem FDA is trying to solve with the proposed rule and guidance.
            *   The IND application is a process to ensure the safety of subjects in drug studies. However, foods, the subject of nutrition research, are required to be inherently safe.
        *   The proposed rule also does not establish a time limit on FDA’s review of nutrition research protocol to determine whether an exemption will be granted.
        *   It indicates CBER or CDER (rather than the Human Foods Program) would be reviewing nutrition research protocols, and it’s unclear if FDA is staffed to undertake these new reviews.
        *   The proposed rule introduces new regulatory hurdles for academia and industries advancing nutrition research and would create a stifling effect on advancements of nutrition science and research in the United States.
        *   It would potentially incentivize movement of research outside of the United States where these regulatory burdens do not exist.
        *   The Final Guidance establishes a framework that differs somewhat from the proposed rule, in that it indicates nutrition research including infants, immunocompromised individuals, or those with serious medical conditions may require an IND.
        *   It appears to indicate that FDA would require a study on a medical food for its intended purpose (dietary management of a disease) to be conducted under an IND application despite the statute containing a carve out of medical food from the definition of drug.
        *   It also appears that FDA would require a nutrition study assessing structure/function endpoints in infants or vulnerable populations to submit an IND even though structure/function (in the sense of a food) is carved out of the statutory definition of drug.
        *   Similarly, it’s unclear what problem FDA was attempting to solve with this guidance in that the IND is a process to ensure the safety of a subjects in drug studies, and foods are required to be inherently safe as food.
    *   **8. FDA – 21 CFR 106.110 (modification)**
        *   Section 412(c) of the FD&C Act establishes registration requirements for new infant formulas introduced into interstate commerce; it does not require registration of infant formulas intended exclusively for export.
        *   However, the codifying regulations at 21 CFR 106.110 added a requirement to register with FDA any new infant formulas that are intended for export only.
        *   We recommend removing the requirement to register “export only” infant formulas with FDA.
        *   Any infant formulas intended solely for export are manufactured in accordance with the receiving country’s regulations (including composition and labeling, which may be in a foreign language), and are reviewed by the receiving country’s regulatory authority.
        *   The utility of this review by FDA is unclear and, given FDA’s resource constraints on reviewing infant formula submissions intended for the US market, and to remove this burden for domestic infant formula manufacturers, we recommend that the “export only” registrations be removed from the regulation.
        *   Specifically, we recommend deleting from 21 CFR§ 106.110, “including a new infant formula for export only” to align the regulation with the statutory provision.
    *   **9. FDA – Guidance / Practice on Obtaining Food Export Certificates as described here: Food Export Certificates | FDA**
        *   We recommend FDA consolidate, simplify criteria, and remove unnecessary documentation for the issuance of certificates that support US export of food products.
        *   Approximately 50 countries to which nutritional products are exported from the United States, require a certificate of free sale (COFS) for the pre-market registration with the local regulatory authority.
        *   FDA supports manufacturers by issuing certificates for products manufactured in the United States but intended for export (requirements noted on the Food Export Certificates | FDA webpage).
        *   FDA issues three types of export certifications for food products manufactured in the United States with the certificate type defined by food regulatory category (e.g., conventional food, infant formula, foods for special dietary use).
        *   The Certificate of Free Sale (COFS) is generally accepted by these countries. However, the US limits its use to only one food category, foods for special dietary use.
        *   The other two certificate types (Certificate of Exportability and Certificate to a Foreign Government) are frequently rejected by foreign authorities.
        *   To reduce bureaucracy, we recommend making all food product regulatory categories eligible for FDA issuance of the Certificate of Free Sale (COFS) when those food products are manufactured in compliance with the receiving country’s regulations for composition, regulatory categorization, and labeling when the foreign authority requires the export certificate.
        *   To simplify, we recommend that FDA omit the labeling requirement for export certificates because the labels are designed to comply with the receiving country’s requirements and will allow FDA to conserve resources currently devoted to reviewing foreign food labeling against US regulations.
        *   Under current practice, the submitter translates the labeling into English, so FDA can review it against US regulations, which is unnecessary because the product is intended for export only and not the US market.
        *   Based on our company’s experience, making these changes will support US export of food products.
    *   **10. CMS – 42 CFR § 493.1405(b) changed by 88 FR 89976.**
        *   Significantly increased laboratory director educational requirements, without evidence of an issue, will reduce qualified medical doctors from functioning as laboratory directors for laboratories associated with their practice.
        *   Specifically, the modifications to the medical residency provision emphasizing the requirement for “clinical laboratory training” and requiring one year of experience supervising in moderate or high complexity testing and 20 hours of continuing education (CE) to qualify for the position of laboratory director will lead to lab closures of physician office laboratories or laboratories in sites of emergency and critical care that are owned and operated by the medical practice owner, impacting patient diagnosis and care, especially in rural areas, and other areas experiencing health care facility closures.
        *   Point-of-Care (POC) testing has become a standard of practice in many healthcare systems, allowing laboratory results to be delivered to the treating healthcare provider as rapidly as possible.
        *   To reduce lab closures, we recommend rescinding these stricter personal requirements that went into effect 12/28/2024 and revert to previous regulation allowing for 1 year of laboratory training, which can be qualified through medical residency, or 20 hours of CE for the position of laboratory director of physician office laboratories or laboratories in sites of emergency and critical care that are owned and operated by the medical practice owner, aligned with the CMS enforcement discretion memorandum issued June 23, 2025 (Ref: QSO-25-21-CLIA).
    *   **11. CMS – 42 CFR 493.1411(4)(i)(A) changed by 88 FR 89976.**
        *   Revised regulations replaced the qualifications to operate as a point of care testing technical consultant from holding a nursing degree to a complex algorithm.
        *   Point of care technical consultants are necessary to document competency of end users to run point of care tests in moderately complex laboratories and are essential workers in critical care and emergency departments.
        *   No issues have been identified with individuals holding a nursing degree to prompt a change in the regulation that will ultimately reduce the ability of nurses to perform this critical function.
        *   Point-of-Care (POC) testing has become a standard of practice in critical care and emergency departments allowing laboratory results to be delivered to the treating healthcare provider as rapidly as possible.
        *   With an existing decline in laboratory professionals, eliminating nursing degrees as a qualifying degree to serve as a technical consultant will lead to overburdened laboratories, which impacts the ability to deliver timely lab results and ultimately patient care.
        *   To reduce the impact to patient care and lab closures, we recommend rescinding this unnecessarily complex personnel requirements that went into effect 12/28/2024 and revert to previous regulation allowing medical doctor degree holders and bachelors of science in nursing to qualify similarly to bachelor’s degree holders of chemical, biological, or clinical laboratory science.
    *   **12. CMS – 42 CFR §493.1804(c)(1) changed by 88 FR 89976.**
        *   Recent regulation changes allowing alternative sanctions, (“that is, civil money penalties”) to be levied against certificate of waiver (CoW) bearing laboratories (laboratories that only perform waived tests, defined as “simple laboratory examinations and procedures that have an insignificant risk of an erroneous result,” creates a financial incentive for accrediting organizations to focus laboratory resources on processes not required for waived laboratories without evidence of need or risk of patient harm.
        *   While the regulation cites the benefit of decreasing the burden for sanction imposed for improper proficiency testing referral, proficiency testing is not a required process for laboratories qualified to only perform CoW tests, and as such creates new incentive monitoring these sites, increasing their cost and burden of compliance (taken directly from the FR “will increase flexibility [in regulation] while moving these laboratories toward compliance”) for processes that are not currently being monitored today, without evidence of need for patient care.
        *   By adding an entirely financial sanction for CoW laboratories with the basis of violation being a process they are not currently responsible for and have no evidenced history of violating, it creates a financial incentive for regulators to apply stricter standards of compliance without evidence of need.
        *   Increasing the financial burden and risk to operate these laboratories reduces access to care.
        *   We recommend revising the regulation by removing the alternative sanctions (civil money penalties).
    *   **13. CMS – 2 CFR part 493, subpart F—General Administration changed by 88 FR 89976.**
        *   In December 2018 (83 FR 67723 through 67728), there was a 20% increase in fees imposed to help ensure the CLIA program could continue to be self-sustaining.
        *   “The 2018 increase was intended to give CMS time to propose a process through rulemaking to allow for ongoing changes to the CLIA fees. Despite that increase, the level of carryover funding available to cover program expenses is projected to decline continuously. As such, the CLIA program will not be self-supporting by the end of FY 2023 without an additional fee increase.”
        *   This current update imposes an across-the-board fee update of 18%, and a change to allocate directly from certificate of waiver laboratories the cost for FDA to categorize clinical laboratory tests as waived.
        *   These changes will significantly increase the cost to operate laboratories, reducing lab viability, specifically in certificate of waiver laboratories.
        *   Furthermore, there is no evidence that these updates will “stabilize” the program financially, as the repeated increases in fees have not done so previously and only serve to exacerbate the existing consolidation of laboratories and shortages of lab professionals and services that impact access to care.
        *   Further increasing the cost of oversight does not benefit innovation and access to care.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: Abbott Laboratories, a global healthcare product manufacturer, urges federal agencies to rescind outdated and burdensome regulations across diagnostics, medical devices, nutrition, and laboratory operations to reduce bureaucracy, foster innovation, improve patient access, and better utilize agency resources.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Abbott Laboratories
- **Type:** Business
- **Role/Expertise:** Manufacturer of nutrition, diagnostics, medical devices, and branded generic pharmaceuticals; input provided by April Veoukas, J.D., Director, Regulatory Affairs, Abbott Quality & Regulatory.
- **Geographic Scope:** National (US-headquartered, provides broad portfolio in US) and International (exports products to approximately 50 countries).
- **Stake in Issue:** A major developer and provider of healthcare products, directly impacted by federal regulations governing product development, approval, manufacturing, export, and clinical laboratory operations; seeks to streamline regulatory pathways to efficiently bring innovative and accessible products to market.
structuredSections.corePosition: Abbott believes that well-intentioned regulations sometimes create unforeseen bureaucracy, ultimately impacting the ability to provide essential health care products to those who need them most. We have identified a cross-section of regulatory areas where recission will improve patient access and optimize the utilization of agency resources. It is time to reassess these areas to ensure appropriate regulatory pathways for innovative health technologies, especially diagnostics used in near-patient settings.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Rescind portions of 21 CFR § 878.9 and related regulations that require premarket notification for in vitro diagnostic devices intended for Point-of-Care (POC) or near-patient testing, aligning with Congressional intent for low-risk devices.
- Reassess the need for and consider rescinding 21 CFR Part 11, Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures, and its associated guidance, given the expansion of electronic systems.
- Withdraw the September 2007 FDA final guidance on Commercially Distributed Analyte Specific Reagents (ASRs) to reduce confusion caused by its unnecessarily narrow interpretation.
- Reassess the implementation of the CLIA Waiver by Application standard, removing the concept of "total allowable error" from the demonstration of accuracy to align with statutory language and legislative history.
- Rescind three specific 2023 FDA draft guidance documents related to 510(k) submissions: "Best Practices for Selecting a Predicate Device," "Evidentiary Expectations for 510(k) Implant Devices," and "Use of Clinical Data in Premarket Notification [510(k)] Submissions," as they are unsupported by existing statutes and inconsistent with longstanding practice.
- Withdraw the draft guidance “Evaluation of Thermal Effects of Medical Devices that Produce Tissue Heating and/or Cooling,” due to its overly broad scope, inconsistency with IDE application criteria, and conflict with established policies.
- Withdraw the December 2022 proposed rule (87 FR 75536) and accompanying guidance regarding Investigational New Drug (IND) applications for nutrition/food research, as it is counterproductive and delays important public health research.
- Remove the requirement from 21 CFR 106.110 to register "export only" infant formulas with FDA, aligning the regulation with the FD&C Act and removing an unnecessary burden.
- Consolidate, simplify criteria, and remove unnecessary documentation for food export certificates, making all food product categories eligible for the Certificate of Free Sale (COFS) and omitting labeling requirements for export-only products.
- Rescind the stricter laboratory director educational requirements in 42 CFR § 493.1405(b) (effective 12/28/2024), reverting to previous regulations to prevent lab closures.
- Rescind the revised regulations in 42 CFR 493.1411(4)(i)(A) (effective 12/28/2024) that changed qualifications for point-of-care testing technical consultants, allowing nursing degrees to qualify.
- Revise 42 CFR §493.1804(c)(1) by removing alternative sanctions (civil money penalties) for Certificate of Waiver (CoW) laboratories, which create undue financial incentives for regulators.
- Reassess the recent fee increases and allocation changes in 2 CFR part 493, subpart F—General Administration, as they significantly increase costs for laboratories without stabilizing the program or benefiting access to care.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Unforeseen Bureaucracy and Stifled Innovation:** Well-intentioned regulations often create excessive bureaucracy, hindering the ability to provide innovative health care products and impacting patient access, particularly in areas like point-of-care diagnostics.
- **Outdated Regulatory Frameworks:** Decades-old regulations governing point-of-care (POC) exemptions and CLIA waiver processes have not kept pace with technological advancements or widespread at-home testing, stifling POC innovation.
- **Unpredictable Regulatory Expectations & Increased Burden:** Recent draft guidances for 510(k) submissions introduce new requirements unsupported by statute or longstanding practice, leading to unpredictable hurdles, increased FDA review resources, and potential disclosure of proprietary information.
- **Broad/Conflicting Guidance Documents:** Overly broad guidance documents (e.g., thermal effects of devices) and those conflicting with existing regulations (e.g., ASR guidance, IND for nutrition research) create confusion, impede device development, and are inconsistent with "least burdensome" principles.
- **Barriers to Nutrition Research:** Proposed rules and guidance requiring IND applications or exemptions for nutrition research are counterproductive, unnecessarily delay important research into population health, are not supported by current FDA staff levels, and could incentivize research to move outside the U.S.
- **Increased Operating Costs and Reduced Access to Care for Laboratories:** New, stricter educational requirements for laboratory directors and technical consultants, combined with new financial sanctions for Certificate of Waiver (CoW) labs and rising CLIA fees, are projected to lead to lab closures, overburdened laboratories, and reduced access to timely patient diagnosis and care, especially in rural and underserved areas.
- **Inefficient Export Processes:** The current FDA system for issuing food export certificates is cumbersome and leads to frequent rejection of US certificates by foreign authorities, hindering US export of food products.
- **Lack of Evidence for Regulatory Changes:** Several recent regulatory changes (e.g., lab director requirements, technical consultant qualifications, CoW lab sanctions) lack clear evidence of an underlying problem or patient harm they are intended to address, instead creating unnecessary burdens.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- Highlighted the demonstrated value of Point-of-Care (POC) in vitro diagnostic testing, including tests for doctor’s offices, schools, workplaces, rural settings, and homes, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic, where the general population learned to use at-home tests.
- Noted that current regulations for near-patient testing are decades old, originating when such testing was novel, and now require reassessment due to significant technological advancements automating elements of the testing process.
- Stated that based on the company's direct experience, changes to the cumbersome food export certificate process are necessary to support US export of food products, as current certificate types are frequently rejected by foreign authorities.
- Expressed concern that new, stricter personnel requirements for laboratory directors and technical consultants could lead to lab closures, particularly in physician office laboratories and emergency/critical care sites, severely impacting patient diagnosis and care in rural areas and those experiencing healthcare facility closures.

- "At times well-intentioned regulations can create unforeseen bureaucracy, ultimately impacting the ability to provide health care products to the people who need it the most."
- "Categorically limiting a device simply because it is POC no longer makes sense. It does not support the public health in today’s health care environment, and it creates unnecessary regulatory hurdles that stifle innovation."
- "Subjecting nutrition research to a process to determine if drug regulations apply is counterproductive and will unnecessarily delay important research with the potential to improve population heath by improved nutrition."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
-   On behalf of the National Small Business Association (NSBA) and its more than 65,000 members, as well as the millions of small businesses across the nation, we write to respond to the Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS) Request for Information (RFI) entitled “Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation to Make America Healthy Again.”
-   This letter identifies unnecessary regulations that are outdated or that should be eliminated pursuant to President Trump’s Executive Order 14192.
-   Specifically, this letter urges HHS to consider the following in its regulatory reform efforts:
    -   Final Rule entitled “Short-Term, Limited-Duration Insurance and Independent, Noncoordinated Expected Benefits Coverage” (STLDI Rule).
    -   Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) Standards for Privacy of Individually Identifiable Health Information (Privacy Rule).
    -   General burdens faced by small businesses in health care affordability and Affordable Care Act (ACA) compliance.
-   STLDI Rule
    -   On April 3, 2024, the Internal Revenue Service, Department of the Treasury, Employee Benefits Security Administration, and HHS’ Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) issued a final rule amending the definition of “short-term, limited-duration insurance” (STLDI).
    -   The rule's stated purpose is to "ensure that consumers can clearly distinguish STLDI from comprehensive coverage, protect the risk pools and stabilize premiums for individual health insurance coverage, and promote access to affordable comprehensive coverage."
    -   Other small business advocacy organizations have expressed concern with this rule, arguing that it "restricts small businesses’ ability to select health coverage by limiting access to flexible, low-cost, short-term health plans."
    -   In response to the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking prior to issuance of the final STLDI rule, commenters noted that self-employed individuals or owners of a small business may benefit from being able to purchase longer-duration STLDI coverage.
    -   The departments acknowledged but failed to incorporate this feedback into their final rule, stating that they were “not persuaded that a longer maximum initial contract term or longer maximum duration, taking into account renewal or extensions, is appropriate.”
    -   Moreover, in the final rule’s Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) analysis, the departments conceded that they were “unable to precisely determine how many small issuers of STLDI and fixed indemnity excepted benefits coverage will be affected by these final rules” and that “there is some uncertainty about the impacts of these rules on the revenue of issuers of STLDI and fixed indemnity insurance.”
    -   Accordingly, NSBA recommends that HHS and CMS conduct a thorough RFA analysis.
    -   They should also work with the Small Business Administration’s (SBA) Office of Advocacy to accurately assess the true extent to which this final rule will impact small businesses and whether a small business carveout is appropriate.
-   HIPAA Privacy Rule
    -   The HIPAA Privacy Rule “requires covered entities to make reasonable efforts to limit use, disclosure of, and requests for protected health information [PHI] to the minimum necessary to accomplish the intended purpose.”
    -   For flexibility purposes, the rule “requires covered entities to make their own assessment of what [PHI] is reasonably necessary for a particular purpose, given the characteristics of their business and workforce, and to implement policies and procedures accordingly.”
    -   This guidance, however well intentioned, was last updated in 2006.
    -   Since that time, considerations involving data, including sensitive data, have become nearly ubiquitous in business practices for businesses of all sizes.
    -   Accordingly, NSBA recommends that HHS consider ways to update HIPAA guidance that will provide clarity to small entities without robust compliance teams.
    -   This update should not unduly burden the day-to-day operations of these entities, since small business owners themselves are often responsible for their business’s compliance.
    -   Alternatively, NSBA also supports a “cybersecurity safe harbor,” similar to one that was just signed into law in Texas.
    -   This safe harbor would protect small businesses from liability in data breach lawsuits so long as they “implement and maintain a compliant cybersecurity program.”
    -   This option should be explored by HHS and, if necessary, the agency should work with Congress to authorize this sort of safe harbor provision.
-   Considerations for Regulatory Reform: Small Business Compliance and Affordability Challenges
    -   Health care affordability has long been a priority for NSBA and its members.
    -   Additionally, a recent survey conducted by NSBA shed light on the compliance challenges that contribute to the crisis of health care affordability, with respondents indicating that health care regulations are one of the most burdensome areas of regulation for their business.
    -   Moreover, two-in-five respondents reported that ACA compliance, specifically, was burdensome to their business.
    -   These types of compliance burdens, the survey demonstrated, often result in a decrease in implementation of growth strategies and in hiring, as well as in higher prices.
    -   In short, as HHS conducts its review of outdated and unnecessary regulations, NSBA urges the agency to account for challenges faced by small businesses in obtaining affordable health coverage as well as in complying with a complex regime of regulations.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The National Small Business Association advocates for significant regulatory reform from HHS, urging the elimination or modification of health regulations like the STLDI Rule and outdated HIPAA guidance, and a reduction in ACA compliance burdens to improve healthcare affordability and foster small business growth.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
-   **Name/Organization:** National Small Business Association (NSBA)
-   **Type:** Advocacy Group
-   **Role/Expertise:** Nation's oldest small-business advocacy organization, founded in 1937, operating on a bipartisan basis to represent the interests of all American small businesses. Represents over 65,000 members.
-   **Geographic Scope:** National (members in every state and every industry across the country).
-   **Stake in Issue:** Represents small businesses nationwide who are directly impacted by federal health regulations, particularly regarding healthcare affordability, compliance burdens, and access to suitable health coverage options.
structuredSections.corePosition: On behalf of its members and millions of small businesses, we are responding to HHS's Request for Information to identify and urge the elimination of unnecessary, outdated regulations, pursuant to Executive Order 14192. We specifically call for reform concerning the Short-Term, Limited-Duration Insurance (STLDI) Rule, the HIPAA Privacy Rule, and the general burdens small businesses face with healthcare affordability and Affordable Care Act (ACA) compliance.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   **For the STLDI Rule:**
    -   HHS and CMS should conduct a thorough Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) analysis.
    -   Work with the Small Business Administration’s (SBA) Office of Advocacy to accurately assess the true extent to which this final rule will impact small businesses.
    -   Determine whether a small business carveout is appropriate for the rule.
-   **For the HIPAA Privacy Rule:**
    -   HHS should consider ways to update HIPAA guidance to provide clarity to small entities without robust compliance teams.
    -   Ensure that any updates do not unduly burden the day-to-day operations of small businesses, as owners often manage their own compliance.
    -   Explore implementing a “cybersecurity safe harbor,” similar to the one recently signed into law in Texas, to protect small businesses from liability in data breach lawsuits if they implement and maintain a compliant cybersecurity program.
    -   If necessary, HHS should work with Congress to authorize this type of safe harbor provision.
-   **For overall regulatory reform:**
    -   HHS should account for the challenges faced by small businesses in obtaining affordable health coverage.
    -   HHS should account for the burdens of complying with a complex regime of regulations.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   **Regarding the STLDI Rule:**
    -   The rule restricts small businesses’ ability to select health coverage by limiting access to flexible, low-cost, short-term health plans, contrary to the needs of self-employed individuals or small business owners.
    -   HHS acknowledged but failed to incorporate feedback from the Notice of Proposed Rulemaking that advocated for longer-duration STLDI coverage.
    -   The departments' own Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA) analysis conceded an inability to precisely determine the rule's impact on small issuers and expressed uncertainty about revenue impacts, indicating an incomplete assessment of burden.
-   **Regarding the HIPAA Privacy Rule:**
    -   The current guidance for the HIPAA Privacy Rule, last updated in 2006, is outdated and inadequate given that data considerations, including sensitive data, have become nearly ubiquitous in modern business practices for all sizes of businesses.
    -   Small businesses often lack the robust compliance teams needed to navigate complex HIPAA requirements, placing the burden directly on small business owners.
-   **Regarding general small business compliance and affordability:**
    -   Health care regulations are consistently identified as one of the most burdensome regulatory areas for small businesses.
    -   Specifically, two-in-five small businesses report that Affordable Care Act (ACA) compliance is burdensome.
    -   These regulatory and compliance burdens directly result in a decrease in the implementation of growth strategies, reduced hiring, and higher prices for consumers.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
-   A recent survey conducted by NSBA highlighted that healthcare regulations are among the most burdensome areas for small businesses, with two-in-five respondents specifically identifying ACA compliance as burdensome.
-   The NSBA survey demonstrated that these compliance burdens negatively impact business operations, leading to decreased implementation of growth strategies, reduced hiring, and higher prices for goods and services.
-   The commenter proposes a "cybersecurity safe harbor" provision, modeled after a recent Texas law, as a viable solution to protect small businesses from data breach liability when they maintain a compliant cybersecurity program, offering a concrete example of a desired policy solution.

-   "This guidance, however well intentioned, was last updated in 2006. Since that time, considerations involving data, including sensitive data, have become nearly ubiquitous in business practices for businesses of all sizes."
-   "These types of compliance burdens, the survey demonstrated, often result in a decrease in implementation of growth strategies and in hiring, as well as in higher prices."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The National Association of Neonatal Nurses (NANN) submitted comments to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Food and Drug Administration's (FDA) Request for Information (RFI) regarding the removal of outdated and unnecessary regulations to lower healthcare costs and empower providers.
*   NANN serves as the professional voice for more than 6,400 neonatal nurses and Advance Practice Registered Nurses (APRNs) across the United States.
    *   We advance the specialty of neonatal nursing through evidence-based education, clinical excellence, and advocacy.
    *   Neonatal nurses and APRNs are essential members of interprofessional teams.
        *   They care for the nation’s most fragile and medically complex patients, including critically ill newborns and premature infants.
        *   They support families during often life-altering experiences in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) and beyond.
*   We appreciate the Department’s recognition that many current regulations are barriers to timely, high-quality care.
*   We highlight three key regulatory areas where meaningful change can reduce costs and expand access to specialized neonatal and maternal care.

*   **1. Remove Barriers to Full Practice Authority for Advanced Practice Providers in Neonatal Care**
    *   NANN strongly urges HHS to eliminate federal regulatory barriers that prevent Neonatal APRNs from practicing to the full extent of their education and clinical training.
        *   Full Practice Authority (FPA) allows APRNs to independently assess, diagnose, and manage care, including prescribing medications, without burdensome or unnecessary physician oversight.
    *   While FPA is permitted in some states, regulatory inconsistencies across jurisdictions constrain the APRN’s ability to deliver consistent, high-quality care to newborns and families.
        *   This is particularly true in underserved and rural areas where physicians may be unavailable or stretched thin.
    *   These barriers not only limit providers but also delay essential neonatal interventions.
        *   Such delays can improve long-term developmental outcomes and reduce rehospitalizations.
    *   The neonatal population requires rapid, continuous, and highly skilled medical decision-making.
        *   Neonatal APRNs are expertly prepared to deliver this care.
    *   Federal health programs such as Medicare, Medicaid, and CHIP should reflect this reality by ensuring that APRNs can deliver services without restrictive collaboration requirements.
    *   HHS has the authority to set national standards within federal programs.
    *   We urge the Department to implement a regulatory framework that allows neonatal APRNs to practice fully and autonomously wherever they serve.

*   **2. Ensure Medicaid Participation for Rural Emergency Hospitals (REHs) to Protect Perinatal Access**
    *   NANN is deeply concerned by the Department’s interpretation that Rural Emergency Hospitals (REHs) are not eligible for Medicaid reimbursement in most cases.
        *   This interpretation directly threatens access to neonatal and perinatal care in rural areas.
        *   These regions are already disproportionately impacted by maternal and newborn care deserts.
        *   Desert counties showed a 36% higher risk for maternal death and a 26% increased risk for pregnancy-related mortality.
    *   Rural hospitals often provide essential maternity and newborn services, including access to Level I and II nurseries.
    *   Without Medicaid funding, many hospitals will not pursue REH designation despite the increased Medicare reimbursement it offers.
        *   Doing so would cut them off from a vital source of revenue for their predominantly Medicaid-covered populations.
    *   This regulatory stance stands in direct contrast to HHS' stated goals of improving maternal and infant health equity and reducing preventable neonatal mortality.
    *   It also contradicts the intent of Congress in creating REHs as a solution to prevent further closures of rural hospitals.
    *   We urge HHS to revise its interpretation of the REH statute to clearly allow Medicaid participation, thereby preserving neonatal and perinatal access in these vulnerable communities.

*   **3. Reform the CPT/RUC Process to Fairly Value Neonatal Nursing Services**
    *   The Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) and Relative Value Scale Update Committee (RUC) processes, currently governed by the American Medical Association (AMA), drive reimbursement decisions across Medicare and private payers.
    *   Unfortunately, this system has consistently undervalued the services provided by neonatal APRNs and RNs due to limited representation of nonphysician providers.
    *   Despite the critical role neonatal nurses and ARPNs play in NICUs and delivery rooms, managing complex ventilator-dependent patients, providing resuscitative care, and coordinating discharge planning, these contributions are often overlooked in reimbursement methodologies.
    *   NANN believes this lack of equitable representation in the CPT/RUC process results in undervaluation of neonatal nursing services.
    *   It also disincentivizes the deployment of advanced practice nurses in high-need settings.
    *   We urge CMS to reform the CPT/RUC structure by increasing transparency, mandating nonphysician participation, and requiring a more balanced panel composition.
        *   Specifically, CMS should renegotiate its contract with AMA.
        *   This renegotiation should ensure that reimbursement decisions are informed by a wider range of healthcare professionals, including neonatal APRNs and RNs.
    *   These reforms are essential to aligning payment models with the realities of modern, team-based neonatal care delivery.

*   **Conclusion**
    *   Neonatal nurses and APRNs are foundational to the care of the nation’s most vulnerable patients.
    *   Yet federal regulations continue to constrain their ability to deliver care efficiently and equitably.
    *   NANN urges HHS to prioritize the following regulatory reforms:
        *   Expand Full Practice Authority for neonatal APRNs across all federal programs.
        *   Ensure Medicaid eligibility for Rural Emergency Hospitals to protect access to maternal and neonatal care.
        *   Reform the CPT/RUC process to better recognize and value nursing contributions.
    *   We thank the Department for its commitment to regulatory reform and for the opportunity to share the perspectives of neonatal nursing professionals.
    *   NANN remains ready to work alongside HHS and FDA to develop thoughtful solutions that strengthen care for newborns, families, and providers alike.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The National Association of Neonatal Nurses urges HHS to remove federal barriers to full practice authority for neonatal APRNs, ensure Medicaid reimbursement for Rural Emergency Hospitals, and reform the CPT/RUC process to fairly value nursing services, all to enhance access to and quality of neonatal and maternal care.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I am commenting on the U.S Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
*   The years of pregnancy to age three set the foundation for a baby’s development, learning and relationships.
    *   Babies rely entirely on the adults around them—parents, caregivers, and early childhood professionals—to provide safe, nurturing care.
    *   When babies or their caregivers face reduced support or program quality, babies can end up facing long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences.
    *   When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health.
*   Regulations matter.
    *   HHS, as the leading Federal agency tasked with enhancing the health and well-being of all Americans, plays a critical role in ensuring that babies, families, and the professionals who care for little ones have access to the resources, protections, and supports they need.
    *   In considering changes to regulations, HHS must preserve regulations that:
        *   Keep young children safe and healthy.
        *   Enable the adults in their lives to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
*   For example, regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings are needed to keep babies safe and developmentally on track.
*   Regulations that keep children and those who care for them healthy, like those that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care, must be maintained.
    *   This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe.
*   HHS rules reach far beyond just Medicaid and early learning, with many HHS programs laying the foundation of quality care and critical support that babies need.
*   Any changes to regulations must be:
    *   Transparent.
    *   Grounded in evidence.
    *   Focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
*   Because each regulation is different, HHS must continue to give the public—including families and early childhood professionals like me—ample time and opportunity to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes.
    *   We need a robust public process to make sure that the rules work for babies and those who care for them.
*   To keep America’s babies healthy, HHS must maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services.
*   Please uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
*   I would also like to add that I am a product of Head Start Services.
    *   I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career.
    *   I have a Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma.
    *   I have been a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for the past twenty-three years servicing the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles.
    *   It gives great pleasure to give back to my community.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An experienced early childhood education professional and Head Start alumna urges HHS to maintain and strengthen regulations that ensure the safety, health, and development of young children, advocating for transparent, evidence-based changes and robust public input.

structuredSections.corePosition: I strongly believe that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) must preserve and uphold regulations that safeguard the health, safety, and development of young children from pregnancy to age three. These foundational years dictate lifelong well-being, and effective regulations, grounded in evidence and developed transparently with public input, are crucial for ensuring access to quality care and services.

    -   Maintain regulations that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care.

-   Provide ample time and opportunity for the public, including families and early childhood professionals, to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes through a robust public process.
-   Maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services for babies.
-   Uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
