structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Response to the HHS Request for Information: Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make America Healthy Again
*   To whom it may concern:
    *   I am writing on behalf of the New Jersey Head Start Association based in Bridgeton, New Jersey.
    *   Our suggestions focus on streamlining Head Start regulations while maintaining program strengths.
    *   The New Jersey Head Start Association represents the Early Head Start and Head Start programs of New Jersey.
    *   In 2024, these programs were funded for 13,376 infants, toddlers, preschool children, and pregnant women.
*   New Jersey Head Start programs provide the foundation for growing future leaders and strong communities.
    *   They foster children’s development, building essential foundations for early childhood learning for success in school and life.
*   New Jersey Head Start Association has observed the significant achievements resulting from being a national network of high-quality, comprehensive early learning programs.
    *   These programs are vested with the capability to design a program that reflects the community, a goal achievable only with local control.
    *   With this freedom and local control, programs in New Jersey have created innovative programs.
        *   Examples include outdoor garden centers, sensory classrooms, child care wrap services, partnerships with school districts and child care, art programs, and classrooms within homeless shelters.
*   New Jersey Head Start programs collaborate to continuously strengthen and improve programs.
    *   This ensures best practices are implemented in classrooms and communities.
    *   We support regulatory simplification aimed at improving our ability to best run our program.
    *   We urge you to maintain what makes Head Start strong in your efforts to improve efficiency and reduce bureaucracy.
*   In the spirit of continuous quality improvement, we recommend your consideration of these changes to regulation:
    *   **CLASS**
        *   Eliminate the use of CLASS as an instrument for monitoring programs.
        *   Instead, design the Aligned Monitoring System to integrate key aspects of classroom environment/interactions into the Focus Area 2 (FA2) monitoring.
        *   This would eliminate one of the three monitoring events that Head Start programs participate in during their five-year grant cycle, reducing monitoring costs.
    *   **CLASS thresholds**
        *   Elimination of CLASS would also eliminate thresholds that automatically place programs in the Designated Renewal System (DRS).
        *   Programs with significant classroom implementation issues can easily be identified during the FA2.
        *   When appropriate, these programs should be given the opportunity to improve through training and technical assistance, as well as follow-ups, rather than placing the entire program in jeopardy of closing.
        *   The DRS process results in numerous hours of ACF/OHS staff time reviewing grant proposals and negotiating with programs for new five-year cycle awards.
        *   It can also result in additional and unnecessary costs for licenses, facilities, and other start-up expenses.
        *   NJHSA recommends the removal of 1304.11(c).
    *   **Triggers for Designation Renewal System (DRS)**
        *   Triggers such as CLASS and non-systems-based Child Safety Incidents should either be eliminated or revised to ensure that only systemic, ongoing issues are included.
        *   While it is important to designate new grant recipients when the current grant recipient is no longer capable of providing appropriate services, the current system often places good, strong, and effective grant recipients in DRS.
        *   This results in time spent by grant recipients in compiling massive amounts of data, documentation, and responses as part of participating in the DRS process.
        *   In addition, during the uncertainty of the DRS process, programs often lose experienced, highly qualified staff to other employers.
        *   As a result, an increased amount of program funds are spent on employee recruitment and training.
        *   NJHSA recommends the overall revision of 1304.11 to ensure that only systemic and substantial issues are included.
        *   “Systemic,” according to the Cambridge Dictionary, is defined as “a systemic problem or change is a basic one, experienced by the whole of an organization or a country and not just particular parts of it.”
        *   “Substantial” is defined as “large in size, value, or importance.”
    *   **Federal Monitoring Events**
        *   Streamline the process of federal oversight of funding.
        *   Currently, federal funding is monitored through the Aligned Monitoring System’s Focus Area I and Focus Area II, Improper Payment Studies, annual audits, Office of Inspector General audits, and Defend the Spend.
        *   Monitoring events require significant staff time on documentation specific to the request of the monitor or auditor.
        *   Streamlining or integrating these monitoring approaches would reduce time spent on these activities and result in cost reductions.
    *   **Mental Health Services as outlined in the Final Rule**
        *   Mental health services to support the development of children is key to school success.
        *   However, the final rule requires ongoing, on-site collaboration with licensed mental health consultants, which for many programs, are not available.
        *   In many areas, especially rural or underserved communities, there is a shortage of qualified professionals and those available command high hourly rates.
        *   Programs must contract with private providers at market rates, which may exceed their budget capacity.
        *   In addition, the Final Rule emphasizes a preventative, continuous mental health approach, rather than episodic interventions.
        *   This includes regular classroom observations, teacher consultation, family engagement, and crisis intervention planning.
        *   This on-going scope of work increases staffing and consulting costs dramatically compared to the previous model.
        *   A mid-sized Head Start program might have to allocate $80,000–$150,000+ annually just to meet the basic mental health service expectations.
        *   These funds could otherwise support hiring more teachers, extending program hours, or enhancing curriculum.
        *   NJHSA recommends removing 1302.45 (a)(4)(i)(ii).
    *   **Transportation**
        *   Current regulations only allow for school buses or allowable alternate vehicles to be used for daily transportation of children.
        *   Transportation services are very expensive, including costs of buses, operations, and drivers.
        *   In addition, there has been a shortage of bus drivers throughout the country.
        *   NJHSA proposes revising 1303.71 to allow programs to develop alternate transportation services, including the use of public transportation, vans, and personal vehicles.
        *   This would require child safety seats, appropriate insurance, and the presence of an aide, parent, or legal caregiver during transportation.
    *   **Eligibility Documentation**
        *   The current process of extensive income verification places a significant administrative burden on staff.
        *   Adopting a simplified verification method and allowing automatic eligibility based on participation in other federal poverty programs (WIC, Child Care, LEA, Subsidized Housing, etc.) would streamline enrollment and reduce the time and resources required for eligibility determination.
        *   NJHSA proposes revisions to 1302.13(i).
    *   **Home Visitor Requirements**
        *   NJHSA recommends revising 1302.91(6)(i) to read “Obtain a minimum of a home-based CDA credential or…within 12 months of employment;and,….
        *   Current standards require the CDA at time of hire, placing an undue burden on programs since candidates rarely have the required certificate.
    *   **Family Partnership Services Ratio**
        *   The decreased ratios for family partnership services are creating a hardship for many programs, forcing them to hire additional staff without additional funding.
        *   NJHSA recommends the revision of 1302.52(d)(2) …no greater than 45:1…, as well as 1302.52(d)(2)(i), eliminating criteria for waiver, relying on programs to provide justification for the waiver based on the program and community needs.
    *   **Parent Education**
        *   Programs currently invest significant funds into research-based parenting curriculum.
        *   NJHSA proposes to revise 1302.51(b) to say “A program must offer opportunities for parents to participate in parenting curriculum that is reflective of the community, the program, and supports parent choice.”
    *   **Wages**
        *   The current standards support wage comparability and a living wage, an important aspect of supporting a high-quality program.
        *   The standards are not supported by funding, and potentially jeopardize programs in 2031.
        *   NJHSA recommends the following revisions:
            *   1302.90(e)(1)(i) – remove “promotes salaries that are comparable to similar services in relevant industries in their geographic area”.
            *   1302.90(e)(2) – Remove the following language from (i): “By August 1. 2031, a program must demonstrate it has made progress to parity with kindergarten through third grade teachers by ensuring that each Head Start teacher receives an annual salary that is at least comparable to the annual salary paid to preschool teachers in public school settings in the program’s local school district, adjusted for responsibilities, qualifications, experience, and schedule or hours worked.
            *   Keep and revise last sentence to say “A program may provide annual salaries to education staff who work directly with children comparable to a local or neighboring school district if the salaries are higher than a program’s local school district.”
            *   Eliminate (ii)-(iv).
            *   1302.90(e)(3) and (4) provide suitable guidance for salary floor and wage comparability and should remain.
            *   1302.90(e)(7)(i) – remove “if over the preceding four fiscal years, the average annual increase in Federal…was less than 1.3 percent.”
            *   Instead, criteria should be focused on program design and community impact.
    *   **Davis Bacon Act**
        *   While it would require a Congressional Act, NJHSA recommends raising the threshold from $2,000 to $75,000.
        *   Currently, programs must pay higher costs due to Davis-Bacon for many of its ongoing maintenance and repair costs such as painting, replacing flooring, and minor renovations like replacing windows as part of reducing heating/cooling costs.
        *   Head Start pays significantly higher costs out of its federal funds as compared to non-federal entities.
    *   **Early Head Start Teacher Requirements**
        *   NJHSA supports the bill currently under consideration in Congress, known as the HEADWAY Act.
        *   This Act aims to address the shortage of Early Head Start teachers by allowing some teachers to work while simultaneously pursuing their Child Development Associate (CDA) credential.
        *   This bipartisan legislation seeks to increase access to Early Head Start programs by providing more flexibility to hire and retain qualified staff.
*   In addition, we urge you to not eliminate requirements that are foundational to Head Start’s success.
    *   The federal framework, when coupled with local flexibility, has been key to maintaining high standards through good times and challenging times.
    *   For example, we highlight these areas of regulation that are essential in driving the high-quality programming that makes Head Start successful:
        *   1303.3 and 1301.4 are foundational to the success of Head Start.
            *   Engaging parents in leadership opportunities strengthens their role as a parent and contributes to the long-term success of their child.
            *   NJHSA has seen many parent Policy Council presidents grow to become leaders in their community as well as grow in their ability to create a self-sufficient household that supports the quality of life for their child.
        *   1302.30-1302.36 provide a framework for impactful high-quality services to children and their families.
            *   Research-based curriculums and child assessment tools ensure children are making progress with school readiness.
            *   Parent and family engagement, including home visits, create a partnership between parents and staff to support a lifetime of learning.
        *   1302.42-1302.44 is crucial for supporting children’s approach to learning.
            *   Children experiencing health, dental, or nutritional issues are unable to fully benefit from the learning environment.
*   Head Start programs in New Jersey have seen the lasting benefits to families, communities, and ultimately American taxpayers.
    *   Children who attend Head Start are more likely to graduate, secure stable employment, and actively contribute to the workforce.
    *   Families of Head Start benefit from greater stability and fewer barriers to workforce participation.
*   We support administrative simplification as part of continuous quality improvement efforts.
    *   Through this process, we prevail on you to recognize and support the core tenets of Head Start and how the flexibilities grant recipients currently have ensure that federal funds are maximized to create a program that is responsive to the community.
    *   And as always when considering changes, we ask for the opportunity to address potential unexpected outcomes of those changes.
*   Thank you for your support of Head Start and our shared desire to improve our ability to partner with families to ensure their and their children’s success.
*   Sincerely,
    *   Bonnie Eggenburg
    *   President
    *   New Jersey Head Start Association

- **Name/Organization:** New Jersey Head Start Association
- **Type:** Advocacy Group
- **Role/Expertise:** Represents Early Head Start and Head Start programs in New Jersey; currently funds 13,376 infants, toddlers, preschool children, and pregnant women.
- **Geographic Scope:** State (New Jersey), based in Bridgeton, New Jersey.

structuredSections.corePosition: We support regulatory simplification geared towards improving our ability to best run our program. We also urge you to maintain what makes Head Start strong in your efforts to improve efficiency and reduce bureaucracy. The New Jersey Head Start Association advocates for streamlining federal regulations to reduce administrative burden and costs, allowing for greater local flexibility and innovation, but emphasizes preserving the foundational aspects of Head Start that ensure high-quality, comprehensive early learning and family support services.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- **Eliminate CLASS as a monitoring instrument:**
  - Integrate key aspects of classroom environment/interactions into Focus Area 2 (FA2) monitoring.
  - This would eliminate one of three monitoring events, reducing costs.
- **Eliminate CLASS thresholds for Designated Renewal System (DRS) and revise DRS triggers:**
  - Remove 1304.11(c).
  - Ensure only systemic, ongoing, and substantial issues trigger DRS, not non-systems-based child safety incidents.
  - Allow programs with implementation issues identified during FA2 to improve through training, technical assistance, and follow-ups instead of DRS.
  - Revise 1304.11 overall.
- **Streamline Federal Monitoring Events:**
  - Integrate current monitoring approaches (Aligned Monitoring System’s Focus Area I & II, Improper Payment Studies, annual audits, OIG audits, Defend the Spend) to reduce staff time and costs.
- **Revise Mental Health Services requirements in the Final Rule:**
  - Remove 1302.45 (a)(4)(i)(ii) to address the shortage of licensed mental health consultants and high costs of continuous services.
- **Revise Transportation regulations:**
  - Revise 1303.71 to allow alternate transportation services like public transportation, vans, and personal vehicles, with requirements for child safety seats, insurance, and an aide/parent/caregiver.
- **Simplify Eligibility Documentation:**
  - Revise 1302.13(i) to adopt a simplified verification method and allow automatic eligibility based on participation in other federal poverty programs (e.g., WIC, Child Care, LEA, Subsidized Housing).
- **Revise Home Visitor Requirements:**
  - Revise 1302.91(6)(i) to allow home-based CDA credential to be obtained within 12 months of employment.
- **Revise Family Partnership Services Ratio:**
  - Revise 1302.52(d)(2) to state "no greater than 45:1."
  - Revise 1302.52(d)(2)(i) to eliminate criteria for waiver, relying on program justification based on program and community needs.
- **Revise Parent Education requirements:**
  - Revise 1302.51(b) to offer opportunities for parents to participate in parenting curriculum "reflective of the community, the program, and supports parent choice."
- **Revise Wage standards due to funding limitations:**
  - Remove 1302.90(e)(1)(i) language about promoting comparable salaries to similar services in relevant industries.
  - Revise 1302.90(e)(2) to remove the 2031 parity deadline with K-3 teachers and allow salaries comparable to local or neighboring school districts if higher than the program's local school district.
  - Remove 1302.90(e)(7)(i) criteria based on average annual Federal increase less than 1.3%, focusing criteria instead on program design and community impact.
  - Maintain 1302.90(e)(3) and (4) for salary floor and wage comparability guidance.
- **Increase Davis Bacon Act threshold (requires Congressional Act):**
  - Raise the threshold from $2,000 to $75,000.
- **Support the HEADWAY Act:**
  - Allow Early Head Start teachers to work while simultaneously pursuing their Child Development Associate (CDA) credential to address teacher shortages.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Burdensome and Costly Monitoring Systems:**
  - CLASS monitoring creates unnecessary monitoring events and automatic triggers for the Designated Renewal System (DRS).
  - The current DRS process is costly in terms of federal and program staff time, requiring massive data compilation and leading to the loss of experienced staff due to uncertainty.
  - Multiple, unintegrated federal monitoring events require significant staff time on documentation and increase overall program costs.
- **Unfunded Mandates and Cost Increases:**
  - Mental health services requirements (1302.45) necessitate expensive, ongoing, on-site collaboration with licensed consultants, who are often unavailable or too costly, especially in rural areas, diverting funds from other critical services like hiring teachers or extending program hours.
  - Decreased Family Partnership Services ratios create hardship by forcing programs to hire additional staff without corresponding additional funding.
  - Current wage comparability standards for teachers are not supported by sufficient funding and could jeopardize programs by 2031.
  - The low Davis Bacon Act threshold ($2,000) significantly increases costs for routine maintenance and repairs, reducing funds available for direct child and family services.
- **Administrative Burdens and Staffing Challenges:**
  - Extensive income verification for eligibility places a significant administrative burden on program staff.
  - The requirement for Home Visitors to have a CDA credential at the time of hire is an undue burden, as qualified candidates rarely possess it immediately, hindering recruitment.
  - High transportation costs and a national shortage of bus drivers limit program efficiency and service delivery under current restrictive regulations.
- **Risk to Program Quality and Stability:**
  - Current DRS triggers (e.g., CLASS, non-systemic child safety incidents) can unnecessarily place "good, strong and effective" grant recipients in DRS, leading to staff attrition and increased recruitment/training costs, rather than focusing on addressing systemic issues and supporting improvement.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- **Impact of Local Control:** New Jersey Head Start programs have leveraged local control to develop innovative initiatives, including outdoor garden centers, sensory classrooms, child care wrap services, partnerships with school districts, art programs, and even classrooms within homeless shelters.
- **Positive Outcomes of Parent Engagement:** The commenter highlights how parent engagement in leadership opportunities (e.g., Policy Council presidents) has fostered individual growth, leading parents to become community leaders and create self-sufficient households, directly contributing to their child's long-term success.
- **Financial Strain of Unfunded Mandates:** A specific example is provided, estimating that a mid-sized Head Start program might allocate "$80,000–$150,000+ annually just to meet the basic mental health service expectations—funds that could otherwise support hiring more teachers, extending program hours, or enhancing curriculum."
- **DRS's Detrimental Effects on Staff:** The Designated Renewal System (DRS) process is noted to cause programs to lose experienced, highly qualified staff due to the inherent uncertainty, consequently increasing costs associated with recruitment and training for replacement personnel.
- **Head Start's Long-term Societal Benefits:** The comment asserts that children who attend Head Start are "more likely to graduate, secure stable employment, and actively contribute to the workforce," demonstrating a significant, lasting return on investment for families, communities, and taxpayers.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "New Jersey Head Start Association has seen the great work that has come from being a national network of high quality comprehensive early learning programs vested with the capability to design a program that reflects the community, a goal that can only be achieved with local control."
- "A mid-sized Head Start program might have to allocate $80,000–$150,000+ annually just to meet the basic mental health service expectations—funds that could otherwise support hiring more teachers, extending program hours, or enhancing curriculum."
- "While it is important to designate new grant recipients when the current grant recipient is no longer capable of providing appropriate services, the current system often places good, strong and effective grant recipients in DRS."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The American Academy of Dermatology Association (AADA) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the Department of Health & Human Services’ (HHS) Request for Information (RFI) titled, "Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again."
*   AADA is the leading society in dermatological care, representing nearly 17,500 dermatologists nationwide.
    *   We are committed to excellence in the medical and surgical treatment of skin disease.
    *   We advocate for high standards in clinical practice, education, and research in dermatology and dermatopathology.
    *   We drive continuous improvement in patient care and outcomes while reducing the burden of disease.
*   To support deregulation in various areas under HHS’ purview and promote the health and well-being of Americans, we urge HHS to consider the following regulatory issues:
    *   I. Medicare Physician Payment Reform and Access to Care
        *   The AADA highlights the urgent need to modernize the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (PFS).
        *   For calendar year 2025, physicians have experienced a 2.83 percent reduction to the PFS conversion factor relative to 2024.
            *   This marks the fifth consecutive year of payment cuts.
        *   These reductions occur as the cost of delivering care continues to rise.
            *   The Medicare Economic Index, which reflects practice cost inflation, is projected to increase by 3.5 percent in 2025.
        *   Despite rising costs, physician payments remain tied to a statutory update frozen at zero percent through 2025, with only minimal updates scheduled to follow for most years thereafter.
            *   H.R. 1, “The One Big Beautiful Bill Act” provides for a temporary 2.5 percent payment increase to fee schedules for 2026.
        *   The Medicare PFS is the only major Medicare payment system that lacks a regular, inflation-based update, leaving physician practices without a reliable path to financial stability.
        *   Without sufficient updates, many practices are forced to scale back services, stop accepting new Medicare patients, or close.
            *   This directly affects access to care for beneficiaries and undermines the goal of a healthy America.
        *   Reports from federal advisors reinforce concerns about physicians' ability to provide care under the current payment system.
            *   In June, the Medicare Trustees again warned that payment updates are not keeping pace with practice costs and that access to Medicare-participating physicians could become a significant challenge.
            *   Similarly, the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) called for replacing scheduled 0.25 and 0.75 percent updates beginning in 2026 with a single permanent inflation-based update tied to a portion of the growth in the Medicare Economic Index.
            *   These recommendations reflect a growing consensus that the current approach for updating payments under the PFS is unsustainable.
        *   Additionally, annual payment updates are subject to statutory budget neutrality adjustments.
            *   These adjustments must be applied if certain policy changes are expected to increase or decrease payments under the PFS by more than $20 million relative to what payments would have been absent such changes.
            *   Congress has not updated this $20 million threshold since 1992, despite significant increases in total PFS spending over this time.
            *   Such budget neutrality adjustments can result in significant reductions to the PFS conversion factor when policy changes have significant payment impacts, as has occurred in recent years.
                *   For example, in the CY 2021 Medicare PFS final rule, CMS finalized changes to office and outpatient (O/O) evaluation and management (E/M) codes that would have led to a 10.2 percent budget neutrality reduction in the PFS conversion factor for the year and steep payment cuts for a broad swath of the physician community.
                *   Congressional intervention averted the majority of these cuts and what would have been substantial financial losses for many physicians and, more importantly, maintained access for patients.
                *   However, Congressional intervention is not guaranteed, as demonstrated by lack of Congressional action to avert the 2025 payment reduction, and the risk to physician payments is real.
        *   Furthermore, it is worth noting that budget neutrality adjustments are often overstated, and high utilization assumptions built into their calculation do not materialize.
            *   When an overestimation occurs, it contributes to budget neutrality reductions that remain uncorrected under current policy, resulting in unwarranted yet sustained reductions in the Medicare physician payment pool.
            *   For example, in 2013, transitional care management services were added to the PFS.
                *   While CMS estimated 5.6 million new claims, actual utilization was under 300,000 in the first year and less than a million after three years.
                *   This overestimation led to an estimated $5.2 billion reduction in Medicare physician payments from 2013 to 2021.
        *   While we recognize that these challenges are largely based on statutory requirements that apply to the PFS, we bring them to your attention given the significant burden they impose on physician practices and their direct impact on beneficiary access.
        *   Solo and small-group dermatology practices, in particular, report challenges retaining staff because they cannot offer wages that compete with local hospitals or even retail employers.
            *   Members frequently say that experienced staff leave for better pay and benefits, leading to constant turnover, increased training demands, added pressure on physicians, and decreased capacity to manage patient loads.
        *   To preserve access to care for Medicare beneficiaries, the AADA recommends that HHS work with Congress to establish a reliable, inflation-based update mechanism for physician payments and to increase the budget neutrality threshold to reflect inflation, as well as pursue corrections of erroneous utilization assumptions that contributed to unjustified budget neutrality adjustments.
    *   II. Drug Shortages
        *   Ongoing drug shortages continue to pose serious challenges for dermatology practices in the United States.
        *   Even routine, generic dermatologic drugs are affected by these shortages, including sodium bicarbonate and lidocaine with epinephrine.
            *   These local anesthetics are necessary for a range of office-based dermatologic procedures, including skin biopsy, excision, wound closure, tissue rearrangement, skin grafting, cauterization, non-ablative lasers, and ablative skin resurfacing.
        *   Access to local anesthetics is critical to ensuring patient comfort and safety during dermatologic procedures.
        *   However, persistent national shortages of medications, like lidocaine, have forced dermatologists, especially those in solo and small group practices, to ration supplies or delay care.
            *   Dermatologists practicing in underserved areas have reported limited to no supplies of lidocaine and lidocaine with epinephrine.
            *   Some are also facing shortages of sodium bicarbonate, which is often used to buffer lidocaine and reduce the pain of injection.
        *   These supply challenges are particularly burdensome for small and solo practices, as wholesalers tend to prioritize hospitals, health systems, and larger groups.
        *   Although supply chain issues contribute to drug shortages, regulatory barriers are often a more significant factor.
            *   Delays in FDA approvals, limited transparency around manufacturing disruptions, and burdensome post-approval requirements reduce manufacturers’ ability to respond to supply challenges.
            *   This is particularly true for commonly used dermatologic medications, such as sterile injectables, which are more complex to produce and less profitable, making them less attractive for sustained production.
        *   These regulatory challenges don’t just impact manufacturers, they have direct clinical consequences.
            *   When essential medications are in limited supply, physicians may be forced to modify treatment plans, delay procedures, or adjust clinical workflows, all of which can impact the efficiency and delivery of high-quality care.
        *   Ongoing shortages of essential medications threaten patients’ access to high-quality care and undermine the stability of clinical practice.
        *   Without regulatory reform, the drug supply will remain vulnerable to future disruptions.
        *   To address drug shortages that disrupt patient care and practice, the AADA urges HHS to direct the FDA to undertake regulatory reforms that strengthen the drug supply chain, reduce administrative burden, and prevent drug shortages.
        *   Additionally, we urge the FDA to prioritize diversifying the generic drug manufacturing base by reducing reliance on single-site production, increasing redundancy, and ensuring a minimum number of manufacturers for essential medications.
        *   Finally, the AADA urges the FDA to make facility inspection reports publicly available to help purchasers assess supply-chain risk, and to continue evaluating the use of buffer supply models to reduce shortages.
    *   III. Conclusion
        *   Thank you again for the opportunity to provide comments on HHS’s deregulation efforts.
        *   We look forward to collaborating with you to reform Medicare payment and strengthen the drug supply chain, ensuring that dermatologists and their patients have timely access to safe and effective treatments.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   University of Utah Health (U of U Health) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation to Make American Healthy Again, AHRQ-2025-0001.
*   CMS Inpatient Quality Reporting (IQR) Program: THA/TKA PRO-PM Response Rates
    *   We appreciate that CMS is incorporating patient-reported outcomes (PROs) measures into the IQR program.
        *   PROs are a meaningful way to track what is most important to the patient.
        *   PROs also contribute to positive clinical outcomes and meaningful performance improvement work.
    *   To avoid Annual Payment Update (APU) penalties with the THA/TKA PRO-PM measure, hospitals must collect both pre-op and post-op questionnaires from at least 50% of joint procedure patients.
        *   Collecting this information is difficult for hospitals and providers to control, and it is financially burdensome.
        *   Specifically, patients may not return to the doctor’s office for a one-year follow-up visit.
        *   Patients may not answer phone calls from our call center.
        *   Patients may not respond to requests sent via our electronic patient portal.
        *   These factors make it especially challenging to obtain a one-year post-op questionnaire from 50% of patients.
    *   CMS recently published information on response rates for organizations that participated in voluntary reporting for this metric.
        *   The number of respondent hospitals was small (under 100).
        *   Only 57% of those organizations had a 50% or higher response rate.
    *   Penalizing a large percentage of organizations with negative payment adjustments due to a patient’s lack of response causes undue administrative and financial burden on the provider.
    *   We urge CMS to review actual pre-op and post-op response rates submitted by providers over the next two years and revise the response rate requirement to a feasible percentage based on data.
*   CMS Physician Fee Schedule Rule: The Quality Payment Program, APMs, MIPS, and MVPs
    *   We appreciate that CMS is mindful of developing policies for the Quality Payment Program that rewards high-quality care for patients and reduces the cost of healthcare for patients and Medicare.
    *   With these goals in mind, U of U Health has concerns with the significant administrative burdens and resource costs that we must incur in order to participate in advanced QPP tracks.
        *   Namely, the Advanced APMs and MIPS Value Pathways (MVP) programs demand substantial administrative, IT, and provider resources to keep pace with annual program changes and new measures, models, and/or MVPs.
        *   It can take multiple years and extensive resources to build and validate measures, communicate and work with providers on performance improvement, and complete annual submissions.
    *   On top of the administrative burden concerns, we are concerned that many providers participate in the MIPS program to avoid negative payment adjustments, not to obtain rewards for high performance.
        *   Under 2023 performance data, the reward for a perfect score of 100 was only +2.15%.
        *   The penalty for not participating is substantial (-9%).
        *   The budget neutrality aspect of the program, along with the removal of the exceptional performance bonus, has made the “reward” for being a high performer so negligible that the program is fundamentally flawed.
        *   Clinicians are now incurring high administrative costs just to avoid penalties.
    *   We appreciate and understand the intent for creating MVPs, with the aim of creating measures and performance categories that are relevant to a specialty or medical condition.
    *   However, we echo concerns shared previously that MVPs substantially increase the administrative burden on providers. For example:
        *   Multi-specialty TINs must build and maintain a significantly higher number of quality measures.
        *   Because some MVPs do not have enough eCQMs, clinicians are often required to partner with costly external registries to select other measures.
        *   Multi-specialty TIN organizations must work on multiple improvement activities simultaneously to meet the different improvement activity requirements of multiple MVPs.
        *   Providers must devote additional staff resources to complete a high number of annual registrations and submissions and to develop increasingly complex reporting tools.
    *   We urge CMS to carefully consider the actual cost that providers incur to successfully participate in these programs.
    *   We believe CMS should carefully consider the administrative and financial burdens that participation in these programs require of providers so that an accurate cost and benefit analyses is an essential component of developing future program plans.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: University of Utah Health urges CMS to reduce the burdensome administrative and financial requirements of quality reporting and payment programs, especially regarding patient-reported outcome response rates and MIPS Value Pathways, which currently penalize providers more than they incentivize high-quality care.

    *   The 50% patient response rate requirement for pre-op and post-op questionnaires is difficult for hospitals and providers to control and financially burdensome.
        *   Patients may not return for one-year follow-up visits.

The budget neutrality aspect of the program, along with the removal of the exceptional performance bonus, has made the “reward” for being a high performer so negligible that the program is fundamentally flawed. Clinicians are now incurring high administrative costs just to avoid penalties."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   OCHIN responds to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again (AHRQ-2025-0001).
*   OCHIN applauds HHS’ leadership in pursuing a historic deregulatory effort that restricts innovation, drives up costs, and punishes small, independent providers, especially in rural and low-resource communities that already operate on tight margins.
*   **Promoting a Level Playing Field in Healthcare**
    *   OCHIN is a national nonprofit health information technology and research network.
    *   It serves over 2,000 community health care sites with 34,000 providers in 43 states.
    *   Members include rural health clinics, critical access hospitals (CAHs), frontier providers, and federally qualified health centers (FQHCs).
    *   These members face the highest barriers with the fewest resources, yet they deliver efficient, high-quality care despite outdated policies that make it harder for them to survive, grow, or innovate.
    *   OCHIN's providers serve on the frontlines and compete in some of the most fragile and resource-constrained healthcare markets in America.
    *   Instead of being supported to innovate, these providers are often penalized by federal regulations that were designed for large, consolidated health systems.
    *   The cost of compliance with outdated or misaligned regulations can mean the difference between survival and closure for these providers.
*   **It’s Time for a Deregulatory Roadmap that Works for All Providers**
    *   As HHS undertakes its largest deregulatory initiative, OCHIN urges the Department to focus on rules and requirements that limit provider flexibility, increase public program costs, and stifle innovation, particularly for providers in rural and low-resourced communities.
    *   The following priorities, detailed further in the Appendix, reflect areas where regulatory reform can reduce unnecessary burden, improve care delivery, and ensure Medicare and Medicaid dollars are spent effectively.
        *   **Address Infrastructure Price Inflations.**
            *   Private equity acquisitions of essential healthcare infrastructure, including electronic health records and digital tools, have led to rising prices without equivalent improvements in service or value.
            *   These costs are passed through to providers and ultimately taxpayers.
            *   CMS should consider oversight mechanisms to promote pricing transparency and prevent cost spikes that disproportionately impact providers in rural and low-resourced communities.
        *   **Modernize Program Integrity Rules.**
            *   Shared staffing models, telehealth collaborations, and pooled infrastructure are essential in low-resourced areas.
            *   Current Anti-Kickback and Stark rules can expose well-meaning providers to compliance risk.
            *   CMS should use its authority to test waivers and safe harbors that support rural innovation without undermining program integrity.
        *   **Remove Licensure Barriers for Rural Trainees.**
            *   Cross-state licensure rules make it too hard for providers, and even harder for medical residents, to serve where they are needed.
            *   CMS should explore deregulatory strategies to enable rural training rotations and expand access through broader licensure mobility, in coordination with state and federal partners.
*   **CONCLUSION**
    *   OCHIN urges HHS to prioritize practical reforms that lift unnecessary burdens and let providers focus on care, not compliance.
    *   Deregulation should work for small, rural, and community-based providers, not just large systems.
    *   This is a chance to cut red tape, lower costs, and build a health system that works for everyone.
*   **APPENDIX**
    *   **Strengthen Oversight of Post-Acquisition Cost Increases in Health IT and Infrastructure.**
        *   Private equity acquisition of essential healthcare infrastructure, including technology used in the delivery of health services, has in some cases resulted in exorbitant price increases that are not always accompanied by meaningful improvements in service or value.
        *   These cost spikes are absorbed by independent providers and passed through to public programs like Medicare and Medicaid, especially in rural markets where options are limited, thereby raising costs for taxpayers.
        *   CMS should coordinate with other federal agencies to establish oversight mechanisms and cost safeguards related to private equity acquisitions of essential health infrastructure, including certified health IT systems and digital platforms required for participation in Medicare and Medicaid.
        *   Such scrutiny is vital to protect public healthcare spending and ensure small and rural providers are not priced out of the systems they need to operate.
    *   **Modernize Anti-Kickback, Stark, and Program Integrity Rules for Rural and Safety-Net Innovation.**
        *   Providers in rural and underserved areas often rely on shared staffing models, virtual specialty networks, pooled infrastructure, and training collaborations to meet patient needs.
        *   Broad application of the Anti-Kickback Statute (42 U.S. Code § 1320a-7b), Stark Law (42 U.S.C. § 1395nn), and other program integrity rules make it legally risky to innovate, even when there is no intent to defraud.
        *   This limits opportunities to expand the training pipeline, strengthen care coordination, and expand patient access.
        *   CMS should initiate or expand waivers and safe harbors to allow rural and low-resourced providers to legally participate in shared infrastructure models and workforce collaborations that would otherwise risk triggering compliance penalties under Stark Law, Anti-Kickback Statute, or other program integrity regulations.
        *   These updates would protect taxpayers, reduce legal risk, and help local clinics survive and grow without fear of penalty.
    *   **Remove Regulatory Barriers to Cross-State Practice for Rural Medical Trainees.**
        *   State-by-state licensure frameworks limit provider flexibility and create regional provider shortages by making it harder for fully licensed doctors and medical residents to practice across state lines, even when rural areas are desperate for care.
        *   These barriers block telehealth expansion, reduce competition among health professionals, and limit the rural training pipeline that helps the next generation of doctors grow.
        *   These steps would increase care access, strengthen rural workforces, and break down anti-competitive barriers that prevent qualified providers from serving where they are needed most.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: OCHIN, a national health information technology and research network, urges HHS to prioritize deregulation efforts that address rising health IT costs, modernize program integrity rules, and remove licensure barriers to specifically benefit rural and low-resource healthcare providers and ensure their survival and ability to innovate.

structuredSections.corePosition: OCHIN applauds HHS's initiative to reduce regulatory burdens and urges the Department to focus its deregulatory efforts on policies that specifically limit flexibility, increase costs, and stifle innovation for rural and low-resourced healthcare providers. We believe a tailored deregulatory roadmap is critical to ensure these providers, who are penalized by regulations designed for large health systems, can survive, grow, and continue delivering high-quality care in fragile markets.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- CMS should consider oversight mechanisms to promote pricing transparency and prevent cost spikes related to essential healthcare infrastructure (like EHRs and digital tools) that disproportionately impact providers in rural and low-resourced communities.
  - Require price transparency reporting for vendors whose products are necessary for CMS program participation.
  - Monitor post-acquisition price increases that exceed medical inflation without clear improvements in value.
  - Prioritize independent provider feedback in rulemaking on vendor certification or compliance programs.
- CMS should initiate or expand waivers and safe harbors to allow rural and low-resourced providers to legally participate in shared infrastructure models and workforce collaborations that would otherwise risk triggering compliance penalties under Stark Law, Anti-Kickback Statute, or other program integrity regulations.
  - Expand pilot waiver authority through CMS Innovation Center for virtual networks.
  - Codify safe harbors for telehealth, shared services, and training collaborations among safety-net providers.
  - Provide clearer carve-outs for arrangements involving Rural Emergency Hospitals, Critical Access Hospitals, and FQHCs.
- CMS should explore deregulatory strategies to enable rural training rotations and expand access through broader licensure mobility, in coordination with state and federal partners.
  - Incentivize state participation in the Interstate Medical Licensure Compact.
  - Establish a CMS-facilitated rural rotation exemption that allows cross-state training and supervision.
  - Recognize uniform credentialing mechanisms for Medicare-participating teaching institutions.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- Private equity acquisitions of essential healthcare infrastructure (e.g., electronic health records, digital tools) have led to exorbitant price increases for providers without equivalent improvements in service or value, with these costs being passed to public programs and taxpayers, disproportionately impacting rural and low-resource communities.
- Current Anti-Kickback and Stark rules broadly applied make it legally risky for well-meaning providers in rural and underserved areas to utilize essential shared staffing models, telehealth collaborations, and pooled infrastructure, even when there is no intent to defraud.

- Outdated or misaligned federal regulations designed for large, consolidated health systems often penalize small, independent, rural, and low-resource providers, making it harder for them to survive, grow, or innovate.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:

- The organization points out a critical disconnect where federal regulations, designed for large, consolidated health systems, inadvertently penalize small, independent providers, with the cost of compliance sometimes meaning the difference between survival and closure.
- They identify a specific, surprising consequence of private equity acquisitions in the healthcare IT sector: these acquisitions have led to significant price increases for essential infrastructure without corresponding improvements in service or value, which directly burdens independent and rural providers and public programs.
- OCHIN provides insight into how existing program integrity rules, like Anti-Kickback and Stark laws, inadvertently create legal risk for essential collaborative models (shared staffing, telehealth, pooled infrastructure) that are crucial for providers in low-resource areas to meet patient needs.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   My ADHD brain has always been a source of originality and energy
    *   I can pitch ideas others would never consider
    *   I can build out complex marketing plans from scratch
    *   I can improvise when things fall apart
    *   It’s a superpower - until it’s not
*   When I’m not on my meds, the thoughts pile up faster than I can process them
    *   Deadlines slip
    *   Priorities vanish
    *   Emails go unanswered
    *   And then comes the shame spiral
*   I was undiagnosed most of my adult life
    *   I lost multiple jobs - not because I lacked skill, but because I couldn’t keep up with the pace of follow-through that neurotypical workplaces demand
    *   At one point, I had a full client list but still ended up broke because I couldn’t manage invoices, emails, or even my calendar
    *   Sleep was impossible
        *   I’d be up till 3 a.m., my mind replaying all the little things I forgot
    *   Social events felt like landmines
        *   I’d either talk too much
        *   I’d zone out mid-conversation
        *   I’d forget I’d even RSVPed
*   Getting properly diagnosed was a turning point
    *   My provider, through telehealth, was the first person who actually understood what I was experiencing
    *   Once I started medication, it felt like my brain had space to breathe
        *   I could sort through the chaos
        *   I could focus on one thing at a time
        *   I could sleep without hours of racing thoughts
    *   But staying on medication has become its own full-time job
*   Every month, I deal with pharmacy roulette
    *   Is it in stock?
    *   Which generic will they give me this time?
    *   Will it work the same?
    *   Will I be able to fill it before the weekend, or will I go days without meds and spiral again?
    *   It’s exhausting. And the fact that this is happening in a regulated healthcare system tells me something is deeply broken.
*   Why are ADHD meds still in the same class with some of the most heavily restricted and abuse-prone substances, such as methadone and fentanyl, when the evidence just doesn’t support that level of control?
    *   These medications have helped millions of people function for decades.
    *   They don’t deserve to be lumped into the same box as substances with wildly different abuse potential and social impact.
    *   Misuse exists, sure - but when the system makes legal use so fragile, what do you expect?
*   I’m not asking for special treatment. I’m asking for a system that doesn’t punish me for having a diagnosable, treatable disabling condition.
*   We need telehealth permanently so people like me can get proper care without jumping through hoops.
*   And we need the DEA to stop treating our meds like illicit substances - we’re creative people trying to build lives, not criminals.
*   And for once, design regulations around how people actually live - not outdated fears and bureaucratic inertia.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An individual with ADHD advocates for permanent telehealth and less restrictive regulation of ADHD medication, citing severe personal and professional struggles caused by current access barriers and misclassification of their essential medication.

The system creates unnecessary barriers to essential medication, leading to significant personal and professional hardship. Regulations should be designed based on how people actually live, not outdated fears or bureaucratic inertia.

- The DEA should cease treating ADHD medications with the same level of restriction as highly abuse-prone illicit substances.
- Regulations concerning ADHD medication should be designed based on the real-world needs and lives of patients, rather than on outdated fears or bureaucratic inertia.

    - Belief that evidence does not support this level of control for ADHD medications.
    - The system's fragility in providing legal access may inadvertently contribute to misuse.
- The healthcare system effectively punishes individuals for having a diagnosable and treatable disabling condition.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I am commenting on the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
*   I am a mother of two children with special needs who have used and benefited from programs under the Medicaid program.
    *   These programs provided services they otherwise would not have received due to both the cost of private therapies and lack of access to healthcare in rural Texas.
    *   Thanks to the services my children have received, they are now in school in the gifted and talented classes, succeeding in ways we did not once think possible.
    *   My oldest child went from 3 years of speech therapy being totally nonverbal to having a solo in her first-grade concert.
    *   We are living testaments that investing 1 dollar into babies and toddlers saves on average 3 dollars down the road.
*   The years of pregnancy to age three set the foundation for a baby’s development, learning, and relationships.
    *   Babies rely entirely on the adults around them—parents, caregivers, and early childhood professionals—to provide safe, nurturing care.
    *   When babies or their caregivers face reduced support or program quality, babies can end up facing long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences.
    *   When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health.
*   Regulations matter.
    *   As the leading Federal agency tasked with enhancing the health and well-being of all Americans, HHS plays a critical role in ensuring that babies, families, and the professionals who care for little ones have access to the resources, protections, and supports they need.
    *   In considering changes to regulations, HHS must preserve regulations that keep young children safe and healthy.
    *   HHS must also preserve regulations that enable the adults in their lives to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
    *   For example:
        *   Regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings are needed to keep babies safe and developmentally on track.
        *   Regulations that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care must be maintained.
        *   This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe.
*   HHS rules reach far beyond just Medicaid and early learning, with many HHS programs laying the foundation of quality care and critical support that babies need.
    *   Any changes to regulations must be transparent, grounded in evidence, and focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
    *   Because each regulation is different, HHS must continue to give the public—including families and early childhood professionals like me—ample time and opportunity to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes.
    *   We need a robust public process to make sure that the rules work for babies and those who care for them.
*   To keep America’s babies healthy, HHS must maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services.
*   Please uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: A mother of special needs children from rural Texas urges HHS to preserve existing regulations for early childhood development and Medicaid programs, emphasizing their crucial role in children's health, safety, and long-term success.

These regulations, from provider ratios to early intervention services, are vital for ensuring all babies have a strong start in life and prevent long-term negative consequences, proving that early investment yields significant societal savings.

- Preserve regulations that enable adults in children's lives to provide care for healthy growth and development.
    - Specifically, maintain regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings.
    - Maintain regulations that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care.
- Ensure any changes to regulations are transparent, grounded in evidence, and focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
- Continue to give the public—including families and early childhood professionals—ample time and opportunity to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes.
    - Implement a robust public process for regulatory changes.
- Uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
- Maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services for America's babies.

- Potential for reduced support or program quality if regulations are not preserved, leading to long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences for babies.
- Risk of children not receiving necessary care (e.g., therapies, screenings, early intervention) due to cost or lack of access, particularly in rural areas.
- Concern that without proper regulations, basic quality and access to services for young children could be compromised.
- Risk that regulatory changes could be made without sufficient transparency, evidence-basis, or focus on child well-being and safety.
- Inadequate public input process for proposed regulatory changes could result in rules that do not work for babies and their caregivers.

- Personal anecdote of her oldest child transitioning from being totally nonverbal after 3 years of speech therapy (accessed via Medicaid) to having a solo in her first-grade concert, demonstrating the profound impact of early intervention services.
- Observation that her special needs children, who benefited from these programs, are now succeeding in gifted and talented classes, illustrating long-term positive outcomes.
- Insight that "investing 1 dollar into babies and toddlers saves on average 3 dollars down the road," highlighting the long-term economic benefits of early childhood programs.
- Experience with the crucial role of Medicaid in overcoming barriers of high costs for private therapies and lack of healthcare access in rural Texas.

- "We are living testaments that investing 1 dollar into babies and toddlers saves on average 3 dollars down the road."
- "When babies or their caregivers face reduced support or program quality, babies can end up facing long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   **Introduction**
    *   The National Indian Child Welfare Association (NICWA) submits comments on the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) request for information regarding deregulation (Docket: AHRQ-2025-0001).
    *   Our comments focus on the impacts to Native children and families regarding human service programs under the Administration for Children and Families (ACF).
    *   Tribal Nations have a unique political relationship with the Federal government based on treaties, the United States Constitution, United States Supreme Court decisions, and Federal law.
    *   This government-to-government relationship reflects the U.S. acknowledgement of Tribal Nations as sovereign governments and the millions of acres of land ceded in exchange for the Federal government assuming a Federal trust obligation to ensure the well-being of Native people.
    *   These trust and treaty obligations apply to all Federal departments, including HHS.
    *   HHS also operates under departmental policies that acknowledge and emphasize this government-to-government relationship and require consultation with Tribal Nations on policies that impact Tribal citizens, such as deregulation.
    *   While NICWA appreciates the department’s desire to improve the effectiveness and efficiency of HHS through deregulation, something also important to Tribal Nations and Native organizations, deregulation that impacts Tribal Nation programs must be conducted pursuant to a nation-to-nation relationship.
    *   This requires adherence to formal government-to-government protocols, which begin with consultation before decisions are made that impact Tribal communities.

*   **Models for Future Policy Change**
    *   For Tribal Nations, policy changes that further Tribal self-governance principles and are in alignment with Federal trust and treaty obligations are priorities.
    *   Examples of current Federal policy that can be a model for future changes include:
        *   Empowering Tribal Nations to utilize community standards for determining program eligibility for Head Start programs operating in Tribal communities.
        *   Allowing Tribal Nations to select which eligible child welfare services to concentrate their Title IV-B, Subpart 2 funding in.
        *   Authorizing Tribal Nations that operate the Title IV-E Prevention Services program to utilize community-based standards to define what is an eligible prevention service.
        *   Public Law 102-477 that allows Tribal Nations to streamline and consolidate administrative requirements between various Federal human service programs that address training, employment, and related services.
    *   The following section provides supplementary information to further emphasize the vital role these policy changes play in enhancing the efficiency and effectiveness of Tribal programs.
        *   **Head Start**
            *   P.L. 118-47 granted Head Start programs additional flexibility to serve children in Tribal communities.
            *   These provisions ensure Tribal Head Start programs can prioritize enrolling children who are Tribal members or whose family or household members are Tribal members, regardless of family income.
            *   The Office of Head Start Program Instruction ACF-OHS-PI-24-03 outlines the discretion that Tribal Head Start programs have regarding determinations of eligibility for Head Start services regardless of income, including both Tribal children and other children in the Tribal service area.
            *   This change is designed to ensure that Tribal Head Start programs can serve more children and have flexibility and decision-making power to determine how best to deliver services to children and families in their service area.
            *   Securing more flexibility in Head Start eligibility helps Tribal programs operate more efficiently by reducing bureaucratic barriers and tailoring services to community needs, which supports long-term program sustainability and family stability.
        *   **Title IV-B**
            *   Title IV-B of the Social Security Act provides the Secretary of HHS with the ability to waive a requirement for Tribal grantees that requires them to spread out their Title IV-B funding equally among all the eligible service categories.
            *   For Tribal Nations, especially Tribes that receive smaller allocations, this created a barrier to designing child welfare programming that was responsive to the needs of their families and the realities of having fewer funds for prevention services overall.
            *   The waiver allows Tribal Nations to use their funding as needed and concentrate the funding in the service categories that provide the most opportunity to prevent out-of-home removal and longer stays in the child welfare system, and partner with State child welfare systems that benefit from accessing Tribal services and support.
        *   **Title IV-E**
            *   The Children’s Bureau published new policies in their Child Welfare Policy Manual that expand flexibility to Tribal Nations that are operating the Title IV-E program under an agreement with a State Title IV-E agency.
            *   The new policies clarify that a Tribe in an agreement with a State may provide prevention programs and services adapted to the needs and standards of their communities—an essential step to strengthen program effectiveness, which both states and Tribes support.
            *   Aligning prevention services with community standards improves program efficiency by reducing the need for future child welfare involvement and supporting families in achieving stability and self-sufficiency sooner.
            *   It also provides States with greater flexibility to partner with Tribal Nations in a manner that supports the best possible services targeted to the needs of Tribal families.
        *   **Public Law 102-477**
            *   Public Law 102-477 allows Tribal Nations to streamline and consolidate administrative requirements between various Federal human service programs that address training, employment, and related services.
            *   477 fits well with HHS’s priorities to increase efficiency by reducing reporting and administrative requirements, allowing Tribal Nations to effectively deliver services to their Tribal citizens.
            *   ACF’s efforts under 477 have broadened the range of consolidated programs to include child welfare services, such as Title IV-B child welfare grants which contribute to parenting capacity and ability to achieve self-sufficiency.
            *   This expansion further streamlines administrative processes, thereby enabling Tribal Nations to provide integrated services that intentionally address the interconnected needs of families—promoting stability and positive health outcomes.
    *   These examples highlight how policy changes drive the development of regulations that serve Tribal Nations and support Tribal self-determination.
    *   Together, policy and regulations ensure Tribal Nations have the necessary resources to operate effective and efficient programs that are responsive to the needs of their communities.

*   **Current Policy that Supports Native Children, Families, and Tribal Nations and Improves Program Effectiveness and Efficiency**
    *   We recognize that Federal regulations serve a critical purpose in improving policy and services to Native children and families and promoting partnership between state and Tribal governments.
    *   Below are a few examples of regulations that we believe align with shared goals of achieving department efficiency and improving program effectiveness.
        *   **AFCARS**
            *   The 2024 Adoption and Foster Care Analysis Reporting System (AFCARS) regulations (RIN 0970-AC98) require collection of new data on Native children and families in State child welfare systems as mandated under the Supporting America’s Children and Families Act (P.L. 118-258, Section 107).
            *   These new data elements will provide Tribal Nations, States, and Federal officials with previously unavailable data and insights into the trends and impacts of services on outcomes for Native children.
            *   The value of this data in developing targeted technical assistance, improving outcomes for Native children, and promoting stronger State and Tribal partnerships is invaluable and should be protected during the deregulation process.
        *   **Foster Care Legal Representation**
            *   The 2024 Foster Care Legal Representation regulations (RIN 0970-AC89) are another example that promote greater protection and support for improved State-Tribal relationships and the potential for improved decision-making in child welfare for Native children and families.
            *   The final rule provides clarification on the use of Title IV-E administrative funds to support legal representation of the child welfare agency, children, and parents in foster care proceedings in either Tribal or state systems and for legal representation of a Tribal Nation in state child welfare proceedings involving their Tribal children.
            *   Studies indicate the criticality of children and parents having legal representation in child welfare proceedings and the benefits of this representation in securing appropriate placements, better judicial decisions, safe return to parents, and reduced stays in foster care.
            *   For many Tribal Nations, their capacity to provide legal representation as parties in state proceedings involving their Tribal children is challenging, which also restricts the court’s access to valuable Tribal knowledge, perspective, and resources that can improve case planning and service outcomes.
            *   Providing reasonable opportunities to support the cost of legal representation for children, parents, and Tribal Nations can save dollars over the long-term with more effective decision-making.
        *   **Child Care**
            *   In November 2024, HHS issued a final rule (RIN 0970-AD11) to increase flexibility for Tribal Nations to use funds from the Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) without a previously imposed income requirement on eligibility to receive services.
            *   The final rule eliminates the previous requirement that only Tribal Nations who received award allocations of less than $250,000 could have flexibility in determining which children could receive child care services supported by CCDF funds.
            *   The final rule extended the flexibility to determine eligibility for tribal CCDF child care services to all Tribal Nations regardless of the size of their CCDF grant.
            *   This flexibility allows Tribal Nations to exercise their sovereignty and make determinations for CCDF funded child care services that reflect community standards and align with service delivery realities that limit access to child care services to Tribal members living on Tribal lands, many in remote locations.
            *   Flexibility in funding also allows Tribal Nations to align child care with other supportive programs that support the stability of Native families, including home visiting, Head Start and Early Head Start, and Tribally funded preschool, all of which can be integrated to strengthen care provided to children and the support offered to their families.
            *   Regulatory changes that increase flexibility give Tribal Nations more control to determine how best to meet the needs of their families and communities, while promoting family unity and self-sufficiency.
        *   **Child Support**
            *   In February 2024, the Office of Child Support Services issued a final rule (RIN 0970-AC99) eliminating the non-federal share of program expenditures requirement for Tribal child support programs.
            *   This change removes a significant financial barrier that has prevented many Tribal Nations from developing and maintaining child support services.
            *   The final rule recognizes the need to ensure that Tribal Nations can focus their attention on meeting the needs of their families and communities and less time trying to meet the non-Federal share requirement.
            *   Commentors underscored in the public comment process that this requirement brought disruption and instability to program operations, especially for Tribal Nations that have few resources or opportunities to generate Tribal revenue.
            *   Eliminating the non-federal share requirement reduces burden on Tribal child support programs and ensures they can focus on expansion of community-based child support services that reflect community needs and support family stability.
            *   This change exemplifies how regulations can be adapted to be more responsive to the needs of Tribal communities and must be safeguarded under HHS deregulation initiatives to respect and strengthen Tribal sovereignty.

*   **Areas for Future Policy Development for Tribal Nations**
    *   As HHS considers areas where new regulations or policy are needed, we encourage them to consult with Tribal Nations on the best approaches to support effective and efficient services.
    *   Title IV-B provides some of the most flexible federal funding for Tribal Nations and states to help children at risk of entering foster care remain safely at home, promoting family unity, enhancing system effectiveness, and reducing both the overall costs and the length of time children spend in out-of-home care.
    *   With the passage of the Supporting America’s Children and Families Act (P.L. 118-258), there are several provisions in the law that will require additional guidance for both States and Tribes.
    *   For example, P.L. 118-258 allows the Secretary to modify reporting requirements for Tribes and States.
    *   Regulations should provide clear guidance on how to exercise this authority to reduce administrative burdens for Tribes and States—ensuring more time and resources are dedicated to delivering essential services to families.
    *   P.L. 118-258 also contains provisions that require:
        *   New data collection.
        *   Authorizes technical assistance to states and Tribes to improve their implementation of the Indian Child Welfare Act.
        *   Maximize engagement of Tribal Nations in state child welfare proceedings involving their Tribal members.
        *   Allow the Secretary of HHS to waive or modify an application requirement or matching requirement for Tribal grants addressing the needs of foster children who have parents that are incarcerated.
    *   These and other provisions in the new law that impact Tribal access and utilization of Title IV-B funding will need guidance that is informed by consultation by Tribal Nations and other experts in Tribal child welfare services.
    *   At a recent Administration of Children and Families Tribal Advisory Committee meeting, ACF committed to holding listening sessions and Tribal consultations to inform and plan for the implementation of the new Tribal provisions under P.L. 118-258.
    *   This commitment is appreciated and will help set the stage for meaningful consultation on the critical issues that will shape the implementation of the new law for Tribal Nations.

*   **Conclusion**
    *   Tribal Nations are ready to work with HHS to support deregulation that enhances program efficiency and effectiveness while advancing the principles of Tribal self-governance and upholds Federal trust and treaty obligations.
    *   Consultation ahead of decisions to propose or make regulation changes will be critical in ensuring that Federal trust and treaty obligations are upheld, federal agencies are exposed to Tribal perspectives and experiences, and changes advance policy that supports effective Tribal administration of federal programs and retains important protections for Native children and families.
