structuredSections.detailedContent:
- I’ve lived with ADHD since childhood but only got a formal diagnosis in my mid-30s
  - Growing up, I was always the “daydreamer” or “spacey” one
    - Teachers thought I wasn’t trying
    - I was constantly reminded that I wasn’t living up to my potential
  - I dropped out of college twice because I just couldn’t keep track of assignments and deadlines
    - That left me with thousands of dollars in student debt and no degree to show for it
  - My untreated ADHD also led to years of insomnia
    - I’d spend countless nights unable to turn my brain off
    - The next day I’d feel exhausted and anxious
    - That anxiety made it even harder to function socially and professionally
- Getting help through virtual healthcare was a game changer
  - My local doctors didn’t really understand ADHD well
  - There was no way I could wait months for an appointment
  - Through online health services, I was finally able to see a specialist and start medication
    - The meds helped me bring order to the chaos in my head and finally made things manageable
  - But every month, there’s this terrible worry about whether my pharmacy will have my meds or if they’ll give me a generic that just doesn’t work
    - Sometimes, I can’t refill early or stockpile in case of shortages
    - That unpredictability causes a ton of stress
- It’s baffling that these medications are still treated like the most dangerous narcotics when the science has moved on decades ago
  - ADHD meds have been used safely for nearly 80 years, yet they sit on the same regulatory shelf as fentanyl or methadone
  - That’s simply outdated and unjust
  - If there’s a problem with diversion, it’s likely because the current rules make legal access so difficult that people have no choice but to turn to other options
  - We desperately need these medications to be moved to a more appropriate category
    - My meds don’t belong in the same legal bracket as Oxycontin
    - Yet here we are - stuck under laws written when Richard Nixon was president
  - Please, fix this classification error that’s hurting millions and keep telemedicine options open
  - Let’s stop treating ADHD like a criminal offense and start treating it like the manageable condition it is
  - This system needs to change - for all of us who just want to live without constant barriers
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An individual with ADHD recounts their lifelong struggles, extols the benefits of virtual healthcare for diagnosis and treatment, and urgently advocates for reclassification of ADHD medications due to outdated regulations that create unnecessary barriers and stress.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Anonymous
- **Type:** Individual
- **Role/Expertise:** Lived experience with ADHD; experience navigating traditional and virtual healthcare systems for chronic condition management.
- **Geographic Scope:** National (implied, given federal regulation context and mention of "local doctors")
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly affected by federal regulations governing ADHD medication classification and access, including the availability of telemedicine services.
structuredSections.corePosition: We desperately need these medications to be moved to a more appropriate category, as my meds don’t belong in the same legal bracket as Oxycontin. This system needs to change for all of us who just want to live without constant barriers created by outdated laws.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Move ADHD medications to a more appropriate regulatory category.
- Keep telemedicine options open for ADHD treatment.
- Stop treating ADHD like a criminal offense and start treating it as a manageable condition.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- Misclassification of ADHD medications as highly dangerous narcotics (e.g., on the same regulatory shelf as fentanyl, methadone, Oxycontin).
  - This classification is outdated and unjust, despite decades of safe use.
  - It makes legal access to medication difficult.
- Resulting unpredictability and stress regarding monthly medication refills.
  - Worry about pharmacy stock.
  - Concern over effectiveness of generic alternatives.
  - Inability to refill early or stockpile medication in case of shortages.
- Negative impacts of undiagnosed and untreated ADHD.
  - Academic struggles (dropping out of college twice, leading to student debt without a degree).
  - Chronic insomnia and associated exhaustion and anxiety.
  - Difficulty functioning socially and professionally.
- Barriers to accessing appropriate care through traditional local healthcare.
  - Lack of understanding of ADHD among local doctors.
  - Long wait times for specialist appointments.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The profound, lifelong impact of undiagnosed ADHD, including being labeled "daydreamer" or "spacey," feeling constantly reminded of not living up to potential, and significant educational and mental health struggles (dropping out of college twice, chronic insomnia).
- Virtual healthcare was a "game changer" for accessing specialist care and medication, highlighting a critical gap in traditional healthcare access for ADHD.
- The insight that if diversion of ADHD medications is a problem, it is likely because current regulations make legal access so difficult, pushing people to seek other options.
- The observation that current regulations are "stuck under laws written when Richard Nixon was president," emphasizing the outdated nature of the legal framework governing ADHD medications.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "Getting help through virtual healthcare was a game changer."
- "It’s baffling that these medications are still treated like the most dangerous narcotics when the science has moved on decades ago."
- "My meds don’t belong in the same legal bracket as Oxycontin. Yet here we are - stuck under laws written when Richard Nixon was president."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The National Milk Producers Federation (NMPF) strongly supports efforts to improve Americans’ diets and increase transparency in food labeling.
    *   However, NMPF is concerned that the "Labeling of Plant-based Milk Alternatives (PBMA) and Voluntary Nutrient Statements" guidance and the "Labeling of Plant-Based Alternatives to Animal-Derived Foods: Draft Guidance for Industry" will fail to achieve FDA’s stated goals.
    *   These documents mislead consumers, distort public understanding of healthful eating, and are both unlawfully promulgated and otherwise unlawful on numerous grounds.
    *   NMPF requests both guidances be revoked in their entirety.
*   The guidances are unlawful and meet several criteria for repeal identified in the Request for Information (RFI):
    *   They are unconstitutional because a federal agency cannot rewrite a Congressional statute, and both guidances do so in numerous instances.
    *   They are unlawful because they contradict existing regulations that were properly promulgated under the Administrative Procedures Act (APA).
    *   They are unlawful because they did not follow the notice and comment provisions of the APA.
    *   They are unlawful because they are based on anything other than the best reading of the underlying statutory authority or prohibition.
    *   They are unlawful because they are based on unlawful delegations and/or usurpations of legislative power.
*   The "Labeling of Plant-based Milk Alternatives and Voluntary Nutrient Statements" draft guidance provides information on labeling plant-based alternatives that include dairy food names, aiming to empower consumers for healthier diets.
    *   However, this guidance does the opposite by creating more uncertainty on the nutritional differences between these products and real dairy milk.
    *   Real dairy milk is a key source of calcium, vitamin D, protein, and many other nutrients.
    *   Allowing these products to use the term "milk" is misleading, even with voluntary nutrient statements.
*   Similarly, the "Labeling of Plant Based Alternatives to Animal Derived Foods" draft guidance claims to emphasize "clear labeling" but creates more confusion.
    *   It misinterprets nutritional information, blurs standards of identity, and undermines the importance of dairy in a healthy diet.
*   Eliminating the plant-based labeling guidance documents directly aligns with the mission of "making sure that providers and caretakers can focus on preventing and treating chronic diseases."
    *   Evidence shows that mislabeling has led to consumer confusion regarding the nutritional deficiencies of plant-based alternatives.
    *   According to a 2018 IPSOS survey, 62% of plant-based beverage buyers cite nutrition as important, and more than 70% thought plant-based substitutes had the same or more protein than dairy milk.
    *   An actual comparison of nutritional profiles shows most non-dairy substitutes are almost uniformly nutritionally inferior to nutrient-dense dairy counterparts.
    *   The inconsistency between consumer perception and reality of nutritional profiles has grave consequences, given dairy’s important role in human nutrition.
    *   Health experts and industry executives know non-dairy substitutes are nutritionally inferior, but consumers are not well informed.
    *   Misleading labels reinforce the false perception that nutritionally inferior imitations are equivalent or even superior to dairy counterparts.
    *   Numerous reports of health incidents, such as malnutrition, are associated with replacing dairy beverages with nutritionally inferior imitations.
    *   These public health consequences are precisely why FDA regulations require truthful, non-misleading common or usual names and require nutritionally inferior substitutes to be labeled as "imitation" products.
*   Under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FFDCA) and the Fair Packaging and Labeling Act, FDA must enforce fair and accurate labeling.
    *   These laws promote fair trade and consumer understanding.
    *   A food is misbranded if it purports to be a food with a definition and standard of identity (SOI) but does not conform, or if its label does not bear the specified name.
    *   Well-established SOIs exist for dairy products like "milk," "yogurt," "cheese," "ice cream," and "butter."
    *   The latest guidance inappropriately relaxes these SOIs in conflict with laws passed by Congress.
    *   SOIs are not just nomenclature; they ensure clear and accurate labels for consumer understanding.
    *   Terms like "yogurt," "cheese," and "butter" have distinct consumer meanings and reflect nutritional composition (e.g., yogurt's protein and probiotic benefits have established SOI thresholds).
    *   Plant-based imitation products may have substantially different nutritional compositions but benefit from the nutritional expectations inherent with the dairy term.
    *   This is the type of consumer confusion Congress sought to remedy.
    *   For example, FDA modified the SOI for yogurt in 2023 through a full rulemaking process (Advanced Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, proposed final rule, stakeholder input).
    *   In contrast, the proposed guidance on plant-based alternatives creates a sweeping policy change for an entire product category through guidance, not rulemaking.
    *   FDA is attempting to revise its own regulations with guidance documents, violating the APA.
    *   Congress defined when products are misbranded; FDA ignores this and substitutes its own policy. FDA does not have legal authority to rewrite federal statute; only Congress does.
    *   Federal courts reinforced this in *American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) v. FDA*: "The power of an agency like the FDA is not the power to make law. Rather, it is the power to adopt regulations to carry into effect the will of Congress as expressed by the statute...neither federal agencies [like the FDA] nor the courts can substitute their policy judgments for those of Congress."
*   Given the conflict with the underlying statute and the Administrative Procedures Act, NMPF requests both guidance documents related to the labeling of plant-based alternatives be withdrawn immediately.
    *   If FDA wishes to change the FFDCA, it can work with Congress to amend the statute.
    *   If FDA wishes to change its regulations, it can do so by following notice-and-comment requirements of the APA.
    *   In developing both plant-based labeling guidances, FDA has egregiously ignored laws and its duties.
*   This is not the first time NMPF has raised concerns about consumer misinformation in labeling.
    *   NMPF previously filed a Citizen Petition on February 21, 2019, to address the Plant-Based Milk Alternative labeling problem.
        *   The petition asked FDA to:
            *   Enforce existing "imitation" labeling requirements against nutritionally inferior non-dairy substitutes for standardized dairy foods (e.g., "milk," "yogurt," "cheese," "ice cream," or "butter") that fail to provide the required "imitation" disclosure statement.
            *   Amend section 101.3(e) of FDA regulations to codify conditions for using standardized dairy food names in the statement of identity of non-dairy substitutes.
    *   NMPF has never asked for an outright ban on dairy terminology for imitation, substitute, or alternative plant-based foods, acknowledging a complete ban would be impermissible under the First Amendment.
        *   NMPF consistently asked for adherence to rules and transparency for informed purchasing decisions.
        *   Current regulations permit "imitation" labeling (e.g., "Imitation Vanilla Extract").
    *   NMPF has focused on consumers not understanding the nutritional inferiority of PBMA, not whether consumers confuse them for real dairy.
        *   PBMA-funded research did show some consumer confusion over what was in a particular PBMA product.
*   PBMA nutritional inferiority matters due to serious public health consequences.
    *   It is long overdue that FDA recognizes most, if not all, PBMA are not nutritionally equivalent to real milk.
    *   The difference is starker when considering protein quality in addition to quantity.
    *   Consumers, especially parents for growing children, need to understand this.
    *   Harm from misbranding is not hypothetical; existing regulations protect consumer and public health by discouraging "nutritional degradation of the American diet."
    *   Consumers unknowingly reduce vital nutrient consumption based on false assumption of nutritional equivalence.
    *   An Oct. 2018 industry-funded survey (IFICF) found 7-9% of consumers believe non-dairy beverages contain cow’s milk, and 16-20% don't know. Federal Trade Commission precedent holds 10-20% confusion sufficient for deception.
    *   The survey failed to ask about perception of nutritional/performance characteristics.
    *   FDA regulations and food standards protect health by establishing nutritional, quality, and compositional benchmarks.
    *   PBMA are marketed as healthy, nutritious alternatives and labeled with explicit references to dairy.
    *   Studies confirm consumers wrongly assume PBMA are nutritionally equivalent or superior.
        *   IPSOS 2018 survey: 62% of PBMA buyers cite nutrition as important; 70%+ thought PBMA had same or more protein than dairy milk.
    *   An August 2017 NMPF survey of 244 non-dairy beverages in Washington, D.C., compared to 1% milk for 13 essential nutrients:
        *   None were nutritionally equivalent to real milk or delivered nine essential nutrients in the same proportions.
        *   Many lacked key essential nutrients like protein and Vitamin D.
        *   Unlike milk's consistent nutrient profile, wide variation existed within and among PBMA categories.
    *   The Dietary Guidelines for Americans separate plant-based products (except fortified soy) from the Dairy Group because their "overall nutritional content is not similar to dairy milk and fortified soy beverages."
    *   A 2023 study by Dr. Abigail Johnson found nutrient amounts varied across PBMA brands/types, with few matching protein, calcium, and vitamin D levels in dairy milk.
    *   Reports of health incidents, like malnutrition, are associated with replacing dairy with nutritionally inferior imitations.
*   Nutrient absorption is a critical factor FDA has missed.
    *   The body's ability to use a nutrient is as important as its quantity.
    *   Calcium absorption differs: Dairy products are a main natural source of absorbable calcium. Fortified products vary based on calcium type (e.g., calcium carbonate vs. tricalcium phosphate in soy drink).
    *   Shkembi 2022 states: "to be considered a suitable source of calcium, it is important that foods not only contain it in adequate quantities, but also that the calcium is also sufficiently bioavailable."
    *   Vitamin D: Dairy is typically fortified with Vitamin D3 (more effective at raising blood levels), whereas many PBMA use plant-based Vitamin D2 (less effective).
*   NMPF's response to FDA's specific invited questions:
    *   **Space for disclosures:** Most PBMA packages (e.g., 97% of soy PBMA in half-gallon or quart sizes) have ample space for additional disclosures.
        *   NMPF asserts there is room on smaller SKUs too.
        *   NMPF is strongly opposed to hiding disclosures on the back of the package, as consumers lack time/inclination to search.
        *   Consumers are misinformed, so front-of-pack disclosure is essential.
    *   **Nutrient disclosure statements:** FDA’s recommendation for disclosure statements on PBMA labels that contain less calcium, protein, vitamin A, vitamin D, magnesium, phosphorus, potassium, riboflavin, and vitamin B12 compared to milk is a great start.
        *   However, dairy is a good or excellent source of 13 nutrients, including niacin (B3), pantothenic acid (B5), cobalamin (B12), iodine, selenium, and zinc.
        *   FDA misses the mark regarding protein, making equivalency solely depend on protein quantity.
        *   Not all proteins are equal: dairy proteins are high quality, containing all essential amino acids; plant proteins are significantly lower quality.
        *   NMPF proposed modifying 21 CFR 103 to include protein quality value based on the protein digestibility-corrected amino acid score (PDCAAS).
        *   FDA should amend the proposed equivalence determination to specifically address protein inferiority.
    *   **USDA criteria:** USDA's efforts in determining minimum nutrient levels for fluid milk substitutes have stood the test of time, though protein quality should be added.
        *   Milk has 13 essential nutrients, including iodine, which is often deficient in American diets.
*   FDA’s Draft Guidance Violates the Administrative Procedures Act (APA) and the U.S. Constitution.
    *   The draft guidance rewrites and contradicts FDA’s existing regulation on misbranding and imitation labeling at 21 CFR 101.3(c).
    *   It violates the U.S. Constitution because Congress drafted the misbranded and imitation labeling requirements and provisions in the FFDCA (21 U.S.C. 343(c) and 343(g)).
    *   21 CFR 101.3(e) states a food is misbranded if it is an "imitation" unless its label bears "imitation" and the name of the food imitated; a food is an imitation if it is a substitute, resembles, and is nutritionally inferior.
    *   21 U.S.C. §343 states a food is misbranded if it is an imitation unless its label bears "imitation" and the name of the food imitated.
    *   The APA violation stems from FDA rewriting a regulation using a guidance document, disregarding the notice-and-comment process.
    *   Congress declared how imitation food should be labeled; FDA chooses to ignore this and substitute its own policy.
    *   Plant-based milk alternatives epitomize imitation: they capture the dairy industry’s health halo, look, feel, packaging, and store placement, and purport to be milk.
    *   FDA has not reinterpreted, amended, or extended Congressional language; it has contradicted it, substituting its judgment for Congress's. This is a clear separation of powers violation.
    *   If FDA wants to eliminate misbranding/imitation provisions of the FFDCA, it must consult Congress for statute amendment, and then follow APA notice-and-comment rulemaking for regulation changes.
*   The case of *American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) v. Food and Drug Administration* (PWG-18-883) is hauntingly familiar.
    *   In March 2018, AAP sued FDA over analogous facts and actions and prevailed.
    *   The court determined that FDA's guidance was *ultra vires* and unconstitutional (violating APA, exceeding authority, violating Constitution's Take Care clause) and an unlawful rule (issued without notice-and-comment).
    *   The court made it clear that an agency cannot make law but can only adopt regulations to carry out Congress's will, and cannot substitute its policy judgments for Congress's.
    *   The court also found FDA's alleged use of enforcement discretion was a "red herring," and blanket non-enforcement was an abdication of statutory responsibilities.
    *   NMPF asserts FDA’s decades-long, across-the-board non-enforcement of existing rules and the FFDCA is inconsistent with the FFDCA and in excess of FDA’s authority and cannot stand.
*   Standards of Identity (SOIs) are important.
    *   SOIs were developed to protect consumers and promote honesty/fair dealing by ensuring consistent characteristics, ingredients, and production processes for specific foods.
    *   Before the FFDCA (1938), the 1906 Act’s "distinctive name proviso" allowed marketing of debased foods (e.g., "Bred-Spred," resembling jam but with less fruit), contributing to proliferation of cheap foods.
    *   The FFDCA aimed to ensure food integrity by establishing SOIs for standardization (sections 401, 403, 701).
    *   SOIs were intended not just to prevent deception but to protect food supply integrity by setting compositional and quality benchmarks.
    *   FDA explained SOIs vary by defining characteristics (ingredients, composition, production processes), e.g., milkfat/solids for milk, manufacturing for cheese.
    *   SOIs promote honesty and ensure consumer expectations (organoleptically, chemically, nutritionally, and performance characteristics).
    *   For basic foods important as nutrient sources (like dairy), SOIs protect consumer and public health.
    *   Dairy SOIs are important due to widespread consumption and nutrient contributions to a healthy diet.
    *   The Dietary Guidelines recommend daily dairy servings and distinguish dairy foods from plant-based substitutes (except fortified soy) due to "overall nutritional content."
    *   FDA has historically addressed issues with cheaper, nutritionally inferior non-dairy substitutes by prohibiting confusing names, prescribing imitation labeling, and promulgating new standards (e.g., margarine).
    *   Amendments under the Nutrition Labeling and Education Act of 1990 (NLEA) allowed nutritionally modified versions of standardized foods (e.g., "low fat milk") if specific requirements were met, including using authorized dairy ingredients in substantial amounts.
*   Establishment of Common and Usual Names:
    *   FFDCA section 403(i)(1) requires a "common or usual name."
    *   FFDCA 403(b) prohibits offering for sale under another food's name.
    *   FFDCA 403(c) prohibits imitation unless labeled as such.
    *   FFDCA 403(a) prohibits false or misleading labeling.
    *   FDA regulations for common/usual names (101.3(b)(2), 101.3(b)(3), 102.5(a)) require accurate identification, uniformity, and no confusing similarity.
    *   There is no provision allowing a common or usual name to be created by "extended and continuous violation of existing labeling rules."
    *   "Scofflaws should not be rewarded."
*   The proliferation of misbranded non-dairy substitutes misappropriating standardized dairy terms:
    *   Non-dairy, plant-based foods resembling dairy products are increasingly labeled and marketed as nutritionally equivalent or superior, despite being nutritionally inferior.
    *   They are derived from diverse plant ingredients (hemp, oat, pea, pecan, rice, quinoa, cashew, hazelnut, pistachio, flax) and combinations (e.g., "coconut hemp milk").
    *   Offerings have expanded to target yogurt and ice cream alternatives.
    *   These products are intentionally formulated with added colors, flavors, and additives to resemble dairy products, and use standardized dairy terms.
    *   FDA's failure to enforce existing regulations has emboldened the industry.
    *   These products are misbranded, implying false nutritional equivalence. Modifiers like "non-dairy" or "vegan" are haphazardly used and don't resolve the issue.
    *   These misleading names are not accepted consistently internationally (e.g., Canada, UK, EU use "soy beverage," "almond drink").
    *   The European Court of Justice found "milk" reserved for animal origin, and that adding plant origin descriptions doesn't exclude consumer confusion. The same rationale applies in the U.S.
    *   Manufacturers complying with U.S. law (e.g., Trader Joe’s, Quaker Oats, Pacific Foods, Kirkland) use names that don't reference standardized dairy foods, showing easy label revision is possible.
    *   NMPF is not stifling innovation but asks FDA to ensure products are labeled consistent with law, preventing labels that falsely suggest nutritional equivalence.
*   Clarification: If a product does not purport to be a dairy product, it can use a dairy term.
    *   Plant-based milk alternatives (PBMA) *do* purport and represent themselves to be real milk.
        *   They are concocted to look like milk (white liquid), have similar viscosity, similar packaging, are placed in the dairy section (often with "slotting allowances").
        *   Their uses are clearly established to be the same as real milk.
        *   WhiteWave CEO Steven Demos (2001): "Why not position fresh soymilk to be as close as possible?"
    *   In contrast, products like peanut butter, milk of magnesia, cocoa butter, and canned coconut milk clearly do not purport to be dairy products.
        *   Their packaging, store placement, and intended uses are not similar, and consumers are not misled.
        *   The dairy industry has never had an issue with these products using dairy terminology because they comply with law and regulations.
    *   FDA's inaction for decades has led to consumer confusion over PBMA nutritional quality, resulting in malnourishment.
*   NMPF Citizen Petition:
    *   Enforcement of "imitation" labeling under FFDCA section 403(c) and FDA section 101.3(e) against nutritionally inferior non-dairy substitutes is consistent with the First Amendment.
    *   Disclosure requirements "trench much more narrowly" on advertiser interests than flat prohibitions.
    *   These disclosures would apply only to manufacturers who affirmatively manufacture, label, and position non-dairy foods to substitute for and resemble standardized dairy foods AND use a standardized dairy term (e.g., "milk").
    *   "Imitation" labeling would be factually accurate and uncontroversial.
    *   "Imitation" or "Substitute"/"Alternative" labeling can be avoided if products are nutritionally equivalent and use distinctive names (e.g., "Rice Beverage").
    *   Proposed section 101.3(e)(6) in the petition would put existing requirements into the specific context of non-dairy substitutes for standardized dairy foods.
        *   It explicitly specifies requirements that prevent consumer deception and allow "substitute"/"alternative" labeling for nutritionally inferior products under certain circumstances.
        *   "Imitation" disclosure would not apply to nutritionally inferior or equivalent non-dairy substitutes if they do not represent themselves as a form of standardized dairy food (e.g., "Oat Beverage" instead of "Oat Milk").
        *   For nutritionally inferior products, no representation suggesting nutritional equivalence or superiority to dairy would be permitted.
        *   Product labeling would require disclosure of material differences in performance (e.g., "not suitable for frying").
        *   Nutritional inferiority of non-imitation labeled products would need prominent disclosure.
        *   Under new proposed section 101.3(e)(6)(v), a standardized dairy term (e.g., "milk") could be used if qualified as "Milk Substitute" or "Milk Alternative."
    *   The requested enforcement and regulatory actions are carefully tailored to advance FDA’s substantial interests in preventing consumer deception and protecting public health.
    *   False and misleading commercial speech is not First Amendment protected. Remedies through factual disclosures (e.g., "Imitation [Milk]," "not suitable for frying") easily satisfy First Amendment requirements (Central Hudson, Zauderer).
    *   These actions are disclosure requirements, not speech bans, requiring "somewhat more information" from advertisers.
    *   The petition also asked FDA to adopt amendments to 21 CFR 101.3(e) (new section 101.3(e)(6)) for all plant-based foods using dairy terminology, codifying existing requirements and policies.
        *   This provision would apply to non-dairy foods that substitute for and resemble standardized dairy foods (milk, yogurt, cheese, ice cream, butter).
        *   It would prohibit claims already prohibited by the Act and specify required disclosures for nutritionally inferior and equivalent products.
        *   For nutritionally inferior foods, "imitation" labeling would not be required if the food adheres to certain labeling practices, including prominent disclosure of nutritional inferiority and no express/implied representation of being a standardized dairy food (except as permitted with "substitute"/"alternative" terms).
        *   For non-nutritionally inferior foods, "imitation" requirements would be avoided if they comply with existing regulations and disclose material limitations.
        *   The proposed amendments expressly permit non-dairy substitutes to use a reference standardized dairy term as part of the statement of identity if the material fact that it is a "substitute" or "alternative" is disclosed (e.g., "Milk Substitute;" "Milk Alternative").
    *   These disclosure requirements apply in limited contexts where manufacturers affirmatively choose to manufacture/label a food that substitutes for/resembles a standardized dairy food AND employ the standardized dairy term.
    *   "Imitation," "alternative," or "substitute" disclosure statements would not be required for non-dairy foods that don't substitute for/resemble standardized dairy foods or use distinctive names (e.g., "Natural Soy Beverage").
    *   The "imitation" labeling requirements the petition seeks to enforce target misbranded products lacking mandatory disclosures and labeled falsely.
*   NMPF commends FDA for recognizing consumer confusion and nutritional inferiority of PBMA.
    *   However, NMPF cannot condone FDA violating the APA and arguably the U.S. Constitution to convey that information instead of using proper legal processes.
    *   FDA needs to enforce existing standards of identity and should modify them as NMPF suggested in its Citizen Petition.
    *   Both FDA's flawed approach and NMPF's approach share a concern for consumers and transparency.
    *   The logical resolution is embodied in NMPF's Citizen Petition.
    *   If FDA does not adopt NMPF's petition, the agency should find a legally compliant way to make nutritional inferiority disclosures mandatory and prominently placed front-of-pack.
    *   NMPF has been frustrated for decades by FDA’s unwillingness to enforce SOIs for milk and milk products.
    *   In the absence of a full resolution focused on SOIs (e.g., via DAIRY PRIDE Act), any legally sound guidance should focus on addressing consumer confusion, be forcefully implemented by FDA, and taken seriously by the plant-based beverage community.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The National Milk Producers Federation demands the immediate withdrawal of FDA's draft guidances on plant-based food labeling, arguing they are unlawful, contradict established dairy standards of identity, mislead consumers about nutritional inferiority, and that FDA should instead enforce existing misbranding laws or pursue changes through a formal rulemaking process as outlined in NMPF's citizen petition.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** National Milk Producers Federation (NMPF)
- **Type:** Trade Association
- **Role/Expertise:** Represents 24 dairy cooperatives and 20,000 dairy producers who collectively produce two-thirds of the U.S. milk supply; organized in 1916 to participate in public policy discussions and advocates for dairy producers and cooperatives.
- **Geographic Scope:** National (U.S.)
- **Stake in Issue:** Direct representatives of the U.S. dairy industry, advocating for policies that ensure fair and accurate labeling of dairy and competing plant-based products, concerned about consumer confusion, public health impacts, and the legal integrity of food standards that define dairy products.
structuredSections.corePosition: We request that both guidance documents related to the labeling of plant-based alternatives be withdrawn immediately because they contradict the requirements of underlying statutes related to labeling, violate the process requirements set forth by the Administrative Procedures Act, and ultimately propagate consumer misinformation. If the FDA wishes to change the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, it can work with Congress to amend the statute itself, or if it wishes to change its regulations, it can do so by following the notice-and-comment requirements established by the Administrative Procedures Act.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Withdraw immediately both guidance documents related to the labeling of plant-based alternatives to animal-derived foods ("Labeling of Plant-Based Alternatives to Animal-Derived Foods: Draft Guidance for Industry" and "Labeling of Plant-based Milk Alternatives and Voluntary Nutrient Statements").
  - If FDA wishes to change the FFDCA, it should work with Congress to amend the statute itself.
  - If FDA wishes to change its regulations, it must follow the notice-and-comment requirements established by the Administrative Procedures Act (APA).
- Enforce existing "imitation" labeling requirements against nutritionally inferior non-dairy substitutes for standardized dairy foods (e.g., "milk," "yogurt," "cheese," "ice cream," or "butter") that fail to provide the required "imitation" disclosure statement.
- Amend section 101.3(e) of FDA regulations to codify more detailed conditions for using standardized dairy food names in the statement of identity of non-dairy substitutes, as proposed in NMPF's Citizen Petition.
  - This would allow use of a standardized dairy term (e.g., "milk") if explicitly qualified as "Milk Substitute" or "Milk Alternative," ensuring clear factual disclosure without implying nutritional equivalence.
  - Require prominent, front-of-pack disclosure of nutritional inferiority and material performance differences for plant-based alternatives that use dairy terms.
- Revise the equivalence determination for plant-based alternatives to specifically address the inferiority of plant-based proteins, including protein quality value based on methods like PDCAAS.
- Consider including all 13 essential nutrients found in milk (including iodine) in any nutrient disclosure comparisons for plant-based alternatives, not just the currently recommended 9.
- Ensure any nutrient disclosure requirements for plant-based alternatives consider nutrient absorption and bioavailability (e.g., Vitamin D3 vs. D2, different forms of calcium).
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Unlawfulness and Unconstitutionality of Guidance Documents:**
  - The guidances contradict underlying statutes (FFDCA, Fair Packaging and Labeling Act) and rewrite existing regulations through guidance, bypassing the Administrative Procedures Act's notice-and-comment requirements.
  - FDA is exceeding its statutory authority and usurping legislative power by substituting its policy judgments for those of Congress, violating the separation of powers.
  - The guidances are based on anything other than the best reading of statutory authority and contradict established federal court precedents (e.g., *AAP v. FDA*).
- **Consumer Misinformation and Misleading Labeling:**
  - The guidances propagate consumer misinformation and distort public understanding of healthful eating by allowing plant-based products to use dairy terms (e.g., "milk," "yogurt," "cheese") despite significant nutritional differences.
  - Surveys show high consumer confusion regarding the nutritional equivalence of plant-based alternatives to dairy milk, with many mistakenly believing them to be nutritionally similar or superior.
  - The "voluntary" nature of nutrient statements and potential placement on the back of packages fail to address widespread consumer confusion effectively.
- **Nutritional Inferiority and Public Health Consequences:**
  - Most plant-based alternatives are not nutritionally equivalent to real milk, particularly regarding protein quality and quantity, and essential vitamins and minerals (e.g., Vitamin D, Calcium, Iodine).
  - Consumers unknowingly reduce vital nutrient intake by substituting dairy with nutritionally inferior plant-based products, leading to potentially grave public health consequences, including documented cases of malnutrition.
  - The guidances undermine the importance of nutrient-dense dairy in a healthy diet as recognized by the Dietary Guidelines for Americans.
- **Undermining Standards of Identity (SOIs):**
  - The guidances inappropriately relax well-established SOIs for dairy products, which are crucial tools for ensuring clear, accurate labels, promoting honesty, and reflecting nutritional composition.
  - FDA's approach to modify SOIs for an entire category of products via guidance is inconsistent with its own prior rigorous rulemaking process for individual SOIs (e.g., yogurt).
- **Abrogation of Enforcement Responsibility:**
  - FDA's decades-long decision to follow an across-the-board non-enforcement of existing misbranding and imitation labeling rules has emboldened the plant-based industry.
  - This non-enforcement is an abdication of FDA’s statutory responsibilities.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- NMPF's long-standing frustration (decades) with FDA's unwillingness to enforce its own standards of identity for milk and milk products, despite consistent requests from the dairy industry.
- The direct link drawn between FDA's inaction on labeling enforcement and documented cases of malnutrition due to consumers replacing dairy with nutritionally inferior, mislabeled plant-based imitations.
- The use of the "Bred-Spred" example from the 1906 Act era to illustrate how the lack of strong SOIs led to "economically adulterated" products, highlighting that SOIs protect food integrity, not just prevent deception.
- The detailed comparison of FDA's rigorous rulemaking process for modifying the yogurt SOI in 2023 (involving ANPR, proposed rule, stakeholder input) versus the broad policy change through guidance for plant-based alternatives, underscoring the perceived procedural hypocrisy.
- The compelling argument that plant-based milk alternatives "purport to be" real milk due to their look (white liquid), similar viscosity, packaging, store placement in the dairy section, and even historical industry intent, contrasting them with other products using "dairy" terms like "peanut butter" or "milk of magnesia" that do not purport to be dairy.
- The revelation that some non-dairy manufacturers (e.g., Trader Joe’s, Quaker Oats, Pacific Foods) already comply with FDA regulations by using non-dairy specific names (e.g., "Rice Beverage"), demonstrating that compliance is feasible and does not stifle innovation.
- The reference to the European Court of Justice's ruling that "milk" is reserved for animal origin, even with descriptive additions, highlighting an international precedent for strict adherence to dairy definitions.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "Simply put, the document is unlawful and should be withdrawn."
- "The power of an agency like the FDA “is ‘not the power to make law. Rather, it is “the power to adopt regulations to carry into effect the will of Congress as expressed by the statute … and moreover, “neither federal agencies [like the FDA] nor the courts can substitute their policy judgments for those of Congress.”"
- "Anyone who says that plant-based milk alternatives are not imitations of real dairy products is exceptionally naïve or simply dead wrong."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The National Milk Producers Federation (NMPF) offers these comments in response to the proposed rule entitled “Food Labeling: Front-of-Package Nutrition Information” published in the Federal Register on January 16, 2025 (Docket No. FDA-2024-N-2910).
*   NMPF also offers comments in response to the Request for Information (RFI) entitled “Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation to Make American Healthy Again,” published in the Federal Register on May 14, 2025 (Docket No. AHRQ-2025-0001).
    *   These comments specifically address the "Food Labeling: Front-of-Package Nutrition Information" proposed rule as an example of a regulation warranting repeal.
    *   Previously submitted comments to FDA on the FOPNL rule (January 17, 2025) are attached for convenience and provide clear insight into why this rule must be withdrawn.
*   NMPF’s 24 cooperatives represent 20,000 dairy producers who collectively produce two-thirds of the U.S. milk supply.
    *   NMPF was organized in 1916 to provide a forum for dairy producers and the cooperatives they own to participate in public policy discussions.
    *   NMPF advocates policies to Congress, U.S. and foreign government agencies, industry organizations, the news media, and the public.
*   While NMPF advocates for healthy diets and consumer education, FDA’s proposed Front-of-Pack (FOP) rule:
    *   Not only fails to improve consumer understanding but instead encourages consumers to make dietary decisions based on a new misleading box that provides an incomplete assessment of a food’s nutritional profile.
    *   Aims to reduce consumption of certain nutrients without regard to beneficial nutrient content that may help consumers meet much-needed dietary targets for key things such as protein, vitamins, minerals, and more.
    *   Is therefore both at odds with public health interests and raises concerns about its legality.
*   This rule involves compelled commercial speech.
    *   To pass muster under the First Amendment, the government not only needs to show a substantial interest justifying a regulation on commercial speech, but it also must show that its regulation directly advances that goal.
    *   NMPF is at a loss as to what substantial interest is being advanced with a rule that duplicates information already on the package in the Nutrition Facts Panel (NFP), but that, in its front-of-pack form, encourages an incomplete and misleading profile of a food’s nutrient content.
    *   Given that the proposed rule provides consumers with little to no new information and may mislead consumers, FDA does not have a substantial interest being advanced.
    *   If FDA’s goal is to improve the diets of Americans, NMPF asserts that this rule will not advance that goal; it will run contrary to it.
    *   FDA touts that 87 percent of U.S. consumers report that they have looked at the Nutrition Facts Panel and that 80 percent report using it sometimes or often.
    *   NMPF believes that if this rule were to go into effect, that number would drop dramatically, and most U.S. consumers would probably completely ignore the Nutrition Facts Panel.
    *   So, FDA is trading a commonly relied upon Nutrition Facts Panel for a snippet of incomplete information in the new box.
    *   Perhaps most problematic is the fact that the front-of-pack label includes no mechanism to direct consumers toward nutrient goals that most Americans fail to meet – for instance, regarding protein, dietary fiber, and beneficial vitamins and minerals.
    *   This rule instead reduces decision-making to an arbitrary set of things to avoid.
*   The proposed rule is unlawful and meets several criteria that warrant repeal, specifically:
    *   It is an unconstitutional regulation that raises serious constitutional difficulties, in that it is unlawful compelled commercial speech and violates the 1st Amendment.
    *   It is a regulation that is based on unlawful delegations of legislative power.
    *   It is a regulation that imposes significant costs upon private parties that are not outweighed by public benefits.
*   The proposed FOPNL—focused exclusively on saturated fat, sodium, and added sugars—presents a distorted picture of a food’s overall nutritional quality.
    *   By isolating these three “nutrients to limit,” the rule implicitly suggests that these alone determine a food's healthfulness.
    *   This approach ignores the substantial contributions of beneficial nutrients that many Americans under-consume, such as calcium, potassium, vitamin D, protein, and dietary fiber.
    *   Dairy products, for example, provide thirteen essential nutrients, including three of the four nutrients of public health concern for under-consumption: calcium, potassium, and vitamin D.
    *   Yet, under this proposed labeling scheme, nutrient-rich dairy foods could be penalized in the consumer’s eye based on a simplistic system without regard to the food’s total nutrient profile or net contribution to dietary quality.
    *   This reductionist approach not only misrepresents foods like milk, yogurt, and cheese but runs counter to the FDA’s own guidance encouraging nutrient-dense dietary patterns.
*   Further, to justify a compelled commercial speech disclosure, assuming the government articulates a substantial governmental interest, the government must show that the disclosure is purely factual, uncontroversial, not unduly burdensome, and reasonably related to the government’s interest.
    *   The proposed rule fails on most of these points, but, in particular, NMPF does not believe it is uncontroversial.
    *   FDA is focused on three nutrients only: added sugar, saturated fat, and sodium.
    *   FDA is ignoring countless beneficial nutrients found in dairy products.
    *   For decades, the Dietary Guidelines for Americans have recommended up to three servings per day of dairy foods and beverages in the diets of Americans based on an overwhelming body of science that demonstrates dairy’s nutritional importance to people of all ages.
    *   By focusing on only these three nutrients, consumers are learning little but that they should only be paying attention to the "bad."
    *   Recent science shows that a food is more than its parts.
        *   For example, the dairy matrix comprises both the nutritional and physical matrix.
        *   Dairy products’ unique variations in structure and interactions create defined matrices that can impact nutrient digestion and therefore impact physiological responses.
        *   This is especially relevant when looking at the saturated fat in dairy products.
        *   There is a growing body of science showing the health benefits of dairy at all fat levels.
        *   This growing body of science finds that consumption of full-fat dairy foods (milk, cheese, and yogurt) is not associated with higher risk of negative health outcomes, including obesity, diabetes, and heart disease; moreover, dairy has protective effects against several chronic diet-related diseases, including type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
    *   NMPF finds it disappointing that the proposed front-of-pack nutrition labeling scheme continues to take the reductionist approach to nutrition, focusing solely on negatives and completely ignoring the four nutrients of public health concern.
    *   NMPF asserts that under this regulatory scheme, rather than providing consumers with more information to make informed decisions, FDA is undermining the utility of the Nutrition Facts Panel and telling consumers to focus on only three nutrients.
    *   NMPF views this compelled commercial speech as very controversial and therefore impermissible under the First Amendment.
*   NMPF also notes an unintended consequence: higher prices for food at a time when consumers are having a difficult time paying their grocery bills.
    *   As the FDA is aware, label changes are expensive.
    *   Food manufacturers have hundreds if not thousands of stock-keeping units (SKUs), each with its own label, and frequently they have multiple years of label inventory on hand.
    *   Not only will the physical labels need to be replaced, but the plates that print those labels will need to be replaced.
    *   The costs to make the changes are substantial, and most food manufacturers operate on tight profit margins, which means the additional costs will be borne by consumers.
    *   The additional burdensome requirement of changing millions of food labels with nothing other than a characterization of what is high, medium, or low regarding three nutrients is arguably absurd.
*   NMPF acknowledges the FDA’s efforts to conduct consumer research, including experimental studies of different FOPNL formats.
    *   However, the finding that consumers made faster decisions based on “high/med/low” descriptors is not sufficient to justify mandating such a system across the entire food industry.
    *   The rule’s justification relies on behavioral research rather than health outcome data.
    *   It relies on the assumption that simplified nutrient warnings will lead to healthier diets overall.
    *   But without evidence that this labeling approach improves actual nutritional intake or health outcomes, the government lacks a compelling interest in overriding commercial speech protections.
*   Given the uncertainty of regulatory actions on the eve of a change in administration, NMPF felt it prudent to file these brief comments in advance of that change and reserve the right to file additional comments in the months ahead.
*   NMPF respectfully asks FDA to withdraw this rule.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The National Milk Producers Federation strongly opposes the proposed Front-of-Package Nutrition Labeling rule, arguing it is unconstitutional compelled commercial speech that misleads consumers by singularly highlighting "bad" nutrients while ignoring beneficial ones crucial to nutrient-dense foods like dairy, all while imposing significant, unjustified costs on the industry.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
-   **Name/Organization:** National Milk Producers Federation (NMPF)
-   **Type:** Trade Association
-   **Role/Expertise:** Represents 24 cooperatives and 20,000 dairy producers who collectively produce two-thirds of the U.S. milk supply; organized in 1916 to provide a forum for dairy producers and their cooperatives to participate in public policy discussions, advocating for the dairy industry.
-   **Geographic Scope:** National (U.S.)
-   **Stake in Issue:** The proposed Front-of-Package Nutrition Labeling rule would directly impact the labeling requirements for dairy products, potentially mischaracterizing nutrient-rich dairy foods and imposing substantial financial burdens on dairy producers and manufacturers.
structuredSections.corePosition: While we support efforts to improve Americans’ diets and increase food label transparency, we are concerned that the proposed "Food Labeling: Front-of-Package Nutrition Information" rule will fail to achieve FDA’s stated goals. We believe this rule threatens to mislead consumers, distort public understanding of healthful eating by focusing solely on "nutrients to limit," and impose significant, unjustified burdens on food manufacturers, making it unconstitutional and unlawful, and therefore request its revocation in its entirety.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   Withdraw the proposed "Food Labeling: Front-of-Package Nutrition Information" rule (Docket No. FDA-2024-N-2910) in its entirety.
    -   The Front-of-Package Nutrition Labeling (FOPNL) box does not improve consumer understanding.
    -   It risks misleading the public.
    -   It oversimplifies complex science.
    -   It imposes undue costs on food producers.
    -   A one-size-fits-all FOPNL scheme promoting only “nutrients to avoid” while ignoring “nutrients to encourage” is inconsistent with the goals of the Dietary Guidelines and fails to empower informed food choices.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   **Constitutional and Legal Concerns (Compelled Commercial Speech):**
    -   The proposed rule is an unconstitutional regulation that raises serious constitutional difficulties, as it is unlawful compelled commercial speech and violates the 1st Amendment.
    -   It is based on unlawful delegations of legislative power.
    -   To pass First Amendment muster, the government must show a substantial interest directly advanced by the regulation, and the compelled disclosure must be purely factual, uncontroversial, not unduly burdensome, and reasonably related to the government’s interest.
    -   NMPF asserts FDA has not met these requirements because the rule:
        -   Provides little to no new information and may mislead consumers.
        -   Compels food manufacturers to carry a subjective, government-endorsed message that elevates three nutrients above all others, despite disagreement among nutrition experts and evolving science.
        -   Is not purely factual, is highly controversial, and not narrowly tailored to achieve the stated goal of improving public health.
-   **Misleading Consumer Information and Dietary Guidance:**
    -   The proposed FOPNL, focused exclusively on saturated fat, sodium, and added sugars, presents a distorted picture of a food’s overall nutritional quality.
    -   By isolating these three “nutrients to limit,” the rule implicitly suggests that these alone determine a food's healthfulness.
    -   This approach ignores the substantial contributions of beneficial nutrients that many Americans under-consume, such as calcium, potassium, vitamin D, protein, and dietary fiber.
    -   It includes no mechanism to direct consumers toward nutrient goals that most Americans fail to meet, instead reducing decision-making to an arbitrary set of things to avoid.
    -   Nutrient-rich dairy foods could be penalized in the consumer’s eye based on a simplistic system without regard to the food’s total nutrient profile or net contribution to dietary quality.
    -   This reductionist approach misrepresents foods like milk, yogurt, and cheese and runs counter to the FDA’s own guidance encouraging nutrient-dense dietary patterns.
    -   The rule undermines the utility of the Nutrition Facts Panel (NFP), which 87% of consumers report using and 80% rely on regularly, by replacing quantitative information with vague qualitative descriptors ("Low," "Med," and "High") for only three nutrients.
    -   It risks oversimplifying food choice decisions and shifting attention away from broader nutrient intake goals, effectively trading a comprehensive nutrition disclosure system for a "soundbite" that may deter consumers from reading the full label.
-   **Economic Burden and Cost to Consumers:**
    -   The rule imposes significant costs upon private parties that are not outweighed by public benefits.
    -   Label changes are expensive, requiring new physical labels and printing plates for potentially thousands of Stock-Keeping Units (SKUs), with manufacturers often holding multiple years of label inventory.
    -   These are major cost burdens, especially for small and mid-sized food manufacturers.
    -   Most food manufacturers operate on tight profit margins, meaning these additional costs will inevitably be borne by consumers, at a time when food affordability is already a growing national concern.
    -   This costly regulatory requirement has no proven net consumer benefit.
-   **Reliance on Outdated Science and Insufficient Justification:**
    -   The proposed rule continues to rely on outdated nutrition models that demonize saturated fat in isolation.
    -   Its justification relies on behavioral research (consumers made faster decisions) rather than health outcome data.
    -   There is no evidence that this labeling approach improves actual nutritional intake or health outcomes, meaning the government lacks a compelling interest in overriding commercial speech protections.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
-   The observation that the proposed rule, by reducing the complex Nutrition Facts Panel to a "snippet of incomplete information," risks causing the majority of U.S. consumers to "completely ignore the Nutrition Facts Panel" which 80% currently rely on regularly.
-   The insight that the rule's focus on only three "nutrients to avoid" prevents consumers from being directed towards essential nutrients (like protein, fiber, calcium, potassium, vitamin D) that most Americans under-consume, as opposed to only highlighting "the bad."
-   The detailed argument about the "dairy matrix," explaining how the unique structure and interactions within dairy products impact nutrient digestion and physiological responses, particularly relevant for saturated fat.
-   The highlight of growing science showing health benefits of dairy at all fat levels, including findings that consumption of full-fat dairy foods (milk, cheese, yogurt) is not associated with higher risk of negative health outcomes (obesity, diabetes, heart disease) and may even have protective effects against chronic diet-related diseases.
-   The specific concern that "nutrient-rich dairy foods could be penalized in the consumer’s eye" due to the simplistic "Low," "Med," "High" system, despite providing 13 essential nutrients, including three of the four "nutrients of public health concern" for under-consumption.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
-   "While NMPF advocates for healthy diets and consumer education, FDA’s proposed Front-of-Pack rule not only fails to improve consumer understanding but instead encourages consumers to make dietary decisions based on a new misleading box that provides an incomplete assessment of a food’s nutritional profile."
-   "So, FDA is trading a commonly relied upon Nutrition Facts Panel for a snippet of incomplete information in the new box. Perhaps most problematic is the fact that the front-of-pack label includes no mechanism to direct consumers toward nutrient goals that most Americans fail to meet – for instance regarding protein, dietary fiber, and beneficial vitamins and minerals. This rule instead reduces decision-making to an arbitrary set of things to avoid."
-   "Recent science shows that a food is more than its parts. For example, the dairy matrix comprises both the nutritional and physical matrix. Dairy products’ unique variations in structure and interactions create defined matrices that can impact nutrient digestion and therefore impact physiological responses. This is especially relevant when looking at the saturated fat in dairy products. There is a growing body of science showing the health benefits of dairy at all fat levels."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- I've always been a creative person, involved in photography, art, and writing.
  - However, ADHD made it almost impossible to turn creativity into a stable career.
  - I dropped out of art school after my second year.
    - I couldn't keep up with deadlines or the structure.
    - I accumulated $27,000 in student loans but left with no degree and significant shame.
    - I constantly wondered why I couldn't finish things like everyone else.
- The reason was ADHD, though I didn't discover this until age 26.
  - Before diagnosis, I struggled, bouncing between jobs, moving in and out of relationships, and barely scraping by.
  - The most difficult part was lying awake at night, intensely criticizing myself for all my failures, which felt like "insomnia with a megaphone."
- After starting medication, things improved, though not completely fixed.
  - I gained the ability to focus, work on edits, sleep better, and consistently show up for clients.
  - Despite the improvement, access to this "lifeline" feels constantly threatened.
- My telehealth doctor is excellent, but I am uncertain what I would do if Congress or the DEA removed the telehealth option.
  - No psychiatrist near me is accepting new ADHD patients.
  - Even with a prescription, the pharmacy supply is unreliable.
    - I receive different brands of medication every month, leading to varying side effects.
    - Sometimes, the pharmacy is completely out of stock.
  - The Schedule II rules for these medications make it impossible to plan ahead.
  - It feels as though ADHD treatment is intentionally designed to fail individuals who already struggle with planning.
- Regarding the scheduling of these medications:
  - These medications have been in use for a longer period than birth control.
  - Yet, they are still classified alongside substances like fentanyl and methadone (Schedule II).
  - In contrast, testosterone is Schedule III and Xanax is Schedule IV.
  - I am not abusing my medication; I am using it to survive.
  - The notion that ADHD patients are "one pill away from becoming drug dealers" is insulting.
  - I question who would manage to photograph a wedding on time, edit 1,200 photos, and then proceed to sell their medication.
- The current scheduling system treats ADHD medications as if they are as dangerous as street fentanyl, which is completely divorced from reality.
- I request the following actions:
  - Please keep telehealth options open.
  - Reform the federal controlled substances tiering to align with modern scientific understanding.
  - Consider offering student loan forgiveness for individuals who dropped out of school before receiving an ADHD diagnosis.
  - We deserve to recover our lives, not just explain why they fell apart.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An individual with ADHD recounts their lifelong struggles, the transformative impact of medication, and urgently advocates for continued telehealth access, federal drug scheduling reform, and student loan forgiveness, arguing that current systems fail those already challenged by ADHD.

- Inappropriate federal scheduling of ADHD medications (Schedule II), placing them alongside highly dangerous substances like fentanyl and methadone, despite their long history of use and therapeutic purpose.
- The insulting implication that ADHD patients are prone to abusing or dealing their medication.
