structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Eli Lilly and Company (Lilly) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments on the Request for Information (RFI) for "Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make America Healthy Again."
*   Lilly is one of the country’s leading innovation-driven, research-based pharmaceutical and biotechnology corporations.
*   Our company is devoted to seeking answers for some of the world’s most urgent medical needs through discovery and development of breakthrough medicines and technologies and through the health information we offer.
*   Ultimately, our goal is to develop products that save and improve patients’ lives.
*   As a member of both the Pharmaceutical Researchers and Manufacturers Association of America (PhRMA) and the Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO), Lilly supports by reference their comments on this RFI and encourages CMS to consider their input.
*   Lilly offers specific comments to highlight a particular regulatory matter for which we have deep expertise and a strong vested interest in better access for the patients we serve.

*   **I. Coverage with Evidence Development Guidance Document (Aug. 7, 2024) Should Be Rescinded**
    *   The Social Security Act (Medicare Act) states that the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) must determine if items and services are “reasonable and necessary” for diagnosis or treatment to be covered by Medicare.
    *   From Medicare’s inception in 1965 until 2006, CMS consistently interpreted this mandate as a categorical approval or denial of Medicare coverage through a National Coverage Determination (NCD).
    *   In 2006, however, CMS asserted a new authority through sub-regulatory guidance, known as "coverage with evidence development" (CED).
    *   Under CED, CMS purports to "approve" Medicare coverage only if the item or service is provided to Medicare beneficiaries who are subjects in Medicare-approved clinical trials, effectively denying ordinary course coverage.
    *   CMS has continued to expand its purported authority to implement CED through guidance documents, most recently in August 2024, demonstrating a clear intention to greatly expand its use of CED over FDA-approved therapies.
    *   As CMS explores opportunities for deregulation while also ensuring Medicare beneficiaries receive high-quality healthcare, we strongly urge CMS to revisit and significantly revise its approach to CED.
    *   The sub-regulatory guidance lacks a firm legal foundation, imposes undue administrative burden, and creates access barriers for patients, especially for Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved pharmaceuticals.

    *   **A. CMS Lacks Statutory Authority for CED**
        *   Lilly is deeply concerned that CMS’s application of CED exceeds its statutory authority.
        *   CED is not mentioned anywhere in the Medicare statute and was invented by CMS without a clear legislative mandate.
        *   In its CED Guidance, CMS cites Section 1862(a)(1)(E) of the Social Security Act as the legal basis for CED, but that provision does not authorize an alternative coverage mechanism based on clinical study participation.
        *   CMS claims section 1862(a)(1)(E) "effectively permits Medicare payment in the case of research conducted pursuant to section 1142 of the Act for items and services that are reasonable and necessary to carry out that section."
        *   However, Section 1862(a)(1)(E) only allows Medicare payment "in the case of research conducted pursuant to section 1320b-12 of this title," which is the statutory authority for AHRQ to "conduct and support research" on health outcomes.
        *   As a matter of plain statutory language, Section 1862(a)(1)(E) applies only to research "conducted and supported" by AHRQ under Section 1142.
        *   CMS stated when finalizing the guidance document that "support" may also take the form of an appropriate AHRQ "endorsement" and that AHRQ has "supported" CED studies by identifying "general characteristics and attributes," being "included" in CED guidance documents, and reviewing studies.
        *   However, HHS’s General Counsel in the First Trump Administration recognized that AHRQ "has not been supporting" these trials, as the word "support" in this context is commonly understood to mean funding.
        *   Accordingly, Section 1862(a)(1)(E) should only apply if AHRQ adequately "supports" the CED study, which will involve more than merely endorsing the clinical study.
        *   Even if CMS could point to some implicit statutory authority to create CEDs for products or uses without FDA approval, CMS lacks any such authority when it comes to drugs that have been approved by FDA for use in the Medicare population and coverage is based on an on-label use.
        *   In such situations, a CED would conflict with FDA’s findings that a drug is safe and effective for on-label use and that the benefits outweigh any risks, as determined by 21 U.S.C. § 355(d).
        *   The CED Guidance would have CMS – an agency without the clinical expertise or personnel capable of making these decisions – use its unauthorized CED structure to replace the FDA’s authority on safety and risks.
        *   In that situation, the risk that a CED determination will conflict with FDA’s prior safety and effectiveness findings is most acute.
        *   As a creation of statute, CMS can have no authority other than what Congress has affirmatively delegated to it.
        *   It is irrelevant that Congress did not explicitly forbid CMS from creating CED as a new paradigm; CMS would have to identify affirmative statutory authorization, and it cannot do so.
        *   The need for clear authority under a statute is particularly present given the drastic change CMS’s CED guidance imposes.
        *   It is not believable that Congress granted CMS the power to create a new paradigm for coverage questions, not mentioned in any statute, under circumstances where it would conflict with determinations already made by FDA on approval of medicines.
        *   The more implausible an agency’s assertion of authority, the clearer Congress must be in delegating the authority.

    *   **B. Inappropriate and Unprecedented Use of CED for FDA-Approved Pharmaceuticals**
        *   Historically, CED has been used in limited circumstances, primarily for technologies—such as medical devices and diagnostics—that, despite FDA approval, were considered to have evolving or limited evidence bases in the Medicare population.
        *   The overwhelming majority of CED applications have involved diagnostics or devices, with only one prior exception for a drug.
        *   The recent expansion of CED to include FDA-approved monoclonal antibody treatments for Alzheimer’s disease represents a concerning departure from precedent.
        *   This departure is concerning both because the product is a therapeutic rather than a device and because the CED requirements apply to the on-label use of an FDA-approved drug.
        *   The differentiator here is not modality, but the fact that CMS is imposing additional evidentiary requirements post-FDA approval.
        *   Further, CMS has taken the unprecedented step of developing, approving, and operating its own CED study, effectively positioning itself as a clinical research sponsor.
        *   This raises serious questions about agency overreach, delays patient access to care, and risks worsening health disparities in populations already underrepresented in research.
        *   Furthermore, drugs approved by the FDA are almost always covered in a straightforward manner.
        *   Patients expect that if they have a condition an FDA-approved drug is intended to treat, and they and their provider believe it is the best option, Medicare coverage is generally predictable and assumed.
        *   This is not the case for new procedures with implantable devices, where the reimbursement landscape is much less straightforward with complex coding and variable coverage policies.
        *   Additionally, the FDA approval pathway—whether traditional or accelerated—should not alter CMS’s coverage obligations.
        *   The FDA has affirmed that drugs approved via accelerated pathways meet the same statutory standards for safety and effectiveness.
        *   CMS should not create additional hurdles that second-guess these expert determinations.
        *   By imposing CED on FDA-approved drugs, CMS risks undermining the FDA's authority and delaying critical access to treatments for patients.
        *   The settings for use also differ significantly:
            *   Implantable devices are generally used at academic medical centers with sophisticated systems for collecting data and are typically implanted once.
            *   Most devices subject to CED are Class III (high risk) devices, including critical implants with serious life-sustaining impacts.
            *   Coverage within a clinical trial under CED may be more feasible for these devices because they are administered through a one-time, major operation, affecting a relatively small number of patients.
            *   Monitoring through a clinical trial as physicians become comfortable with the technology could be a preferred route to coverage.
        *   Moreover, when examining the application of CED to FDA-approved drugs, it becomes clear the framework is ill-suited to medicines.
            *   The FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research (CDER) requires “Substantial Evidence” of safety and effectiveness—typically through randomized, placebo-controlled trials—as a condition of approval.
            *   In contrast, medical devices, regulated by the Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH), are often cleared based on a “Reasonable Assurance” standard, which may not require RCTs.
            *   These structural differences may make CED more appropriate in select device cases, but they do not justify extending the model to drugs that have already met a significantly higher evidentiary threshold through FDA approval.
            *   Drugs are prescribed in various care settings and are used chronically or on a long-term basis, often in places without the necessary capabilities or staff to collect research data.
            *   For example, most approved drugs and investigational assets in the amyloid therapeutic class are administered every 2-4 weeks, making the requirements of CED much more onerous for patients seeking approved therapies compared to approved medical devices subject to CED.

    *   **C. CED Creates Redundant and Duplicative Evidence Requirements**
        *   Lilly and other manufacturers already conduct rigorous Phase 3 clinical trials regulated by—and subject to extensive review by—the FDA, often followed by real-world evidence (RWE) studies to meet both regulatory and payer needs.
        *   Imposing a separate set of evidence requirements under CED unnecessarily duplicates this scientific and operational work, offering no incremental learnings.
        *   This duplication creates inefficiencies, drives up administrative costs, and introduces avoidable delays in patient access.
        *   The burden extends to providers, who are asked to enroll patients in CMS-mandated studies that often conflict with clinical workflows and may not be feasible or appropriate in routine care settings.
        *   Requiring 100% patient participation in these studies is not only operationally unrealistic but also scientifically unnecessary, as no credible research standard requires total enrollment to draw robust conclusions.

    *   **D. CED Undermines Patient-Centered Care and Exacerbates Access Barriers**
        *   Requiring Medicare beneficiaries to enroll in trials or registries as a condition of coverage undermines the foundational principles of patient-centered care.
        *   It creates unnecessary barriers to timely treatment, particularly for older adults, rural populations, communities of color, and individuals of lower socioeconomic status who are less likely to participate in clinical research due to logistical, geographic, or resource-related constraints.
        *   These mandates not only delay access to FDA-approved therapies but also entrench health disparities across the Medicare population.
        *   The Alzheimer’s Treatment Target (ATT) registry—a central component of CMS’s CED framework for monoclonal antibodies targeting amyloid—offers a clear case study in these consequences.
        *   While the registry may appear administratively straightforward on paper, it imposes a substantial operational burden on the very providers who serve vulnerable populations.
        *   Small and independent neurology practices, which are often the only option for patients in rural areas, frequently lack the staffing, infrastructure, and technical expertise required to comply with CMS’s reporting protocols.
        *   At a Congressional briefing in 2023, a leader from Dent Neurology in New York highlighted the complexity involved in navigating the CED process:
            *   “While this registry [the CMS portal] may not be cumbersome in and of itself, for somebody in a standalone neurology practice this might be quite a burden…To get someone from the point of a probable Alzheimer's diagnosis to sitting in the infusion chair to receive this treatment, it is many steps. Even though we have everything all under one roof, it's a process that took up two pages when I wrote it out step by step.”
        *   Similarly, a neurologist at a large academic medical center with extensive clinical trial experience noted that while their institution could manage the CMS portal, they were deeply concerned that smaller practices—those without trial infrastructure or dedicated regulatory staff—would be unable to navigate the same requirements.
        *   As a result, access to these treatments may become concentrated in large academic centers, leaving rural and underserved patients behind.
        *   This model of conditional coverage not only disrupts continuity of care but also places untenable documentation and compliance burdens on frontline clinicians.
        *   Instead of empowering providers to deliver timely, evidence-based care, the CED model shifts their focus toward regulatory administration—without generating any meaningful improvements in clinical outcomes or safety monitoring beyond what has already been established through FDA review and post-market evidence.
        *   CMS must reconsider whether mandating registry participation as a prerequisite to coverage is aligned with its own fairness goals and the statutory obligation to provide reasonable and necessary care to all beneficiaries.
        *   The current CED framework, particularly as implemented through the ATT registry, has the unintended but foreseeable effect of restricting access to breakthrough therapies based on geography and provider capacity—precisely the populations Medicare is charged with protecting.

        *   **Issues with the TAVR Registry**
            *   The TVT Registry, approved by CMS as part of the National Coverage Determination (NCD) for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), is often cited as the “gold standard” for CED implementation.
            *   However, while it may represent a model for data collection, it should not be considered a gold standard for equitable patient access—nor should it be used as a precedent for the application of CED to anti-amyloid therapies in Alzheimer’s disease.
            *   First, the TAVR NCD and its associated CED requirements have now been in place for nearly a decade, despite widespread agreement among clinical experts that sufficient data have been generated to answer the original CED questions.
            *   This extended duration raises concerns about the self-perpetuating nature of CED requirements and the lack of clear endpoints or off-ramps for affected technologies.
            *   More importantly, the TAVR experience demonstrates that even well-structured registries can impose significant barriers to patient access—particularly for underserved populations.
            *   Strict requirements on both providers and patients have limited the availability of TAVR to those treated at major academic centers or high-volume institutions.
            *   Many community hospitals lack the infrastructure or resources to participate in the TVT Registry, effectively excluding patients in rural areas and lower-resourced health systems.
            *   These access limitations have had measurable consequences: In 2018, only 4% of patients receiving TAVR in the United States were African American, underscoring the inequitable distribution of care.
            *   Patients from rural counties or minority communities are frequently forced to travel long distances to meet coverage requirements—a pattern that disproportionately affects the populations already facing structural barriers to care.
            *   The registry itself imposes substantial operational and financial burdens on participating providers.
            *   In 2019, the practice enrollment fee for the TVT Registry was $25,000, not including additional staff hours, training, data entry, and compliance costs.
            *   Providers who are unable to meet these requirements are denied reimbursement for the procedure, creating an artificial gatekeeping mechanism that limits access based on administrative capacity rather than clinical need.
            *   Extrapolating this model to Alzheimer’s disease therapies—particularly in the context of the ATT registry—would be highly problematic.
            *   Unlike TAVR, which is typically performed in tertiary care centers, anti-amyloid treatments are often administered in outpatient settings and rely heavily on community-based neurology practices.
            *   These practices are even less likely to have the staffing or financial resources required to meet registry mandates, and any attempt to replicate the TAVR model would exacerbate disparities in care delivery and disrupt the physician-patient relationship.
            *   In sum, while the TVT Registry may offer lessons in data infrastructure, it also illustrates the unintended consequences of CED when applied without sufficient attention to real-world implementation challenges.
            *   It should not serve as the template for future CED applications, especially for therapeutics already approved by the FDA and poised to address urgent unmet needs in aging and underserved populations.

        *   **Challenges with the Amyloid PET CED Registry**
            *   Although the Amyloid PET NCD with CED has since been retired, the experience of the IDEAS and the NEW IDEAS registries offers important lessons about the persistent harm of CED, particularly for underserved and under-represented populations.
            *   The legacy of these CED requirements continues to shape patient access and provider behavior in the diagnostic pathway for Alzheimer’s disease.
            *   Coverage with Evidence Development (CED) is particularly harmful and burdensome for underserved patient populations, reinforcing disparities in both access and outcomes.
            *   For minority patients, CED historically exacerbates persistent issues of diversity and inclusion in care.
            *   The original IDEAS CED registry was approximately 92% white, prompting the American College of Radiology (ACR) and the Alzheimer’s Association to design the New IDEAS study with a specific goal of enrolling a more diverse population.
            *   Despite this intentional focus, as of June 2022, only 27% of participants in New IDEAS identified as Black, Hispanic, or Latino (14% Black/African American; 13% Hispanic/Latino).
            *   Moreover, interviews conducted at the time the New IDEAS study was still active with minority recruitment team members in Tennessee and North Carolina revealed that patient misunderstanding of CED—particularly confusion about the need to enroll in a clinical trial despite Aβ PET being FDA-approved—was a major barrier to diverse enrollment.
            *   This highlights how the complex and opaque nature of CED can disproportionately discourage participation by historically underrepresented communities.
            *   For rural patients, the burdens of CED are compounded by geographic and logistical limitations.
            *   Many rural providers and hospitals struggle to meet the complex infrastructure and participation requirements associated with CED studies.
            *   As an example, 18 states—many of them rural—had no New IDEAS site, forcing patients to cross state lines in order to receive Medicare-covered amyloid PET scans.
            *   This not only delayed care but also imposed significant travel burdens on already underserved populations while this CED was in effect.
            *   Further, the adverse impact on patient access is intensified by the rapid growth of Medicare Advantage (MA) enrollment.
            *   As of 2024, Medicare Advantage accounts for more than 54% of eligible Medicare beneficiaries, with projections suggesting enrollment could exceed 60% by 2030.
            *   A 2022 Office of Inspector General (OIG) report found that MA organizations frequently applied clinical criteria not found in Medicare coverage rules and requested unnecessary documentation, even for services that should be covered.
            *   In response, bipartisan members of Congress urged HHS to finalize rules that would streamline prior authorization, improve transparency, and ensure timely access to care.
            *   While CMS took important steps in 2023, additional fairness-focused reforms proposed for CY 2026 have yet to be finalized.
            *   As CMS is well aware, national coverage decisions apply equally to beneficiaries enrolled in Traditional Medicare and Medicare Advantage.
            *   However, a burdensome and inconsistently implemented CED framework threatens to create substantial disparities in beneficiary access and outcomes, particularly when overlaid with the known limitations of the MA program.
            *   These inequities are especially troubling given that CED lacks a clear statutory basis and continues to be used in ways that diverge from congressional intent and administrative law norms.
            *   A continued reliance on CED—especially in the context of FDA-approved technologies like amyloid PET—raises serious concerns about both equity and legality.

*   **II. CED Is Unnecessary Where Other Post-Market Data Commitments Exist**
    *   Lilly strongly believes CMS should take a step back and consider the fundamental question of whether CED, in its current form and application, accomplishes the stated goal of efficiently providing patients with access to new therapies while continuing to learn about them.
    *   As stated, the application of Medicare’s CED policy to FDA-approved drugs, particularly anti-amyloid therapies for Alzheimer’s disease, has inadvertently created barriers to patient access.
    *   These therapies have already met the FDA's rigorous standards for safety and efficacy through both Accelerated and Traditional approval pathways.
    *   Requiring additional study participation as a condition for Medicare coverage duplicates existing evidence requirements and delays beneficiary access to necessary treatments.
    *   To be clear, ongoing evidence generation and the pursuit of optimal patient care is important.
    *   Continued research is foundational to the U.S. innovation ecosystem, and Lilly is a leader in this effort.
    *   We have a longstanding commitment to real-world evidence (RWE) generation, investing in post-market studies to assess long-term, clinically meaningful outcomes.
    *   In the case of Alzheimer's disease, Lilly has dedicated over 30 years to research and is actively conducting RWE studies in the U.S. and Europe on therapies like donanemab.
    *   This work evaluates outcomes such as the delay in functional decline and time to dependence on caregiver support.
    *   Specifically, Lilly’s US RWE Study plan:
        *   Compares amyloid-positive, early symptomatic Alzheimer’s patients treated with donanemab plus supportive care to those receiving supportive care alone.
        *   Includes over 3,000 participants (1,020 treated, 2,040 controls) and will assess how donanemab impacts time to caregiver dependence and other functional outcomes over five years.
        *   Expects final results in 2030, with interim analyses providing early insight into real-world clinical benefit, value, and patient experience.
    *   Importantly, this approach is not unique to Alzheimer’s disease.
    *   Across therapeutic areas, including oncology, migraine, and diabetes, Lilly has consistently used RWE to refine clinical understanding, inform regulatory changes, and support broader health system learning. Examples include:
        *   Supporting FDA label updates in oncology based on RWE of less frequent dosing regimens.
        *   Conducting migraine studies (TRIUMPH and OVERCOME) to assess real-world treatment patterns and outcomes.
        *   Evaluating how out-of-pocket costs and treatment adherence differ across diabetes therapies to support more equitable patient access.
    *   These studies reflect a broader industry standard: nearly all large biopharmaceutical companies invest in robust post-market data generation for new medicines.
    *   In short, RWE is already being generated, rigorously, transparently, and voluntarily.
    *   Imposing duplicative and government-administered requirements under CED not only delays access but disregards the extensive, real-time data that manufacturers, providers, and payers are already working to generate and apply.
    *   CMS should recognize this evolving evidence ecosystem and remove unnecessary registry mandates that risk delaying benefits to patients, especially in areas as urgent and devastating as Alzheimer’s disease.

*   **III. Conclusion**
    *   The current CED construct falls short and is inefficient.
    *   It not only undermines FDA authority by requiring additional enrollment in studies as a condition of Medicare coverage, but it duplicates ongoing research efforts by imposing redundant data collection, even as industry-led post-market studies are already underway and generating valuable insights.
    *   To enhance beneficiary access to FDA-approved treatments while supporting the generation of valuable real-world evidence, CMS should:
        *   Differentiate drug and device pathways: CED may be better suited for certain medical devices, but it is ill-fitting for FDA-approved therapeutics and diagnostic agents, where its application delays access rather than enabling it.
        *   Respect the FDA’s gold standard: FDA approval—whether via Accelerated or Traditional pathways—is based on substantial evidence. Once granted, it should be the basis for full Medicare coverage without further conditions.
        *   Leverage industry-led RWE efforts: Companies like Lilly are already generating high-quality RWE for all newly approved medicines. These efforts can and should inform clinical and payer decision-making without redundant requirements imposed through CED.
        *   De-link access from data collection: CED currently functions at the individual beneficiary level—requiring participation in additional studies to gain access. This is not patient-centered. A better approach would allow full coverage for all Medicare beneficiaries consistent with the FDA label, while RWE studies continue in parallel. Access should never be contingent on enrollment in a research protocol.
        *   Examine differences in beneficiary access to services approved under CED between Traditional Medicare and Medicare Advantage to reinforce the need for reform.
    *   In sum, Medicare policy should streamline and evolve to support timely access to FDA-approved therapies while encouraging meaningful, non-duplicative post-market research.
    *   Doing so respects scientific standards, empowers patients, and sustains the innovation-ecosystem that continues to deliver breakthroughs for devastating diseases like Alzheimer’s.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: Eli Lilly urges CMS to rescind or significantly revise its Coverage with Evidence Development (CED) guidance, arguing it lacks legal basis, duplicates industry's post-market real-world evidence generation, and severely impedes timely patient access to FDA-approved drugs, particularly for vulnerable populations.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:

structuredSections.corePosition: Eli Lilly urges CMS to revisit and significantly revise its approach to Coverage with Evidence Development (CED), specifically calling for the rescission of the August 7, 2024 guidance document. We contend that CED lacks a firm legal foundation, imposes undue administrative burden, and creates access barriers for patients, especially for Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved pharmaceuticals, undermining both FDA authority and patient-centered care.

- Respect the FDA’s gold standard for approval:

- De-link access from data collection:

structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Lack of Statutory Authority:** CMS's application of CED exceeds its statutory authority as CED is not mentioned in the Medicare statute and was invented by CMS without a clear legislative mandate, and its cited legal basis is misinterpreted.
- **Conflict with FDA Authority:** The CED Guidance would have CMS, an agency without clinical expertise, replace FDA’s authority on safety and risks for on-label use of approved drugs, risking conflict with FDA’s findings.
- **Inappropriate and Unprecedented Use for FDA-Approved Drugs:** CED has historically been limited to devices/diagnostics, and its recent expansion to FDA-approved therapeutics (e.g., Alzheimer's monoclonal antibodies) is a concerning departure, imposing additional evidentiary requirements post-FDA approval.
- **CMS as Research Sponsor:** CMS has taken the unprecedented step of developing, approving, and operating its own CED study, raising questions about agency overreach and potential worsening of health disparities.
- **Duplicative Evidence Requirements:** CED unnecessarily duplicates rigorous Phase 3 clinical trials and post-market RWE studies already conducted by manufacturers, creating inefficiencies, administrative costs, and avoidable delays.
- **Operational Burden on Providers:** CED imposes undue burden on providers who are asked to enroll patients in studies that conflict with clinical workflows and are often infeasible in routine care settings, especially for small or independent practices.
- **Undermines Patient-Centered Care:** Requiring trial/registry enrollment as a condition of coverage creates unnecessary barriers to timely treatment, particularly for vulnerable populations (older adults, rural, communities of color, lower socioeconomic status), entrenching health disparities.
- **Registry Limitations and Inequities:**
    - The Alzheimer’s Treatment Target (ATT) registry imposes substantial operational burdens on small neurology practices.
    - The TAVR Registry, despite being cited as a "gold standard," has limited access for underserved populations, concentrated care in academic centers, and failed to achieve equitable distribution (e.g., only 4% African American patients).
    - The Amyloid PET CED registries (IDEAS, NEW IDEAS) showed poor diversity (original 92% white, New IDEAS 27% minority) and patient misunderstanding of CED despite FDA approval, disproportionately discouraging participation.
    - Registries impose significant financial burdens on participating providers (e.g., $25,000 enrollment fee for TVT Registry in 2019).
- **Compounding Medicare Advantage Issues:** The growth of Medicare Advantage (MA) enrollment, combined with a burdensome CED framework, threatens substantial disparities, as MA organizations have historically applied clinical criteria not found in Medicare rules and requested unnecessary documentation.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- **Dent Neurology Case Study:** A leader from Dent Neurology highlighted the immense complexity of navigating the CED process for a standalone neurology practice, detailing a multi-step process that "took up two pages when I wrote it out step by step" to get a patient from diagnosis to infusion chair for Alzheimer's treatment.
- **Academic Medical Center Concern:** A neurologist at a large academic medical center, despite their own institution's ability to manage the CMS portal, expressed deep concern that smaller practices, lacking trial infrastructure or dedicated regulatory staff, would be unable to navigate the same CED requirements.
- **TAVR Registry Disparities:** The TVT Registry, often cited as a CED "gold standard," demonstrated significant access barriers for underserved populations, with only 4% of TAVR patients in 2018 being African American and many community hospitals unable to participate, forcing rural and minority patients to travel long distances.
- **Amyloid PET CED Registry Diversity Failures:** Despite intentional design to be more diverse, the New IDEAS study (Amyloid PET) still had only 27% Black, Hispanic, or Latino participants, with patient misunderstanding and confusion about needing to enroll in a clinical trial for an FDA-approved diagnostic being a major barrier to diverse enrollment.
- **Lilly's Robust Real-World Evidence (RWE) Programs:** Lilly highlights its extensive, voluntary RWE generation, including a 5-year US RWE study for donanemab with over 3,000 participants assessing caregiver dependence and functional outcomes, and examples across oncology, migraine, and diabetes, demonstrating that industry already provides valuable post-market data, rendering CED duplicative.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "While this registry [the CMS portal] may not be cumbersome in and of itself, for somebody in a standalone neurology practice this might be quite a burden…To get someone from the point of a probable Alzheimer's diagnosis to sitting in the infusion chair to receive this treatment, it is many steps. Even though we have everything all under one roof, it's a process that took up two pages when I wrote it out step by step."
- "It is not believable that Congress granted CMS the power to create a new paradigm for coverage questions, not mentioned in any statute, under circumstances where it would conflict with determinations already made by FDA on approval of medicines."
- "Access should never be contingent on enrollment in a research protocol."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The National PACE Association (NPA) is providing deregulation recommendations to enhance access to the Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE), consistent with the Administration's "Make America Healthy Again" initiative.
*   As a provider and health plan, PACE is poised for growth, demonstrating promise and potential to serve older Americans with chronic needs who want and are safely able to receive care in the community.
*   Currently, an estimated two million individuals eligible for PACE lack access to the program.
*   To ensure more PACE-eligible individuals have geographic access, especially in rural communities, we recommend HHS remove administrative barriers in the provider and participant PACE application processes.
*   The following federal PACE regulations and/or policies meet criteria outlined in E.O. 14219 and should be modified or rescinded to reduce undue beneficiary and provider burden and enhance access to the innovative PACE care model.

*   **PACE Participant Enrollment Recommendations**
    *   Permit mid-month enrollment in PACE by revising or eliminating the outdated federal requirement at 42 CFR § 460.158, which limits the effective date of a participant’s enrollment to the first day of the calendar month following the date the PACE organization (POs) receives the signed enrollment agreement.
        *   CFR § 460.158 imposes burdens without clinical justification, adding layers of cost for taxpayers by unnecessarily delaying access to the value-based PACE care model without delivering corresponding value or improved outcomes.
        *   Unlike any other Medicare or Medicaid provider, federal PACE regulations require PACE enrollment to begin on the first day of the calendar month after the signed agreement is received.
        *   If an enrollment application is delayed and misses the cut-off for the first of the month, individuals must wait another full month, which can lead to health deterioration or necessitate finding a different long-term care option.
        *   It should be as easy to enroll in PACE as it is to enter a nursing home, if it is the individual’s choice.
        *   This counterproductive limitation is not grounded in statutory requirement and raises concerns under E.O. criteria for rules that "impose significant costs not outweighed by public benefits" and "impede disaster response and healthcare access" by unduly limiting access.
        *   The PACE model supports medically complex, frail older adults in remaining safely at home, delivering significantly better outcomes at a fraction of the cost compared to institutional care.
        *   There is no empirical medical or economic justification for a regulatory requirement that delays prospective participants from entering PACE.
        *   Modifying this rule to allow mid-month enrollment would lead to better patient outcomes and more timely care, with minimal administrative burden.
    *   Allow POs to determine nursing home level of care (LOC) eligibility for enrollment in PACE, with specified state review and audit requirements to ensure accuracy.
        *   This would be consistent with the clinical expertise and responsibilities of the Interdisciplinary Team (IDT) to conduct initial comprehensive assessments, periodic reassessments, and develop/execute participant care plans.
        *   Allowing POs to determine LOC eligibility would streamline enrollment, as state-based or third-party LOC determinations often delay enrollment, resulting in avoidable health deterioration, hospitalization, or institutionalization.
        *   Limitations on provider-determined LOC eligibility act as a barrier to enrollment, especially for individuals urgently needing community-based services.
        *   Allowing providers to determine LOC eligibility, consistent with IDT clinical authority, would reduce delays caused by inconsistent or duplicative state-based evaluations.
        *   This aligns with E.O. criteria to eliminate burdens that "impede private enterprise and entrepreneurship" and "harm the national interest by unjustifiably impeding access to care."

*   **PACE Accessibility Recommendations**
    *   Streamline CMS’ review of applications for new PACE programs and service area expansions (SAEs).
        *   The current PACE application process is overly complex, restrictive, and misaligned with operational realities of providers and needs of older adults.
        *   It generally takes 18-24 months to initiate a new PACE program, with a medium cost of approximately $5.83 million (adjusted for inflation 2003-2022).
        *   The extensive time and cost to start or expand a PACE program unnecessarily delays or prevents beneficiaries from accessing PACE.
        *   NPA urges CMS to modernize and streamline the PACE application process to better support timely access, reduce administrative burden, and facilitate program growth.
        *   Specifically, we request CMS to:
            *   Allow POs to have multiple applications under concurrent CMS review, not precluding a PO with one application from submitting another.
                *   Developing a PACE provider application can take over 180 days and involves close coordination with the State Administering Agency (SAA).
                *   The current one-application-at-a-time limitation unduly constrains a PO’s ability to scale, especially in states with multiple underserved areas.
                *   This change does not require a federal PACE regulation change and could be effected via clarifying CMS guidance.
            *   Permit established POs to add a new PACE center in an existing service area through a public notice process, foregoing the current SAE application requirement (42 CFR §§ 460.10, 460.12).
                *   The current requirement for an extensive SAE application, even for adding a new PACE center within an existing CMS-approved service area, creates unnecessary delays and administrative burden.
                *   These center-only expansions do not alter the geographic service area or provider’s capacity, yet are subject to the same rigorous review as full SAEs.
                *   Requiring a full SAE application in these cases results in costs and delays disproportionate to the regulatory benefit, meeting E.O. criteria for regulations that "impose significant costs upon private parties that are not outweighed by public benefits" and "unduly burden small businesses."
                *   NPA recommends CMS create a streamlined, expedited pathway for center-only expansions focusing on operational readiness rather than duplicative documentation.
            *   Provide expedited and coordinated CMS and SAA concurrent review, rather than the costly and protracted process of sequential agency review (42 CFR §§ 460.12, 460.18).
                *   This is consistent with, if not encouraged by, federal PACE regulations, given the required coordinated review process.
                *   Further coordination reduces administrative and financial burden on CMS and SAAs, reduces redundancies for applicants, and importantly, ensures timely participant access to PACE.
            *   Clarify in the CMS Readiness Review Tool, used by SAAs to review non-operational PO applicants, that states may accept attestations from the PO that staff will be employed by the time the PACE center becomes operational.
                *   Doing so would ease the administrative and financial burden on POs.
                *   This is an administrative action CMS could take without rulemaking or statutory change, significantly extending geographic access to PACE.
            *   Increase the frequency at which CMS accepts applications for new and expanding POs from quarterly to monthly.
                *   To eliminate potential delays, we urge CMS to remove the current restriction limiting applicants to four days a year and allow more continuous submissions.
                *   If a PO applicant misses a deadline, they must wait three months, causing significant delays in prospective participants’ access to PACE.
                *   This change requires no statutory or regulatory change as CMS conveyed the limitation through sub-regulatory guidance.
    *   To expand access to PACE in geographically underserved areas, including rural communities, we encourage CMS to partner with the Administration for a Healthy America (AHA) to reinstate the Rural PACE Planning and Development Grants, which were issued and subsequently withdrawn by HRSA earlier this year.
        *   PACE has a proven track record of improving care outcomes for older adults.
        *   These reissued grants would provide resources to reach populations in rural communities who can benefit from this care model.
        *   This is consistent with NACRHHS recommendations to expand PACE in rural America.
    *   Remove the anti-competitive and outdated federal regulatory limitation at 42 CFR § 460.24 that limits the total number of PACE programs that can be operational.
        *   This arbitrary and outdated limitation exacerbates barriers to PACE access for beneficiaries and puts POs on an uneven playing field with Medicare Advantage (MA) plans, which are not subject to such anti-competitive requirements.

*   **Regulations for Reconsidering to Achieve Chronic Disease Reversal (E.O. 14212)**
    *   To support the goals of E.O. 14212, particularly reversing chronic disease through prevention and person-centered care, NPA strongly recommends HHS reconsider several outdated regulations that create avoidable delays and limit access to the innovative PACE care model.
    *   Please refer to NPA’s comprehensive response to Question 1, as these regulatory reforms would collectively expand access, accelerate preventive interventions, and advance the MAHA Commission’s goals by empowering older adults and individuals with disabilities to manage chronic conditions effectively in the community.

*   **General Deregulatory Considerations (E.O. 14192)**
    *   Certain federal PACE regulations and guidance present unnecessary complexity, impose burdensome documentation requirements, and ultimately impede PACE access to care for older adults with chronic health needs.
    *   These should be reconsidered for administrative inefficiency and misalignment with the person-centered, integrated care philosophy PACE delivers.
    *   Specifically, we strongly recommend HHS consider the following:

*   **PACE Excessive Administrative Burden (Regulatory Compliance)**
    *   Reassess onerous new (CY 2025) federal PACE regulatory requirements.
        *   In the Contract Year (CY) 2025 MA, Part D, and PACE Final Rule, CMS codified significant new federal regulatory requirements for POs effective January 1, 2025.
        *   These provisions include new service delivery and care coordination timeframes where the onus is placed on both the PO and the contracted provider (e.g., hospitals, care facilities) for the PO to be compliant (42 CFR §§ 460.98 and 460.102).
        *   CMS estimated POs would incur $2.1 million in costs in CY 2025 to implement these PACE provisions.
        *   These provisions primarily address the arrangement and scheduling of IDT-approved services, not the actual provision (furnishing or delivery) of services.
        *   A more effective approach to evaluating participant protections and service delivery is through review of documentation such as care plans, progress notes, and service logs to assess prompt service delivery according to needs and to ensure responsiveness to individual needs, upholding the person-centered philosophy.
    *   Mitigate burden related to PACE personnel requirements for contracted entities providing staff that provide direct participant care.
        *   NPA recognizes the importance of ensuring all staff, direct or contracted, possess necessary competencies for high-quality, safe care.
        *   However, current regulatory mandates under 42 CFR §§ 460.64(a)(3) and 460.71(a)(2) impose significant administrative burdens on POs by requiring direct oversight and validation of contracted personnel training and competency.
        *   These provisions necessitate extensive documentation and monitoring, diverting valuable resources from direct participant care and potentially hindering PO agility in responding to participant needs.
        *   To balance patient safety with operational realities, NPA suggests alternative approaches that maintain rigorous oversight without undue administrative strain, including:
            *   **Leverage contractual accountability for training and competency:** POs already have detailed contracts with contracted entities that include compliance with CMS and state requirements. These contracts should be the primary mechanism for ensuring training and competency, rather than direct PO obligations. Additional training requirements on contractors may discourage high-quality entities from partnering with POs, especially in underserved areas.
            *   **Accept attestations as sufficient documentation:** While POs can accept attestations from contracted providers for personnel standards (background checks, OIG screenings, medical clearances), CMS audits still require POs to obtain and produce underlying documentation. This creates significant operational burden and unnecessary duplication. NPA recommends CMS allow POs to rely on signed attestations as evidence of compliance and acceptable audit documentation. To ensure accountability, CMS could establish a framework requiring POs to implement internal oversight (e.g., periodic monitoring) to validate accuracy.
            *   **Align federal PACE personnel requirements with state and industry standards:** NPA encourages CMS to ensure federal PACE personnel requirements for contracted providers align with applicable industry and state standards (e.g., state licensure for EMTs). This addresses burdensome additional requirements when existing regulatory frameworks already ensure workforce competency and safety.
            *   **Permit chart reviews in lieu of conducting in-person reassessments in response to service determination request (SDR) denials under specified conditions:** Federal PACE regulations at §§ 460.104(d)(2), 460.121(h)(1), and 460.104(d)(2) require appropriate IDT members to conduct an in-person reassessment before a final decision on an anticipated denial or partial denial of an SDR.
                *   POs often must conduct a full reassessment even when the participant’s condition has not changed and clinical information is documented.
                *   This approach is inefficient, burdensome, consumes clinical resources, diverts staff from direct care, and delays timely decision-making, especially for non-urgent services. It also contributes to participant fatigue.
                *   NPA recommends CMS provide greater discretion to POs to respond to SDRs, particularly when the request pertains to services already addressed in the care plan or recently evaluated.
                *   Specifically, we request CMS permit POs to, in certain circumstances, conduct a targeted chart review (or virtual assessment) instead of a full reassessment when the participant has been recently assessed (e.g., within 30 days), the requested service is already in the care plan or under active review, and no significant change in condition has occurred.
                *   This revised approach preserves clinical integrity and participant safety, reduces administrative burden, and supports more timely and efficient responses. POs would continue to document rationale and ensure IDT review.

*   **PACE Quality Monitoring and Reporting Burden**
    *   One of the most significant administrative challenges stems from duplicative and inconsistent quality reporting requirements outlined at §§460.130(d), 460.200(b)(1), 460.200(c), and 460.202.
    *   POs are required to submit both aggregate and individual PACE Quality Data to CMS through the PACE Quality Monitoring Module in the Health Plan Management System (HPMS).
    *   Region-specific mandates add unnecessary redundancy, with CMS Regional Office Account Managers often requiring the same data in separate spreadsheets, sometimes monthly, despite quarterly HPMS submissions.
    *   Further duplication occurs at the state level, where SAAs require the same data in different formats already provided to CMS.
    *   This forces POs to report the same data through multiple channels, increasing administrative burden without improving data quality or utility, diverting critical provider resources, and creating confusion.
    *   We strongly advocate for a centralized and streamlined reporting process using a standardized format, allowing CMS Central Office, ROs, SAAs, and POs to access consistent data through a single unified platform.
    *   Reducing duplicative reporting is essential to alleviating provider burden and enabling more effective, consistent, and meaningful quality oversight.

*   **PACE Audit Burden**
    *   NPA is deeply concerned about the continued retrofitting of MA and Part D audit processes for use in the PACE program.
    *   The current audit framework fails to reflect PACE’s integrated provider-based care model, imposing data collection and reporting demands that are disproportionately complex and misaligned with how POs deliver and document care.
    *   Many required data elements presume automated, plan-level retrieval capacities that do not exist in PACE’s provider-centric infrastructure.
    *   As a result, CMS burden estimates significantly understate the time, staffing, and administrative resources POs need to manually extract and prepare clinical documentation, diverting critical staff time from direct care.
    *   The proposed 2026 PACE Audit Protocol introduces new templates, cover sheets, and impact analysis requirements that, while aiming to standardize, continue to impose excessive burden.
    *   Demand for highly specific clinical data and participant-level medical records involves time-intensive manual reviews by clinical and interdisciplinary staff.
    *   While CMS has taken some steps to reduce duplicative reporting, the audit protocol still demands an uncommon level of per-participant information not typically expected of other Medicare or Medicaid provider types.
    *   NPA urges CMS to revisit its burden assumptions and recommends piloting audit elements to develop a more appropriate, provider-informed oversight model tailored specifically to PACE’s unique structure and care delivery.

*   **Alternative Approaches for Lesser Burden**
    *   Please refer to NPA’s responses under Question 3 regarding opportunities to mitigate excessive administrative burden, such as those related to PACE personnel requirements for contracted entities.
    *   We also call attention to recommendations in response to Question 3 to reduce the complexity of time-intensive data retrieval aspects of the PACE audit process, and opportunities to streamline PACE quality data monitoring and reporting.
    *   Further, we recommend that CMS issue guidance recommending states explicitly include PACE participants in their Medicaid paid caregiver programs.
        *   Currently, only a limited number of states allow PACE participants to access state Medicaid-paid caregiver programs.
        *   These programs compensate family members, friends, and neighbors who assist individuals with activities of daily living (ADLs) and other non-skilled services in their homes.
        *   Allowing PACE participants access to paid caregivers would advance aging-in-place strategies, reduce caregiver strain, and lower long-term healthcare costs by avoiding institutional care and preventable hospitalizations.

*   **Outdated Technology and Leveraging New Technologies**
    *   NPA offers the following recommendations for HHS to better align Medicare requirements with current and new technologies to better serve participants and achieve potential cost-savings:
        *   **Leverage PACE model tests to further the reach of PACE to additional high-cost, high-need individuals and geographic areas:** There is considerable upside for HHS to leverage PACE, a proven, risk-adjusted care model, as an innovative incubator. These model tests could provide important data to inform PACE scaling and policy refinements, leading to expanded access. PACE is well-positioned to pilot and test innovative technologies through CMS-supported model tests, generating real-world evidence to inform broader regulatory reforms and ensure federal PACE rules keep up with evolving care delivery methods. By embracing a more tech-enabled, risk-adjusted approach, rooted in participant needs and clinical judgment, HHS can achieve regulatory goals with lower burdens and better outcomes.
        *   **Permit targeted telehealth flexibilities:** POs provide comprehensive, person-centered care for older adults with chronic conditions in the PACE center and participants’ homes. Telehealth is an important tool to ensure uninterrupted access to essential services, especially for rural individuals. However, current federal regulations (42 CFR § 460.104) significantly limit POs’ ability to leverage telehealth for participant assessments. While in-person assessments are essential, regulations broadly prohibiting telehealth alternatives, even when medically appropriate and with participant consent, are outdated. Allowing targeted, condition-specific use of telehealth assessments would increase flexibility, reduce avoidable care disruptions, and align with best practices adopted by state Medicaid programs and private-sector models.
        *   **Foster collaborative models between POs and contracted providers—predicated on reasonable Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement principles—to ensure participants have access to a robust PACE provider network:** Except for emergency services (42 CFR § 460.100), federal regulations at 42 CFR § 460.70(a) require POs to have written contracts with outside organizations, agencies, or individuals providing administrative or care-related services not directly furnished by the PO, including stipulated medical specialties.
            *   Unlike non-contract providers providing Medicare-covered services, CMS does not delineate the minimum amount POs must reimburse (and the provider must accept in full) contracted providers for Medicare or Medicaid-covered services.
            *   Several PO members, particularly those in their initial trial period, report significant challenges securing contracts with providers, especially hospitals and specialty providers, who charge rates above typical Medicare rates due to market leverage or scarcity.
            *   To address this, NPA requests CMS consider changes to federal regulations that would require hospitals within a PO’s geographic service area to demonstrate good-faith contracting efforts, develop CMS-endorsed model contracts with fair reimbursement clauses, and/or potentially facilitate regional contracting pools.
            *   Regarding Medicaid payments, NPA appreciates the 2025 PACE Medicaid Capitation Rate Setting Guide’s specificity on how the Amount Would Otherwise be Paid (AWOP) and rates should be established, hoping for a more transparent rate-setting process.
            *   We strongly recommend that states acknowledge the administrative and support costs associated with the direct provision of care, by POs and their contracted entities, in developing payment rates.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The National PACE Association requests comprehensive deregulation of federal PACE requirements to remove administrative barriers, streamline processes, and enhance access for eligible older Americans to the Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** National PACE Association
- **Type:** Organization
- **Role/Expertise:** Represents Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) providers and health plans; expert in delivering integrated care to older Americans with chronic needs in the community.
- **Geographic Scope:** National
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly represents organizations providing PACE services, seeking to reduce regulatory burdens that impede program growth, participant access, and operational efficiency across the country.
structuredSections.corePosition: We believe the Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly (PACE) is poised for significant growth, yet it is currently hindered by outdated, complex, and burdensome federal regulations and policies. These administrative barriers unnecessarily delay or prevent millions of eligible older adults from accessing vital community-based care, leading to higher costs and poorer health outcomes. Comprehensive deregulation is essential to unleash PACE's full potential, consistent with the Administration's health initiatives.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Permit mid-month enrollment in PACE by revising or eliminating 42 CFR § 460.158 to allow enrollment to begin immediately upon signing the agreement, not just on the first day of the subsequent month.
- Allow PACE Organizations (POs) to determine nursing home Level of Care (LOC) eligibility for enrollment, consistent with the Interdisciplinary Team's clinical authority, while maintaining state review and audit requirements for accuracy.
- Streamline CMS’ review of applications for new PACE programs and service area expansions (SAEs).
    - Allow POs to have multiple applications under concurrent CMS review.
    - Permit established POs to add a new PACE center in an existing service area through a public notice process, foregoing the full SAE application requirement.
    - Provide expedited and coordinated CMS and State Administering Agency (SAA) concurrent review, rather than sequential agency review.
    - Clarify in the CMS Readiness Review Tool that states may accept attestations from the PO that staff will be employed by the time the PACE center becomes operational.
    - Increase the frequency at which CMS accepts applications for new and expanding POs from quarterly to monthly.
- Partner with the Administration for a Healthy America (AHA) to reinstate the Rural PACE Planning and Development Grants to expand access in underserved areas.
- Remove the anti-competitive and outdated federal regulatory limitation at 42 CFR § 460.24 that limits the total number of operational PACE programs.
- Reassess onerous new (CY 2025) federal PACE regulatory requirements, especially those concerning service delivery and care coordination timeframes, and focus on evaluating actual service provision via documentation.
- Mitigate burden related to PACE personnel requirements for contracted entities providing direct participant care by:
    - Leveraging contractual accountability for training and competency as the primary mechanism for compliance.
    - Accepting signed attestations from contracted providers as sufficient documentation for personnel standards during audits.
    - Aligning federal PACE personnel requirements with state and industry standards.
- Permit targeted chart reviews, instead of full in-person reassessments, for Service Determination Request (SDR) denials under specified conditions (e.g., recent assessment, no significant change in condition).
- Implement a centralized and streamlined quality reporting process using a standardized format to reduce duplicative reporting across CMS Central Office, Regional Offices, and SAAs.
- Pilot PACE audit elements to develop a more appropriate, provider-informed oversight model tailored to PACE's unique structure, rather than retrofitting Medicare Advantage/Part D audit processes.
- Issue guidance recommending that states explicitly include PACE participants in their Medicaid paid caregiver programs.
- Leverage PACE as an innovative incubator for model tests to inform scaling and policy refinements, especially for new technologies, to generate real-world evidence for regulatory reforms.
- Permit targeted telehealth flexibilities for participant assessments when medically appropriate and with participant consent.
- Foster collaborative models between POs and contracted providers by:
    - Requiring hospitals within a PO’s service area to demonstrate good-faith contracting efforts.
    - Developing CMS-endorsed model contracts with fair reimbursement clauses.
    - Potentially facilitating regional contracting pools.
    - Recommending states acknowledge administrative and support costs in Medicaid payment rates.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- The current regulatory framework unnecessarily delays access to PACE for an estimated two million eligible individuals, leading to health deterioration and avoidable institutionalization.
- Federal regulations impose significant, clinically unjustified costs and burdens on POs and taxpayers by delaying access to value-based care.
- State-based or third-party Level of Care (LOC) determinations cause enrollment delays and impede access to urgent community-based services.
- The overly complex, restrictive, and prolonged (18-24 months, costing $5.83M) application process for new PACE programs and service area expansions stifles program growth.
- Limitations on concurrent application reviews and the requirement for full Service Area Expansion (SAE) applications for simple center additions within existing service areas create undue administrative burden and restrict scaling.
- The quarterly application submission window creates significant delays for prospective programs missing deadlines.
- The outdated federal regulatory limitation on the total number of operational PACE programs is anti-competitive and puts PACE at a disadvantage compared to Medicare Advantage (MA) plans.
- New (CY 2025) federal regulatory requirements for service delivery and care coordination timeframes place an onerous burden on POs and contracted providers without focusing on actual service provision.
- Current mandates for POs to directly oversee and validate contracted personnel training and competency impose significant administrative burdens, diverting resources from direct care and potentially hindering agility.
- The requirement for in-person reassessments for every Service Determination Request (SDR) denial, even when conditions haven't changed, is inefficient, consumes clinical resources, and causes participant fatigue.
- Duplicative and inconsistent quality reporting requirements across federal and state levels (HPMS, CMS ROs, SAAs) increase administrative burden without improving data utility.
- The retrofitting of Medicare Advantage (MA) and Part D audit processes to PACE creates disproportionately complex data collection and reporting demands, understating the actual time and resources required from POs.
- Challenges in securing contracts with hospitals and specialty providers due to reimbursement rates charged above typical Medicare levels, especially for new POs in their trial period.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The direct comparison that "it ought to be as easy to enroll in PACE as it is for an individual to enter a nursing home" highlights a core frustration with the current regulatory hurdles.
- The explicit cost ($5.83 million) and time (18-24 months) estimates for initiating a new PACE program vividly illustrate the significant barriers to growth.
- The revelation that many data elements required for CMS audits presume automated, plan-level retrieval capacities which do not exist in PACE’s provider-centric infrastructure, forcing time-intensive manual extraction, reveals a fundamental misalignment between regulatory expectations and operational realities.
- The observation that an "arbitrary and outdated regulatory limitation" caps the total number of operational PACE programs, unlike Medicare Advantage plans, points to an anti-competitive and inequitable playing field.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "Simply put, it ought to be as easy to enroll in PACE as it is for an individual to enter a nursing home, if it is their choice to do so."
- "This arbitrary and outdated regulatory limitation serves to further exacerbate beneficiaries’ barriers to accessing PACE, not to mention puts POs on an uneven playing field with Medicare Advantage (MA) plans, the latter of which are not subject to such anti-competitive requirements."
- "Many of the data elements required during CMS audits presume automated, plan-level retrieval capacities that simply do not exist in PACE’s provider-centric infrastructure."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I am commenting on the U.S Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
*   The years of pregnancy to age three set the foundation for a baby’s development, learning and relationships.
    *   Babies rely entirely on the adults around them—parents, caregivers, and early childhood professionals—to provide safe, nurturing care.
    *   When babies or their caregivers face reduced support or program quality, babies can end up facing long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences.
    *   When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health.
*   Regulations matter.
    *   HHS, as the leading Federal agency tasked with enhancing the health and well-being of all Americans, plays a critical role in ensuring that babies, families, and the professionals who care for little ones have access to the resources, protections, and supports they need.
    *   In considering changes to regulations, HHS must preserve regulations that:
        *   Keep young children safe and healthy.
        *   Enable the adults in their lives to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
*   For example, regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings are needed to keep babies safe and developmentally on track.
*   Regulations that keep children and those who care for them healthy, like those that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care, must be maintained.
    *   This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe.
*   HHS rules reach far beyond just Medicaid and early learning, with many HHS programs laying the foundation of quality care and critical support that babies need.
*   Any changes to regulations must be:
    *   Transparent.
    *   Grounded in evidence.
    *   Focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
*   Because each regulation is different, HHS must continue to give the public—including families and early childhood professionals like me—ample time and opportunity to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes.
    *   We need a robust public process to make sure that the rules work for babies and those who care for them.
*   To keep America’s babies healthy, HHS must maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services.
*   Please uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
*   I would also like to add that I am a product of Head Start Services.
    *   I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career.
    *   I have a Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma.
    *   I have been a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for the past twenty-three years servicing the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles.
    *   It gives great pleasure to give back to my community.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An experienced early childhood education professional and Head Start alumna urges HHS to maintain and strengthen regulations that ensure the safety, health, and development of young children, advocating for transparent, evidence-based changes and robust public input.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
-   **Name/Organization:** Elizabeth Villanueva
-   **Type:** Individual
-   **Role/Expertise:** Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma; 23 years as a vendor for the state of California Early Start system; former Head Start recipient.
-   **Geographic Scope:** Local (South Central Los Angeles, San Pedro, CA) / State (California)
-   **Stake in Issue:** As an early childhood professional directly involved in providing services to vulnerable children and a beneficiary of early childhood programs, she has a direct interest in regulations that ensure quality care and support for young children and their caregivers.
structuredSections.corePosition: I strongly believe that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) must preserve and uphold regulations that safeguard the health, safety, and development of young children from pregnancy to age three. These foundational years dictate lifelong well-being, and effective regulations, grounded in evidence and developed transparently with public input, are crucial for ensuring access to quality care and services.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   Preserve regulations that keep young children safe and healthy.
-   Preserve regulations that enable adults to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
    -   Specifically, maintain regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings.
    -   Maintain regulations that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care.
-   Ensure any changes to regulations are transparent, grounded in evidence, and focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
-   Provide ample time and opportunity for the public, including families and early childhood professionals, to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes through a robust public process.
-   Maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services for babies.
-   Uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   Reduced support or program quality for babies and caregivers could lead to long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences for children.
-   Regulatory changes that are not transparent, evidence-based, or child-focused could negatively impact the well-being and safety of children, families, and their service providers.
-   Inadequate public involvement in the regulatory process may result in rules that do not effectively serve the needs of babies and their caregivers.

-   Extensive professional experience as a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for 23 years, specifically servicing "the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles."
-   Expresses deep personal satisfaction and commitment to her work, stating "It gives great pleasure to give back to my community."
