structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The American Academy of Hospice and Palliative Medicine (AAHPM) thanks the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for the opportunity to comment on the Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation to Make America Healthy Again [AHRQ-2025-0001].
    *   AAHPM is the professional organization for physicians specializing in Hospice and Palliative Medicine (HPM).
    *   Membership includes over 5,200 physicians, nurses, social workers, spiritual care providers, and other health professionals.
    *   They are deeply committed to improving quality of life for the expanding population of patients facing serious illness, as well as their families and caregivers.
    *   They strive to advance the field and ensure that patients across all communities and geographies have access to high-quality palliative and hospice care.
*   AAHPM supports HHS efforts to promote health and well-being, and to undertake deregulatory actions that reduce administrative burden while upholding patient safety and well-being.
    *   AAHPM previously submitted comments in response to the Medicare RFI “Unleashing Prosperity through Deregulation of the Medicare Program (Executive Order 14192),” offering feedback on unnecessary and excessive burdens for HPM physicians and/or hospice providers.
    *   They underscore the need to address concerns and act on recommendations from that prior submission.
*   AAHPM appreciates the opportunity through this RFI to broaden the lens beyond the Medicare program.
    *   They call attention to the value of palliative care in managing the nation’s chronic disease burden.
    *   They urge the Department to consider policy changes that would facilitate broader patient access to palliative care services.
    *   They highlight the burden that prior authorization imposes on physicians and patients, including across Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, and private health plans, impeding access to and delivery of medically necessary treatments and services.
*   Recognizing the Value of Palliative Care
    *   Palliative care is an interdisciplinary model of care aimed at preventing and managing the debilitating effects of serious illness, including serious chronic illness.
        *   It can be provided from the time of diagnosis and involves the relief of pain and other symptoms causing discomfort.
        *   Hospice is a type of palliative care for patients near the end of life.
    *   Palliative care is patient- and family-centered, focusing on matching treatment to achievable patient goals to maximize quality of life.
        *   This involves detailed and skilled communication with patients and families to elicit goals and preferences.
        *   It includes expert assessment and management of physical, psychological, and other sources of suffering.
        *   It involves coordination of care across multiple settings (e.g., hospital, post-acute care, ambulatory clinics, home).
        *   High-quality palliative care also supports caregivers by offering education, emotional support, tools, social work assistance, and more.
    *   Enhanced access to palliative care would support policy objectives outlined in Executive Order 14212, “Establishing the President’s Make America Healthy Again Commission.”
        *   Specifically, those focused on "aggressively [combatting] the critical health challenges facing our citizens," ensuring "our healthcare system promotes health rather than just managing disease," and ensuring "availability of expanded treatment options and the flexibility for health insurance coverage to provide benefits that support beneficial lifestyle changes and disease prevention."
    *   A growing body of medical research documents the benefits of high-quality palliative and hospice care for seriously and chronically ill patients and their families.
        *   Benefits include relieving pain and other distressing symptoms, addressing psychosocial and spiritual needs, and improving capacity to contend with illness stresses.
        *   Benefits also accrue for hospitals, payers, and the healthcare system, such as enhanced quality of life, higher patient and family satisfaction, reduced hospital expenditures and lengths of stay.
        *   Palliative care achieves these outcomes at a lower cost than usual care by helping patients better understand and address their needs, choose effective interventions, and avoid unnecessary/unwanted hospitalizations and interventions.
        *   Palliative care is holistic and person-centered, understanding patient needs and preferences (including culture, history, community, spiritual orientation) and considering psychosocial factors.
    *   Current policies and payment systems pose numerous barriers limiting palliative care teams’ ability to receive adequate reimbursement for comprehensive services, thereby limiting patient access to high-quality palliative care.
    *   To expand access to palliative care services, AAHPM offers the following recommendations:
        *   Pursue opportunities to expand access to palliative care services, including through models implemented by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid (CMS) Innovation Center and modifications to the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (MPFS).
            *   AAHPM has advocated for a robust Medicare alternative payment model (APM) for community-based palliative care, including submitting a proposed model to PTAC and informing CMS.
            *   Increased coverage for and access to community-based palliative care services is necessary for patients with serious illness, including serious chronic illness.
            *   Models could also focus on integrating palliative care into primary care delivery.
            *   AAHPM has also supported MPFS payment changes for care management services, communication technology-based services, caregiver training, and principal illness navigation (PIN) services.
            *   Increasing availability and utilization of these services would expand palliative care teams’ ability to support seriously ill patients.
        *   Work with Congress to achieve permanent Medicare telehealth flexibilities.
            *   AAHPM members and patients experienced tremendous benefits from telehealth, especially for seriously ill patients who face challenges accessing in-person care.
            *   Permanently eliminating geographic and originating site restrictions on Medicare telehealth services is imperative for ongoing palliative care access, regardless of location, including in homes.
        *   Pursue all available avenues for expanding the number of Medicare-supported residency slots for HPM.
            *   This includes expanded graduate medical education funding and prioritization of slots for high-value/significant shortage specialties like HPM.
            *   The nation faces a shortage of HPM specialists, critical for Americans with serious or complex chronic illness, a population expected to grow.
            *   This shortage largely stems from policies limiting Medicare-funding of residency slots based on historical allocations.
            *   Increased HPM residency positions will build a physician workforce aligned with evolving healthcare needs and improve care for millions.
        *   Ensure access to a wide range of pain management therapies, from multimodal and nonpharmacological treatment to appropriate opioid prescriptions.
            *   AAHPM recognizes the public health imperative to curb opioid misuse but urges balanced policy that also recognizes the need for ready access to appropriate pain medications for seriously ill or end-of-life patients, for whom high-dose opioids may be necessary.
            *   Timely and effective pain management is central to high-quality palliative care.
            *   This includes considering guidelines for opioid and other pain management therapies, coverage and payment policies across Medicare, Medicaid, and private plans, and quality measurement efforts.
        *   Support enhanced funding for palliative care research, including through the Consortium for Palliative Care Research Across the Lifespan.
            *   More research is needed to understand and address pain and other distressing symptoms, and to improve serious illness care delivery models, communication science, and caregiving science.
            *   HHS should prioritize continued support for the National Institute on Aging (NIA) to coordinate the multi-disease Consortium for Palliative Care Research Across the Lifespan.
*   Addressing Prior Authorization and Other Utilization Management Challenges
    *   Prior authorization tools and similar utilization management requirements create significant burden for physicians delivering timely and effective care to seriously ill patients, for both medical services and prescription drugs.
        *   Members report that a single prior authorization request can take an hour or more of physician or clinical staff time, diverting attention and resources from patient care.
        *   These requirements delay patient access to medically necessary care in best-case scenarios and deny access altogether in worst-case scenarios.
        *   Either outcome can lead to significant patient harm.
    *   In members’ experience, payers create inappropriate and burdensome hurdles inconsistent with best evidence for treating seriously ill patients.
        *   For example, some step therapy protocols require a trial of an atypical opioid (e.g., tramadol or methadone) before a typical sustained-release opioid, without regard for safety concerns or appropriateness for seriously ill patients with significant pain.
        *   Policies that essentially require physicians to practice bad medicine can harm patients and contribute to poor outcomes.
    *   Prior authorization guidelines may not account for reasonable flexibilities necessary to protect access to treatments and services.
        *   For example, if a patient has approval for thirty 10-milligram immediate-release oxycodone tablets but only 5-milligram tablets are available due to supply chain issues, new prior authorization requests are often required for twice the quantity.
        *   If the lack of availability is regional and not on the official national back-order list, the second prior authorization request is often denied, delaying treatment.
        *   Commonsense policies limiting such obstacles would significantly improve timely access to medically necessary prescriptions and minimize poor patient outcomes from medication access challenges.
    *   Prior authorization and other utilization management challenges apply across Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, and private plans.
    *   AAHPM believes relief from prior authorization policies is needed to support patient access and timely delivery of medically necessary care.
        *   They encourage HHS to consider policies that limit prior authorization and other utilization management-related burden on physicians and patients.
        *   Changes finalized for Medicare Advantage plans offer a good starting point for broader application to other payers. These include requiring plans to:
            *   Provide publicly accessible information on the evidence and rationale used for utilization management policies.
            *   Ensure prior authorizations remain valid for the duration of an entire approved course of treatment or services.
            *   Limit the use of prior authorization to confirm the presence of diagnoses or other medical criteria.
    *   CMS previously finalized requirements for applicable private plans to give providers notice of coverage decisions, including specific reasons for denial, but excluded drug prior authorization decisions.
        *   AAHPM recommends CMS consider new requirements for private payers, including Medicare Part D plans, or their contracted pharmacies to inform prescribers when drug coverage is denied and the specific reason.
        *   Too often, physicians are not informed of denials or patient challenges in obtaining medications.
        *   Patients may not understand next steps or be able to advocate for themselves, potentially resulting in devastating consequences such as increased emergency department utilization, unnecessary hospitalization, or life-threatening complications.
        *   Requiring plan sponsors or contracted pharmacies to close the loop with prescribers could help prevent negative outcomes.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The American Academy of Hospice and Palliative Medicine advocates for policy changes to expand patient access to high-quality palliative care services and reduce the burden of prior authorization across all health plans, emphasizing its critical role in managing chronic illness and improving patient outcomes at lower costs.

structuredSections.corePosition: We support deregulatory actions that reduce administrative burden while upholding patient safety and well-being. We advocate for policy changes that would facilitate broader patient access to palliative care services, recognizing their value in managing the nation’s chronic disease burden. Additionally, we call for relief from prior authorization and other utilization management policies that impede patient access to and delivery of medically necessary treatments and services.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Pursue opportunities to expand access to palliative care services through CMS Innovation Center models and modifications to the Medicare Physician Fee Schedule (MPFS).
  - Advocate for a robust Medicare alternative payment model (APM) for community-based palliative care, potentially integrating it into primary care.
  - Support MPFS payment changes for care management services, communication technology-based services, caregiver training, and principal illness navigation (PIN) services.
- Work with Congress to achieve permanent Medicare telehealth flexibilities by permanently eliminating geographic and originating site restrictions on Medicare telehealth services.
- Pursue all available avenues for expanding the number of Medicare-supported residency slots for Hospice and Palliative Medicine (HPM).
  - Include expanded graduate medical education funding and prioritization for high-value/shortage specialties like HPM.
- Ensure access to a wide range of pain management therapies, balancing opioid misuse prevention with ready access to appropriate pain medications for seriously ill patients.
  - Consider guidelines for opioid use, coverage and payment policies across all plans, and quality measurement efforts.
- Support enhanced funding for palliative care research, including through the Consortium for Palliative Care Research Across the Lifespan, coordinated by the National Institute on Aging (NIA).
- Limit prior authorization and other utilization management-related burden on physicians and patients by applying changes similar to those finalized for Medicare Advantage plans more broadly to other types of payers.
  - Require plans to provide publicly accessible information on the evidence and rationale used for utilization management policies.
  - Require prior authorizations to remain valid for the duration of an entire approved prescribed or ordered course of treatment or services.
  - Limit the use of prior authorization to confirm the presence of diagnoses or other medical criteria.
- Consider new requirements for private payers (including Medicare Part D plans) or their contracted pharmacies to inform prescribers when drug coverage is denied and the specific reason for denial.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- Current policies and payment systems pose numerous barriers that limit palliative care teams’ ability to receive adequate reimbursement, consequently limiting patients’ ability to receive high-quality palliative care.
- The nation is facing a shortage of Hospice and Palliative Medicine (HPM) specialists, largely stemming from policies that limit Medicare-funding of residency slots based on reliance on historical allocations.
- Prior authorization tools and other utilization management requirements create significant administrative burden for physicians, diverting attention and resources away from patient care (e.g., a single request taking an hour or more).
- Prior authorization delays or denies patient access to medically necessary and appropriate care, leading to significant patient harm.
- Payer-created hurdles are often inconsistent with the best available evidence for treating seriously ill patients.
  - Examples include step therapy protocols that require a trial of atypical opioids before typical sustained-release opioids, without regard to safety concerns or appropriateness, potentially forcing "bad medicine."
- Prior authorization guidelines do not account for reasonable flexibilities necessary to protect access to treatments and services.
  - Example: Supply chain issues requiring new prior authorization requests for equivalent doses (e.g., 5mg tablets instead of 10mg) often result in denial if the issue is regional, leading to delayed treatment.
- Physicians are too often not informed of drug coverage denials or other challenges patients experience in obtaining needed medications.
  - This can lead to patients not understanding next steps or being unable to advocate for themselves, potentially resulting in devastating consequences such as increased emergency department utilization, unnecessary hospitalization, or life-threatening complications.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The administrative burden of prior authorization is significant, with members reporting that a single request can take an hour or more of physician or clinical staff time, directly diverting resources from patient care.
- Payer-imposed step therapy protocols can force physicians to "practice bad medicine" by requiring trials of less appropriate or potentially unsafe medications (e.g., atypical opioids) before more suitable ones for seriously ill patients, leading to patient harm.
- Real-world supply chain issues highlight a critical flaw in prior authorization systems, where a simple change in medication dosage availability (e.g., 5mg vs. 10mg tablets) can necessitate a new prior authorization, often denied if not on a "national back-order" list, delaying medically necessary treatment.
- Palliative care is presented as a cost-effective solution, achieving better patient and system outcomes (enhanced quality of life, reduced hospital expenditures, lower costs) compared to usual care.
- The lack of communication from plans to prescribers regarding drug coverage denials creates a critical gap, leaving vulnerable patients without clear next steps and potentially leading to severe health consequences.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "Indeed, our members report that a single prior authorization request can take an hour or more of physician or clinical staff time to process, diverting attention and resources away from patient care."
- "When such policies essentially require physicians to practice bad medicine, they can harm patients and contribute to poor outcomes."
- "Unfortunately, patients may not understand the next steps they should take or may not be able to advocate on their own behalf, potentially resulting in devastating consequences, such as increased emergency department utilization, potential unnecessary hospitalization, or life-threatening complications."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Response from Wolters Kluwer on the HHS Request for Information on Deregulation
    *   This is Wolters Kluwer’s response to the Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS) Request for Information (RFI) entitled Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation to Make America Healthy Again (AHRQ-2025-0001).
    *   Wolters Kluwer is a leading global provider of clinical technology and evidence-based solutions that assist effective decision-making and outcomes across the healthcare continuum.
        *   Key solutions include UpToDate®, UpToDate® Lexidrug™, UpToDate® Patient Engagement, Medi-Span®, Sentri7®, Lippincott® Solutions, Ovid®, and Health Language®.
        *   Wolters Kluwer had annual revenue in 2024 of $6.4 billion.
    *   We commend the Trump Administration and HHS for seeking opportunities to rescind outdated or overly expansive regulations and reduce administrative burden.
    *   We also appreciate the Department’s view that any deregulatory effort should scrutinize policy guidance and other regulatory “obligations” that might be ill-conceived and/or create undue burden.
    *   Our comments address the policy guidance entitled Clinical Decision Support Software (FDA-2017-D-6569) issued by FDA in September 2022.
        *   We believe this guidance is a good candidate for deregulatory efforts because it meets two criteria from Executive Order 14219:
            *   The guidance is not based on the best reading of the underlying statutory authority delegated by Congress.
            *   The guidance is impeding technological innovation.
    *   In December 2016, Congress passed the 21st Century Cures Act, which carved out low-risk Clinical Decision Support (CDS) software from the definition of ‘medical device,’ exempting such software from FDA oversight.
        *   Specifically, Section 520(o) was added to the Food, Drug and Cosmetic (FD&C) Act, excluding certain software functions from the device definition if four criteria are met:
            *   The software function is not intended to acquire, process or analyze a medical image or a signal from an in vitro diagnostic device or a pattern from a signal acquisition system.
            *   The software function is intended for the purpose of displaying, analyzing or printing medical information about a patient or other medical information.
            *   The software function is intended for the purpose of supporting or providing recommendations to a health care professional about the prevention, diagnosis or treatment of a disease or condition.
            *   The software function is intended for the purpose of enabling such health professional to independently review the basis for such recommendations that such software presents so that it is not the intent that such health care professional rely primarily on any of such recommendations to make a clinical diagnosis or treatment decision regarding an individual patient.
    *   In September 2022, FDA issued its Clinical Decision Support Software final guidance, interpreting the 21st Century Cures Act statutory language.
        *   In our view, FDA’s interpretation did not adhere to the plain language of the Act.
        *   Instead, FDA introduced concepts such as the “time-critical nature” of the medical decision and “automation bias,” defined as the “propensity of humans to over-rely on a suggestion from an automated system.”
        *   FDA noted that automation bias was more likely if the software provided a “single, specific, selected output or solution rather than a list of options or complete information.”
        *   FDA also stated the “time-critical nature” of the medical decision might increase automation bias because there is not sufficient time for the user to adequately consider other information.
        *   Thus, in FDA’s view, software providing a specific output/directive and/or addressing a time-critical decision would be interpreted as “directing the (health care professional) to take action and substituting for their judgment,” making it likely subject to FDA regulation as a medical device.
    *   First, neither “automation bias,” nor the “time-critical nature” of the medical decision appear in the 21st Century Cures Act, either as statutory language or concepts to be considered by FDA.
        *   To the contrary, the statute clearly emphasized that the “intended” purpose or design of the underlying software should be the primary factor for the 4 criteria related to product exemption.
    *   Second, while we agree CDS software should present clinicians with recommendations incorporating all appropriate options and allow clinicians to adequately consider all relevant information, we do not agree that CDS presenting only a single recommendation and/or supporting time-critical medical decisions necessarily increases automation bias.
        *   There are many instances in clinical care when compelling scientific and medical evidence indicates only a single selected output or solution is correct for the patient.
            *   For example, if a particular infection can be treated by multiple antibiotics, but a patient is allergic to all but one, it would be inappropriate to suggest anything other than the one safe antibiotic.
            *   Similarly, if one treatment has overwhelmingly been shown to be the best approach for a condition, suggesting alternatives could lead to suboptimal care.
        *   CDS software should provide a range of options when appropriate, but if only one best option is dictated by evidence and the patient’s situation, then only one should be presented.
        *   An important way CDS solutions increase transparency is by assigning confidence levels to their output based on the certainty of the medical evidence (e.g., GRADE methodology).
    *   FDA recently addressed regulating CDS software that issues a single recommendation in its response to a Citizen’s Petition challenging its CDS Guidance (Docket Number FDA-2023-P-O422).
        *   FDA argued its decision is consistent with Section 520(o) because Congress used the plural, “recommendations,” in Criteria 3 and 4, implying software delivering a single recommendation would not be exempt.
        *   We strongly disagree with this interpretation.
        *   A more accurate read is that Congress understood CDS software provides many “recommendations” over its lifecycle to many clinicians covering multiple patients, addressing thousands of care events.
        *   Most CDS output will provide multiple options, but in some clinical situations, there is only one right recommendation.
        *   Even CDS software used twice daily in a small practice could be classified as having issued “recommendations,” even if those two outputs were single best options.
    *   Regarding the time-critical nature of medical decision-making, the 21st Century Cures Act does not authorize FDA to consider this factor in defining which CDS software remains under regulatory purview.
        *   Congress clearly indicated the developer’s design or “intended use” should control.
        *   In practice, identifying time-critical decisions is not clear due to numerous factors (patient, presentation, setting).
            *   For example, managing gastrointestinal bleeding may be emergent if the patient is severely bleeding and in shock, but less urgent if they had a single episode an hour earlier and are hemodynamically stable.
        *   Given the context-specific nature of time-critical decisions, its use as a factor to determine CDS regulation is impracticable, unfeasible, and beyond FDA’s statutory authority.
    *   The ramifications of FDA’s overly narrow interpretation of Section 520(o) have led to fewer CDS solutions being exempt from FDA oversight.
        *   New product innovations and features, possibly including AI-enablement, could be (and likely already have been) abandoned.
        *   This deprives providers and patients of enhanced functionality that could improve health outcomes and lower costs.
    *   In sum, FDA’s guidance on Clinical Decision Support Software is not based on the best reading of statutory authority and is impeding technological innovation in the CDS marketplace.
    *   We urge the Trump Administration to direct the FDA’s Center for Device and Radiological Health to rescind the guidance and issue a revised interpretation that aligns with Congress’ intent to exempt low-risk CDS software from FDA regulation.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: Wolters Kluwer, a leading global provider of clinical technology, urges the Trump Administration to rescind the FDA's "Clinical Decision Support Software" guidance, arguing it misinterprets the 21st Century Cures Act and stifles innovation by regulating low-risk software that Congress intended to exempt.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Wolters Kluwer
- **Type:** Organization
- **Role/Expertise:** Leading global provider of clinical technology and evidence-based solutions that assist effective decision-making and outcomes across the healthcare continuum. They offer key solutions such as UpToDate®, UpToDate® Lexidrug™, Medi-Span®, Sentri7®, Lippincott® Solutions, Ovid®, and Health Language®. Had annual revenue of $6.4 billion in 2024.
- **Geographic Scope:** Global
- **Stake in Issue:** As a major developer and provider of Clinical Decision Support (CDS) software, their products are directly impacted by FDA's interpretation and regulation of such software, affecting their ability to innovate and provide solutions to healthcare professionals and patients.
structuredSections.corePosition: We commend efforts to reduce regulatory burden but believe the FDA's "Clinical Decision Support Software" guidance misinterprets the 21st Century Cures Act. This guidance expands FDA oversight beyond congressional intent, particularly concerning software that provides single recommendations or supports time-critical decisions, thereby stifling technological innovation and potentially hindering patient care improvements.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Direct the FDA’s Center for Device and Radiological Health to rescind the current "Clinical Decision Support Software" guidance (FDA-2017-D-6569).
- Issue a revised interpretation of Section 520(o) of the FD&C Act that aligns with Congress’ intent to exempt low-risk Clinical Decision Support (CDS) software from FDA regulation.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- FDA's "Clinical Decision Support Software" guidance is not based on the best reading of the underlying statutory authority granted by Congress in the 21st Century Cures Act.
- The guidance is impeding technological innovation in the Clinical Decision Support (CDS) marketplace.
- FDA's interpretation introduces concepts like "time-critical nature" and "automation bias" that are not present in the 21st Century Cures Act.
- FDA's narrow interpretation of the plural "recommendations" in the statute incorrectly subjects software that provides a single, evidence-based best option to regulation.
  - This misinterpretation implies that CDS software must always provide multiple options, even when overwhelming evidence points to only one correct solution, potentially leading to suboptimal patient care.
- Considering the "time-critical nature" of medical decisions as a regulatory factor is impracticable, unfeasible, and beyond the scope of FDA’s statutory authority due to its context-specific variability.
- The overly broad interpretation of Section 520(o) has resulted in fewer CDS solutions being exempt from FDA oversight.
  - This leads to new product innovations and features, including potential AI-enablement, being abandoned.
  - This abandonment deprives providers and patients of enhanced functionality that could improve health outcomes and lower costs.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- Clinical examples illustrate situations where presenting a single, best recommendation is appropriate and necessary:
  - If a patient is allergic to all but one antibiotic for an infection, suggesting other options would be inappropriate.
  - When one treatment overwhelmingly stands as the best approach for a condition, suggesting alternatives could lead to suboptimal patient care.
- CDS solutions enhance transparency by assigning confidence levels to their output based on the certainty of medical evidence (e.g., using methodologies like GRADE).
- The concept of "time-critical decisions" is context-specific and not uniformly identifiable, making it an impractical regulatory factor (e.g., severity of gastrointestinal bleeding varies by patient presentation and setting).
- The statutory use of "recommendations" (plural) should be interpreted to mean the many recommendations a CDS software provides over its *lifecycle* to *many clinicians* for *multiple patients* and thousands of care events, rather than requiring multiple options for every single instance.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "CDS software should be designed to provide a range of options for the clinician when appropriate, but if there is only one best option dictated by the evidence and the patient’s situation, then only one should be presented."
- "A more accurate read is that Congress understood that CDS software is designed to provide many recommendations over the course of its lifecycle to many clinicians covering multiple patients, addressing thousands of care events that require a corresponding number of clinical decisions."
- "New product innovations and features, possibly including AI-enablement, could be (and likely already have been) abandoned, thus depriving providers and patients of enhanced functionality that could improve health outcomes and lower costs."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Submitted by Chris Diefenthaler, Director, on behalf of Assistance Dogs International.
*   Subject: Request for Information – Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation to Make America Healthy Again.
*   Comment Topic: CDC Dog Importation Regulation – Impact on People with Disabilities and the Assistance Dog Community.
*   Administering Division: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
*   1. Introduction
    *   As a representative of Assistance Dogs International (ADI)—a global coalition of non-profit assistance dog organizations and the leading authority in the assistance dog field—we respectfully submit this comment.
    *   The comment addresses critical unintended consequences of the CDC’s current dog import regulations and proposes recommendations for improvement.
    *   As Director, I have extensive knowledge of the challenges these regulations pose for individuals with disabilities who rely on assistance dogs for independent travel.
    *   While the goal of preventing disease transmission, particularly rabies, is valid, the implementation of these rules—especially for dogs arriving from high-risk countries—creates unnecessary barriers for users of medically essential, highly trained assistance dogs whose risk profile differs significantly from that of pet imports.
    *   ADI defines an assistance dog as a guide, hearing, or service dog specifically trained to perform a task to mitigate the effects of an individual’s disability.
    *   These comments refer to assistance dogs for people with disabilities pursuant to the ADA (Americans with Disabilities Act) and section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, not emotional support or companion dogs.
*   2. Background
    *   The CDC’s dog import regulations, updated in 2024, require extensive documentation and port-of-entry restrictions for dogs entering the U.S. from countries classified as high-risk for dog rabies variant.
    *   These requirements apply equally to pet dogs and assistance dogs, including those trained by internationally recognized accreditation organizations such as Assistance Dogs International (ADI) and the International Guide Dog Federation (IGDF).
    *   Under the current regulations, assistance dogs arriving from high-risk rabies countries—despite being fully vaccinated and highly trained—must enter the U.S. through CDC-approved animal facilities, restricting individuals to a limited number of designated entry points.
    *   In some instances, assistance dogs have been separated from their handlers for revaccination or paperwork verification, resulting in undue stress and disruption.
    *   Furthermore, the required photo documentation submission process is inaccessible to individuals who are blind, creating additional barriers for blind travelers.
*   3. Analysis
    *   Impact on Assistance Dog Users:
        *   These rules disproportionately burden people with disabilities who depend on their dogs for independence, safety, and medical support.
        *   Unlike pet owners, these individuals are not merely choosing to travel with their dogs; they are traveling with essential medical aids.
        *   Requiring CDC facility reservations and inaccessible online procedures places an unfair and discriminatory burden on this population.
    *   Unintended Consequences for Breeding Programs:
        *   ADI and IGDF member organizations operate cooperative international breeding programs, which require the movement of puppies under 6 months of age because of critical development and socialization landmarks that are scientifically proven in dog development.
        *   Current CDC regulations inhibit timely puppy transport, threatening the long-term socialization outcomes of these animals.
        *   This directly impacts the quality and availability of future assistance dogs and the sustainability of breeding populations.
    *   Risk Profile Not Properly Differentiated:
        *   Assistance dog programs accredited through ADI and IGDF follow strict vaccination protocols and veterinary oversight.
        *   Treating them the same as unregulated pet imports ignores this significantly lower risk profile.
        *   The agency’s assumption that all dogs pose equal rabies risk lacks nuance and creates avoidable enforcement burdens.
    *   Barriers to Equal Access:
        *   Handlers with visual impairments returning home or traveling to the US from high-risk dog rabies countries cannot effectively take required photos of their dogs without sighted assistance.
        *   These requirements are not aligned with disability access mandates and do not allow for reasonable accommodation requests.
*   4. Recommendations
    *   A. Create an exemption from CDC dog import requirements for assistance dogs from ADI and IGDF accredited members, applicable to both low- and high-risk rabies countries.
    *   B. Accept the following forms of documentation as valid proof at the point of entry:
        *   ADI Digital ID.
        *   Hard copy ID from the accredited ADI/IGDF member organization.
        *   Letter on official letterhead with ADI or IGDF logo attesting to the dog’s training by the member organization.
        *   The CDC can verify current accredited members via ADI's and IGDF's Websites.
    *   C. Allow entry for all dogs under 6 months of age as follows:
        *   From low-risk border countries (Canada, Mexico, and the U.S. have all eliminated dog-mediated human rabies according to the USDA): dogs aged 8+ weeks with [CDC Dog Import Document].
        *   From other low-risk countries: dogs aged 16+ weeks with [CDC Dog Import Document + Rabies Vaccination Proof].
        *   From high-risk countries: dogs aged 16+ weeks follow the guidelines listed here: Approved Rabies Serology Laboratories for Testing Dogs - Importation - CDC.
    *   CI. Establish clear guidelines for providing reasonable accommodations for people with disabilities who need assistance complying with the CDC Dog Import Regulation.
    *   CII. Refrain from separating handlers from their service dogs.
*   5. Conclusion
    *   CDC’s dog import regulation has created a harmful and avoidable barrier to travel and international cooperation for individuals who depend on assistance dogs.
    *   These rules not only interfere with equal access required by law but also hamper breeding programs vital to future service dog availability.
    *   We appreciate the commitment to reviewing public feedback and eliminating burdensome and excessive regulations while considering the needs of people with disabilities and the organizations that serve them.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: Assistance Dogs International (ADI), a global coalition, urges the CDC to exempt highly trained assistance dogs from restrictive import regulations, citing their essential role for people with disabilities and lower rabies risk, while proposing specific documentation and accommodation guidelines.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The American Podiatric Medical Association (APMA) appreciates the opportunity to respond to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again; AHRQ-2025-0001.
*   APMA supports HHS’ efforts to remove excessive and inappropriate regulations to ultimately improve access to care.
*   APMA has identified three opportunities for deregulation and streamlining under the Medicare program:
    *   The first two are related to durable medical equipment (DME), as implemented by the DME Medicare Administrative Contractors (DME MACs).
    *   The third deregulatory opportunity falls under addressing the overly burdensome and confusing regulations related to the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS).
*   All of these regulations stifle physician practices’ ability to deliver high-quality, medically necessary care to Medicare beneficiaries by imposing excessively burdensome requirements whose costs exceed benefits.
*   APMA also strongly believes CMS and the DME MACs have exceeded their lawful role in implementation.
*   Specifically, APMA is asking that HHS remove unnecessary and/or unlawfully burdensome regulations related to:
    *   DME policy for coverage and payment of medically necessary “same or similar” items;
    *   Medicare local coverage requirements for documenting medical necessity of therapeutic shoes for persons with diabetes; and
    *   The MIPS program.

*   DME “Same or Similar”
    *   Policy 42 CFR § 414.210(f) specifies requirements for Medicare payment for replacement of DME.
    *   If an item of DME previously paid under Medicare Part B has been in continuous use by the patient for the equipment’s reasonable useful lifetime or if the item is determined to be lost, stolen, or irreparably damaged, the patient may elect to obtain new equipment.
    *   The regulation also specifies that the reasonable useful lifetime of DME items can be no less than 5 years unless CMS issues separate program instructions.
    *   HHS, through CMS, has delegated the implementation of this policy to the DME MACs.
    *   DME MACs have developed “same or similar” policies that deny coverage and payment of any items identified as “same or similar” to initial items.
    *   Currently, the only way for a provider to supply a medically necessary, covered, and allowable “same or similar” item is to submit the claim, receive the denial, and then submit a redetermination.
    *   This is an incredibly burdensome process that creates uncertainty for patients and DME suppliers and unnecessarily delays payment.
    *   These challenges are exacerbated by the fact that “same or similar” policies too often result in payment denial for DME items that are not replacement items and should not be subject to the requirements at 42 CFR § 414.210(f).
    *   These are new medically necessary items intended for different diagnoses or reflecting a change in therapy for the same site and condition.
    *   As a result, patients may have trouble accessing new medically necessary DME items if the items are “same or similar” to DME items they already possess.
    *   APMA is certain the method by which the DME MACs have implemented this policy is not consistent with this Administration’s efforts to reduce burden.
    *   This inefficiency exemplifies the type of stifling, unnecessary, and unduly burdensome hurdle that HHS seeks to rescind through the RFI.
    *   This burden could be eliminated if HHS were to instruct CMS to require that the DME MACs allow coverage of medically necessary “same or similar” items when the claim is submitted with the KX modifier.
    *   The KX modifier is a billing modifier that indicates the billing provider has ensured coverage criteria have been met and that documentation exists to support medical necessity.
    *   Allowing attestation through the use of the modifier would eliminate the burden and cost associated with providers needing to navigate the redetermination process for an item that is allowed, without compromising program integrity.
    *   Providers would still need to confirm whether the item is “same or similar” in nature to an original item, would still need to document the medical necessity of the “same or similar” item, and would still be subject to review of their claims.

*   Therapeutic Shoes for Persons with Diabetes (TSD) Program
    *   Under §1861(s)(12) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1395x(s)(12)), Medicare covers diabetic shoes prescribed and furnished by a podiatrist (or other qualified physician) when the physician managing the patient’s diabetes documents certain diabetic sequelae and certifies the need for shoes, among other requirements.
    *   In the implementation of these requirements, DME MACs have imposed undue burden, exceeding statutory requirements.
    *   Specifically, through DME MAC Policy Article A52501, MACs are requiring that the physician managing the diabetes:
        *   “obtain, initial, date (prior to signing the certification statement), and indicate agreement with information from the medical records of an in-person visit with a podiatrist, other M.D or D.O., physician assistant, nurse practitioner, or clinical nurse specialist that is within 6 months prior to delivery of the shoes/inserts …”
    *   These additional requirements imposed upon managing physicians create unnecessary paperwork and burden and delay access to therapeutic shoes for patients who may be at significant risk for ulceration.
    *   The elimination of this duplicative step would not compromise program integrity, as a requirement for the managing physician to submit a statement certifying the patient’s need for diabetic shoes would remain.
    *   This co-signing requirement serves no purpose in furthering patient safety or improving care for patients but rather creates obstacles that prevent patients from receiving medically necessary diabetic footwear.
    *   Providers often report that this documentation requirement is unnecessarily burdensome, leading to delays or denials of care for patients who need it most.
    *   As a result, many qualified providers have opted out of the TSD program, leaving patients without access to this critical service.

*   Merit-Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS)
    *   MIPS was authorized under the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 (MACRA) to, in part, replace and improve upon historically disjointed federal quality reporting programs.
    *   The program—which ties Medicare Part B physician payments to performance on quality, cost, the promotion of electronic health record (EHR) interoperability, and engagement in clinical improvement activities—is now in its ninth year.
    *   Over that period of time, it has evolved into a senselessly complex and burdensome program that requires physician practices to focus more on avoiding penalties than moving the needle on quality.
    *   Numerous studies and reports have documented the flaws and failures of MIPS.
    *   A Journal of American Medical Association (JAMA) study found that, on average, it cost practices $12,811 per physician to participate in MIPS, with clinicians and administrators spending more than 200 hours per physician on MIPS-related activities.
        *   This study evaluated the 2019 MIPS performance year, when the program was not yet fully implemented, and likely reflects an underestimate of today’s cost of compliance—particularly for small practice specialties, like podiatry.
    *   Another JAMA study found that MIPS scores were inconsistently associated with performance on process and outcome measures, suggesting that MIPS may be ineffective at measuring and incentivizing quality improvement among physicians.
    *   A more recent U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report expressed concern that MIPS performance feedback is neither timely nor meaningful, questioned whether the program helps to improve quality and patient outcomes, and highlighted the program’s low return on investment.
    *   In this already challenging environment for physicians, the expense of keeping up with ever-changing and overly burdensome regulatory requirements has become unsustainable, for both APMA and their members.
    *   Recently, CMS introduced a new MIPS Value Pathways (MVP) framework, aimed at providing more streamlined and relevant participation options for physicians.
    *   Unfortunately, MVPs do little to address what is fundamentally broken in the program and carry over many of the same flawed policies from traditional MIPS.
        *   This includes a one-size-fits-all approach to measurement and flawed assessments of value due to misaligned quality and cost measures.
    *   In the face of these limitations, CMS has continued to express its intent to make reporting via MVPs mandatory.
    *   APMA believes this would overstep the initial intent of MACRA by limiting clinician choice and further hampering podiatrists’ ability to succeed under MIPS.
        *   This is not because they are providing low quality care, but because of structural limitations in the program that do not allow them to demonstrate their true quality performance.
    *   APMA strongly recommends that HHS critically review and evaluate the MIPS program to identify opportunities for burden reduction, while ensuring that quality reporting programs enhance delivery of patient care, instead of impeding.

*   Recommendations
    *   APMA recommends that HHS, through instruction to CMS, remove these unnecessary, unduly burdensome, and unsound regulations that stifle American business and burden healthcare providers by:
        *   Instructing the DME MACs to allow coverage of medically necessary “same or similar” items when the claim is submitted using the KX Modifier.
        *   Instructing the DME MACs to remove a specific sentence from “Therapeutic Shoes for Persons with Diabetes - Policy Article” (A52501):
            *   “Obtain, initial, date (prior to signing the certification statement), and indicate agreement with information from the medical records of an in-person visit with a podiatrist, other M.D or D.O., physician assistant, nurse practitioner, or clinical nurse specialist that is within 6 months prior to delivery of the shoes/inserts, and that documents one of more of criteria a – f.”
        *   Removing unnecessary regulatory requirements from MIPS and providing clinicians with more flexibility to demonstrate high value care in a way that makes sense for their specific patient populations.

*   Conclusion
    *   APMA appreciates the Administration’s continued focus on removing unnecessary and unlawful regulations, and values the opportunity to provide these comments.
    *   APMA is available to provide additional information or discuss these recommendations further.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The American Podiatric Medical Association urges HHS to deregulate burdensome Medicare policies for durable medical equipment and the MIPS program, arguing they stifle care access and practice efficiency for podiatrists.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** American Podiatric Medical Association (APMA)
- **Type:** Advocacy Group
- **Role/Expertise:** The premier professional organization representing the vast majority of the nation’s doctors of podiatric medicine (podiatrists or podiatric physicians and surgeons).
- **Geographic Scope:** National
- **Stake in Issue:** Represents podiatrists whose practices are directly impacted by burdensome and overly complex Medicare regulations related to durable medical equipment (DME) and the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS), which they state impede their ability to deliver high-quality, medically necessary care and cause significant financial and administrative burdens.
structuredSections.corePosition: We appreciate and support HHS’ efforts to remove excessive and inappropriate regulations to ultimately improve access to care. We believe current Medicare regulations regarding durable medical equipment (DME) "same or similar" items, therapeutic shoes for persons with diabetes (TSD), and the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) are excessively burdensome, costly, and stifle physician practices' ability to deliver high-quality, medically necessary care. We strongly believe CMS and the DME Medicare Administrative Contractors (DME MACs) have exceeded their lawful role in implementing these policies.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Instruct the DME Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs) to allow coverage of medically necessary “same or similar” items when the claim is submitted using the KX Modifier.
- Instruct the DME MACs to remove the specific co-signing requirement from the "Therapeutic Shoes for Persons with Diabetes - Policy Article" (A52501) that mandates the managing physician to obtain, initial, date, and indicate agreement with information from medical records of an in-person visit within 6 months prior to delivery of shoes/inserts.
- Remove unnecessary regulatory requirements from MIPS and provide clinicians with more flexibility to demonstrate high-value care in a way that makes sense for their specific patient populations.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **DME “Same or Similar” Policy:**
    - The current implementation by DME MACs forces providers to submit claims, receive denials, and then pursue redeterminations for medically necessary "same or similar" items, which is incredibly burdensome, creates uncertainty, and delays payment.
    - These policies often incorrectly deny new medically necessary DME items intended for different diagnoses or changes in therapy, simply because they are "same or similar" to previously possessed items, limiting patient access.
    - DME MACs have exceeded their lawful role in implementing this policy in a manner inconsistent with burden reduction efforts.
- **Therapeutic Shoes for Persons with Diabetes (TSD) Program:**
    - DME MACs have imposed additional requirements, specifically a co-signing mandate from the managing physician, that exceed statutory requirements.
    - This co-signing requirement creates unnecessary paperwork, delays patient access to critical footwear, serves no purpose for patient safety or care improvement, and has led many qualified providers to opt out of the program.
- **Merit-Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS):**
    - The program has evolved into a "senselessly complex and burdensome program" that requires practices to focus on avoiding penalties rather than truly improving quality.
    - It imposes significant financial and time costs on practices (e.g., $12,811 per physician and over 200 hours per physician on MIPS-related activities in 2019).
    - Studies suggest MIPS scores are inconsistently associated with actual performance and that the program may be ineffective at incentivizing quality improvement or providing timely/meaningful feedback, resulting in a low return on investment.
    - The new MIPS Value Pathways (MVP) framework fails to address fundamental flaws, carrying over issues like a one-size-fits-all measurement approach and misaligned quality/cost measures.
    - Mandatory MVP reporting would overstep MACRA's intent, limiting clinician choice and hindering podiatrists' ability to demonstrate quality due to structural program limitations, not low-quality care.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The current method of denying "same or similar" DME items requires providers to submit a claim, receive a denial, and then submit a redetermination, which is described as an "incredibly burdensome process that creates uncertainty for patients and DME suppliers and unnecessarily delays payment."
- The specific co-signing requirement for Therapeutic Shoes for Persons with Diabetes is criticized for serving "no purpose in furthering patient safety or improving care for patients" and instead creates obstacles leading to delays or denials of care.
- Many qualified providers have opted out of the Therapeutic Shoes for Persons with Diabetes program due to the documentation burden, leaving patients without access to this critical service.
- Data from a JAMA study revealed MIPS participation cost practices, on average, $12,811 per physician and clinicians/administrators spent over 200 hours per physician on MIPS-related activities, suggesting a high and potentially underestimated cost of compliance, especially for small practices like podiatry.
- Research indicates that MIPS scores are "inconsistently associated with performance on process and outcome measures," leading to the insight that the program may be "ineffective at measuring and incentivizing quality improvement."
- The U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) reported that MIPS performance feedback is "neither timely nor meaningful" and questioned whether the program truly helps improve quality and patient outcomes, highlighting its "low return on investment."
- APMA asserts that CMS and DME MACs have "exceeded their lawful role in implementation" of certain policies, particularly regarding "same or similar" DME items and Therapeutic Shoes for Persons with Diabetes.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "All of these regulations stifle physician practices’ ability to deliver high-quality, medically necessary care to Medicare beneficiaries by imposing excessively burdensome requirements whose costs exceed benefits. We also strongly believe CMS and the DME MACs have exceeded their lawful role in implementation."
- "This co-signing requirement serves no purpose in furthering patient safety or improving care for patients but rather creates obstacles that prevent patients from receiving medically necessary diabetic footwear."
- "MIPS... has evolved into a senselessly complex and burdensome program that requires physician practices to focus more on avoiding penalties than moving the needle on quality."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Understanding the Scope and Procedures of Executive Order 14192 “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation”
    *   This Request for Information (RFI): “Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation to Make America Healthy Again” helps implement the President’s deregulatory initiatives, including Executive Order (EO) 14192: “Unleashing Prosperity through Deregulation.”
    *   Section 1 of EO 14192 states its purpose as: “for each new regulation issued, at least 10 prior regulations be identified for elimination.”
    *   The Scope of EO 14192
        *   Section 5 of EO 14192 (“Definitions”) explicitly states that guidance documents are included in the term “regulation” or “rule”:
            *   "For purposes of this order, the term “regulation” or “rule” means an agency statement of general or particular applicability and future effect designed to implement, interpret, or prescribe law or policy or to describe the procedure or practice requirements of an agency, including, without limitation, regulations, rules, memoranda, administrative orders, guidance documents, policy statements, and interagency agreements, regardless of whether the same were enacted through the processes in the Administrative Procedure Act..."
*   ACRO’s concerns
    *   We support the RFI and Executive Order 14192 goal of “unleashing innovation” and the Secretary’s commitment to “radical transparency.”
    *   However, we believe the consequences of including guidance documents within the scope of EO 14192 will be anti-innovation and anti-transparency.
    *   Guidance documents are a distinct tool in the regulatory armamentarium.
        *   While the Executive Order groups regulations and guidance documents together, it is important to recognize their differences.
        *   FDA notes that guidance documents describe its interpretation of or policy on a regulatory issue (21 CFR 10.115(b)).
        *   In general, FDA’s guidance documents do not establish legally enforceable responsibilities and are not binding on FDA or the public; they are recommendations.
        *   FDA explains in each draft guidance that "the use of the word should in Agency guidances means that something is suggested or recommended, but not required."
        *   While regulations are “restrictive” due to their legally binding status, guidance documents are properly understood as “permissive” or “enabling” due to their legally non-binding status.
        *   Guidance documents facilitate three important goals:
            *   They provide transparency into the Agency’s current thinking.
            *   They announce and explain regulatory innovation.
            *   Both of these, in turn, facilitate biomedical innovation.
    *   Guidance documents as tools for regulatory transparency
        *   Although not legally binding, they provide valuable insight into the Agency’s current thinking and approaches that may help regulated industry reach their regulatory goals.
    *   Guidance documents as vehicles for regulatory innovation
        *   The FDA is recognized globally as a forward-leaning Agency that maintains the gold standard for patient safety, data integrity, and evidence generation.
        *   A key component of FDA’s leadership is its prescient, timely issuance of guidance documents.
        *   Examples of FDA’s global leadership in regulatory innovation through guidances include:
            *   Considerations for the Use of Artificial Intelligence to Support Regulatory Decision-Making for Drug and Biological Products (draft guidance)
            *   Integrating Randomized Controlled Trials for Drug and Biological Products into Routine Clinical Practice (draft guidance)
            *   Conducting Clinical Trials with Decentralized Elements (final guidance)
            *   Digital Health Technologies for Remote Data Acquisition in Clinical Investigations (final guidance)
        *   FDA’s draft guidance on AI in drug development, which embraces a risk-based, flexible, and pragmatic approach, is globally influential and will be studied by regulators worldwide.
    *   Guidance documents help de-risk drug development and enable biomedical innovation
        *   Biomedical innovation and investment are cautious and risk averse about adopting innovative trial design (e.g., decentralized trials) and technologies in clinical research.
        *   FDA issuance of draft guidance helps mitigate this risk aversion by providing industry with transparency into FDA’s current thinking, which is especially valuable for complex, rapidly evolving technology.
        *   Guidance documents are "engines of biomedical innovation," not part of “an overbearing and burdensome administrative state.”
        *   They provide transparency into the FDA’s current thinking while offering industry the flexibility for a nimble, agile approach to drug development.
        *   This balance between direction and flexibility is essential for creating a stable and predictable regulatory environment where drug developers can make business decisions with confidence.
*   ACRO’s Recommendation
    *   Inclusion of guidance documents within the scope of EO 14192 could have negative consequences for maintaining a stable, predictable regulatory environment and ensuring a world-leading supportive regulatory environment for drug development in the U.S.
    *   One plausible scenario is that fewer draft guidances might be issued by FDA or converted into final guidance, thereby exacerbating industry caution and risk aversion.
        *   This slowdown could make the U.S. less globally competitive for the placement of clinical trials.
        *   If the number of FDA guidance documents decreases while other regions (e.g., the European Union and the United Kingdom) maintain or increase theirs, other regions could be viewed as more predictable, transparent, and attractive.
    *   Another plausible scenario is that draft guidances continue to be issued (and finalized) but with negative repercussions due to the 10:1 requirement.
        *   In a typical year, ACRO responds to as many as 12 draft guidances issued by FDA, which is only a subset of the total.
        *   Application of the 10:1 requirement would mean that for the 12 draft guidances ACRO responds to, 120 guidances would have to be repealed.
        *   Many, if not most, draft guidances focus on supporting patient safety and data integrity.
        *   It is difficult to imagine repealing 120 guidance documents without negative repercussions for both patient safety and data integrity.
        *   The FDA CDER 2025 Guidance Agenda contains over four pages of proposed draft guidances for the year.
        *   Issuing even half of these under the 10:1 requirement is difficult to imagine.
        *   For the categories of “clinical/medical” and “ICH” draft guidances alone, 22 draft guidances are planned, which would trigger the repeal of 220 guidances.
        *   It is impossible to imagine identifying 220 guidances whose repeal would not have a material impact on patient safety, data integrity, and biomedical innovation.
    *   We support both the RFI and EO 14192 goal of “unleashing innovation” and the Secretary’s commitment to “radical transparency.”
    *   However, we urge HHS to take a more targeted approach to guidance documents specifically (as distinct from rules and regulations).
    *   Guidance documents that are truly outdated (e.g., due to technological advances) are appropriate candidates for removal.
    *   We believe the current blanket approach to guidance documents is counterproductive.
    *   In the spirit of advancing innovation and transparency; in acknowledgment of the unique nature of guidance documents (vis-à-vis regulations); and in recognition of the essential de-risking role of guidance documents in enabling transparency, regulatory innovation, and biomedical innovation; we ask that “guidance documents” be removed from Section 5 and the 10:1 requirement of EO 14192.
