    *   It would better promote the health and well-being of individuals like my identical twin brothers who have autism, intellectual disability, and a history of chronic, treatment-resistant, dangerous, and life-threatening self-injurious and aggressive behaviors.
*   The proposed ban targets the court-approved ESD treatment my one brother received at the Judge Rotenberg Education Center (JRC) for severe self-injury and aggression.
    *   This treatment has never caused any harm and saved his life.
    *   His treatment plan was written and supervised by a licensed psychologist.
    *   His treatment plans, including the ESD, have always been developed and supervised by licensed professionals and medically cleared by a physician after other treatments were determined ineffective.
*   I also have a daughter with severe autism.
*   I am a board-certified psychiatrist who completed a fellowship at the Seaver and New York Autism Center at Mount Sinai Hospital.
    *   I have authored a book and psychiatry articles on autism.
    *   I have lectured on autism spectrum disorders at professional conferences, including the American Psychiatric Association.
    *   I am also the president of the Judge Rotenberg Center Parents’ Association.
*   I have tried the shock myself and neither my brother nor I have ever experienced a side effect.
*   The GED electrical stimulation device was approved by a court proceeding where my brother had his own attorney.
*   The school never pressured my mother to consent to the device; rather, my brother’s life-threatening behaviors pressured her.
*   My brother has even asked to wear the device and is on seven positive behavior contracts, earning preferred items throughout the day for being safe.
*   When living at home, my brother
    *   Banged his head into sharp corners.
    *   Developed symptoms of neuroleptic malignant syndrome from haloperidol.
    *   Required surgery to his head from self-injury, resulting in five and a half months in the hospital, where he continued to need repeated suturing for head banging despite 24/7 staff presence.
    *   This occurred despite polypharmacy with five medications (Klonopin, Ativan, Prolixin, Artane, Inderal), which caused adverse effects such as obesity, tardive dyskinesia, loss of verbal communication, drooling, and excessive daytime sedation.
    *   The Board of Education told my mother no educational facility would accept him and requested she waive his right to an education, which she refused.
    *   Medical insurance was running out, and my parents were told they could be held responsible for hospitalization costs, leading my father to worry if their house could be taken.
    *   Through my mother's physician, she learned about the Judge Rotenberg Center.
*   When he first arrived at JRC, he had 900-1000 episodes of aggression and 400-500 episodes of self-injury a month.
    *   He has been there for over 36 years and is doing quite well without any head banging and is on no medication.
    *   We have taken him on trips to other states, including Niagara Falls.
    *   He works a paid job at the school.
    *   In 2011, when an attempt was made to remove the skin shock device, he perforated both his tympanic membranes and had to go to the hospital, for the first time since entering JRC.
    *   He had 200 applications of skin shock in the first year, but now has not needed any for over ten years, though he may wear the device after engaging in dangerous behavior to prevent escalation.
*   My other brother, who is not at JRC or on an aversive conditioning device:
    *   Was functioning quite well in the past, holding a full-time job for about three years without medication and was travel-trained.
    *   Moved into a New York State Organization for People with Developmental Disabilities funded agency residence while working.
    *   Lost his job after a co-worker teased him about work hours, leading him to become agitated and grab the co-worker’s butcher knife.
    *   Subsequently became obsessed with setting fires and has tried to set a peer and himself on fire.
    *   Has had numerous hospitalizations.
    *   Has failed positive behavior supports with functional behavior assessment.
    *   Has had at least fifteen medication trials, causing obesity, tardive dyskinesia, sedation, seizures, and osteoporosis, resulting in numerous foot fractures.
    *   Has been prescribed up to 20 different medications at once, mostly psychiatric or to treat side effects of psychotropic medications.
    *   A few years ago, he was hospitalized for bowel obstruction due to psychiatric medications.
    *   At a family gathering, he became agitated, obsessed with material, and hit my 99-year-old grandmother in the face.
    *   He was too agitated to attend her 100th birthday party, unlike his twin brother from JRC.
    *   He is sometimes too agitated to go on trips and visit his twin brother.
    *   We cannot get him the help he needs due to the aversives ban in New York.
    *   He was best friends with his identical twin, but they cannot live together due to New York’s refusal to allow aversives.
    *   It is very sad that our family must live in different parts of the country due to politics.
*   The "state of the art" treatments described by the FDA ban proposal are not always backed up by research to be effective.
    *   As a result, direct care workers, primarily women and people of color, daily risk their lives.
    *   They have suffered injuries requiring surgeries, finger amputations, and permanent opiate use for intractable pain.
    *   One worker provided a video I have used at my lectures.
    *   Although my daughter has not required this treatment and my brother was successfully faded years ago, another student who needs the device and cannot access it, and is aggressive, places my family and other students at risk of injuries and subsequent trauma.
*   In practice, at least in NY, individuals are discharged or suspended from day programs due to their behaviors, leaving them alone with elderly parents in potentially dangerous situations.
    *   Two prior JRC students taken off skin shock devices returned to New York and died from self-injury in their 20s.
    *   I do not want my brother to die too.
*   Many so-called positive behavior plans include calling 911 when someone is dangerous.
    *   This intervention is aversive, as police often use pepper spray or tasers, which are more intensive than JRC’s skin shock and have killed people.
    *   When these individuals arrive at the hospital, they are given painful intramuscular medications that sometimes have toxic and life-threatening side effects.
*   Research
    *   Aversives and skin shock have been debated for decades.
    *   Eric Schopler, originator of the research-based TEACCH program, discussed aversives in 1990, calling critics "self-serving ideologues" who oversimplify the issue.
    *   There are 130 peer-reviewed articles and a PhD dissertation supporting the efficacy of skin shock treatment for behaviors.
    *   A literature analysis on punishment, including skin shock, recommended using moderate or high-intensity punishers for problem behavior and cautioned against gradual intensity increases.
    *   Research on positive-only treatments shows significant limitations, including how "severe" behaviors are defined, often including commonplace classroom behaviors rather than life-threatening ones like my brother's head banging requiring surgery.
    *   Positive behavior supports are only effective in about half of cases to suppress behavior frequency by 90%, which is insufficient for life-threatening behaviors.
    *   There are many problems with medication management for self-injury.
        *   Millions of Americans are hospitalized and thousands die each year due to adverse drug reactions.
        *   Estimates from 1998 suggested 106,000 deaths annually from adverse reactions to prescribed medications, making it the fourth leading cause of death.
        *   A 2013 study suggested 210,000 to 440,000 deaths per year from iatrogenic causes, potentially making it the third leading cause of death; these numbers are estimated due to inaccurate medical records and reluctance to disclose mistakes, with adverse drug events being the most common medical errors.
        *   Risperidone received FDA approval for autism, but placebo-controlled trials did not differentiate between mild and severe behavior, lacked line-by-line analyses of the Aberrant Behavior Checklist (only three components relate to self-injury), and had a 49% sedation rate.
        *   Aripiprazole trials showed no significant improvement in self-injury for autism patients compared to placebo.
        *   Up to 60% of individuals with autism without clinical seizures have epileptiform discharges on EEGs, and these medications increase seizure risk.
        *   Using medication is particularly dangerous for individuals who cannot communicate side effects or comply with prescribing guidelines (e.g., blood pressure, blood tests).
        *   Using aversives decreases or stops the need for psychotropic medications, as it did for my brother.
        *   It has also prevented deadly restraints.
        *   It has allowed individuals with significant cognitive impairments, unable to make risk-benefit decisions, to have physical exams.
        *   It is unethical to take away the only treatment proven effective for them.
    *   Research on skin shock has shown positive side effects.
        *   One study documented "Positive side effects indicating an improved affective state and increased interaction with the environment," with treatment gains maintained at a 1-year follow-up, and an increase in self-initiated toy play.
        *   Another study at JRC found that contingent shock (CS) treatment either significantly improved or showed no change in positive verbal/nonverbal utterances, socially appropriate behaviors, and time off work, with no negative side effects found.
    *   Placebo-controlled trials have not been done on skin shock for good reasons.
        *   It may be unethical to give someone a placebo for acute life-threatening behavior.
        *   Observers could not be blind to who received a shock due to observable reactions (I made a vocalization myself when I tried the shock).
        *   Placebo-controlled trials have limitations: statistically significant results may not be clinically meaningful, or magnitude of change may be small, which is unacceptable for life-threatening behavior.
        *   Single-case and multiple-case studies with baselines are useful in behavior analytic research, including skin shock, for observing individual clinically meaningful change.
    *   The FDA ban proposal mentioned a 2019 PhD dissertation on efficacy, risks, and ethics of aversive/positive therapy in identical twins but stated no robust experimental control group existed.
        *   This reflects bias, as the dissertation used an identical twin as a control, contradicting the ban agenda.
        *   The "medical literature" cited by FDA for ESD side effects also lacks control groups.
    *   The FDA proposal suggesting studies by JRC-affiliated authors are invalid is inconsistent with FDA routinely approving products based on company-sponsored studies.
*   Improper Investigations
    *   When New York investigated aversives, they did not obtain collateral information from family or staff for reported symptoms.
        *   JRC only learned a student reported being suicidal through the NY State report; investigators never alerted staff or family.
    *   Regarding documented side effects, the FDA never obtained collateral information from a treating physician, therapist, or treatment record.
    *   I find it disturbing that the FDA has never toured JRC or visited a program treating life-threatening behaviors with polypharmacy, routinely using emergency medical services and hospitalizations.
    *   I doubt the FDA has observed placements where individuals are so sedated they cannot be safely evacuated in case of fire, all of which I have observed.
    *   The United Nations never investigated, visited, or spoke to a parent; they gave an opinion based on a third-hand report.
        *   The UN has condemned involuntary treatment, despite involuntary hospital admissions saving lives.
        *   This view implies depressed individuals have the right to commit suicide or starve to death if they believe food is poisoned, despite these behaviors being absent without psychiatric illness.
*   Conclusions
    *   I do not understand why the shock device is held to a different standard than medication, especially when the risk of no treatment can be death, and off-label polypharmacy trials examining adverse effects have never been done on this population.
    *   I have worked with a developmentally disabled population exclusively for twelve years in New York.
    *   Like my brother in New York, there is no choice but to administer polypharmacy that often makes these individuals sleep much of the day to control behavior.
        *   They develop diabetes, heart disease, liver toxicity, among other ailments.
        *   Sometimes, they die very young, even in early adulthood, due to adverse effects.
        *   Without access to skin shock, they sometimes end up either sick or dead.
    *   Some of my patients with intellectual disability and autism in New York, unable to access effective behavioral treatments, ended up unhoused and serving prison time.
    *   No one has ever died from a skin shock device, while people have died from side effects of psychiatric medication, restraints, and tasers, which are the current, often ineffective, alternatives.
    *   It is also traumatic when staff cannot manage behaviors, leading inexperienced police to handcuff and taser individuals, who then arrive at the hospital, are mechanically restrained, and administered injectable medications.
    *   This situation frightens families, including myself, that our children will lose effective treatment and forces us to relive our trauma.
    *   Withdrawing the proposed ban aligns with the Trump Administration’s goals of "ensuring the availability of expanded treatment options," "protecting expert recommendations from inappropriate influence," and "reducing over-reliance on medication."
    *   Please rethink the FDA ban proposal on electrical stimulation devices, leave treatment planning to the families, treating professionals, and courts, and let my brother and others continue to live, function, and have a quality of life.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: A board-certified psychiatrist and mother of a child with autism, whose twin brothers both have severe autism and intellectual disability, strongly urges the FDA to withdraw its proposed ban on electrical stimulation devices, citing their life-saving efficacy for one brother and the devastating, life-threatening failures of alternative treatments for the other in a state with a ban.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Ilana Slaff-Galatan, M.D.
- **Type:** Individual, Healthcare Provider, Advocacy Group (President of Judge Rotenberg Center Parents’ Association)
- **Role/Expertise:** Board certified psychiatrist; completed a fellowship at the Seaver and New York Autism Center at Mount Sinai Hospital; authored a book and psychiatry articles on autism; lectured on autism spectrum disorders; specializes in developmentally disabled population.
- **Geographic Scope:** Local/State (Oakland Gardens, NY); addresses national FDA policy; discusses impacts in New York and Massachusetts (Judge Rotenberg Center).
- **Stake in Issue:** Has identical twin brothers with autism and intellectual disability, one of whom relies on the banned device for life-saving treatment at JRC, and the other who suffers severe, dangerous behaviors in New York where the device is banned; has a daughter with severe autism; professional experience treating this population in New York where effective treatments are limited.
structuredSections.corePosition: I am requesting that the FDA’s proposed ban on electrical stimulation devices to treat severe self-injury and aggression should be withdrawn, as this treatment has saved my brother's life and is a safe, effective option when other interventions, including polypharmacy, fail and lead to severe harm or death. It is unethical to remove the only proven effective treatment for individuals with life-threatening behaviors who cannot communicate or make risk-benefit decisions.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Withdraw the FDA’s proposed ban on electrical stimulation devices (ESDs) for treating severe self-injury and aggression.
- Leave treatment planning for individuals with severe behaviors to families, treating professionals, and courts.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- The proposed FDA ban will impede access to a life-saving treatment (ESDs) for individuals with severe, treatment-resistant self-injurious and aggressive behaviors.
- "State of the art" alternatives like positive behavior supports and polypharmacy are often ineffective for life-threatening behaviors and carry significant risks.
    - Positive behavior supports are only 50% effective in suppressing behavior by 90%, which is insufficient for life-threatening actions.
    - Medication management for self-injury causes severe adverse effects, including obesity, tardive dyskinesia, loss of communication, sedation, seizures, bowel obstruction, and can be fatal (cited as a leading cause of death).
    - Polypharmacy in this population often leads to sedation that prevents safe evacuation in emergencies (e.g., fire) and can cause early death from organ damage (diabetes, heart, liver).
    - Individuals on extensive medication regimens cannot communicate side effects or comply with prescribing guidelines (e.g., blood tests), making treatment dangerous.
- Current crisis interventions for dangerous behaviors, such as calling 911, often involve more harmful "aversives" like police use of pepper spray or tasers (which can be lethal), mechanical restraints, and painful intramuscular medications with toxic side effects.
- Lack of access to effective behavioral treatments due to bans leads to severe negative outcomes.
    - Individuals are discharged or suspended from programs, leaving elderly parents in dangerous situations.
    - Former JRC students died from self-injury after returning to New York and losing access to skin shock.
    - Patients in New York who could not access effective behavioral treatments ended up unhoused or in prison.
- Investigations by regulatory bodies (New York State, FDA, United Nations) into aversives and ESDs are "improper" and biased.
    - Investigations failed to obtain collateral information from families or staff regarding reported symptoms or side effects.
    - Investigators did not alert staff or family when a student reported being suicidal.
    - FDA has never toured JRC or observed programs treating life-threatening behaviors with polypharmacy and frequent emergency services use.
    - UN opinions are based on third-hand reports without direct investigation or speaking to parents.
    - The FDA shows bias by dismissing research from JRC-affiliated authors while routinely approving products based on studies sponsored by companies that profit from approval.
- The UN Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities' view that all persons have legal capacity at all times effectively condemns involuntary life-saving treatment, which could lead to preventable deaths (e.g., depressed individuals choosing suicide, or individuals starving due to delusions).
- The FDA applies a different, stricter standard to ESDs compared to medications, despite the clear risks and lack of specific trials for off-label polypharmacy in this population.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The commenter's identical twin brother with autism and intellectual disability experienced life-threatening self-injury (banging head into sharp corners, requiring surgery, repeated suturing in hospital for 5.5 months despite 24/7 staff) and polypharmacy failure (5 medications with severe side effects including neuroleptic malignant syndrome), leading to their family facing potential financial ruin and loss of his right to education, before finding life-saving ESD treatment at JRC.
- This brother's transformation at JRC included cessation of head banging, no medication, working a paid job, going on trips, and regaining a quality of life, demonstrating the profound efficacy of the ESD over 36 years.
- A critical incident in 2011 revealed the ESD's necessity when an attempt to remove it resulted in the brother perforating both tympanic membranes and needing hospitalization for the first time since entering JRC.
- The commenter's other identical twin brother, living in New York (with an aversives ban), suffered severe, life-threatening behaviors including grabbing a butcher knife, trying to set himself and others on fire, hitting their 99-year-old grandmother, and experiencing numerous hospitalizations and 15+ failed medication trials (up to 20 medications at once) leading to severe side effects and conditions like bowel obstruction, highlighting the catastrophic impact of treatment limitations.
- The commenter personally tried the ESD shock and experienced no side effects, challenging perceptions of the device's aversiveness.
- Observations of direct care workers suffering severe injuries (requiring surgeries, finger amputations, permanent opiate use) from aggressive individuals when effective behavioral treatments are unavailable.
- Awareness of two former JRC students who died from self-injury in their 20s after returning to New York and losing access to their skin shock devices.
- Direct observation of individuals so sedated by polypharmacy that they could not be safely evacuated in case of a fire, illustrating a severe unintended consequence of medication-centric treatment.
- Experience with patients in New York with intellectual disability and autism who, lacking effective behavioral treatments, ended up unhoused and incarcerated.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "The proposed ban seeks to ban the court-approved Electrical stimulation device treatment that my one of my brothers has received at the Judge Rotenberg Education Center for his severe self-injury and aggression, treatment that has never caused any harm and saved his life."
- "No one has ever died from a skin shock device while people have died from side effects of psychiatric medication, restraints and tasers, which are the alternatives currently being used, although sometimes ineffective."
- "It is unethical to take away the only treatment that has been proven to be effective for them."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- In the spirit of continuous quality improvement, we recommend your consideration of this review of the regulation:
  - Maintain comprehensive services.
    - These are critical to the success of Head Start.
    - Health services are essential to ensure the success of children’s education.
    - Family services are essential to supporting parents becoming thriving citizens, supporting their own needs and expenses.
  - Maintain National to Local funding.
  - Ensure high-quality standards.
  - Ensure comprehensive services that work.
  - Decrease documentation of nonfederal match requirements to 5%.
    - Programs must balance their budgets to be successful.
    - Nonfederal match or in-kind will be required to support the budget.
    - The documentation is an administrative burden.
    - Documentation of a 20% match diverts staff efforts away from child and family support, parent choice, nutrition, and health and safety.
    - If match must be a requirement, require documentation of 5% to show community buy-in but not to create an administrative burden.
  - Expand the definition of children with disabilities to reach the 10% threshold by including more children with health challenges, not covered with an IFSP or IEP.
    - Include children with allergy plans who must be monitored extensively.
    - Include children who receive private speech, physical, and occupational therapy and were not accepted by the public schools or whose parents chose not to participate in the public school’s options.
    - Include children with diabetes, epilepsy, and other significant health conditions.
  - Asset Disposals: Set a fair market value (FMV) threshold required for regional approval for disposal of asset inventory items to a value of $5,000 or less.
    - For example, a dated copier with a FMV of $425.00 requires board, policy council, and regional approval.
    - For example, presently an outdated server worth $0 requires board, policy council and regional approval.
    - For example, presently, a 22-year-old air conditioning unit worth $0 requires board, policy council, and regional approval.
    - Items are backlogged with no place to store, dispose of, or recycle for over 180 days due to the multi-layered regional approval process.
  - Simplify re-budget and carry-over requests such that timelines are met by the grantee for requesting and by the regional program for approval.
    - Simplify the process and hold both parties accountable for timelines.
    - Requests that get caught in long timeline reviews inhibit efficiency for serving children.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An anonymous individual with Head Start program experience recommends streamlining regulations to reduce administrative burdens, particularly related to nonfederal match documentation, asset disposal, and re-budget requests, while maintaining essential comprehensive services and expanding the definition of children with disabilities.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Anonymous
- **Type:** Individual
- **Role/Expertise:** Implied Head Start program administrator or staff with operational experience in budgeting, compliance, asset management, and child/family support.
- **Geographic Scope:** National (addresses federal regulation impacting local programs)
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly involved in the administration and operation of Head Start programs, impacted by federal regulations that dictate operational efficiency and resource allocation.
structuredSections.corePosition: We recommend simplifying and streamlining federal regulations to reduce the administrative burden on Head Start programs, ensuring that staff efforts are directed towards direct child and family support rather than excessive documentation. It is crucial to maintain comprehensive services and high-quality standards that are critical to the success of Head Start.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Maintain comprehensive services, including health and family services, as they are critical to the success of Head Start programs and children's education.
- Maintain National to Local funding structure.
- Ensure high-quality standards and effective comprehensive services.
- Decrease the documentation requirement for nonfederal match from 20% to 5% to reduce administrative burden while still showing community buy-in.
- Expand the definition of children with disabilities to help programs meet the 10% threshold by including:
  - Children with health challenges not covered by an IFSP or IEP.
  - Children with allergy plans requiring extensive monitoring.
  - Children receiving private speech, physical, or occupational therapy who were not accepted by public schools or whose parents opted out of public school options.
  - Children with diabetes, epilepsy, and other significant health conditions.
- Set a fair market value (FMV) threshold of $5,000 or less for regional approval of asset inventory item disposals.
- Simplify re-budget and carry-over requests, ensuring that both grantees and regional programs adhere to established timelines for requests and approvals.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- The current 20% nonfederal match documentation requirement imposes a significant administrative burden on Head Start programs.
- Excessive documentation diverts staff efforts away from direct child and family support, parent choice, nutrition, and health and safety.
- The current definition of "children with disabilities" makes it challenging for programs to meet the mandated 10% threshold.
- The multi-layered regional approval process for disposing of low-value or zero-value assets is overly cumbersome and inefficient.
- This asset disposal process leads to a backlog of items that cannot be stored, disposed of, or recycled, sometimes for over 180 days.
- Long timeline reviews for re-budget and carry-over requests inhibit efficiency in serving children.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- Specific examples of low-value assets (e.g., a $425 copier, a $0 outdated server, a $0 22-year-old air conditioning unit) requiring extensive board, policy council, and regional approval, highlighting the disproportionate administrative effort for negligible value.
- The direct consequence of the burdensome approval process, resulting in items being backlogged for over 180 days with no place for storage, disposal, or recycling.
- The insight that excessive documentation, specifically for the 20% match, directly diverts staff time and resources from critical child and family support services.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "Documentation of a 20% match diverts staff efforts away from child and family support, parent choice, nutrition, and health and safety."
- "Items are backlogged with no place to store, dispose of, or recycle for over 180 days due to the multi-layered regional approval process."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Modernizing Food-Health Regulations to Enable Evidence-Based Chronic Disease Claims
    *   Our regulatory system should be an enabler of innovation, not an obstacle.
*   Introduction
    *   Chronic diseases linked to diet are straining America’s health and economy.
    *   Under current regulations, food producers are largely forbidden from informing consumers about scientifically supported health benefits of real foods and natural compounds.
    *   Any claim suggesting prevention or management of diseases (e.g., diabetes, heart disease) can cause a food to be legally classified as an unapproved "drug," leading to enforcement actions.
    *   This has created a stark imbalance:
        *   Innovators in “food as medicine” are constrained from making evidence-based health claims.
        *   Ultra-processed food incumbents freely market products with implied health benefits by fortifying with vitamins or fiber.
    *   For example, a blueberry farmer cannot label blueberries as “may reduce cancer risk,” but a sugary cereal fortified with folic acid can claim to “support prenatal health.”
    *   This report outlines specific FDA and USDA regulations that hinder honest health communications about food, and recommends reforms to balance safety with innovation.
    *   The goal is to enable structure-function and chronic disease-related claims for foods based on emerging science and real-world biomarkers.
    *   This would level the playing field for small food innovators like Brightseed, One Bio, Holobiome, and Bonumose, and empower consumers to make healthier choices.
*   Regulatory Barriers to Evidence-Based Health Claims for Foods
    *   FDA’s Stringent Restrictions on Health Claims
        *   Under the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA), any statement that a food can treat, cure, mitigate, or prevent a disease transforms that food into a “drug” in the eyes of the law.
        *   The Nutrition Labeling and Education Act (NLEA) of 1990 allows “health claims” on conventional food labels only if pre-approved by FDA based on “significant scientific agreement” (SSA) among experts.
        *   These authorized health claims are limited to specific disease-nutrient relationships (e.g., calcium and osteoporosis, soluble fiber and heart disease) and must be worded exactly as FDA prescribes.
        *   Any unapproved disease claim, even if supported by studies, renders the product “misbranded.”
            *   For instance, when a walnut company cited research on omega-3s and heart health, FDA warned that “your walnut products are drugs” and “misbranded” because of the health claims, since walnuts were not an approved treatment.
            *   In another case, FDA warned a cereal brand that claimed it “lowers cholesterol” (a biomarker for heart disease) caused the cereal to be an unapproved drug; only the authorized phrasing “may reduce the risk of heart disease” was acceptable.
        *   These rules make it practically impossible for whole foods or new ingredients to truthfully advertise disease-related benefits without undergoing a drug-like approval process.
        *   FDA does allow “structure/function” claims (statements about maintaining normal body structure or function) for dietary supplements, e.g., “supports healthy immunity,” with a disclaimer.
        *   However, for conventional foods, even structure/function-style language is policed if it implies disease prevention.
            *   FDA has objected to phrases like “promotes healthier blood sugar levels” on supplements, deeming them implied drug claims for diabetes.
            *   On a food label, a claim such as “helps lower A1C” (a blood sugar marker) would likewise be treated as an illegal drug claim under current policy.
            *   Thus, emerging biomarker-based benefits cannot be mentioned for foods, despite growing evidence that certain diets and ingredients can improve clinical metrics (like hemoglobin A1c, LDL cholesterol, or blood pressure).
        *   FDA’s health claim regulations impose additional hurdles:
            *   The substance in the claim must be a “nutritive” component of food (contributing taste, aroma, or nutritional value).
            *   The food must not exceed “disqualifying” levels of saturated fat, sodium, cholesterol, or total fat.
            *   This nutritive-value rule has prevented some bioactive plant compounds, which may have health effects but aren’t traditional nutrients, from being the subject of authorized claims.
                *   It also complicates claims for probiotics or botanical extracts discovered by companies like Brightseed, since they may not fit the classic definition of a nutrient.
            *   The disqualifying-nutrient rule, while intended to ensure overall “healthy” products, can bar inherently nutritious foods from making claims.
                *   For example, nuts and avocados (high in fats) historically could not carry heart-health claims due to fat content limits, even though science now recognizes their cardiovascular benefits.
                *   Meanwhile, a fat-free sugary product could make a health claim if fortified appropriately, illustrating a misalignment with modern nutrition science.
        *   Qualified health claims (QHC) offer a narrow alternative: they allow disease risk reduction claims with weaker evidence, accompanied by disclaimers.
            *   However, the QHC petition process is cumbersome and slow.
            *   By FDA’s own procedures, a QHC petition must undergo extensive evidence review, and FDA often finds that “no credible evidence” exists to support a claim, effectively denying even carefully worded, preliminary claims.
            *   In 2024, FDA rejected a petition to say D-tagatose “may reduce risk of type 2 diabetes” on the grounds that evidence, while suggestive, was not yet “credible” in FDA’s view.
            *   The bar for what constitutes acceptable evidence remains high and somewhat subjective.
            *   Additionally, FDA’s turnaround time for health claim petitions has been notoriously slow, creating uncertainty for innovators.
            *   FDA’s interim guidance on QHC timelines conflicted with formal regulations and led to backlogs, with petitions pending far beyond the 270-day statutory decision deadline.
            *   Such delays and ambiguity disproportionately burden small companies that cannot wait years or spend millions to win claim approval.
    *   USDA/FSIS Labeling Hurdles for Meat and Produce
        *   For meat, poultry, and egg products regulated by USDA’s Food Safety and Inspection Service (FSIS), the barriers are similar, with extra steps.
        *   FSIS requires pre-approval of any “special statement” on labels, including health claims and structure/function claims, before the product can go to market.
        *   A beef or poultry producer wishing to cite a health benefit must submit supporting documentation to FSIS, and FSIS will only approve claims that meet the same standards as FDA (since FSIS mirrors FDA’s definitions of health claims).
            *   For example, a lean beef producer cannot unilaterally label their product as “heart healthy” without demonstrating it meets the FDA-authorized claim criteria (e.g., “low in saturated fat and cholesterol”) and getting FSIS sign-off.
            *   This pre-market approval adds cost and time that small producers often cannot afford, effectively discouraging any health-related labeling.
        *   Whole fresh foods like fruits and vegetables face a different challenge: they are generally sold without extensive packaging, so producers rely on marketing or commodity promotions to communicate benefits.
        *   Yet these promotions are restricted too; for instance, federally mandated commodity checkoff programs (for beef, pork, dairy, etc.) are prohibited from making disease prevention claims or disparaging other foods.
            *   A vegetable growers’ association using checkoff funds cannot run ads saying “cruciferous vegetables reduce cancer risk,” even if supported by research, because that would be an impermissible health claim.
        *   The result is that “real foods” (produce, single-ingredient foods) get out-marketed by processed foods, which can make nebulous health-suggestive claims by virtue of added nutrients.
        *   As one analysis noted, “Real food producers are restricted from making health claims unless they meet strict FDA evidentiary standards... In contrast, ultra-processed foods can add a synthetic nutrient and claim ‘supports heart health.’”.
        *   This inequity in marketing freedoms allows nutritionally poor products to don a health halo (e.g., a sugary cereal with added fiber proclaiming “heart healthy”), while truly nutritious foods remain mute about their benefits.
        *   Current regulations (21 CFR §101.14; 21 USC §§321 & 343) tightly control health-related statements on foods.
        *   They require lengthy and expensive approval for explicit disease risk reduction claims and outright forbid disease treatment claims, regardless of the strength of the science.
        *   Structure-function claims on conventional foods are constrained to very general terms.
        *   These barriers protect consumers from false cures, but they also impede the communication of legitimate, emerging science.
        *   They favor large companies (which can fund compliance and petition processes) and status quo claims (such as fiber and vitamins) over small disruptors and novel bioactives.
        *   Next, we examine how these rules have impacted specific innovators and ingredients.
*   Impact on Innovative Food Companies: Case Examples
    *   Brightseed: Bioactive Compounds Trapped Outside the Regulatory Definition
        *   Brightseed is a startup using AI to discover bioactive compounds in plants (“dark matter” of nutrition) with promising benefits for metabolic and liver health.
        *   For instance, Brightseed has identified novel phytonutrients that may help manage conditions such as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and enhance microbiome function.
        *   However, because these bioactives are neither essential nutrients nor traditional supplements, current FDA frameworks do not formally recognize them.
        *   They are absent from dietary guidelines and lack even a standard definition in regulation.
        *   This means Brightseed cannot easily integrate its discoveries into food products that make health claims.
        *   Even if strong science links a new plant compound to reduced inflammation or improved insulin sensitivity, the FDA’s “nutritive value” requirement in 21 CFR 101.14 would question whether that compound qualifies as a legitimate claim substance.
        *   Moreover, any claim about the effect of a disease or biomarker would trigger drug status.
        *   Brightseed’s response has been to form a Bioactives Coalition to advocate for updating guidelines and definitions to include these compounds.
        *   Until regulations evolve, Brightseed’s bioactives can only be marketed in the shadows of the supplement world or with very careful structure-function wording, limiting their impact on mainstream food-as-medicine innovations.
    *   One Bio: Fibers Targeting Chronic Inflammation, Muzzled on Disease Claims
        *   One Bio, a UC Davis spinoff, has developed technology to convert agricultural waste into odorless, tasteless fibers (oligosaccharides) that nourish specific gut bacteria and combat inflammation.
        *   The company’s mission is to “end inflammatory disease” and “restore healthspan” via these functional fibers.
        *   Scientific rationale suggests that tailor-made prebiotic fibers could reduce chronic inflammation, benefiting metabolic health and immunity.
        *   However, One Bio faces the reality that it cannot put “prevents inflammatory diseases” or any such claim on a food label under FDA rules.
        *   Even referencing improved immune function or reduced inflammatory markers would likely be deemed an implied disease claim (since chronic inflammation underlies many diseases).
        *   One Bio can describe its ingredient in general terms, e.g., “supports gut health” or “nourishes beneficial microbiota,” but it cannot explicitly market its fiber’s role in, say, reducing risk of diabetes or autoimmune conditions without regulatory approval.
        *   Achieving an authorized health claim for fiber and, for example, reduced risk of a specific disease would require extensive clinical evidence and FDA petitioning.
        *   Big cereal manufacturers succeeded in obtaining a qualified claim that diets rich in whole grain foods (high in fiber) may reduce the risk of heart disease and certain cancers, but a start-up fiber company lacks the resources to pursue such approvals for novel fiber sources.
        *   In effect, One Bio’s innovative ingredient is regulated as just “fiber,” and the company must rely on educated consumers to make the connection between fiber intake and health.
        *   The affordability gap looms large: a pharmaceutical anti-inflammatory can go through FDA trials and explicitly claim to treat disease, whereas a food-derived fiber with similar potential cannot afford that route and thus can’t legally highlight its benefits.
    *   Holobiome: Microbiome-Based Mental Health Caught in Drug/Food Dichotomy
        *   Holobiome is exploring the gut-brain axis, formulating probiotics and microbial metabolites aimed at improving mental health and neurological conditions.
        *   They have identified specific bacterial strains that produce neurotransmitters or anti-inflammatory compounds that could help with depression, anxiety, or cognitive decline.
        *   The promise of these “psychobiotics” is exciting, but our regulatory system offers only two extreme paths:
            *   Develop them as prescription drugs (costly and lengthy).
            *   Sell them as foods/supplements with no mental health claims.
        *   If Holobiome markets a probiotic yogurt or supplement, it cannot say “for anxiety” or “reduces depression symptoms” without instantly becoming an unapproved drug.
        *   Even a statement like “supports a positive mood” walks a fine line, as FDA and FTC have scrutinized mental health-related claims in supplement advertising.
        *   Holobiome might pursue medical food status for a product (which would allow disease-specific marketing for patients under physician supervision), but FDA currently does not recognize chronic conditions like depression or diabetes as eligible for medical foods.
            *   The agency has stated that regular diets can be modified for these conditions, thus “diabetes is not a category for which medical foods are indicated.”
        *   This stance closes off a potentially useful middle category for conditions that diet could ameliorate.
        *   As a result, Holobiome’s innovations may be steered toward the drug route (with full FDA trials), which would substantially increase costs and time to market.
        *   Alternatively, they remain in the supplement domain with vague claims.
        *   In either case, consumers and doctors miss out on clear, validated information about how certain probiotic strains or prebiotic foods could improve mental well-being.
        *   Holobiome’s predicament highlights the need for a new regulatory model that can accommodate foods targeting microbiome and health outcomes more directly, without defaulting to drug designation.
    *   Bonumose: A Rare Sugar’s Regulatory Battle
        *   Bonumose produces D-tagatose, a naturally occurring “rare sugar” that is 90% as sweet as table sugar but with only 38% of the calories and a negligible glycemic impact.
        *   Tagatose has been shown to improve glycemic control, act as a prebiotic, and not promote tooth decay.
        *   In essence, it could be a game-changer for diabetic-friendly foods and beverages.
        *   Yet Bonumose ran headlong into regulatory roadblocks: FDA insisted that tagatose must be labeled as an “Added Sugar” on Nutrition Facts, just like ordinary sugar.
            *   This is despite the FDA acknowledging in its own review that tagatose does not have the same metabolic effects as traditional sugars, and noting its health benefits (better blood sugar response and dental friendliness).
            *   FDA had exempted another rare sugar, allulose, from added-sugar labeling in 2020, but denied the same for tagatose, citing a slight difference in calorie count.
            *   Bonumose argued this was “arbitrary and capricious” under the Administrative Procedures Act, especially as the decision ignored tagatose’s positive impact on health.
            *   In 2024, a federal court agreed that FDA’s denial of the tagatose petition was inadequately justified; the judge noted FDA failed to explain why tagatose’s reduced tooth decay and glycemic benefits were disregarded, and vacated the denial order.
            *   This legal victory is paving the way for tagatose to be labeled more fairly.
            *   However, it came only after 6+ years of Bonumose’s advocacy and litigation, an enormous burden for a startup, taken on principle as much as profit.
            *   And even after 10 months since the court Order, FDA still has not acted on it.
        *   Bonumose also sought to make a qualified health claim that replacing sugar with tagatose may reduce the risk of type 2 diabetes.
        *   Given tagatose’s effects on blood glucose, such a claim is biologically plausible.
        *   Yet in February 2024, FDA rejected it outright, stating “no credible evidence” supported the claim.
            *   In FDA’s assessment, short-term studies on blood sugar and insulin were not enough; only long-term outcomes, like fewer diabetes diagnoses, might have swayed them.
        *   This illustrates how even modest, qualified claims with careful wording (“scientific evidence suggests but does not prove…”) are barred without near-drug-level proof.
        *   Bonumose’s experience encapsulates the plight of many small food innovators: their product is demonstrably safer than the status quo (sugar) and offers positive health benefits, but regulatory standards designed for absolute assurance prevent them from making any medical-style claims.
        *   Meanwhile, consumers still see “Added Sugar” on tagatose-sweetened foods (sending a discouraging message) and have to dig through research on their own to learn of tagatose’s benefits.
        *   Without reform, only large corporations or industry coalitions can muster the time and money to overturn such regulatory decisions (or endure the petition process), leaving most startups stuck marketing on vague wellness promises rather than evidence-based claims.
        *   These case studies demonstrate that the current regulatory regime stifles innovation and communication.
        *   Legitimate food-health solutions, whether bioactives, fibers, probiotics, or sugar alternatives, struggle to navigate rules that were designed decades ago for a different context.
        *   In the next section, we propose targeted reforms to unlock food-based health innovation while upholding safety and truthfulness.
*   Recommendations for Regulatory Reform
    *   To maintain public safety and trust, we do not propose eliminating standards for scientific substantiation.
    *   Rather, we recommend modernizing the framework so that it scales evidence requirements to the risk and nature of foods, leverages new science (including real-world data), and removes unnecessary hurdles that favor big players.
    *   The following reforms would enable responsible health claims for foods and natural compounds, preserving safety and accuracy while accelerating innovation:
    *   1. Create a Tiered System for Health Claims Based on Evidence Strength
        *   Not all health claims need the same evidentiary bar as drug approvals.
        *   FDA could establish multiple tiers of claims (Similar to the proposal from the Grocery Manufacturers Association in 2006):
            *   Authorized Health Claims (High Confidence): The current gold-standard claims backed by Significant Scientific Agreement would remain for well-proven relationships (e.g., folic acid preventing neural tube defects).
            *   Qualified Health Claims (Moderate Evidence): This existing tier can be improved.
                *   FDA should clarify and possibly lower the threshold for “credible evidence,” so that promising diet-disease links can be communicated with appropriate qualifiers rather than being denied entirely.
                *   For instance, if preliminary human studies suggest a food bioactive reduces inflammation, allow a claim like “Emerging research suggests that [bioactive] may help reduce markers of inflammation, although more research is needed,” instead of banning any mention.
                *   The disclaimers can be standardized and prominent.
                *   Further, the FDA must expedite review of QHC petitions, adhering to the FDAMA mandate for a 120-day review, to make this pathway viable for small firms.
                *   Dedicate additional staffing or utilize external scientific advisory panels could help alleviate the backlog.
                *   If necessary, Congress should mandate a faster petition process or a “deem approved” provision if FDA fails to respond within the set time.
            *   Structure/Function and “Biomarker” Claims (Basic and Specific Support): We propose expanding the allowable claims for conventional foods to include specific functional benefits tied to biomarkers or normal health functions, analogous to what supplements can claim.
                *   FDA could issue guidance recognizing that statements about maintaining healthy levels of blood glucose, blood pressure, cholesterol, etc., are permissible structure/function claims for foods, so long as no disease is mentioned and the claim is truthful.
                *   For example, “Helps maintain healthy blood sugar levels as part of a balanced diet” or “supports microbiome balance for digestive wellness.”
                *   Currently, agencies treat terms like “lower blood sugar” as implicit disease claims, but this can be nuanced: a claim to “lower the spike in blood sugar after eating” could be allowed with evidence from continuous glucose monitor (CGM) data, as it refers to a physiological response rather than treating diabetes outright.
                *   To maintain accountability, such claims should be substantiated by clinical or valid real-world studies, and perhaps notified to FDA similar to supplement claims (21 USC 343(r)(6) notification) with the ability for FDA to intervene if claims are misleading.
                *   By liberalizing structure/function claims for foods, innovators could communicate measurable benefits (e.g., “low glycemic response”) without crossing into explicit disease language, addressing the gap between bland marketing and full health claims.
    *   2. Develop a Fast-Track “Food as Medicine” Approval Process
        *   Not every food-related health benefit will initially have authoritative backing or decades of research.
        *   We recommend establishing an alternative approval pathway for high-impact food-health innovations, akin to “fast track” or “accelerated approval” in drugs.
        *   Key features might include:
            *   Surrogate Endpoint Acceptance: Allow certain claims to be approved based on surrogate health markers (A1C, LDL, blood pressure, microbiome diversity) rather than waiting for long-term disease outcomes.
                *   This parallels FDA’s accelerated drug approvals using surrogate endpoints.
                *   For example, if a new fiber consistently lowers LDL cholesterol, permit a claim about “heart health” benefits (with explanation) before a 10-year trial on heart attacks is done.
                *   This encourages early adoption of beneficial foods, with the understanding that surrogates are well-validated proxies.
            *   Conditional Approval with Post-Market Research: FDA could grant time-limited, conditional authorization for a health claim if initial evidence is compelling.
                *   The company would then conduct additional studies or collect real-world data to confirm the benefit within a certain timeframe.
                *   If the benefit is confirmed, the claim stays; if not, the claim authorization could sunset or be revised.
                *   This risk-sharing approach lets consumers benefit sooner and motivates companies to invest in research (or lose the claim if they don’t follow through).
            *   Priority Review for Public Health Needs: FDA’s Human Foods Program should prioritize review of claims addressing prevalent diet-related diseases (obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease).
                *   For example, a claim about a new sweetener reducing sugar intake or a probiotic aiding metabolic health deserves faster handling due to its public health relevance.
                *   A formal “Food for Chronic Disease Prevention” priority track could be created, similar to how breakthrough therapies for serious illnesses get expedited.
                *   This would involve tighter FDA-industry communication during the petition process and perhaps rolling submission of evidence.
            *   Safe Harbor for Small Businesses: To address the affordability gap, waive or reduce petition fees and simplify the paperwork for companies below a certain size.
                *   FDA could provide a template petition format for common types of emerging evidence (like a standard dossier for glycemic claims) to lower legal costs for applicants.
                *   By lowering these barriers, more scientifically-sound petitions will come from startups and research spin-offs, not just from cereal and pharma giants.
    *   3. Leverage Real-World Data and Tech for Substantiation
        *   In the age of wearables, apps, and big data, FDA and USDA can harness real-world evidence (RWE) to substantiate food-health relationships:
            *   Biomarker Data from Wearables: Encourage companies to incorporate data from continuous glucose monitors, fitness trackers, blood pressure cuffs, and other consumer devices as part of their evidence.
                *   For instance, a meal product shown (via CGM in hundreds of users) to flatten post-meal glucose spikes could use that aggregated data to substantiate a “lower glycemic response” claim.
                *   FDA’s evidence-based review guidance should be updated to include well-designed RWE studies (with appropriate controls and statistical rigor) as valid support, complementing traditional trials.
            *   Citizen Science and “Blockchain-Verified” Outcomes: We see an opportunity for a consumer-verified health outcome program, possibly managed by a neutral third party or a blockchain-based platform.
                *   Companies could invite consumers to opt-in to anonymously share health metrics and outcomes while using a product.
                *   By securing this data on a tamper-evident ledger (blockchain), all parties can trust that the results are real and not manipulated.
                *   If, say, thousands of consumers using a fiber supplement record improved bowel regularity and reduced inflammatory markers (confirmed by home test kits or labs), that dataset could support broader claims.
                *   Regulators could allow provisional claims accompanied by a QR code or link to a public dashboard of aggregated outcomes, increasing transparency.
                *   This turns post-market surveillance into a two-way street: consumers get validation of benefits, and regulators get large-scale data on efficacy.
                *   We recommend HHS pilot a “Food as Medicine Blockchain” initiative to test this approach with willing companies, ensuring privacy and data integrity.
                *   Such a model could revolutionize the speed at which evidence is gathered and updated, far outpacing traditional trials.
            *   Crowdsourcing and Challenges: FDA and USDA might also hold challenges or grants for validating food-health claims with real-world evidence.
                *   For example, an NIH or AHRQ-sponsored prize for the first company to demonstrate (with wearables and labs) that its product can lower average A1c by a certain margin in a population.
                *   This would spur data-driven innovation.
                *   By welcoming modern data science, regulators can maintain rigorous standards while reflecting the real-life effectiveness of food interventions, which often show up in broad population data even when RCTs are hard to fund.
    *   4. Introduce a New Category for Functional Foods and Expand “Medical Foods”
        *   Current law shoehorns products into either “conventional food,” “dietary supplement,” or “drug,” with medical foods as a narrow niche.
        *   We propose carving out a clearer regulatory category for Functional Foods or expanding the Medical Foods definition:
            *   Functional Foods Category: Define a category (through new legislation or FDA rulemaking) for foods that are specifically formulated or scientifically shown to benefit health or reduce disease risk beyond basic nutrition.
                *   This could be similar to Japan’s FOSHU (Foods for Specified Health Use) model, which approves foods to bear certain health claims after review.
                *   The U.S. version could allow a “Functional Food” seal or statement on products that meet criteria: proven safe (e.g., GRAS ingredients or long dietary use), and with evidence for a health benefit that is significant but not yet SSA-level.
                *   Functional Foods could be allowed to make moderately worded health claims on labels and in marketing, subject to pre-market notification to FDA rather than full approval, unless FDA objects.
                *   This flips the burden: if a company has, for example, a smoothie clinically shown to improve gut microbiome diversity, it could label it for “supports gut health and digestive regularity” without waiting for FDA authorization, provided it has notified FDA with its evidence dossier.
                *   FDA would retain the power to disallow or demand changes if the claim is not adequately supported.
                *   Essentially, it’s an expanded structure/function regime for conventional foods, coupled with transparency and oversight.
                *   This would particularly help companies like Brightseed and One Bio bring forth foods enhanced with bioactives or fibers and communicate their purpose.
            *   Reform the Medical Foods Scope: Medical foods (defined in 21 CFR 101.9(j)) are intended for dietary management of diseases under physician supervision, but FDA’s interpretation excludes common chronic diseases (e.g., they allow inborn errors of metabolism or severe malabsorption, but not diabetes or hypertension).
                *   This is a missed opportunity.
                *   We recommend FDA expand the list of conditions eligible for medical foods to include certain chronic diseases or risk conditions that have well-established dietary needs.
                *   Diabetes is a prime example: managing blood glucose is fundamentally dietary, and one could formulate nutritionally balanced shakes or meals specifically for type 2 diabetics.
                *   Allowing these to be marketed as medical foods would let companies state “for the dietary management of diabetes” (with a doctor's oversight), which is currently disallowed.
                *   Similarly, medical foods for mild cognitive impairment (with specific nutrients), for arthritis (with anti-inflammatory diets), etc., could be recognized.
                *   To maintain rigor, such products must still meet the medical food criteria (specially processed or formulated, intended for patients who need them, used under medical supervision) and provide nutrient combinations supported by clinical guidelines.
                *   Expanding medical foods would give innovators like Holobiome or One Bio an alternate path: if they can convince medical professionals and gather some clinical data, they could market a product explicitly for a condition via healthcare channels, potentially even insurance reimbursed, without going through drug trials.
                *   This addresses the “food or drug” dichotomy by populating the middle ground.
            *   Clarify FSDU vs. Supplements: Foods for Special Dietary Use (an older FDA category) and supplements overlap somewhat.
                *   FDA could issue guidance to clarify that foods or beverages fortified for a specific health purpose (e.g., a cognitive health drink with choline and polyphenols) may be marketed with intended use statements as FSDU or functional foods, rather than being forced into supplement labeling.
                *   This would let companies choose a conventional food form factor (e.g., a snack bar) and still communicate health uses beyond general nutrition.
                *   Such guidance, combined with oversight for truthfulness, would legitimize a sector of functional packaged foods that currently operate in a gray area.
    *   5. Align Incentives and Definitions to Support Small Innovators
        *   Many of the existing rules inadvertently favor large companies with regulatory lawyers and lobbying arms.
        *   Reforms should strive to level the playing field and remove perverse incentives that favor ultra-processed foods:
            *   Update Nutrient Definitions and “Healthy” Criteria: FDA’s recent revision of the “healthy” claim definition is a step in the right direction, acknowledging that foods like nuts, salmon, and avocado can be healthy despite higher fat.
                *   Continuing this science-based update of criteria will help small producers of genuinely healthy foods compete.
                *   We recommend reviewing the “disqualifying nutrient levels” for health claims in 21 CFR 101.14.
                *   For example, excluding naturally occurring beneficial fats from “total fat” limits or raising the cap for foods with high unsaturated fat could allow foods like walnuts or flaxseed to make heart health claims (with appropriate language) rather than being automatically barred.
                *   Similarly, consider added sugar differently when it’s a functional sweetener with proven lower glycemic effect (as in tagatose or allulose).
                *   By refining these definitions, we ensure legacy fortifiers, like a bit of added fiber in a sugary cereal, aren’t given an edge over truly nutrient-rich whole foods.
            *   Permit Comparative and Contextual Claims: Small innovators often position their foods as better alternatives to unhealthy staples (e.g., a low-glycemic sweetener vs sugar, a veggie-based snack vs chips).
                *   Currently, explicit comparative health claims (“X has lower risk than Y”) are generally not allowed in food labeling.
                *   Regulators should explore allowing relative risk claims or substitution claims grounded in evidence.
                *   For instance, “Replacing sugar with tagatose reduces blood sugar spikes” or “Diets with plant-based fiber in place of refined carbs show reduced inflammation.”
                *   These could be qualified with “US dietary guidelines recommend…” or other context.
                *   Allowing well-substantiated comparative claims would directly attack the ultra-processed incumbents’ dominance by educating consumers on healthier swaps.
                *   The FTC and FDA would need to coordinate here to ensure advertising can echo these claims without being accused of disparagement, as long as they are factual.
            *   Support Claim Substantiation for Small Businesses: Government agencies (USDA, NIH) and public-private partnerships could assist in research needed for claim approval.
                *   For example, USDA’s NIFA or ARS could fund clinical trials on promising functional crops (fruits, legumes, biofortified foods) to generate evidence that could be used in health claim petitions.
                *   The results would be published for any producer to use.
                *   This would be especially helpful for small farmers or co-ops that cannot afford to sponsor studies alone.
                *   A shared evidence base lowers the cost for each company to make science-based claims.
                *   Moreover, FDA could maintain a public database of authorized and qualified health claims, and importantly, those under consideration, so innovators know where the science threshold lies and can collaborate rather than duplicate efforts.
            *   Revise Labeling to Empower Real Foods: Beyond claims, labeling rules can be adjusted to avoid unduly penalizing innovative products.
                *   Bonumose’s tagatose fight is illustrative: the FDA should proactively consider exempting or footnoting novel healthy ingredients in nutrition labeling (as they did for allulose) so that the label accurately reflects the true health impact.
                *   When an ingredient like tagatose or a new fiber doesn’t act like traditional sugar or carbs in the body, the label should inform consumers of that distinction (e.g., via a note on digestible vs. non-digestible carbs).
                *   Such nuance helps small companies that introduce these ingredients, rather than entrenching the old guard of corn syrup and refined flour.
                *   We commend FDA for recognizing allulose and urge similar treatment for other emerging ingredients after evaluation.
            *   Ensure Consistent Enforcement on “Dubious” Claims: The reforms above focus on enabling good actors, but it’s equally important to tighten oversight of misleading health messaging by big players.
                *   The FDA and FTC should continue to scrutinize implied health claims on ultra-processed foods, for example, sugary cereals adorned with heart symbols or terms like “immunity boost” simply due to vitamin additives.
                *   If a product’s claim is technically within regulations but fundamentally misleading (e.g., implying a disease benefit from a token fortification), agencies should issue warning letters or require corrective disclosures.
                *   This evens the field for small companies that take a science-first approach.
                *   No company, big or small, should be able to claim “heart healthy” unless the overall product truly supports cardiovascular health.
                *   By holding all to high truth-in-advertising standards, regulators prevent a race to the bottom and build consumer trust in any new claims regime.
    *   6. Encourage USDA and Cross-Agency Support for Food as Medicine
        *   FDA’s regulations do not exist in isolation. We urge USDA, HHS, and other agencies to collaborate in creating a conducive ecosystem:
            *   USDA Dietary Guidelines Integration: The Dietary Guidelines for Americans (DGA) could start to recognize certain food-health relationships more explicitly, which would provide a basis for authorized claims.
                *   For example, if DGA states “diets rich in bioactive polyphenols from berries are associated with cognitive health,” industry can build on that.
                *   Brightseed’s coalition push to include bioactives in guidelines is a model.
                *   Policymakers should direct the DGA committee to review emerging nutrient categories (bioactives, fermentable fibers, probiotic foods) so that they provide guidance that can translate into claims.
                *   Under FDAMA 1997, an “authoritative statement” from a federal scientific body can allow a health claim without FDA’s full petition (via notification), so getting authoritative statements in place is key.
            *   FSIS Harmonization: USDA’s FSIS should be ready to mirror any new flexibilities FDA enacts for health-related claims on labels.
                *   If FDA creates an expedited claim pathway or new functional food category, FSIS can issue parallel directives so that meat and poultry producers can utilize them.
                *   This might include FSIS accepting the use of specified structure/function claims on labels without sketch approval, as long as they are defined in policy (e.g., allowing “protein helps build muscle” on meats generically, which is common-sense but still technically a claim about body structure).
                *   For novel claims (like a pastured egg high in omega-3s claiming “supports brain health”), FSIS can use FDA’s evaluation as a basis to approve the label, reducing duplicative burden on producers.
            *   Healthcare and Payment Models: Although beyond labeling laws, it’s worth noting that if these reforms succeed, we will have more foods making legitimate health claims.
                *   CMS and insurers could then consider covering certain food products or ingredients under health benefits (as they do for medical foods or diabetes self-management).
                *   For instance, a shake proven to lower A1c could be eligible for reimbursement or HSAs.
                *   Government pilot programs could test “food prescription” models where products with proven claims are prescribed to patients (FreshRx programs have shown success in lowering A1c with produce).
                *   Regulatory reform that legitimizes claims will facilitate these food-as-medicine interventions on a broad scale.
            *   Education and Oversight: Agencies should invest in educating consumers and industry about any new claim categories.
                *   A public registry of functional food claims and the evidence behind them (perhaps maintained by FDA or NIH) would ensure transparency.
                *   Blockchain-verified consumer data, as discussed, could even feed into this registry, creating a living database of how foods affect health in practice.
                *   Meanwhile, regulatory oversight via random audits of claims (checking that companies have the promised evidence on file) can keep the system honest without requiring pre-approval of every claim.
                *   This balances speed with accountability.
*   List of Regulatory Changes
    *   To implement the above reforms, we identify key statutes, regulations, and guidance to revise or create. This “punch list” highlights specific clauses and pathways for change:
        *   21 U.S.C. §321(g)(1)(B), Definition of “Drug”: Amend this FDCA section to exclude foods or ingredients marketed with FDA-sanctioned health claims or structure-function claims from the “drug” definition.
            *   This legal tweak would ensure that a food making an allowed claim about disease risk (or a supported functional claim) is not automatically an unapproved drug.
            *   It provides a statutory safe harbor for the outcomes of FDA’s new claims approval processes.
        *   21 U.S.C. §343(r), Nutrition Labeling (Health Claims): Revise NLEA provisions to institute the tiered claims system. Specifically:
            *   Authorize FDA to define an “emerging science qualified health claim” level with streamlined evidence requirements.
            *   Require FDA to respond to health claim petitions within e.g., 180 days, with extensions only by mutual consent (addressing Senators’ concerns on delays).
            *   Empower FDA to allow interim marketing of a claim with disclaimers if evidence meets a credible threshold, pending final review.
            *   Congress could also instruct FDA to accept federal research findings (NIH, CDC) as a sufficient basis for certain claims to speed up the dissemination of public health information.
        *   21 CFR §101.14, Health Claims General Requirements: Update FDA’s regulation to remove or adjust outdated criteria.
            *   We recommend deleting the strict “nutritive value” requirement in §101.14(b)(3)(i) so that non-nutritive bioactives and probiotics can be claim subjects, provided they are safe and part of the food.
            *   Additionally, update §101.14(a)(4) “disqualifying nutrient levels”: raise or exempt limits for inherently healthy fats (e.g., if saturated fat is from nuts/avocado in a food that meets other heart-healthy criteria) and consider a lower Added Sugar threshold for products making metabolic health claims.
            *   The regulation could insert an exception that disqualifying levels may be waived if the food has a net positive effect backed by evidence (for example, a dark chocolate could exceed fat limits but still claim antioxidant benefits if proven).
            *   These changes will remove blanket barriers for foods like nuts and bioactive-rich ingredients.
        *   21 CFR §101.70, Petition Process for Health Claims: Amend this to streamline petitions.
            *   For instance, shorten the required content (smaller businesses can reference generally accepted scientific reviews rather than reproduce them entirely) and mandate a provisional response from FDA by 120 days (even if just a scientific opinion).
            *   Add a clause that if FDA fails to respond in 180 days, the claim may be used with a conspicuous “FDA evaluation pending” disclaimer, spurring the agency to act.
            *   Clarify that petitions can include real-world evidence and observational studies as part of the substantiation, not just RCTs.
        *   21 CFR §101.93, Dietary Supplement Claims Notification: Expand this regulation (or create a parallel one) to cover conventional foods making structure/function or general wellness claims.
            *   For example, a new §101.93a could allow food marketers to notify FDA of claims like “supports healthy blood pressure” on a beverage, including the required disclaimer “not intended to treat or prevent disease” if needed.
            *   FDA’s Small Entity Compliance Guide on structure/function claims can be updated and extended to food companies, giving examples of permissible vs. impermissible phrasing for foods.
            *   This change uses the DSHEA model (which has worked for supplements) to give foods more latitude in communicating benefits without pre-approval, as long as they steer clear of explicit disease terms.
        *   21 CFR §101.9(j), Medical Foods Definition: Modify the medical foods criteria to include certain chronic diseases or conditions.
            *   Specifically, remove the clause in FDA’s guidance that excludes conditions like diabetes from medical food eligibility.
            *   Replace it with language permitting medical foods for any disease or condition with distinctive nutritional requirements documented by scientific evidence.
            *   Additionally, require notification to FDA when a medical food for a new disease category is introduced, so FDA can monitor misuse.
            *   This opens the door for products addressing diabetes, prediabetes, early-stage kidney disease, mild cognitive impairment, etc., under medical supervision.
        *   New FDA Guidance on Functional Foods/RWE: Develop guidance (or a FDA rule) on utilizing real-world evidence for food claims.
            *   This would detail how companies can collect and submit RWE (from wearables, patient registries, blockchain logs) and how FDA will weigh it alongside clinical trials.
            *   It should set quality standards for data (sample size, endpoints, statistical significance) so that such evidence is credible.
            *   A section could cover fast-track functional food designation, criteria a product must meet (safety, mechanistic plausibility, some human data) to be considered for accelerated claim approval.
            *   This guidance would signal FDA’s openness to modern evidence and give industry a clear roadmap for innovative claim substantiation.
        *   9 CFR §§412.1 & 412.2, FSIS Label Approval: Update USDA’s regulations to align with FDA changes.
            *   Amend 9 CFR 412.1(c)(3) to state that if a health or structure/function claim is defined in FDA regulations or guidance, FSIS will generically approve it on meat/poultry labels without requiring separate sketch approval.
            *   This means if FDA says “X may reduce the risk of osteoporosis” is an allowable claim, a milk or meat producer meeting the criteria can use it by notification.
            *   Also, instruct FSIS labeling policy to accept the expanded structure/function claims for meats (e.g., “protein for muscles”) as generically approved since they are factual statements.
            *   This harmonization prevents a two-track system where even after FDA reform, USDA-regulated foods lag behind.
        *   Federal Trade Commission (FTC) Coordination: Issue a joint FDA-FTC guidance or Memorandum of Understanding clarifying that FTC will defer to FDA’s determinations on qualified health claims and functional claims substantiation.
            *   This avoids situations where a company approved to make a qualified claim by FDA might face an FTC false advertising challenge due to different standards.
            *   Essentially, if a claim is allowed on the label, it should be acceptable in advertising, provided the contextual caveats are included.
            *   The guidance should also emphasize that marketing of foods with health claims must not mislead, e.g., imagery and overall context shouldn’t imply a greater benefit than substantiated.
