structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   On behalf of our more than 350 member hospitals, we suggest how the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) can reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens for hospitals that serve a safety net role.
*   As HHS responds to President Trump’s Executive Order 14219, implementing the president’s deregulatory initiatives, we hope to partner with HHS to ensure changes do not undermine access to care for the patients our members serve.
*   America’s Essential Hospitals is the leading association and champion for hospitals and health systems dedicated to keeping all Americans healthy, including people who cannot afford other options for care.
    *   Since 1981, we have advanced policies and programs that ensure access to critical services meeting patient needs.
    *   We support over 350 members with advocacy, policy development, research, education, and leadership development.
*   Although essential hospitals account for only 5% of acute-care hospitals nationwide, they provided 28% of the nation’s charity care in 2022.
    *   About three-quarters of our members' patients are uninsured or enrolled in Medicare or Medicaid.
    *   Essential hospitals do this at a financial loss because much care is uncompensated or under-reimbursed by government payers.
    *   Members had an aggregate operating margin of -9.0% in 2022, far worse than all other hospitals (-2.8%).
        *   Miu R, Kelly K, Nelb R, et al. Essential Data: Our Hospitals, Our Patients—Results of America’s Essential Hospitals 2022 Annual Member Characteristics Survey. America’s Essential Hospitals. December 2024. essentialdata.info. Accessed June 25, 2025.
*   It is difficult for our members to take on additional costs from unnecessary regulations due to their financial challenges.
    *   As a result, we support the administration’s efforts to identify regulations that impose undue burdens on businesses without clear public benefits.
*   In health care, we encourage HHS to focus deregulatory efforts on reducing overly complex and burdensome regulations that divert staff time and resources from direct patient care.
    *   We encourage HHS to consider policies to:
        *   Simplify the administration of Medicaid state directed payments (SDPs).
        *   Streamline quality measurement.
        *   Expand telehealth coverage.
        *   Simplify administrative aspects of the 340B program.
        *   Remove unnecessary conditions of participation.
*   We also encourage HHS to ensure its deregulatory initiatives do not undermine access to care for Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries.
    *   For example, as CMS considers regulatory changes to improve SDP administration, it is important to preserve states’ ability to use this payment authority to ensure access to quality care for Medicaid beneficiaries.
*   Efforts to make federal regulations more efficient and effective work best if affected stakeholders are involved in policymaking.
    *   We remain willing to work with HHS to identify ways to further streamline federal regulations.
    *   We encourage HHS to solicit feedback from other stakeholders to avoid potential unintended consequences.
*   Improving Medicaid SDP Administration
    *   SDPs are a vital tool many states use to offset low Medicaid payment rates and ensure access to quality care for Medicaid beneficiaries.
    *   Without SDPs, Medicaid managed care payments to hospitals would be less than half the rate paid by other payers, which is not enough to sustain access to essential services (e.g., maternity, trauma, behavioral health care).
    *   During the first Trump administration, the president recognized the importance of providing states with flexibility to implement SDPs.
        *   In 2018, the Trump administration allowed states to use SDPs to close gaps in hospital payments between Medicaid and the average commercial rate (ACR).
        *   Many states adopted this policy to keep rural hospitals open, reduce infant and maternal mortality, and improve care quality, value, and access.
            *   Kozminski J. State Directed Payments: Closing Medicaid Payment Gaps for Essential Hospitals. America’s Essential Hospitals. September 2024. https://essentialhospitals.org/state-directed-payments-closing-the-medicaid-payment-gap-for-essential-hospitals/. Accessed June 25. 2025.
    *   To promote efficient and effective administration of SDPs, most states use separate payment terms and interim payments based on historic utilization.
    *   Unfortunately, the 2024 Medicaid managed care rule requires states to phase out the use of these authorities (42 CFR 438.6(c)(2)(vii)(B) and 42 CFR 436.6(c)(6)).
    *   We urge HHS to repeal these two provisions of the final regulation because they will add substantial administrative costs to states, health plans, and providers with no meaningful benefit for patients.
        *   Moreover, these provisions reduce payment transparency and make it more difficult to ensure SDPs are advancing their intended goals.
    *   By simplifying SDP administration, CMS can better focus on monitoring policies that matter for patients.
        *   We encourage HHS to accelerate SDP payment application approval to advance the agency’s goals of improving federal and state program administration, which are part of the Medicaid and CHIP Scorecard.
            *   Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS). Medicaid and CHIP Scorecard. https://www.medicaid.gov/state-overviews/scorecard/measure/State-Directed-Payment-Review-Administrative-Data. Accessed April 11, 2025.
    *   a. Separate payment terms (42 CFR 436.6(c)(6))
        *   In the final rule, CMS noted that the use of separate payment terms has grown as more stakeholders realize the benefit of this payment flexibility.
        *   In 2021, more than half (55%) of SDPs used separate payment terms.
        *   CMS noted that commenters reported these arrangements "provide greater transparency, ensure that payments flow to providers as intended, minimize administrative burden for states, and make it easier for states to track SDPs."
            *   89 Fed. Reg. 41,002, 41,285. (May 10, 2024.)
        *   In our own analysis, we found that separate payment terms are particularly helpful for states that target SDPs to essential hospitals because they reduce the risk that health plans would have an incentive to steer patients away from the providers the state intended to help.
        *   The American Academy of Actuaries highlighted similar findings, noting that "prohibiting these separate payment terms could result in access issues or steerage away from certain providers, including some who may be essential safety net providers."
            *   American Academy of Actuaries. Letter to CMS regarding “Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program Managed Care Access, Finance, and Quality (CMS-2439-P)” on June 30, 2023. https://www.regulations.gov/comment/CMS-2023-0071-0104. Accessed June 25, 2025.
        *   Despite the proven benefits, CMS chose to eliminate these provisions due to concerns they are inconsistent with "the risk-based nature of managed care."
            *   The agency does not explain why it prioritizes this goal over states' statutory responsibilities to safeguard access and ensure managed care payments benefit Medicaid beneficiaries.
            *   There is no statutory reason for CMS to restrict the use of separate payment terms.
        *   CMS’ concerns appear based on a mistaken view that separate payment terms remove health plans’ responsibility for managing utilization.
            *   SDPs continue to be based on actual utilization, and plans remain at full risk for base payments.
            *   Separate payment terms reduce the incentive for health plans to steer patients away from essential hospitals receiving targeted SDPs, consistent with the goal to target resources where most needed.
        *   Eliminating separate payment terms adds administrative risk that SDPs flowing to providers will be less than the amount targeted by the state or funded through capitation rates.
            *   Actuaries will need to account for this risk, adding new administrative costs into capitated rates that do not benefit patients.
        *   To mitigate consequences, CMS noted states can add risk corridors or require health plans to contract with essential hospitals.
            *   However, these policies do not fully eliminate the possibility that health plans will pay providers differently than intended, and they add substantial administrative costs that do not benefit patients.
            *   Moreover, they do not mitigate other actions health plans could take to reduce SDP amounts, such as delaying or denying claims.
    *   b. Interim payments based on historic utilization (42 CFR 438.6(c)(2)(vii)(B))
        *   Interim payments based on historic utilization help states make more timely and predictable payments to providers.
            *   Though ultimately reconciled to actual utilization, interim payments allow providers to be paid more quickly before the claims runout process is complete.
            *   This process also reduces administrative burden of recalculating directed payment amounts throughout the year, adding costs without meaningful impact on final amounts.
            *   Historical data is commonly used in Medicaid managed care capitation to estimate future costs and is the most appropriate estimate for actuarial projections.
        *   Timely SDP payment is important for maintaining cash for financially vulnerable essential hospitals.
            *   CMS noted the claims run-out process can be as long as 16 months in some states, meaning hospitals might wait over a year for full payment without interim historic utilization payments.
                *   89 Fed. Reg. 41,002, 41,285. (May 10, 2024).
            *   While states can use interim payments based on actual utilization, this is not a good substitute due to the same claims runout challenges and unnecessary administrative burden of re-running claims data.
        *   In states relying on hospitals to finance the nonfederal share of SDPs, hospitals incur added costs months or years before payment, creating cash flow challenges for states.
        *   Combined with uncertainty and complexity from eliminating separate payment terms, this misalignment of hospital costs and payments increases risk.
        *   CMS applied the same "risk-based nature of managed care" standard to prohibit interim payments based on historic utilization, ignoring providers' legitimate need for timely and accurate payments.
            *   Prepaid payments to health plans do not mean provider payments need to be delayed.
        *   If SDPs are otherwise consistent with federal managed care rate regulations, it is unclear why CMS would preclude states from using interim payments based on historical utilization, especially when reconciled.
            *   CMS’ new policies only add uncertainty about timely receipt of intended SDP amounts.
            *   For safety net providers on thin margins, these delays and uncertainties increase the risk of losing access to essential services.
        *   To mitigate consequences, CMS noted states can make interim payments based on utilization during the rating period.
            *   However, recalculating payments monthly or quarterly requires substantial administrative costs and is still subject to claims runout delays.
            *   This constant recalculation adds administrative costs to states and health plans with no patient benefit, as it does not alter final reconciled payments.
*   Streamlining Quality Measurement
    *   Essential hospitals are committed to high-quality care and improving health outcomes.
    *   However, the current quality measurement landscape is overly complex, often duplicative, and imposes significant administrative burden.
    *   Many existing measures and reporting requirements pull valuable time and resources away from patient care rather than supporting improvements.
        *   Saraswathula A, Merck S, Bai G, et al. The Volume and Cost of Quality Metric Reporting. JAMA. 2023;329;(21):1840–1847. https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2805705. Accessed June 27, 2025.
    *   We urge CMS to streamline and better align quality measures across programs, focusing on a targeted set of evidence-based measures clearly linked to improved health outcomes.
        *   CMS should remove structural measures from hospital quality programs and instead focus on outcome measurement.
            *   Examples include Patient Safety Structural, Age-Friendly Hospital, and Maternal Morbidity Structural Measures.
            *   While focusing on important issues, these measures are burdensome, resource-intensive, and frequently do not provide actionable insights into care quality or patient outcomes.
        *   Structural measures rely on subjective attestations or documentation of organizational capabilities rather than actual safety events or clinical outcomes.
        *   These measures add administrative burden and fail to meaningfully support hospitals' efforts to improve care.
        *   Their inclusion increases compliance costs without delivering clear value to patients, providers, or Medicare.
    *   We encourage CMS to prioritize simplification of quality reporting and focus on well-tested, actionable measures that promote better care and efficient use of provider resources.
        *   This approach will support hospitals in improving community health while reducing unnecessary compliance burden.
*   Removing Unnecessary Conditions of Participation
    *   As major providers to Medicaid and Medicare patients, essential hospitals adhere to regulatory requirements and Conditions of Participation (CoP).
    *   CoP were put in place to protect health and safety, but some have become obsolete as the health system evolved.
    *   New CoP have added complexity without clear connection to improved care, straining hospitals with limited compliance resources.
    *   CMS should review and remove CoPs that are obsolete, duplicative, or unnecessarily burdensome.
    *   Notably, HHS should remove the Respiratory Illness Reporting Requirement from CoP finalized in 2024 under the Infection Prevention and Control and Antibiotic Stewardship Programs CoP (42 C.F.R. §§ 482.42(e), 485.640(d)).
        *   Beginning Nov. 1, 2024, the final rule requires all Medicare- and Medicaid-participating hospitals and critical access hospitals to electronically report certain COVID-19, influenza, and respiratory syncytial virus data to the CDC weekly.
        *   Failure to comply may result in termination from Medicare and Medicaid.
            *   QSO-25-05-Hospitals/CAHs
        *   While we recognize the public health value of certain infectious disease data, using CoP as a mechanism to compel data reporting is inconsistent with their original intent.
*   Removing Barriers to Telehealth
    *   Essential hospitals rely on telehealth to expand access for underserved populations, reduce no-show rates, and extend scarce specialists to hard-to-reach communities (rural and urban).
    *   Telehealth is a vital tool to mitigate persistent structural barriers such as lack of transportation, provider shortages, and limited appointment availability.
    *   During the COVID-19 public health emergency, CMS used its authority to waive geographic and site-of-service restrictions on originating sites, allowing Medicare patients to receive telehealth services in various settings, including their homes.
    *   CMS also allowed hospitals to bill an originating-site facility fee when the patient gets the service at home.
    *   These changes have been instrumental in allowing essential hospitals to expand telehealth use.
    *   Removing geographic restrictions is particularly important for improving access for essential hospitals in urban areas, as transportation barriers affect more than just rural patients.
    *   For many patients of essential hospitals, timely telehealth can lead to early diagnosis of life-threatening conditions and cost-effective follow-up care.
    *   Unfortunately, CMS’ authority for these flexibilities is scheduled to expire Sept. 30, 2025, threatening access gains.
    *   CMS should eliminate the geographic and site-of-service restrictions on Medicare telehealth services.
*   Withdraw Information Blocking Disincentives for Health Care Providers
    *   We urge HHS to withdraw the final rule establishing disincentives for health care providers found to have committed information blocking (89 FR 54662, July 1, 2024).
    *   Under the rule, hospitals and providers determined by OIG to have committed information blocking may face punitive consequences, including:
        *   Reductions in Medicare payment updates.
        *   Adjustments to reimbursement rates.
        *   Lower performance scores.
        *   Potential ineligibility for certain incentive programs.
    *   These penalties are disproportionate to alleged violations and create a stacked, variable, unpredictable, and unsustainable financial burden, particularly for essential hospitals treating high volumes of Medicare patients on thin/negative margins.
    *   We support the overarching goal of improving access to health information and fostering interoperability.
    *   Achieving that objective requires a more balanced and constructive approach.
    *   Rather than punitive financial disincentives, HHS should focus on supporting provider compliance through education, technical assistance, and clear, actionable guidance on what constitutes information blocking.
*   Modify the 340B Recertification Process
    *   We urge HHS to modify the current 340B covered entity recertification process to reduce administrative burden and improve efficiency.
    *   Specifically, the agency should explore how existing Medicare and Medicaid data can be leveraged to automate and streamline the annual recertification process for 340B hospitals and other covered entities.
    *   Currently, covered entities must manually re-enter information CMS already collects (e.g., provider identifiers, site-level enrollment status, eligibility data).
        *   This creates unnecessary duplication and burden.
    *   By coordinating to prepopulate or cross-validate required fields using CMS datasets, HHS can ease compliance efforts, reduce data inconsistency risk, and allow HRSA to redirect limited resources toward more targeted program needs.
    *   This effort is timely given HHS’ planned reorganization to move OPA under CMS, presenting an opportunity to better align the 340B program with Medicare and Medicaid operations.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: America's Essential Hospitals, representing over 350 safety-net hospitals operating at significant financial losses, urges HHS to simplify overly complex regulations, including those affecting Medicaid state directed payments, quality measurement, and telehealth, to reduce administrative burden and prevent undermining access to care for vulnerable populations.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** America's Essential Hospitals
- **Type:** Advocacy Group
- **Role/Expertise:** Leading association and champion for hospitals and health systems dedicated to keeping all Americans healthy, particularly those who cannot afford other care options, providing advocacy, policy development, research, education, and leadership development.
- **Geographic Scope:** National (represents over 350 member hospitals nationwide)
- **Stake in Issue:** Their member hospitals provide a disproportionate amount of charity care (28% of the nation's total in 2022) while accounting for only 5% of acute-care hospitals, operate at significant financial losses (aggregate operating margin of -9.0% in 2022), and serve a high proportion of uninsured or Medicare/Medicaid patients (three-quarters), making them acutely vulnerable to unnecessary regulatory costs that divert resources from patient care and threaten access to essential services.
structuredSections.corePosition: "We write to suggest how the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) can reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens for hospitals that serve a safety net role. We support the administration’s efforts to identify regulations that impose undue burdens on businesses that do not have clear public benefits, but we hope to continue to partner with you and your team to ensure that these changes are implemented in ways that do not undermine access to care for the patients our members serve."
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Repeal two provisions of the 2024 Medicaid managed care rule (42 CFR 438.6(c)(2)(vii)(B) and 42 CFR 436.6(c)(6)) which require phasing out the use of separate payment terms and interim payments based on historic utilization for State Directed Payments (SDPs).
  - Simplify SDP administration and accelerate SDP payment application approval.
- Streamline and better align quality measures across programs, focusing on a targeted set of evidence-based measures clearly linked to improved health outcomes.
  - Remove structural measures (e.g., Patient Safety Structural, Age-Friendly Hospital, Maternal Morbidity Structural Measure) from hospital quality programs and instead focus on outcome measurement.
- Review and remove Conditions of Participation (CoP) that are obsolete, duplicative, or unnecessarily burdensome.
  - Specifically, remove the Respiratory Illness Reporting Requirement from CoP finalized in 2024 (42 C.F.R. §§ 482.42(e), 485.640(d)).
- Eliminate the geographic and site-of-service restrictions on Medicare telehealth services.
  - Make permanent the flexibilities granted during the COVID-19 public health emergency, which are scheduled to expire Sept. 30, 2025.
- Withdraw the final rule establishing disincentives for health care providers found to have committed information blocking (89 FR 54662, July 1, 2024).
  - Instead, focus on supporting provider compliance through education, technical assistance, and clear, actionable guidance on information blocking.
- Modify the 340B covered entity recertification process to reduce administrative burden and improve efficiency.
  - Leverage existing Medicare and Medicaid data to automate and streamline the annual recertification process for 340B hospitals and other covered entities.
  - Coordinate to prepopulate or cross-validate required fields using CMS datasets.
  - Better align the 340B program with Medicare and Medicaid operations, especially given HHS' planned reorganization to move OPA under CMS.
- Ensure deregulatory initiatives do not undermine access to care for Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries.
- Involve stakeholders affected by policies in the policymaking process and solicit feedback to avoid unintended consequences.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Increased Administrative Costs and Burden:** New regulations, particularly the 2024 Medicaid managed care rule provisions on SDPs, add substantial administrative costs to states, health plans, and providers with no meaningful benefit for patients.
  - Eliminating separate payment terms for SDPs adds administrative risk and costs due to actuaries needing to account for risk.
  - Prohibiting interim payments based on historic utilization for SDPs creates unnecessary administrative burden of recalculating payments, adding costs without altering final payments.
  - The current quality measurement landscape is overly complex and duplicative, imposing significant administrative burden and pulling valuable staff time and resources from direct patient care.
  - New Conditions of Participation (CoP) add regulatory complexity and strain hospitals with limited compliance resources, without clear connection to improved care.
- **Undermining Access to Care for Vulnerable Populations:** Regulatory changes could undermine access to care for Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, especially given essential hospitals' existing financial fragility.
  - Eliminating separate payment terms for SDPs increases the risk that health plans will have an incentive to steer patients away from essential safety-net providers, potentially leading to access issues.
  - Delays and uncertainties created by changes to SDP administration increase the risk of losing access to essential services for safety-net providers operating on thin margins.
  - The scheduled expiration of Medicare telehealth flexibilities threatens gains in access to care, particularly for underserved urban and rural populations facing transportation barriers and provider shortages.
- **Financial Instability of Essential Hospitals:** Already operating at a significant aggregate operating margin loss (-9.0% in 2022), essential hospitals cannot absorb additional costs from unnecessary regulations.
  - Delaying SDPs through changes to interim payment rules creates cash flow challenges for financially vulnerable hospitals.
  - Hospitals that finance the nonfederal share of SDPs incur added costs months or years before being paid.
  - The information blocking disincentives create a "stacked and variable financial burden" that is "unpredictable and unsustainable," especially for essential hospitals with high Medicare patient volumes and thin margins.
- **Reduced Payment Transparency and Unintended Consequences:**
  - The repeal of separate payment terms for SDPs reduces payment transparency and makes it harder to ensure SDPs advance their intended goals.
  - CMS's mitigation strategies for SDP changes (risk corridors, required contracts) do not fully eliminate the risk of misaligned payments and add administrative costs without patient benefit, potentially leading to health plans delaying or denying claims.
- **Misaligned Regulatory Intent:**
  - Using CoP to compel infectious disease data reporting is inconsistent with the original intent of these conditions, which were established for patient health and safety.
  - Information blocking disincentives are disproportionate to alleged violations and are punitive rather than constructive, despite the shared goal of improving health information access.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- Essential hospitals, though only 5% of acute-care hospitals, provided 28% of the nation's charity care in 2022, highlighting their disproportionate role in serving vulnerable populations.
- These hospitals operate at significant financial losses, with an aggregate operating margin of -9.0% in 2022, compared to -2.8% for all other hospitals, demonstrating their extreme financial precarity.
- The insight that separate payment terms for Medicaid State Directed Payments (SDPs) reduce the risk of health plans "steering" patients away from essential hospitals the state intended to help, thereby safeguarding access.
- The concern that prohibiting interim SDP payments based on historic utilization could force hospitals, often financially vulnerable, to wait over a year for full payment (given claims run-out processes of up to 16 months in some states).
- The argument that structural quality measures (e.g., Patient Safety Structural, Age-Friendly Hospital) are burdensome, resource-intensive, and fail to provide actionable insights into care quality, suggesting a focus on outcome measures instead.
- The observation that telehealth's benefit in urban areas, for patients facing transportation or access barriers, is as critical as its role in rural areas, countering a common perception that it primarily addresses rural access.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "Although essential hospitals account for only 5% of acute-care hospitals nationwide, they provided 28% of the nation’s charity care in 2022."
- "It is difficult for our members to take on additional costs from unnecessary regulations due to the financial challenges they face."
- "Rather than relying on punitive financial disincentives, HHS should focus on supporting provider compliance through education, technical assistance, and clear, actionable guidance on what constitutes information blocking."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The AAMC (Association of American Medical Colleges) welcomes the opportunity to comment on the Department’s Request for Information (RFI) regarding deregulatory initiatives to promote health and well-being.
*   The AAMC is a nonprofit association dedicated to improving health through medical education, health care, biomedical research, and community collaborations.
    *   Its members include 160 U.S. medical schools, 12 Canadian medical schools, nearly 500 academic health systems and teaching hospitals (including VA medical centers), and over 70 academic societies.
    *   It serves millions of individuals in academic medicine, including 210,000+ faculty, 99,000 medical students, 162,000 resident physicians, and 60,000 graduate students/postdoctoral researchers.
    *   Through the Alliance of Academic Health Centers International, AAMC membership extends to over 60 international academic health centers.
*   Reports from the AAMC, National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, and Government Accountability Office have called for federal agencies to harmonize regulations, reduce administrative burden, and adopt a coordinated regulatory approach.
    *   The National Academies' 2016 report noted a lack of rigorous data on regulatory burden and costs to researchers, highlighting the AAMC Conflicts of Interest Metrics Project as a model for assessing operational impact.
    *   HHS should consider the output of a current National Academies initiative ("Improving the Regulatory Efficiency and Reducing Administrative Workload to Strengthen Competitiveness and Productivity of U.S. Research"), expected to deliver a data-driven roadmap for reform this fall.
*   The AAMC appreciates the Trump Administration's emphasis on regulatory reform to reduce burden on health care providers, simplify the system, and ensure optimal patient care.
    *   The increasing administrative responsibility on providers is unsustainable, diverts time from patient care, and leads to burnout.
    *   Reducing this burden will improve care quality, decrease costs, and enhance access.
*   A meaningful regulatory review must be deliberate, transparent, and grounded in sustained dialogue between agencies and the regulated community.
    *   The AAMC's May 2025 letter to OMB emphasized the need for government-wide coherence in eliminating duplicative or outdated requirements.
    *   It also underscored the value of an evidence-based approach that improves efficiency while preserving regulatory intent and value.
    *   Any regulatory changes must adhere to the Administrative Procedure Act’s notice and comment requirements for transparency, accountability, and public participation.
    *   HHS should establish an inter-agency framework for ongoing retrospective regulatory review, guided by defined prioritization criteria.
*   The AAMC has identified numerous federal requirements that create disproportionate burden without clear benefits, and the following recommendations reflect specific regulations that should be revisited, revised, or harmonized.
*   **Reducing Health Care Delivery Burden**
    *   **Regulations that require an excessive number of reports or unreasonable record keeping, or information that is not needed or used effectively**
        *   **Remove Respiratory Illness Reporting Requirement from Conditions of Participation**
            *   CMS added mandatory weekly respiratory illness reporting (COVID-19, influenza, RSV) for Medicare/Medicaid participating hospitals and critical access hospitals (CAHs) via Conditions of Participation (CoPs), effective November 1, 2024.
            *   Failure to report can lead to termination from Medicare/Medicaid programs.
            *   While acknowledging the value of data, using CoPs to compel data sharing is inconsistent with their intent.
            *   HHS should invest in infrastructure for voluntary, less burdensome, and more meaningful data sharing.
        *   **Re-Evaluate New Obstetrical Service Standards Conditions of Participation and Other Maternal Health CoP Changes**
            *   The agency should re-evaluate new Obstetrical Service Standards CoPs and changes to Emergency Services and Discharge Planning CoPs related to maternal health.
            *   The new CoP requires hospitals offering obstetrical services to implement changes in service organization, staffing, delivery, and training, and to use QAPI findings to assess/improve outcomes and disparities.
            *   While supporting efforts to improve maternal health, the AAMC does not support using CoPs to drive these improvements.
            *   The new CoP is considered optional, meaning only hospitals electing to offer the service must comply, which creates varying burdens.
            *   Failure to meet CoP requirements can result in sanctions, potentially leading struggling providers to eliminate obstetrical services to avoid penalties, making requirements overly burdensome.
        *   **Eliminate Duplicative “Look Back” Validation Surveys of Accrediting Organizations and Permanently Adopt Concurrent Validation Surveys**
            *   Current CMS "look back" validation surveys of accrediting organizations (AOs) are duplicative, conducting full re-surveys of hospital compliance and comparing results with AO surveys.
            *   These surveys cause rework and disruption for hospitals instead of assessing AO performance.
            *   CMS should permanently adopt concurrent validation surveys, allowing direct observation of AO performance.
        *   **Withdraw Proposed HIPAA Security Rule to Strengthen the Cybersecurity of Electronic Protected Health Information**
            *   The proposed HIPAA Security Rule by HHS Office for Civil Rights was misguided, lacked a consensus-driven stakeholder approach, and grossly underestimated implementation costs.
            *   The Trump administration should withdraw this rule and collaboratively work with stakeholders on requirements that advance shared goals of protecting patient health information and preventing costly disruptions.
        *   **Reform Hospital Quality Performance and Reporting Programs**
            *   Hospital quality measurement entails considerable burden.
            *   CMS should remove chart-abstracted and structural measures from hospital quality programs to maximize resources for meaningful quality improvements.
            *   Resources should instead be focused on outcomes measurement.
            *   Chart-abstracted and structural measures require significant clerical effort, diverting resources from clinical care (e.g., SEP-1 measure in IQR and VBP programs).
            *   Structural measures (Maternal Morbidity, Patient Safety, Age-Friendly Hospital) do not directly measure outcomes or safety events but require manual data abstraction or attestations to resources and documented activities.
            *   Removing these measures and prioritizing outcomes would more effectively use resources for quality improvement.
        *   **Removed Duplicative Measurement in Hospital Quality Performance Programs**
            *   CMS should simplify by removing duplicative measurement across performance programs to maximize resources for meaningful quality improvements.
            *   Specifically, remove the Safety Domain from the Hospital VBP program as it duplicates measures in the Hospital-Acquired Condition Reduction Program (HACRP).
            *   Eliminating overlap would reduce mixed signals due to different measure versions and scoring approaches.
            *   Removing the Safety Domain from VBP could double the weight of the Clinical Outcomes Domain, incentivizing improved care effectiveness.
        *   **Reform the Quality Payment Program (QPP)**
            *   Members find the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) under QPP administratively burdensome and clinically irrelevant.
            *   The budget-neutral design of MIPS, where rewards cannot exceed penalties, is a growing concern and should be replaced with payment adjustments based on the Medicare Economic Index to account for inflation.
            *   The current program is too costly, requires unnecessary reporting, and diverts time from patient care (estimated 586,877 hours and $70,166,672 burden for CY 2025).
            *   **Specific recommendations for QPP:**
                *   Retain MVP reporting as a voluntary MIPS option and traditional MIPS while developing comprehensive measures for MVP adoption.
                *   Ensure rules for subgroup reporting allow practices to best represent clinical context.
                *   All cost measures in MIPS should be appropriately adjusted for clinical complexity and economic risk factors.
                *   Utilize HITECH Act authority to permit Promoting Interoperability (PI) reporting through yes/no attestations, with points for each "yes."
                *   An attestation-based approach would relieve burden, facilitate EHR development responsive to patient/physician needs, and prioritize health IT functionality gaps.
        *   **Reform and Reduce Reporting Burdens for Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) in the Medicare Shared Savings Program (SSP)**
            *   **CMS should modify quality measurement policies to support ACO participation and reduce burden:**
                *   Provide time to ramp up reporting new electronic clinical quality measures under QPP’s APM Performance Pathway (APP) Plus.
                *   Reverse the policy requiring ACOs to report QPP PI data regardless of Qualified APM Participant (QP) status.
            *   **CMS should delay the sunsetting of Web Interface and MIPS CQM reporting options until at least 2028**, and assure that the Medicare CQM option remains available until digital quality measure reporting is feasible and successful.
            *   **CMS should expand the significant, anomalous, and highly suspect billing activity policy** to allow ACOs to report suspected fraudulent Medicare billing to CMS to expedite investigations and partner against fraud, waste, and abuse.
    *   **Regulations that impose requirements on the wrong individual or group**
        *   **Reconsider Price Transparency Rules to Avoid Duplication, Reduce Burden, and Ensure Patients Have Meaningful Information**
            *   The AAMC supports increasing price transparency and believes patients need information for informed decisions.
            *   Hospitals/health systems have invested significantly to comply with the Hospital Price Transparency Rule and No Surprises Act, with many adopting online tools for out-of-pocket cost estimates.
            *   Concerns exist with the current approach, which is overly burdensome, costly, does not enable patients to understand actual payment, and causes widespread confusion.
            *   Hospitals/health systems and insurers are subject to multiple different policies:
                *   Hospital Price Transparency Rule: Requires public posting of five "standard charges" via machine-readable files (gross charges, payer-specific negotiated rates, de-identified min/max negotiated rates, discounted cash prices) and consumer-friendly display for 300 shoppable services (e.g., online estimator).
                *   No Surprises Act - Good Faith Estimates: Requires hospitals/providers to share GFEs with uninsured/self-pay patients for most scheduled services. "Convening providers" must seek and combine estimates from unaffiliated providers for a single, comprehensive GFE.
                *   Advanced Explanation of Benefits: No Surprises Act requires insurers to share AEOBs with enrollees (not yet implemented due to operational challenges); hospitals will eventually need to provide GFEs to insurers for this.
                *   Transparency in Coverage Rules: Apply to insurers/group health plans, requiring monthly posting of three machine-readable files (in-network negotiated rates, out-of-network allowed amounts/billed charges, negotiated rates/historical net prices for prescription drugs).
            *   Given patient confusion and regulatory burden, the AAMC urges review and streamlining of existing price transparency policies.
            *   Hospital-provided machine-readable files are too large and complex for patients to navigate to find "payer-specific negotiated charges" (e.g., 100+ plans with multiple negotiated rates).
            *   CMS itself acknowledged MRFs are not consumer-friendly and not intended for direct patient use.
            *   Patients need to know their out-of-pocket costs, which depend on their insurance coverage, plan-specific cost-sharing (deductible, co-pay), and where they are in meeting these.
            *   Only the insurer is in a position to provide this personalized information, making insurer-provided information under Transparency in Coverage rules more relevant than provider pricing information.
            *   For uninsured/self-pay patients, the No Surprises Act requires GFEs from hospitals, making much of the hospital price transparency rule unnecessarily redundant and burdensome.
        *   **Under the No Surprises Act Good Faith Estimates, Eliminate the Requirement that the Convening Provider Obtain Information About Charges from Unaffiliated Providers as it is Not Feasible to Operationalize**
            *   GFE requirements are currently in place for uninsured/self-pay patients, requiring the convening provider to contact co-providers/co-facilities within 1 business day for expected charges.
            *   Creating GFEs that include unaffiliated providers is challenging, requiring new workflows (often manual) and costly technology updates for information exchange.
            *   The No Surprises Act also requires health plans to deliver an Advanced EOB (AEOB) to patients using provider GFEs.
            *   This AEOB approach provides meaningful, personalized price transparency.
            *   CMS has delayed AEOB enforcement until a standard industry process for information exchange is adopted.
            *   When implemented, CMS should allow each billing provider to submit a GFE directly to the health plan for their billed items/services.
            *   The responsibility for combining GFEs into one AEOB should rest with insurers, as they already process claims from distinct providers.
            *   Accurate AEOBs could be best established by leveraging existing provider and health plan workflows, standards, and technologies for claims submission and adjudication.
    *   **Regulations that carry excessive penalties**
        *   **Withdraw Information Blocking Disincentives Rule**
            *   The AAMC asks agencies to withdraw the 2024 policy imposing Medicare payment disincentives on health care providers found to have committed information blocking.
            *   This withdrawal would support critical real-world educational efforts to allow providers a fair opportunity to self-correct and ensure compliance.
            *   CMS and OIG should ensure the investigative process and appeal rights are fair and consistent across all regulated actors.
            *   Alternative approaches are needed to reduce significant financial impact and outsized variance across provider types, where some are penalized for others' actions while some avoid reductions regardless of conduct.
            *   An overly punitive approach could critically impact care delivery and reinvestment in value-based health care, negatively affecting patients.
    *   **Regulations that impede access to delivery of care or services**
        *   **Ensure Prior Authorization Requirements do not Limit Patients’ Access to Care by Streamlining Processes and Coverage Criteria**
            *   Hospitals/health systems contract with numerous plans, each with different clinical criteria, rules, and documentation for prior authorization.
            *   These rules and processes should be streamlined to improve patient access and reduce provider burden.
            *   CMS has taken steps by finalizing rules (effective 2026/2027) for standardized electronic prior authorization and securing a voluntary industry pledge.
            *   The Administration should ensure timely implementation and enforcement, and continue discussions with payers, providers, and patients to prevent prior authorization from hindering access.
        *   **Prohibit Restrictive Uses of Prior Authorization by Medicare Advantage Plans That Depart from Traditional Medicare Fee-for-Service**
            *   MA plan prior authorization continues to impact timely patient care.
            *   CMS regulations (CY 2024) require MA plans to adhere to original Medicare coverage criteria, limiting adoption of their own policies unless Medicare policies are not fully established.
            *   Frequent phone calls, faxes, EHR connectivity issues, and different forms for prior authorization hinder efficient care.
            *   Prior authorization rules and criteria must be transparent and available at the point of care.
            *   If a service or medication is denied, both patient and physician need specific reasons, appeal rights, and covered alternatives.
            *   Medically necessary care should not be denied due to complicated, opaque hoops.
            *   In 2021, over 2 million of 35+ million MA prior authorization requests were fully or partially denied; 82% of appealed denials were overturned.
            *   The burden of responding to denials falls on providers, contributing to burnout; beneficiaries often forego care due to appeal complexities.
            *   To reduce requests, CMS should require MA Organizations to submit prior authorization request numbers and results (approval/denial) to track and identify abuse of utilization management tools.
            *   Timely decisions are needed (currently 72 hours for expedited, 7 days for standard). These standards still burden providers and can jeopardize patient access.
            *   CMS should consider faster response times: 24 hours for urgent items/services and 48 hours for non-urgent care.
        *   **Withdraw Prior Authorization Requirement for Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) Services**
            *   CMS should withdraw regulations establishing prior authorization for OPPS services due to tenuous statutory authority and clinical/access repercussions.
            *   This marked the first time CMS required prior authorization for hospital outpatient department services in Medicare fee-for-service (beginning 2020, now 8 categories).
            *   Prior authorization causes delays, administrative burden, and increased costs for providers and patients.
            *   The Medicare statute explicitly allows prior authorization for durable medical equipment but has no such reference for OPPS.
        *   **Ensure Alignment in Care Management Services and Remote Mental Health Services by Allowing Hospital Staff to Provide Care Management Services Remotely**
            *   OPPS regulations allow mental health services provided to beneficiaries at home to be excepted from the "incident to" requirement for in-hospital presence.
            *   However, CMS currently requires hospital staff providing care management services to be physically present in the hospital, even when the patient is not.
            *   CMS has developed codes and payments for chronic care management services under OPPS general supervision (physician not immediately available).
            *   To ensure parity with remote mental health services, CMS should revise 42 CFR § 410.27(a)(1)(iii) to explicitly allow care management services when the patient is not physically present in the hospital.
        *   **Expand Medicare Coverage of Telehealth and Communication Technology-based Services by Removing Outdated Restrictions**
            *   Starting October 1, 2025, CMS will reapply geographic and site-of-service limitations on Medicare telehealth unless Congress acts.
            *   The AAMC supports permanently adopting COVID-19 waivers and regulatory changes that expanded telehealth access.
            *   **Specific recommendations:**
                *   Remove geographic site restrictions on telehealth.
                *   Remove originating site restrictions to enable patients to receive telehealth at home.
                *   Remove in-person visit requirements for behavioral health telehealth.
            *   CMS should also permanently allow practitioners to use their enrolled practice location instead of their home address when providing telehealth from home (currently through CY 2025).
            *   Requiring home addresses discourages telehealth from home, limits access, and raises privacy/safety concerns for practitioners.
        *   **Permanently Allow Direct Supervision Through Virtual Supervision**
            *   The AAMC strongly supports CMS defining direct supervision to permit the presence and "immediate availability" of the supervising practitioner via audio-video technology permanently.
            *   This would expand healthcare access and reduce infectious disease exposure risk.
            *   Members found virtual supervision safe, effective, and beneficial for access.
        *   **Allow Virtual Supervision of Residents for Both Telehealth and In-person Services**
            *   The AAMC strongly supports revising regulations to permanently allow virtual supervision of residents for both in-person and telehealth services in all residency training locations where safe and effective.
            *   At a minimum, allow virtual supervision in underserved areas and non-metropolitan statistical areas.
            *   This is safe, effective, expands access, and promotes training opportunities.
        *   **Address Barriers to Uptake & of Interprofessional Consults**
            *   CMS finalized payment for six CPT® codes for interprofessional consultations in 2019, found to be an effective way to improve access (provider-to-provider modalities, peer-mentored care).
            *   Patients benefit from timely specialist guidance, and payers benefit from less costly service compared to new patient visits.
            *   CMS requires coinsurance for CPT® codes 99451 and 99452. While acknowledging CMS's limited authority to waive coinsurance, this requirement creates barriers.
            *   Patients are responsible for two coinsurance payments for a single consultation, causing confusion, especially as they may not know the consulting provider.
            *   Guidance for CPT® code 99452 clarifies it covers 16-30 minutes of the treating physician/QHP preparing referral/communicating with consultant.
            *   This guidance should be changed to include all activities associated with the interprofessional exchange, including follow-through on recommendations, to expand use and ensure value.
        *   **Work with Model Participants to Improve the Mandatory Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM)**
            *   TEAM is a mandatory model requiring over 700 acute care hospitals to assume financial responsibility for post-procedural care through bundled payments for five surgical episodes, even if implementation is not feasible.
            *   It targets hospitals with low experience in voluntary episodic payment models, risking financial destabilization and threatening community access to care.
            *   CMS should work with participants to improve model design and mitigate risk.
            *   **Recommendations include:**
                *   Revising the pricing methodology.
                *   Implementing a consistent, well-tested set of quality metrics for the model's duration.
                *   Amending the primary care referral requirement to reduce hospital burden.
            *   **Specific to pricing methodology:** Ensure adequate risk adjustment for elective vs. non-elective procedures, increase lookback period for hierarchical condition categories, establish low-volume threshold with no downside risk, and use the Community Deprivation Index (in addition to dual-eligibility) for beneficiary economic risk adjustment.
        *   **Modify Stark Law and Anti-kickback Statute Regulations that Restrict Hospital and Health System Activity that is Beneficial to Patients and Communities**
            *   The Stark Law and Anti-kickback Statute impede arrangements that improve patient care delivery, historically impeding value-based arrangements.
            *   While steps were taken during the "Regulatory Sprint to Coordinated Care," challenges remain for beneficial arrangements by hospitals and health systems.
            *   CMS should consider additional stakeholder feedback on regulatory revisions to remove or mitigate these obstacles.
*   **Reducing Biomedical Research Burden**
    *   Efforts to reduce administrative burden on biomedical research are critical for preserving U.S. science productivity, efficiency, and global leadership.
    *   **Harmonize Federal Conflict of Interest Disclosure Requirements Across Agencies**
        *   In accordance with the 21st Century Cures Act, OMB (with HHS and relevant agencies, in consultation with the regulated community) should identify and adopt common elements for financial conflict of interest (FCOI) disclosure and evaluation.
        *   A harmonized approach would maintain research integrity while reducing burden and improving regulatory efficiency.
        *   Researchers and institutions face multiple, overlapping FCOI requirements across federal agencies (FDA, NIH, CMS, NSF) that differ in definitions, disclosure thresholds, and reporting timelines.
        *   This variation imposes significant financial/administrative burden, diminishing productivity and return on federal investment.
        *   HHS should convene a cross-agency working group to explore a unified FCOI framework (shared definitions, reporting thresholds, interoperable disclosure timelines).
        *   A streamlined framework would minimize institutional burden and maximize consistency/transparency in federally supported research.
    *   **Establish a Research Policy Board to Improve Regulatory Efficiency**
        *   Consistent with the 21st Century Cures Act and National Academies recommendations, HHS should establish a permanent research policy board.
        *   This board would serve as a formal mechanism for federal agencies and the regulated community to coordinate regulatory policy, reduce administrative burden, and promote transparency/consistency in oversight.
        *   The current fragmented, complex, and inconsistent regulatory landscape creates significant compliance challenges, leading to overlapping/duplicative requirements that reduce productivity.
        *   Despite authorization in the 21st Century Cures Act, this board has not been implemented.
        *   The AAMC has repeatedly supported this, emphasizing it would be a powerful tool for transparency and burden reduction, providing a trusted forum for engagement.
        *   HHS should prioritize establishing this board with other federal agencies to advance regulatory coherence and reduce redundancy.
    *   **Clarify and Align FDA Advisory Committee Conflict Standards to Improve Transparency and Efficiency**
        *   The FDA should issue clear, final guidance clarifying distinctions between statutory COI (18 U.S.C. § 208(b)) and "appearance issues" (5 C.F.R. § 2635.502).
        *   FDA should align its internal procedures for evaluating both and streamline the review process.
        *   Clear, consistent guidance would improve transparency of advisory committee determinations and reduce confusion for nominees (e.g., from academic medical community).
        *   Currently, FDA uses two separate legal frameworks (statutory COI, government-wide ethical conduct regulation) with final guidance only for the former and draft guidance for the latter.
        *   This lack of clarity leads to confusion and inconsistencies in disclosure/eligibility, as these distinctions are not common in other federal COI regulations.
        *   Finalizing and consolidating guidance on COI determinations would greatly improve understanding of expectations, rationale for eligibility, and increase participation from qualified experts.
    *   **Harmonize FDA’s Single IRB Requirement with the HHS Common Rule and NIH Single IRB Policy**
        *   FDA should align its single institutional review board (sIRB) requirement for cooperative research (21 C.F.R. Part 56) with federal sIRB requirements under the revised Common Rule (45 C.F.R. §46.114) and the NIH Single IRB policy.
        *   A minimum two-year implementation period is recommended to evaluate operational impact (e.g., need for additional guidance, exceptions, flexibilities).
        *   While appreciating FDA's efforts toward harmonization, many institutions face significant operational/logistical challenges with existing sIRB mandates, often experiencing administrative burden without measurable improvements in participant protection.
        *   FDA should work with HHS and the regulated community to finalize the cooperative research proposed rule in a way that promotes shared best practices, coordinated oversight, and consistent guidance.
*   The AAMC appreciates the opportunity to submit these recommendations and looks forward to continued engagement to reduce regulatory burden on the academic medical community and improve health for all Americans.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The AAMC urges comprehensive regulatory reform to reduce administrative burden, streamline redundant requirements, and enhance patient access and research efficiency across healthcare delivery and biomedical research.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** AAMC (Association of American Medical Colleges)
- **Type:** Advocacy Group
- **Role/Expertise:** Represents 160 U.S. medical schools, 12 Canadian medical schools, nearly 500 academic health systems and teaching hospitals, over 70 academic societies, and millions of individuals (faculty, students, residents, researchers) involved in medical education, healthcare delivery, biomedical research, and community collaborations.
- **Geographic Scope:** National with international affiliations (U.S. medical schools and academic health systems, with Canadian and global academic health center members).
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly represents the academic medical community, including medical schools, teaching hospitals, and researchers, who are significantly impacted by federal regulations that impose administrative burdens, divert resources from patient care and research, and hinder innovation and access to care.
structuredSections.corePosition: The AAMC advocates for substantial regulatory reform within the healthcare system and biomedical research enterprise. We believe current regulations create excessive administrative burden, impede patient access to care, stifle innovation, and reduce the efficiency of federally funded research, necessitating a deliberate, transparent, and evidence-based approach to review and eliminate duplicative or outdated requirements while preserving regulatory intent.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- **General Regulatory Reform:**
    - Harmonize regulations across federal agencies and adopt a coordinated approach.
    - Implement an inter-agency framework for ongoing retrospective regulatory review guided by defined criteria.
    - Adhere to Administrative Procedure Act’s notice and comment requirements for all regulatory changes.
- **Reducing Health Care Delivery Burden:**
    - Remove the mandatory Respiratory Illness Reporting Requirement from Conditions of Participation; instead, invest in infrastructure for voluntary data sharing.
    - Re-evaluate new Obstetrical Service Standards Conditions of Participation and other maternal health CoP changes to ensure feasibility without undue burden.
    - Eliminate duplicative "look back" validation surveys of accrediting organizations and permanently adopt concurrent validation surveys.
    - Withdraw the proposed HIPAA Security Rule to strengthen cybersecurity and instead collaborate with stakeholders on requirements.
    - Reform Hospital Quality Performance and Reporting Programs by removing chart-abstracted and structural measures, focusing on outcomes measurement.
    - Remove duplicative measurement across hospital quality performance programs, specifically the Safety Domain from the Hospital Value-Based Purchasing (VBP) program.
    - Reform the Quality Payment Program (QPP) by:
        - Making MIPS less administratively burdensome and clinically relevant.
        - Replacing its budget-neutral design with payment adjustments tied to the Medicare Economic Index.
        - Retaining MVP reporting as a voluntary option and traditional MIPS, while developing comprehensive MVP measures.
        - Adjusting all MIPS cost measures for clinical complexity and economic risk factors.
        - Permitting Promoting Interoperability (PI) reporting through yes/no attestations.
    - Reform and reduce reporting burdens for Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) in the Medicare Shared Savings Program (SSP) by:
        - Modifying quality measurement policies to support ACO participation and reduce burden (e.g., providing ramp-up time for eCQMs, reversing QPP PI data requirement).
        - Delaying the sunsetting of Web Interface and MIPS CQM reporting options until at least 2028.
        - Expanding the significant, anomalous, and highly suspect billing activity policy to allow ACOs to report suspected fraudulent Medicare billing.
    - Reconsider Price Transparency Rules to avoid duplication, reduce burden, and ensure patients receive meaningful information by streamlining existing policies.
    - Eliminate the No Surprises Act requirement that the convening provider obtain information about charges from unaffiliated providers for Good Faith Estimates; instead, place responsibility for combining GFEs into an Advanced EOB with insurers.
    - Withdraw the Information Blocking Disincentives Rule to support educational efforts and ensure fair investigative and appeal processes.
    - Ensure Prior Authorization requirements do not limit patient access by streamlining processes and coverage criteria, and ensure timely implementation and enforcement of new rules.
    - Prohibit restrictive uses of prior authorization by Medicare Advantage plans that depart from Traditional Medicare fee-for-service, and require MA organizations to submit prior authorization request and result data to CMS.
    - Withdraw the Prior Authorization Requirement for Hospital Outpatient Prospective Payment System (OPPS) Services due to tenuous statutory authority and negative impacts.
    - Ensure alignment in care management and remote mental health services by allowing hospital staff to provide care management services remotely.
    - Expand Medicare coverage of telehealth and communication technology-based services by permanently removing outdated geographic limitations, originating site restrictions, and in-person visit requirements for behavioral health.
    - Permanently allow direct supervision through virtual supervision.
    - Allow virtual supervision of residents for both in-person and telehealth services in all residency training locations permanently, especially in underserved areas.
    - Address barriers to uptake of interprofessional consults by reconsidering coinsurance requirements and clarifying CPT® code 99452 guidance to include all associated activities.
    - Work with model participants to improve the mandatory Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM) design to mitigate financial risk, revise pricing methodology (e.g., adequate risk adjustment, increased lookback period, low-volume threshold, economic risk adjustment), implement consistent quality metrics, and amend primary care referral requirements.
    - Modify Stark Law and Anti-kickback Statute regulations to remove obstacles to beneficial arrangements that improve care delivery.
- **Reducing Biomedical Research Burden:**
    - Harmonize federal Conflict of Interest (FCOI) disclosure requirements across agencies by adopting common elements and convening a cross-agency working group.
    - Establish a permanent Research Policy Board to coordinate regulatory policy, reduce administrative burden, and promote transparency and consistency in oversight.
    - Clarify and align FDA Advisory Committee conflict standards by issuing clear, final guidance distinguishing statutory COI from "appearance issues" and streamlining review processes.
    - Harmonize FDA’s Single IRB requirement with the HHS Common Rule and NIH Single IRB Policy, allowing a minimum two-year implementation period to evaluate operational impact.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- The increasing amount of administrative responsibility on healthcare providers is unsustainable, diverting time and focus from patient care and leading to provider burnout.
- A lack of rigorous data quantifies regulatory burden and costs to researchers, leading to inefficient and uncoordinated regulatory approaches across federal agencies.
- The use of Conditions of Participation (CoPs) to compel hospitals to share data (e.g., respiratory illness reporting) or drive maternal health improvements is inconsistent with the intent of CoPs and may lead to hospitals eliminating services to avoid penalties.
- Duplicative "look back" validation surveys of accrediting organizations result in rework and disruption for hospitals instead of effectively assessing AO performance.
- The proposed HIPAA Security Rule approach was misguided, lacked consensus, and grossly underestimated implementation costs, potentially creating costly disruptions.
- Current hospital quality measurement programs include chart-abstracted and structural measures that impose considerable clerical burden, diverting resources from clinical care and meaningful quality improvements.
- Duplicative quality measurement across performance programs (e.g., Safety Domain in Hospital VBP and HACRP) leads to mixed signals on performance and unnecessary provider burden.
- The budget-neutral design of MIPS under the QPP is problematic, as rewards cannot exceed penalties, and the program is too costly and administratively burdensome, diverting time from patient care.
- Current ACO SSP reporting requirements are burdensome and may hinder continued participation in the largest value-based care model.
- The administration's current approach to price transparency is overly burdensome and costly, does not enable patients to understand actual out-of-pocket costs, and has resulted in widespread confusion.
    - Machine-readable files are too large and complex for patients to navigate effectively, and CMS itself acknowledges they are not consumer-friendly.
- The requirement for "convening providers" to obtain Good Faith Estimate information from unaffiliated providers under the No Surprises Act is difficult and costly to operationalize, involving new (often manual) workflows and costly technology updates.
- The finalized information blocking disincentives rule is overly punitive, has significant financial impacts, and disparate effects across provider types, potentially negatively affecting care delivery and reinvestment in value-based care.
- Prior authorization requirements by various insurance plans impede patients' access to timely care due to varying clinical criteria, rules, and processes, causing significant administrative burden.
    - Restrictive uses of prior authorization by Medicare Advantage plans that deviate from traditional Medicare coverage criteria hinder efficient care and contribute to provider burnout.
    - Denial rates for MA prior authorizations are high (e.g., 82% of appealed denials were overturned in 2021), and the burden to respond falls on providers.
    - Current prior authorization decision timelines (72 hours expedited, 7 days standard) still create barriers to urgent care.
- CMS's prior authorization requirement for Hospital OPPS services lacks explicit statutory authority and causes delays, administrative burden, and increased costs.
- CMS regulations requiring hospital staff to be present in the hospital for care management services, even when the patient is not, create an inconsistency with remote mental health services and limit service delivery.
- Outdated statutory restrictions on Medicare telehealth services will limit patient access starting October 1, 2025, if not permanently waived.
    - Requiring practitioners to report home addresses for telehealth enrollment raises privacy and safety concerns and may discourage providing services from home.
- The current structure of interprofessional consultation CPT codes and associated coinsurance requirements creates confusion for patients and acts as a barrier to providing these valuable services.
- The mandatory Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM) poses a significant financial risk to hospitals, particularly those with limited experience in episodic payment models, potentially destabilizing them and threatening community access to care.
- Stark Law and Anti-kickback Statute regulations continue to impede beneficial arrangements that could improve care delivery for patients and communities.
- The current regulatory landscape for biomedical research is fragmented, complex, and often inconsistent across agencies, leading to significant compliance challenges, overlapping/duplicative requirements, reduced productivity, and diluted effectiveness of the U.S. research enterprise.
    - Federal conflict of interest disclosure requirements across agencies differ in definitions, thresholds, and timelines, imposing significant administrative burden on institutions and researchers.
    - The authorized Research Policy Board has not been implemented, leaving a critical gap in cross-agency regulatory coordination.
    - Lack of clear and consistent FDA guidance on advisory committee conflict standards (statutory vs. "appearance issues") leads to confusion and inconsistencies, potentially limiting participation from qualified experts.
    - Operational and logistical challenges remain in implementing existing single IRB mandates without measurable improvements in research participant protections.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The AAMC Conflicts of Interest Metrics Project is cited as a model for systematically assessing the operational impact of federal regulatory requirements, demonstrating a data-driven approach to burden evaluation.
- The stark observation that "the increasing amount of administrative responsibility forced upon health care providers is unsustainable, diverts time and focus away from patient care and leads to provider burnout."
- AAMC members report significant difficulty and cost in operationalizing the No Surprises Act's requirement for convening providers to obtain Good Faith Estimate information from unaffiliated providers, often necessitating new, manual workflows and costly technology updates.
- The surprising statistic that "Just 11 percent of prior authorization denials were appealed, but of those a whopping 82 percent resulted in the initial prior authorization denial being fully or partially overturned," highlighting a significant flaw in the prior authorization system and immense burden on providers.
- The insight that hospital-provided machine-readable files for price transparency are so large and complex that patients cannot effectively use them, a point reinforced by CMS's own acknowledgment that "MRF formats are not consumer friendly."
- The concern that an "overly punitive approach" to information blocking disincentives could "critically impact care delivery and reinvestment in value-based health care for health systems," ultimately harming patients.
- The direct experience of AAMC members finding "virtual supervision of clinical staff to be safe and effective, and improved access to care."
- The observation that interprofessional consultations are "an effective way to improve access to care" and are "less costly" than new patient visits, but face barriers due to outdated billing guidance and confusing coinsurance requirements.
- The specific risk identified for the mandatory Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM): it particularly targets hospitals with low levels of existing experience with voluntary bundled payment models, increasing the risk of financial destabilization and threatening community access to care.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "The increasing amount of administrative responsibility forced upon health care providers is unsustainable, diverts time and focus away from patient care and leads to provider burnout."
- "Ultimately, for patients the information that is most important and useful to them is knowing their financial obligation or out of pocket costs for the services they receive, which will be based on their insurance coverage."
- "Just 11 percent of prior authorization denials were appealed, but of those a whopping 82 percent resulted in the initial prior authorization denial being fully or partially overturned."
- "Medically necessary care should not be denied because a physician and/or patient cannot jump through complicated, opaque hoops."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The core purpose of government is to protect our religious freedoms, which include our inalienable human rights and civil liberties.
*   In an era of rapid advancements in healthcare technology, such as implantable devices and bioinformatics, we rely on the government to implement essential regulations.
*   These regulations must actively impede technological innovation, infrastructure development, and research and development in healthcare that violate individual privacy and autonomy without explicit, informed consent.
*   To this end, I propose the following legislation, titled Subdermal Warrants Opt-In Academic, Medical, and Predictive Surveillance (SWOAMPS), to establish a robust framework for protecting individuals from unauthorized tracking and data exploitation via sub-dermal implants:
    *   Proposal for Legislation to Protect Individuals from Unwanted Tracking via Sub-Dermal Implants
        *   Title: Subdermal Warrants Opt-In Academic, Medical, and Predictive Surveillance (SWOAMPS)
        *   Preamble: Given the increasing prevalence of sub-dermal medical and GPS implants, there is an urgent need to safeguard individual privacy and autonomy.
        *   This proposal aims to establish a legal framework that ensures these devices cannot be used for unauthorized tracking or data exploitation without explicit consent.
        *   Legislative Proposal:
            *   1. Definition of Terms:
                *   Sub-Dermal Implants: Any device implanted under the skin, including but not limited to medical sensors, GPS trackers, or RFID chips.
                *   Bioinformatics Projects: Research or commercial activities involving the collection, analysis, or use of biological data from such implants.
                *   Tracking: The use of technology to monitor or locate an individual via an implant.
            *   2. Right to Privacy:
                *   Invisibility from Tracking: Individuals with sub-dermal implants shall have the legal right to remain invisible to all forms of tracking unless they opt-in to such monitoring.
                *   Data Control: Any data collected from these implants shall be under the full control of the individual, with stringent regulations on how and when this data can be accessed by external entities.
            *   3. Consent Mechanism:
                *   Opt-In System: All uses of data from sub-dermal implants for tracking, advertising, or bioinformatics projects must require explicit, informed, and periodic consent from the individual.
                *   Revocation of Consent: Individuals can revoke consent at any time, and all tracking and data use must cease immediately upon such revocation.
            *   4. Exceptions:
                *   Criminals: The rights provided by this act may be suspended for individuals legally convicted of crimes where judicial oversight determines tracking is necessary for public safety or law enforcement purposes.
                    *   Such exceptions must be:
                        *   Court-ordered with clear justification.
                        *   Time-limited with regular review.
                        *   Subject to stringent privacy protections even under surveillance.
            *   5. Education and Public Awareness:
                *   Mandatory Education: This legislation will be part of the curriculum in elementary schools to educate young citizens on the rights regarding personal data and privacy.
                *   Public Announcements: There will be a national campaign to inform the public about:
                    *   The right to privacy concerning implants.
                    *   The implications to health, privacy, and safety.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An individual proposes comprehensive federal legislation (SWOAMPS) to ensure explicit opt-in consent and control over personal data and tracking from sub-dermal implants, with provisions for public education and limited exceptions for convicted criminals.
