To achieve this, I propose the Subdermal Warrants Opt-In Academic, Medical, and Predictive Surveillance (SWOAMPS) legislation to establish a robust framework for protecting individuals from unauthorized tracking and data exploitation via sub-dermal implants.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Establish the Subdermal Warrants Opt-In Academic, Medical, and Predictive Surveillance (SWOAMPS) legislation.
- Define key terms: sub-dermal implants (medical sensors, GPS, RFID), bioinformatics projects, and tracking.
- Guarantee the right to privacy for individuals with sub-dermal implants:
  - Individuals shall have the legal right to remain invisible to all forms of tracking unless they opt-in.
  - Data collected from implants shall be under the full control of the individual, with stringent regulations on access by external entities.
- Implement an explicit, informed, and periodic opt-in consent system for all uses of data from sub-dermal implants (tracking, advertising, bioinformatics projects).
- Allow individuals to revoke consent at any time, immediately ceasing all tracking and data use upon revocation.
- Permit exceptions for legally convicted criminals only when judicial oversight determines tracking is necessary for public safety or law enforcement purposes, under strict conditions:
  - Court-ordered with clear justification.
  - Time-limited with regular review.
  - Subject to stringent privacy protections even under surveillance.
- Mandate education on personal data rights and privacy as part of the elementary school curriculum.
- Launch a national public awareness campaign to inform the public about the right to privacy concerning implants and their health, privacy, and safety implications.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- Unauthorized tracking and data exploitation via sub-dermal implants (including medical sensors, GPS trackers, or RFID chips).
- The violation of individual privacy and autonomy by rapidly advancing healthcare technology and bioinformatics without explicit, informed consent.
- The potential for sub-dermal devices to be used for surveillance, advertising, or data collection without individual control.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   **Definition of Federal Interest and Major Renovation (§ 1305.2) Pages 80869**
    *   We prioritize the health and safety of children attending our Head Start facilities.
    *   To ensure child health and safety, we must have the ability to quickly and efficiently address facility repairs and renovations.
    *   Unfortunately, OHS’s misinterpretation of the Davis Bacon Act of 1931, applying it to “repairs” of Head Start facilities, has:
        *   Delayed needed repairs.
        *   Increased the cost of those repairs.
        *   In some circumstances, delayed classrooms from being open.
    *   We have educated lawyers and senior policy officials on this incorrect interpretation, but OHS has made no effort to correct it.
    *   The cumbersome, expensive, and time-consuming process for major renovations also raises safety concerns.
    *   Currently, prior to major renovations, Head Start Agencies must complete and have approved a facility application under Part 1303, Subpart E of the HSPPS.
    *   These facility applications require, among other things:
        *   Hiring independent certified appraisers.
        *   Hiring environmental consultants to complete certain due diligence activities before the Head Start Agency can commence a “major renovation.”
    *   The time and cost of these activities is enormous.
    *   Moreover, the spike in construction costs experienced during the COVID-19 pandemic (which has not relented) means that more renovations are now considered “major” because of the $250,000 threshold.
    *   This threshold has been in place since 2016.
    *   In today’s construction dollars, the 2016 threshold is, based upon our experience of completing new construction during the COVID-19 pandemic, much closer to $500,000 than $250,000.
*   **Workforce Supports: Staff Wages (§ 1302.90(e)), Pages 80822 to 80832**
    *   We welcome the proposed standard, § 1302.90(e)(2)(i), requiring programs to make progress towards pay parity for Head Start and Early Head Start teachers with kindergarten through 3rd grade teachers.
    *   This aligns with the Power to the Profession Task Force, a national collaboration established to define and elevate the early childhood education profession to receive equitable compensation.
    *   The initiative led to the Unifying Framework for the Early Childhood Education Profession document, which acknowledges early childhood educators are professionally prepared, so they must be professionally compensated.
    *   Specifically, the Unifying Framework recommends compensation:
        *   To be comparable for those with similar qualifications, experience, and job responsibilities, regardless of whether they work in a community-based center, elementary school, or family-based childcare home.
        *   To include an adequate benefits package, increase commensurate with increased preparation and competency, and not be differentiated because of the ages of children served.
        *   To be based upon public school salaries serving as the minimum benchmark.
    *   It is time for early childhood educators to be well prepared and compensated in accordance with the complex and demanding work they perform.
    *   However, the regulatory language implementing the changes to § 1302.90(e) is far too prescriptive and will be very difficult, if not impossible, to implement.
    *   When Head Start Agencies struggle to implement the too prescriptive regulatory language, those Agencies will likely be embroiled in costly litigation with their employees challenging whether the Agency has met its pay obligations under § 1302.90(e).
    *   One example of the many challenges raised for us is the requirement that “[b]y August 1, 2031, a program must demonstrate it has made progress to parity by ensuring that each Head Start teacher receive an annual salary that is at least comparable to the annual salary paid to preschool teachers in public school setting in the program’s local school district[.] (emphasis added).
    *   We directly employ Head Start teachers in thirty-seven (37) Head Start centers across eight different states.
    *   We fund two delegate agencies that employ Head Start teachers in six Head Start centers across two states.
    *   There is no “local school district” that we or our delegate agencies can use as a point of comparison for setting the salary scale for Head Start teachers across our vast operational footprint.
    *   In addition, in Oklahoma, local school districts underpay their public-school teachers.
    *   As a result, the mandate to pay Head Start teachers at the level of public-school teachers may, in some instances, have the opposite effect of what is desired.
*   **Workforce Supports: Staff Benefits (§ 1302.90(f)), Pages 80832 to 80837**
    *   Here again, the regulatory language implementing the changes to § 1302.90(e) is far too prescriptive.
    *   Some of the most significant challenges raised by the standard include the following:
        *   Requiring paid leave to encompass “sick leave,” and “vacation” or “personal time,” which does not account for the fact that Head Start Agencies use a variety of terms to describe paid time off benefits.
        *   Requiring family leave to be “paid,” unless the intent of OHS is to have employees substitute any accrued paid leave for an unpaid family leave of absence.
        *   The expanded paid leave rules will impact the ability of Head Start Agencies to staff classrooms.
*   **Mental Health Services (Subpart D, Subpart H, Subpart I), Pages 80840 to Pages Unknown**
    *   The importance of mental health services for families is reflected in the observation of our parent and Policy Council leader.
    *   We previously implemented most of the strategies outlined in the regulation to enhance mental health services for Head Start children, families, and staff.
    *   There are, however, a few new mandates in the regulations that may be impossible for us to implement.
    *   For example, Head Start programs “must have a multidisciplinary team responsible for mental health that . . . [s]ecures mental health consultation services no less than once a month to ensure a mental health consultant is available to partner with staff and families in a timely and effective manner[.]”
    *   We struggle to contract with mental health consultants to provide needed mental health services in our rural service areas.
    *   Requiring the engagement of mental health consultants monthly does not account for the significant barriers that currently exist in rural areas to engage mental health consultants.
*   **Adjustment for Excessive Housing Costs for Eligibility Determinations (§ 1302.12) Pages 80850 to 80851.**
    *   We applaud the acknowledgement in the regulations that the Federal Poverty Guidelines do not accurately reflect poverty in the United States of America.
    *   However, the proposed solution will be, at a minimum, burdensome to implement.
    *   The Policy Council Executive Committee comments: "My thoughts on the new rule that is being proposed, it would just create a lot more work for the eligibility departments across the board. Would it not be easier to raise the low-income guidelines to qualify for the Head Start program?"
    *   According to the 2024 Federal Poverty Guidelines, a family of three with two parents working are not living in poverty if each parent makes $6.46 per hour (based upon 2,000 hours of paid employment for each parent in a year).
    *   This family of three exceeds 130 percent of the Federal Poverty Guideline if each parent makes $8.40 per hour.
    *   Under no circumstances, anywhere in the contiguous 48 states, are these wage levels an accurate assessment of a threshold when a family of three is living in poverty.
*   **Transportation & Other Barriers to Enrollment and Attendance (§ 1302.14 and 1302.16) Pages 80851 to 80852**
    *   The regulations acknowledge the lack of transportation services serve as a significant barrier to children’s enrollment and attendance in Head Start programs.
    *   However, OHS has failed to offer any practical solutions to this dilemma.
    *   In 2016, parents requested the Office of Head Start to provide waivers of the requirement for transportation to and from Head Start facilities to only be provided in school buses or allowable alternative vehicles.
    *   This request was made to enhance child safety – our parents knew their children are always safer in our Head Start program than when they were excluded from our Head Start program and left with babysitters or kincare because of transportation barriers.
    *   Our parents' request to OHS, sadly, fell on deaf ears.
    *   We again request the Office of Head Start permit waivers of the requirement that transportation to and from Head Start facilities only occur in school buses or allowable alternate vehicles.
    *   We have implemented a Family Childcare Home (FCCH) model of services to serve agricultural worker families in small communities, which do not have concentrations of families to support center-based services.
    *   However, we cannot feasibly purchase buses or alternate allowable vehicles to transport the small number of children who require transportation to and from each of those Family Childcare Home programs.
    *   The opportunity for a transportation waiver is particularly appropriate here because we serve some of the hardest to serve families of any Head Start program in the country.
    *   We need the flexibility to serve families through Family Childcare Home providers and, to do that, we need to be able to use standard eight-passenger vans to transport children to and from the FCCH provider.
    *   Caring for Our Children Policy 9.2.5 and 9.2.5.2 acknowledge vehicle suitability for transportation in FCCH programs.
    *   This highlights an incongruity between HSPPS regulations and actual safety risks associated with certain vehicles with larger passenger capacity.
    *   CFOC recommends specific mitigation measures for FCCH homes, emphasizing first aid provisions, pickup/drop-off protocols, maintenance procedures, communication devices, and travel time limitations for children.
    *   Some states also regulate transportation for FCCH providers due to frequency of use.
    *   North Carolina's Administrative code 10A NCAC 09.1723, for example, governs transportation in FCCH programs, offering safety-oriented policies.
    *   It mandates safe loading/unloading areas, ensures vehicles are equipped for hazardous weather conditions, and necessitates safety gear such as fire extinguishers and communication devices in the transporting vehicle.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: ECMHSP, a national Head Start provider, urges AHRQ to revise overly prescriptive regulations on facility renovations, staff compensation and benefits, mental health services, poverty eligibility, and transportation waivers, arguing they create impractical burdens, increase costs, delay services, and hinder effective support for vulnerable families.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** ECMHSP
- **Type:** Organization
- **Role/Expertise:** Provider of Head Start and Early Head Start services, particularly to agricultural worker families. Operates 37 centers across 8 states and funds 2 delegate agencies in 2 states.
- **Geographic Scope:** National (operates in 8 states, funds in 2 states)
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly affected by federal regulations governing Head Start programs, including facility maintenance, staff employment, and service delivery, impacting their ability to provide effective and timely care to children and families.
structuredSections.corePosition: We believe that current and proposed regulations from the Office of Head Start are often too prescriptive, failing to account for real-world operational challenges such as rising costs, diverse geographic needs, and existing workforce limitations. These prescriptive mandates lead to increased costs, delays in crucial services, and hinder our ability to flexibly and effectively serve the vulnerable children and families in our programs.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
*   **For facility renovations:**
    *   Raise the threshold for a “major” renovation from $250,000 to $500,000 to reflect current construction costs.
*   **For staff wages:**
    *   Revise § 1302.90(e) to remove the mandate concerning staff wages being tied to “the program’s local school district.”
    *   Consider expressing requirements regarding staff wages as aspirational goals for Head Start agencies to attain over time.
    *   Publish these aspirational goals, and the strategies to achieve them, in an Information Memorandum.
*   **For staff benefits:**
    *   Revise § 1302.90(f) to remove mandates concerning staff benefits.
    *   Express requirements regarding benefits as aspirational goals for Head Start Agencies to attain over time.
    *   Publish these aspirational goals, and the strategies to achieve them, in an Information Memorandum.
*   **For mental health services:**
    *   Consider revising 1302.45(a)(3) to express monthly mental health consultations as an aspirational goal, rather than a strict mandate.
*   **For eligibility determinations:**
    *   Adjust the low-income guidelines to accurately reflect poverty in the United States of America, rather than implementing burdensome solutions related to housing costs.
*   **For transportation:**
    *   Permit waivers of the requirement that transportation to and from a Head Start facility only occur in a school bus or allowable alternate vehicle.
        *   Such waivers would be particularly appropriate for Head Start Agencies implementing the Family Childcare Home model of services.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
*   **Facility Renovation & Repair Burdens:**
    *   OHS’s misinterpretation of the Davis Bacon Act to apply to "repairs" delays needed repairs, increases costs, and can delay classroom openings.
    *   The "major renovation" process is cumbersome, expensive, and time-consuming, requiring costly independent appraisals and environmental consultants.
    *   The static $250,000 threshold for "major renovation" (unchanged since 2016) is outdated, with current construction costs making more renovations fall under the "major" category, effectively increasing administrative burden.
*   **Staff Wage and Benefit Prescriptiveness:**
    *   The proposed regulatory language for staff wages (§ 1302.90(e)) is too prescriptive, making implementation difficult, potentially impossible, and risking costly litigation for agencies.
    *   Tying teacher salaries to a "local school district" is unfeasible for organizations operating across multiple states and diverse school districts, as there is no single comparable entity.
    *   In some areas (e.g., Oklahoma), public school teachers are underpaid, meaning a parity mandate could have the unintended consequence of depressing Head Start teacher wages.
    *   The prescribed paid leave definitions (e.g., "sick leave," "vacation," "personal time") do not account for the variety of paid time off benefits used by Head Start agencies.
    *   The mandate for "paid" family leave creates challenges, especially regarding how it interacts with existing accrued leave or staffing capabilities.
    *   Expanded paid leave rules will negatively impact the ability of Head Start Agencies to staff classrooms.
*   **Mental Health Service Accessibility in Rural Areas:**
    *   The mandate for monthly mental health consultations via a multidisciplinary team (§ 1302.45(a)(3)) is impossible to implement in rural service areas due to significant barriers in contracting with mental health consultants.
*   **Burdensome Eligibility Determinations:**
    *   The proposed solution for adjusting for excessive housing costs for eligibility determinations (§ 1302.12) is burdensome and creates more work for eligibility departments.
    *   The Federal Poverty Guidelines, even at 130%, do not accurately reflect poverty, as families with two parents working at wages as low as $6.46-$8.40 per hour are considered above poverty, which is unrealistic anywhere in the contiguous 48 states.
*   **Transportation Barriers and Lack of Flexible Solutions:**
    *   OHS acknowledges transportation as a barrier but offers no practical solutions, maintaining restrictive requirements for vehicle types.
    *   The mandate that transportation must only occur in school buses or allowable alternate vehicles prevents the use of more feasible options like standard eight-passenger vans, particularly for the Family Childcare Home model serving dispersed agricultural worker families.
    *   This lack of flexibility prevents Head Start from serving some of the hardest-to-serve families.
    *   There is an incongruity between HSPPS regulations and vehicle suitability acknowledged in other policies (e.g., Caring for Our Children Policy) and state regulations.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
*   OHS's ongoing misinterpretation of the Davis Bacon Act to apply to routine facility "repairs" has led to tangible delays, increased costs, and even prevented classrooms from opening, despite efforts to educate policy officials.
*   The significant spike in construction costs post-COVID-19 has rendered the 2016 "major renovation" threshold of $250,000 obsolete, with real-world experience showing $500,000 is a more accurate reflection of current costs, forcing more projects into a burdensome approval process.
*   The commenter operates across 8 states directly and 2 states through delegates, illustrating the impracticality of using a "local school district" for salary comparisons due to the geographic and structural diversity of their operations.
*   The specific example of Oklahoma where public school teachers are underpaid highlights an unintended negative consequence of the salary parity mandate.
*   The profound difficulty in contracting mental health consultants in rural areas makes the monthly consultation mandate impossible to fulfill.
*   A parent and Policy Council leader's insight on the need for public advocacy and integration of mental health support due to fears of judgment within families.
*   A Policy Council Executive Committee member's direct feedback that the proposed housing cost adjustment rule "would just create a lot more work" and suggesting it would be "easier to raise the low-income guidelines."
*   Parents' 2016 request for transportation waivers, based on the belief that "their children are always safer in our Head Start program than when they were excluded from our Head Start program," underscores the critical need for transportation flexibility as a matter of child safety and access.
*   The implementation of the Family Childcare Home model to serve dispersed agricultural worker families, which necessitates flexible transportation solutions (e.g., 8-passenger vans) that are currently disallowed by regulations.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
*   "Throughout the years mental health has been handled privately or not at all because of fears of being judged, I feel it needs to be advocated publicly and openly. Families would be able to better understand the problems that their children are going through if a mental health support system was integrated into their services being offered to the families if needed by the Head Start programs to better understand mental health and issues from younger ages.”
*   “My thoughts on the new rule that is being proposed, it would just create a lot more work for the eligibility departments across the board. Would it not be easier to raise the low-income guidelines to qualify for the Head Start program?”
*   "Our parents knew their children are always safer in our Head Start program than when they were excluded from our Head Start program and left with babysitters or kincare because of transportation barriers."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I am commenting on the U.S Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
*   The years of pregnancy to age three set the foundation for a baby’s development, learning and relationships.
    *   Babies rely entirely on the adults around them—parents, caregivers, and early childhood professionals—to provide safe, nurturing care.
    *   When babies or their caregivers face reduced support or program quality, babies can end up facing long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences.
    *   When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health.
*   Regulations matter.
    *   HHS, as the leading Federal agency tasked with enhancing the health and well-being of all Americans, plays a critical role in ensuring that babies, families, and the professionals who care for little ones have access to the resources, protections, and supports they need.
    *   In considering changes to regulations, HHS must preserve regulations that:
        *   Keep young children safe and healthy.
        *   Enable the adults in their lives to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
*   For example, regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings are needed to keep babies safe and developmentally on track.
*   Regulations that keep children and those who care for them healthy, like those that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care, must be maintained.
    *   This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe.
*   HHS rules reach far beyond just Medicaid and early learning, with many HHS programs laying the foundation of quality care and critical support that babies need.
*   Any changes to regulations must be:
    *   Transparent.
    *   Grounded in evidence.
    *   Focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
*   Because each regulation is different, HHS must continue to give the public—including families and early childhood professionals like me—ample time and opportunity to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes.
    *   We need a robust public process to make sure that the rules work for babies and those who care for them.
*   To keep America’s babies healthy, HHS must maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services.
*   Please uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
*   I would also like to add that I am a product of Head Start Services.
    *   I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career.
    *   I have a Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma.
    *   I have been a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for the past twenty-three years servicing the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles.
    *   It gives great pleasure to give back to my community.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An experienced early childhood education professional and Head Start alumna urges HHS to maintain and strengthen regulations that ensure the safety, health, and development of young children, advocating for transparent, evidence-based changes and robust public input.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
-   **Name/Organization:** Elizabeth Villanueva
-   **Type:** Individual
-   **Role/Expertise:** Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma; 23 years as a vendor for the state of California Early Start system; former Head Start recipient.
-   **Geographic Scope:** Local (South Central Los Angeles, San Pedro, CA) / State (California)
-   **Stake in Issue:** As an early childhood professional directly involved in providing services to vulnerable children and a beneficiary of early childhood programs, she has a direct interest in regulations that ensure quality care and support for young children and their caregivers.
structuredSections.corePosition: I strongly believe that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) must preserve and uphold regulations that safeguard the health, safety, and development of young children from pregnancy to age three. These foundational years dictate lifelong well-being, and effective regulations, grounded in evidence and developed transparently with public input, are crucial for ensuring access to quality care and services.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   Preserve regulations that keep young children safe and healthy.
-   Preserve regulations that enable adults to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
    -   Specifically, maintain regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings.
    -   Maintain regulations that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care.
-   Ensure any changes to regulations are transparent, grounded in evidence, and focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
-   Provide ample time and opportunity for the public, including families and early childhood professionals, to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes through a robust public process.
-   Maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services for babies.
-   Uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   Reduced support or program quality for babies and caregivers could lead to long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences for children.
-   Regulatory changes that are not transparent, evidence-based, or child-focused could negatively impact the well-being and safety of children, families, and their service providers.
-   Inadequate public involvement in the regulatory process may result in rules that do not effectively serve the needs of babies and their caregivers.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
-   Personal testimony as a "product of Head Start Services," attributing her education and career advantages to the program.
-   Extensive professional experience as a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for 23 years, specifically servicing "the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles."
-   Expresses deep personal satisfaction and commitment to her work, stating "It gives great pleasure to give back to my community."
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
-   "When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health."
-   "This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe."
-   "I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The American Feed Industry Association (AFIA) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments to the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) Notice of Request for Information (RFI) on ideas for deregulation that can reduce regulatory burden on the animal food industry without compromising safety.
    *   AFIA hopes AHRQ and the Food and Drug Administration’s (FDA) Center for Veterinary Medicine (CVM) will review comments in the spirit offered and appreciates the administration’s willingness to consider regulatory reform.
*   **About AFIA:**
    *   Founded in 1909, based in Arlington, Va.
    *   The world’s largest organization exclusively representing the business, legislative, and regulatory interests of the U.S. animal food industry and its suppliers.
    *   Membership comprises over 650 domestic and international companies, representing the total feed industry, including manufacturers of commercial and integrated feed, pet food, ingredient suppliers, pharmaceutical companies, industry support, and equipment manufacturers.
    *   Members manufacture more than 75% of the feed and 70% of the non-whole grain ingredients used in the country.
*   AFIA provides responses to questions 1 and 3 of the RFI to reduce regulatory burdens on the animal food industry.

*   **1. What HHS regulations and/or guidance meet one or more of the following seven criteria identified in E.O. 14219? Should they be modified or repealed? What would be the impact of this change, especially the costs and savings?**
    *   **Regulations that impose significant costs upon private parties that are not outweighed by public benefits.**
    *   **Request: Elimination of Part 11 Requirements for Veterinary Feed Directive and Medicated Feed Records**
        *   Modification of 21 C.F.R. § 558.6 and 21 C.F.R. § 225.
        *   **Cost savings:** Reduction in time spent filing information that does not contribute to public or animal safety.
        *   Removal of requirement to develop record keeping compliant computer systems at an approximate cost of $300,000 per facility to meet requirements for medicated feeds.
        *   In 2016 and 2017, AFIA, joined by the National Grain and Feed Association (NGFA), filed two citizen petitions requesting exemption from Part 11 requirements for records kept under the Veterinary Feed Directive (VFD) and medicated feed current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) regulations.
            *   These petitions are under Docket No. FDA-2016-P-2533.
            *   In 2022, FDA responded, indicating it was initiating rulemaking, but no action has been taken, and this priority has fallen off FDA’s unified agenda.
        *   **Proposed Change:** Amend regulations so that 21 CFR Part 11 electronic records and electronic signatures requirements do not apply to records maintained under two specific animal feed regulations:
            *   Records kept under 21 C.F.R. § 558.6, specifically:
                *   Veterinary Feed Directives (VFDs) issued by veterinarians for animal drugs in medicated feed.
                *   Records required from feed manufacturers and distributors related to medicated feeds containing VFD drugs.
            *   Records kept under 21 C.F.R. § 225 requirements for medicated feeds.
        *   These petitions are based on FDA’s September 2015 action to grant a Part 11 exemption in the final Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA) regulations for human and animal food.
            *   FDA CVM did not grant similar exemptions for VFD records during rulemaking finalized just three months prior (June 2015).
            *   Medicated feed CGMP regulations were adopted in 1976 and modified in 1986, preceding the Part 11 rulemaking process which began in 1992.
        *   **Rationale:**
            *   The animal feed industry seeks a similar exemption for VFD and medicated feed records and swift rulemaking to update outdated Part 11 regulations to reduce onerous requirements.
            *   To AFIA’s knowledge, none of their members (including large corporations) currently have a fully Part 11-compliant computer system.
            *   Costs for developing/maintaining such a system are extremely burdensome: estimated $150,000 per facility in 1997, now approximately $300,000 with inflation.
            *   The feed industry is competitive with low profit margins; these costs would likely be passed to American consumers without discernable public or animal health benefits.
            *   FDA issued guidance in 2003 stating it would "narrowly interpret the scope of Part 11" and use enforcement discretion, indicating the need for updated regulations.
            *   An exemption would also benefit FDA by enabling facilities to provide documents to inspectors more quickly, improving inspection efficiency.
    *   **Request: Elimination of Drug Establishment Registration for Feed Mills**
        *   Elimination of requirements for drug establishment registration and drug listing as set forth in section 510 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act), section 351 of the Public Health Service Act (PHSA), and 21 CFR Part 207.
        *   **Cost savings:** Reduction in time spent filing information that does not contribute to public or animal safety.
        *   FDA has clarified that the annual Drug Establishment Registration (DER) requirement, originally for drug manufacturers, also applies to medicated feed mills manufacturing feed using Category II, Type A medicated articles.
        *   These facilities submit duplicative information for annual DER and Medicated Feed Mill License applications.
        *   **Proposed Change:** Eliminate the DER requirement for feed mills, as it is primarily meant for drug manufacturers.
        *   **Rationale:**
            *   The annual DER requires medicated feed mills to resubmit information FDA already received and approved in medicated feed mill license applications.
            *   FDA never utilizes extra details required in a DER (e.g., plant manager name).
            *   The overly complicated annual reregistration system is a major burden; FDA administrative personnel often tell firms they will finish reregistration after receiving paper records.
            *   Medicated feed mills also have a separate biennial food facility registration requirement (initial under Bioterrorism Act 2002, amended by FSMA 2010).
            *   Requiring many different registrations on different timelines is confusing and should be simplified.
            *   Since the medicated feed mill license requirement began in 1996, the number of licensed mills has dropped from 1,000 to 769.
            *   AFIA is concerned facilities may not have reregistered due to the cumbersome DER process, and members often outsource this effort at considerable expense.
            *   AFIA members report receiving "drug listing" notices around reregistration time, even though drug lists are not required for medicated feed manufacturers, indicating agency or system confusion.
            *   These nonsensical requests waste time for both the agency and industry and add to confusion regarding the requirement’s purpose for feed manufacturers.

*   **3. For more general deregulatory consideration under E.O. 14192, are there additional HHS regulations and/or guidance that: impede efforts to innovate?**
    *   **Request: Streamlined Review of Ingredients for Use in Animal Food**
        *   Modification of the food additive petition (FAP) and the generally recognized as safe (GRAS) notification program.
        *   Remove existing regulatory roadblocks to marketing innovative animal food ingredients.
        *   CVM plays an important role in reviewing and approving animal food ingredients through FAP, GRAS notification, and Animal Food Ingredient Consultation (AFIC) processes.
            *   Food additives are reviewed under 21 CFR 571 and described in 21 CFR 573.
            *   GRAS status can be achieved via scientific procedures or common use before 1958, per FD&C Act sections 201(s) and 409, and FDA regulations 21 CFR 570.3 and 570.30.
        *   AFIA has long supported CVM’s vital role in ingredient reviews for safety and reliability, benefiting industry and customers.
            *   Historically, CVM’s reviews were globally recognized and relied upon by foreign governments.
            *   However, the U.S. ingredient review process has diminished in efficiency and predictability, hindering effectiveness.
        *   It is time for CVM to reduce the complexity of the animal food ingredient review process to achieve faster approvals and spur innovation.
        *   CVM opened a docket in 2024 (Docket No. FDA-2024-N-2979) to hear stakeholder concerns regarding FAP and GRAS notification inefficiencies, which is seen as a positive step.
        *   AFIA urges the administration to allow CVM to complete this review and implement timely changes to improve regulatory functions and enable market innovation.
            *   Addressing these barriers and implementing improvements can restore CVM’s position as a global leader in regulatory efficiency and safety assurance.
            *   It will also allow the U.S. animal food industry to provide innovations that advance animal nutrition and U.S. manufacturing.
        *   AFIA is committed to collaborating with CVM to enhance the effectiveness and efficiency of animal food ingredient review processes.
*   **Conclusion**
    *   AFIA appreciates the opportunity to provide information to reduce unnecessary regulatory burden and drive innovation.
    *   Meaningful regulatory reform would provide tremendous benefit in time and resources to both industry and FDA.
    *   AFIA commends the administration for tackling this initiative and is available for further discussion.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The American Feed Industry Association urges the Department of Health and Human Services to streamline regulations for the animal food industry, specifically by eliminating outdated electronic record-keeping mandates, simplifying redundant drug establishment registrations, and improving the inefficient ingredient review process to reduce costs and foster innovation without compromising safety.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** American Feed Industry Association (AFIA)
- **Type:** Trade Association
- **Role/Expertise:** World’s largest organization representing the business, legislative, and regulatory interests of the U.S. animal food industry and its suppliers; members manufacture over 75% of feed and 70% of non-whole grain ingredients in the country.
- **Geographic Scope:** National (U.S.) and international membership
- **Stake in Issue:** Direct impact on its 650+ member companies who face significant regulatory burdens, costs, and hindrances to innovation due to current HHS/FDA regulations affecting animal feed manufacturing and ingredient approval.
structuredSections.corePosition: The American Feed Industry Association advocates for significant regulatory reform within the animal food industry, arguing that current mandates from the FDA, particularly those related to electronic record-keeping and drug establishment registration, are outdated, duplicative, and impose substantial, uncompensated costs on businesses without providing public or animal health benefits. We believe that streamlining these regulations and improving the efficiency of ingredient approval processes are critical to reducing industry burden, fostering innovation, and maintaining the U.S. as a global leader in animal nutrition.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Eliminate Part 11 requirements for Veterinary Feed Directive (VFD) and medicated feed records (21 C.F.R. § 558.6 and 21 C.F.R. § 225).
  - Amend regulations so Part 11 electronic records and electronic signatures do not apply to these specific records.
  - This would align with FDA's 2015 exemption for human and animal food under FSMA.
- Eliminate Drug Establishment Registration (DER) requirements for medicated feed mills.
  - Remove requirements set forth in section 510 of the FD&C Act, section 351 of the PHSA, and 21 CFR Part 207.
  - This would eliminate duplicative and unnecessary annual submissions, as feed mills already undergo medicated feed mill license applications and biennial food facility registrations.
- Streamline the review of ingredients for use in animal food.
  - Modify the food additive petition (FAP) and generally recognized as safe (GRAS) notification programs.
  - Reduce the complexity of the animal food ingredient review process to achieve faster approvals and spur innovation.
  - Urge CVM to complete its ongoing review of pre-market animal food ingredient review programs (Docket No. FDA-2024-N-2979) and implement timely changes.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Burdensome and Costly Part 11 Requirements for Electronic Records:**
  - Members generally lack fully Part 11-compliant computer systems.
  - Developing and maintaining such systems is extremely burdensome, costing approximately $300,000 per facility today (inflation-adjusted).
  - These costs are likely passed to consumers, without discernable public or animal health benefits.
  - Regulations are outdated, originating before Part 11, and FDA's own 2003 guidance suggests a narrow interpretation and enforcement discretion.
- **Duplicative and Complicated Drug Establishment Registration (DER) for Feed Mills:**
  - Requires annual resubmission of information already provided and approved in medicated feed mill license applications.
  - FDA reportedly does not utilize the extra details required in DERs.
  - The annual reregistration system is overly complicated, often requiring firms to provide paper records for FDA personnel to complete.
  - Causes confusion due to multiple, different registration timelines (DER, food facility registration).
  - Contributed to a significant drop in licensed medicated feed mills (from 1,000 to 769 since 1996), potentially due to the cumbersome DER process.
  - Members often outsource DER efforts at considerable expense and receive "nonsensical" drug listing notices not applicable to them, wasting time.
- **Inefficient and Unpredictable Animal Food Ingredient Review Process:**
  - The once globally recognized "gold-standard" U.S. ingredient review process (FAP and GRAS) has diminished in efficiency and predictability.
  - Hinders the marketing of innovative animal food ingredients.
  - Prevents the U.S. animal food industry from providing innovations to advance animal nutrition and U.S. manufacturing.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The cost of developing a Part 11-compliant computer system is estimated at $300,000 per facility today, based on informal inquiries and inflation from an original $150,000 estimate in 1997.
- FDA's Center for Veterinary Medicine did not grant Part 11 exemptions for VFD records in June 2015 rulemaking, despite granting similar exemptions for human and animal food in September 2015 under FSMA.
- The number of licensed medicated feed mills in the U.S. has significantly decreased from 1,000 in 1996 to 769, raising concerns that the cumbersome Drug Establishment Registration (DER) process may be a contributing factor.
- AFIA members report often having to outsource their DER efforts at considerable company expense due to the process's complexity.
- Members frequently receive "drug listing" notices from FDA around reregistration time, despite drug lists not being required for medicated feed manufacturers, indicating confusion within the agency's systems or personnel.
- The U.S. animal food ingredient review process, once a globally recognized "gold standard" relied upon by foreign governments, has diminished in efficiency and predictability in recent years.
- FDA's CVM recently opened a docket (FDA-2024-N-2979) in 2024 to specifically hear concerns from stakeholders regarding inefficiencies in the FAP and GRAS notification processes, acknowledging the problem.

- "Thus, these costs – which would not result in any discernable public health or animal health benefits – would undoubtedly be passed on to American consumers."
- "This complicated DER process is not necessary for feed mills."
- "It is time for the CVM to reduce the complexity of the animal food ingredient review process to achieve faster approvals and spur innovation."
