structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The National Community Pharmacists Association (NCPA) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments to the US Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS’) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
*   NCPA represents America’s community pharmacists, including 18,900 independent community pharmacies.
    *   Almost half of all community pharmacies provide long-term care services.
    *   They play a critical role in ensuring patients have immediate access to medications in both community and long-term care (LTC) settings.
    *   Our members employ 205,000 individuals and provide an expanding set of healthcare services to millions of patients every day.
    *   Our members are small business owners who are among America’s most accessible healthcare providers.
    *   NCPA submits these comments on behalf of both community and LTC independent pharmacies.
*   In this RFI, HHS seeks input on how to dramatically deregulate across all areas the Department touches.
*   CENTERS FOR MEDICARE AND MEDICAID SERVICES (CMS)
    *   CMS should eliminate pharmacies’ mandatory participation in the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation (MDPN) Program via PBM/plan contracts.
        *   To preserve the viability of Medicare Part D, access of beneficiaries to the pharmacy of their choice, and the viability of independent pharmacies, NCPA asks CMS to make this reform.
        *   CMS has required such participation in the recent Part D final rule by amending § 423.505 by adding paragraph (q).
        *   This paragraph requires Part D sponsors’ network contracts with pharmacies to require pharmacies to be enrolled in the MDPN Program’s Medicare Transaction Facilitator Data Module (‘‘MTF DM’’).
        *   NCPA opposes mandatory participation in the MDPN Program via PBM/plan contracts via this mandatory requirement.
        *   NCPA does not believe that CMS has the authority to tie participation in Part D as a whole with participation in the MDPN Program.
    *   CMS should rescind the Medicare Part B requirement for a beneficiary’s signature on a reimbursement claim.
        *   This requirement is under 42 C.F.R. 424.32 and 42 C.F.R. 424.36.
        *   It is outdated in today’s era of electronic claim submission.
        *   Capturing a signature—both on paper and electronically—is administratively burdensome and not an effective deterrent for fraud and abuse.
        *   Specific regulations cited:
            *   42 C.F.R. 424.32 Basic requirements for all claims.
                *   (a) A claim must meet the following requirements:
                    *   (3) A claim must be signed by the beneficiary or on behalf of the beneficiary (in accordance with § 424.36).
            *   42 C.F.R. 424.36 Signature requirements.
                *   (a) General rule. The beneficiary's own signature is required on the claim unless the beneficiary has died or specific provisions apply.
                *   (c) Who may sign if the beneficiary was not present for the service. A representative may sign if there was no personal contact (e.g., a physician sent a blood sample to the provider for diagnostic tests).
        *   This requirement was more appropriate when pharmacies were more regularly submitting paper claims.
        *   It is no longer viable today as pharmacies engage predominantly in real-time, electronic claims submission.
        *   It is unclear what, if anything, these rules do to protect the Medicare program from fraud or abuse.
        *   These rules do substantially add to administrative burden on pharmacies and cause delays in patient care.
        *   Specific administrative burdens include lost time attempting to mail a form to the beneficiary requesting signature and repeatedly following up seeking a response.
    *   CMS should revise its interpretation of 42 CFR 424.57(c)(12) - Signature for In Person Pickup of Items.
        *   42 CFR 424.57(c)(12) states: Must be responsible for the delivery of Medicare covered items to beneficiaries and maintain proof of delivery.
            *   The supplier must document that it or another qualified party has at an appropriate time provided beneficiaries with necessary information and instructions on how to use Medicare-covered items safely and effectively.
        *   NCPA believes CMS should interpret this regulation to mean that a signature capture is not required for in person pickup.
        *   Requiring a signature for items that are picked up in person at a supplier is contrary to this regulation and unnecessarily burdensome.
        *   The federal regulation does not specifically state that signature must be captured to document proof of delivery.
        *   A supplier can rely on receipt of delivery confirmation from the carrier.
        *   It is especially burdensome since a signature is not required for home delivery.
        *   It is unclear how the signature requirement protects against fraud or abuse in the Medicare program.
        *   A supplier has other forms of documentation it can produce for items picked up in person (e.g., electronic documentation of sales transactions, use of/form of payment collected for copayments), similar to a third-party carrier delivery confirmation.
*   SUBSTANCE ABUSE AND MENTAL HEALTH SERVICES ADMINISTRATION (SAMHSA) / DRUG ENFORCEMENT ADMINISTRATION (DEA)
    *   SAMHSA and DEA should rescind joint rules requiring pharmacists to verify the identity of patients filling prescriptions for buprenorphine to treat opioid use disorder (OUD) that were issued on the basis of a telemedicine encounter.
        *   These rules are 42 CFR § 12.3 (b)(4) and 21 CFR § 1306.51 (b)(4).
        *   This requirement perpetuates the stigma that individuals seeking OUD treatment can experience.
        *   It thereby undermines the underlying purpose of the Final Rule to “increase patient access to legitimate medical treatment.”
        *   Further, these requirements impose burdensome, costly, and unworkable requirements on pharmacies.
        *   They were never properly noticed for public comment.
*   FOOD AND DRUG ADMINISTRATION (FDA)
    *   Any Future MOU
        *   In 1997, Congress amended the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act to require FDA to develop a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with state boards of pharmacy.
        *   NCPA welcomed FDA’s delay of implementation of the MOU on October 21, 2022.
            *   This delay was until the effective date of a final rule regarding certain distributions of compounded human drug products and publication of an updated standard MOU.
        *   NCPA also supported FDA’s past suspension of the October 2020 MOU, its plans to establish a new MOU through rulemaking, and its "plans to further extend the period during which FDA does not intend to enforce the statutory 5 percent limit during the rulemaking process."
        *   NCPA supports FDA suspending this MOU indefinitely, given our multiple concerns.
        *   NCPA hopes that any future MOU, if it were promulgated, will address our previously stated concerns.
            *   States should be given sufficient time to assess any conflicts of law.
            *   If states choose to sign, they need to modify existing laws to comply with the MOU.
            *   Already, several state boards of pharmacy have raised issues about the potential conflicts between the old MOU and existing state laws regarding confidentiality of information, which conflicts with the reporting requirements of the old MOU.
            *   Some of these states have significant patient populations who use compounded drugs.
        *   NCPA also remains concerned about the consequences of not signing the MOU on patient access to essential compounded medications.
            *   Pharmacies in states that sign the MOU will be permitted to provide patients with personalized medications unimpeded.
            *   In states that choose not to sign, a five percent cap on interstate shipments would be imposed on pharmacies.
            *   NCPA is also concerned that patients who rely on compounded medications from pharmacies in states that cannot or do not sign the final MOU deadline will be penalized by disruption of care and inability to receive therapy from their pharmacy of choice.
        *   NCPA also disapproves of the way FDA has structured the past MOU.
            *   NCPA continues to have issues with both the process and the content of the old MOU.
            *   NCPA believes FDA conflates the definitions of “distribute” and “dispense” without Congressional authorization.
        *   The statutory language in section 503A of the FDCA directing FDA to establish an MOU with states requiring reporting of interstate distributions of compounded drugs is now outdated.
        *   It does not make sense in the context of the establishment of 503B outsourcing facilities under the DQSA.
        *   NCPA hopes that FDA will work with NCPA, NABP and other pharmacy stakeholders on consensus legislation to update this statute.
            *   This update should require reporting by pharmacies of interstate dispensing and distributions of compounded drugs without the need for states to sign an MOU that may conflict with state laws.
            *   It should also remove the arbitrary and punitive 5% cap in the current law.
    *   Demonstrably Difficult to Compound Federal Register Notice
        *   FDA should eliminate its proposed rule on demonstrable difficulties for compounding.
        *   FDA’s proposed rule seeks to establish criteria for two lists of drug products or categories of drug products that present demonstrable difficulties for compounding (Demonstrable Difficulties for Compounding Lists or DDC Lists) under certain sections of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
        *   Drug products or categories of drug products that appear on the DDC Lists cannot qualify for certain statutory exemptions, and therefore may not be compounded under, either section 503A or section 503B, respectively.
        *   FDA is also proposing to establish criteria for evaluating drug products or categories of products for inclusion on one or both lists, including: formulation complexity, drug delivery mechanism complexity, dosage form complexity, complexity of achieving or assessing bioavailability, compounding process complexity, and complexity of physicochemical or analytical testing.
        *   Additionally, FDA is proposing to identify the first three categories of drug products on both DDC Lists: (1) oral solid modified-release drug products that employ coated systems (MRCs), (2) liposome drug products (LDPs), and (3) drug products produced using hot melt extrusion (HMEs).
        *   Both sections 503A and 503B of the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act give FDA authority to prohibit compounding of certain medications deemed “demonstrably difficult to compound in a manner that reasonably demonstrates an adverse effect on the safety or effectiveness” of the drug.
        *   But according to Congress, the authority is different in these sections:
            *   In 503A, FDA may bar specific drug products from compounding — a narrow authority focused on individual formulations.
            *   In 503B, FDA is authorized to restrict both drug products and categories of drugs — a broader power that reflects the scale and manufacturing practices of outsourcing facilities.
        *   Despite this distinction, FDA’s proposed regulations apply the broader category-based prohibition to 503A pharmacies — an approach not supported by the statute.
        *   In the March 2024 proposed rule, FDA proposed six vague criteria for evaluating whether a drug is “demonstrably difficult to compound,” and stated that it may choose to use them to justify banning entire drug classes from 503A compounding.
        *   This is not a permissible interpretation of the statute.
        *   Section 503A refers only to “drug products”—not categories—and makes no provision for banning entire classes of medications.
        *   By attempting to impose the 503B framework into 503A, FDA is acting beyond its authority.
        *   Therefore, NCPA urges HHS to:
            *   Prevent FDA from finalizing any rule that exceeds its statutory authority under Section 503A.
            *   Ensure that only individual drug products—not entire categories—may be added to the 503A DDC list, consistent with congressional intent.
    *   Veterinarian GFI #256
        *   FDA should rescind its 2023 Guidance for Industry #256 (GFI 256).
        *   FDA seeks to regulate veterinary compounding, despite having no clear congressional mandate to do so.
        *   GFI 256 imposes broad restrictions on the use of bulk drug substances in veterinary compounding.
        *   These restrictions undermine the clinical judgment of veterinarians and unnecessarily restrict access of compounded drugs for animals.
        *   If FDA insists on maintaining GFI 256, a much more revised GFI 256 would be appropriate.
            *   It should respect veterinary practice, prescribing veterinarians, and the essential role of compounded medications in animal health.
            *   It should streamline the bulk substance nomination process, incorporating transparency in its evaluations.
    *   Nonprescription Drug Products with Additional Conditions for Nonprescription Use (ACNU)
        *   FDA should modify its Nonprescription Drug Products with Additional Conditions for Nonprescription Use (ACNU) final rule to standardize the ACNU process and incorporate the role of the pharmacist.
        *   In December 2024, FDA issued a final rule establishing requirements for the approval, labeling and post-marketing reporting of Nonprescription Drug Products with Additional Conditions for Nonprescription Use (“ACNU”).
        *   FDA created ACNU drugs as a new category of over-the-counter drug products that can be sold at retail to consumers without a prescription if the product manufacturer implements an additional condition to ensure appropriate self-selection or appropriate actual use, or both, by consumers without a prescribing healthcare provider’s supervision.
        *   Consumers must complete a self-assessment process designed by the product manufacturer to screen and determine whether that individual is eligible to purchase the product based on their health.
        *   NCPA believes this final rule creates operational burdens and costs at pharmacies.
        *   NCPA proposes revisions to make the rule workable for pharmacies and patients alike.
        *   Lack of Standardization:
            *   The Final Rule allows for different manufacturers to establish and deploy varying methods for consumers to complete the self-assessment process.
            *   Therefore, each manufacturer may operationalize ACNU differently, resulting in significant administrative burden for pharmacies as they would need to operationalize and implement sales processes to accommodate myriad ACNU requirements, which would necessitate the training of sales clerks.
            *   NCPA instead recommends that FDA standardize the ACNU process such that there is a common way for patients to prove that they fulfilled the ACNU.
        *   Costs and Time to Modify Point of Sale Systems:
            *   The ACNU final rule will require costly modifications for point-of-sale systems in pharmacy establishments.
            *   These systems would need to enter a “stop” in order to ask the patient to show their “proof” that they did the self-assessment, and the product is right for them.
            *   The POS systems will also have to add some type of documentation that the patient provided the self-assessment showing it was appropriate for that patient.
            *   This too would create great administrative burden, as pharmacies would be hesitant to modify their systems without knowing how manufacturers are going to approach the self-assessment.
            *   This is why NCPA supports standardization of the ACNU self-assessment, as well as pharmacy input in the development of the systems.
        *   Patient concerns:
            *   Additionally, there will likely be significant patient confusion of the same product being available both for prescription and over-the counter.
            *   Insurance plans may also stop covering the prescription version of the drug, which will contribute to greater out-of-pocket costs to patients and possible medication adherence/access issues.
        *   Ideally, the ACNU class of drugs should leverage the expertise of the pharmacist by being available only from state licensed pharmacies where pharmacists can assist with the necessary assessment processes for determining whether a particular medication is appropriate for the individual seeking the therapy.
*   NCPA thanks HHS for the opportunity to provide feedback and stands ready to work with the agency to offer possible solutions and ideas.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The National Community Pharmacists Association (NCPA), representing independent community and long-term care pharmacies, urges HHS to deregulate various areas, including mandatory Medicare Drug Price Negotiation participation, outdated signature requirements, and current compounding and OTC drug rules, advocating for reforms that reduce administrative burden, protect patient access, and respect pharmacists' expertise.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** National Community Pharmacists Association (NCPA)
- **Type:** Trade Association
- **Role/Expertise:** Represents 18,900 independent community pharmacies, including those providing long-term care services; advocates on behalf of small business owners who are accessible healthcare providers. Steve Postal, JD, Senior Director, Policy & Regulatory Affairs.
- **Geographic Scope:** National (representing America’s community pharmacists)
- **Stake in Issue:** Direct impact on the operational viability, administrative burden, and ability to provide patient care for independent community and long-term care pharmacies across various federal regulations impacting Medicare, drug compounding, and over-the-counter medication sales.
structuredSections.corePosition: We are urging HHS to dramatically deregulate across all areas the Department touches, as the current regulatory environment imposes significant administrative burdens, threatens the viability of independent pharmacies, and often restricts patient access to essential medications and services. Our fundamental stance is that regulations should be updated to reflect current practices, leverage the expertise of pharmacists, and truly protect patients without imposing unnecessary barriers or costs.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   **CMS:**
    -   Eliminate pharmacies’ mandatory participation in the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation (MDPN) Program via PBM/plan contracts.
        -   NCPA does not believe CMS has the authority to tie Part D participation to MDPN program enrollment.
    -   Rescind the Medicare Part B requirement for a beneficiary’s signature on a reimbursement claim (42 C.F.R. 424.32 and 42 C.F.R. 424.36).
    -   Revise interpretation of 42 CFR 424.57(c)(12) to not require signature capture for in-person pickup of Medicare-covered items.
-   **SAMHSA/DEA:**
    -   Rescind joint rules (42 CFR § 12.3 (b)(4) and 21 CFR § 1306.51 (b)(4)) requiring pharmacists to verify identity of buprenorphine patients for OUD from telemedicine encounters.
-   **FDA:**
    -   Suspend indefinitely any future Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with state boards of pharmacy regarding compounded human drug products.
        -   If an MOU is promulgated, it must:
            -   Grant states sufficient time to assess conflicts of law and modify existing laws.
            -   Avoid conflating "distribute" and "dispense" definitions without Congressional authorization.
            -   Update statutory language in section 503A of the FDCA to require reporting by pharmacies of interstate dispensing and distributions of compounded drugs without the need for states to sign an MOU.
            -   Remove the arbitrary and punitive 5% cap on interstate shipments for non-signing states.
    -   Eliminate the proposed rule on demonstrable difficulties for compounding.
        -   Prevent FDA from finalizing any rule that exceeds its statutory authority under Section 503A.
        -   Ensure only individual drug products—not entire categories—may be added to the 503A Demonstrable Difficulties for Compounding (DDC) list.
    -   Rescind its 2023 Guidance for Industry #256 (GFI 256) on veterinary compounding.
        -   If GFI 256 is maintained, revise it to:
            -   Respect veterinary practice and prescribing veterinarians.
            -   Recognize the essential role of compounded medications in animal health.
            -   Streamline the bulk substance nomination process and incorporate transparency.
    -   Modify the Nonprescription Drug Products with Additional Conditions for Nonprescription Use (ACNU) final rule.
        -   Standardize the ACNU process for all manufacturers.
        -   Incorporate the role of the pharmacist, ideally by making ACNU drugs available only from state licensed pharmacies where pharmacists can assist with assessments.
        -   Ensure pharmacy input in the development of ACNU systems.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   **Medicare Part D Viability & Patient Access:**
    -   Mandatory participation in Medicare Drug Price Negotiation (MDPN) Program via PBM/plan contracts threatens the viability of Medicare Part D and independent pharmacies, and restricts beneficiary access to their pharmacy of choice.
    -   CMS lacks authority to tie Part D participation to MDPN enrollment.
-   **Administrative Burden & Delays in Patient Care:**
    -   The Medicare Part B beneficiary signature requirement for reimbursement claims is outdated and creates significant administrative burden for pharmacies (e.g., mailing forms, follow-ups), without effectively deterring fraud or abuse in today's electronic claim submission era.
    -   Requiring signatures for in-person pickup of Medicare-covered items is unnecessarily burdensome and inconsistent with home delivery (which doesn't require a signature).
    -   The ACNU final rule creates significant operational burdens and costs for pharmacies due to lack of standardization and the need for costly point-of-sale system modifications.
-   **Stigma and Access to OUD Treatment:**
    -   Joint SAMHSA/DEA rules requiring pharmacists to verify identity for buprenorphine prescriptions from telemedicine encounters perpetuate stigma for OUD patients, undermining patient access to legitimate OUD treatment, and were implemented without proper public comment.
-   **Compounding Regulation Overreach and Patient Disruption:**
    -   FDA's proposed MOU for compounded drugs risks conflicts with existing state laws (e.g., confidentiality), penalizing states that cannot sign.
    -   A 5% cap on interstate shipments for non-signing states would disrupt patient care and deny patient choice for essential compounded medications.
    -   FDA conflates "distribute" and "dispense" definitions without Congressional authorization regarding compounding.
    -   FDA's proposed rule on "Demonstrably Difficult to Compound" drugs exceeds its statutory authority under Section 503A by attempting to ban entire *categories* of drugs rather than just *individual drug products*.
    -   FDA's GFI #256 on veterinary compounding lacks clear congressional mandate and imposes broad restrictions that undermine veterinary clinical judgment and patient access.
-   **Patient Confusion and Cost for ACNU Drugs:**
    -   The ACNU final rule will likely lead to significant patient confusion for products available both by prescription and over-the-counter.
    -   Insurance plans may stop covering prescription versions, leading to greater out-of-pocket costs and potential medication adherence/access issues.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
-   The observation that the Medicare Part B signature requirement for claims, while perhaps appropriate for historical paper claims, is no longer viable or effective in the current era of real-time, electronic claim submission.
-   The insight that requiring a signature for in-person pickup of Medicare-covered items is more burdensome and less justifiable than for home delivery, which does not require it.
-   The critical point that joint SAMHSA/DEA rules for buprenorphine identity verification perpetuate stigma against individuals seeking OUD treatment, thereby undermining the stated goal of increasing access to legitimate medical treatment.
-   The argument that FDA's attempt to ban entire *categories* of compounded drugs for 503A pharmacies, rather than individual drug products, constitutes an overreach of its statutory authority and misinterprets Congressional intent.
-   The concern that allowing different manufacturers to implement varying self-assessment methods for ACNU drugs will lead to "myriad ACNU requirements" for pharmacies, causing significant administrative burden and necessitating extensive training for sales clerks.
-   The foresight that ACNU drugs could create patient confusion if the same product is available both prescription and OTC, potentially leading to insurance plans ceasing coverage for the prescription version and increasing patient out-of-pocket costs and adherence issues.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
-   "NCPA does not believe that CMS has the authority to tie participation in Part D as a whole with participation in the MDPN Program."
-   "Requiring a signature for items that are picked up in person at a supplier is contrary to this regulation and unnecessarily burdensome, especially since a signature is not required for home delivery."
-   "This requirement [for buprenorphine] perpetuates the stigma that individuals seeking OUD treatment can experience, thereby undermining the underlying purpose of the Final Rule to “increase patient access to legitimate medical treatment.”"
-   "By attempting to impose the 503B framework into 503A, FDA is acting beyond its authority."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I have been a public school teacher for almost ten years, I love my students, and I take my work seriously.
*   Living with ADHD and trying to manage a classroom is a constant mental tug-of-war.
    *   I forget small instructions.
    *   I lose track of time.
    *   I miss minor but important details.
*   The perfectionist in me obsesses over every mistake, every missed email, every parent interaction I could’ve handled better.
    *   This stress is taken home, into the night and into my sleep, which I rarely get.
*   Insomnia and anxiety have followed me for most of my adult life.
    *   Even when I manage to fall asleep, it’s restless and shallow.
    *   I wake up feeling like I never really went to bed.
*   ADHD medication was a turning point for me.
    *   I could think more clearly.
    *   I could get through the school day.
    *   I could sleep without five hours of overthinking first.
    *   It helped me be the teacher my students deserve.
*   However, the fight to maintain treatment makes me feel like the system isn’t just indifferent—it’s cruel.
*   There are no new-patient psychiatrists in my area.
*   My Primary Care Physician (PCP) does not manage my ADHD medications.
*   I finally started telehealth during the pandemic, and it saved me.
*   But with Schedule II restrictions, every single refill is a high-stakes game.
    *   My local pharmacy is often out of stock.
    *   I cannot get it filled early.
    *   I’ve had to take unpaid days off because I couldn’t function without my medications.
*   I do not understand why these medications are still treated like deadly substances.
    *   Stimulant medications for ADHD are currently classified on the same legal shelf as some of the most dangerous narcotics.
    *   This classification is outdated bureaucracy, not medicine.
*   Addiction to Adderall is no longer a recognized diagnosis.
*   These medications have been used safely for nearly a century, and the evidence supporting their safety is available.
    *   It is the system that has not caught up.
*   Telehealth needs to be permanently available.
*   The substance classification framework requires a full overhaul.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: A public school teacher with ADHD describes the critical role medication plays in managing her condition and performing her job, advocating for the permanent availability of telehealth and a reclassification of ADHD stimulants due to current, harmful restrictions.

structuredSections.corePosition: As a dedicated teacher living with ADHD, I have found stimulant medication to be crucial for my professional performance and personal well-being, including managing severe insomnia and anxiety. The current classification of these medications as Schedule II narcotics, along with restrictive dispensing rules and limited access to prescribing providers, creates an unnecessarily cruel and bureaucratic system that prevents me from reliably accessing essential treatment.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Telehealth services must remain available and be permanently continued.
- The substance classification framework, specifically for stimulant medications used to treat ADHD, needs a full overhaul to reflect current medical understanding and evidence of safety.

    - Inability to get early refills.
    - Forced unpaid days off from work due to medication unavailability and subsequent functional impairment.
- The outdated and harmful classification of ADHD stimulant medications alongside dangerous narcotics, despite evidence of their safety and long-term use.
- The "cruelty" and "indifference" of a system that impedes access to necessary and effective treatment.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:

- The transformative positive impact of ADHD medication on professional performance and quality of life, enabling the commenter to be the "teacher my students deserve" and achieve restful sleep.
- The critical role telehealth played in maintaining access to care during the pandemic when in-person options were unavailable.
- The specific and severe real-world consequences of Schedule II restrictions, such as pharmacy shortages leading to missed workdays and functional impairment.
- The insight that "Addiction to Adderall? Not a recognized diagnosis anymore," which directly challenges the rationale for the medication's current classification.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The National Grocers Association (NGA) appreciates the opportunity to submit comments in response to the Request for Information concerning the impact of existing regulations on market competition and innovation.
*   NGA commends the Trump Administration’s initiative to identify and eliminate outdated or unnecessary regulations.
*   NGA is the national trade association representing independent grocery retailers and wholesalers who serve them.
    *   An independent retailer is a privately owned or controlled company operating in a variety of formats.
    *   Having often been in business for generations, independent grocers are dedicated to their customers, associates, and communities.
    *   Much of NGA’s membership is comprised of family-owned and family-operated businesses.
    *   Nearly half of NGA’s members are single-store operators, and another quarter operate less than five stores.
    *   Independent retail and wholesale grocers are an important part of America’s economy.
        *   They account for a third of all grocery sales, exceeding $250 billion in sales.
        *   They support more than one million American jobs.
    *   We are inherently tied to the strength and vitality of the markets we serve – at the heart of local communities and the U.S. economy.
*   We ask that you review the FDA Traceability Rule for its impact on the independent grocery industry and consider this rule for delay or intervention.
*   Requirements for Additional Traceability Records for Certain Foods (FDA-2014-N-0053)
    *   The final Traceability Rule establishes recordkeeping requirements for food entities who manufacture, process, pack, or hold foods on the Food Traceability List (FTL).
    *   It requires that these food entities provide their supply chain partners Key Data Elements (KDE) for certain Critical Tracking Events (CTE) in the handling of the food.
    *   This rule creates an immense burden for independent retailers.
        *   The requirements of this overly complex and expansive rule are expensive to implement due to the technological needs for implementation.
        *   They require additional labor that many stores cannot spare.
        *   This burden will, at a minimum, substantially and permanently raise costs and add to inflationary pressures.
            *   This would very well lead to increased food costs for consumers.
    *   FDA substantially underestimated the economic impact of the rule.
        *   As drafted, the rule imposes both one-time and continuing costs for NGA’s retail grocery and wholesale grocery members.
            *   They will be required to develop new business systems.
            *   They will need to invest in new capital improvements to information infrastructure.
            *   They will need to train personnel to mind these new systems.
            *   They will need to respond to both FDA- and industry-initiated tracing exercises.
        *   As small businesses, our members do not get to dictate what their technology providers prioritize and create, so we are at the mercy of their timeline.
    *   As an attempt to lessen burdens on small business, FDA exempted companies with ten or fewer full-time employees.
        *   However, that is essentially meaningless for independently owned community grocers.
        *   Even a small, single-store operation is likely to have more than 50 full-time employees.
            *   This includes cashiers to staff a six- or seven-day-a-week schedule with stores open for at least twelve hours a day.
            *   It includes specialized clerks to ensure the purchase, stocking, and care of healthful foods in meat/fish, produce, and deli departments.
            *   It also includes stocking clerks and management.
        *   The exemption for small retailers is set so low that no full-service grocery store could qualify.
    *   Additionally, we believe that FDA exceeded its statutory authority with this rulemaking.
        *   The rule would be not merely difficult but well-nigh impossible to implement absent case-level tracking, which the agency is specifically prohibited from imposing under section 204(d)(1)(L)(iii).
        *   The requirement for production of a sortable electronic spreadsheet becomes a de facto imposition of an electronic recordkeeping system.
            *   It would be impossible otherwise to comply with the 24-hour production requirement in the absence of existing electronic records to populate the sortable electronic spreadsheet.
            *   This requirement would therefore violate the statutory limitations under section 204(d)(1)(C).
        *   Moreover, by mandating the production of information in this form, the Proposed Rule violates section 204(d)(1)(E) by requiring a record that is overly complex, burdensome, and duplicative of other extant records.
    *   This rule, while well intended, does not consider implementation realities for the food industry and independent grocers specifically.
*   We ask that your review of this rule’s impact to our industry and thank you for considering our comments.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The National Grocers Association, representing independent grocery retailers nationwide, urges the FDA to review, delay, or intervene on the burdensome Traceability Rule, asserting it significantly underestimates economic impact, is unworkable for small grocers, and exceeds statutory authority.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** National Grocers Association (NGA)
- **Type:** Trade Association
- **Role/Expertise:** National trade association representing independent grocery retailers and wholesalers; members are often family-owned and family-operated businesses, with nearly half being single-store operators and another quarter operating fewer than five stores.
- **Geographic Scope:** National
- **Stake in Issue:** Represents independent grocery retailers and wholesalers who are directly impacted by the FDA Traceability Rule's requirements, which impose significant technological, labor, and cost burdens on their small business members.
structuredSections.corePosition: We ask that you review the FDA Traceability Rule for its impact on the independent grocery industry and consider this rule for delay or intervention. This rule creates an immense burden for independent retailers due to its complexity, technological needs, and labor requirements, which will substantially and permanently raise costs for businesses and consumers.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Review the FDA Traceability Rule (Requirements for Additional Traceability Records for Certain Foods, FDA-2014-N-0053) for its impact on the independent grocery industry.
- Consider delaying or intervening on the FDA Traceability Rule.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Immense Burden and Underestimated Economic Impact:**
    - The rule is overly complex and expansive, leading to high implementation costs due to technological needs and required additional labor that many stores cannot spare.
    - This burden will substantially and permanently raise costs for independent retailers and wholesalers, contributing to inflationary pressures and potentially increasing food costs for consumers.
    - FDA substantially underestimated the rule's economic impact, imposing significant one-time and continuing costs on members for developing new business systems, investing in information infrastructure, training personnel, and responding to tracing exercises.
    - Members, as small businesses, are at the mercy of their technology providers' timelines, as they cannot dictate their priorities or development schedules.
- **Inadequate Small Business Exemption:**
    - The exemption for companies with ten or fewer full-time employees is "meaningless" for independently owned community grocers.
    - Even a small, single-store operation is likely to have over 50 full-time employees (including cashiers, specialized clerks for various departments, stocking clerks, and management), meaning no full-service grocery store could qualify for the exemption.
- **Exceeding Statutory Authority:**
    - The rule effectively mandates case-level tracking, which the agency is specifically prohibited from imposing under section 204(d)(1)(L)(iii).
    - The requirement for producing a sortable electronic spreadsheet implicitly forces the adoption of an electronic recordkeeping system, as 24-hour compliance would otherwise be impossible, thus violating statutory limitations under section 204(d)(1)(C).
    - By mandating information in this form, the rule violates section 204(d)(1)(E) by requiring records that are overly complex, burdensome, and duplicative of existing records.
- **Lack of Consideration for Implementation Realities:**
    - The rule, though well-intended, does not account for the practical realities of implementation within the food industry, particularly for independent grocers.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The critical insight that FDA's small business exemption (10 or fewer full-time employees) is "meaningless" for independent grocers, as even the smallest full-service store typically employs over 50 people.
- The unique challenge faced by small businesses like independent grocers: they are "at the mercy" of their technology providers' timelines and priorities, unable to dictate the development of necessary compliance tools.
- The detailed legal argument that the rule implicitly requires case-level tracking and electronic recordkeeping, despite explicit statutory prohibitions, highlighting a potential overreach of regulatory authority.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "This rule creates an immense burden for independent retailers. The requirements of this overly complex and expansive rule are expensive to implement due to the technological needs for implementation and require additional labor that many stores cannot spare."
- "The exemption for small retailers is set so low that no full-service grocery store could qualify."
- "The rule would be not merely difficult but well-nigh impossible to implement absent case-level tracking, which the agency is specifically prohibited from imposing under section 204(d)(1)(L)(iii)."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
-   As an early childhood advocate and Head Start employee for over 26 years, I appreciate the opportunity to offer information in response to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS’s) recent Request for Information (RFI) on “Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.”
-   Prenatal-to-five programs like Head Start/Early Head Start provide locally controlled, community-driven services to families in every state.
-   The regulations and standards that HHS creates for the early care and learning field are critical to continued service to families and accountability for taxpayer-funded programs.
    -   They provide important guidance to the state- and community-based organizations that are entrusted with carrying out critical services.
    -   They promote program consistency, quality, accountability, and continuous improvement.
-   While every Head Start program is designed to meet the needs of their own community, performance standards provide the guidance necessary to ensure that we are both accountable for federal dollars and providing the essential services necessary to most effectively support children and families.
-   I strongly caution HHS against broad removal of accountability measures with the following key considerations:
    -   Ensuring Success in All States and Communities:
        -   In early childhood services, accountability measures from HHS uphold key pillars like program quality, child safety, and workforce supports.
        -   These ensure that the taxpayer-funded programs that yield positive outcomes can be replicated in all types of communities – rural, urban, exurban, suburban, and tribal.
        -   HHS’s standards are a critical tool for ensuring consistently positive outcomes across the U.S.’s vast range of geographies.
    -   Honoring Parent Choice:
        -   Local Systems of Care:
            -   Communities across the country have shaped their early care and learning and maternal health landscapes to be responsive to the needs of parents in their local community.
            -   Standards and accountability measures from HHS provide a key framework from which communities can operate to implement services that are consistent in quality and unique in the specific services, delivery methods, and curriculum they offer in response to parent input.
            -   I urge HHS to uphold standards as essential frameworks that communities build and innovate from.
            -   These standards allow parents the opportunity to take advantage of community services with the confidence that HHS is holding programs accountable on quality and safety.
        -   Family Leadership:
            -   In order to preserve parents’ rights to choose the best education for their child starting in the earliest years, I strongly urge HHS to maintain a robust public comment process on regulations pertaining to maternal health and child and family services.
                -   This will allow families to engage with HHS to create the types of early care and learning opportunities that will best align with their personal views on the type of early childhood education they want their child to receive.
            -   I strongly urge HHS to uphold the integrity of family leadership and feedback loop opportunities that are embedded into the structures of child and family services, including Head Start Parent Policy Councils and Head Start and Child Care Development Block Grant and Maternal, Infant, Early Childhood Home Visiting program community needs assessments.
            -   These opportunities to inform accountability measures and policies play a critical role in uncovering and promoting parent choice in early care and learning and maternal health services.
    -   Preserve Accountability for Public Funds:
        -   Through its standards, HHS supports state- and community-based entities in remaining accountable to their communities and to the federal government by requiring public disclosure around the use of federal funds.
        -   This is a critical function of regulations that I urge HHS to maintain, as it re-enforces principles that child and family serving services consider core to their mission: transparency, fiscal integrity, and accountability to families.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: A 26-year Head Start employee and early childhood advocate urges HHS to maintain robust regulations and accountability measures, highlighting their critical role in ensuring quality, promoting parent choice, and safeguarding public funds across diverse communities.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
-   **Name/Organization:** Margaret Tazewell / Head Start employee
-   **Type:** Individual
-   **Role/Expertise:** Early childhood advocate; Head Start employee for over 26 years
-   **Geographic Scope:** National (as Head Start operates across all states and communities)
-   **Stake in Issue:** Direct involvement in implementing and benefiting from the regulations governing early childhood and family services, with deep experience in Head Start.
structuredSections.corePosition: As a long-time Head Start employee, I strongly caution HHS against broad removal of accountability measures in early childhood and family services. These regulations and standards are critical for maintaining service quality, ensuring child safety, promoting parent choice, fostering innovation within frameworks, and preserving accountability for taxpayer-funded programs across all communities.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   Maintain robust regulations and accountability measures for early childhood and family services.
    -   Uphold these standards as essential frameworks that communities can build and innovate from.
-   Maintain a robust public comment process on regulations pertaining to maternal health and child and family services.
-   Uphold the integrity of family leadership and feedback loop opportunities embedded into service structures.
    -   Specifically mentioning Head Start Parent Policy Councils and community needs assessments for Head Start, Child Care Development Block Grant, and Maternal, Infant, Early Childhood Home Visiting programs.
-   Maintain the critical function of requiring public disclosure around the use of federal funds to ensure transparency, fiscal integrity, and accountability.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   Broad removal of accountability measures could undermine key pillars of early childhood services, including program quality, child safety, and workforce supports.
-   Weakening HHS standards could jeopardize the consistent replication of positive outcomes across the U.S.'s diverse geographies (rural, urban, exurban, suburban, tribal).
-   Erosion of parent choice if standards no longer provide confidence that programs are held accountable for quality and safety.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
-   I got diagnosed with ADHD two years ago, after I wrecked two relationships, lost my job, and almost lost custody of my daughter.
    -   I ain’t proud of it, but I didn’t know I had it.
    -   I just thought I was bad with time, lazy, forgetful.
    -   People would get mad because I’d forget stuff they said or space out halfway through talking.
    -   I’d feel like crap, but I couldn’t help it.
-   I couldn’t sleep either.
    -   My brain never shut up.
    -   I’d lie awake replaying every dumb thing I said or forgot.
    -   Then I’d oversleep, show up late, mess up a job.
        -   That’s how I lost three HVAC gigs.
    -   Then I lost my marriage.
        -   My ex said I couldn’t be trusted, and I didn’t even know what to say.
-   Getting on meds changed a lot.
    -   I can keep my job now.
    -   I show up, remember details, get stuff done.
-   But getting those meds every month? That’s a battle.
    -   My doctor won’t prescribe Schedule II.
    -   No ADHD specialists near me are taking new people.
    -   I had to go through telehealth, which worked, so of course now they’re talking about taking it away.
-   Pharmacy stuff is just stupid.
    -   They run out, or give me different brands that don’t feel right.
    -   I can’t refill early even when I know they’ll be out.
    -   It’s like the system is built to fail.
-   Why is Adderall treated like fentanyl?
    -   Fentanyl kills people.
    -   I’m just trying to keep my head clear and my daughter fed.
-   People with ADHD shouldn’t be penalized because their medication is stuck in a 1970s regulatory classification.
    -   These drugs aren’t opioids.
    -   They're not fentanyl.
    -   But they’re regulated like they are.
-   Make telehealth permanent, and reclassify ADHD meds appropriately.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I didn’t ask for this brain; I got ADHD and didn’t know it until I was 29.
    *   Before diagnosis, I made a mess of everything.
        *   Dropped out of college three times.
            *   I owe Sallie Mae over $60,000 for a degree I never finished.
        *   Had about a dozen jobs and was fired from most.
            *   Reasons included being late, forgetting things, or spacing out mid-shift.
        *   Two relationships ended because I would zone out during conversations or forget to pick up kids.
            *   Partners thought I didn’t care, but I did; I just couldn’t stay focused.
    *   Sleep was a major issue; I used to stay up all night obsessing over mistakes.
        *   I would then crash around 6 AM.
        *   Anxiety from lack of sleep made everything worse.
*   I was finally diagnosed by a telehealth doctor.
    *   It took a few tries, but I received medication.
    *   Things started to calm down after beginning medication.
        *   I could actually follow through on tasks.
        *   I could sleep.
        *   I could keep a job.
*   Every month, I face challenges accessing my medication.
    *   The pharmacy is often out of stock.
    *   Sometimes I receive the wrong generic, which causes heartburn and brain fog.
    *   Because it’s a Schedule II medication, I cannot easily go to a different pharmacy.
        *   I have to wait for stock.
        *   I try to ration pills.
        *   I fall behind again on my responsibilities.
*   I question why these medications are still treated like heroin.
    *   It's insane that Xanax is easier to obtain than ADHD medications.
    *   If these medications were truly addictive, half of America would be hooked, given they've been around since WWII.
    *   People are not robbing banks for Ritalin.
*   Telehealth is the only reason I am still managing to keep my life together.
    *   Please do not take telehealth away.
*   These medications need to be reclassified; they do not belong on the same list as fentanyl.
    *   We deserve better.
*   If ADHD is truly this disabling—and it is—why am I still paying student loans for a degree my brain never allowed me to earn?

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I was diagnosed with ADHD when I was 33 years old.
    *   Before diagnosis, I had already:
        *   Dropped out of community college.
        *   Been fired from about six different jobs.
        *   Been divorced once.
    *   I am not unintelligent; I actually loved school.
        *   However, I couldn't keep track of assignments, dates, or reading materials.
        *   My brain "just wouldn't do it."
    *   I felt like a loser, and this experience killed my self-esteem.
    *   Insomnia worsened the situation:
        *   I would stay up all night worrying about unfinished tasks.
        *   I would then sleep only two hours.
        *   This led to showing up late or not at all to obligations.
    *   Despite advice to "just work harder," I tried:
        *   I would show up early, stay late, and write notes on my arm.
        *   But I would still forget things, space out, or get overwhelmed.
    *   When I dropped out of college, I still owed loans for a degree I didn't finish, which I question if that is fair.
    *   ADHD "wrecked my chances," and "no one cared until I got so low I begged for help."
*   Medication has been significantly helpful for me.
    *   It allows me to keep my job, show up, and fulfill my responsibilities.
    *   I am also able to sleep at night.
*   However, maintaining medication is difficult:
    *   I had to drive three hours to find a psychiatrist who treats ADHD.
    *   My regular doctor is unwilling to prescribe it because it is a Schedule II controlled substance.
    *   I question why Adderall is treated with the same scrutiny as meth or fentanyl, as I am trying to survive, not abuse it.
*   The pharmacy presents another set of challenges:
    *   They frequently switch medication brands, and some brands cause negative side effects like jitters or sickness for me.
    *   They are consistently out of stock of the medication.
    *   I am unable to fill prescriptions early, even when planning a trip.
    *   Missing even two or three days of medication makes me feel like I am "drowning in my own head."
*   I urge for changes to these regulations.
    *   Do not penalize individuals for having a diagnosis.
    *   Maintain telehealth options for treatment.
    *   Address and fix the current scheduling regulations for these medications.
    *   Stop assuming the worst intentions of people who simply want to function.
    *   Consider establishing disability protections for ADHD, given its impact on college completion, employment, and relationships, instead of imposing punishments.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- As someone who spent over 35 years in a detail-heavy profession, living with untreated ADHD felt like trying to keep a hundred marbles from rolling off a table every single day.
  - I was only formally diagnosed after retirement.
  - This diagnosis explained a lifetime of struggles I had blamed on character flaws:
    - Forgetting deadlines
    - Working twice as long to complete tasks
    - Feeling emotionally reactive
    - Never sleeping through the night
- When I started medication, the difference was profound.
  - It didn’t solve everything, but it gave me just enough clarity and calm to feel like I wasn’t constantly failing.
  - For the first time in decades, I could rest, sleep, and think without every thought fighting for attention.
  - It was a gift.
- But it’s a gift I now have to fight to keep due to various barriers.
  - My psychiatrist retired, and I couldn’t find anyone locally taking new patients.
  - I had to turn to a telehealth provider, which has been a crucial option.
  - The barriers don’t end there:
    - I can’t fill my prescription early, even if I’m traveling.
    - The pharmacy switches manufacturers without warning, and sometimes the new version just doesn’t work.
    - The looks I get when I mention I take stimulants are degrading, as though I’m doing something illicit.
- Having worked in finance, I understand risk and also understand outdated policy.
  - Schedule II placement made sense in 1971, but it does not in 2025.
  - These medications are not causing mass addiction, as reflected by the DSM-5.
  - I question why the DEA is still clinging to 50-year-old fear-based models.
  - Meanwhile, drugs like Xanax, with far greater abuse potential, sit comfortably on schedule IV.
- I urge you to consider this Request for Information (RFI) an opportunity for meaningful change.
  - Please don’t dismantle telehealth, as it’s been the only consistent lifeline for people like me.
  - It’s time to reclassify ADHD medications.
  - Right now, they’re lumped in with fentanyl and OxyContin, which makes no medical sense.
  - We’re being penalized under a drug policy that hasn’t evolved in 50 years.
  - Adults with ADHD are not criminals; we are citizens seeking access to the tools that allow us to participate fully in society.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I am writing to comment on the U.S Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
*   The years of pregnancy to age three set the foundation for a baby’s development, learning and relationships.
    *   Babies, toddlers and children rely entirely on the adults around them—parents, caregivers, and early childhood professionals—to provide safe, nurturing care.
*   As a pediatric physical therapist who worked for 30+ years in Early Intervention (birth to 3 years old), I have seen firsthand how federal programs help babies in these crucial years of development.
    *   I have witnessed how access to or lack of health insurance, healthcare, safe daycare/childcare and preschool have long term consequences.
    *   When babies face reduced support or program quality, it can lead to emotional, physical, and developmental impacts throughout their childhood.
*   HHS plays a critical role in ensuring that babies, families, and the professionals who care for little ones have access to the resources, protections, and supports they need.
    *   In considering changes to regulations, HHS must preserve regulations that keep young children safe and healthy.
    *   HHS must also preserve regulations that enable the adults in their lives to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
*   Regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and childcare settings are needed to keep babies safe and developmentally on track.
*   Safeguards that keep children healthy, like pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care, must be maintained.
*   Many HHS programs and regulations lay the foundation for quality care and critical support that babies need.
    *   Any changes to those programs and regulations must be transparent, grounded in evidence, and focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
*   I appreciate HHS giving the public—including families and early childhood professionals like me—an opportunity to weigh in on any proposed changes.
*   To keep America’s babies healthy and safe, HHS must maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services.
*   Please uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
-   As an early childhood advocate and Head Start employee for over 26 years, I appreciate the opportunity to offer information in response to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS’s) recent Request for Information (RFI) on “Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.”
-   Prenatal-to-five programs like Head Start/Early Head Start provide locally controlled, community-driven services to families in every state.
-   The regulations and standards that HHS creates for the early care and learning field are critical to continued service to families and accountability for taxpayer-funded programs.
    -   They provide important guidance to the state- and community-based organizations that are entrusted with carrying out critical services.
    -   They promote program consistency, quality, accountability, and continuous improvement.
-   While every Head Start program is designed to meet the needs of their own community, performance standards provide the guidance necessary to ensure that we are both accountable for federal dollars and providing the essential services necessary to most effectively support children and families.
-   I strongly caution HHS against broad removal of accountability measures with the following key considerations:
    -   Ensuring Success in All States and Communities:
        -   In early childhood services, accountability measures from HHS uphold key pillars like program quality, child safety, and workforce supports.
        -   These ensure that the taxpayer-funded programs that yield positive outcomes can be replicated in all types of communities – rural, urban, exurban, suburban, and tribal.
        -   HHS’s standards are a critical tool for ensuring consistently positive outcomes across the U.S.’s vast range of geographies.
    -   Honoring Parent Choice:
        -   Local Systems of Care:
            -   Communities across the country have shaped their early care and learning and maternal health landscapes to be responsive to the needs of parents in their local community.
            -   Standards and accountability measures from HHS provide a key framework from which communities can operate to implement services that are consistent in quality and unique in the specific services, delivery methods, and curriculum they offer in response to parent input.
            -   I urge HHS to uphold standards as essential frameworks that communities build and innovate from.
            -   These standards allow parents the opportunity to take advantage of community services with the confidence that HHS is holding programs accountable on quality and safety.
        -   Family Leadership:
            -   In order to preserve parents’ rights to choose the best education for their child starting in the earliest years, I strongly urge HHS to maintain a robust public comment process on regulations pertaining to maternal health and child and family services.
                -   This will allow families to engage with HHS to create the types of early care and learning opportunities that will best align with their personal views on the type of early childhood education they want their child to receive.
            -   I strongly urge HHS to uphold the integrity of family leadership and feedback loop opportunities that are embedded into the structures of child and family services, including Head Start Parent Policy Councils and Head Start and Child Care Development Block Grant and Maternal, Infant, Early Childhood Home Visiting program community needs assessments.
            -   These opportunities to inform accountability measures and policies play a critical role in uncovering and promoting parent choice in early care and learning and maternal health services.
    -   Preserve Accountability for Public Funds:
        -   Through its standards, HHS supports state- and community-based entities in remaining accountable to their communities and to the federal government by requiring public disclosure around the use of federal funds.
        -   This is a critical function of regulations that I urge HHS to maintain, as it re-enforces principles that child and family serving services consider core to their mission: transparency, fiscal integrity, and accountability to families.
