structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   We appreciate the opportunity to provide comments to the Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS) request for information to address "regulations that are unnecessary, inconsistent with the law, overly burdensome, outdated, out of alignment with current Executive orders, or otherwise unsound."
*   Consumer health products that contribute to nutritional adequacy and support overall health and wellness align with national public health goals and the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) vision.
*   Rescinding outdated, unnecessarily burdensome, or scientifically misaligned regulations, guidances, policies, and other requirements within the consumer health product space would enhance businesses' ability to develop, market, and distribute products like dietary supplements and functional foods.
*   In support of deregulatory initiatives, our client submits four suggestions for rescission or revision:
    *   I. Nutrition Labeling for Food Final Rule & Guidance for Industry: Frequently Asked Questions About Medical Foods – Third Edition
    *   II. Draft Guidance for Industry: Dietary Supplements: New Dietary Ingredient Notifications and Related Issues (April 2024) & Guidance for Industry: New Dietary Ingredient Notification Procedures and Timeframes - Dietary Supplements (March 2024) & Draft Guidance for Industry: New Dietary Ingredient Notification Master Files for Dietary Supplements: Guidance for Industry (April 2024)
    *   III. Health Claims: General Requirements – General Health Claim Labeling Requirements
    *   IV. Small Entity Compliance Guide on Structure/Function Claims

*   **I. Nutrition Labeling for Food Final Rule & Guidance for Industry: Frequently Asked Questions About Medical Foods – Third Edition**
    *   Agency: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
    *   Sections to be rescinded:
        *   21 C.F.R. §§ 101.9(j)(8)(ii) & (iii)
        *   Guidance for Industry: Frequently Asked Questions About Medical Foods – Third Edition
    *   Type of rule/guidance: Final Rule and Guidance
    *   Name of regulation:
        *   Nutrition Labeling for Food – 21 C.F.R. §§ 101.9(j)(8)(ii) & (iii)
        *   Guidance for Industry: Frequently Asked Questions About Medical Foods – Third Edition
    *   Justifications for rescission:
        *   The statutory definition of a medical food (21 U.S.C. § 360ee(b)(3)) is "A food which is formulated to be consumed or administered enterally under the supervision of a physician and which is intended for the specific dietary management of a disease or condition for which distinctive nutritional requirements, based on recognized scientific principles, are established by medical evaluation.”
        *   FDA’s final rule adopts an unjustifiably narrow interpretation in 21 C.F.R. §§ 101.9(j)(8)(ii) by stating medical foods are *only* for individuals whose dietary management "cannot be achieved by the modification of the normal diet alone."
            *   This effectively excludes conditions manageable by diet modification, even when practical barriers (access, affordability, palatability, complexity) impair a patient's ability to meet distinctive nutritional requirements without medical foods.
            *   Medical foods serve as a clinically appropriate and necessary tool in such cases.
        *   FDA’s definition in subsections (ii) and (iii) of 21 C.F.R. §§ 101.9(j)(8) limits "distinctive nutritional requirements" to "nutrients," and to those with "limited or impaired capacity to ingest, digest, absorb, or metabolize ordinary foodstuffs or certain nutrients."
            *   This narrow, essential-nutrient model does not align with advances in nutritional science, as bioactives like probiotics can play a critical role but don't meet the "nutrient" definition.
            *   The current CFR definition appears to limit medical foods far beyond statutory intent, primarily to rare genetic disorders, and disregards functional impairments common in chronic diseases that create distinctive nutritional needs without overt nutrient deficiencies.
            *   This interpretation limits access to medical foods that could provide meaningful clinical benefit.
        *   The FDA’s Guidance, "Frequently Asked Questions About Medical Foods – Third Edition," echoes these unduly narrow interpretations.
        *   FDA’s current interpretation may inadvertently restrict patient access to medical foods despite scientifically recognized nutritional needs, undermining the statute's intent to support disease management through scientifically grounded, medically supervised nutrition.
        *   A more inclusive interpretation consistent with the statutory definition, recognizing both clinical and practical dimensions of dietary management, is essential.
        *   This aligns with the MAHA goal of focusing on preventing and treating chronic diseases rather than unnecessary paperwork or burdensome administrative requirements with no clear health benefit.
    *   Reasons for rescission: (1) inconsistent with statute; (5) bad policy, unreasoned, or unsound (scientifically).
    *   Proposed C.F.R. text after rescission (showing sections (ii) and (iii) removed):
        *   21 C.F.R. § 101.9(j)(8):
            *   (8) Medical foods as defined in section 5(b) of the Orphan Drug Act (21 U.S.C. 360ee(b)(3)). A medical food is a food which is formulated to be consumed or administered enterally under the supervision of a physician and which is intended for the specific dietary management of a disease or condition for which distinctive nutritional requirements, based on recognized scientific principles, are established by medical evaluation. A food is subject to this exemption only if:
                *   (i) It is a specially formulated and processed product (as opposed to a naturally occurring foodstuff used in its natural state) for the partial or exclusive feeding of a patient by means of oral intake or enteral feeding by tube;
                *   (ii) …
                *   (iii) …
                *   (iv) It is intended to be used under medical supervision; and
                *   (v) It is intended only for a patient receiving active and ongoing medical supervision wherein the patient requires medical care on a recurring basis for, among other things, instructions on the use of the medical food.
        *   The Guidance for Industry: Frequently Asked Questions About Medical Foods – Third Edition should also be rescinded.
    *   Agency Head: Martin A. Makary, Commissioner of Food and Drugs.

*   **II. Draft Guidance for Industry: Dietary Supplements: New Dietary Ingredient Notifications and Related Issues (April 2024); Dietary Supplements: New Dietary Ingredient Notification Procedures and Timeframes: Guidance for Industry (March 2024); New Dietary Ingredient Notification Master Files for Dietary Supplements: Guidance for Industry (Draft Guidance) (April 2024)**
    *   Agency: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
    *   Guidances to be rescinded:
        *   Dietary Supplements: New Dietary Ingredient Notifications and Related Issues: Guidance for Industry (Draft Guidance) (April 2024)
        *   Dietary Supplements: New Dietary Ingredient Notification Procedures and Timeframes: Guidance for Industry (March 2024)
        *   New Dietary Ingredient Notification Master Files for Dietary Supplements: Guidance for Industry (Draft Guidance) (April 2024)
    *   Type of guidance: Draft Guidance (2) and Final Guidance (1)
    *   Name of regulation: As listed above.
    *   Justifications for rescission:
        *   The 2016 "Dietary Supplements: New Dietary Ingredient Notifications and Related Issues: Guidance for Industry" had problems, including overly broad interpretations of "new" dietary ingredients and chemical alteration, retroactive application, confidentiality/IP risks, lack of clear review standards, and ingredient vs. finished product submission requirements.
        *   While FDA is prioritizing and segmenting the finalization of the 2016 draft guidance, the updated sections (April 2024 draft, March 2024 final, April 2024 draft master file guidance) continue to impose inappropriate burdens.
        *   These guidances impose regulatory burdens that exceed the statutory intent of the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994 (DSHEA).
        *   The New Dietary Ingredient (NDI) guidance interprets DSHEA in a way that expands FDA’s authority beyond Congressional intent and imposes unnecessarily burdensome premarket obligations resembling a drug-like regulatory framework.
        *   The final guidance, "Dietary Supplements: New Dietary Ingredient Notification Procedures and Timeframes: Guidance for Industry," requires a separate NDIN for *each individual dietary supplement product* containing the same NDI.
        *   The draft guidance, "New Dietary Ingredient Notification Master Files for Dietary Supplements: Guidance for Industry," introduces a "master file" concept similar to the drug master file (DMF) process for drug active ingredients.
            *   This "master file" process seemingly implements the requirement for each individual product to submit an NDIN by allowing manufacturers to reference NDI "master files."
        *   Requiring an NDIN for each individual product containing the same NDI is inconsistent with the statutory framework of section 413 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (21 U.S.C. § 350b).
            *   The statute states that the "manufacturer or distributor of the dietary ingredient or dietary supplement provides the Secretary…", which can reasonably refer to a single ingredient dietary supplement.
            *   Congress recognized that an NDIN need not be submitted for every dietary supplement containing an NDI; rather, a supplier of a dietary ingredient may submit the NDIN.
        *   FDA has disregarded this statutory language, creating a drug-like regulatory regime inconsistent with DSHEA and Congress’ determination that dietary supplements are a subcategory of food.
        *   An ingredient-based approach to safety is consistent with GRAS (generally recognized as safe) ingredient notifications, which rely solely on ingredient safety, not each food product.
        *   Considering the vast number of dietary ingredients and potential products, requiring an NDIN for every dietary supplement containing an NDI is inconsistent with regulatory efficiency and proportionality, and imposes undue burden on industry and FDA itself.
        *   This current requirement imposes redundant administrative costs and creates barriers to innovation and market entry.
        *   A more appropriate approach would allow for ingredient-based notifications, permitting multiple individual products to rely on a single, well-supported NDIN.
        *   Rescinding these three guidances and redrafting the 2016 draft guidance, incorporating industry feedback, current practices, and safety data, would restore regulatory balance, realign policy with DSHEA, and foster innovation, investment, and consumer access.
    *   Reasons for rescission: (1) inconsistent with statute; (3) costs outweigh benefits; (5) bad policy, unreasoned, or unsound (scientifically).
    *   Proposed C.F.R. text after rescission: N/A (as these are guidances, not C.F.R. provisions).
    *   Agency Head: Martin A. Makary, Commissioner of Food and Drugs.

*   **III. Health Claims: General Requirements – General Health Claim Labeling Requirements**
    *   Agency: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
    *   Section to be rescinded: 21 C.F.R. § 101.14 (d)(2)(iv) – General health claim labeling requirements
    *   Type of rule: Final Rule
    *   Name of regulation: Health Claims: General Requirements, General health claim labeling requirements
    *   Justifications for rescission:
        *   The Nutrition Labeling and Education Act of 1990 (NLEA) defines a health claim as characterizing the relationship of a nutrient to a disease or health-related condition.
        *   Section 403(r) of the FD&C Act (21 U.S.C. § 343(r)) and relevant regulations (21 C.F.R. §§ 101.14, 101.70–71) permit health claims when FDA approves based on "totality of publicly available scientific evidence" and "significant scientific agreement."
        *   FDA-permitted health claims (21 C.F.R. §§ 101.72 to 101.83) are lengthy.
        *   Permitting abbreviated forms of these health claims can enhance consumer understanding without compromising scientific integrity, especially for front-of-pack labeling on dietary supplements.
        *   If FDA supports the full claim scientifically, a shortened version, clearly marked with an asterisk directing consumers to the complete claim, should not be considered misleading.
    *   Reasons for rescission: (5) bad policy and unreasoned.
    *   Proposed C.F.R. text after revisions to 21 C.F.R. § 101.4(d)(2)(iv):
        *   All information required to be included in the claim appears in one place without other intervening material, except that the principal display panel of the label or labeling may bear an abbreviated health claim, provided that the abbreviated health claim is a truthful and not misleading summary of the authorized claim; and the abbreviated claim includes a clear reference, such as an asterisk, directing consumers to the complete claim elsewhere in labeling. the reference statement, “See ______ for information about the relationship between ______ and ______,” with the blanks filled in with the location of the labeling containing the health claim, the name of the substance, and the disease or health-related condition (e.g., “See attached pamphlet for information about calcium and osteoporosis”), with the entire claim appearing elsewhere on the other labeling, Provided that, where any graphic material (e.g., a heart symbol) constituting an explicit or implied health claim appears on the label or labeling, the reference statement or the complete claim shall appear in immediate proximity to such graphic material;
    *   Agency Head: Martin A. Makary, Commissioner of Food and Drugs.

*   **IV. Small Entity Compliance Guide on Structure/Function Claims**
    *   Agency: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)
    *   Guidance to be rescinded: Small Entity Compliance Guide on Structure/Function Claims
    *   Type of guidance: Guidance
    *   Name of regulation: Small Entity Compliance Guide on Structure/Function Claims
    *   Justifications for rescission:
        *   The Guidance discusses factors FDA applies to determine whether a claim is a structure/function claim or a disease claim.
        *   The Guidance states that heart symbols (with and without an EKG line) are ordinarily implied disease claims.
            *   However, these symbols can imply heart health and are commonly used in the dietary supplement industry to represent heart health, and do not imply disease unless accompanied by claims or other depictions that convey disease.
        *   Similarly, the Guidance states that claims about maintaining intestinal flora in people on antibiotics are disease claims because they imply prevention of pathogenic bacterial overgrowth (a disease condition).
            *   However, current science supports that probiotics can help maintain healthy or normal intestinal flora for those taking antibiotics.
            *   This effect is distinct from preventing bacterial overgrowth and does not imply disease treatment.
    *   Reasons for rescission: (2) inconsistent with the Constitution (implied due to speech restrictions); (5) bad policy, unreasoned, or unsound (scientifically).
    *   Proposed Guidance text after revisions:
        *   Are there some symbols that are implied disease claims?
            *   Yes. Some symbols, like the heart symbol, are so widely recognized as symbols for disease treatment and prevention that their use is ordinarily an implied disease claim. Symbols such as EKG tracings are also implied disease claims because they are strongly associated with heart disease and the average consumer cannot distinguish a healthy tracing from an unhealthy one to provide context to remove the implied disease treatment or prevention claim. It would be an unusual circumstance in which the use of these two symbols would not be implied disease claims.
        *   Criterion 9: Claims to treat, prevent, or mitigate adverse events associated with a therapy for a disease (see section R, starting on page 1029 of the preamble to the rule).
            *   A claim that a product will affect adverse events associated with a therapy for disease is a disease claim if the adverse event is itself a disease. For example, "to maintain the intestinal flora in people on antibiotics" is a disease claim because the a claim that implies that the product will prevent pathogenic bacterial overgrowth (a disease condition) associated with antibiotic use is a disease claim. If the adverse event is not a disease, then this type of claim is acceptable. For example, a claim that a product is useful because it counterbalances the effect of a drug in depleting a nutrient or interfering with the metabolism of a nutrient would be an acceptable structure/function claim.
    *   Agency Head: Martin A. Makary, Commissioner of Food and Drugs.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: KKB, on behalf of its client in the consumer health products industry, urges HHS and FDA to rescind or revise specific regulations and guidances related to medical foods, dietary supplement notifications, and labeling claims, arguing they are unduly burdensome, scientifically outdated, and inconsistent with statutory intent, hindering innovation and access to products promoting health.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
-   **Name/Organization:** KKB
-   **Type:** Organization (Law Firm)
-   **Role/Expertise:** Represents a client in the consumer health products industry, providing legal and regulatory expertise on federal regulations concerning dietary supplements and functional foods.
-   **Geographic Scope:** National (based in Washington, DC, representing clients affected by federal regulations).
-   **Stake in Issue:** Represents businesses involved in the development, marketing, and distribution of consumer health products, whose ability to innovate and provide products to Americans is directly impacted by the clarity, burden, and consistency of current FDA regulations and guidances.
structuredSections.corePosition: We believe that current regulations and guidances from the FDA, particularly concerning medical foods, new dietary ingredients, and health/structure/function claims, are often inconsistent with statutory intent, scientifically outdated, and unnecessarily burdensome. These restrictive interpretations and requirements hinder the consumer health product industry's ability to innovate and provide products that align with national public health goals, ultimately limiting consumer access to beneficial health and wellness solutions.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
*   **Rescind 21 C.F.R. §§ 101.9(j)(8)(ii) & (iii) and the March 2023 Guidance for Industry: Frequently Asked Questions About Medical Foods – Third Edition.**
    *   Rationale: Current interpretations are unjustifiably narrow and do not fully account for clinical and practical realities of dietary management, nor do they align with advances in nutritional science regarding non-nutrient bioactives, thus restricting patient access.
*   **Rescind the three guidances related to New Dietary Ingredient (NDI) notifications and master files.**
    *   Dietary Supplements: New Dietary Ingredient Notifications and Related Issues: Guidance for Industry (Draft Guidance) (April 2024)
    *   Dietary Supplements: New Dietary Ingredient Notification Procedures and Timeframes: Guidance for Industry (March 2024)
    *   New Dietary Ingredient Notification Master Files for Dietary Supplements: Guidance for Industry (Draft Guidance) (April 2024)
    *   Rationale: These guidances exceed statutory intent, impose drug-like premarket burdens, require redundant product-specific notifications instead of ingredient-based ones, and create undue administrative costs and barriers to innovation.
    *   Recommendation also includes: Initiating a comprehensive redrafting process of the 2016 draft guidance, incorporating industry feedback, current practices, and safety data.
*   **Revise 21 C.F.R. § 101.14(d)(2)(iv) to permit abbreviated health claims on labels.**
    *   Rationale: Abbreviated claims enhance consumer understanding without compromising scientific integrity, especially for front-of-pack labeling, provided they are truthful, not misleading, and direct consumers to the full claim.
*   **Revise the Small Entity Compliance Guide on Structure/Function Claims.**
    *   Rationale: The guidance's interpretations regarding heart symbols and claims related to maintaining intestinal flora with antibiotics are inconsistent with common understanding, current science, and unnecessarily classify non-disease claims as implied disease claims.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
*   **Overly Narrow Interpretation of Medical Foods:** The FDA's current definition limits medical foods to conditions not manageable by diet modification alone and restricts "distinctive nutritional requirements" to "nutrients," excluding functional impairments and beneficial bioactives like probiotics. This unduly restricts patient access to clinically appropriate nutritional interventions.
*   **Burdensome and Misaligned NDI Regulations:** The FDA's NDI guidances are seen as expanding FDA's authority beyond DSHEA's intent, creating a "drug-like regulatory framework" for dietary supplements.
    *   Concerns include overly broad interpretations of "new" dietary ingredients, retroactive application, confidentiality risks, lack of clear review standards, and requiring a separate notification for each individual dietary supplement product containing the same NDI, rather than an ingredient-based approach.
    *   This leads to redundant administrative costs, barriers to innovation, and inefficiency for both industry and the agency.
*   **Restrictive Health Claim Labeling Requirements:** Current regulations for health claims result in lengthy and complex statements that can hinder consumer understanding, especially for front-of-pack labeling. The prohibition of abbreviated claims prevents more effective consumer communication without loss of scientific integrity.
*   **Scientifically Outdated Structure/Function Claim Guidance:** The guidance misclassifies common symbols (e.g., heart symbol) and scientifically supported effects (e.g., probiotics maintaining intestinal flora during antibiotic use) as implied disease claims. This is out of step with current scientific understanding and common industry practice.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
*   The insight that while certain conditions might theoretically be managed through diet alone, numerous practical barriers (limited access, affordability, palatability, complexity) can significantly impair a patient's ability to meet their distinctive nutritional requirements, making specially formulated medical foods clinically appropriate and necessary.
*   The observation that FDA's medical food definition relies on a narrow, essential-nutrient model that does not align with advances in nutritional science, which recognizes the critical role of non-nutrient bioactives like probiotics in managing diseases and conditions.
*   The critical analysis that the FDA's new "master file" concept for New Dietary Ingredient Notifications, while seemingly helpful, still reinforces the burdensome requirement for product-specific NDINs, thereby creating a regulatory regime "quite similar to the long-established drug master file (DMF) process" but inconsistent with DSHEA's intent for dietary supplements.
*   The argument that "abbreviated forms of these health claims can enhance consumer understanding without compromising scientific integrity" and are particularly suitable for front-of-pack labeling, suggesting a practical solution for effective consumer communication.
*   The assertion that current science supports the fact that probiotics can help maintain healthy or normal intestinal flora for those taking antibiotics, and that this effect is distinct from preventing bacterial overgrowth, meaning it should not be classified as a disease claim.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
*   "A more inclusive interpretation consistent with the controlling statutory definition, one that recognizes both the clinical and practical dimensions of dietary management, is essential to ensure that patients with legitimate nutritional needs are not excluded from access to medical foods due to overly restrictive regulatory interpretation."
*   "The NDI guidance interprets DSHEA in a manner that expands FDA’s authority beyond what Congress intended and imposes unnecessarily burdensome premarket obligations that resemble a drug-like regulatory framework."
*   "Rescinding these three guidances and initiating a comprehensive redrafting process of the 2016 draft guidance, incorporating industry feedback, current practices and safety data, would serve to restore regulatory balance, realign agency policy with the original intent of Congress as articulated in DSHEA, and foster a regulatory environment that supports innovation, investment, and consumer access within the dietary supplement sector."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
-   As an early childhood advocate and Head Start employee for over 26 years, I appreciate the opportunity to offer information in response to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS’s) recent Request for Information (RFI) on “Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.”
-   Prenatal-to-five programs like Head Start/Early Head Start provide locally controlled, community-driven services to families in every state.
-   The regulations and standards that HHS creates for the early care and learning field are critical to continued service to families and accountability for taxpayer-funded programs.
    -   They provide important guidance to the state- and community-based organizations that are entrusted with carrying out critical services.
    -   They promote program consistency, quality, accountability, and continuous improvement.
-   While every Head Start program is designed to meet the needs of their own community, performance standards provide the guidance necessary to ensure that we are both accountable for federal dollars and providing the essential services necessary to most effectively support children and families.
-   I strongly caution HHS against broad removal of accountability measures with the following key considerations:
    -   Ensuring Success in All States and Communities:
        -   In early childhood services, accountability measures from HHS uphold key pillars like program quality, child safety, and workforce supports.
        -   These ensure that the taxpayer-funded programs that yield positive outcomes can be replicated in all types of communities – rural, urban, exurban, suburban, and tribal.
        -   HHS’s standards are a critical tool for ensuring consistently positive outcomes across the U.S.’s vast range of geographies.
    -   Honoring Parent Choice:
        -   Local Systems of Care:
            -   Communities across the country have shaped their early care and learning and maternal health landscapes to be responsive to the needs of parents in their local community.
            -   Standards and accountability measures from HHS provide a key framework from which communities can operate to implement services that are consistent in quality and unique in the specific services, delivery methods, and curriculum they offer in response to parent input.
            -   I urge HHS to uphold standards as essential frameworks that communities build and innovate from.
            -   These standards allow parents the opportunity to take advantage of community services with the confidence that HHS is holding programs accountable on quality and safety.
        -   Family Leadership:
            -   In order to preserve parents’ rights to choose the best education for their child starting in the earliest years, I strongly urge HHS to maintain a robust public comment process on regulations pertaining to maternal health and child and family services.
                -   This will allow families to engage with HHS to create the types of early care and learning opportunities that will best align with their personal views on the type of early childhood education they want their child to receive.
            -   I strongly urge HHS to uphold the integrity of family leadership and feedback loop opportunities that are embedded into the structures of child and family services, including Head Start Parent Policy Councils and Head Start and Child Care Development Block Grant and Maternal, Infant, Early Childhood Home Visiting program community needs assessments.
            -   These opportunities to inform accountability measures and policies play a critical role in uncovering and promoting parent choice in early care and learning and maternal health services.
    -   Preserve Accountability for Public Funds:
        -   Through its standards, HHS supports state- and community-based entities in remaining accountable to their communities and to the federal government by requiring public disclosure around the use of federal funds.
        -   This is a critical function of regulations that I urge HHS to maintain, as it re-enforces principles that child and family serving services consider core to their mission: transparency, fiscal integrity, and accountability to families.

-   Uphold the integrity of family leadership and feedback loop opportunities embedded into service structures.
    -   Specifically mentioning Head Start Parent Policy Councils and community needs assessments for Head Start, Child Care Development Block Grant, and Maternal, Infant, Early Childhood Home Visiting programs.

-   Broad removal of accountability measures could undermine key pillars of early childhood services, including program quality, child safety, and workforce supports.
-   Weakening HHS standards could jeopardize the consistent replication of positive outcomes across the U.S.'s diverse geographies (rural, urban, exurban, suburban, tribal).
-   Erosion of parent choice if standards no longer provide confidence that programs are held accountable for quality and safety.
-   Compromising family leadership and feedback loop opportunities that are vital for families to shape early care and learning services.
-   Failure to preserve accountability for public funds, risking transparency and fiscal integrity in child and family serving services.

-   The commenter's 26 years of experience as a Head Start employee provides significant long-term perspective on the practical impact of regulations.
-   An insightful perspective that HHS standards serve as "essential frameworks that communities build and innovate from," rather than stifling local responsiveness.
-   Emphasis that accountability measures are crucial for ensuring positive outcomes can be replicated across "all types of communities – rural, urban, exurban, suburban, and tribal," highlighting the broad applicability and necessity of consistent standards.

submitter: National Association of Long Term Hospitals

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The National Association of Long-Term Hospitals (NALTH) is the only hospital trade association devoted exclusively to the needs of medically complex patients requiring services from long-term acute care hospitals (LTCHs).
*   NALTH is committed to research, education, and public policy development that furthers the interests of very ill and often debilitated patient populations receiving services in LTCHs nationwide.
*   In May 2025, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) launched a public Request for Information (RFI) to identify and eliminate outdated or unnecessary regulations.
*   The American Hospital Association (AHA) responded to this RFI, sharing 100 recommendations to reduce burden on hospitals and health systems, grouped into four categories: Billing, Payment and Other Administrative Requirements; Quality and Patient Safety; Telehealth; and Workforce.
*   On behalf of its members, which include the nation’s leading LTCHs (free-standing, hospital-within-hospital, for-profit, and non-profit), NALTH applauds the Trump administration’s efforts to identify and eliminate outdated and unnecessary regulations and supports AHA’s response.
*   In addition to AHA’s recommendations, NALTH has shared several specific areas where the administration could reduce the regulatory burden on LTCHs.
*   Excessive and Unnecessary Regulatory Burdens Place LTCHs at High Risk for Closure and Reduced Beneficiary Access
    *   LTCHs play a special role in caring for the most complex patients, with staff and resources to treat those too medically complex for many other settings.
    *   LTCHs must satisfy the same Medicare Conditions of Participation (CoP) as short-term acute care hospitals (STACHs).
    *   There are currently fewer than 330 LTCHs operating in the U.S., with more than 90 LTCHs closing since 2017 following the implementation of the site-neutral policy.
    *   Address Failed Payment Methodologies for High-cost Outlier Cases:
        *   Current Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) payment structures do not adequately reflect the rising costs associated with inflation, labor shortages, and increased expenses for equipment and supplies.
        *   The high-cost outlier (HCO) fixed-loss threshold creates financial strain on providers delivering complex care to the most critically ill.
        *   To limit potential negative consequences from a rapidly rising HCO fixed-loss threshold, policymakers could take several steps:
            *   In the short term, limit the increase in the HCO fixed-loss threshold to minimize disruptions to LTCH care.
            *   Further identify the underlying causes for the growth in the LTCH PPS HCO fixed-loss threshold to help target solutions.
            *   Consider alternative approaches to calculating the HCO fixed-loss threshold.
            *   Assess approaches to improve the payment accuracy for LTACH cases, particularly for the highest acuity cases, including modifying the MS-LTC-DRGs.
        *   Without policy interventions, access to LTACH care for the most critically ill and medically complex Medicare beneficiaries may be negatively impacted.
    *   Reduce Burden of Quality Reporting through Measure Alignment and Prioritization:
        *   Over the past few years, the LTCH Care Data Set has nearly doubled in size.
        *   CMS has consistently underestimated the additional effort required to incorporate new requirements for new measures, some of which are of uncertain value to patients and providers.
        *   Quality reporting requirements should be aligned with the actual care being delivered and focused on improving patient outcomes, being meaningful without placing undue administrative burden on providers.
        *   NALTH urges CMS to remove burdensome social determinants of health, cognitive, and depression screening data elements such as A1005 (Ethnicity), A1010 (Race), A1100 (Language), A1250 (Transportation), B1300 (Health Literacy), and D0700 (Social Isolation).
        *   NALTH members have experienced that asking these personal and intrusive questions of patients, their families, or caregivers can result in annoyance, agitation, and even threats of violence, particularly when these or similar questions have already been asked by the short-term hospital.
        *   CMS should remove these and other data elements that impose unnecessary burden on patients and staff at LTCHs.
        *   NALTH also encourages CMS to consider all aspects of data collection and reporting costs and to prioritize the appropriateness of the measures selected in terms of accountability of the reporting entity and suitability of the measures to the patient population over alignment with other reporting programs.
    *   Fix Excess Burdens Associated with 25-Day Average Length of Stay Requirement:
        *   To be recognized as an LTCH by CMS, a hospital must have an average Medicare inpatient length of stay (ALOS) of greater than 25 days (including all covered and noncovered days).
        *   The length of stay requirement is intended to differentiate LTCHs from short-term acute care hospitals (STACHs) and is the primary mechanism to ensure LTCHs admit high acuity cases.
        *   However, the threshold has remained fixed at 25 days despite treatment advances and significant reductions in the ALOS at short-term acute care hospitals over the last several years.
        *   As a result, the ALOS requirement has become an important barrier for traditional Medicare beneficiaries to access LTCH care.
        *   NALTH urges CMS to reconsider the 25-day ALOS requirement.
        *   Specifically, NALTH requests that short-stay outlier cases that expire in LTCHs, or were discharged to a hospice or against medical advice, be excluded from the 25-day ALOS requirement calculation.
    *   Reduce Burdens Associated with the LTCH Qualifying Period:
        *   To be classified as an LTCH, a Medicare-certified hospital must demonstrate an ALOS of greater than 25 days for at least five consecutive months within a designated six-month assessment window.
        *   After that period, the hospital may request an exemption from its current payment system (i.e., Inpatient Prospective Payment System) and be classified as an LTCH.
        *   NALTH members find this six-month qualifying period significantly burdensome as LTCHs are paid at short-term acute care hospital rates (under the IPPS) during the demonstration period, while their ALOS (and costs) far exceed those in IPPS hospitals.
        *   Inpatient Rehabilitation Facilities (IRFs), which are also certified as acute care hospitals similar to LTCHs, are certified under a different process that allows these facilities to be paid under the Medicare IRF payment system much sooner than an LTCH can be paid under the Medicare LTCH payment system.
        *   NALTH requests that CMS align its approach for certifying an LTCH for payment purposes with the approach used for IRFs.
    *   Streamline Administrative Processes for Prior Authorization and Denial Management:
        *   Simplifying prior authorization and denial management processes is critical.
        *   A more efficient payment system would allow providers to focus on delivering high-quality care rather than navigating bureaucratic hurdles.
        *   Specifically, eliminate the following:
            *   The requirement that physicians need to sign the 90-day plan of care.
            *   The duplicative requirement for outpatient therapy time in billing (i.e., requirements to note CPT codes, number of minutes, and the time of day in/time of day out of the session).
            *   The KX modifier process.
*   NALTH appreciates the opportunity to submit these comments.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The National Association of Long-Term Hospitals (NALTH) supports federal efforts to reduce healthcare regulations, but specifically advocates for critical changes to payment methodologies, quality reporting, length-of-stay requirements, qualifying periods, and administrative processes that disproportionately burden LTCHs and threaten patient access.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** National Association of Long Term Hospitals (NALTH)
- **Type:** Trade Association
- **Role/Expertise:** The only hospital trade association exclusively devoted to the needs of medically complex patients requiring services from long-term acute care hospitals (LTCHs), representing the nation's leading free-standing, hospital-within-hospital, for-profit, and non-profit LTCHs; committed to research, education, and public policy development.
- **Geographic Scope:** National
- **Stake in Issue:** Represents long-term acute care hospitals (LTCHs) whose operations, financial viability, and ability to provide access to care for critically ill and medically complex Medicare beneficiaries are directly impacted by the discussed federal regulations and payment methodologies. They argue that current regulations place LTCHs "at High Risk for Closure and Reduced Beneficiary Access."
structuredSections.corePosition: The National Association of Long-Term Hospitals applauds the administration's efforts to identify and eliminate outdated and unnecessary regulations and supports the American Hospital Association's broad recommendations. However, we specifically advocate for targeted regulatory changes that address the unique and excessive burdens faced by long-term acute care hospitals, which currently jeopardize their operations and patient access. Our aim is to ensure payment accuracy, reduce administrative overhead, and allow providers to focus on delivering high-quality care to the most complex patients.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- **Address Failed Payment Methodologies for High-cost Outlier Cases:**
    - In the short term, limit the increase in the High-Cost Outlier (HCO) fixed-loss threshold to minimize disruptions to LTCH care.
    - Further identify the underlying causes for the growth in the LTCH Prospective Payment System (PPS) HCO fixed-loss threshold to help target solutions.
    - Consider alternative approaches to calculating the HCO fixed-loss threshold.
    - Assess approaches to improve the payment accuracy for LTCH cases, particularly for the highest acuity cases, including modifying the MS-LTC-DRGs.
- **Reduce Burden of Quality Reporting through Measure Alignment and Prioritization:**
    - Urge CMS to remove burdensome social determinants of health, cognitive, and depression screening data elements (e.g., Ethnicity, Race, Language, Transportation, Health Literacy, Social Isolation) from the LTCH Care Data Set.
    - Encourage CMS to consider all aspects of data collection and reporting costs and to prioritize the appropriateness of measures selected based on accountability and suitability to the patient population, rather than solely alignment with other reporting programs.
- **Fix Excess Burdens Associated with 25-Day Average Length of Stay Requirement:**
    - Reconsider the 25-day average length of stay (ALOS) requirement for LTCH recognition.
    - Exclude short-stay outlier cases (patients who expire in LTCHs, or are discharged to hospice or against medical advice) from the 25-day ALOS requirement calculation.
- **Reduce Burdens Associated with the LTCH Qualifying Period:**
    - Align CMS's approach for certifying an LTCH for payment purposes with the approach used for Inpatient Rehabilitation Facilities (IRFs).
- **Streamline Administrative Processes for Prior Authorization and Denial Management:**
    - Eliminate the requirement for physicians to sign the 90-day plan of care.
    - Eliminate the duplicative requirement for outpatient therapy time in billing (e.g., noting CPT codes, number of minutes, and time in/out of the session).
    - Eliminate the KX modifier process.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Inadequate Payment for High-Cost, Complex Cases:** Current CMS payment structures, particularly the High-Cost Outlier (HCO) fixed-loss threshold, do not adequately reflect rising costs due to inflation, labor shortages, and increased expenses for equipment and supplies, creating significant financial strain on providers delivering complex care.
- **Risk of LTCH Closures and Reduced Beneficiary Access:** Excessive and unnecessary regulatory burdens, combined with payment inadequacies, place LTCHs at high risk for closure, with over 90 LTCHs having closed since 2017, potentially negatively impacting Medicare beneficiaries' access to critical care.
- **Burdensome and Inefficient Quality Reporting:** The LTCH Care Data Set has nearly doubled in size, imposing additional effort for new requirements that CMS consistently underestimates, with some measures being of uncertain value to patients and providers.
- **Patient and Staff Distress from Intrusive Data Collection:** Members report that asking personal and intrusive social determinants of health, cognitive, and depression screening questions (e.g., ethnicity, race, language, transportation, health literacy, social isolation) can cause annoyance, agitation, and even threats of violence from patients, their families, or caregivers, especially if previously asked by short-term hospitals.
- **Outdated and Restrictive Length of Stay Requirement:** The fixed 25-day average length of stay (ALOS) requirement, unchanged despite treatment advances and reduced ALOS in short-term hospitals, has become a significant barrier for traditional Medicare beneficiaries to access LTCH care.
- **Burdensome and Costly LTCH Qualifying Period:** The requirement to demonstrate an ALOS greater than 25 days for five consecutive months while being paid at lower short-term acute care hospital rates (IPPS) during a six-month qualifying period creates a significant financial burden for new LTCHs, unlike the more streamlined certification process for Inpatient Rehabilitation Facilities (IRFs).
- **Inefficient Administrative Processes:** Current prior authorization and denial management processes are overly bureaucratic, diverting provider focus from delivering high-quality care.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- NALTH highlights that over 90 LTCHs have closed since 2017, linking this directly to the implementation of the site-neutral policy and underscoring the severe impact of current regulatory and payment environments.
- A distinctive insight is the reported negative patient and staff experience related to specific quality reporting data elements (A1005, A1010, A1100, A1250, B1300, D0700). NALTH members have observed that asking these "personal and intrusive questions" can lead to "annoyance and sometimes lead to agitation and even threats of violence" from patients, their families, or caregivers, particularly when the questions are duplicative of those already asked by short-term hospitals.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "There are currently fewer than 330 LTCHs operating in the U.S., with more than 90 LTCHs closing since 2017 and the implementation of the site-neutral policy."
- "NALTH members have experienced that asking these personal and intrusive questions of patients, their families or caregivers can result – particularly when they have already been asked these or similar questions by the short-term hospital –in annoyance and sometimes lead to agitation and even threats of violence."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The Federation of American Hospitals (FAH) represents nearly 1,000 leading tax-paying hospitals and health systems throughout the United States.
    *   FAH members provide patients and communities with access to high quality, affordable care in both urban and rural areas across 46 states, plus Washington, DC, and Puerto Rico.
    *   Our members include teaching, acute, inpatient rehabilitation, behavioral health, and long-term care hospitals and provide a wide range of inpatient, ambulatory, post-acute, emergency, children’s, and cancer services.
*   The FAH commends HHS’ leadership in issuing this Request for Information (RFI).
    *   Many regulations and related requirements divert resources from patient care, contribute to inefficiencies, and create financial strains.
    *   These regulations prevent patients and our health care system from achieving maximum health.
    *   The FAH appreciates the opportunity to provide comments regarding this critical effort to reduce burdensome and unnecessary regulations that divert the focus on patient care.

*   Rein in Abuses of Prior Authorization in Medicare Advantage Plans
    *   The FAH and our members support the Medicare Advantage (MA) program and its ability to offer private options and flexibility beyond Traditional Medicare.
    *   Our members increasingly serve more seniors with MA coverage than through Traditional Medicare fee-for-service.
    *   However, we are increasingly concerned by alarming practices of MA plans that harm patients by eroding access to and affordability of medically necessary care.
    *   Abusive practices by MA plans include systematically inappropriately denying, limiting, and delaying the delivery of services and care.
    *   This behavior often requires hospitals and caregivers to divert precious resources and time to respond to care denials and delay tactics, away from their core mission of patient care.
    *   MA delays and denials through prior authorization and inconsistent administrative processes add tremendous costs to the health care system.
    *   Hospitals and physicians must hire teams of clinical and non-clinical staff, as well as costly information systems, to keep up with the prior authorization and payment hurdles that MA plans erect.
    *   By design, these practices lead to Medicare Advantage beneficiaries receiving a lower standard of appropriate care than those in Traditional Medicare.
    *   We urge HHS and CMS to improve MA by taking steps that would simplify these administrative barriers.
    *   This includes requiring plans to ensure that MA patients receive at least the same levels of coverage as patients in Traditional Medicare.
    *   One easy way to significantly reduce burdensome paperwork, processes, and costs would be to ensure that plans comply with the Medicare Two-Midnight Rule and Inpatient Only List.
    *   This would save time and money for hospitals, physicians, nursing staff, and plans, as well as for Medicare overall.
    *   Medicare beneficiaries that ultimately receive authorization for inpatient admission often face additional hurdles upon discharge.
    *   MA patients that need post-acute care (PAC) often have much longer lengths of stay in the inpatient setting.
    *   This is due to a combination of lengthy PAC prior authorization delays as well as inadequate PAC networks.
    *   For patients, it means they are stuck in the hospital longer than they want or need to be.
    *   For hospitals, it means increased administrative costs trying to access PAC for the patient and unreimbursed costs for care, since most inpatients are paid at a per case rate (using DRGs).
    *   In some cases, it can also lead to denied claims as MA plans deny care that is not “medically necessary” at the end of the stay, even though their inadequate PAC provider networks and lengthy prior authorization processes caused the delay.
    *   These overly burdensome and varied MA practices are a rich opportunity for HHS regulatory relief efforts.
    *   We also urge HHS and CMS to track and report prior authorization denials and appeals at discrete service levels and provide this information to Medicare enrollees.
    *   Doing this will add transparency to the MA prior authorization processes and allow seniors to be informed of their practices and more easily choose plans they know will cover the care they need.

*   Reject Site-Neutral Cuts to Medicare
    *   The FAH strongly opposes site neutral cuts to Medicare payments and urges HHS/CMS not to implement such a payment strategy in the guise of regulatory relief.
    *   This is especially critical in light of the $1.1 trillion in devastating health care cuts included in the recently enacted budget reconciliation bill, HR 1, that will leave an estimated 11.8 million people uninsured.
    *   Site neutral payments will only exacerbate this coverage gap and leave many more patients without access to care.
    *   Focusing solely on payment rates, site neutrality does not account for the significant regulatory burdens and 24/7 essential services provided by hospitals to sicker patients that need higher resource care.
    *   Thus, site neutrality would be a short-sighted and flawed approach to regulatory relief and threatens to compromise patient access to care.
    *   Specifically, site-neutral payments do not consider one simple fact: hospitals and doctors' offices are not the same.
    *   Hospitals require a different payment structure because they provide critical services to communities including 24/7/365 access to emergency care, disaster and trauma response, and treatment of high-acuity patients.
    *   Hospital-affiliated sites offer patients more integrated care across health care settings, services for which hospitals need proper payment to maintain coordinated, high-quality care for patients.
    *   Hospital outpatient departments (HOPDs) treat more underserved populations and sicker, more complex patients than other ambulatory care sites.
        *   A study by the American Hospital Association, as updated in January 2025, indicates that relative to patients seen in independent physician offices and ambulatory surgical centers, Medicare patients seen in HOPDs tend to be:
            *   Lower-income.
            *   From medically underserved populations.
            *   Eligible for Medicare based on disability and/or end-stage renal disease.
            *   More severe comorbidities or complications.
            *   Dually-eligible for Medicare and Medicaid.
            *   Previously seen in an emergency department or hospital setting.
    *   In addition, hospitals also are held to more rigorous licensing, accreditation, and regulatory requirements.
    *   Implementing site-neutral payment policies could force outpatient clinics to close or cut back on critical services, resulting in reduced patient access and job losses.
    *   Notably, on average, Medicare pays only 82 cents for every dollar of hospital care provided to Medicare beneficiaries, leaving hospitals with nearly $100 billion in Medicare shortfalls.
    *   As a result, two-thirds of all hospitals report negative Medicare margins.
    *   Additional site-neutral cuts will only exacerbate these shortfalls and reduce access to care for seniors.
    *   Therefore, it is vital that payment for outpatient services provided in HOPDs reflects the higher overhead costs associated with providing care in that setting.
    *   We urge HHS/CMS to reject a site-neutral approach for Medicare hospital payment, which would reduce patient access to care and further contribute to Medicare’s chronic failure to cover the cost of caring for beneficiaries.

*   Eliminate the Inpatient Rehabilitation Facility (IRF) Review Choice Demonstration (RCD)
    *   HHS should eliminate CMS’ IRF RCD program that requires pre-payment review of 100 percent of all IRF admissions in Alabama and Pennsylvania.
    *   The IRF RCD program began in Alabama with 100 percent prior authorization review of all IRF admissions.
    *   More than 85 percent of claims received during the first one and a half years of this program receive approval, and appeals raise the total approval rate even higher.
    *   This program is administratively burdensome for CMS and IRFs and is unnecessary.
    *   The program is slated for expansion to California and Texas IRFs and will ultimately be expanded to IRFs in other states that use the same MACs in the four RCD states.
    *   HHS should eliminate this costly and unnecessary program.

*   Enforce No Surprises Act (NSA) Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) Process
    *   Hospitals fully support the surprise billing patient protections under the NSA.
    *   We urge the Administration and HHS, however, to enforce health insurer compliance with the NSA, including the IDR process.
    *   The IDR process establishes a mechanism intended to resolve insurer-provider disputes over payment for certain out-of-network services.
    *   Appropriate incentives must be implemented to ensure that health insurers:
        *   Provide greater payment transparency.
        *   Meaningfully participate in the IDR 30-day open negotiation process.
        *   Timely, appropriately, and efficiently pay out-of-network amounts and any related IDR awards.
        *   Are subject to enforcement for noncompliance.
    *   Without appropriate incentives for health insurers, the NSA’s IDR process is broken, ineffective, and anticompetitive for hospitals vis-à-vis health insurers.
    *   Insurers’ ability to bypass the requirements for the NSA IDR process presents an anticompetitive dynamic in hospital and other provider negotiations with insurers.
    *   Insurers can threaten to bar provider participation in their networks knowing the provider would then be subject to the broken and anticompetitive IDR dispute resolution for out-of-network claims.
    *   We urge HHS to adopt its pending proposed rule containing provisions intended to establish an IDR process, with appropriate incentives, for health insurers as envisioned by the NSA when enacted in December 2020.

*   Nursing Staff Ratio Interpretations in Conditions of Participation
    *   CMS has issued interpretive guidance under 42 C.F.R. § 482.23(b), governing nursing services, that increasingly reflect rigid expectations around nurse-to-patient ratios.
    *   The FAH strongly opposes any move toward implementing specific ratios in regulation or sub-regulatory guidance.
    *   Section 1861(e) of the Social Security Act allows CMS to ensure that hospitals maintain adequate nursing services to meet patient needs.
    *   However, it does not authorize the agency to mandate fixed ratios irrespective of staffing realities, patient acuity, or local market conditions.
    *   As detailed in our FY 2023 IPPS comments, the imposition of nurse staffing ratios would severely burden hospitals struggling with nursing workforce shortages.
    *   Such mandates may lead to care delays or temporary closures of units, particularly in rural and underserved areas.
    *   Rather than improving care, rigid ratios reduce flexibility and could result in unintended safety risks.
    *   HHS/CMS should rescind interpretive guidance implying ratio requirements and confirm hospital discretion in establishing staffing plans responsive to patient needs.

*   Remove Patient-Reported Outcomes Measure for Hip/Knee Arthroplasty (PRO-PM)
    *   The PRO-PM for Total Hip and Knee Arthroplasty, adopted under the Hospital IQR Program, requires hospitals to collect and submit survey-based patient-reported outcomes before and after surgery.
    *   Although CMS adopted this under the same statutory authority as other IQR measures, the FAH has raised strong concerns in multiple IPPS comment cycles regarding its feasibility, fairness, and alignment with statutory intent.
    *   The implementation of this measure is complex and costly.
    *   Hospitals must procure survey platforms, maintain consistent follow-up processes, and manage response rate bias.
    *   Moreover, these data are heavily influenced by social and demographic variables unrelated to hospital care quality.
    *   Smaller and rural hospitals may lack the technical or staffing capacity to comply, raising significant rural-urban equity issues.
    *   These challenges render the measure incompatible with Section 1886(b)(3)(B)(viii), which envisions accurate and equitable quality assessment across all hospitals.
    *   Until methodological concerns are addressed, HHS/CMS should withdraw the PRO-PM.

*   Remove Low-Value Structural Measures in the Hospital IQR and VBP Programs
    *   CMS has adopted a range of structural measures in the Hospital IQR and Value-Based Purchasing (VBP) Programs, also authorized under Section 1886(b)(3)(B)(viii) of the Social Security Act.
    *   While initially intended to incentivize quality infrastructure, these measures now impose a significant reporting burden with little utility for hospital performance differentiation.
    *   Key structural measures currently implemented in the IQR Program include:
        *   Maternal Morbidity Structural Measure (hospital participation in PQCs and use of safety bundles).
        *   Patient Safety Structural Measure (attestation of safety culture strategies across five domains).
        *   Age-Friendly Hospital Measure (five-domain assessment of geriatric care practices).
    *   Although these measures are well-intentioned, the FAH’s recent FY 2026 IPPS proposed rule comments noted that they present limited variation across hospitals and add burdensome documentation requirements.
    *   Many hospitals already meet the basic expectations of these measures, and there is minimal evidence that they lead to improved outcomes.
    *   For example, the Age-Friendly Hospital measure is primarily a self-attestation exercise, prone to subjective interpretation and lacking rigorous validation.
    *   CMS’ continued use of these structural measures raises questions about statutory alignment.
    *   Section 1886(b)(3)(B)(viii) authorizes the collection of "measures of quality of care," which are more accurately represented by patient outcome measures rather than attestation-based infrastructure inputs.
    *   The FAH recommends that the measures be removed and that outcomes-based, actionable quality indicators be implemented.

*   Remove Hybrid Clinical/Claims-Based Quality Measures
    *   CMS implemented hybrid measures in the Hospital Inpatient Quality Reporting (IQR) Program under the authority of Section 1886(b)(3)(B)(viii) of the Social Security Act.
    *   These measures, including the Hybrid Hospital-Wide Readmission and Mortality Measures, require hospitals to extract and report structured clinical data elements from electronic health records (EHRs) alongside claims data.
    *   The FAH stated in comments on the FY 2023 IPPS proposed rule that these measures present a disproportionate burden with little evidence of added clinical value.
    *   Data elements such as troponin levels, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation are often not captured in structured fields, necessitating costly manual abstraction.
    *   These measures unfairly penalize smaller, resource-constrained hospitals and should be withdrawn until standardized EHR interoperability and infrastructure are universally available.

*   Suspend Hospital Star Ratings and Develop Better Model
    *   The FAH urges HHS/CMS to suspend the Hospital Star Ratings program and initiate a transparent, collaborative process to develop a more accurate and equitable model.
    *   The current Star Ratings oversimplify complex hospital performance data and often mislead patients by failing to reflect important contextual factors, such as the hospital’s case mix, social risk factors, and service lines.
    *   The program’s methodology remains volatile, particularly for smaller, rural, and critical access hospitals, due to the limited number of measures reported and inconsistent peer grouping.
    *   Additionally, hospitals are scored on differing combinations of measure groups, making direct comparisons unreliable and confusing.
    *   Public display of these ratings can unintentionally penalize hospitals that serve high-risk or underserved populations, potentially exacerbating disparities in access and perception.
    *   The FAH recommends that HHS/CMS replace the existing system with one that promotes transparency, reflects clinical realities, and supports informed decision-making without distorting public perception or undermining hospitals committed to serving vulnerable communities.

*   Remove eCQMs from Mandatory Reporting
    *   The FAH urges HHS/CMS to remove the mandatory reporting requirements for electronic clinical quality measures (eCQMs) under both the Hospital Inpatient Quality Reporting (IQR) Program and the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program.
    *   While the FAH supports the broader goal of advancing digital measurement, the current mandates place an outsized burden on hospitals, particularly small, rural, and critical access facilities.
    *   These facilities often lack the health IT infrastructure and technical support needed to comply.
    *   Many of these hospitals use electronic health record systems that are not fully interoperable or cannot extract standardized data without manual abstraction, undermining the efficiency and reliability of the process.
    *   Additionally, the complex data requirements of eCQMs often span multiple clinical domains and care settings, further straining limited staff and resources.
    *   The FAH recommends that HHS/CMS make eCQM reporting voluntary across both programs, allowing hospitals to adopt digital quality reporting in a manner aligned with their technical readiness and resource capacity.

*   Ensure Appropriate Pre-Deployment Testing of all Federal Systems for Collecting and Reporting Hospital Quality Data Both at CMS and CDC
    *   HHS should ensure full testing of any changes to quality measures and the reporting structures to which the data is reported before the new/updated systems are deployed.
    *   Hospitals are required to report a series of quality measures to CMS and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).
    *   FAH members welcome the opportunity to improve patient care and value the feedback received from reporting data.
    *   However, inordinate resources are expended in reporting data to and retrieving data from faulty federal reporting systems.
    *   This year alone, CMS has had to recall preview reports, suspend reporting for several weeks, or change reporting deadlines three times in the first quarter due to problems with QualityNet reporting.
    *   Deploying systems that cannot either accurately receive the data or report data back to hospitals costs both the government and hospitals hundreds of thousands of dollars each year.
    *   Additionally, more robust testing of CDC National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) quality reporting systems prior to deployment of any new upgrade would avoid challenges, downtime, and inability of hospitals to effectively and efficiently retrieve their data to either check that it was recorded appropriately or inform improved patient care.
    *   Each time an upgrade is issued, hospitals experience significant challenges and down time in submitting and retrieving data at CDC.

*   Right-Size CMMI Models and Halt Mandatory Approaches
    *   The FAH urges HHS/CMS to halt the implementation of mandatory models developed by the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI), including the Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM) and the Increasing Organ Transplant Access (IOTA) Model.
    *   The FAH does not believe that section 1115A authorizes HHS/CMS to mandate provider participation in CMMI models such as the TEAM and the IOTA. As such, HHS/CMS should make them voluntary.
    *   CMMI authority is designed to test models and make recommendations to Congress for permanent or mandatory changes to the Medicare program.
    *   Specifically, CMMI’s general authority is to test innovative payment and services delivery models to reduce program expenditures while preserving or enhancing quality of care.
    *   The law further directs HHS/CMS to evaluate CMMI models and, if appropriate, allows HHS/CMS to expand “the scope and duration” of an existing model to a “Phase II,” provided certain requirements are met.
    *   HHS/CMS is required to report periodically to Congress on CMMI models and make proposals for legislative action on models it deems appropriate.
    *   Notably, nowhere does the law expressly state that HHS/CMS can make models mandatory.
    *   While the FAH supports innovation in care delivery and payment, mandating participation in untested or underdeveloped models imposes significant financial and operational risk on providers.
    *   This is especially true during a time of workforce shortages, inflationary cost pressures, and regulatory fatigue.
    *   The TEAM model, scheduled to begin on January 1, 2026, is a mandatory, episode-based payment model.
        *   It requires selected acute care hospitals to coordinate care for patients undergoing specific surgical procedures.
        *   It also requires them to assume responsibility for the cost and quality of care from surgery through the first 30 days post-discharge.
        *   Despite minor technical updates proposed in the FY 2026 IPPS Proposed Rule (e.g., adjustments to quality measures and risk adjustment methodologies), the model's fundamental structure remains unchanged, maintaining significant financial risk for participating hospitals without adequate piloting or stakeholder engagement.
    *   Similarly, the IOTA model, set to commence on July 1, 2025, is a six-year mandatory model aimed at increasing access to kidney transplants for patients with end-stage renal disease.
        *   While CMS has made some adjustments in response to stakeholder feedback (e.g., delaying the start date and modifying performance metrics), the model still imposes substantial operational and financial burdens on transplant hospitals.
        *   Concerns remain regarding the model's potential to incentivize inappropriate organ-recipient matches due to an overemphasis on transplant volume, as well as the lack of sufficient risk adjustment to ensure equity.

*   Provide Payment and Regulatory Flexibility for IRFs in CMMI Bundling Programs
    *   HHS/CMS should provide IRFs an optional, voluntary discount to the standard payment amount, or otherwise enable them to assume more risk, for relevant IRF cases discharged from an acute care hospital participating in a CMMI bundling program.
    *   At the same time, regulatory relief under the 60 Percent Rule and Three-hour Rule should be granted to provide IRFs treating these patients at payments below the current IRF prospective payment system rates.
    *   This flexibility is needed to participate in the program without jeopardizing their Medicare status.
    *   This shared accountability payment model would strengthen the relationship between acute care hospitals and IRFs and reduce costs by enabling IRFs to pass along savings from accepting payments lower than the IRF discharge-based PPS.

*   Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program
    *   We urge HHS to phase out or significantly simplify the Promoting Interoperability Program (formerly Meaningful Use).
    *   While it once played a vital role in advancing health information technology, its continued complexity adds administrative burden without delivering proportional value.
    *   Should the program continue, we propose the following recommendations to enhance its efficiency and reduce unnecessary complexity:
        *   Phase In Higher Program Scoring Thresholds:
            *   A passing score above 70 may disadvantage smaller hospitals, particularly those without access to a national Health Information Exchange (HIE) and unable to earn full points for the HIE Objective.
            *   Instead of increasing the scoring threshold to 70 in the 2025 reporting year and 80 in the 2026 reporting year, we recommend gradually increasing the threshold by 5–10 points over several years.
            *   This would allow time for resource allocation and reduce compliance burden.
        *   Allow Flexibility in Public Health Data Exchange Progression:
            *   The FY2023 IPPS final rule requires eligible hospitals and critical access hospitals (CAHs) to advance from Option 1: Pre-production and Validation to Option 2: Validated Data Production after just one reporting period per measure.
            *   However, since this rule was implemented, public health agencies (PHAs) have faced resource and capacity constraints, making it difficult to support timely onboarding, testing, and validation across all required data types.
            *   These limitations have caused delays in establishing standard connections.
            *   As CMS acknowledged in the FY 2016 IPPS final rule, hospitals should not be held accountable for factors beyond their control, particularly the readiness and technical capabilities of PHAs.
        *   Expand Exclusions for Onboarding Challenges:
            *   HHS/CMS should allow exclusions for hospitals in states where integration with PHAs is not feasible due to legal, technical, or infrastructure barriers.
            *   Hospitals facing persistent onboarding delays or difficulties demonstrating progress should be protected from penalties tied to circumstances beyond their control.
        *   Allow Flexibility for Safety Assurance Factors for EHR Resilience (SAFER) Guides:
            *   The FAH supports the goal of enhancing EHR safety and appreciates CMS’ effort to update the Safety Assurance Factors for EHR Resilience (SAFER) Guides.
            *   However, we continue to have significant concerns regarding the SAFER guides and recommend making the attestation requirements for the SAFER Guides measure optional beginning in CY2026, due to the following concerns:
                *   Duplicative Requirements and Limited Added Benefit: The SAFER Guides assessment contains duplicative content and considerations already addressed through other facets of the Promoting Interoperability Program, particularly within the Protect Patient Health Information objective through the Security Risk Analysis (SRA). Performing both assessments annually creates unnecessary administrative burden without commensurate benefit to providers or their EHR systems.
                *   Resource Intensive: The comprehensive assessment of all required SAFER Guides places a substantial burden on providers and personnel, diverting valuable time and resources from direct patient care and other essential activities.
                *   Lack of Clarity and Potential for Inconsistent Implementation: Ambiguity in several recommended practices within the SAFER Guides poses significant challenges and necessitates additional resources for proper completion.
            *   To address these concerns and promote a more streamlined and effective approach to EHR safety assessment, we recommend HHS/CMS consider the following alternatives:
                *   Reconsider Measure Requirements: Reconsider mandating the SAFER Guides measure due to the above concerns.
                *   Recognize Alternative EHR Safety Demonstrations: Allow organizations to submit evidence of their participation in recognized EHR safety programs or certifications as an alternative means of demonstrating compliance. Providers and vendors already attest to many of the existing best practices through ASTP/ONC’s health IT certification program. As an example, the Office of Civil Rights (OCR) also requires consideration of “recognized security practices” when determining HIPAA fines.
                *   Share Responsibility with Certified Health IT Vendors: Re-evaluate the requirements for hospitals and providers to be a shared responsibility with certified health IT vendors. Both parties should be accountable for attesting “Yes” to the SAFER Guides and their functional assessment.
    *   We urge HHS/CMS to carefully consider these concerns and alternatives to ensure that the SAFER Guides measure is streamlined in a manner that promotes EHR safety without placing an undue burden on healthcare providers.

*   Data Exchange & Interoperability – TEFCA
    *   Ensuring seamless data exchange is crucial for a functional health technology ecosystem.
    *   The Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) is beginning to advance provider access to health information, particularly by simplifying connections to health information exchange networks and standardizing the agreements between participating entities.
    *   We strongly support the continued advancement of TEFCA as a critical foundation for nationwide health data exchange, regardless of the future of the Promoting Interoperability Program.
    *   We urge action on the following recommendations:
        *   Concentrate on making the TEFCA framework fully operational and effective, rather than introducing new or parallel interoperability models.
        *   In particular, standardized patient matching and record-locator methods should be developed and mandated under TEFCA to improve the accuracy of nationwide data exchange.
        *   Provide incentives or regulatory options to encourage providers to participate in TEFCA.
        *   For example, CMS could facilitate or reward a hospital’s connection to a designated Qualified Health Information Network (QHIN) under TEFCA, accelerating adoption and the flow of key health information across networks.

*   Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) Value Pathways (MVP)
    *   HHS/CMS should continue the Traditional MIPS program (with some modifications discussed below) and discontinue the development of further MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs).
    *   Although we understand CMS’ desire to move away from Traditional MIPS toward MVPs so that eligible clinician performance would be judged against measure sets that are more tailored to their specialty and scope of practice, this move would greatly increase the complexity of maintaining compliance and avoiding penalties.
    *   Traditional MIPS still serves as a solid baseline to ensure eligible clinicians obtain and leverage advanced EHR/Health IT platforms.
    *   With MIPS, eligible clinicians still have the opportunity to select a quality measure set that aligns with their specialty and scope of practice, so it is somewhat unclear what problem CMS is trying to solve with MVPs.

*   Traditional MIPS
    *   We believe that the Traditional MIPS program serves as a solid baseline to ensure eligible clinicians obtain and leverage advanced EHR/Health IT platforms.
    *   However, the Improvement Activities and Cost categories of Traditional MIPS offer negligible benefits when compared to the administrative overhead required to support them, making them ripe for streamlining.
    *   Any eligible clinician that has implemented a Traditional-MIPS-compliant EHR platform can easily meet the required number of Improvement Activities.
    *   However, the documentation effort required to support compliance in these areas is incongruous with the real-world value of implementing the features themselves in an era where these kinds of functionality have simply become table stakes for even the most basic EHR platforms.
    *   Further, the Cost category exists as a sort of “black box” into which eligible clinicians have little visibility.
    *   To make matters worse, eligible clinicians have limited ability to influence the outcome of CMS’ calculation of this category. As such, it does little to truly influence eligible clinician behavior in a positive way.

*   Submission Methods
    *   HHS/CMS should work to streamline MIPS measure collection and submission methods in a manner that reduces burden for eligible clinicians.
    *   This same logic could be applied across many CMS programs, but an example where it would be immediately beneficial is in quality measure reporting.
    *   While CMS has developed a strategic roadmap for transitioning all quality measures to Digital Quality Measures (dQM), the roadmap has dQMs being fully implemented by 2030 at the earliest.
    *   In the current state, there are so many different clinical quality measures (CQM), some of which can be electronically collected/reported and others of which must be chart-abstracted.
