    *   Depending on the type of measure and program under which it is reported, eligible clinicians may report via QRDA files (at the provider-level, practice-level [CMMI projects], TIN-level, or the ACO-level—yet another layer of complexity), APIs, or QCDRs.
    *   While this variation may seem helpful to offer multiple options for eligible clinicians, it often means vendors, providers, and healthcare systems end up having to support multiple submission methods, creating a significant amount of duplicative work that wastes precious time and resources.
    *   While awaiting the full implementation of dQMs, CMS should select an interim gold standard that balances the fidelity of the data received against the burden it places on vendors and providers both to support it.
    *   We acknowledge and appreciate that dQMs are intended to measure quality as a passive byproduct of normal healthcare operations.
    *   However, until they are fully implemented, the lack of standardization in the current state of quality measurement reporting will continue to be a drain on the same resources that should be focused on actually improving the quality of the care we provide.

*   Public Health Reporting
    *   HHS/CMS should continue to move toward a more centralized model for public health reporting, leveraging what has been learned in certain areas like Electronic Case Reporting (eCR).
    *   Public health reporting continues to be a huge drain on resources.
    *   For eligible clinicians, immunization registry reporting is the most challenging public health reporting requirement at present.
    *   The experience of working with different public health agencies across different jurisdictions, each with their own resource constraints and interpretation/application of the HL7 standards, can be extremely demoralizing.
    *   Everyone wants to achieve the same thing—a robust public health system that can react in an informed way when an emergency arises.
    *   However, we all lack some version of the tools required to achieve this goal.
    *   Creating either a national registry or, as was done in the case of eCR, implementing a federated model with an independent intermediary that can harmonize the differences between what each public health agency needs and what each EHR platform can (without technical intervention by its users) provide would create a much stronger foundation on which to build a better public health system that can truly serve the needs of all parties and the general population when the next crisis inevitably occurs.

*   Electronic Prior Authorization Final Rule
    *   Under the Advancing Interoperability and Improving Prior Authorization Processes final rule, during the 2027 EHR reporting period, eligible hospitals and CAHs must attest “yes” to submitting at least one prior authorization request electronically via a Prior Authorization API using data from certified EHR technology (CEHRT) or claim an applicable exclusion.
    *   The payer implementation deadline is January 2027.
    *   Additionally, the Health IT vendor certification requirements initially proposed in the Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability: Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (HTI-2) rule were not finalized.
    *   Therefore, the FAH recommends that HHS/CMS take the following actions:
        *   Postpone Provider Requirement: Given the payer implementation deadline of January 1, 2027, and the absence of finalized vendor Prior Authorization API certification requirements, we urge postponement of the provider deadline accordingly to allow adequate time for industry-wide readiness and adoption.
        *   Finalize Health IT Vendor Certification Requirement: We urge CMS to collaborate with the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy (ASTP) to establish clear certification criteria for electronic Prior Authorization functionality within the Health IT Certification Program. A formal framework would provide essential guidance for developers, payers, and providers, ensuring consistent and effective implementation.

*   Expand 60 Percent Rule Data Transparency
    *   HHS/CMS should provide IRFs with access to their patient-level data submitted for presumptive testing under the 60 Percent Rule.
    *   Currently, IRFs do not know which cases satisfied the rule and which cases did not and have been unable to access this patient-level data from CMS.
    *   This information would enable IRFs to reconcile their internal 60 Percent Rule testing procedures against CMS’ presumptive testing procedures and thus reduce the burden and cost of compliance.

*   Harmonize IRF Appeal Rights Under the PRRB
    *   HHS/CMS should grant IRFs access to the Provider Reimbursement Review Board (PRRB) process for Low-Income Patient (LIP) appeals.
    *   While acute care hospitals can appeal DSH payment determinations by their contractors to the PRRB, IRFs cannot appeal parallel LIP payment adjustment determinations by their contractors.
    *   Instead, IRFs are forced to seek such appeals through the federal court system, which is more burdensome, costly, and time-consuming.

*   CMS Conditions of Participation (CoPs) on Respiratory Illness Reporting
    *   The COVID-19 public health emergency prompted CMS to establish new requirements under 42 C.F.R. § 482.42(e), mandating that hospitals report data on respiratory illnesses such as COVID-19, influenza, and RSV.
    *   While appropriate in the context of a national emergency, these provisions were extended beyond the statutory emergency authority and now continue without a clear statutory mandate under Section 1861(e) of the Social Security Act.
    *   That section authorizes the Secretary to impose hospital Conditions of Participation to ensure the health and safety of patients receiving services, not to require duplicative, long-term epidemiological surveillance.
    *   The FAH has highlighted in prior IPPS rulemaking (FY 2023) that these CoPs duplicate data submissions already required by the CDC under the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) and add administrative burden without improving patient care or clinical operations.
    *   Hospitals must dedicate health information technology (HIT), clinical, and compliance resources to maintain daily reporting, which is an inefficient use of personnel post the public health emergency.
    *   We urge HHS/CMS to rescind §42 C.F.R. § 482.42(e) as an outdated and burdensome provision inconsistent with statutory authority.

*   Maternal Health CoPs
    *   CMS has finalized new CoPs for maternal health under 42 C.F.R. § 482.82, which require hospitals to establish and maintain policies and procedures addressing obstetric emergencies such as severe hypertension and obstetric hemorrhage.
    *   While these are critical issues, Section 1861(e) of the Social Security Act does not authorize CMS to impose clinical protocol mandates under CoPs.
    *   That section provides facility standards to protect patient health and safety but does not empower CMS to standardize clinical decision-making across vastly diverse hospital settings.
    *   In comments on the CY 2024 and 2025 OPPS proposed rules, the FAH cautioned that such regulations disproportionately affect small, low-volume, or rural hospitals that may not offer labor and delivery services or have the infrastructure to comply with one-size-fits-all mandates.
    *   These hospitals are already engaged in evidence-based maternal safety work through the Alliance for Innovation on Maternal Health (AIM) or state perinatal collaboratives.
    *   The proposed CoPs risk closure of obstetric services in areas where maternal care access is already limited, thus undermining the very safety goals the rule seeks to advance.
    *   These provisions should be withdrawn to align with CMS statutory limits.

*   Conditions of Participation (CoP)
    *   We urge HHS/CMS to narrow the focus of new CoPs issued in late 2024 for hospital emergency services, focusing on emergency readiness, including staff training on the emergency protocols and a call-in system for each patient in the emergency services treatment area.
    *   These requirements are unnecessary and extremely burdensome for providers while diverting resources away from patient care.
    *   In addition, we urge HHS/CMS to update life safety code CoPs to allow hospitals to comply with more up-to-date requirements and reduce potential conflicts with State and local requirements.

*   Streamline Care Plan Documentation Requirements
    *   To provide higher quality, more holistic care, patients are increasingly cared for by interdisciplinary teams, with clinical professionals ranging, for example, from nurses and therapists to social workers.
    *   These teams develop what an “interdisciplinary care plan” although outdated regulations require nursing-specific care plans.
    *   As care delivery trends increasingly move toward interdisciplinary teams that work collaboratively to address a patient's needs from a more patient-centered approach framework, clinicians must create duplicate paperwork to document the care plan.
    *   Therefore, we urge that the care plan documentation requirements at 42 CFR 483.23(b)(4) be streamlined.

*   Repeal Information Blocking/Provider Disincentive Regulations
    *   Providers are encountering significant challenges in complying with overlapping federal and state regulations governing health information sharing.
    *   Regulations such as HIPAA, the ONC Information Blocking rules, and 42 CFR Part 2 governing certain substance use disorder records often impose conflicting obligations, creating undue burdens and legal uncertainty.
    *   Additionally, state laws (such as those in California and Texas requiring delays in releasing test results) further complicate compliance, particularly given the current limitations of robust data segmentation technology necessary for selectively withholding sensitive information.
    *   The FAH strongly emphasizes the necessity and urgency of advancing technology capabilities that support data segmentation.
    *   Certified health IT currently lacks sufficient functionality to effectively segment data, especially sensitive information relating to behavioral health, reproductive health, and adolescent health records.
    *   Without appropriate data segmentation capabilities, providers face substantial operational hurdles and complexity in ensuring patient confidentiality while responding to information requests and managing APIs.
    *   We recommend that HHS/ONC prioritize accelerating the development and implementation of standardized data segmentation solutions to meet these critical privacy needs, as previously noted in our communications.
    *   Moreover, providers invest significant resources in managing complex and varied jurisdictional privacy and health information management requirements.
    *   We urge HHS/ONC to collaborate with the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) and other relevant agencies to develop resources assisting providers in navigating these myriad obligations, thereby alleviating confusion and enhancing clarity.
    *   Data segmentation capabilities could also operationalize privacy protections and prevent harm under the information blocking rules.
    *   Many physicians express concerns that immediate sharing of sensitive or life-altering test results via patient portals, without contextual clinical discussion, could cause psychological distress or potential physical harm in sensitive situations such as intimate partner abuse.
    *   Technologies must support patient preferences regarding the timing and manner of information sharing, enabling clinicians to responsibly manage sensitive data disclosures.
    *   In light of the foregoing, the FAH recommends that HHS, including CMS and ASTP/ONC:
        *   Conduct comprehensive reviews and harmonization of federal and state privacy laws to clarify and eliminate contradictory requirements, helping providers avoid conflicting legal obligations.
        *   Repeal the provider disincentives included in the Disincentives for Health Care Providers That Have Committed Information Blocking final rule (July 1, 2024).
            *   This rule provides that hospitals and providers determined to have engaged in information blocking may face reductions in Medicare payment updates, adjustments to payment rates, lower performance scores, and potential ineligibility for certain incentive programs.
            *   The FAH supports ensuring that critical health information is available to patients, clinicians treating those patients, and those with appropriate reasons for having access, among which are payment, care oversight, and research.
            *   However, the disincentive structure in this rule is excessive and puts hospitals’ stability at risk, especially for small and rural hospitals.
            *   Further, the Office of the Inspector General processes for determining whether information blocking has occurred are not sufficiently clear and lack transparency, including the appeals process, thus making providers subject to a rule that seems arbitrary and capricious.
            *   Alternatively, at a minimum, we recommend:
                *   Prioritizing education and collaborative guidance efforts over punitive measures for information blocking compliance, fostering enhanced understanding and cooperation across provider communities.
                *   Clearly defining the term "intent" regarding information blocking, ensuring providers have precise guidance to mitigate unfair penalties due to ambiguous regulations.
                *   Revisiting and refining penalties associated with information blocking, linking severity directly to the violation's nature, scope, and resultant harm.
        *   Implement phased approaches for providers to adopt information-sharing best practices, supported by practical guidelines and clear examples provided collaboratively by CMS, ONC, and OIG.
        *   Leverage ASTP/ONC convening capabilities and resources to accelerate the development and real-world testing of standards-based data segmentation solutions.
            *   This includes assessing and potentially refining existing standards such as the HL7 CDA and FHIR Data Segmentation for Privacy Implementation Guides and the HCS Security Label Vocabulary.
            *   The FAH recommends funding pilot tests that explicitly evaluate patient outcomes, provider usability, and system efficiency, with transparent public dissemination of these findings.
            *   Advancing robust data segmentation functionalities will significantly aid providers in effectively navigating complex regulatory landscapes, safeguarding patient privacy, and ensuring compliance with evolving federal and state mandates.

*   Withdraw Cybersecurity Proposed Regulations
    *   The FAH urges HHS to withdraw the HHS/OCR HIPAA Security Rule to Strengthen the Cybersecurity of Electronic Protected Health Information, proposed on December 27, 2024, with comments due on March 7, 2025.
    *   Many provisions in the proposal are not operationally feasible and do not recognize the nuance and complexities of applying cyber protections in a complex health IT environment.
    *   They are not scalable to multiple types and sizes of hospitals and health care systems.
    *   They drastically underestimate implementation costs and impose prohibitively costly and unnecessary burden.
    *   Therefore, we urge HHS to withdraw the proposed rule and engage in a stakeholder process to develop a new approach for a cybersecurity regulatory framework.

*   Expand Eligibility for 340B Drug Pricing Program to Tax-Paying Hospitals
    *   The FAH urges HHS/CMS to consider reforms to the 340B Drug Pricing Program that would expand eligibility to tax-paying hospitals and protect 340B status during hospital acquisitions.
    *   Currently, approximately 20% of community hospitals—those that are tax-paying—are categorically excluded from the program.
    *   This exclusion applies even when they serve high concentrations of Medicaid and uninsured patients and exceed the Medicare low-income thresholds.
    *   This arbitrary tax status-based restriction undermines the original intent of the 340B program, which is to stretch federal resources and improve access to care for vulnerable populations.
    *   FAH data show that our member hospitals provide greater levels of charity and uncompensated care, as a percentage of operating costs, than many current 340B participants.
    *   To promote continuity of care and preserve community benefit, we recommend that CMS support legislative or regulatory action to:
        *   Allow tax-paying hospitals serving low-income populations to participate in the 340B program.
        *   Grandfather 340B eligibility for hospitals that are acquired by tax-paying systems, provided that the safety-net services and patient mix remain substantially the same post-acquisition.
    *   This policy would extend critical cost savings to underserved communities regardless of tax status and reinforce the program’s intent to improve access and affordability for those most in need.

*   Telehealth
    *   The FAH supports the value of telehealth in providing critically needed services to Medicare beneficiaries, especially as technology has evolved.
    *   Telehealth flexibilities help ensure that hospitals are able to meet the needs of their patients and communities.
    *   To continue to leverage value of telehealth and make it accessible on a widespread basis to Medicare beneficiaries, we urge that HHS/CMS support legislation to achieve the following:
        *   Remove telehealth originating site restrictions within the Medicare program at Sec. 1834(m)(4)(C)(ii)(X) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1395m) and 42 CFR 410.78(b)(3) to enable patients to receive telehealth in their homes.
        *   Remove telehealth geographic site restrictions within the Medicare program at Sec. 1834(m)(4)(C)(i) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1395m) and 42 CFR 410.78(b)(4) to enable beneficiaries in non-rural areas to have the same access to virtual care as those in rural areas.
        *   Remove the in-person visit requirements for behavioral health telehealth at Sec. 1834(m)(7) of the Social Security Act (42 U.S.C. 1395m) and 42 CFR 410.78(b)(3)(xiv), which is unnecessary, is a barrier to accessing care and on a timely basis, and creates a disparity between physical and mental health services.

*   Medicare Parts A and B Overpayment Provisions of the Affordable Care Act
    *   The FAH broadly supports CMS’ policy that applies the False Claims Act standard of “knowing” and “knowingly” to the identification of overpayments and suspends the report and return deadline during a timely, good-faith investigation of related overpayments.
    *   The FAH, however, is concerned that the suspension provision assumes a relatively straightforward investigation of related overpayments and the 180-day proposed period is insufficient for more complicated overpayment investigations.
    *   Therefore, the FAH urges HHS/CMS to revise proposed 42 C.F.R. § 401.305(b)(3)(ii) to provide that the deadline is suspended for the entirety of a timely, good-faith investigation to minimize the piecemeal report and return of overpayments.
    *   The 180-day limit proposed in subsection (b)(3)(ii)(B) may be a useful benchmark for many simple overpayment investigations, but it is not uncommon for a good-faith investigation conducted with reasonable diligence to necessitate additional time, particularly where the overpayment issue involves complex factual and legal questions.
    *   If a timely, good-faith investigation cannot be concluded in the 180-day period, the provider would likely revert to the piecemeal report and return of overpayments, addressing the initially identified overpayments with an initial report and return while continuing its larger investigation and then subsequently reporting and returning any further overpayments that are later identified.
    *   Certainly, there are situations where a timely, good-faith investigation can be concluded within 180 days such that the related overpayments can be identified within this time frame and then reported and returned along with the initially identified overpayments.
    *   But providers frequently confront circumstances where the underlying facts and circumstances are sufficiently complicated that a reasonable, good-faith investigation would not conclude within 180 days.
    *   For example, in some cases the investigation of related overpayments requires complex factual development, including the clinical review of individual medical charts and interviews of staff.
    *   These complicated, multi-stage investigations are particularly common for hospitals given the breadth and complexity of their operations.
    *   In order to appropriately minimize piecemeal reports and returns of overpayments, the FAH strongly urges HHS/CMS to revise 42 C.F.R. § 401.305(b)(3)(ii) to provide for the reasonable suspension of deadlines over the entirety of a timely, good-faith investigation.
    *   In the alternative, HHS/CMS should provide a process for reasonably extending the 180-day period in appropriate circumstances.
    *   Flexibility to go beyond 180 days in appropriate cases is necessary in light of the range of complexity in investigations of related overpayments.

*   Accrediting Organizations (AOs) and Preventing AO Conflict of Interest
    *   The FAH has previously provided comments to CMS regarding a proposed rule addressing Strengthening Oversight of Accrediting Organizations (AOs) and Preventing AO Conflict of Interest, and Related Provisions.
    *   Our hospital system members demonstrate compliance with Conditions of Participation (CoPs) by achieving accreditation through a CMS-approved national AO that is authorized to “deem” compliance, rather than through a State Survey Agency certification, in accordance with Section 1865(a) of the Social Security Act.
    *   Our members have established effective working relationships with the AOs, which ensures that Medicare’s health and safety requirements for beneficiaries are met or exceeded.
    *   While the proposed rule reference above has not been finalized, we urge HHS/CMS to ensure the following:
        *   The Definition of “Fee-Based Consulting Services” Should Not Include Subscription-Based Generic Consultative Tools
            *   CMS has proposed to restrict AOs from providing “fee-based consulting services” prior to a provider’s initial survey and providing such services to their accredited providers during the 12-month period prior to each provider’s reaccreditation survey.
            *   The FAH urges HHS/CMS to clarify that the definition of “fee-based consulting services” does not include use of AOs’ subscription-based generic consultative tools.
            *   If “fee-based consulting services” is defined too broadly, this could prove detrimental and undermine hospital efforts to ensure they meet the CoPs and appropriately advance quality and safety initiatives.
            *   Our members often utilize annual subscription web-based, generic tools and seminars offered by an AO or its consulting arm, including during the 12 months prior to a survey, to generate self-assessment reports that help hospitals meet the CoPs and prepare for a survey.
            *   These commonly used AO tools and seminars would not represent a conflict of interest because they do not result in the: (i) AO or its consulting arm facilitating or advising on hospital-specific situations or complaints being evaluated by an AO; or (ii) development of a material personal relationship with a representative of the AO or its consulting arm.
            *   Hospitals may contact technical or tool navigation support at the AO consulting arm, including within 12 months prior to an initial or reaccreditation survey, but these interactions are on a sporadic, as needed basis, and are not tailored to a hospital’s individual survey needs or a specific complaint being assessed about a hospital.
            *   Hospitals would be adversely impacted if these types of resources could no longer be used during the 12-month period prior to a survey.
            *   Such a restriction would leave hospitals without a source of guidance to self-assess and ensure appropriate compliance with the quality and safety requirements of the Medicare CoPs.
        *   Reconsider the Parameters of an “Unannounced Survey”
            *   Under the proposed rule, the AO would be required to cease any advance notification to the hospital and its staff so that the facility would be unaware of the survey until the time that the survey team arrives.
            *   AOs also would be required to schedule surveys so that their timing or occurrence would not be predictable to the facility being surveyed.
            *   Further, in June 2023, CMS released guidance that parallels the intentions of the proposed rule, with similar requirements for “unannounced surveys.”
            *   The proposed rule’s new definition of “unannounced survey” reinforces an inefficient policy that overestimates the value of providing a facility a brief advance notice of a survey.
            *   Both the June 2023 guidance and the proposed rule give too much credence to what a facility could do to improve the results of an impending survey in the short amount of advance notice that an AO may provide, often inadvertently.
            *   The FAH recommends that HHS/CMS encourage AOs to provide hospitals 24 hours’ advance notice of a survey.
            *   This would allow time for hospitals to ensure appropriate staff are available for the survey.
            *   While there may be instances in which a hospital’s staff members may not be available for the survey due to travel or illness, for example, providing the hospital with a brief advance notice would allow the hospital to resolve simple scheduling issues that could ensure maximum access to hospital leadership and other staff who could better facilitate a smooth survey process and answer surveyors’ questions accurately and completely.
            *   This would allow surveyors to garner robust feedback in a more efficient manner, making the survey results more useful and reflective of the care the hospital provides for the facility, public, and CMS’ consideration.
            *   CMS discussed in the proposed rule its concern that unannounced surveys are required “to prevent the provider or supplier from making unusual preparations for the survey that would not represent the ongoing typical condition of the provider and true nature and quality of care provided.” 89 Fed. Reg. 12,004.
            *   Yet, a 24-hour window of time would represent an appropriate balance to these concerns—this window would not allow enough time to make unusual preparations while at the same time it would allow hospitals an opportunity to ensure a more efficient, robust, and smoother survey process.
        *   Surveys Need Greater Transparency
            *   AOs often combine the triennial deemed status surveys with a complaint survey during a survey visit.
            *   Each of these surveys has very different rules and requirements.
            *   Combining them into one evaluation, especially when each type of survey is not identified by the surveyor, is confusing for hospital staff and risks conflating results against varying standards, increasing the possibility that a hospital will receive inaccurate results.
            *   Thus, we urge HHS/CMS to ensure that surveyors clearly identify the purpose of each survey being conducted, along with providing appropriate instruction for each such survey, with outreach to hospital staff to assess any issues that arise and develop a plan to address them.

*   National Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Standard
    *   We urge HHS/CMS to support Congressional enactment of a national privacy law under HIPAA that pre-empts all state privacy laws that apply to protected health information (PHI).
    *   The FAH has long advocated for strong national privacy standards and believes this is the best approach for both PHI and personal health data that falls outside HIPAA.
    *   Covered entities and their business associates have struggled for many years with the patchwork of different, sometimes conflicting state laws governing PHI, especially as many more states have enacted comprehensive privacy laws.
    *   While some of these laws carve out PHI, others do not or are unclear as to the application to PHI, which makes compliance a significant challenge, for both large and small hospital systems that operate in multiple states.
    *   Requiring organizations to comply with multiple different, often inconsistent, privacy laws for the same health data creates complexities and compliance challenges that take away from patient care.
    *   The FAH therefore urges:
        *   (i) a national privacy standard under HIPAA that pre-empts all state privacy laws that apply to PHI.
        *   (ii) any federal privacy law for non-HIPAA personal health data should similarly preempt state privacy laws that might otherwise apply to that data.

*   Eliminate 96-Hour Rule
    *   The 96-hour average length of stay requirement for Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs), originally enacted in the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, is outdated and no longer reflects the realities of rural health care.
    *   While intended to limit costs and define the scope of CAH services, this statutory provision — along with the regulatory 96-hour physician certification requirement — imposes unnecessary administrative burdens and limits flexibility in care delivery.
    *   Today, CAHs often manage higher-acuity patients, face limited transfer options due to hospital closures, and leverage technology to provide safe, effective care beyond the original 96-hour assumption.
    *   The 96-hour average inpatient stay limit is too restrictive and not clinically appropriate for many patients, particularly those with more complex needs or in areas with limited access to higher-level care.
    *   Realizing the challenges for rural providers, CMS announced in 2014 it would not enforce the requirement that physicians certify at admission that a patient will likely be discharged or transferred within 96 hours (per 42 CFR § 412.3).
    *   CMS justified this moratorium by saying it would reduce administrative burden and preserve access to care in rural areas.
    *   Further, during the first Trump Administration, CMS granted waivers during COVID-19 and other public health emergencies that suspended enforcement of the 96-hour rule entirely, reinforcing arguments that the requirement is not essential for quality or safety.
    *   This regulation is outdated and administratively burdensome.
    *   The FAH urges HHS/CMS to work with Congress to amend the statute to eliminate the length-of-stay requirement (42 U.S.C. § 1395i–4(c)(2)(B)(iii)).
    *   Moreover, we urge HHS/CMS to take immediate steps to remove the corresponding Conditions of Participation (42 CFR § 485.620(a)), which mandates that the average annual length of stay not exceed 96 hours.
    *   We also urge to eliminate the separate 96-hour payment condition that obligates physicians to certify at admission that a patient is likely to be discharged or transferred within 96 hours (42 CFR § 412.3).
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The Federation of American Hospitals (FAH), representing nearly 1,000 tax-paying hospitals, urges HHS to dramatically deregulate across numerous areas, including Medicare Advantage, quality reporting, interoperability, and CoPs, to reduce administrative burdens, improve patient access, and ensure appropriate payment.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Federation of American Hospitals
- **Type:** Trade Association
- **Role/Expertise:** National representative of nearly 1,000 leading tax-paying hospitals and health systems throughout the United States. Members include teaching, acute, inpatient rehabilitation, behavioral health, and long-term care hospitals, providing a wide range of inpatient, ambulatory, post-acute, emergency, children’s, and cancer services.
- **Geographic Scope:** National (across 46 states, Washington, DC, and Puerto Rico)
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly affected by federal healthcare regulations that impact their operations, patient care delivery, financial viability, and ability to provide high-quality, affordable care. We aim to reduce regulatory burdens that divert resources from patient care and create financial strains.
structuredSections.corePosition: The Federation of American Hospitals commends HHS's deregulatory efforts, asserting that many current regulations and requirements divert critical resources from patient care, foster inefficiencies, and impose significant financial strains on hospitals. We believe dramatic deregulation across all areas HHS touches is necessary to unleash innovation, improve the health and well-being of the American people, and allow our healthcare system to achieve maximum health.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Rein in abuses of Prior Authorization in Medicare Advantage plans.
  - Require plans to ensure MA patients receive at least the same levels of coverage as Traditional Medicare, including compliance with the Medicare Two-Midnight Rule and Inpatient Only List.
  - Track and report prior authorization denials and appeals at discrete service levels, providing this information to Medicare enrollees.
- Reject site-neutral cuts to Medicare payments.
  - Ensure payment for outpatient services provided in Hospital Outpatient Departments (HOPDs) reflects the higher overhead costs of that setting.
- Eliminate the Inpatient Rehabilitation Facility (IRF) Review Choice Demonstration (RCD) program.
- Enforce health insurer compliance with the No Surprises Act (NSA) Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process.
  - Adopt the pending proposed rule establishing an IDR process with appropriate incentives for health insurers (e.g., greater payment transparency, meaningful participation in open negotiation, timely payment).
- Rescind interpretive guidance implying rigid nursing staff ratio requirements in Conditions of Participation (CoPs).
  - Confirm hospital discretion in establishing staffing plans responsive to patient needs.
- Withdraw the Patient-Reported Outcomes Measure for Hip/Knee Arthroplasty (PRO-PM) from the Hospital IQR Program.
- Remove low-value structural measures from the Hospital IQR and Value-Based Purchasing (VBP) Programs.
  - Implement outcomes-based, actionable quality indicators instead.
- Remove hybrid clinical/claims-based quality measures from the Hospital Inpatient Quality Reporting (IQR) Program until standardized EHR interoperability and infrastructure are universally available.
- Suspend the Hospital Star Ratings program and initiate a transparent, collaborative process to develop a more accurate and equitable model.
- Remove mandatory reporting requirements for electronic clinical quality measures (eCQMs) under both the Hospital Inpatient Quality Reporting (IQR) Program and the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program, making it voluntary.
- Ensure appropriate pre-deployment testing of all federal systems for collecting and reporting hospital quality data at both CMS and CDC.
- Halt the implementation of mandatory models developed by the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI), including the Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM) and the Increasing Organ Transplant Access (IOTA) Model, making them voluntary.
- Provide Inpatient Rehabilitation Facilities (IRFs) an optional, voluntary discount to the standard payment amount, or allow them to assume more risk, for relevant IRF cases discharged from acute care hospitals participating in CMMI bundling programs.
  - Grant regulatory relief under the 60 Percent Rule and Three-hour Rule for IRFs treating these patients at payments below current IRF prospective payment system rates.
- Phase out or significantly simplify the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program. If continued:
  - Gradually increase program scoring thresholds (e.g., 5-10 points over several years) instead of large jumps.
  - Allow flexibility in Public Health Data Exchange Progression, not holding hospitals accountable for Public Health Agency (PHA) readiness/capacity.
  - Expand exclusions for hospitals facing persistent onboarding challenges with PHAs due to legal, technical, or infrastructure barriers.
  - Make attestation requirements for the Safety Assurance Factors for EHR Resilience (SAFER) Guides measure optional beginning CY2026.
    - Reconsider mandating the SAFER Guides measure entirely.
    - Recognize alternative EHR safety demonstrations (e.g., participation in recognized programs or certifications).
    - Share responsibility for SAFER Guides attestation with certified health IT vendors.
- Continue to advance the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA).
  - Concentrate on making TEFCA fully operational and effective, avoiding new/parallel interoperability models.
  - Develop and mandate standardized patient matching and record-locator methods under TEFCA.
  - Provide incentives or regulatory options to encourage provider participation in TEFCA.
- Continue the Traditional MIPS program with modifications, and discontinue the development of further MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs).
  - Streamline Improvement Activities and Cost categories within Traditional MIPS.
- Streamline MIPS measure collection and submission methods to reduce burden for eligible clinicians.
  - Select an interim "gold standard" for quality measure reporting that balances data fidelity and burden, while awaiting full Digital Quality Measure (dQM) implementation.
- Move toward a more centralized model for public health reporting, leveraging lessons from Electronic Case Reporting (eCR).
  - Create either a national registry or implement a federated model with an independent intermediary for immunization registry reporting.
- Postpone the provider deadline for electronic prior authorization requests via API, given payer implementation deadlines and unfinalized vendor certification.
  - Finalize Health IT Vendor Certification Requirements for electronic Prior Authorization functionality within the Health IT Certification Program.
- Provide Inpatient Rehabilitation Facilities (IRFs) with access to their patient-level data submitted for presumptive testing under the 60 Percent Rule.
- Grant Inpatient Rehabilitation Facilities (IRFs) access to the Provider Reimbursement Review Board (PRRB) process for Low-Income Patient (LIP) appeals.
- Rescind CMS Conditions of Participation (CoPs) on Respiratory Illness Reporting (42 C.F.R. § 482.42(e)).
- Withdraw new CMS Conditions of Participation (CoPs) for maternal health (42 C.F.R. § 482.82).
- Narrow the focus of new late 2024 CoPs for hospital emergency services to emergency readiness (staff training on protocols, call-in system).
- Update life safety code CoPs to allow hospitals to comply with more up-to-date requirements and reduce conflicts with State and local requirements.
- Streamline care plan documentation requirements at 42 CFR 483.23(b)(4) to allow for interdisciplinary care plans.
- Repeal the provider disincentives included in the Disincentives for Health Care Providers That Have Committed Information Blocking final rule (July 1, 2024).
  - Alternatively: Prioritize education/collaborative guidance over punitive measures, clearly define "intent" for information blocking, and refine penalties based on violation nature/scope/harm.
  - Implement phased approaches for providers to adopt information-sharing best practices.
  - Accelerate the development and real-world testing of standards-based data segmentation solutions, including funding pilot tests.
- Withdraw the HHS/OCR HIPAA Security Rule to Strengthen the Cybersecurity of Electronic Protected Health Information proposed on December 27, 2024.
  - Engage in a stakeholder process to develop a new cybersecurity regulatory framework.
- Expand eligibility for the 340B Drug Pricing Program to tax-paying hospitals.
  - Allow tax-paying hospitals serving low-income populations to participate.
  - Grandfather 340B eligibility for hospitals acquired by tax-paying systems, provided safety-net services/patient mix remain substantially the same.
- Support legislation to remove telehealth originating site restrictions, geographic site restrictions, and in-person visit requirements for behavioral health telehealth within Medicare.
- Revise 42 C.F.R. § 401.305(b)(3)(ii) related to Medicare Parts A and B overpayment provisions.
  - Suspend the report and return deadline for the entirety of a timely, good-faith investigation of related overpayments.
  - Alternatively, provide a process for reasonably extending the 180-day period in appropriate circumstances.
- Ensure that the definition of "fee-based consulting services" for Accrediting Organizations (AOs) does not include subscription-based generic consultative tools.
- Reconsider the parameters of an "unannounced survey" for AOs, recommending a 24-hour advance notice to hospitals.
- Ensure surveyors clearly identify the purpose of each survey being conducted (e.g., triennial deemed status vs. complaint survey) and provide appropriate instruction.
- Support Congressional enactment of a national privacy law under HIPAA that preempts all state privacy laws that apply to Protected Health Information (PHI).
  - Similarly, any federal privacy law for non-HIPAA personal health data should preempt state privacy laws.
- Work with Congress to amend the statute to eliminate the 96-hour average length of stay requirement for Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs).
  - Immediately remove corresponding Conditions of Participation (42 CFR § 485.620(a)) and the separate 96-hour physician certification payment condition (42 CFR § 412.3).
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- Medicare Advantage plans' abusive practices harm patients by eroding access and affordability through inappropriate denials, limitations, and delays of medically necessary care, diverting hospital resources and staff time from patient care.
  - These practices lead to MA beneficiaries receiving a lower standard of appropriate care than those in Traditional Medicare.
  - Lengthy post-acute care (PAC) prior authorization delays and inadequate PAC networks lead to longer inpatient lengths of stay and unreimbursed hospital costs.
- Site-neutral cuts to Medicare payments would exacerbate coverage gaps and reduce patient access to care, as they do not account for significant regulatory burdens and 24/7 essential services provided by hospitals to sicker patients.
  - They could force hospital outpatient clinics to close or cut critical services, and Medicare already underpays hospitals, leading to negative margins for two-thirds of hospitals.
- The Inpatient Rehabilitation Facility (IRF) Review Choice Demonstration (RCD) program is administratively burdensome, unnecessary, and costly given its high approval rates.
- The No Surprises Act (NSA) Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process is broken, ineffective, and anticompetitive without appropriate incentives for health insurers, allowing them to bypass requirements.
- CMS interpretive guidance on nursing staff ratios increasingly reflects rigid expectations, which would severely burden hospitals facing workforce shortages, potentially leading to care delays, unit closures, and unintended safety risks.
- The Patient-Reported Outcomes Measure for Hip/Knee Arthroplasty (PRO-PM) is complex, costly, influenced by irrelevant variables, and presents rural-urban equity issues for smaller hospitals.
- Low-value structural measures in quality programs impose significant reporting burdens with little utility for differentiating hospital performance or evidence of improved outcomes.
- Hybrid clinical/claims-based quality measures impose disproportionate burden with little added clinical value, requiring costly manual abstraction and unfairly penalizing resource-constrained hospitals.
- The current Hospital Star Ratings oversimplify complex performance data, mislead patients, fail to reflect contextual factors (case mix, social risk), and can unintentionally penalize hospitals serving high-risk populations.
- Mandatory reporting requirements for electronic clinical quality measures (eCQMs) place an outsized burden on hospitals lacking sufficient health IT infrastructure and technical support.
- Faulty federal reporting systems for quality data (CMS QualityNet, CDC NHSN) cause inordinate resource expenditure, downtime, and delays for hospitals.
- Mandatory Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI) models (e.g., TEAM, IOTA) impose significant financial and operational risks on providers without adequate testing or stakeholder engagement, with concerns the IOTA model could incentivize inappropriate organ-recipient matches.
- The continued complexity of the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program adds administrative burden without proportional value, compounded by challenges with achieving scoring thresholds, public health agency (PHA) readiness, and the duplicative nature of SAFER Guides attestation.
- The current lack of standardization in MIPS measure collection and submission methods creates duplicative work and wastes time/resources.
- Public health reporting, particularly immunization registry reporting, is a significant resource drain due to varied agency requirements and technical constraints.
- Delays in finalizing Health IT vendor certification requirements for the electronic prior authorization API will hinder provider readiness for the upcoming mandate.
- Inpatient Rehabilitation Facilities (IRFs) lack transparency regarding their patient-level data for the 60 Percent Rule, making compliance reconciliation difficult.
- IRFs lack access to the Provider Reimbursement Review Board (PRRB) for Low-Income Patient (LIP) appeals, forcing them into more burdensome and costly federal court appeals.
- CMS Conditions of Participation (CoPs) on Respiratory Illness Reporting are outdated, duplicate CDC requirements, and impose administrative burden without statutory mandate post-public health emergency.
- New Maternal Health CoPs impose clinical protocol mandates beyond CMS's statutory authority, disproportionately affecting small/rural hospitals and risking closure of obstetric services.
- New general CoPs for hospital emergency services are unnecessary and burdensome, diverting resources.
- Outdated care plan documentation requirements force clinicians to create duplicate paperwork for interdisciplinary teams.
- Overlapping and conflicting federal/state regulations (HIPAA, Information Blocking, 42 CFR Part 2) create undue burdens, legal uncertainty, and compliance challenges for information sharing, exacerbated by a lack of robust data segmentation technology.
  - Concerns exist that immediate sharing of sensitive test results via patient portals without clinical context could cause psychological distress or harm, and provider disincentives for information blocking are excessive with unclear determination processes.
- The proposed HHS/OCR HIPAA Security Rule to Strengthen Cybersecurity of Electronic Protected Health Information is not operationally feasible, not scalable, drastically underestimates costs, and imposes prohibitive burdens.
- The arbitrary exclusion of tax-paying hospitals from the 340B Drug Pricing Program undermines its intent to stretch federal resources and improve access for vulnerable populations, despite many providing high levels of charity care.
- Existing Medicare telehealth restrictions (originating site, geographic site, in-person visit requirements for behavioral health) limit access to critically needed services.
- The 180-day suspension period for Medicare Parts A and B overpayment investigations is often insufficient for complex cases, leading to piecemeal reporting.
- A broad definition of "fee-based consulting services" for Accrediting Organizations (AOs) could detrimentally prevent hospitals from using valuable generic self-assessment tools.
- The "unannounced survey" policy for AOs is inefficient and overestimates the value of preventing brief advance notice, hindering smooth survey processes.
- Lack of transparency when AOs combine different types of surveys (e.g., deemed status and complaint) is confusing for hospital staff and risks inaccurate results.
- The patchwork of different, sometimes conflicting state privacy laws governing Protected Health Information (PHI) creates significant compliance challenges for multi-state hospital systems, diverting resources from patient care.
- The 96-hour average length of stay requirement for Critical Access Hospitals (CAHs) is outdated, administratively burdensome, not clinically appropriate for many patients, and limits flexibility in care delivery.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- Medicare Advantage delays and denials through prior authorization systematically harm patients and lead to MA beneficiaries receiving a lower standard of appropriate care than those in Traditional Medicare, often forcing hospitals to divert precious resources and time to respond to care denials.
- Hospital outpatient departments (HOPDs) disproportionately serve lower-income, medically underserved, dually-eligible, and sicker patients with more severe comorbidities compared to independent physician offices, highlighting their unique role and need for appropriate payment structures.
- The experience with the IRF RCD program in Alabama showed over 85% of claims were approved (higher with appeals), demonstrating the program's administrative burden is unnecessary.
- The breakdown of the NSA's IDR process is anticompetitive, allowing insurers to threaten to bar provider participation in networks, knowing providers will be stuck in a broken dispute resolution system.
- The complexity of eCQM data requirements often spans multiple clinical domains and care settings, further straining limited staff and resources, especially for smaller hospitals lacking advanced IT infrastructure.
- CMS's QualityNet reporting system problems (recalled preview reports, suspended reporting, changed deadlines multiple times in a quarter) illustrate the financial and operational burden of faulty federal systems on hospitals.
- The experience with public health reporting, particularly immunization registries, reveals demoralizing challenges due to varying state/jurisdictional requirements and technical constraints, hindering the goal of a robust national public health system.
- Physicians express concerns that immediate sharing of sensitive or life-altering test results via patient portals without contextual clinical discussion could cause psychological distress or potential physical harm, such as in intimate partner abuse situations, underscoring the need for data segmentation and patient-preferred timing of information release.
- FAH data indicates that tax-paying member hospitals provide greater levels of charity and uncompensated care (as a percentage of operating costs) than many current 340B participants, challenging the arbitrary exclusion based on tax status.
- The temporary suspension of the CAH 96-hour rule during COVID-19 and other public health emergencies reinforced arguments that the requirement is not essential for quality or safety, demonstrating its outdated and burdensome nature.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "By design, these practices lead to Medicare Advantage beneficiaries receiving a lower standard of appropriate care than those in Traditional Medicare."
- "Focusing solely on payment rates, site neutrality does not account for the significant regulatory burdens and 24/7 essential services provided by hospitals to sicker patients that need higher resource care. Thus, site neutrality would be a short-sighted and flawed approach to regulatory relief and threatens to compromise patient access to care."
- "The program’s methodology remains volatile—particularly for smaller, rural, and critical access hospitals—due to the limited number of measures reported and inconsistent peer grouping. Additionally, hospitals are scored on differing combinations of measure groups, making direct comparisons unreliable and confusing. Public display of these ratings can unintentionally penalize hospitals that serve high-risk or underserved populations, potentially exacerbating disparities in access and perception."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
-   As an early childhood advocate and Head Start employee for over 26 years, I appreciate the opportunity to offer information in response to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS’s) recent Request for Information (RFI) on “Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.”
-   Prenatal-to-five programs like Head Start/Early Head Start provide locally controlled, community-driven services to families in every state.
-   The regulations and standards that HHS creates for the early care and learning field are critical to continued service to families and accountability for taxpayer-funded programs.
    -   They provide important guidance to the state- and community-based organizations that are entrusted with carrying out critical services.
    -   They promote program consistency, quality, accountability, and continuous improvement.
-   While every Head Start program is designed to meet the needs of their own community, performance standards provide the guidance necessary to ensure that we are both accountable for federal dollars and providing the essential services necessary to most effectively support children and families.
-   I strongly caution HHS against broad removal of accountability measures with the following key considerations:
    -   Ensuring Success in All States and Communities:
        -   In early childhood services, accountability measures from HHS uphold key pillars like program quality, child safety, and workforce supports.
        -   These ensure that the taxpayer-funded programs that yield positive outcomes can be replicated in all types of communities – rural, urban, exurban, suburban, and tribal.
        -   HHS’s standards are a critical tool for ensuring consistently positive outcomes across the U.S.’s vast range of geographies.
    -   Honoring Parent Choice:
        -   Local Systems of Care:
            -   Communities across the country have shaped their early care and learning and maternal health landscapes to be responsive to the needs of parents in their local community.
            -   Standards and accountability measures from HHS provide a key framework from which communities can operate to implement services that are consistent in quality and unique in the specific services, delivery methods, and curriculum they offer in response to parent input.
            -   I urge HHS to uphold standards as essential frameworks that communities build and innovate from.
            -   These standards allow parents the opportunity to take advantage of community services with the confidence that HHS is holding programs accountable on quality and safety.
        -   Family Leadership:
            -   In order to preserve parents’ rights to choose the best education for their child starting in the earliest years, I strongly urge HHS to maintain a robust public comment process on regulations pertaining to maternal health and child and family services.
                -   This will allow families to engage with HHS to create the types of early care and learning opportunities that will best align with their personal views on the type of early childhood education they want their child to receive.
            -   I strongly urge HHS to uphold the integrity of family leadership and feedback loop opportunities that are embedded into the structures of child and family services, including Head Start Parent Policy Councils and Head Start and Child Care Development Block Grant and Maternal, Infant, Early Childhood Home Visiting program community needs assessments.
            -   These opportunities to inform accountability measures and policies play a critical role in uncovering and promoting parent choice in early care and learning and maternal health services.
    -   Preserve Accountability for Public Funds:
        -   Through its standards, HHS supports state- and community-based entities in remaining accountable to their communities and to the federal government by requiring public disclosure around the use of federal funds.
        -   This is a critical function of regulations that I urge HHS to maintain, as it re-enforces principles that child and family serving services consider core to their mission: transparency, fiscal integrity, and accountability to families.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: A 26-year Head Start employee and early childhood advocate urges HHS to maintain robust regulations and accountability measures, highlighting their critical role in ensuring quality, promoting parent choice, and safeguarding public funds across diverse communities.
