structuredSections.corePosition: We believe the FDA's current approach to pharmaceutical compounding includes regulations and guidance that exceed statutory authority, are unnecessarily burdensome, and stifle innovation, thereby limiting patient access to essential personalized and shortage-bridging medications. We urge HHS to enact reforms that align FDA's actions with Congressional intent, reduce regulatory overreach, and support the critical role of compounding in American healthcare.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Rescind the March 2024 proposed rule "Drug Products or Categories of Drug Products That Present Demonstrable Difficulties for Compounding Under Sections 503A or 503B of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act" [FDA-2023-N-0061].
  - This would better align FDA actions with statute by preventing the banning of entire drug categories under 503A, which only permits banning specific drug products.
  - It would relieve unnecessary burdens on State-regulated pharmacies and preserve innovation in compounding practices.
- Amend the January 2025 Guidance for Industry, “Interim Policy on Compounding Using Bulk Drug Substances Under Section 503A of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act” [FDA-2015-D-3517].
  - This amendment should remove the exclusion of USP’s Dietary Supplement Monographs (USP-DS) for compounding under Section 503A.
  - This would remove an unnecessary barrier to care, better align with the DQSA, and foster innovation for patients requiring specialized therapies.
- Rescind the Center for Veterinary Medicine’s GFI #256, “Compounding Animal Drugs from Bulk Drug Substances” [FDA-2018-D-4533] and amend any associated regulations.
  - This would remove broad restrictions on the use of bulk drug substances in veterinary compounding that appear to lack statutory basis and hinder the preparation of suitable formulations for animals.
- Automatically deem any active ingredient compoundable by a 503A pharmacy as part of the 503B Bulks List.
  - This would streamline compounding and harmonize Sections 503A and 503B.
  - This could be accomplished by rescinding, reissuing, or amending the guidance titled, “Evaluation of Bulk Drug Substances Nominated for Use in Compounding Under Section 503B of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act” [FDA-2018-D-1067] and any related guidance.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- FDA's proposed rule regarding Section 503A's "Demonstrably Difficult to Compound List" attempts to ban entire drug *categories* for 503A pharmacies, which appears to exceed the statutory authority limited to individual "drug products."
  - This overreach would impose unnecessary burdens on thousands of family-owned, State-regulated pharmacies.
  - It would hinder innovation in patient care by reducing the prescriptive power of physicians and pharmacists' ability to develop personalized formulations.
- FDA's interpretation of Section 503A excludes USP’s Dietary Supplement Monographs (USP-DS) for compounding.
  - This unnecessrily limits patients’ access to medically necessary therapies.
  - It restricts prescribers and compounders from developing tailored solutions, creating a barrier to innovation.
- FDA’s Guidance for Industry #256 (GFI #256) on veterinary compounding imposes broad restrictions on bulk drug substances, effectively banning their use without clear statutory basis in AMDUCA.
  - This forces compounders to rely on finished drug products as starting materials, which may not be appropriate in dosage/strength or may contain excipients harmful to specific animal species.
  - Using finished products increases costs with no quality improvement and minimizes the foundational compounding principle of starting with suitable materials.
- The FDA's slow progress in populating the 503B Bulks List, with only five substances added in ten years, creates significant uncertainty for outsourcing facilities.
  - This impedes their ability to quickly meet hospital and patient demand for medications.
  - It limits outsourcing facilities' capacity to bridge gaps in drug supply and provide innovative, U.S.-produced pharmaceutical solutions.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The comment highlights the practical impact of current regulations on the compounding industry's ability to respond to national emergencies, specifically referencing "address[ing] national emergencies like the cisplatin drug shortage in 2023."
- It points out a counterintuitive consequence where FDA's restrictions on using bulk substances in veterinary compounding force the use of finished drug products, which can introduce "unwanted excipients" and "drive up the cost... with no demonstrable increase in quality."
- The fundamental principle of compounding, "starting with materials that meet requirements for both a suitable and stable formulation," is noted as being "minimized" by current FDA policies, revealing a disconnect between regulatory approach and core compounding practice.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "Our comments center on several Food and Drug Administration (“FDA”) matters that are thwarting access to individualized therapies, stymying innovation, and inhibiting American small business enterprise."
- "This action appears to exceed the statutory authority granted by Congress in the DQSA and, if finalized, would impose unnecessary burdens on thousands of family-owned, State-regulated pharmacies that fulfill the unique needs of patients requiring personalized medications."
- "A foundational principle associated with compounding is starting with materials that meet requirements for both a suitable and stable formulation; this principle is minimized when compounding is restricted to the use of only finished drug products as a starting material, which may fall short of being most appropriate, when more appropriate and qualified bulk drug substances are available."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The Association for Behavioral Health and Wellness (ABHW) looks forward to collaborating with the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Administration to eliminate unlawful and unduly burdensome regulations that stifle market competition and innovation.
    *   The Trump Administration has the opportunity to reduce government waste while better meeting patients' behavioral health needs.
    *   ABHW has identified opportunities that are inconsistent with statutory text, waste behavioral health care dollars, and stifle healthcare innovation.
*   ABHW is the national voice for payers managing behavioral health (BH) insurance benefits.
    *   Our member companies provide coverage to 200 million people in the public and private sectors to treat mental health (MH), substance use disorder (SUD), and other behaviors that impact health and wellness.
*   At a time when one in five adults in the U.S. experiences a mental illness each year and we continue to face record-high rates of suicide and overdose, the provisions below compromise the ability of health plans to ensure their members receive the highest quality of appropriate care.
*   I. Rescind Certain Provisions in MHPAEA Final Rule
    *   Since its inception, ABHW has been a leader for MH and SUD parity and was instrumental in drafting the legislation for the initial Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA) of 2008.
    *   Our member health plans have worked tirelessly over the past 16 years to implement parity for behavioral health services, innovating new approaches and benefits, addressing provider shortages and lack of access, and driving quality to improve patient outcomes.
    *   ABHW is grateful to the Trump Administration for issuing the non-enforcement policy covering portions of the MHPAEA Final Rule applicable for plan years beginning or after January 1, 2025, and January 1, 2026.
    *   We understand that the Departments are re-examining the current MHPAEA Final Rule and enforcement programs more broadly.
    *   Since January 2025, ABHW has asked the Trump Administration for:
        *   A one-year enforcement delay for the Biden Administration’s Final Rule “Requirements Related to the Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA Final Rule, Final Rule or Rule),” published on September 23, 2024.
        *   To withdraw certain provisions.
        *   To reform other provisions to ensure that the application and enforcement are practical, effective, and efficient.
    *   The Final Rule imposes vague guidelines and extensive new requirements, which require substantive guidance that health plans have not yet received, despite the 1/1/2025 and 1/1/2026 implementation dates for key provisions.
    *   We encourage the administration to draft a new parity rule consistent with the 2008 parity act and the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2021 (CAA).
    *   We welcome further conversations with the Trump administration to improve mental health parity compliance.
    *   In light of the non-enforcement policy for the 2024 MHPAEA final rule, we want to reiterate our concerns with the top five provisions listed below because they are inconsistent with the MHPAEA statute and/or create unsound, unworkable, and burdensome policies.
        *   These provisions divert funding, time, and resources away from helping patients with MH and SUD conditions and create new, onerous administrative requirements.
    *   1. Meaningful Benefits, 26 C.F.R. § 54.9812-1(c)(2)(ii)(A) (Treasury); 29 C.F.R. § 2590.712(c)(2)(ii)(A) (DOL); 45 C.F.R. § 146.136(c)(2)(ii)(A) (HHS)
        *   We urge HHS to withdraw the regulatory requirements for plans to cover meaningful benefits for every covered MH/SUD condition in every classification to avoid the direct conflict of this requirement with the MHPAEA statute.
        *   The Final Rule creates a “Meaningful Benefits” provision that exceeds the Department’s statutory authority because it effectively imposes a benefit mandate that the Departments lack the authority to impose.
        *   The Final Rule mandates that if a health plan covers an MH/SUD condition in a benefit classification (e.g., inpatient, outpatient, pharmacy), it must provide “meaningful benefits” for that condition in all classifications in which M/S benefits are provided.
        *   The Rule defines “meaningful benefits” as generally recognized, independently formulated standards for current medical practice and stipulates that coverage must include at least one “core” or “primary” treatment for the condition in each classification.
        *   The Rule is inconsistent with MHPAEA’s statutory intent to establish a methodology for comparing M/S benefits to MH benefits and instead mandates access.
        *   The statute clearly states, “nothing in this section shall be construed … as requiring a group health plan … to provide any [MH] or [SUD] benefit.”
        *   The MHPAEA 2013 regulations clearly state that the Departments “did not intend to impose a benefit mandate through the parity requirements.”
        *   The meaningful benefits provision violates the Administrative Procedures Act (APA) as it is a significant course reversal, incorrectly insisting that the MHPAEA Rule is “not intended to mandate coverage of any particular benefits.”
        *   What constitutes a “core or primary” treatment is ambiguous.
            *   In some cases, a “core treatment” may include a suite of items and services (e.g., prescription drugs and psychotherapy for major depressive disorder).
            *   However, there may also be no “core treatment” for certain conditions in certain classifications.
        *   The Rule also violates the APA’s Arbitrary and Capricious standard because it outsources the definition of “core treatment” to third-party authors of clinical literature rather than allowing medical professionals within health plans to determine what qualifies as a core treatment.
    *   2. Material Difference, 26 C.F.R.§ 54.9812-1(c)(4)(iii)(B) (Treasury); 29 C.F.R. § 2590.712(c)(4)(iii)(B) (DOL); 45 C.F.R.§ 146.136(c)(4)(iii)(B) (HHS).
        *   The “Material Difference” provision should be withdrawn because it exceeds statutory authority.
        *   The final rule mandates that where a health plan’s outcomes data suggests a difference in access to MH/SUD benefits as opposed to M/S benefits, the health plan must determine whether the numerical difference is “material” and whether the differences are attributable to an NQTL (non-numerical limits).
        *   If the plan uncovers material differences in data outcomes measures, they’re required to take “reasonable actions” to address any material differences as necessary to ensure compliance.
        *   Congress did not impose a requirement of parity in access to MH/SUD and M/S benefits in MHPAEA; MHPAEA requires only parity in plan terms and the application of those terms.
        *   The Departments themselves acknowledged in the 2013 regulations that “[d]isparate results alone” do not amount to a parity violation.
        *   The material differences in access provision:
            *   Relies on ambiguous, open-ended terms that determine compliance with the material standard including, “material differences,” “access,” and “relevant data.”
            *   Treats mere differences in access between MH/SUD and M/S benefits as indicative of a plan’s lack of parity.
            *   Incorrectly assumes that MH/SUD and M/S treatments are comparable.
            *   Operates as a one-way ratchet in treating material differences in access as presumptive evidence of a violation, without treating a lack of such differences as presumptive evidence of compliance.
        *   This failure to provide fair notice to regulated parties about what conduct is required violates the Fifth Amendment’s guarantee of due process.
    *   3. New Comparative Analyses Requirements, 26 C.F.R. § 54.9812-2(c) (Treasury); 29 C.F.R. § 2590.712-1(c) (DOL); 45 C.F.R. § 146.137(c) (HHS).
        *   ABHW urges HHS to withdraw the new regulatory requirements for comparative analyses and revise them to align with the statutory requirements.
        *   The Rule’s changes to the comparative analyses of NQTLs add significant new documentation requirements not required by MHPAEA and lack the specificity and clarity necessary for health plans to understand whether their documentation will be determined to be sufficient to demonstrate parity.
        *   Health plans are still awaiting clarifying information and illustrative de-identified examples regarding the development and application of NQTLs, which were required by the 21st Century CURES Act of 2016 and the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2021 (CAA 2021) but have yet to be produced.
        *   The Final Rule significantly reconfigures the 5-part test outlined by MHPAEA to a 6-part test in the regulations.
            *   The Departments do not justify this arbitrary departure from the clearly delineated structure of the statute.
            *   More troublingly, the Final Rule adds new requirements that are not addressed by the statute.
                *   First, the Final Rule substantively transforms the text that identifies what types of “factors” to analyze, requiring health plans to analyze the factors and evidentiary standards “used to design or apply the NQTL.”
                *   Second, the Final Rule adds a new step 3 that does not exist in MHPAEA, requiring plans to provide a “description of how factors are used in the design and application of the nonquantitative treatment limitation.”
                    *   The Departments do not attempt to identify any statutory basis for this new requirement.
                *   Third, the Final Rule creates a new requirement for plans to provide documentation of each factor, including, as relevant, documentation of evidence of whether MH/SUD and M/S benefits met or did not meet any applicable threshold in the evidentiary standard.
        *   This interpretation departs significantly from both the statute and previous guidance.
        *   This Final Rule imposes burdensome make-work requirements for health plans to develop written documentation to justify their every decision, rather than aligning with MHPAEA to require an analysis of the comparability of the types of processes, strategies, evidentiary standards, and other factors that the plan applies to its decision-making.
        *   The new comparative analysis requirements violate the APA's Arbitrary and Capricious standard as they use undefined terms and fail to specify the information health plans must provide for compliance.
        *   This is heightened by the fact that Departments’ continue to assert that not a single comparative analysis they have reviewed to date meets their expectations (as stated in the 2023 and 2024 Report to Congress on MHPAEA), coupled with the fact that the Departments have yet to create a model comparative analysis that would satisfy their expectations.
    *   4. Non-Quantitative Treatment Limitations (NQTL) Cease and Desist Provision, 26 CFR 54.9812-1(c)(4)(v)(A), 29 CFR 2590.712(c)(4)(v)(A), and 45 CFR 146.136(c)(4)(v)(A).
        *   ABHW requests that HHS withdraw the regulatory section authorizing regulators to prohibit the application of an NQTL that the regulator finds to violate MHPAEA because this provision is unconstitutional.
        *   The Final Rule includes a new enforcement provision that authorizes federal and state regulators to prohibit health plans from applying an NQTL if the plan’s comparative analysis does not adequately demonstrate compliance.
        *   The Departments indicate that inadequate documentation is now a strong indication of substantive non-compliance.
        *   Prior to the Final Rule, regulators found that all initial documentation submitted to date was insufficient.
        *   The fact that, to date, regulators have not found any comparative analysis submitted by a health plan to be fully adequate will raise the arbitrary and capricious nature of this new enforcement authority.
        *   Our members’ concerns are further exacerbated by the highly subjective nature of interpreting the exceedingly ambiguous new regulations and the near certainty that different federal and state regulators will arrive at differing conclusions about the sufficiency of plans’ analyses.
            *   Indeed, federal and state investigations to date have already arrived at different conclusions, with plans that operate in multiple markets submitting virtually identical documentation to different regulators and receiving findings of non-compliance from some and no findings from others.
        *   This is especially problematic given that the Departments have not adopted an appeals process to provide a formal review of these decisions.
        *   Health plans and insurers should have the opportunity to be heard at a meaningful time and in a meaningful manner.
        *   Substantial procedural protections are required here, as the consequences of following a final determination of noncompliance are severe.
    *   5. Mental Health Benefits Definition, 26 CFR 54.9812-1(a)(2), 29 CFR 2590.712(a)(2), and 45 CFR 146.136(a)(2).
        *   ABHW urges HHS to withdraw and revise the definition of “Mental Health Benefits” because it is unduly burdensome and unsound.
        *   The Final Rule interprets the regulatory definitions for “mental health benefits,” “substance use disorder benefits,” and “medical/surgical benefits” to require plans and issuers to “characterize items and services as medical/surgical benefits, mental health benefits, or substance use disorder benefits based on the condition or disorder being treated.”
        *   This provision means that claims and authorizations for “cross-over services” that are delivered to treat both MH/SUD and M/S conditions—including speech and occupational therapy, urgent care, surgeries (e.g., for gender dysphoria), and a wide range of other services—must be treated as MH/SUD benefits or M/S benefits based on the condition being treated.
            *   In other words, the same service delivered by the same provider might be characterized as an MH or M/S benefit depending on the condition being treated.
        *   This interpretation, which has never before been included in guidance and, to our knowledge, has never been enforced, will cause several perverse consequences.
        *   This non-sensical approach requires significant and costly changes to general industry practices related to benefit authorizations, claims determinations, and related health plan operations, most of which are not currently designed to process claims and authorizations differently based on the condition being treated.
            *   Health plans with more complex cost-sharing must implement new procedures that apply cost-sharing to diagnosis codes for the first time, and many systems were already set up and filed for 2025 when this rule was published.
            *   Additionally, there is an impact on Quantitative Treatment Limitation (QTL) testing.
                *   Under parity regulations, plans must analyze QTLs as well as NQTLs.
                *   QTLs are numerical limits on the scope or duration of benefits, such as visit limits, day limits, or episode limits, and these have never been a problem.
                *   However, this definition requires us to reexamine and restructure our QTL analyses.
            *   Lastly, pharmacy claims and authorizations, which have never been linked to pharmacy codes, must now somehow be linked for Parity implementation.
        *   The Department’s regulatory impact assessment does not account for the high cost and significant disruption to health plan operations across the country, which require plans to reconfigure their claims and authorization platforms to accommodate this new interpretation.
        *   Finally, the Departments definition for “Mental Health Benefits” confirms that health plans must define MH benefits to include all covered conditions that fall under any of the diagnostic categories listed in the mental, behavioral, and neurodevelopmental disorders chapter of the most current version of the International Classifications of Diseases (ICD) or that are listed in the current Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM).
            *   The rule thus defines intellectual and neurodevelopmental disorders, including dementia and autism spectrum disorder, as MH conditions, even if applicable state laws define these conditions as M/S conditions.
            *   This overrides state law definitions for MH/SUD benefits, which creates confusion and is difficult to implement.
                *   For example, some states, such as Ohio and New Mexico, currently classify autism as an M/S benefit.
            *   Historically, intellectual and neurodevelopmental disorders have not been considered MH conditions.
            *   This also diverges from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) guidance for Medicaid and CHIP, under which many state Medicaid agencies have defined benefits for intellectual and developmental disabilities as M/S benefits.
    *   State Parity Laws
        *   Another issue that arises with parity broadly and the provisions we outlined above is the intersection with state parity regulations.
        *   Several states have passed laws that impose unique parity compliance requirements, which have caused much confusion among stakeholders regarding compliance with the MHPAEA Final Rule.
        *   We also request that the Trump Administration work with states to rescind state-specific rules that have codified unlawful and unsound federal MHPAEA provisions or adopted their own burdensome parity provisions.
        *   If the federal provisions above are rescinded, these state laws that contain the same or similar provisions would remain.
        *   For example, in March 2025, Colorado adopted provisions from the federal MHPAEA final rule, such as meaningful benefits, changes to the definitions of mental health benefits, new definitions for evidentiary standards, factors, processes, and strategies, and requirements for the design and application of NQTLs that we listed above in items 1 – 5.
            *   If the federal MHPAEA Rule provisions above are invalidated, these provisions would remain in Colorado’s law.
        *   Another example, on June 23, 2025, Illinois issued a bulletin stating that it will continue to enforce the 2024 MHPAEA final parity rule “unless the 2024 Final Rule becomes void or is superseded by new legislation or rules, or unless the Department is otherwise enjoined from enforcement, provisions that took effect on January 1, 2025 will continue to be enforced without interruption in Illinois for issuers and plans subject to 215 ILCS 5/370c.1.”
            *   Illinois has committed to implementing the 2024 rule, despite the administration burden and statutory overreach, unless a new federal rule is developed.
        *   ABHW recommends that HHS promote uniformity between state and federal parity requirements by ensuring that states use federal standards as the basis for parity compliance evaluations to mitigate variations in enforcement and requirements.
        *   Federal and state governments should utilize the Office of Inspector General (OIG) MHPAEA Work Plan as a model for promoting consistency among the DOL regional offices.
    *   Improve Efficiency and Consistency of Audits and Investigations
        *   There is an overall need to improve the efficiency and consistency of NQTL investigations.
        *   We urge HHS to reevaluate the rules pertaining to NQTLs generally, as the existing compliance regime is unworkable and uses significant federal government resources.
        *   The current MHPAEA NQTL investigations are neither effective nor efficient.
        *   These investigations result in multi-year investigations and effectually require the plan to prove the nonexistence of an MHPAEA violation in a piecemeal fashion.
        *   The final rule failed to provide meaningful structure and due process for these investigations, and its new documentation requirements and vague new standards (e.g., meaningful benefits and material difference standards) will increase the complexity of these investigations.
*   II. Network Adequacy Regulations
    *   Certain network adequacy regulations limit health plans' ability to design cost-efficient narrow network plans, curb differentiation, and stifle market innovation.
    *   Some provisions below add complex network adequacy requirements that don’t account for the behavioral health workforce shortage and add administrative burden to business operations.
    *   Maintaining compliance with complex network adequacy standards increases business administrative overhead, diverting resources from consumer-focused improvements and competitive pricing.
    *   A. CMS Medicaid Managed Care Regulation
        *   Rescind Key Provisions in the 2024 Medicaid Managed Care Rule 42 CFR 438.68(3), 457.1218, 438.69 (f), 457.1207, 457.121
        *   1) Appointment Wait Time Standards
            *   The Center for Medicaid and Medicare Services (CMS) finalized the Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Managed Care Access, Finance, and Quality Rule in April 2024 that requires states to establish and enforce wait time standards for Medicaid managed care plans.
            *   The Rule mandates that routine outpatient MH and SUD appointments (for adults and children) be available within 10 business days. It also sets a 15-business-day standard for routine primary care and OB/GYN services.
            *   Medicaid Managed Care Organizations (MCOs) must achieve 90% compliance with state-established appointment wait time standards within federal maximums, consistent with Marketplace standards (applicable for the first rating period, January 1, 2027).
            *   Annual independent secret shopper surveys will be required to assess compliance with these wait-time standards and provider directory accuracy, requiring provider errors to be reported to the state within three business days. The first rating period is applicable July 10, 2028.
            *   ABHW has significant concerns with the behavioral health appointment wait time standards, expressing that they should not be more stringent than primary care standards.
            *   MCOs have no ability to manage provider scheduling practices; providers are best equipped to determine the urgency and timing of a patient visit.
            *   This Rule will not improve access to care but instead add a burden to providers, states, and health plans.
            *   We request that the HHS rescind the Medicaid Managed Care wait times requirement. These provisions overstep into state management of Medicaid, and national standards cannot account for states’ market dynamics.
    *   B. CMS Medicare Laws and Regulations
        *   1) Prohibition on Dual-Listing Providers Across Specialties; Rescind Provision: 422.116(b)(2)
            *   In CMS’s Contract Year 2025 Medicare Advantage and Part D Final Rule, CMS finalized a provision restricting a single provider from being counted in multiple network adequacy specialty categories.
            *   This increases the administrative burden without allowing providers to be valued for their specific expertise.
            *   For example, a provider cannot be counted in the psychiatry and outpatient behavioral health categories.
            *   ABHW requests that this requirement be eliminated.
        *   2) Limited Telehealth Credit Towards Network Adequacy, Amend Provision § 422.116(d)(5)
            *   CMS finalized a provision in the 2025 Medicare Advantage and Part D Final Rule that offers only a 10-percentage-point credit for telehealth providers in meeting network adequacy standards, which does not sufficiently account for telehealth's role in expanding access.
            *   Telehealth has proven an effective way to expand access to high-quality care, particularly in behavioral health.
            *   HHS and CMS have acknowledged the benefits of telehealth and should continue to evaluate ways to improve access, particularly in rural areas or areas with significant provider shortages.
            *   Given the acute workforce challenges limiting the supply of behavioral health providers and the efficacy of delivering behavioral health services via telehealth, CMS should increase the telehealth credit above 10%.
        *   3) Minimum Patient Volume Requirements for Behavioral Health Providers: Rescind Provision § 422.116(b)(2)(xiv)(B)(1) and (2)
            *   A new requirement in the Contract Year 2025 Medicare Advantage and Part D Final Rule requires certain providers, including nurse practitioners (NP), physicians assistants (PA), and certified nurse specialists (CNS), to treat a minimum number of patients before they can be included in network adequacy assessments, potentially excluding qualified providers.
            *   For an NP, PA, or CNS to satisfy the Outpatient Behavioral Health network adequacy standards, they must have furnished certain psychotherapy or SUD prescribing services to at least 20 patients within the previous 12 months.
            *   We ask CMS to rescind the 20-patient requirement, as providers should not have to prove they have served a minimum number of patients.
            *   By arbitrarily shutting certain providers out of networks, this requirement impedes access to services.
        *   4) Appointment Wait Time Standards: Rescind Guidance
            *   In the April 2025 Final Letter to Issuers in the FFEs and April 2024 Appointment Wait Time Secret Shopper Survey Technique Guidance for Qualified Health Plan Issuers in the Federally-facilitated Exchanges, which include Medicare Advantage plans, CMS established specific 10-day wait time requirements for behavioral health services.
            *   Given current provider availability, these requirements are challenging and could lead to compliance issues.
            *   We request that HHS rescind this provision for the MA behavioral wait times.
            *   The administration should align wait times for behavioral health services with existing standards already applied in the industry, such as the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) standards, which are already standardized across provider types and will eliminate confusion among stakeholders – plans, providers, and patients.
            *   At minimum, CMS should implement a different timeframe for non-emergency behavioral health services, which should be fourteen days, versus the proposed one week.
            *   Since emergency or urgent care is generally made available across the industry within 72 hours, there should be a more differentiated standard for non-urgent care. This seems warranted for non-emergency behavioral health, with the unprecedented demand for services and limitations in the system and workforce today.
*   III. Eliminate the DEA’s Prohibition on the Prescribing of Methadone for OUD; Rescind Provision 21 C.F.R. § 1306.07
    *   Methadone for the treatment of opioid use disorder (OUD) can only be dispensed directly by federally regulated opioid treatment programs (OTPs), with limited exceptions.
    *   21 C.F.R. § 1306.07 prohibits qualified practitioners from prescribing methadone for OUD and qualified pharmacies from dispensing it.
    *   Specifically, the language in the underlying statute does not have this prohibition. Instead, it requires practitioners, including pharmacies that dispense narcotic drugs for maintenance or detoxification, to obtain a separate registration for that purpose annually.
    *   Federal statute defines “dispense” (21 U.S.C. 802 (10)) as “deliver[ing] a controlled substance to an ultimate user . . . by . . . a practitioner, including the prescribing and administering of a controlled substance.”
    *   The Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) has restricted methadone to OTPs that directly dispense it rather than to qualified practitioners more broadly.
    *   This restriction limits the number of access points for methadone, thereby preventing competition.
    *   21 C.F.R. § 1306.07 is an incorrect interpretation of the underlying statute (21 U.S.C. 823(h)) and should be removed since it constitutes a significant regulatory action that materially harms competition in health care delivery.
    *   By essentially restricting access to methadone for OUD through OTPs that directly dispense it, rather than qualified practitioners more broadly, current regulations prevent competition in methadone treatment.
    *   The limited number of methadone treatment practitioners harms patients who do not live near OTPs, especially patients in rural areas.
*   IV. DEA’s Buprenorphine Final Rule, Eliminate Mandatory Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP) Review; Rescind 21 CFR 1306.51(b)(1)
    *   The DEA’s Expansion of Buprenorphine Treatment via Telemedicine Encounter final rule is scheduled to be implemented at the end of December 2025.
    *   A provision within the Buprenorphine Final Rule requires practitioners to review the Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP) data and notate the date and time such a review occurred within the patient's electronic health record (EHR) or paper record.
    *   If the PDMP data is inaccessible for any reason, the prescribing practitioner must notate the date and time that such review was attempted, indicate why the PDMP was inaccessible, and be limited to prescribing a seven-day supply.
    *   ABHW believes that HHS should rescind this requirement for a PDMP review, as patients should not be penalized if the PDMP is inaccessible or inoperable.
    *   States operate PDMPs independently of one another, and not all states capture the same sets of information.
        *   While one state may capture all information from prescribing controlled substances, another may exclude the name of the controlled substance and the location of the patient receiving the prescription or fail to note whether the prescription was provided through telehealth or in person.
        *   The lack of uniformity across the states challenges the implementation of this provision.
*   Conclusion
    *   ABHW is ready to support HHS and this administration in ensuring that regulations:
        *   Do not impede fair market competition.
        *   Are consistent with statute.
        *   Reduce unnecessary complexity.
        *   Safeguard fair access to MH and SUD services.
    *   We look forward to working with you to achieve the goal of improving all Americans' behavioral health.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The Association for Behavioral Health & Wellness, representing health plans covering 200 million people, urges HHS to rescind or revise several provisions in the MHPAEA Final Rule, CMS network adequacy regulations, and DEA rules on opioid treatment, arguing they are unlawful, burdensome, stifle innovation, and impede access to quality behavioral health care.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Association for Behavioral Health & Wellness (ABHW)
- **Type:** Organization
- **Role/Expertise:** National voice for payers managing behavioral health (BH) insurance benefits; member companies provide coverage to 200 million people; instrumental in drafting the initial Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA) of 2008.
- **Geographic Scope:** National
- **Stake in Issue:** Represents health plans whose ability to ensure members receive high-quality, appropriate behavioral health care is compromised by current regulations, which they argue are inconsistent with statutory text, waste healthcare dollars, and stifle innovation.
structuredSections.corePosition: We believe the Administration has a significant opportunity to eliminate unlawful and unduly burdensome regulations that stifle market competition and innovation, ultimately improving behavioral health care. The current MHPAEA Final Rule, certain CMS network adequacy provisions, and DEA regulations are inconsistent with statutory intent, create administrative burdens, waste resources, and impede patients' access to quality mental health and substance use disorder services.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Rescind certain provisions in the MHPAEA Final Rule, specifically:
    - Requirements for "Meaningful Benefits."
    - The "Material Difference" provision.
    - New comparative analyses requirements; revise them to align with statutory requirements.
    - The Non-Quantitative Treatment Limitations (NQTL) cease and desist provision.
    - The current definition of “Mental Health Benefits”; revise it to be less burdensome and more sound.
- Draft a new parity rule consistent with the 2008 MHPAEA Act and the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2021 (CAA).
- Promote uniformity between state and federal parity requirements by ensuring states use federal standards as the basis for compliance evaluations.
    - Utilize the Office of Inspector General (OIG) MHPAEA Work Plan as a model for consistency among DOL regional offices.
- Reevaluate rules pertaining to NQTLs generally to improve the efficiency and consistency of audits and investigations.
- Rescind key provisions in the 2024 CMS Medicaid Managed Care Rule, specifically:
    - Behavioral health appointment wait time standards, arguing they should not be more stringent than primary care standards.
- Rescind provisions in CMS Medicare Laws and Regulations, specifically:
    - The prohibition on dual-listing providers across specialties.
    - Minimum patient volume requirements for behavioral health providers (e.g., 20-patient rule for NPs, PAs, CNSs).
    - Appointment wait time standards (10-day rule for MA behavioral health services); instead, align with NCQA standards or implement a 14-day timeframe for non-emergency services.
- Amend the limited telehealth credit towards network adequacy (§ 422.116(d)(5)) to increase the telehealth credit above 10%.
- Eliminate the DEA’s prohibition on the prescribing of methadone for Opioid Use Disorder (OUD) by qualified practitioners (Rescind 21 C.F.R. § 1306.07).
- Eliminate the mandatory Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP) review requirement in the DEA’s Buprenorphine Final Rule (Rescind 21 CFR 1306.51(b)(1)).
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- The MHPAEA Final Rule (Biden Administration's version) imposes vague guidelines and extensive new requirements, lacking substantive guidance for health plans despite upcoming implementation dates, diverting resources from patient care.
    - The "Meaningful Benefits" provision effectively imposes an unauthorized benefit mandate, is inconsistent with MHPAEA's statutory intent, uses ambiguous terms for "core or primary" treatment, and illegally outsources definitions.
    - The "Material Difference" provision exceeds statutory authority by mandating parity in access (not just terms), relies on ambiguous terms, incorrectly assumes MH/S benefits are comparable, and operates as a one-way ratchet, violating due process.
    - New comparative analyses requirements add significant, unjustified documentation burdens, reconfigure statutory tests, and lack clarity, made worse by regulators consistently finding submitted analyses insufficient and failing to provide a model.
    - The NQTL "Cease and Desist" enforcement provision is unconstitutional, as it authorizes regulators to prohibit NQTL application based on inadequate documentation, is subjective, and allows inconsistent federal and state findings without an appeals process, leading to severe consequences.
    - The "Mental Health Benefits" definition is unduly burdensome and unsound, requiring costly changes to industry practices (e.g., claims processing based on condition treated, re-examining QTLs, linking pharmacy claims to codes).
        - It overrides state law definitions for MH/SUD benefits by defining intellectual/neurodevelopmental disorders as MH conditions, creating confusion and implementation difficulties, and diverging from CMS Medicaid/CHIP guidance.
- State parity laws that have codified or adopted burdensome federal MHPAEA provisions will remain in effect even if federal rules are invalidated, causing continued confusion and varied enforcement (e.g., Colorado, Illinois).
- The current MHPAEA NQTL investigation regime is unworkable, inefficient, and consumes significant federal resources, resulting in multi-year investigations requiring plans to prove non-violation piecemeal without sufficient due process.
- Certain network adequacy regulations limit health plans' ability to design cost-efficient narrow network plans, curb differentiation, stifle market innovation, don't account for behavioral health workforce shortages, and add administrative burden, diverting resources from consumer improvements.
    - CMS Medicaid Managed Care wait time standards (10 days for BH) are too stringent, MCOs cannot manage provider scheduling, and these standards add burden without improving access, overstepping into state management.
    - CMS's prohibition on dual-listing providers across specialties increases administrative burden and undervalues specific provider expertise.
    - The limited 10% telehealth credit for network adequacy does not sufficiently account for telehealth's proven role in expanding behavioral health access, especially in rural or underserved areas.
    - Minimum patient volume requirements for behavioral health providers (e.g., 20 patients for NPs/PAs/CNSs) arbitrarily exclude qualified providers and impede access to services.
    - Medicare Advantage behavioral health wait time guidance (10 days) is challenging given current provider availability and could lead to compliance issues.
- The DEA’s restriction of methadone for OUD to Opioid Treatment Programs (OTPs) limits access points, prevents competition, is an incorrect interpretation of statute, harms patients (especially in rural areas), and should be removed.
- The mandatory Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP) review provision in the DEA’s Buprenorphine Final Rule will penalize patients if PDMP data is inaccessible and is challenging to implement due to lack of uniformity in state PDMP data collection.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- ABHW was instrumental in drafting the initial Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act (MHPAEA) of 2008, demonstrating their long-standing expertise and commitment to parity.
- The Departments continually assert that no submitted comparative analyses have met expectations (as per 2023 and 2024 Reports to Congress on MHPAEA), yet they have not provided a model comparative analysis for health plans to follow.
- Federal and state investigations into parity compliance have resulted in inconsistent findings for plans operating in multiple markets, with virtually identical documentation leading to non-compliance findings from some regulators and no findings from others.
- The new "Mental Health Benefits" definition could lead to "perverse consequences" by requiring the same service from the same provider to be characterized differently (MH or M/S) based on the patient's underlying condition, which is a significant departure from current industry practices.
- Health plans had already set up and filed their systems for 2025 based on previous regulations, making the late publication of the new definition of "Mental Health Benefits" particularly disruptive and costly for implementing changes to claims and authorization platforms.
- States like Colorado have adopted federal MHPAEA Final Rule provisions into their state laws, meaning that even if federal provisions are invalidated, these burdensome rules could persist at the state level, highlighting a critical challenge in achieving national regulatory consistency.
- Illinois has explicitly stated its intent to continue enforcing the 2024 MHPAEA final rule unless it becomes void or superseded, demonstrating state-level resistance to potential federal regulatory shifts.
- Telehealth has proven to be an effective means of expanding access to high-quality behavioral health care, especially in rural areas, making the current limited credit towards network adequacy standards insufficient.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "The Final Rule imposes vague guidelines and extensive new requirements, which require substantive guidance that health plans have not yet received, despite the 1/1/2025 and 1/1/2026 implementation dates for key provisions."
- "The material differences in access provision... operates as a one-way ratchet in treating material differences in access as presumptive evidence of a violation, without treating a lack of such differences as presumptive evidence of compliance."
- "Our members’ concerns are further exacerbated by the highly subjective nature of interpreting the exceedingly ambiguous new regulations and the near certainty that different federal and state regulators will arrive at differing conclusions about the sufficiency of plans’ analyses."
- "This interpretation, which has never before been included in guidance and, to our knowledge, has never been enforced, will cause several perverse consequences."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO) thanks the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ) for the opportunity to submit comments regarding the Request for Information: Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make America Healthy Again.
*   BIO is the premier biotechnology advocacy organization, representing biotech companies, industry leaders, and state biotech associations in the United States and over 35 countries.
    *   BIO members range from biotech start-ups to large biopharmaceutical companies.
    *   Their shared goal is to develop medical and scientific breakthroughs that prevent and fight disease, restore health, and improve patients’ lives.
    *   BIO also organizes the BIO International Convention and annual conferences to drive partnerships, investment, and progress in the sector.
*   BIO’s submission responds to the request for information on regulations and guidance documents appropriate for repeal, replacement, or modification.
    *   This submission identifies statutes and guidance documents that are outdated, redundant, or inconsistent with current scientific standards and practices.
    *   These provisions impose unnecessary burdens on industry without providing commensurate public health benefits.
    *   BIO has identified specific regulations and guidances recommended for deregulatory action in a detailed table.
*   Manufacturing-related regulations are cited as examples where requirements delay product improvements or introduce inefficiencies.
    *   Annual review mandates and lot release procedures often duplicate internal quality systems, offering little added value.
    *   There is value and efficiency to be gained by harmonizing these requirements with international standards and modern quality practices.
*   In post-market and clinical trial contexts, outdated, unneeded, and duplicative regulations contribute to delays in patient access to therapies and increased development costs.
    *   For example, the requirement for pre-use submission of promotional materials for accelerated approval products is unnecessary due to current labeling practices and FDORA provisions.
    *   Several guidance documents and regulations that are obsolete or misaligned with current law are highlighted.
    *   HHS is urged to revise or rescind these requirements to reduce regulatory burden, promote innovation, and ensure alignment with modern scientific and legal standards.
*   I. Detailed Comments
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: 21 CFR 211.170b
        *   Description: Visual inspection of reserve samples
        *   Rationale: Visual examination has a cost while providing no value beyond what is required by stability testing programs.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: 21 CFR 211.180(e)
        *   Description: Annual review of all quality standards, drug product specifications and manufacturing or control procedure specifications
        *   Rationale: Manufacturers already update these specifications and related documents as necessary; requiring annual reviews is arbitrary.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: 21 CFR 211.86
        *   Description: Components, drug product containers, and closures approved for use shall be rotated so that the oldest approved stock is used first.
        *   Rationale: By contrast, the standard in Europe for medicinal products is a “first expiry, first out” approach. Without greater clarity, companies may implement and maintain additional controls of their inventories that are needlessly inefficient and burdensome, requiring expenditure of additional resources.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: 21 CFR 314.50(e)
        *   Description: Samples and methodology submission
        *   Rationale: FDA no longer routinely performs testing during NDA/BLA review, so this regulation requires firms to hold samples for no purpose. The methods package can be provided in eCTD format on demand to FDA laboratories if requested. Labeling is also submitted electronically, so multiple copies are no longer submitted. Therefore, this section is outdated and should be removed.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: 21 CFR 314.50(f)(2)
        *   Description: This regulation requires the submission of case report forms (CRFs) with every submission.
        *   Rationale: This requirement is redundant as information contained within CRFs is already included within case report tabulations. They can be provided upon request as stated within 21 CFR 314.50(f)(3).
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: 21 CFR 314.530
        *   Description: Accelerated Approval – Withdrawal procedures
        *   Rationale: BIO suggests revising the guidance to align with current law. Under FDORA, the Accelerated Approval withdrawal procedures were revised, so 21 CFR 314.530 no longer reflects current law (e.g., the need for a hearing). This outdated regulation could create confusion for applicants about how FDA will fulfill its withdrawal requirements.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: 21 CFR 314.550
        *   Description: The regulation mandates that applicants for Accelerated Approved products submit copies of all promotional materials intended for dissemination or publication for consideration prior to use within 120 days after approval or subsequently, 30 days prior to use.
        *   Rationale: Currently, product labels explicitly describe the accelerated approval basis and the need for confirmatory studies, rendering this regulation unnecessary and burdensome and in conflict with FDORA requirements.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: 21 CFR 601(g)(1)
        *   Description: This regulation prohibits the reference of master files in BLAs.
        *   Rationale: Applicants must duplicate application information that could more easily utilize Master Files, just as FDA allows for NDAs and deemed BLAs. This is a burdensome and redundant requirement that should be eliminated.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: 21 CFR 610.13(b)
        *   Description: Rabbit pyrogen testing
        *   Rationale: This method of testing has been replaced by more modern/appropriate endotoxin testing, which ensures the safety of biological products (e.g., LAL and MAT).
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: 21 CFR Part 11
        *   Description: Electronic signatures
        *   Rationale: The regulations do not reflect advancements in electronic systems in the last two decades and should be modified and updated. Data Integrity standards are encompassed in updated GMP guidelines. Subsequent issuance by other agencies has given legal status to electronic records and signatures. Any standards needed for filing should be internationally harmonized.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: FDA Guidance - Submission Documentation for Sterilization Process Validation in Applications for Human and Veterinary Drug Products
        *   Description: Sterilization guidance
        *   Rationale: This guidance, published in 1994, is obsolete.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: FDA Guidance - Format and Content of the Nonclinical Pharmacology/Toxicology Section of an Application (1987)
        *   Description: Document format for submissions
        *   Rationale: This guidance, published in 1987, is obsolete.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: FDA Guidance - Glass Syringes for Delivering Drug and Biological Products: Technical Information to Supplement International Organization for Standardization (ISO) Standard 11040-4 (April 2013)
        *   Description: Glass syringes
        *   Rationale: This guidance is outdated as a revised version of ISO 11040-4 was issued in 2015, and later added by FDA as a recognized consensus standard, without corresponding updates to this guidance.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: FDA Guidance - Medical Devices with Sharps Injury Prevention Features (August 2005)
        *   Description: Sharps injury prevention
        *   Rationale: This guidance is outdated and redundant given the 2011 release of a new International Organization for Standardization (“ISO”) standard to address sharps injury prevention—ISO 23908—which FDA added as a recognized consensus standard in 2014.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: FDA Guidance - Pediatric Drug Development Under the Pediatric Research Equity Act and the Best Pharmaceuticals for Children Act: Scientific Considerations AND FDA Guidance - Pediatric Drug Development: Regulatory Considerations--Complying With the Pediatric Research Equity Act and Qualifying for Pediatric Exclusivity Under the Best Pharmaceuticals for Children Act
        *   Description: Written requests under BPCA and/or PREA
        *   Rationale: BIO suggests revising the guidance to align with current law. FDA was not granted authority under BPCA and/or PREA to deny a Written Request (WR) because a study is a requirement under PREA. The law specifically states: SEC. 505A.(b)(1) “the Secretary determines that information relating to the use of a new drug in the pediatric population may produce health benefits in that population...”. Any drug with any study requirements under PREA meets this definition, and thus the Agency does not have the discretion to deny a WR on these grounds. In addition, this is not consistent with observed regulatory precedence.
        *   The policy to not issue WR based on PREA studies alone is a major change and is not justified based on data included in the guidance.
        *   There are several products that can only be used to treat a specific condition, such as HIV, and cannot be developed to treat any other condition. The current change in policy makes such products no longer eligible to seek incentives. This change will have a major impact across therapeutic areas and significantly impact pediatric drug development.
        *   The observation that PREA has resulted in more labeling changes than BPCA does not support the change in position that FDA will only issue WRs for additional studies beyond those required by PREA. If the PREA required studies exhaust the indications in which there is a meaningful health benefit for a pediatric patient, and the sponsor submits a Pediatric Study Plan (PPSR), a WR should be issued. The language used in the cited USC 355a is "may" (allowing WRs for PREA-required studies) and not "must" (not precluding WRs or associated exclusivity for PPSRs) which does not support the FDA position as stated in this draft guidance.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: MAPP 5019.1
        *   Description: Allowable excess volume
        *   Rationale: MAPP 5019.1 introduces new drug product specification requirements. Introduction of new policies and requirements through MAPPs precludes industry ability to provide input to new policies and requirements.
        *   The MAPP does not align with the ICH Q6(R1) Final Concept Paper in that it does not consider the specifications setting in the context of the control strategy of the product.
    *   Regulation or Guidance to be rescinded or modified: Section 510(j)(3) and (4) of the FFDCA
        *   Description: Reporting requirements
        *   Rationale: The rationale behind the distribution reporting regulation is to support the tracking of adverse events (AEs). However, the information submitted to the FDA every six months has limited utility for this purpose.
        *   It is challenging for the FDA to accurately correlate specific lots with reported AE due to the long shelf life of many biologics and the large number of lots potentially in distribution at any given time.
        *   In practice, manufacturers’ records are the most reliable source for determining whether particular lots are associated with adverse events. The FDA can obtain this information directly from the manufacturer as needed.
        *   FDA should exercise its enforcement discretion to exclude products licensed under section 351 of the PHSA from these CARES Act reporting requirements.
        *   Alternatively, BIO recommends that FDA consider consolidating the Drug Establishment, Lot Distribution, and CARES Act reports/reporting requirements to avoid redundancy and the resource burden created by having to format data into multiple, complex formats required by the Agency. Consolidation of these reports will allow sponsors to generate a single report to meet the requirements.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The Biotechnology Innovation Organization requests that AHRQ repeal, replace, or modify numerous outdated, redundant, or inconsistent regulations and guidance documents across manufacturing, clinical trials, and post-market contexts to reduce burdens, foster innovation, and accelerate patient access to therapies.

- **Name/Organization:** Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO)
- **Type:** Trade Association
- **Role/Expertise:** Premier biotechnology advocacy organization representing biotech companies, industry leaders, and state biotech associations; focused on developing medical and scientific breakthroughs. Steve Berman is VP, Science & Regulatory Affairs Strategy.

structuredSections.corePosition: We believe that many existing statutes and guidance documents are outdated, redundant, or inconsistent with current scientific standards and practices, imposing unnecessary burdens on industry without providing commensurate public health benefits. These provisions contribute to delays in patient access to therapies and increased development costs. We urge the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality to revise or rescind these requirements to reduce regulatory burden, promote innovation, and ensure alignment with modern scientific and legal standards.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Rescind or modify 21 CFR 211.170b (Visual inspection of reserve samples)
- Rescind or modify 21 CFR 211.180(e) (Annual review of quality standards and specifications)
- Rescind or modify 21 CFR 211.86 (Rotation of components and closures)
  - Align with the "first expiry, first out" standard in Europe to avoid inefficient and burdensome controls.
- Rescind or modify 21 CFR 314.50(e) (Samples and methodology submission)
  - Remove requirements for holding samples and submitting multiple copies of labeling, as FDA no longer routinely tests during review and electronic submissions (eCTD) are standard.
- Rescind or modify 21 CFR 314.50(f)(2) (Submission of case report forms)
  - Eliminate redundancy with case report tabulations and allow provision upon request.
- Revise 21 CFR 314.530 (Accelerated Approval – Withdrawal procedures)
  - Align with updated withdrawal procedures under FDORA.
- Rescind or modify 21 CFR 314.550 (Submission of promotional materials for Accelerated Approved products)
  - Eliminate as current labels explicitly describe accelerated approval, rendering this unnecessary and conflicting with FDORA.
- Eliminate 21 CFR 601(g)(1) (Prohibition of referencing master files in BLAs)
  - Allow master file usage similar to NDAs and deemed BLAs to avoid duplication.
- Rescind or modify 21 CFR 610.13(b) (Rabbit pyrogen testing)
  - Replace with modern endotoxin testing methods (e.g., LAL and MAT).
- Modify and update 21 CFR Part 11 (Electronic signatures)
  - Reflect advancements in electronic systems and align with updated GMP guidelines and internationally harmonized standards for data integrity.
- Rescind FDA Guidance - Submission Documentation for Sterilization Process Validation in Applications for Human and Veterinary Drug Products (1994) as obsolete.
- Rescind FDA Guidance - Format and Content of the Nonclinical Pharmacology/Toxicology Section of an Application (1987) as obsolete.
- Update FDA Guidance - Glass Syringes for Delivering Drug and Biological Products: Technical Information to Supplement International Organization for Standardization (ISO) Standard 11040-4 (April 2013)
  - Align with the revised ISO 11040-4 (2015) and FDA's recognition of it as a consensus standard.
- Rescind FDA Guidance - Medical Devices with Sharps Injury Prevention Features (August 2005)
  - Eliminate as outdated and redundant given the ISO 23908 (2011) standard for sharps injury prevention.
- Revise FDA Guidance - Pediatric Drug Development Under the Pediatric Research Equity Act and the Best Pharmaceuticals for Children Act: Scientific Considerations AND FDA Guidance - Pediatric Drug Development: Regulatory Considerations--Complying With the Pediatric Research Equity Act and Qualifying for Pediatric Exclusivity Under the Best Pharmaceuticals for Children Act
  - Align with current law regarding FDA's authority to deny Written Requests (WRs) under BPCA/PREA, ensuring eligibility for incentives for PREA-required studies where meaningful health benefits exist.
- Modify MAPP 5019.1 (Allowable excess volume)
  - Address concerns about new policies and requirements being introduced without industry input and ensure alignment with ICH Q6(R1).
- Exercise enforcement discretion to exclude products licensed under section 351 of the PHSA from Section 510(j)(3) and (4) of the FFDCA (CARES Act reporting requirements).
  - Alternatively, consolidate Drug Establishment, Lot Distribution, and CARES Act reporting requirements to avoid redundancy and reduce resource burden.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- Regulatory requirements delay product improvements and introduce inefficiencies in manufacturing.
- Annual review mandates and lot release procedures often duplicate internal quality systems, offering little added value.
- Lack of harmonization with international standards and modern quality practices creates inefficiencies.
- Outdated, unneeded, and duplicative regulations in post-market and clinical trial contexts contribute to delays in patient access to therapies and increased development costs.
- Regulations and guidances are inconsistent with current scientific standards and practices (e.g., visual inspection, rabbit pyrogen testing, electronic signatures, outdated ISO standards).
- Provisions that are obsolete or misaligned with current law, such as those affected by FDORA, create confusion and unnecessary burdens.
- Introduction of new policies and requirements through MAPPs (e.g., MAPP 5019.1) precludes industry ability to provide input.
- Current distribution reporting requirements (e.g., CARES Act) for adverse events have limited utility due to challenges in correlating specific lots with reported AEs for products with long shelf lives and large distribution volumes.
- Current FDA policy regarding Written Requests under PREA/BPCA may significantly impact pediatric drug development, especially for products treating specific conditions (e.g., HIV), by making them ineligible for incentives.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The contrast between U.S. "oldest approved stock first" rule for components and Europe's "first expiry, first out" approach, highlighting potential for unnecessary controls and resource expenditure.
- The observation that FDA no longer routinely performs testing during NDA/BLA review makes existing regulations requiring sample submission obsolete and burdensome.
- The insight that FDORA provisions have rendered previous requirements for promotional material submission unnecessary, as product labels now explicitly describe accelerated approval and confirmatory studies.
- The clear articulation that modern endotoxin testing methods (LAL, MAT) have replaced outdated rabbit pyrogen testing, making the old requirement obsolete.
- The critical insight that 21 CFR Part 11 for electronic signatures is significantly outdated, failing to reflect advancements in electronic systems over two decades, while other agencies have already given legal status to electronic records and signatures.
- The specific argument regarding FDA's interpretation of BPCA/PREA, contending that FDA lacks the authority to deny Written Requests for PREA-required studies if they provide meaningful pediatric health benefits, and highlighting the negative impact on pediatric drug development for certain therapeutic areas.
- The concern that agency policies introduced through "MAPPs" (Manuals of Policies and Procedures) bypass the standard public comment process, thus precluding industry input on new requirements.
- The practical assessment that current bi-annual distribution reporting for adverse event tracking has limited utility due to the long shelf life of biologics and the sheer volume of lots, suggesting manufacturers' internal records are more reliable.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
-   As an early childhood advocate and Head Start employee for over 26 years, I appreciate the opportunity to offer information in response to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS’s) recent Request for Information (RFI) on “Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.”
-   Prenatal-to-five programs like Head Start/Early Head Start provide locally controlled, community-driven services to families in every state.
-   The regulations and standards that HHS creates for the early care and learning field are critical to continued service to families and accountability for taxpayer-funded programs.
    -   They provide important guidance to the state- and community-based organizations that are entrusted with carrying out critical services.
    -   They promote program consistency, quality, accountability, and continuous improvement.
-   While every Head Start program is designed to meet the needs of their own community, performance standards provide the guidance necessary to ensure that we are both accountable for federal dollars and providing the essential services necessary to most effectively support children and families.
-   I strongly caution HHS against broad removal of accountability measures with the following key considerations:
    -   Ensuring Success in All States and Communities:
        -   In early childhood services, accountability measures from HHS uphold key pillars like program quality, child safety, and workforce supports.
        -   These ensure that the taxpayer-funded programs that yield positive outcomes can be replicated in all types of communities – rural, urban, exurban, suburban, and tribal.
        -   HHS’s standards are a critical tool for ensuring consistently positive outcomes across the U.S.’s vast range of geographies.
    -   Honoring Parent Choice:
        -   Local Systems of Care:
            -   Communities across the country have shaped their early care and learning and maternal health landscapes to be responsive to the needs of parents in their local community.
            -   Standards and accountability measures from HHS provide a key framework from which communities can operate to implement services that are consistent in quality and unique in the specific services, delivery methods, and curriculum they offer in response to parent input.
            -   I urge HHS to uphold standards as essential frameworks that communities build and innovate from.
            -   These standards allow parents the opportunity to take advantage of community services with the confidence that HHS is holding programs accountable on quality and safety.
        -   Family Leadership:
            -   In order to preserve parents’ rights to choose the best education for their child starting in the earliest years, I strongly urge HHS to maintain a robust public comment process on regulations pertaining to maternal health and child and family services.
                -   This will allow families to engage with HHS to create the types of early care and learning opportunities that will best align with their personal views on the type of early childhood education they want their child to receive.
            -   I strongly urge HHS to uphold the integrity of family leadership and feedback loop opportunities that are embedded into the structures of child and family services, including Head Start Parent Policy Councils and Head Start and Child Care Development Block Grant and Maternal, Infant, Early Childhood Home Visiting program community needs assessments.
            -   These opportunities to inform accountability measures and policies play a critical role in uncovering and promoting parent choice in early care and learning and maternal health services.
    -   Preserve Accountability for Public Funds:
        -   Through its standards, HHS supports state- and community-based entities in remaining accountable to their communities and to the federal government by requiring public disclosure around the use of federal funds.
        -   This is a critical function of regulations that I urge HHS to maintain, as it re-enforces principles that child and family serving services consider core to their mission: transparency, fiscal integrity, and accountability to families.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: A 26-year Head Start employee and early childhood advocate urges HHS to maintain robust regulations and accountability measures, highlighting their critical role in ensuring quality, promoting parent choice, and safeguarding public funds across diverse communities.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
-   **Name/Organization:** Margaret Tazewell / Head Start employee
-   **Type:** Individual
-   **Role/Expertise:** Early childhood advocate; Head Start employee for over 26 years
-   **Geographic Scope:** National (as Head Start operates across all states and communities)
-   **Stake in Issue:** Direct involvement in implementing and benefiting from the regulations governing early childhood and family services, with deep experience in Head Start.
structuredSections.corePosition: As a long-time Head Start employee, I strongly caution HHS against broad removal of accountability measures in early childhood and family services. These regulations and standards are critical for maintaining service quality, ensuring child safety, promoting parent choice, fostering innovation within frameworks, and preserving accountability for taxpayer-funded programs across all communities.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   Maintain robust regulations and accountability measures for early childhood and family services.
    -   Uphold these standards as essential frameworks that communities can build and innovate from.
-   Maintain a robust public comment process on regulations pertaining to maternal health and child and family services.
-   Uphold the integrity of family leadership and feedback loop opportunities embedded into service structures.
    -   Specifically mentioning Head Start Parent Policy Councils and community needs assessments for Head Start, Child Care Development Block Grant, and Maternal, Infant, Early Childhood Home Visiting programs.
-   Maintain the critical function of requiring public disclosure around the use of federal funds to ensure transparency, fiscal integrity, and accountability.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   Broad removal of accountability measures could undermine key pillars of early childhood services, including program quality, child safety, and workforce supports.
-   Weakening HHS standards could jeopardize the consistent replication of positive outcomes across the U.S.'s diverse geographies (rural, urban, exurban, suburban, tribal).
-   Erosion of parent choice if standards no longer provide confidence that programs are held accountable for quality and safety.
-   Compromising family leadership and feedback loop opportunities that are vital for families to shape early care and learning services.
-   Failure to preserve accountability for public funds, risking transparency and fiscal integrity in child and family serving services.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
-   The commenter's 26 years of experience as a Head Start employee provides significant long-term perspective on the practical impact of regulations.
-   An insightful perspective that HHS standards serve as "essential frameworks that communities build and innovate from," rather than stifling local responsiveness.
-   Emphasis that accountability measures are crucial for ensuring positive outcomes can be replicated across "all types of communities – rural, urban, exurban, suburban, and tribal," highlighting the broad applicability and necessity of consistent standards.
-   Highlighting specific mechanisms for family leadership and feedback loops, such as Head Start Parent Policy Councils and community needs assessments, as critical to upholding parent choice.

-   "These standards allow parents the opportunity to take advantage of community services with the confidence that HHS is holding programs accountable on quality and safety."
-   "This is a critical function of regulations that I urge HHS to maintain, as it re-enforces principles that child and family serving services consider core to their mission: transparency, fiscal integrity, and accountability to families."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Blue Cross Blue Shield Association (BCBSA) comments on the Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation to Make American Healthy Again (90 FR 20478).
    *   BCBSA is a national federation of independent, community-based and locally operated BCBS companies (Plans).
    *   These Plans collectively cover, serve, and support 1 in 3 Americans in every ZIP code across all 50 states and Puerto Rico.
    *   BCBS Plans contract with 96% of hospitals and 95% of doctors across the country.
    *   They serve those covered through Medicare, Medicaid, an employer, or self-purchased coverage.
    *   BCBSA offers a balanced perspective on health insurance given Plans' long history of serving members.
    *   Over time, regulators have implemented both helpful and unnecessary, unduly burdensome, costly requirements, some exceeding statutory scope.
    *   Health insurance is one of the most heavily regulated industries in America.
    *   Unnecessary state and federal requirements can:
        *   Limit insurers' flexibility to deliver innovative solutions.
        *   Force insurers to invest heavily in administrative infrastructure instead of patient care.
        *   Result in compliance costs (legal fees, auditing, reporting systems, specialized staffing) being passed to patients through higher premiums, deductibles, and out-of-pocket (OOP) costs.
        *   Drive up costs for patients and create barriers to streamlined access to care.
    *   We share the Administration’s interest in reducing unnecessary costly and/or burdensome regulations.
    *   Agencies exceeding statutory authority can produce results inconsistent with Congressional intent.
    *   Commonsense, streamlined rules can support robust, competitive health insurance markets offering high-quality, affordable coverage choices.
    *   As health care expenditures rise, payers and policymakers must collectively shift payments from volume-based to high-quality, cost-effective care.
    *   Embracing flexibilities and streamlined regulatory requirements can drive creative thinking and advance this shift towards lower cost, person-centered care.
    *   To support HHS' efforts to streamline government regulations, reduce costs, and make government more effective, BCBSA recommends HHS focus on the following key actions:
        *   Improve the surprise billing Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR) process to address bias and gaming of the system.
            *   Departments should reduce burden, costs, and misuse of IDR, which drives up patient costs.
            *   Actions should focus on:
                *   Reducing incentives for providers to submit ineligible cases to IDR.
                *   Improving IDR entity decision-making quality through increased accountability and oversight.
                *   Many of these actions can be done by improving existing guidance, in addition to finalizing the IDR Operations Rule.
        *   Pause implementation of the Excellent Health Outcomes for All (EHO4all) reward under Medicare Star Ratings and retain the current reward factor until the methodology can be transparently evaluated.
