structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Comment in response to HHS Request for Comment, 90 Fed. Reg. 20,478 (May 14, 2025)
    *   This comment is submitted in PDF form so that relevant images can be included.
    *   The comment reproduces HHS’s online form and then provides responses in blue text.
*   If you have ideas for cutting existing rules or regulations, we want to hear from you.
    *   Which agency/agencies promulgated the regulation?
        *   Food and Drug Administration (FDA), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)
    *   Which title, parts, and/or sections of the Code of Federal Regulations (C.F.R.) should be rescinded?
        *   21 C.F.R. Part 1141; 85 Fed. Reg. 15,638 (Mar. 18, 2020).
    *   What is your name?
        *   [Blank]
    *   Is your proposed rescission a notice of proposed rulemaking, final rule, direct final rule, interim final rule, or interpretive rule?
        *   Final Rule
    *   What is the name of the regulation being rescinded, if applicable?
        *   Required Warnings For Cigarette Packages And Advertisements
    *   Please provide a short summary of the justifications for the rescission.
        *   In a concededly unprecedented regulatory imposition, FDA’s graphic warnings rule mandates massive, provocative, and misleading graphic warnings that commandeer the top 50% of the front and back of every cigarette package and 20% of all cigarette advertisements.
        *   The rule should be rescinded because it violates the First Amendment, the Tobacco Control Act, the Administrative Procedure Act, and is fundamentally unsound and unreasonable.
    *   Please insert the address of the agency.
        *   [Blank]
    *   Please insert the contact information for the agency.
        *   Center for Tobacco Products, Food and Drug Administration, Document Control Center, 10903 New Hampshire Ave., Bldg. 71, Rm. G335, Silver Spring, MD 20993, 877-287-1373, AskCTP@fda.hhs.gov
        *   Michele Mital, michele.mital@fda.hhs.gov
    *   What is the background for the regulation being rescinded?
        *   The Tobacco Control Act (“TCA”) requires cigarette packages and advertising to bear one of nine statutorily specified textual warnings.
            *   15 U.S.C. § 1333(a)(1), (b)(1).
        *   It also requires FDA to “issue regulations that require color graphics depicting the negative health consequences of smoking to accompany” these warnings.
            *   Id. § 1333(d)[1].
        *   Together, the textual warnings and color graphics must occupy the top 50% of the front and back of cigarette packages and 20% of cigarette advertising.
            *   Id. § 1333(a)(2), (b)(2).
        *   For nearly fifteen years, FDA has failed to promulgate a legally sound rule.
            *   In 2011, FDA issued its first version of the rule, requiring disturbing images (body with incision, diseased body parts, wailing baby).
                *   Required Warnings for Cigarette Packages and Advertisements, 76 Fed. Reg. 36,628 (June 22, 2011).
                *   FDA claimed the rule would “reduc[e] the number of Americans … who use cigarettes” by making consumers “depressed, discouraged, and afraid” to buy them.
                    *   76 Fed. Reg. at 36,629, 36,638 (quotation marks omitted).
                *   The U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia and the D.C. Circuit quickly invalidated the rule as a First Amendment violation.
                    *   R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. v. FDA, 845 F. Supp. 2d 266, 277 (D.D.C. 2012); R.J. Reynolds v. FDA, 696 F.3d 1205 (D.C. Cir. 2012).
            *   In 2020, after eight years of inaction, FDA issued a second graphic warnings rule.
                *   This rule again required warnings to occupy the top 50% of front/back of cigarette packages and 20% of advertisements.
                    *   21 C.F.R. Part 1141; Tobacco Products; Required Warnings for Cigarette Packages and Advertisements, 85 Fed. Reg. 15,640, 15,709, 15,641 (Mar. 18, 2020) (“the Rule”).
                *   The Rule replaced seven of the TCA’s nine textual warnings with nine FDA-drafted warnings (totaling eleven textual warnings) and adopted eleven graphic images.
                    *   Id. at 15,685, 15,708–09.
                *   The eleven required warnings, including images materially similar to those invalidated by the D.C. Circuit, are viewable on FDA’s website.
                    *   See FDA, Cigarette Labeling and Health Warning Requirements (Jan. 15, 2025), https://tinyurl.com/msv85tm5.
                *   In contrast to its 2011 rule, FDA did not attempt to justify the new rule on the grounds that it would affect smoking behavior.
                *   Instead, it justified the new rule solely on the grounds that it would “promote greater public understanding of the negative health consequences of cigarette smoking,” particularly focusing on “less-known health consequences of smoking.”
                    *   85 Fed. Reg. at 15,640.
        *   The Rule has been subject to extensive litigation.
            *   A group of tobacco manufacturers and retailers challenged the rule in 2020 under the First Amendment, TCA, and APA.
                *   In 2022, the district court held the Rule violates the First Amendment and vacated it.
                    *   R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. v. FDA, 2022 WL 17489170 (E.D. Tex. Dec. 7, 2022) (Barker, J.).
                *   The Fifth Circuit reversed on the First Amendment claim and remanded on the statutory claims.
                    *   R J Reynolds Tobacco Co. v. FDA, 96 F.4th 863 (5th Cir. 2024).
                *   In January 2025, the district court entered a preliminary injunction, postponing the Rule’s effective date, holding that plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of at least some statutory claims.
                    *   R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. v. FDA, 762 F. Supp. 3d 529 (E.D. Tex. 2025).
                *   FDA has since appealed that postponement order to the Fifth Circuit.
                    *   See R J Reynolds Tobacco Co. v. FDA, No. 25-40137 (5th Cir.).
            *   Separately, in December 2024, another group of plaintiffs challenged the Rule in another district court, alleging violations of the TCA, APA, and First Amendment.
                *   Philip Morris USA Inc. v. FDA, No. 2:24-cv-00143 (S.D. Ga. Dec. 13, 2024).
                *   The case remains pending with cross-motions for summary judgment filed.
    *   Explain the reasons for the rescission.
        *   Rescission of the rule is compelled by all three of President Trump’s de-regulatory executive orders cited in the Department of Health and Human Services’ public comment request.
            *   90 Fed. Reg. at 20,480–81 (citing Exec. Order No. 14219, 90 Fed. Reg. 10,583 (Feb. 25, 2025); Exec. Order 14212, 90 Fed. Reg. 9833 (Feb. 13, 2025); and Exec. Order 14192, 90 Fed. Reg. 9065 (Feb. 6, 2025)).
        *   FDA’s unprecedented and onerous graphic warnings rule is unlawful because it violates the First Amendment, the TCA, and the APA.
        *   The Rule does not reduce chronic disease; it places an unnecessary burden on the American people; it imposes undue costs on free enterprise; and there are several obvious less-burdensome alternatives, all of which the agency failed to consider. It should be rescinded.
        *   I. The Rule is Unconstitutional Because It Violates the First Amendment.
            *   The Rule meets the criteria identified in E.O. 14219 because it is unconstitutional.
                *   Exec. Order No. 14219, 90 Fed. Reg. 10,583 (Feb. 25, 2025).
            *   The First Amendment protects “both the right to speak freely and the right to refrain from speaking at all.”
                *   Janus v. Am. Fed’n of State, Cnty., & Mun. Emps., Council 31, 585 U.S. 878, 892 (2018) (quotation marks omitted).
            *   The government therefore may not compel cigarette manufacturers to “use their private property as a ‘mobile billboard’ for the State’s ideological message.”
                *   Wooley v. Maynard, 430 U.S. 705, 715 (1977); see 303 Creative LLC v. Elenis, 600 U.S. 570, 586 (2023).
            *   The Zauderer exception (compelled disclosure of “purely factual and uncontroversial information” related to preventing deception) does not apply.
                *   Zauderer v. Off. of Disciplinary Couns. of Supreme Ct. of Ohio, 471 U.S. 626, 651 (1985).
                *   The warnings are not “purely factual,” “accurate,” or “uncontroversial”; they convey the government’s ideological anti-smoking message and are susceptible to multiple false or misleading interpretations.
                    *   Examples: images of a woman with a baseball-sized tumor, a sick child wearing a breathing mask, bloody diseased lungs, and diseased feet with missing toes.
                        *   See FDA, Cigarette Labeling and Health Warning Requirements (Jan. 1, 2025), https://tinyurl.com/msv85tm5.
                    *   Many images are similar to the “inflammatory images” from the first graphic-warnings rule, which the D.C. Circuit declared “cannot rationally be viewed as pure attempts to convey information to consumers.”
                        *   R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., 696 F.3d at 1216–17.
                    *   The head-and-neck cancer image is ambiguous and misleading; FDA defended it by asserting such tumors are "not unusual" in "underserved communities," but the image does not indicate this limitation.
                        *   85 Fed. Reg. at 15,674.
                        *   An image is subject to misinterpretation if it could cause consumers to believe a rare consequence is common.
                            *   R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., 696 F.3d at 1216.
                    *   FDA’s position has no limit; it could compel shocking warnings on products from fast food to guns to bully consumers.
                *   Zauderer also does not apply because the warnings are not related to preventing consumer deception but are purportedly designed to simply “promote greater public understanding.”
                    *   85 Fed. Reg. at 15,668.
                    *   The government cannot compel private actors to simply educate the public absent evidence of consumer deception.
            *   Since Zauderer does not apply, strict scrutiny should apply to this compelled speech.
                *   See, e.g., 303 Creative LLC, 600 U.S. at 583, 588.
            *   At minimum, the Rule is subject to the standard set forth in Cent. Hudson Gas & Elec. Corp. v. Pub. Serv. Comm'n of New York, 447 U.S. 557, 664–66 (1980), as Judge Barker held.
                *   The Rule fails this three-pronged test:
                    *   1. No substantial government interest: FDA lacks interest in compelling misleading disclosures, cannot sustain the Rule on a purely informational interest, and the public is nearly universally aware of smoking harms.
                    *   2. The regulation does not directly advance the governmental interest: FDA cannot show the Rule will meaningfully advance even its purely academic interest.
                    *   3. The regulation is more extensive than necessary: It commandeers 50% of package space and 20% of advertising for gruesome warnings.
                        *   The administrative record reflects that several readily available less-restrictive warnings would likely have been at least as effective.
                            *   An expert’s study in the administrative record compared FDA’s warnings to less-restrictive alternatives and found very few statistically significant differences in “new information” conveyed or beliefs about smoking risks.
                                *   Administrative Record (“AR”) 28001–28093.
                        *   FDA needed, at a minimum, to consider less burdensome alternatives, which it entirely failed to do.
            *   For the same reasons, even if the Zauderer test applied, the Rule would fail it.
        *   II. The Rule violates the TCA.
            *   The Rule meets two criteria identified in E.O. 14219 because it is not based “on the best reading of the underlying statutory authority”—the Tobacco Control Act—and accepting FDA’s understanding of its authority to alter the statutory textual warnings would work an “unlawful delegation of legislative power to the agency.”
                *   90 Fed. Reg. 20,480; see also Exec. Order No. 14219, 90 Fed. Reg. 10,583 (Feb. 25, 2025).
            *   A. FDA violated the TCA by changing the total number of warnings from nine to eleven.
                *   The TCA requires nine specified textual warnings (15 U.S.C. § 1333(a)(1)). The Rule’s eleven warnings are inconsistent with this.
                    *   Exec. Order No. 14219, 90 Fed. Reg. 10,583 (Feb. 25, 2025).
                *   Judge Barker held that Congress did not give the agency authority to increase the number of compelled warnings.
                    *   R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co., 762 F. Supp. 3d at 544.
                *   This is reinforced by Congress’s policy choice and the material, additional cost of incorporating each additional warning.
                    *   Id. at 545.
                *   Congress “struck [a] balance with a rule of nine, allowing the agency only to adjust the text of any of those nine labels.”
                    *   Id.
                *   FDA acted against clear instructions and materially increased costs by changing the total number of warnings.
            *   B. FDA violated the TCA by changing the textual warnings without first promulgating a rule requiring graphics to accompany the statements specified in the statute.
                *   FDA relied on 15 U.S.C. § 1333(d)[2] to rewrite textual warnings, which permits adjustment of format, type size, color graphics, and text to promote greater public understanding.
                *   The TCA’s text and structure clarify that FDA can invoke this authority only after first promulgating a rule under § 1333(d)[1] to require graphics to accompany the statutorily specified textual warnings.
                    *   TCA § 201(b) triggers graphic warning effectiveness 15 months after § 1333(d)(1) regulations are issued.
                    *   The rule under subsection (d)[1] must require color graphics “to accompany the label statements specified” in the statute.
                    *   FDA concedes it did not promulgate such a rule.
                *   The statute does not permit FDA to invoke subsection (d)[2] until a valid graphic warnings rule is issued under subsection (d)[1].
                    *   Subsection (d)[2] includes the power to adjust “the … color graphics,” which presupposes an existing rule requiring color graphics.
                        *   See, e.g., Corner Post, Inc. v. Bd. of Governors of the Fed. Rsrv. Sys., 603 U.S. 799, 817 (2024); Slack Techs., LLC v. Pirani, 598 U.S. 759, 767 (2023).
            *   C. FDA violated the TCA by substantively rewriting the Act’s textual warnings.
                *   FDA replaced seven statutory warnings with its own, addressing unmentioned risks like erectile dysfunction, cataracts, and bladder cancer.
                    *   85 Fed. Reg. at 15,658, 15,708–09.
                *   Nothing in the statutory text allows FDA to substantively rewrite Congress’s enumerated warnings.
                *   Subsection (d)[2] allows FDA to “adjust the format, type size, color graphics, and text of any of the label requirements.”
                    *   15 U.S.C. § 1333(d)[2].
                *   This limited authority to “adjust the … text” means “to alter [it] slightly,” not to rewrite it wholesale.
                    *   Adjust, Collins English Dictionary (7th ed. 2005).
                *   FDA’s arguments are an attempt to arrogate authority to draft statutory text, which Congress has not (and cannot) delegate.
                    *   E.g., Clinton v. City of New York, 524 U.S. 417, 439–40.
        *   III. The Rule violates the APA.
            *   The Rule also violates the APA, making it unlawful.
                *   Exec. Order No. 14219, 90 Fed. Reg. 10,583 (Feb. 25, 2025).
            *   The Rule impedes addressing chronic health conditions and promoting American wellbeing because FDA cannot show it affects smoking rates, and its studies don't show improved public understanding of risks.
            *   The agency failed to consider other, less-burdensome alternatives.
            *   The Rule burdens small businesses and private enterprise with no quantifiable benefit.
                *   Exec. Order 14212, 90 Fed. Reg. 9833 (Feb. 13, 2025); Exec. Order 14192, 90 Fed. Reg. 9065 (Feb. 6, 2025); 90 Fed. Reg. 20481 (May 14, 2025).
            *   A. The Rule is unreasoned and unsound.
                *   FDA violated the APA by acting arbitrarily and capriciously in five distinct ways, showing the Rule is unreasoned and unsound.
                    *   Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass’n of U.S., Inc. v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 29, 43 (1983).
                *   First, FDA acted arbitrarily and capriciously because its explanation for the Rule defied all available evidence.
                    *   Exec. Order No. 14219, 90 Fed. Reg. 10,583 (Feb. 25, 2025).
                    *   An agency acts arbitrarily and capriciously when its explanation runs counter to evidence.
                        *   Motor Vehicle Mfrs., 463 U.S. at 43; see Rest. L. Ctr. v. Dep’t of Lab., 120 F.4th 163, 175 (5th Cir. 2024).
                    *   FDA failed to show its warnings are superior to TCA warnings and failed to demonstrate its graphic-text pairings were reasonable.
                    *   FDA’s own peer reviews criticized the Agency’s choices as “arbitrary,” “inconsistent,” “not convincing,” contrary to “any sense of what the word” “understanding” “ordinarily means,” and based on “results [that] undermined the legitimacy and utility of the warnings.”
                        *   AR.54059, AR.54063, AR.54070–78.
                *   Second, FDA acted arbitrarily and capriciously because it improperly adopted warnings that evidence showed are already known, not believable, or misleading.
                    *   Exec. Order No. 14219, 90 Fed. Reg. 10,583 (Feb. 25, 2025).
                    *   FDA’s own Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health survey shows 99.5% of individuals believe smoking is harmful.
                        *   AR.27896–03.
                    *   Higher percentages believe smoking causes lung disease (94%) and heart disease (88%) than know the Earth revolves around the Sun (74%).
                        *   AR.27897. It would be difficult to improve these numbers.
                    *   FDA’s studies showed many FDA-created textual warnings were not believable.
                    *   FDA’s studies also demonstrated consumers would take away misleading and inaccurate messages from the Rule’s images and text.
                *   Third, FDA acted arbitrarily and capriciously because it failed to consider an important aspect of the problem: whether the Rule would actually affect smoking rates.
                    *   Cigar Ass’n of Am. v. FDA, 964 F.3d 56, 62 (D.C. Cir. 2020); AR.27529, AR.36105–06; See Exec. Order No. 14219, 90 Fed. Reg. 10,583 (Feb. 25, 2025); Exec. Order 14212, 90 Fed. Reg. 9833 (Feb. 13, 2025); Exec. Order 14192, 90 Fed. Reg. 9065 (Feb. 6, 2025).
                    *   FDA has not disputed it must consider important aspects of the problem or that it did not consider effects on smoking rates.
                    *   The impact on smoking rates is an important aspect of the problem, as a matter of “common sense.”
                        *   Cigar Ass’n, 964 F.3d at 62.
                        *   “[W]hen requiring a product to bear such obtrusive and expensive health warnings, it is difficult to imagine a more important ‘aspect of the problem’ than whether the warnings will actually affect product usage.”
                            *   Cigar Ass’n, 964 F.3d at 62 (citation omitted).
                        *   The current warnings are far more “obtrusive and expensive” than those in Cigar Association.
                    *   Requiring consideration of effects on smoking rates is consistent with common sense and the objective of the Make America Healthy Again Commission to reduce chronic disease (E.O. 14212).
                    *   The Rule could backfire and increase smoking rates, e.g., if disgusting images cause consumers to avoid reading warnings.
                        *   AR.28514-15.
                        *   Multi-country studies show up to 30% of smokers regularly avoid thinking about or looking at warnings.
                        *   One U.S. study found 74% of participants would likely avoid graphic warning information by concealing packs.
                            *   Id.
                    *   FDA failed to consider the emotional impact of the warnings, even though its own study respondents reported emotional reactions.
                        *   FDA concededly ignored this issue and made no effort to assess the emotional impact.
                            *   See 85 Fed. Reg. at 15,668 (“[A]n assessment of emotional responses or behavioral study outcomes is not aligned with the final rule”).
                *   Fourth, FDA acted arbitrarily and capriciously by ignoring several obviously less-burdensome alternatives to the provocative warnings.
                    *   Exec. Order No. 14219, 90 Fed. Reg. 10,583 (Feb. 25, 2025); 90 Fed. Reg. 20481 (May 14, 2025).
                    *   Agency action is arbitrary and capricious if an agency ignores an alternative approach that is “neither frivolous nor out of bounds.”
                        *   Chamber of Com. v. SEC, 412 F.3d 133, 144–45 (D.C. Cir. 2005).
                    *   Despite the significant burdens, FDA failed to consider alternative approaches including: less-provocative warnings; non-misleading warnings; text-only warnings; smaller, differently placed warnings; or a public-information campaign.
                        *   AR.27518.
                    *   In 2018, Reynolds urged FDA to test less-restrictive alternatives to assess their effectiveness compared to graphic warnings.
                        *   Reynolds suggested a study comparing current textual warnings, new textual warnings, and new textual warnings with graphic images to determine the graphics’ contribution to information conveyance.
                            *   See AR.27519 (quoting RAIS Comments at 4, Docket No. FDA-2018-N-3552 (Nov. 16, 2018)).
                        *   FDA refused to test this or any other alternative.
                            *   See 85 Fed. Reg. at 15,650.
                    *   FDA could have achieved its goals of highlighting “less-known health consequences of smoking” by changing Surgeon General’s warnings text or running a public-education campaign.
                        *   FDA has repeatedly promoted public education campaigns as “highly successful” and “yielding tremendous results.”
                            *   Norman E. Sharpless, Press Announcement (Aug. 20, 2019), https://tinyurl.com/y3kmouoa.
                        *   FDA touted a study asserting its Real Cost youth anti-smoking campaign prevented up to 587,000 youth nationwide from initiating smoking between 2014-2016.
                            *   Id.
                    *   An expert study in the administrative record found very few statistically significant differences between FDA’s warnings and less-restrictive alternatives regarding new information conveyed and beliefs about smoking risks.
                        *   AR.28014–17.
                        *   No statistically significant differences for “new information” between FDA’s warnings and text-only warnings on the side of the pack.
                            *   AR.28014.
                        *   No statistically significant differences for knowledge of smoking risks between FDA’s warnings and text-and-graphics warnings on the side of the pack.
                            *   AR.28015.
                        *   Other studies on less-restrictive alternatives reached similar conclusions.
                            *   AR.27925–26; AR.27519–20 (citing studies); AR.28513 (same).
                    *   FDA conceded it did not consider smaller and differently placed warnings, generically asserting that bigger is better.
                        *   85 Fed Reg. 15,650.
                        *   If this reasoning prevails, nothing would prevent the agency from commandeering 90% of the package.
                *   Fifth, FDA acted arbitrarily and capriciously by failing to engage in a proper cost-benefit analysis.
                    *   Exec. Order No. 14219, 90 Fed. Reg. 10,583 (Feb. 25, 2025); 90 Fed. Reg. 20481 (May 14, 2025).
                    *   A serious flaw undermining a cost-benefit analysis can render a rule unreasonable.
                        *   Idaho Conservation League v. Wheeler, 930 F.3d 494, 507 (D.C. Cir. 2019).
                    *   FDA completely failed to quantify the Rule’s purported benefits, expressly disclaiming any attempt.
                        *   FDA stated “there is a high level of uncertainty around quantitative economic benefits”—presumably because there are none—and chose to “describe them qualitatively.”
                            *   AR.19593.
                        *   FDA claimed it could not “compare benefits and costs directly.”
                            *   AR.19599.
                    *   FDA invented an analysis, suggesting $1.6 billion in costs would be offset by an imagined $0.01 benefit for each cigarette package sold.
                        *   AR.19628–29.
                        *   If permissible, this ersatz analysis would allow justification of any cost with unquantified benefits, contrary to Supreme Court instruction that “reasonable regulation ordinarily requires paying attention to the advantages and the disadvantages of agency decisions.”
                            *   Michigan v. EPA, 576 U.S. 743, 753 (2015).
                    *   In other contexts, FDA is willing to quantify benefits (e.g., Real Cost campaign prevented 587,000 youth from smoking and would save over $53 billion).
                        *   Norman E. Sharpless, Press Announcement (Aug. 20, 2019), https://tinyurl.com/y3kmouoa.
                    *   FDA’s refusal to quantify the Rule’s benefits is telling.
                    *   The failures of this cost-benefit analysis are notable given FDA’s experience with the original graphic warnings rule, where its analysis showed a de minimis, statistically insignificant reduction in smoking.
                        *   R.J. Reynolds, 696 F.3d at 1219–20.
                        *   The agency’s cost-benefit analysis did not amount to “a shred of evidence—much less the ‘substantial evidence’ required by the APA—showing that the graphic warnings will ‘directly advance’ its interest in reducing the number of Americans who smoke.”
                            *   Id. at 1219.
                    *   FDA, mindful of this rebuke, remarkably did the opposite and declined to attempt to quantify benefits at all, which is hard to interpret as anything other than a tacit admission that those benefits simply do not exist.
                *   Each of these five ways in which FDA acted arbitrarily and capriciously compels rescission of the Rule.
            *   B. FDA failed to provide meaningful notice and opportunity to comment.
                *   The Rule is unlawful because FDA failed to provide the public with meaningful notice of the bases for the Rule.
                    *   Exec. Order No. 14219, 90 Fed. Reg. 10,583 (Feb. 25, 2025).
                *   The APA requires a notice of proposed rulemaking to include “a description of the subjects and issues involved.”
                    *   5 U.S.C. § 553(b)(3).
                *   Agencies have a duty to identify and make available data used in proposing rules; failure to reveal technical basis in time for meaningful commentary is a serious procedural error.
                    *   Airlines for Am. v. DOT, 127 F.4th 563, 579 (5th Cir. 2025) (quoting Solite v. EPA, 952 F.2d 473, 484 (D.C. Cir. 1991)).
                *   FDA concealed vital information when it issued the proposed rule, relying on qualitative and quantitative studies but not releasing underlying data.
                    *   84 Fed. Reg. at 42,765–72, 42,777–78.
                    *   FDA initially released only short descriptions of qualitative studies, belatedly releasing reports without sufficient time for comment.
                        *   Id. at 42,767, 42,771.
                    *   Final data sets from quantitative or qualitative studies were not released until litigation.
                    *   FDA’s “Memo to File” explained not disclosing data, fearing “third party attempts to analyze the data in different and potentially selective, biased or misleading ways.”
                        *   AR.23863.2.
                    *   FDA also hid important information by not providing notice or opportunity to comment on peer review reports for the two quantitative reports.
                        *   85 Fed. Reg. at 15,658.
                *   FDA failed to provide meaningful opportunity to comment by giving only 15 days to comment on qualitative study reports.
                    *   84 Fed. Reg. at 60,966–68.
                    *   This failure was a “serious procedural error.”
                        *   Airlines for Am., 127 F.4th at 579 (quoting Solite Corp., 952 F.2d at 484); accord Kern Cnty. Farm Bureau v. Allen, 450 F.3d 1072, 1076 (9th Cir. 2006).
        *   IV. The Rule is bad policy.
            *   FDA has never attempted to show that the warnings will meaningfully change smoking behavior and has conceded that it cannot quantify the Rule’s purported benefits.
                *   Exec. Order No. 14219, 90 Fed. Reg. 10,583 (Feb. 25, 2025); Exec. Order 14192, 90 Fed. Reg. 9065 (Feb. 6, 2025).
            *   Its own studies indicate the warnings would not have a meaningful effect on public beliefs.
            *   The burdensome Rule compels private companies to promote FDA’s ideological message through grotesque, misleading graphics on 50% of the package, with no benefit to the public.
            *   This is textbook bad policy. The Rule should be rescinded.
    *   Describe the text of the relevant C.F.R. provisions as it will exist after the rescission.
        *   21 C.F.R. §§ 1141.10 and 1141.12 will be deleted.
    *   Please insert the name of the current agency head.
        *   Martin A. Makary, M.D., M.P.H.
    *   Please insert the title of the agency head.
        *   Commissioner of Food and Drugs
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An individual commenter asserts that the FDA's graphic cigarette warning rule is an unlawful, unprecedented, and unreasonable imposition that violates the First Amendment, the Tobacco Control Act, and the Administrative Procedure Act, and should be immediately rescinded.

- **Type:** Individual

Likely represents or is affiliated with entities impacted by the regulation (e.g., tobacco manufacturers or retailers), given the depth of argument and specific citations to industry comments and ongoing litigation.
- **Geographic Scope:** National (commenting on federal regulation applicable across the U.S.)
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly affected by the graphic warning rule's requirements, likely due to implications for the manufacturing, advertising, and sale of cigarettes, incurring compliance costs and First Amendment concerns.
structuredSections.corePosition: The FDA's graphic warnings rule (21 C.F.R. Part 1141; 85 Fed. Reg. 15,638) is an unconstitutional, statutorily unauthorized, and arbitrary imposition that should be rescinded. It mandates massive, provocative, and misleading graphic warnings on cigarette packaging and advertisements without quantifiable public benefit, violating core constitutional rights and administrative procedure.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- The FDA's graphic warnings rule (21 C.F.R. Part 1141; 85 Fed. Reg. 15,638) should be rescinded immediately as a final rule.
  - Rescission is compelled by President Trump’s de-regulatory executive orders (E.O. 14219, 14212, 14192).
  - Rescission would delete 21 C.F.R. §§ 1141.10 and 1141.12.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Violation of the First Amendment:**
  - The compelled graphic warnings are not "purely factual" or "uncontroversial" and convey an ideological anti-smoking message, rendering the Zauderer exception inapplicable.
  - The warnings are ambiguous and misleading (e.g., disproportionate images like baseball-sized tumors, or images defended by FDA with unstated limitations).
  - The government cannot compel private actors to simply "educate the public" without evidence of consumer deception.
  - The rule fails the Central Hudson test: no substantial government interest, no direct advancement of interest, and more extensive than necessary.
  - FDA failed to consider less-burdensome alternatives despite evidence suggesting their comparable effectiveness.
- **Violation of the Tobacco Control Act (TCA):**
  - FDA unlawfully changed the statutory total number of warnings from nine to eleven, exceeding its authority.
  - FDA improperly altered statutory textual warnings without first promulgating a valid rule requiring graphics to accompany the *statutorily specified* statements, as required by the TCA.
  - FDA substantively rewrote the Act’s textual warnings (e.g., adding risks like erectile dysfunction, cataracts, bladder cancer) instead of merely "adjusting" them as permitted by statute.
- **Violation of the Administrative Procedure Act (APA):**
  - **Unreasoned and Unsound Rulemaking:**
    - FDA’s explanation defied available evidence and peer reviews, which deemed its choices "arbitrary" and "inconsistent."
    - FDA adopted warnings for risks already widely known (e.g., 99.5% believe smoking is harmful) and warnings that its own studies found to be unbelievable or misleading.
    - FDA failed to consider the rule's actual impact on smoking rates, despite this being a "common sense" and "important aspect of the problem."
    - FDA failed to consider the emotional impact of the shocking and disturbing warnings on the public.
    - FDA ignored several obviously less-burdensome alternatives (e.g., less-provocative, non-misleading, text-only, smaller warnings, or public-information campaigns), refusing to test them.
  - **Failure of Proper Cost-Benefit Analysis:**
    - FDA completely failed to quantify the rule's purported benefits, instead using a qualitative description and an "invented" ersatz analysis to offset $1.6 billion in costs with an imagined $0.01 benefit per pack.
    - This contrasts with FDA's willingness to quantify benefits for other programs (e.g., "Real Cost" campaign).
    - This failure suggests a "tacit admission that those benefits simply do not exist," especially given the previous rule's de minimis impact.
  - **Lack of Meaningful Notice and Opportunity to Comment:**
    - FDA concealed vital underlying data for studies used in the proposed rule, releasing it only during litigation.
    - FDA failed to provide public notice or opportunity to comment on peer review reports for its quantitative studies.
    - FDA provided only 15 days to comment on qualitative study reports, which is considered a "serious procedural error."
- **Bad Policy:** The rule compels private companies to promote FDA’s ideological message through grotesque, misleading graphics on 50% of the package with no quantifiable public benefit, making it burdensome and ineffective.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The comment highlights the extensive and ongoing legal challenges to FDA's graphic warning rules, noting that FDA has failed for nearly 15 years to promulgate a legally sound rule after its first attempt was invalidated on First Amendment grounds.
- It provides a striking insight into public awareness, citing FDA's own data showing 99.5% of individuals already believe smoking is harmful and that awareness of smoking's link to lung/heart disease (94%/88%) is higher than knowing the Earth revolves around the Sun (74%).
- The commenter raises a counterintuitive insight: the rule could backfire and *increase* smoking rates if disgusting images cause consumers to avoid reading accompanying warnings, citing studies where up to 30% of smokers avoid warnings and 74% might conceal packs.
- It details specific instances of FDA's arbitrary and capricious behavior, such as ignoring its own peer reviews that "lambasted" the agency's choices as "arbitrary" and "inconsistent," and refusing to test less-restrictive alternatives despite being urged to by industry.
- The comment points out the contradiction in FDA's approach to cost-benefit analysis, where it claimed inability to quantify benefits for the graphic warning rule while readily quantifying substantial benefits for its "Real Cost" public education campaign.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "In a concededly unprecedented regulatory imposition, FDA’s graphic warnings rule mandates massive, provocative, and misleading graphic warnings that commandeer the top 50% of the front and back of every cigarette package and 20% of all cigarette advertisements."
- "Indeed, FDA’s own Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health survey, a 'nationally representative longitudinal dataset,' shows that 99.5% of individuals already believe that cigarette smoking is harmful to health. The same data shows that a higher percentage of adults believe smoking causes lung disease (94%) and heart disease (88%) than know the Earth revolves around the Sun (74%)."
- "It is hard to interpret this decision [FDA's refusal to quantify benefits] as anything other than a tacit admission that those benefits simply do not exist."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   ADHD has affected every corner of my life since I was a kid, but I didn’t get diagnosed until I was 32.
    *   For years, I thought I was just bad at life.
        *   Missing deadlines
        *   Forgetting simple tasks
        *   Struggling to keep a job or a relationship stable
    *   Once I finally got a diagnosis, things made sense.
        *   I wasn’t lazy - I had a brain that processes the world differently.
    *   Medication helped me get a grip on my responsibilities.
        *   I could finally hold down a job in tech support.
        *   Focus on tickets.
        *   Remember appointments.
        *   Even feel a little more present with my wife and kids.
*   It is ridiculously hard to keep that treatment going.
    *   Most psychiatrists in my area don’t accept new ADHD patients anymore.
        *   When they do, the waitlists are six to eight months.
    *   My PCP tries his best, but he’s not confident managing my meds.
    *   Every month, I go through the same song and dance with the pharmacy.
        *   Since my medication is classified as Schedule II, they won’t even process it a day early.
        *   They’re constantly out of stock.
        *   I’ve been handed pills from different manufacturers that feel completely different in my body.
            *   It throws me off.
            *   Messes up my sleep.
            *   Makes me even more anxious.
*   The Schedule II label alone creates this cloud of suspicion.
    *   It doesn’t reflect the actual medical risk.
    *   It signals to everyone - providers, pharmacists, even family members - that these meds are inherently “dangerous.”
    *   That label has done more to damage access and increase stigma than anything else.
    *   People talk about “diversion,” but these rules weren’t written for patients.
        *   They were written for the tiny percentage of potential abusers.
        *   In trying to block a few bad actors, the system ends up punishing 100% of the people who are actually using these medications responsibly and desperately need them.
*   It’s absurd that these meds are still sitting in the same category as fentanyl and methadone, while drugs like Xanax and testosterone are on lighter schedules.
    *   These medications have been used since WWII.
    *   If they were really so addictive, we would have a stimulant crisis on our hands by now.
        *   We don’t - because the majority of patients are managing ADHD, not getting high.
    *   The DSM-5 doesn’t even list amphetamine addiction anymore.
    *   These restrictions are not protecting us from overdose deaths, and they are not improving care.
*   We’re not criminals.
*   We’re not drug seekers.
*   We’re adults with a neurodevelopmental condition trying to stay functional, productive, and present in our lives.
*   Telehealth gave us a way to finally access care - don’t take that away.
*   Stop letting 1970s drug war thinking dictate how modern medicine is handled in 2025.
*   More than 30 million people with ADHD deserve better.

These restrictions, based on outdated "drug war thinking," punish the vast majority of people who genuinely need these medications to function, rather than effectively preventing abuse.

    - It should ideally place these medications on a lighter schedule, similar to Xanax or testosterone.
    - This would reduce stigma and improve access for the over 30 million people with ADHD.

- Difficulty in maintaining consistent ADHD treatment due to systemic access barriers.

    - Ongoing monthly issues with pharmacies regarding Schedule II medications:
        - Inability to process refills even one day early.
        - Persistent out-of-stock situations.
        - Receiving pills from different manufacturers that vary in effect, causing physiological disruption (throws me off, messes up sleep) and increased anxiety.
- The Schedule II classification of ADHD medication.
    - It creates a "cloud of suspicion" and signals to all involved parties (providers, pharmacists, family) that the medications are inherently “dangerous.”
    - It disproportionately damages patient access and increases stigma.
    - The regulations are designed for a tiny percentage of potential abusers, effectively punishing 100% of responsible patients who desperately need the medication.
    - The classification is inconsistent and absurd, placing ADHD meds in the same category as fentanyl and methadone, while drugs like Xanax and testosterone are on lighter schedules.
    - The premise of high addictiveness is unfounded, given their long history of use since WWII without a "stimulant crisis" and the DSM-5's removal of amphetamine addiction.
    - Current restrictions do not protect against overdose deaths nor do they improve patient care.
- The potential removal of telehealth access, which has been crucial for obtaining care.
- Outdated "1970s drug war thinking" continues to dictate modern medical policy in 2025, to the detriment of patients.

- A compelling argument that current regulations, in attempting to block a few bad actors, "end up punishing 100% of the people who are actually using these medications responsibly and desperately need them."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The Child Care Association of Louisiana (CCAL) endorses the comments submitted by the National Child Care Association (NCCA).
    *   CCAL is the longest standing advocacy organization representing licensed childcare centers.
    *   NCCA also responded to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) invitation for stakeholders to submit deregulatory actions through Regulations.gov, docket number AHRQ-2025-0001.
    *   We appreciate the opportunity to provide input on HHS’s comprehensive deregulatory effort.
    *   We support the Administration’s goals to reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens while maintaining the integrity of protecting children in licensed childcare facilities.
*   Comments Regarding 45 C.F.R. § 98 - Background Check Implementation
    *   History
        *   There are several components that make it difficult to enforce full compliance with the federal background check requirements for child care workers, as mandated by the Child Care and Development Block Grant (CCDBG) Act of 2014.
        *   We urge the Department to revise interpretations that go beyond the plain meaning of the statute authorizing background checks.
        *   Individuals with histories of child abuse, violent crimes, or sexual offenses are not permitted to work in licensed child care settings.
        *   These requirements include FBI fingerprint checks, in-state and inter-state criminal history and sex offender registry reviews, and child abuse and neglect registry searches.
        *   Unfortunately, several states, most notably California, remain out of compliance with one or more of these provisions—despite federal deadlines and technical support made available through HHS.
        *   California’s continued failure to conduct required cross-state registry checks and fully implement screening requirements undermines the integrity of the national child care safety framework.
        *   It also places children at avoidable and unacceptable risk.
*   Comment Regarding Interpretation of “Supervision” in Background Check Requirements under 45 C.F.R. § 98.43
    *   We respectfully request HHS to revise its interpretation of “supervision of provisional employees” as used in the implementation of 45 C.F.R. § 98.43, which governs the background check requirements for childcare providers under the CCDBG Act.
    *   Background
        *   The CCDBG Act of 2014 and its implementing regulations require that child care staff who have not yet completed comprehensive background checks may only begin employment provisionally, under certain conditions.
        *   Specifically, if they are “supervised at all times by an individual who has received a background check.”
        *   While the statute provides necessary safeguards for children’s health and safety, the federal interpretation of “supervision” has led to operational burdens and misaligned state-level enforcement practices.
        *   Specifically, HHS has defined this term more narrowly than the statutory language passed by Congress, interpreting “supervision” to mean one-on-one, line-of-sight oversight by a staff member with a comprehensive background check, effectively tethering the new provisional employee to a supervisor and undermining operational flexibility.
    *   Impact on Providers
        *   Staffing Strain: Requiring a fully vetted staff member to shadow a new hire restricts classroom coverage and reduces ratio capacity, particularly in small centers and family childcare homes.
        *   Hiring Delays: Providers, especially in rural or underserved areas, are reluctant to hire needed staff when immediate supervision obligations are functionally or financially unworkable.
        *   Barrier to Entry: The rigidity of supervision standards discourages otherwise qualified individuals from entering the early childhood workforce due to administrative and logistical hurdles.
        *   Child Safety Risks: Ironically, the narrow interpretation may compromise safety by limiting the number of adults available to meet supervision ratios in classrooms, thereby increasing the risk of oversight or fatigue among cleared staff.
    *   Implications of the Chevron Decision
        *   The recent U.S. Supreme Court decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024), which overturned the Chevron doctrine, has important implications for this issue.
        *   By eliminating judicial deference to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes, the Court restored the principle that agencies must remain within the bounds of clear congressional intent.
        *   HHS’s interpretation of “supervision” under 45 C.F.R. § 98.43 appears to go beyond what the CCDBG Act itself requires.
        *   The statute permits provisional employment with supervision but does not define that term, nor does it mandate a one-size-fits-all application.
        *   In light of Loper Bright, we urge HHS to:
            *   Reexamine whether the current federal interpretation imposes unjustified burdens not supported by the statutory text.
            *   Refrain from imposing overly prescriptive definitions that limit states and providers’ ability to implement safe and effective supervision practices.
            *   Affirm that states may adopt reasonable, risk-based interpretations of supervision, consistent with health and safety and operational feasibility.
    *   Recommended Revision
        *   We recommend that HHS issue revised guidance or initiate formal rulemaking to adopt a more functional definition of supervision, such as:
            *   “Supervision means on-site oversight by a cleared staff member who is physically present, readily accessible, and responsible for monitoring the activities of a provisionally employed individual through appropriate methods consistent with the child care setting, including visual checks, classroom presence, or proximity-based observation.”
        *   This language allows for safe, structured oversight of new staff while enabling providers to maintain staff-child ratios and preserve operational flexibility.
        *   It mirrors the practical application already in use in many states for substitute teachers and classroom aides.
*   Comment Regarding Unlawful Restriction on Provisional Child Care Employment Under the CCDBG Act in 45 C.F.R. § 98.43(d)(4) as interpreted by HHS in light of the United States Supreme Court decision Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. ___ (2024)
    *   HHS is currently requiring that child care providers wait until background checks state and federal background checks in the state of employment are completed and cleared before permitting a “prospective staff member” to begin employment, in a supervised, provisional capacity.
    *   This policy is not only inconsistent with the statute, but it now stands in direct violation of the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo.
    *   I. The Plain Text of the Statute Permits Provisional Employment Upon Submission of Background Check Requests
        *   Under the CCDBG Act of 2014, codified at 42 U.S.C. § 9858f(h)(1)(C), Congress made clear that:
            *   “A child care staff member may begin work for a child care provider after the staff member has submitted a request for a criminal background check… and while awaiting the results… provided that such individual is supervised at all times by an individual who has received a qualifying result.”
        *   Congress in their wisdom recognized that child safety is multifaceted, and it essential for providers to be in ratio to ensure the physical safety and protection of children.
        *   Foreseeing situations where employees fail to show to work quit unexpectedly, the statutory language plainly permits supervised provisional employment once a background check application has been submitted—not after it is completed or returned.
        *   Congress considered and rejected the idea of delaying employment until clearance was issued.
        *   Instead, it balanced child safety with the operational realities of childcare programs by allowing supervised employment during the processing period.
    *   II. HHS’s Implementation Adds Unauthorized Conditions
        *   Despite this clear directive, the Department’s implementation of 45 C.F.R. § 98.43(d)(4)—and subsequent agency guidance—has created a de facto requirement that no employment may begin until background checks are fully returned.
        *   In many states, this has been interpreted and enforced to mean:
            *   Staff may not be scheduled or onboarded in any capacity.
            *   Staff may not have any contact with children, even under supervision.
            *   Supervision must occur with line-of-sight or one-to-one monitoring.
            *   Providers cannot count supervised provisional staff toward ratios.
        *   These additional restrictions are nowhere found in the statute, nor is it reasonably derived from its plain meaning.
        *   It imposes a requirement Congress deliberately did not adopt.
    *   III. The Loper Bright Decision Invalidates Chevron Deference for This Rule
        *   In Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. ___ (2024), the Supreme Court overturned the Chevron doctrine, holding that:
            *   “Courts may not defer to an agency interpretation that goes beyond the bounds of statutory text. Courts must exercise independent judgment in determining whether an agency has acted within its lawful authority.”
        *   In light of this decision, HHS may no longer rely on regulatory interpretations or guidance that conflict with or extend beyond the clear language of the CCDBG statute.
        *   When the statute allows provisional employment after submission of a background check, HHS has no authority to require providers to wait for completed results as a precondition of employment.
        *   By imposing requirements more burdensome than those authorized by Congress, the Department exceeds its statutory authority and runs afoul of Loper Bright and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
    *   IV. Real-World Implications for Providers and Families
        *   The unlawful policy has real-world consequences:
            *   Providers cannot hire when needed, exacerbating already critical workforce shortages.
            *   Enrollment is capped, leaving families without care and preventing them from going to work in many instances.
            *   New employees are deterred from entering the field due to unnecessary onboarding delays.
            *   Low-income and rural providers suffer most, as they have fewer staffing reserves to absorb delays.
        *   In short, the Department’s unlawful policy is harming the very system CCDBG is meant to strengthen.
*   Comment Regarding Challenges Obtaining Child Abuse Registry Checks Under the CCDBG Act in 45 C.F.R. § 98.43(d)(4) as interpreted by HHS.
    *   As of January 2024, approximately 37 states, plus the District of Columbia, American Samoa, Guam, and Puerto Rico, maintain statutory “central registries”—statewide databases for reporting and investigating child abuse and neglect cases.
    *   Moreover, when focusing specifically on the ability to conduct out-of-state child abuse and neglect registry checks—a key requirement under the 2014 CCDBG reauthorization—recent federal surveys show that:
        *   35 states and territories have implemented out-of-state child abuse and neglect registry checks.
        *   Roughly 37 states (out of 50) have central registries by law.
        *   35 states currently conduct cross-state registry checks under CCDBG requirements.
    *   In the CCDBG statutory text, it specifically outlines a 45-day window by which states must make a determination of whether a prospective employee has received a satisfactory background check, including the child abuse registry check.
    *   We strongly urge the HHS to interpret this 45 day rule to deem an employee to have a satisfactory comprehensive background check at the 45 day mark if the prospective employee has submitted all background checks regardless of whether the state has responded to the child abuse registry request.
    *   Using Texas as an example, the Texas Health and Human Services Commission (TTHHS) currently requires child care providers to wait 45 days before declaring a background check complete when another state fails to respond to a request for a child abuse and neglect registry check (also known as the “Child Straight” component).
    *   The National Child Care Association (NCCA) raises the following key concerns with this policy:
        1.  Disproportionate Impact on Providers and Families
            *   This rigid 45-day delay punishes providers and applicants for delays caused by other states.
            *   It creates staffing shortages and hiring delays, particularly in high-need or rural areas.
            *   Families experience delays in access to child care, affecting workforce participation and stability.
        2.  Inconsistent with Federal Flexibility
            *   Federal CCDBG guidance permits states to document good-faith efforts when other states do not respond.
            *   States like TTHHS’s strict 45-day policy exceeds federal requirements and lacks flexibility.
        3.  Operational Challenges and Misaligned Incentives
            *   Delays harm provider operations while failing to enhance safety, as other background check components (e.g., FBI, state criminal) are typically completed.
            *   The current policy shifts systemic inter-state issues onto local providers instead of addressing them through interstate cooperation or federal escalation.
*   Comment Regarding 45 C.F.R. § 98.33(a)(4) — Public Posting of Child Care Provider Inspection Reports
    *   We respectfully request that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) rescind or revise 45 C.F.R. § 98.33(a)(4), which mandates that state Lead Agencies publicly post inspection and monitoring reports for all eligible and licensed childcare providers.
    *   While the goal of transparency is important, this rule has had unintended consequences that undermine the long-term stability of the childcare provider network.
    *   Specifically, providers are reporting that inspection reports posted on public-facing consumer education websites are increasingly used by insurance companies and legal entities as a basis for denying liability insurance or raising premiums.
    *   This occurs even in cases where violations are minor, one-time, or fully corrected.
    *   In some cases, the very presence of a citation—regardless of severity or resolution—triggers adverse insurance decisions.
    *   This practice has become a barrier to sustaining childcare operations, especially for small providers or those serving high-need communities.
    *   The loss of or cost-prohibitive increase in liability insurance coverage makes it difficult or impossible for providers to obtain liability insurance to protect both business owners and the children in their care.
    *   Furthermore, the increase in cost, which has been in the triple digits for some providers over the past five years, is being passed on to families making childcare cost prohibitive expensive for some families.
    *   In other cases, providers are ceasing operations altogether, directly undermining access to care for working families.
    *   In light of these concerns, we urge HHS to either:
        *   Rescind the requirement in 45 C.F.R. § 98.33(a)(4), or
        *   Amend the regulation to include the following:
            1.  Require states to allow each posted inspection report to include a provider’s written response or explanation, giving context to the findings and any corrective action taken.
            2.  Require states to offer summarized or tiered reporting formats that reduce the risk of misinterpretation by non-regulatory third parties such as insurance companies.
            3.  Clarify through guidance or rulemaking that these reports are intended solely for family consumer awareness—not for use by insurers to assess provider risk or eligibility.
    *   This proposed revision strikes a balance between transparency and fairness.
    *   While public access to inspection results supports parental awareness, the current one-sided presentation exposes providers, especially small, community-based operations—to reputational and financial harm.
    *   A required provider response ensures due process and more accurate public understanding, while preserving oversight goals without collapsing the fragile childcare insurance market.
    *   Without such a revision, the industry is at risk of the following:
        1.  Chilling Effects on Child Care Supply: Providers report that publicly accessible inspection reports—particularly those reflecting minor, corrected, or first-time violations—are being used by commercial liability insurers to deny coverage, restrict eligibility, or significantly raise premiums.
        2.  Risk of Market Contraction: The increasing difficulty in securing affordable liability insurance is driving some providers to exit the market or operate at reduced capacity, exacerbating the existing national shortage of childcare options.
        3.  Misuse of Context-Free Citations: In the absence of context or provider explanation, posted reports can create a misleading or incomplete public record. Insurers and families alike may misinterpret the seriousness or resolution status of a cited issue, further harming providers’ reputations and viability.
    *   (b) Alternative Implementation
        *   If rescission is not adopted, the regulation shall be amended to include the following safeguard:
            *   “The Lead Agency shall ensure that any posted inspection report includes, alongside the citation or violation, a written response from the provider. This response shall be posted in equal prominence and may include:
                *   Factual clarification or correction,
                *   Description of corrective actions taken,
                *   Explanation of any mitigating or contributing circumstances.”
    *   (c) Limitation on Insurer Use
        *   HHS is further encouraged to issue non-binding guidance discouraging insurers from relying solely on publicly posted inspection reports—absent a formal adjudication or finding of gross negligence—as a basis for denying or limiting liability coverage.
    *   Rationale:
        *   This provision strikes a balance between transparency and fairness.
        *   While public access to inspection results supports parental awareness, the current one-sided presentation exposes providers, especially small, community-based operations—to reputational and financial harm.
        *   A required provider response ensures due process and more accurate public understanding, while preserving oversight goals without collapsing the fragile child care insurance market.
*   Comment Regarding Payment Based on Enrollment Versus Attendance the 2024 Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) Final Rule in 45 C.F.R. § 98
    *   We recommend that HHS revise the rule in 45 C.F.R. § 98 regarding paying providers based on enrollment versus attendance to require that states may not repurpose or redirect any current funds used to serve children in order to meet the enrollment-based payment requirement outlined in the recent rule.
    *   The rule requiring states to pay child care providers based on enrollment rather than attendance is part of the 2024 Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) Final Rule, issued by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
    *   This rule was published in the Federal Register on March 1, 2024, and became effective on April 30, 2024.
    *   Under this rule, states and territories are mandated to implement payment practices that align with those commonly used in the private-pay market.
    *   Specifically, child care providers must be paid prospectively (i.e., in advance) and based on the child’s authorized enrollment rather than actual attendance.
    *   This change aims to provide a more stable and predictable funding stream for providers, thereby improving the financial stability of child care operations and increasing access to care for families.
    *   The shift to enrollment-based payments is intended to reduce administrative burdens on providers and ensure they receive consistent payments, regardless of fluctuations in daily attendance.
    *   This approach supports the goal of enhancing the quality and accessibility of child care services for families participating in the CCDF program.
    *   This clarification is critical to ensure that existing funding streams dedicated to direct services for children are not reduced or compromised in the implementation of the new policy.
    *   Without this safeguard, there is a risk that states could reallocate resources away from services in an effort to comply with the rule, ultimately undermining the goal of improving access and quality of care.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The Child Care Association of Louisiana, a long-standing advocate for licensed childcare centers, strongly endorses the National Child Care Association's recommendations to streamline federal regulations related to background checks and public reporting, and to safeguard funding for children, while still prioritizing child safety.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Child Care Association of Louisiana
- **Type:** Advocacy Group
- **Role/Expertise:** Longest standing advocacy organization representing licensed childcare centers in Louisiana.
- **Geographic Scope:** State (Louisiana), with a national scope through endorsement of the National Child Care Association.
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly represents licensed childcare centers affected by federal regulations concerning staffing, background checks, operational transparency, and funding mechanisms, aiming to reduce burdens and ensure viability while protecting children.
structuredSections.corePosition: We believe that while protecting children in licensed childcare facilities is paramount, current federal interpretations and requirements under HHS regulations regarding background checks and public reporting create unnecessary burdens, stifle operational flexibility, and have unintended negative consequences for providers, families, and the childcare supply. We strongly urge HHS to align its guidance and rules with the plain meaning of the CCDBG Act and recent Supreme Court precedent, and to ensure funding policies support direct services to children.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   **Regarding "Supervision" in Background Checks (45 C.F.R. § 98.43):**
    -   HHS should reexamine whether its current interpretation imposes unjustified burdens not supported by statutory text.
    -   HHS should refrain from imposing overly prescriptive definitions that limit states and providers’ ability to implement safe and effective supervision practices.
    -   HHS should affirm that states may adopt reasonable, risk-based interpretations of supervision, consistent with health and safety and operational feasibility.
    -   HHS should issue revised guidance or initiate formal rulemaking to adopt a more functional definition of supervision: "Supervision means on-site oversight by a cleared staff member who is physically present, readily accessible, and responsible for monitoring the activities of a provisionally employed individual through appropriate methods consistent with the child care setting, including visual checks, classroom presence, or proximity-based observation."
-   **Regarding Provisional Employment (45 C.F.R. § 98.43(d)(4)):**
    -   Rescind any guidance, regulation, or enforcement action that prohibits provisional employment after a background check application is submitted.
    -   Issue updated guidance to all states, affirming that supervised employment is permissible immediately upon submission of the background check request, consistent with 42 U.S.C. § 9858f(h)(1)(C).
    -   Affirm the Department’s commitment to operating within statutory authority, particularly in the post-Loper Bright legal environment.
-   **Regarding Child Abuse Registry Checks (45 C.F.R. § 98.43(d)(4)):**
    -   HHS should interpret the 45-day rule to deem an employee to have a satisfactory comprehensive background check at the 45-day mark if the prospective employee has submitted all background checks, regardless of whether the state has responded to the child abuse registry request.
    -   HHS should instruct all states to allow completion of checks at the 45-day expiration after documented good-faith attempts when other states don't respond.
    -   HHS should permit supervised provisional employment while registry responses are pending.
    -   HHS should collaborate with the Office of Child Care to escalate issues with persistently non-responsive states.
-   **Regarding Public Posting of Inspection Reports (45 C.F.R. § 98.33(a)(4)):**
    -   Rescind the requirement in 45 C.F.R. § 98.33(a)(4), OR
    -   Amend the regulation to include the following:
        -   Require states to allow each posted inspection report to include a provider’s written response or explanation, giving context to the findings and any corrective action taken.
        -   Require states to offer summarized or tiered reporting formats that reduce the risk of misinterpretation by non-regulatory third parties such as insurance companies.
        -   Clarify through guidance or rulemaking that these reports are intended solely for family consumer awareness—not for use by insurers to assess provider risk or eligibility.
    -   If rescission is not adopted, the regulation should be amended to ensure any posted inspection report includes, alongside the citation or violation, a written response from the provider, posted in equal prominence, including factual clarification, description of corrective actions, or explanation of mitigating circumstances.
    -   HHS should issue non-binding guidance discouraging insurers from relying solely on publicly posted inspection reports—absent a formal adjudication or finding of gross negligence—as a basis for denying or limiting liability coverage.
-   **Regarding Payment Based on Enrollment Versus Attendance (45 C.F.R. § 98):**
    -   HHS should revise the rule to require that states may not repurpose or redirect any current funds used to serve children in order to meet the enrollment-based payment requirement.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   **Overly narrow interpretation of "supervision" for provisional employees:**
    -   Leads to staffing strain by requiring one-on-one, line-of-sight shadowing, restricting classroom coverage and reducing ratio capacity, especially in smaller centers.
    -   Causes hiring delays, particularly in rural or underserved areas, as immediate supervision obligations are financially or functionally unworkable.
    -   Acts as a barrier to entry, discouraging qualified individuals from entering the early childhood workforce due to administrative and logistical hurdles.
    -   Ironically, may compromise child safety by limiting the number of adults available to meet supervision ratios, increasing risk of oversight or fatigue among cleared staff.
-   **HHS's unlawful restriction on provisional employment:**
    -   Requires providers to wait for *completed and cleared* background checks before provisional employment, despite the CCDBG Act stating employment can begin *upon submission* of a background check request while awaiting results.
    -   This policy, and its state-level enforcement, prevents staff from being scheduled, onboarding, having contact with children (even supervised), and being counted towards ratios.
    -   Exacerbates critical workforce shortages and caps enrollment, leaving families without care and preventing them from working.
    -   Deters new employees and disproportionately harms low-income and rural providers.
-   **Challenges in obtaining child abuse registry checks:**
    -   A rigid 45-day delay for incomplete child abuse registry checks (like Texas's "Child Straight" component) punishes providers and applicants for delays caused by other states.
    -   Creates staffing shortages and hiring delays, and delays families' access to childcare.
    -   Is inconsistent with federal CCDBG guidance that permits states to document good-faith efforts when other states do not respond.
    -   Shifts systemic inter-state issues onto local providers rather than addressing them through inter-state cooperation or federal escalation.
-   **Negative consequences of public posting of inspection reports:**
    -   Inspection reports, even for minor or corrected violations, are increasingly used by insurance companies and legal entities to deny liability insurance or significantly raise premiums (triple digits increase for some providers over five years).
    -   The very presence of a citation can trigger adverse insurance decisions, creating a barrier to sustaining operations and leading providers to cease operations or operate at reduced capacity, worsening the national childcare shortage.
    -   Context-free citations lead to misuse and misinterpretation by insurers and families, harming providers' reputations and viability.
    -   Threatens the childcare supply and risks market contraction by making affordable liability insurance difficult to secure.
-   **Risk of fund redirection for enrollment-based payments:**
    -   Concerns that states might repurpose or redirect existing funds dedicated to direct services for children to meet the new enrollment-based payment requirement, rather than securing new funding.
    -   This would undermine the goal of improving access and quality of care by reducing resources available for children.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
-   The comment directly leverages the *Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo* (2024) Supreme Court decision, asserting that HHS's current interpretations regarding background checks exceed its statutory authority and invalidate prior agency deference. This highlights a sophisticated legal argument challenging regulatory overreach.
-   It provides a tangible example of regulatory burden where the federal interpretation of "supervision" for provisional employees requires impractical one-on-one, line-of-sight oversight, leading to staffing strain, hiring delays (especially in rural/underserved areas), and ironically, potential child safety risks by limiting available cleared staff.
-   The comment offers a specific, functional alternative definition for "supervision" that mirrors existing practical applications in many states (e.g., for substitute teachers), showcasing a pragmatic, real-world solution to a regulatory challenge.
-   A surprising unintended consequence is revealed regarding public posting of inspection reports: insurers and legal entities are using these reports (even for minor or corrected violations) to deny liability insurance or drastically increase premiums (up to triple digits over five years), which directly threatens the viability of childcare businesses and leads to market contraction.
-   The comment uses the specific example of Texas’s 45-day wait for "Child Straight" child abuse registry checks to illustrate how state-level policies, despite federal flexibility, disproportionately impact providers and families due to inter-state inefficiencies.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
-   "HHS’s interpretation of “supervision” under 45 C.F.R. § 98.43 appears to go beyond what the CCDBG Act itself requires. The statute permits provisional employment with supervision but does not define that term, nor does it mandate a one-size-fits-all application."
-   "This rigid 45-day delay punishes providers and applicants for delays caused by other states."
-   "The Department’s unlawful policy is harming the very system CCDBG is meant to strengthen."
-   "Providers are reporting that inspection reports posted on public-facing consumer education websites are increasingly used by insurance companies and legal entities as a basis for denying liability insurance or raising premiums. This occurs even in cases where violations are minor, one-time, or fully corrected."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
-   Every month, I dread making that call to the pharmacy.
    -   The anxiety usually starts days ahead.
    -   I’m checking my pill supply obsessively.
    -   I’m counting down the hours until refill day.
    -   I feel a tight knot in my stomach, wondering what will happen if they’re out again.
-   The last time they didn’t have my medication for almost a week, and it was brutal.
    -   I couldn’t sleep for nights on end.
    -   My mind raced, anxiety spiraled out of control.
    -   Focusing on my studies became impossible.
    -   I ended up behind on coursework and terrified about my future.
-   The meds themselves are another source of stress.
    -   Because of ongoing supply issues, sometimes I get a different manufacturer’s brand.
    -   I notice the difference right away.
    -   One brand helps me feel calm and focused, like I can manage my day.
    -   Another makes me jittery or is barely effective at all.
    -   It feels like my treatment is a frustrating guessing game every single month.
    -   That unpredictability just makes my anxiety and insomnia worse – two things that go hand in hand with ADHD for me.
-   Telehealth was a lifesaver when I needed it most.
    -   Without it, I doubt I’d have gotten diagnosed or started treatment in time to finish my program.
    -   If those flexibilities are taken away, and stimulant medications remain locked behind outdated, overly strict rules, I don’t know how people like me are supposed to manage.
    -   We didn’t ask to have ADHD.
    -   We’re just trying to live our lives, go to school, hold jobs, and be functional adults.
    -   What we need is consistent, reliable access to care – not endless barriers, suspicion, and stigma.
-   It’s especially frustrating knowing these stimulant meds are in the same category as methadone and oxycodone – drugs known for their high abuse and overdose risk.
    -   That classification makes no sense based on the actual risks of these ADHD medications.
    -   It creates a cloud of fear and misinformation that makes pharmacies reluctant to stock them and providers hesitant to prescribe.
    -   Meanwhile, we’re left caught in the middle, struggling every month just to keep up.
-   Please don’t roll back telehealth access.
    -   It’s literally the only reason I have a shot at staying employed and finishing school.
-   Please reclassify these medications to reflect modern science and real patient experiences.
    -   34 millions with ADHD deserve better than this broken system.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An individual with ADHD advocates for maintaining telehealth access and reclassifying stimulant medications, emphasizing the profound anxiety and functional challenges caused by current unpredictable supply, varying efficacy, and stigmatizing regulations.
