            *   regulations that implicate matters of social, political, or economic significance that are not authorized by clear statutory authority;
            *   regulations that impose significant costs upon private parties that are not outweighed by public benefits;
            *   regulations that harm the national interest by significantly and unjustifiably impeding technological innovation, infrastructure development, disaster response, inflation reduction, research and development, economic development, energy production, land use, and foreign policy objectives; and
            *   regulations that impose undue burdens on small business and impede private enterprise and entrepreneurship.
        *   Such regulations would be subject to rescission or modification.
    *   Pursuant to this order, on May 14, 2025, the Health and Human Services department (HHS) issued a Request for Information (RFI) seeking stakeholder input to identify regulations or other administrative policies and actions falling within the scope of EO 14219 or other deregulatory executive orders.
    *   AHPA members manufacture and market conventional foods, dietary supplements, and other consumer products that contain herbal ingredients, and these products and ingredients are subject to and regulated by HHS.
    *   These comments are submitted on behalf of AHPA and its members and address numerous matters responsive to the remit of the May 14 RFI and EO 14219.
*   Note on the format of these comments
    *   For ease of consideration, the first proposed actions involve simple revocations or rescissions of existing rules or policies.
    *   Subsequent proposed actions, which may entail more complex rulemaking to achieve their deregulatory purposes, are organized by regulatory area.
    *   Each proposed action is organized as follows:
        *   “Administering HHS division” – All of the comments included here relate to products regulated by FDA; for convenient processing of individual elements of these comments, this field identifies the relevant FDA division or divisions in each case.
        *   “Citation to C.F.R.” and “Statutory Citation” (as applicable) – Each of the comments included here that is relevant to a regulatory issue is related to a regulation under Title 21 of the Code of Federal Regulations (21 C.F.R.). In all cases, HHS’s authority to act upon the provided recommendations flows from the original authority permitting the creation of the cited regulation. The specific part or section of 21 C.F.R. addressed in each comment is identified at each separate comment in a field identified as “Citation to C.F.R.” In addition, a few comments are relevant to statutory issues under Title 21 of the United States Code (21 U.S.C.).
        *   “Matter of concern” – A description of the matter of concern to AHPA and its members.
        *   “Recommendation” – AHPA’s suggested approach to address each identified concern.
        *   “Available data on cost or economic impact” – Many of the matters raised in these comments provide self-confirmatory or obvious savings to regulators and/or regulated industry with no negative economic impact. In most cases, AHPA has not conducted formal economic research regarding these matters; where available, sources regarding economic impact are provided.
        *   “Relevance to EO 14219” – Formal relevance of the raised matter to the criteria identified in EO 14219.
    *   In many matters raised in these comments, AHPA proposes specific textual revisions to federal regulations. Where such recommended language is provided, proposed added language is in bold underline text and proposed deleted language is in strikethrough text.
*   Issues requiring simple deregulatory withdrawals and rescissions
    *   FDA should withdraw its “Homeopathic Drug Products” guidance and return to its prior regulatory framework under Compliance Policy Guide 400.400, “Conditions Under Which Homeopathic Drugs May be Marketed”
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA Center for Drug Evaluation and Research and Center for Biologics Evaluation and Research
        *   Citation: “Homeopathic Drug Products: Guidance for FDA Staff and Industry”
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   In 2019, FDA withdrew its longstanding regulatory framework for homeopathic drug products marketed without otherwise-required FDA premarket approval, Compliance Policy Guide Section 400.400, “Conditions Under Which Homeopathic Drugs May be Marketed” (CPG 400.400).
            *   It proposed to replace CPG 400.400 with a draft version of “Homeopathic Drug Products: Guidance for FDA Staff and Industry” (Homeopathic Drug Guidance), issuing a final version in December 2022.
            *   The Homeopathic Drug Guidance states that “all homeopathic drug products remain subject to the premarket approval requirements” applicable to new drugs under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) and that “there are currently no homeopathic drug products that are approved by FDA.”
            *   It further states that “any homeopathic drug product that is being marketed illegally is subject to FDA enforcement at any time.”
            *   These statements, taken together, threaten enforcement against any homeopathic product, even if the product presents no material health risk and has remained marketed without FDA objection for decades, including previously under CPG 400.400.
            *   This enforcement risk places a significant burden on marketers of homeopathic products, especially considering the immense time, money, and research necessary to sponsor a premarket application for a new drug.
            *   Under FDA’s prior regulatory framework of CPG 400.400, homeopathic drug products could generally be marketed without premarket approval, as long as they complied with enumerated conditions such as requirements pertaining to ingredients, compliant labeling (sections 502 and 503 of FDCA and 21 C.F.R. 201), registration of drug establishments (section 510 of FDCA and 21 C.F.R. 207), and compliance with current good manufacturing practice.
            *   The prior regulatory approach under CPG 400.400 provided sufficient safeguards for the manufacture and marketing of homeopathic drug products without forcing manufacturers to undertake the tremendous burden of traditional premarket drug approval or risk constant threat of regulatory action.
            *   AHPA previously presented its concerns in 2015 that a move away from CPG 400.400 could present an increased regulatory burden and potentially limit consumer access, a prediction that has since come true.
            *   AHPA understands that businesses have left the homeopathic drug product market as a result of the issuance of the Homeopathic Drug Guidance and the withdrawal of CPG 400.400, which has resulted in decreased competition and consumer choice.
            *   The Homeopathic Drug Guidance also delineates specific categories of homeopathic drug products for which FDA “intends to prioritize enforcement and regulatory actions,” including those with a route of administration other than oral or topical, effectively chilling the continued marketing of entire categories of previously marketed products.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   FDA should revoke the 2022 Homeopathic Drug Guidance and return to its prior enforcement approach under CPG 400.400.
            *   CPG 400.400 permitted the marketing of homeopathic drug products that met reasonable requirements to ensure product quality and safety.
            *   Such a return to prior practice would allow firms to manufacture and market homeopathic drug products (many of which consumers have relied upon for decades) without undue regulatory burdens.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: The Homeopathic Drug Guidance presents an unjustified burden on industry not supportable by any putative public health benefit; CPG 400.400 provided sufficient safeguards for the manufacture and marketing of homeopathic drug products.
    *   FDA should remove requirements for “written assurances” except where explicitly established by statute
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. Parts 1, 11, 16, 106, 110, 111, 112, 114, 117, 120, 123, 129, 179, 211, and 507
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   FDA regulatory provisions implementing the Food Safety Modernization Act’s (FSMA) Preventive Controls for Human and Animal Foods, Foreign Supplier Verification Program, and Produce Safety Rule each require sellers (farmers and food processors) to obtain from their customers (downstream food processors and distributors), and buyers to obtain from their vendors, various “written assurances” on an annual or biannual basis.
            *   This requirement to obtain annual written assurances is highly impractical and imposes an extreme compliance burden to all participants.
            *   An analysis by the Grocery Manufacturers Association (GMA) determined that the written assurances requirements found under 21 C.F.R. § 117.136 could require an individual firm with a sufficiently complex role in the supply chain to obtain in excess of a million written assurances every year.
            *   The expense and burden created by this requirement for buyers and sellers includes not only the generation and exchange of such assurance documents, but the associated requirement to maintain them on file.
            *   Some companies could find it impossible to obtain the required assurances (e.g., small firms who have little leverage over larger business partners, or farmers who are several steps removed from food processors).
            *   Even if written assurances were consistently obtainable and required only upon initiation of sales, as opposed to annually or biannually, the burden would be significant and without any commensurate public health benefit.
            *   The maintenance of these documents does nothing to materially improve the safety of the food supply.
            *   Other elements of the regulation already require that the existence of any hazards must be disclosed in documentation accompanying the sale of the food, and that food processors adequately mitigate any relevant hazards as appropriate for their products and customers.
            *   Furthermore, the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) makes any entity, including retailers, and their chief executives that knowingly or unknowingly distribute adulterated or misbranded food, strictly liable under the Act, which provides strong incentive for entities throughout the supply chain to ensure the safety of the food they sell.
            *   The U.S. Department of Commerce (DOC) on October 6, 2017, issued a report reflecting stakeholder comments on a Request for Information (RFI) to identify “the most burdensome regulations and permitting requirements” faced by U.S. domestic manufacturers.
            *   One of the specific “priority areas for reform” recommended in the DOC Report addresses written assurances: “The Department of Health and Human Services, Food and Drug Administration (HHS, FDA) should rescind requirements to obtain written assurances from downstream customers on an annual basis, or alternatively consider revision of requirement to reduce frequency and burden.”
            *   Such rescission should be extended to each of the FSMA-implementing rules that impose extensive burdens to obtain written assurances.
            *   This set of requirements was previously the subject of an implementation delay, and FDA has maintained an open-ended policy of enforcement discretion for these requirements.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   FDA should remove regulatory requirements for farmers and food companies to exchange and maintain “written assurances” received from their customers and/or provided to their vendors.
            *   No replacement requirements are necessary, since other existing regulatory and legal frameworks adequately require farmers, food processors, and retailers to disclose the existence of hazards that require mitigation and to ensure food safety prior to sale to consumers.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data, however, even given highly conservative time per record estimates FDA reported in the associated written assurance records in the final produce safety rule, adjusted to reflect inputs from the GRMA above, suggest an annual cost orders of magnitude higher than the 365 hours FDA estimated.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: The assurance requirements at issue are a prime example of a regulation that imposes significant costs upon private parties that are not outweighed by public benefits. The recordkeeping requirements involved are the very essence of unreasonable recordkeeping that is not needed or used effectively, and are especially burdensome upon small businesses high in the supply chain.
*   Issues related to labeling of food (inc. conventional food and dietary supplements)
    *   The following issues are specifically addressed to certain FDA regulations that affect labeling of conventional food products and that may also, to the degree that conventional food labeling rules also apply to dietary supplement labeling, affect labeling of dietary supplements.
    *   Except for nutrients that have an established RDI or DRV, the use of ingredient and constituent names should be allowed on food labels without collocated quantity declarations
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. §§ 101.13 and 101.54
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   Under the present regulations for nutrient content claims, a claim that a particular substance is contained in a food must be accompanied by the amount of the substance in the food.
            *   FDA has communicated this expectation further in guidance:
                *   “N21. Is there any way that a manufacturer can let consumers know that a product contains nutrients without DVs [daily values], such as omega-3 fatty acids? Answer: A manufacturer may make a statement about a nutrient for which there is no established daily value as long as the claim specifies only the amount of the nutrient per serving and does not implicitly characterize the level of the nutrient in the product. Such a claim might be “x grams of omega3 fatty acids.” Such claims must be outside the Nutrition Facts label. 21 C.F.R. 101.13(i)(3)”
                *   “N22. May a label make statements using the words “contains” and “provides” (e.g., “Contains x grams of omega3 fatty acids”) for nutrients without DVs? Answer: To use the words “contains” or “provides” for nutrients without DVs, the specific amount of the nutrient must be stated. The statements “Contains x grams of omega-3 fatty acids per serving” or “Provides x g of omega-3 fatty acids” are permitted. However, "Contains omega-3 fatty acids" or "Provides omega-3 fatty acids" (without the specific amount statement) would not be permitted. Such claims would be synonyms for a "good source" claim which is not permitted for nutrients that do not have established DVs. 21 CFR 101.54(c)”
            *   This interpretation of FDA’s nutrient content claim regulations unnecessarily restricts how substances may be identified on a food label.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   FDA should revise the Food Labeling Guide to provide that, except for nutrients that have an established RDI or DRV, the presence of ingredients or constituents is allowed to be highlighted on food labels outside the Nutrition Facts or Supplement Facts label.
            *   This is allowed so long as the amount of the ingredient or constituent appears in the ingredient declaration or in the Supplement Facts label of the food.
            *   Thus, the statement “Contains omega-3 fatty acids” would be allowed to appear on the label of the food (outside the Nutrition Facts or Supplement Facts label) so long as the amount of omega-3 fatty acids appears in the ingredient declaration or Supplement Facts.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: The current regulation places a restriction upon the conduct of private industry with no equivalent public benefit.
    *   The current rule for foreign language labeling should be amended
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. § 101.15
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   A food in packaged form is required at 21 C.F.R. § 101.3 to bear on its principal display panel a statement of the identity of the commodity, in terms of: (1) The name specified in Federal law/regulation; or, (2) The common or usual name; or, (3) An appropriately descriptive term or fanciful name.
            *   Under current regulation, codified at 21 C.F.R. § 101.15(c)(2), if a food label contains “any representation in a foreign language” then, with certain specified exceptions, “all words, statements, and other information required by or under authority of the act to appear on the label shall appear thereon in the foreign language.”
            *   This means such a food label with, for example, Italian or Spanish words interpreted as “representation(s)” of the food would be required to include Italian or Spanish words for each declared nutrient in the Nutrition Facts panel (e.g., “Calories / Calorías”).
            *   In some instances, FDA has taken the position that the use of ethnic product names on dietary supplements triggers this bilingual label requirement.
            *   In particular, in connection with nutrition labeling exemptions (21 C.F.R. § 101.9(j)(18)), FDA may reject a firm’s annual notification if labels include ethnic words in the product name but do not present all required information in both languages.
            *   The standard to trigger this bilingual labeling requirement has been applied broadly and inconsistently, and absent a specific basis has a number of deleterious effects on consumer understanding.
                *   Ethnic names are often the names most familiar to the consumer. For example, Americans are far more likely to recognize Euterpe oleracea fruit when called by its ethnic name “açaí” rather than its English name “cabbage palm.” Similarly, for typical consumers of dietary supplements and specialty produce “dong quai” is more familiar than “Chinese angelica”; “shiitake” is more familiar than “Japanese forest mushroom”; and “habañero” is at least as recognizable as “bonnet pepper.” In many other cases, there is not even an English equivalent to the ethnic name: chayote, yerba santa, and copaiba are known exclusively by their ethnic names.
                *   This approach to language regulation has not been applied consistently in other product categories. For example, while it may be that many of the Italian words that describe commonly available pasta shapes (such as spaghetti) could now be considered to be English, there are numerous other pasta shapes marketed in the U.S. that are described on product labels with their Italian language names and which have not come to be commonly used in English. Such products are not required to bear bilingual nutrition labeling in Italian, nor is there reason to believe the public would be benefitted by so stringent an application of the rule.
                *   FDA has previously applied this requirement in the context of pinyin names in product statements of identity. However, pinyin is a transliteration of the Chinese language, not a language itself. No person fluent in Chinese reads or writes in pinyin; rather, they use Chinese logogram characters.
                *   Under 21 C.F.R. § 101.4(h), each botanical ingredient is required to be listed using its Latin name, except when the Latin is available in Herbs of Commerce for the common or usual name listed on the label. Therefore, even if a consumer finds an ethnic product name confusing, the consumer will be able to accurately determine the actual contents of the product by way of the Supplement Facts and/or ingredient statement.
            *   FDA has provided no justification for dietary supplement products to be subject to a different bilingual labeling standard than is required for conventional foods.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   FDA should make the following amendment to 21 C.F.R. § 101.15(c)(2): “If the label contains any representation in a foreign language **except in the name of the food**, all words, statements, and other information required by or under authority of the act to appear on the label shall appear thereon in the foreign language: Provided, however, That individual serving size packages of foods containing no more than 11⁄2 avoirdupois ounces or no more than 11⁄2 fluid ounces served with meals in restaurants, institutions, and passenger carriers and not intended for sale at retail are exempt from the requirements of this paragraph (c)(2), if the only representation in the foreign language(s) is the name of the food.”
            *   This revision may be similarly accomplished by a clear communication from the agency of its intention to exercise enforcement discretion in this matter.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: AHPA believes the regulation as currently selectively interpreted is both ineffective and imposes unnecessary costs on private parties to no public benefit. This burden is also seemingly applied particularly to small businesses.
*   Issues related to labeling of dietary supplements
    *   The following issues are specifically addressed to certain FDA regulations that affect labeling of dietary supplements.
    *   The requirement for multiple DSHEA disclaimers is redundant
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. § 101.93(d)
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   21 C.F.R. 101.93(d) requires, with regard to the disclaimer accompanying structure/function claims: “(d) Placement. The disclaimer shall be placed adjacent to the statement with no intervening material or linked to the statement with a symbol (e.g., an asterisk) at the end of each such statement that refers to the same symbol placed adjacent to the disclaimer specified in paragraphs (c)(1) or (c)(2) of this section. On product labels and in labeling (e.g., pamphlets, catalogs), the disclaimer shall appear on each panel or page where there such is a statement. The disclaimer shall be set off in a box where it is not adjacent to the statement in question.”
            *   This regulation is unnecessarily restrictive, particularly for products or labeling contexts with limited available space that could otherwise bear structure/function claims on multiple panels.
            *   AHPA understands that FDA shares this perspective and has not, in practice, enforced this requirement; however, it has been a periodic source of civil litigation targeting industry.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   FDA should revise 21 C.F.R. § 101.93(d) to provide that the disclaimer is required to be placed only once on the label of a dietary supplement making multiple structure/function claims, even if the claims appear on more than one panel of the label, and only once on any labeling where the claims appear, provided that the label or labeling connects each structure/function claim and the disclaimer using a symbol (e.g., an asterisk).
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: Costs associated with defending and resolving threatened or filed private lawsuits can vary dramatically by company and depend on, for example, the particular state law(s) used to attempt to indirectly enforce an alleged violation of § 101.93(d), the quantity of challenged products sold to consumers over the relevant period, and the retail price(s) paid for the challenged products by the representative(s) and members of the (putative) class. Pre-litigation private settlements related to a single product or product line often require payments exceeding $100,000 along with tens of thousands of dollars (or more) in attorneys’ fees and the associated costs of relabeling and discarding existing label inventories. Post-complaint settlements or judgments, with associated attorneys’ fees, often increase these costs into the millions of dollars per challenged product or product line.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: The current regulation imposes a burden on industry speech, communication, and conduct with no concomitant public benefit.
    *   Allow citations of scientific references on websites
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. § 101.93(g)(2)(iv)(C)
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   21 C.F.R. 101.93(g)(2)(iv)(C) provides that citations to published literature in labeling can be construed as a disease claim: “(C) Citation of a publication or reference, if the citation refers to a disease use, and if, in the context of the labeling as a whole, the citation implies treatment or prevention of a disease, e.g., through placement on the immediate product label or packaging, inappropriate prominence, or lack of relationship to the product's express claims;”
            *   This section has been used by FDA to prohibit the use of citations to published literature and the use of published literature on the websites of companies marketing dietary supplements, especially literature that discusses the diagnosis, treatment, cure, or prevention of a disease.
            *   This regulatory approach is unsupported by the Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act (DSHEA), which expressly permits the use of published literature:
                *   “(a) IN GENERAL.- A publication, including an article, a chapter in a book, or an official abstract of a peer-reviewed scientific publication that appears in an article and was prepared by the author or the editors of the publication, which is reprinted in its entirety, shall not be defined as labeling when used in connection with the sale of a dietary supplement to consumers when it – (1) is not false or misleading; (2) does not promote a particular manufacturer or brand of a dietary supplement; (3) is displayed or presented, or is displayed or presented with other such items on the same subject matter, so as to present a balanced view of the available scientific information on a dietary supplement; (4) if displayed in an establishment, is physically separate from the dietary supplements; and (5) does not have appended to it any information by sticker or any other method. (21 U.S.C. 343B)”
            *   Freedom to communicate scientifically accurate information is a foundational element of DSHEA and certain of the “findings” underlying it:
                *   “(5) preventive health measures, including education, good nutrition, and appropriate use of safe nutritional supplements will limit the incidence of chronic diseases, and reduce long-term health care expenditures; […] (7) there is a growing need for emphasis on the dissemination of information linking nutrition and long-term good health; (8) consumers should be empowered to make choices about preventive health care programs based on data from scientific studies of health benefits related to particular dietary supplements; […] (13) although the Federal Government should take swift action against products that are unsafe or adulterated, the Federal Government should not take any actions to impose unreasonable regulatory barriers limiting or slowing the flow of safe products and accurate information to consumers.”
            *   Congress intended the American public to be provided unfettered access to a wide variety of scientific literature.
            *   There is no logical justification for regulatory distinction between third-party literature presented in electronic form as opposed to physically printed form, or for prohibiting firms from using citations to direct the attention of the public to the relevant literature.
            *   Finally, there is no evidence Congress intended to exclude disease-oriented studies from use as third-party literature. Such studies are often relevant to dietary supplement claims.
            *   For example, a scientific study on the use of an ingredient in the treatment of a disease (i.e., a claim that dietary supplements are not allowed to make) may contain information relevant to the mechanism of action of the ingredient; and this latter information may be important for understanding and substantiating the use of the ingredient in health maintenance (i.e., claims that are permitted for dietary supplements).
            *   Free and open communication of publications is especially important with regard to companies making such information available to practitioners on limited-access websites. Practitioners are knowledgeable intermediaries who often present sophisticated questions about a product, and scientific literature is often the best source of answers to their questions.
            *   These company-practitioner communications should also be respected. In this regard, companies should be free on such sites to respond to practitioner questions regarding the use of their products.
            *   While companies cannot make claims for their products outside their established labeling, they should be permitted to respond with truthful and not misleading information regarding the use of their products so long as such responses make clear that the products are labeled and intended only as dietary supplements and are not recommended or suggested for use in the diagnosis, treatment, cure, or prevention of a disease.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   Paragraph (C) of 21 C.F.R. § 101.93(g)(2)(iv) (i.e., 21 C.F.R. § 101.93(g)(2)(iv)(C)) should be deleted.
            *   Furthermore, FDA’s policies with respect to Warning Letters should be revised to conform to the intent of Congress.
            *   Dietary supplement companies should be permitted to cite scientific studies in labeling, including literature relating to use of an ingredient or product in treatment of disease, so long as in the context of the labeling as a whole it is clear that the product is intended only as a dietary supplement and is not recommended or suggested for use in the diagnosis, treatment, cure, or prevention of a disease.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: The current regulatory policy of FDA regarding citations to the scientific literature is not supported by the best reading of the underlying statutory authority or prohibition.
*   Issues related to regulations that affect conventional food and dietary supplement operations and farms
    *   The following issues are specifically addressed to certain of FDA’s regulations, including current good manufacturing practice regulations, that affect operations that manufacturer, package, label or hold food or dietary supplements; and to farms.
    *   FDA inspectors should cite the specific regulation associated with each observation issued on FDA Form 483
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. Part 117
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   FDA has established an internal policy to not cite regulations when reporting what an inspector believes to be objectionable conditions or other violations of applicable law in an inspectional observations report (Form 483).
            *   As a result, when a firm receives a Form 483, it is often unclear what element of the regulation FDA considers to be applicable to the observation or deficiency.
            *   While inspectors are instructed to verbally explain the relationship of both reportable and nonreportable observations to applicable laws and regulations, this policy of establishing no written record creates a wide latitude for inconsistency and miscommunication in the conveyance of inspectional outcomes.
            *   This information is necessary for consistent enforcement, transparency, accurate communication, and ease of comprehension by the regulated trade.
            *   Inclusion of such information would assist the regulated industry in coming into compliance with FDA regulations and thereby promote the public health benefits underlying their promulgation.
            *   Furthermore, inclusion of such information would help ensure that FDA food facility inspections accurately reflect the provisions of the applicable regulations.
            *   FDA previously received a citizen petition requesting that the agency (1) formally rescind its policy of prohibiting investigators from quoting or citing the regulatory basis for inspectional observations in Form 483; and (2) revise the Inspections Operations Manual (IOM) to require that Form 483s such references.
            *   FDA denied the petition. With regard to the first action requested, FDA replied that “there is no such policy,” on the basis that investigators are limited to “describing their factual observations in the FDA 483,” and that “investigator observations or conclusions, quotations from regulations, or characterizations of conditions as ‘violative’ are not ‘factual observations’”.
            *   As such, this denial appears to establish that FDA does in fact have a policy of prohibiting investigators from quoting or citing the regulatory basis for inspectional observations in Form 483s.
            *   With regard to the second action requested in the petition, i.e., to revise the IOM as described, the Agency replied that “FDA’s current practices further the Agency’s interests,” that “The IOM’s procedures promote understanding, compliance, and transparency”; and that “The IOM is consistent with the RPM’s [Regulatory Procedures Manual] ‘prior notice’ policy.”
            *   The decision not to cite the link between the investigator’s observation and the applicable provision of the regulations disserves the Agency’s goal of promoting the public health.
            *   AHPA is aware of circumstances in which federal inspectors have made regulatory claims verbally, including significant assertions of evidence, conduct, and necessary actions to enter compliance, that were not reflected in Form 483 and were not in alignment with federal regulation.
            *   It is in the public interest to ensure understanding within the regulated trade by citing the regulatory provisions that apply to each observation asserted in a Form 483.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   FDA should revise the Inspections Operations Manual (IOM) to require that Agency investigators include references to the underlying cGMP regulations in relation to each cGMP-related observation listed in Form 483s issued to conventional food and dietary supplement facilities.
            *   Such references should make clear reference to the inspected party’s obligations as identified in the final rule establishing cGMP requirements for human foods.
            *   AHPA recognizes that such statements would be claims regarding regulatory violations; in practice, these claims are already being made by investigators (and relied upon by industry) without an established record.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: FDA’s current policy imposes an unnecessary cost on the regulated trade (especially on small businesses) by creating an environment of significant regulatory uncertainty with no concomitant benefit. Any business, especially small businesses, would benefit from receiving as much information as possible about the regulatory basis of each Form 483 observation, so that management can clearly understand the basis for the problem and what is required to address it. In the absence of a transparent and accountable process of regulatory communication, compliance suffers as regulated industry undertakes misaligned compliance costs.
*   Issues related to cGMP for dietary supplements (21 C.F.R. Part 111)
    *   The following issues are specifically addressed to certain of FDA’s current good manufacturing practice regulations that affect operations that manufacturer, package, label or hold dietary supplements.
    *   FDA cannot require compliance with 21 C.F.R. Part 111 on the basis of downstream sale of dietary ingredients as finished supplements
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. § 111.1
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   21 C.F.R. Part 111, by its own terms, applies to dietary supplement manufacturers and does not apply to dietary ingredient manufacturers.
            *   21 C.F.R. § 111.1(a) states, “you are subject to this part if you manufacture, package, label, or hold a dietary supplement….”
            *   However, companies that perform these operations with dietary ingredients are sometimes subjected to the requirements of 21 C.F.R. Part 117 as if they were conventional food ingredient operations.
            *   In the preamble accompanying the issuance of 21 C.F.R. Part 111 as a final rule (the preamble), FDA states: “…those who manufacture, package, label, or hold dietary ingredients (emphasis added) are not subject to the final rule. To illustrate, assume you manufacture a dietary ingredient and sell that bulk dietary ingredient to Company X. Company X then utilizes the bulk dietary ingredient in a dietary supplement. Under final §111.1(a), you would not be subject to these dietary supplement CGMP requirements because you are not manufacturing a dietary supplement, rather you are manufacturing a dietary ingredient for further incorporation into a dietary supplement by Company X.”
            *   However, FDA has created a policy of enforcing Part 111 compliance on dietary ingredient manufacturers under a number of circumstances. For example, the preamble goes on to state: “If, however, you sell herbs in bulk to Company X, and Company X simply packages the herbs into smaller units for sale as a dietary supplement, you would be subject to the dietary supplement CGMP requirements because you are manufacturing a dietary supplement that Company X is simply packaging and labeling, and not further processing into a dietary supplement. In other words, in the latter example, you would have acted as a manufacturer whose finished product is simply repackaged or relabeled.”
            *   It has long been the law that a manufacturer determines the nature of its product by labeling it as a food, drug, or dietary supplement. The actions of a subsequent manufacturer or packager utilizing a food ingredient or a “dietary ingredient” does not change the character of the ingredient as sold by the ingredient manufacturer.
            *   Part 111 compliance may be useful to ensure that the ingredient manufacturer’s products meet their specifications. Indeed, some manufacturers of finished dietary supplements require their dietary ingredient vendors to comply with Part 111, so that the supplement manufacturer can confidently rely on the vendor’s representations about the ingredient. However, such a burden is undertaken voluntarily by the ingredient manufacturer as part of a freely negotiated agreement. It cannot lawfully be imposed based on a preamble statement.
            *   As a matter of regulatory transparency and practicality such an obligation cannot be triggered by the actions of buyers downstream from the dietary ingredient manufacturer, the identity and actions of which the dietary ingredient manufacturer has no knowledge of or control over. In particular, an upstream supplier cannot be aware of circumstances where a downstream manufacturer or processor may choose to change the actions taken regarding product material, thereby changing its regulatory status and applicable requirements.
            *   Furthermore, while Part 111 compliance may be useful to ensure dietary ingredient quality, it is no longer needed to ensure ingredient safety. Since 2007 when Part 111 was published, the new food safety requirements of Part 117 have come into force and dietary ingredient manufacturers who forego Part 111 compliance are now required to ensure safety through compliance with 21 C.F.R. Part 117 Subparts C and G. Ad hoc requirements for Part 111 compliance by firms that are dietary ingredient manufacturers and not dietary supplement manufacturers are no longer needed to protect the public health.
            *   In the preamble to the final rule on Foreign Supplier Verification Programs, FDA rejects a request to include certain importers that comply with Part 111, noting “Attempting to enforce compliance with the dietary supplement CGMP regulation by firms that are not legally required to comply with the regulation could present problems for the Agency if we sought to take an enforcement action against [such a firm]…” Such an analysis equally applies to the imposition of Part 111 requirements on firms that are not dietary supplement manufacturers.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   FDA should regulate food manufacturers solely based on the representations made on their product labels.
            *   Firms whose labels state that the dietary ingredient-containing foods they manufacture are dietary supplements should be regulated under Part 111 (and Part 117 Subpart B insofar as it does not overlap with Part 111).
            *   Firms whose food labels make no mention of dietary supplements should be regulated solely under Part 117.
            *   To the extent that additional regulatory requirements are necessary to ensure product quality under circumstances where a dietary ingredient is purchased for packaging as a dietary supplement, these burdens must fall on the firm performing the packaging; they cannot retroactively fall on vendors upstream from that firm.
            *   Since the packager is the party responsible for deciding what ingredient to buy and how to process it prior to packaging, the packager must bear any additional burdens related to those decisions.
            *   Furthermore, the packager is the only entity with knowledge of what processing the firm intends to do, or not do, prior to packaging; and is the only entity with the information (e.g., serving size, target population, package size, packaging material, shelf life, etc.) necessary to set proper specifications for the ingredient used in the product.
            *   Therefore, if FDA believes that elements of Part 111 such as setting appropriate ingredient specifications and verifying compliance with those specifications are critical in situations where an ingredient is packaged as a supplement, FDA must place those burdens on the packager, not the ingredient vendor.
            *   In the event that such an expansion of the applicability of Part 111 is necessary, FDA may issue a technical correction to the preamble: “If, however Similarly, if you sell herbs in bulk as a dietary ingredient to Company X, and Company X simply packages the herbs into smaller units for sale as a dietary supplement, you would not be subject to these dietary supplement CGMP requirements. In this scenario, Company X acts as a dietary supplement manufacturer whose manufacturing process consists of subdividing the bulk herbs into smaller portions; Company X would be required to establish specifications under §111.70 for the herbs that they repackage into smaller units for sale as a dietary supplement and to ensure that their specifications are met under §111.73 and §111.75. because you are manufacturing a dietary supplement that Company X is simply packaging and labeling, and not further processing into a dietary supplement. In other words, in the latter example, you would have acted as a manufacturer whose finished product is simply repackaged or relabeled.”
            *   The proposed policy of determining GMP requirements based on the labeling of the ingredients in question will relieve dietary ingredient vendors from duplicative regulatory schemes and provide clarity for both FDA and the regulated trade, thereby reducing legal and enforcement costs and improving compliance.
            *   Such effect may alternately be achieved through the release of a guidance document indicating an equivalent policy position.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: The ad hoc application of 21 C.F.R. 111 requirements described above is an application of regulation that imposes undue burdens on industry without a basis for public benefit – one which is particularly burdensome for small businesses. The above recommendation presents a less costly means to meet the regulation’s goal with improved public health protection.
    *   Definitions should be provided for the terms “manufacturing,” “packaging,” “labeling,” and “holding” in 21 C.F.R. Part 111
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. Part 111
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   21 C.F.R. Part 111 is titled Current Good Manufacturing Practice in Manufacturing, Packaging, Labeling, or Holding Operations for Dietary Supplements, but nowhere defines “manufacturing,” “packaging,” “labeling,” or “holding.”
            *   In regulations for current good manufacturing practice, hazard analysis, and risk-based preventive controls for human foods at 21 C.F.R. Part 117 and for animal foods at 21 C.F.R. Part 507, FDA provides a definition for one of these terms (“holding”) and for another similar and possibly synonymous term (“manufacturing / processing”), but does not provide definitions for the other two terms (“packaging” and “labeling”). The definition for “manufacturing / processing” given for both human foods and animal foods in 21 C.F.R. § 117.3 and 21 C.F.R. § 507.3, respectively, includes both packaging and labeling within that definition.
            *   Definitions of regulated activities are necessary to the clear functioning of rules intended to cover the conduct of those activities.
            *   However, the specific definitions provided in Parts 117 and 507 are not appropriate direct incorporation in Part 111 due to significant differences between these rules and the respective product categories they regulate.
            *   FDA indicates by the preamble accompanying the issuance of final 21 C.F.R. Part 111 that a company’s specific operations are relevant to determining which specific sections of the rule apply to their operations: “…you need to comply with the CGMP requirements that apply to your operations related to the manufacture, packaging, labeling, and holding of dietary supplements” (emphasis added).
            *   FDA provides an example of a company that is a packager/labeler but not a finished product manufacturer, and which “would not need to comply with requirements that do not apply to it; for example, the packager/relabeler would not have to conduct testing on the finished batch of dietary supplement since it does not manufacture the finished batch of dietary supplement.”
            *   The agency also notes, “if you are a wholesaler, you would be subject to the requirements in final §111.470 for the dietary supplements you are holding for distribution as well as other applicable requirements, such as those related to personnel, physical plant and grounds, equipment and utensils, quality control, returned dietary supplements, and product complaints.”
            *   Because there are different obligations under 21 C.F.R. Part 111 for different operations it is essential that the regulated trade clearly understand exactly what FDA means by each of the terms, “manufacturing,” “packaging,” “labeling,” and “holding.” Otherwise, ambiguities about the classification of activities such as encapsulation (potentially treated as a packaging or manufacturing operation) will create unnecessary and burdensome compliance and enforcement activity.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   The following definitions should be added to 21 C.F.R. § 111.3:
                *   Manufacturing means to conduct operations to make from one or more components a dietary supplement intended for ingestion in the form of a tablet, capsule, powder, softgel, gelcap, liquid or other form for ingestion, such as a teabag.
                *   Packaging means to conduct operations to place a dietary supplement into the container in which it will be sold.
                *   Labeling means to conduct operations to place labels on packaged dietary supplements, or to form and/or fill packages bearing such labels.
                *   Holding means maintaining and storing components and bulk or retail packaged dietary supplements.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: The definition gap identified herein creates significant costs to private industry to no public benefit; uncertainty regarding the rules applicable to different activities impedes technological innovation in the manufacturing of dietary supplements.
    *   Comments regarding the terms “identity,” “purity,” “strength,” and “composition” in 21 C.F.R. Part 111
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. § 111
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   21 C.F.R. Part 111 requires manufacturers of dietary supplements to establish specifications, and to meet these specifications, for “the identity, purity, strength, and composition of the finished batch of the dietary supplement.”
            *   The rule does not, however, define these four terms.
            *   FDA instead elaborated upon its “interpretation” of these terms in the preamble to the final rule on this matter.
            *   These informal definitions possess some utility as applied to finished dietary supplement products, but must be formalized in regulation.
            *   In being so formalized, these definitions must be revised to apply consistently to the full range of dietary supplement products. In particular, the term “purity” should be omitted.
            *   It is essential that FDA maintains a clear, generally applicable definition for each of these terms, (including “purity” if maintained in the rule.
            *   In the absence of clear, fully applicable definitions for these terms, the agency and regulated trade have struggled with several elements of compliance and inconsistent enforcement activity regarding specifications requirements at 21 C.F.R. §§ 111.70 and 111.75.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   Due to their layered use in regulation and enforcement and the detail necessary to accommodate their full use in dietary supplements, each term is addressed separately below. Each section begins with a quotation of the preamble material describing FDA’s current informal exploration of the term, followed by recommendations and considerations for the needed formal definition.
            *   (a) Identity:
                *   The preamble defines the “identity” of a dietary supplement as consistency with the master manufacturing record (MMR): “The ‘identity’ of a dietary supplement refers to the dietary supplement’s consistency with the master manufacturing record and/or that it is the same as described in the master manufacturing record.”
                *   This definition is generally applicable, but it requires refinement to provide for deviations from the MMR where appropriate, documented, and approved by assigned personnel.
                *   With respect to the “identity” of a dietary supplement as defined, conformance to identity specifications can only be evaluated through review of the batch record; there is no scientifically valid “test” to ensure that the batch is consistent with the MMR.
                *   However, in enforcing the requirement to set specifications for the “identity” of supplements, FDA inspectors have been known to interpret “identity” specifications to mean descriptive or quantitative characteristics such as size, weight, color, odor, taste, viscosity, chemical fingerprint, content of claimed substances, etc.
                *   While such tests provide evidence that the product (or a component) is the intended item, requiring these specifications is inconsistent with the definition provided in the preamble. This causes inconsistent enforcement and confusion among the regulated trade.
                *   If FDA intends to maintain that the “identity” of a supplement refers to the supplement’s consistency with the MMR, then FDA must stipulate that the identity is confirmed by the manufacturer through review of the batch record. A separate definition or at least an explanation is then needed for the “identity” of a component, since the rule requires “identity specifications” to be set for components.
                *   If FDA intends to maintain that “identity” specifications consist of descriptive or quantitative characteristics that, when tested or examined, will provide evidence that a component or product is the intended item, then FDA should adjust the definition provided for the “identity” of a finished product or define “identity specifications” separately from “identity.”
            *   (b) Strength:
                *   The current informal definition of “strength” relates to concentration or amount per serving: “Strength. The strength of a dietary supplement relates to its concentration. By concentration, we mean the quantitative amount per serving (for example, weight/weight, weight/ volume, or volume/volume). Therefore, for purposes of this final rule, strength does not refer simply to the quantity of an ingredient, rather it refers to the amount of a stated ingredient per a specified unit of measure.”
                *   In further discussing this term, FDA notes, “We do not consider the rule’s requirements on dietary supplement strength as necessarily relating to the individual constituents of such products. Whether the requirements regarding dietary supplement strength apply to one or more constituents of dietary ingredients in a dietary supplement depends on what you are manufacturing. For example, if you are manufacturing vitamin C, and your source of vitamin C is rosehips, you would establish a strength specification for vitamin C in the finished batch of the dietary supplement (e.g., ‘x milligrams (mg) of vitamin C per tablet’). Alternately, if you are manufacturing rosehips and not vitamin C from rosehips, the strength specification that you establish for the finished batch of the dietary supplement is the strength of the rosehips themselves (i.e., the concentration of rosehips in the final product, such as ‘x mg of rosehips per tablet’).”
                *   This approach is potentially appropriate, but is not consistently communicated in the preamble, leading to inconsistent application and confusion with pharmaceutical dosage concepts.
                *   This definition also does not adequately describe the range of conventional strength expressions applicable to dietary supplement products.
                *   FDA begins by giving dietary supplement “strength” examples as “weight/weight, weight/volume, or volume/volume,” but makes no mention of “amount per tablet” until later in the preamble, and omits other units such as “per capsule.” Since tablets and capsules are the most common form of dietary supplements, these should be explicitly discussed at the outset along with weight/weight, weight/volume, and volume/volume.
                *   The current informal definition does not address extracts from natural materials, including botanical extracts, for which “strength” is often best expressed as an extract ratio. This conveys the same information as concentration presented as weight/weight, weight/volume, or volume/volume, but is in a format that uses a colon rather than a forward slash. The extract ratio is a common measure of extract “strength” already identified and used in regulation. Labeling regulations at 21 C.F.R. § 101.36(b)(3)(ii)(B) specify how liquid extract ratios should be expressed. For powdered or solid extracts, the ratio should be defined as X:Y where X is the amount of starting botanical material and Y is the amount of finished extract including excipients, with X being dried botanical unless specified as fresh. The option of expressing the “strength” as the extract ratio should be explicitly discussed in the definition, as the ratio is, in practice, the most familiar expression of the concept for a range of dietary supplement industry and consumer stakeholders.
                *   Additional examples should be provided wherein “strength” is expressed as an amount per unit of weight or volume. For example, the strength of a Vitamin D liquid may be described as “X mg per mL”; the strength of enzymes may be described as “X USP units (or other units) per g”; the strength of probiotic products may be expressed as “X billion cfu/g”.
                *   The option of expressing “strength” in terms of percent should also be explicitly discussed. Percent is one of the most common expressions of concentration, equates to “amount of units per 100 units,” and is expressed as weight/weight, weight/volume, or volume/volume. It is therefore entirely consistent with the “strength” discussion provided by FDA in the preamble. For example, 90% ascorbic acid granules consist of vitamin C mixed with appropriate excipients to form a granule.
                *   FDA mentions in the preamble that it is not necessary to establish specifications for the strength of excipients, at least if such a specification is not necessary to ensure the finished dietary supplement specifications are met; AHPA is aware of no case in which such a specification would be necessary. FDA should clarify in its formal definition of the term that “strength” is relevant only with respect to dietary ingredients, not excipients.
            *   (c) Composition:
                *   FDA’s informal discussion of “composition,” uses the phrase “product and product-related substances” in a manner inconsistent with intuition or general practice: “Composition. A dietary supplement’s ‘composition’ refers to the specified mix of product and product-related substances in a dietary supplement. For example, a dietary supplement manufactured to provide vitamin C may contain, in addition to vitamin C, a tablet coating agent and substances used as binders. The composition could be described as the percent of the dietary supplement that is vitamin C, the tablet-coating agent, and each binder.”
                *   In normal usage, the “product” of a manufacturing process is the totality of the material or item resulting from the manufacturing process, not some subcomponent of the final material. In FDA’s example, the “product” would normally be considered the entire vitamin C tablet, not the vitamin C within.
                *   The composition of a dietary supplement would be more clearly defined in a manner such as, “The formula for the dietary supplement, in which each ingredient is identified and the level of each ingredient is expressed as a percent.”
                *   There is no generally available, scientifically valid test for many elements of product composition (unless each ingredient consists of a single molecular entity that is easily separated from the other ingredients and readily measured, which is almost never the case). Often, composition can be determined only (but still reliably) through review of batch records. There is no good reason, public health or otherwise, to impose this requirement on dietary supplement manufacturers.
                *   As a result, the rule should be modified to stipulate that composition specifications for dietary supplements are to be confirmed through review of properly-completed batch records.
            *   (d) Purity:
                *   The term “purity” as described by FDA is either redundant to “strength” and/or “composition” or is irrelevant: “Purity. The ‘purity’ of a dietary supplement refers to that portion or percentage of a dietary supplement that represents the intended product.” FDA provides as an example that if “a dietary supplement provide[s] the amino acid L-arginine, and you determine that 90 percent of the manufactured product is L-arginine and 10 percent of the manufactured product is D-arginine, you could describe your L-arginine product as ‘90 percent pure.’”
                *   In the example provided by FDA, a dietary supplement containing 90% L-arginine and 10% D-arginine is sufficiently described by stating the “strength” as “90% L- arginine” and the “composition” as “100% arginine.”
                *   As another example, a 1000-mg dietary supplement containing 500 mg calcium carbonate, 300 mg ascorbic acid, 180 mg cellulose, and 20 mg silica is sufficiently described by stating the “strength” as 500 mg calcium carbonate per tablet and 300 mg ascorbic acid per tablet and the “composition” as 50% calcium carbonate, 30% ascorbic acid, 18% cellulose, and 2% silica. To additionally describe the product as “50% pure calcium carbonate,” “30% pure ascorbic acid,” “18% pure cellulose,” and/or “2% pure silica” is at best redundant and at worst confusing.
                *   Insofar as FDA intends “purity” to be used to describe different forms of a dietary ingredient within a single component (e.g., a naturally occurring mixture of L and D isomers of arginine), there is still no clear scope of application for a purity specification that is not addressed by strength and composition.
                *   A powder dietary supplement that contains 90% L-arginine and 10% D-arginine, and for which the serving size is 1 g, has a strength of 900 mg L-arginine per g and a composition of “100% arginine”; there is no additional benefit to specifying the “purity” as “90% L-arginine.” If in fact “10% D-arginine” is critical to the supplement’s specifications, this can be established as an additional “strength” specification.
                *   The term “purity” in particular has been a source of longstanding confusion among stakeholders in the regulated trade, because it most commonly refers to freedom from contaminants, not to the percentage of a target ingredient.
                *   “Purity” should thus be removed from the regulation. If FDA maintains “purity” in the regulation, FDA needs to clarify its role and ensure that the resulting regulation does not require such a specification where it is not relevant.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data. Regarding the proposal to test individual markers, the cost to develop and validate a new test for an individual marker compound may vary between $3,000 and $10,000. In the context of businesses that sell a range of multi-ingredient formulations, such costs become immediately prohibitive. In practice, such methods may be flatly impossible to generate in the testing of a finished multi-ingredient botanical product.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: Inconsistent and unclear application of the above terms has been a lasting problem increasing enforcement and compliance costs across the dietary supplement trade since the passage of the final rule 10 years ago. The malformed nature of a highly specific regulation that does not formally or appropriately define its definitions for specifications is a severe and ironic example of a regulation that imposes significant burdens on private enterprise to no public benefit. The additional compliance costs created by these unclear specification standards (in particular uncertainty around the creation and testing of specifications that will satisfy these terms) are a major impediment to innovation in the dietary supplement industry, as well as a significant burden upon small businesses least able to accommodate them.
    *   Master manufacturing records should be able to declare a range of batch sizes
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. § 111.205
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   21 C.F.R. § 111.205 describes the requirement to establish a written master manufacturing record (MMR).
            *   This requirement further states: “(a) You must prepare and follow a written master manufacturing record for each unique formulation of dietary supplement that you manufacture, and for each batch size, to ensure uniformity in the finished batch from batch to batch.”
            *   A different MMR may be appropriate for different batch sizes in many cases, as the quantity of each component must be accurately recalculated for each batch size to maintain correct proportions.
            *   Batch sizes that differ greatly may also require different equipment or other procedural changes.
            *   However, these concerns do not apply in every case, and where they do, there are often other means to ensure quality and consistency.
            *   Therefore, the requirement to create an MMR for every batch size is cumbersome, impractical, and overly prescriptive.
            *   (a) Flexibility to accommodate yield variance: Some companies prepare and follow MMRs that cover various batch sizes within a known range. This is especially necessary for herbal products manufactured from agricultural products where exact crop yield varies from harvest to harvest.
            *   Thus, one harvest may yield 73.5 pounds of an herb and the next may yield 128 pounds. The MMR for a tincture from that herb must be flexible. If a separate MMR is required for each individual batch size, companies must maintain numerous MMRs for a single product, creating a tremendous recordkeeping and filing burden, especially with revision control.
            *   FDA declined to address this concern in the preamble, arguing such a change would not reduce burdens because “a new “formula,” based on the master formula, would still need to be prepared for each batch.” In essence, FDA denies the problem by acknowledging the scale of the burden it creates; a new formula, and a new MMR, for every batch of a product.
            *   An MMR that covers a defined range of batch sizes should be acceptable so long as the (a) relative proportions of all components in the formulation, (b) equipment, (c) in-process specifications, and (d) packaging components used all remain the same for all sizes within the range, and so long as each batch record created from the MMR is reviewed and approved prior to use by quality control personnel to ensure accuracy and appropriateness (e.g., to ensure any ingredient quantities were calculated correctly based on the proportions specified in the product formula).
            *   (b) Lot versus batch flexibilities: In some manufacturing environments, size-dependent manufacturing specifications are established on the basis of a defined lot size rather than a defined batch size. Procedures may occur whereby the manufacture of one batch of product involves producing, during a specified period of time and under one manufacturing record, a series of identical lots of a defined mixture which are then combined to become the finished batch (e.g., by using the lots as the feed for a continuous manufacturing process). In such cases it is more appropriate for the MMR to be established on the basis of the lot size rather than the batch size. The batch size may vary based on how many lots are combined to make the batch, but different batch sizes do not require a separate MMR because there are no process parameters (such as ingredient quantities or equipment settings) that change based on the batch size. Therefore, in these cases the regulation should provide flexibility for MMRs to be established based on a fixed lot size rather than a fixed batch size.
            *   (c) Packaging variance: Packaging operations typically do not include process parameters that vary based on batch size; furthermore, it is typical for each packaging batch to be a different size. The batch size may be slightly different due to minor variations in the output of each manufacturing batch or significantly different because a different batch size was manufactured. It may also differ because one manufactured batch is packaged under a number of different, smaller packaging batches in varying quantities.
            *   In any case, since there are typically no process parameters such as ingredient quantities or equipment settings that vary based on the packaging batch size, it is both onerous and pointless to require a separate MMR for each packaging batch size.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   The rule should be amended to allow a written master manufacturing record to be prepared for a range of lot or batch sizes, and that flexibility be provided such that the requirement may apply to either lots or batches as appropriate to the facility’s operations.
            *   The following specific amendments to current § 111.205(a) address all of the above concerns: “(a) You must prepare and follow a written master manufacturing record for each unique formulation of dietary supplement that you manufacture, and for each lot or batch size, to ensure uniformity in the finished batch product from lot to lot and batch to batch, except that a master manufacturing record may cover a range of lot or batch sizes so long as the (a) relative proportions of all components in the formulation, (b) equipment, (c) in- process specifications, and (d) packaging components used all remain the same for all sizes within the range, and so long as each batch record created from the master manufacturing record is reviewed and approved prior to use by quality control personnel to ensure accuracy and appropriateness. Alternately, in cases where ingredient quantities and other manufacturing parameters vary based on lot size rather than batch size, master manufacturing records may cover a range of batch sizes wherein the lot size fixed but the number of lots per batch may vary. For packaging operations, a separate MMR is not required for each batch size so long as there are no process parameters that vary based on the batch size.”
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: A small manufacturing concern with a moderate number of products estimates that the burdens of multiple batch MMR generation require 50% of time for a midlevel regulatory compliance employee at $40,000 annually.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: For the reasons stated above the regulation at 21 C.F.R. § 111.205(a) to require a separate master manufacturing record for each batch size of a dietary supplement is both ineffective and imposes unnecessary costs on a range of dietary supplement manufacturers. These burdens are especially punishing to small businesses due to their general applicability and generation of duplicative overhead costs; they also severely restrain innovation in manufacturing processes to no public benefit.
    *   FDA should discontinue the practice of imposing manufacturing cGMP requirements under 21 C.F.R. Part 111 on “own label distributors”
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. Part 111
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   There is no cGMP regulation in 21 C.F.R. Part 111 that establishes any specialized obligations for a company that sells supplement products under its own brand that are manufactured and/or labeled by one or more other firms.
            *   Since the rule was promulgated, FDA has begun to informally describe such companies as “own label distributors” (although the rule nowhere defines such a term), and enforce novel cGMP requirements for such firms and their contract manufacturers without regulation.
            *   In doing so, FDA has created an onerous and impractical regulatory environment both for “own label” distributors and contract manufacturers and has acted in contravention of the requirements of 21 U.S.C. 342(g) and 374(a)(1).
            *   In the preamble to the rulemaking establishing the cGMP regulation at 21 CFR Part 111, FDA stated: “A manufacturer who contracts with a person to do packaging and labeling, but who later distributes the packaged and labeled product, is ultimately responsible for the dietary supplement it releases for distribution. The manufacturer would be responsible for the CGMP requirements for the operations that it performs, including those related to the release of the product for distribution.”
            *   FDA has cited this preamble to the regulation in warning so-called “own label” distributors that they must comply with various parts of the cGMP with regard to products manufactured for them by contract manufacturers, including in particular recordkeeping requirements relating to master manufacturing records, batch manufacturing records, and raw material testing records.
            *   These obligations, however, are not stated in the cGMP regulations for any type of distribution company, and in fact cannot as a practical matter be implemented by a firm engaged in distribution rather than manufacturing.
            *   This extraregulatory obligation has shifted and expanded over time through other agency communications. For example, in reference to strict liability provisions of the Federal Food, Drug, & Cosmetic Act, FDA stated in a Warning Letter to Mannatech Incorporated, that: “In particular, the Act prohibits a person from introducing or delivering for introduction, or causing the delivery or introduction, into interstate commerce a dietary supplement that is adulterated under section 402(g) for failure to comply with dietary supplement CGMP requirements (see 21 U.S.C. 342(g) and 331(a)). Thus, a firm that contracts out some or all of its operations must establish a system of production and process controls to ensure the quality of the dietary supplement and that the dietary supplement is packaged and labeled as specified in the master manufacturing record (21 C.F.R. 111.55). The quality control personnel must ensure that the manufacturing, packaging, labeling, and holding operations ensure the quality of the dietary supplement and that the dietary supplement is packaged and labeled as specified in the master manufacturing record (21 C.F.R. 111.105).”
            *   Thus, from the preamble to a regulation, to a summary of that preamble, to strict liability case law, to the general provisions of the Act, FDA in this and similar Warning Letters imposes on distributors various cGMP provisions that are directed toward manufacturers in regulation.
            *   This is contrary to the mandate of the underlying provision cited by FDA, 21 U.S.C. 342(g) which states in subparagraph (2) that: “(2) The Secretary may by regulation prescribe good manufacturing practices for dietary supplements. Such regulations shall be modeled after current good manufacturing practice regulations for food (emphasis added) and may not impose standards for which there is no current and generally available analytical methodology. No standard of current good manufacturing practice may be imposed unless such standard is included in a regulation promulgated after notice and opportunity for comment in accordance with chapter 5 of title 5, United States Code.”
            *   FDA ‘s assertions in Warning Letters regarding the specific cGMP responsibilities of “own label” distributors under the cGMP regulations appear to be improvised. Regulated industry has, as a result, experienced an inconsistent and unpredictable array of expectations for cGMP documentation from inspectors, with similarly unpredictable bases for successful compliance.
            *   In some cases, companies treated as “own label distributors” are permitted to refer the inspector to the contract manufacturer, to provide batch records and/or ingredient testing records from the contract manufacturer, and to provide a quality agreement with the contract manufacturer.
            *   In other cases, investigators retracted requests for these documents when pushed by the “own label” distributor to cite where in the regulation such a burden is placed on the distributor (since no such provision exists).
            *   Under the most severe circumstances, inspectors will require that a distributor obtain all covered documents from the contract manufacturer within 24 hours.
            *   Notably, FDA insistence on reviewing the contract manufacturer’s documents during an inspection of the “own label” distributor fail to provide the contract manufacturer with the protections of 21 U.S.C. 374(a)(1), which require FDA to present a Notice of Inspection to the facility (in this case, the contract manufacturer) prior to seeking access to the facility’s records, and the corresponding protections regarding confidential treatment for proprietary and confidential information within those records.
            *   Dietary supplement firms are subject to a wide variety of requirements under the law, but it does not follow that all such requirements are subject to review by FDA during a cGMP inspection. FDA’s authority during a dietary supplement cGMP inspection is limited to those requirements promulgated in the dietary supplement cGMP regulations.
            *   The application of manufacturer requirements to an “own label” distributor is further impracticable because such a firm does not and often cannot have the detailed knowledge necessary to create, evaluate, or justify to FDA documents such as master manufacturing records, batch records, or ingredient specifications. Only the manufacturer has the prerequisite knowledge of the applicable facilities, equipment, processes, procedures, and other information necessary to establish these documents or evaluate their adequacy.
            *   Where an investigator seeks manufacturer records through a distributor inspection, the resulting mediated request (requiring compilation and support of documentation without notice through a client intermediary) has proven highly disruptive to contract manufacturer operations. Since any one contract manufacturer may process supplements on behalf of hundreds or even thousands of distributors, the manufacturer can find itself continuously disrupted by such requests.
            *   Distributors, including “own label” distributors bear responsibility under the law for the dietary supplements they distribute. In some circumstances, especially where responsibility for the quality and safety of the finished product is divided amongst multiple parties, a formal quality agreement or other contract may be useful to clearly delineate responsibilities and liabilities among the parties. However, any regulatory requirement placed upon industry must have a regulatory, and a legal, basis. Present FDA practices in this area lack such a justification.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   FDA should direct the Office of Food Chemical Safety, Dietary Supplements, and Innovation and the Office of Compliance and Enforcement to discontinue the practice of imposing manufacturing cGMP requirements under 21 CFR Part 111 on “own label” distributors until such time as appropriate notice and comment rulemaking has occurred to clearly define such entities and establish such requirements.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data.
