        *   Relevance to EO 14219: FDA’s current expansive reading of the preamble to the cGMP rule raises the prospect that FDA’s treatment of “own-label distributors” is not based on the best reading of its underlying statutory authority, and indeed violates the associated prohibition. The resulting set of regulatory practices creates significant confusion, cost, and duplicative burden to industry with no public health benefit. Of particular note, the own label distribution model often serves as a market entry point for small business innovators; the current regulatory approach creates an especially severe burden upon these entities.

        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP

        *   Matter of concern:
            *   The FDCA authorizes establishment of good manufacturing practice regulations for dietary supplements, now codified at 21 C.F.R.         *   Relevance to EO 14219: The current regulatory approach regarding specification establishment creates an environment of uncertainty and risk around product innovation, and where new test method establishment is required, incurs great costs not in alignment with public benefit. *   Issues related to Produce Safety rule (21 C.F.R. Part 112)
    *   The following issue is specifically addressed to details in 21 C.F.R. Part 112 and to related rules in 21 C.F.R. Part 117.
    *   Adjust definitions and scope of 21 C.F.R. Part 112 for Produce Safety, and related definitions in Part 117 for food manufacturing, to conform to Congressional intent
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. §§ 112.1, 112.2, 112.3, 117.3
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   In promulgating regulations under the Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA), FDA adopted a formal definition of “produce” and an interpretation of “processed food” which, taken together, will place the burdens of Part 112 on a large proportion of farmers, and further regulate many farmers as food manufacturers subject to the heavy expenses of compliance with food Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) regulations.
            *   AHPA believes these proposals exceed the Congressional intent of FSMA. In passing FSMA, Congress directed FDA to develop regulations to ensure the safety of “produce” consumed by the American public. The term “produce” is ordinarily understood to encompass those fruits and vegetables (and arguably also nuts, sprouts, mushrooms, and culinary herbs such as parsley or basil) that are commonly consumed in fresh, unprocessed form.
            *   In promulgating the implementing regulations for FSMA, however, FDA has defined “produce” to encompass every crop meeting the botanical definition of a “fruit” (i.e., the reproductive structure of a plant that develops from a flower) or “vegetable” (i.e., any part of a plant or fungus other than the fruit) with the sole exception of food grains.
            *   FDA also promulgated in 21 C.F.R. § 112.1(b)(1) a list of examples of produce covered by the rule and in § 112.2(a)(1) a defined list of produce excluded from the rule.
            *   FDA describes this latter list as an “exhaustive” list of produce that is rarely consumed raw, but this list fails to include many food crops that are rarely consumed raw (e.g., yuca (cassava) root; taro root; yams; tepary beans; mashua tubers; ginkgo nuts).
            *   These provisions collectively subject a large variety of crops to the burdens of Part 112 “Produce Safety” compliance that are not commonly understood as “produce” and which are always or almost always cooked or otherwise processed prior to consumption.
            *   This includes a range of crops used to make the flavors, colors, excipients, process aids, and dietary ingredients used in food, including dietary supplements (“non-fresh-produce botanicals”). For example, unless the farmer qualifies for an exemption (and maintains the associated documentation), Part 112 regulatory burdens are applied to the cotton used to make microcrystalline cellulose; the acacia used to make gum arabic; the alfalfa used to make green food color; the oak chips used to make food flavorings; and the hops used to make beer.
            *   Part 112 Produce Safety compliance is not necessary to protect the public health regarding crops that are not, in fact, “produce” consumed in fresh, unprocessed form, especially in view of other food manufacturing safety requirements imposed under 21 C.F.R. Part 117. As these products are outside the scope of “produce,” subjecting them to the full scope of Part 112 compliance goes outside Congressional intent in passing FSMA.
            *   Additional concerns arise with the regulatory classification of commodities as either “raw agricultural commodities” (RACs) or “processed foods”. 21 USC § 321(gg) defines “processed food” to mean “any food other than a raw agricultural commodity and includes any raw agricultural commodity that has been subjected to processing, such as canning, cooking, freezing, dehydration, or milling.” 21 USC § 321(r) defines “raw agricultural commodity” to mean “any food in its raw or natural state, including all fruits that are washed, colored, or otherwise treated in their unpeeled natural form prior to marketing.”
            *   The application of these statutory terms to the food supply chain requires a degree of nuance. For example, while dehydration is listed as an activity that creates a processed food, FDA had long interpreted this provision to apply only when the dehydration creates a new or distinct commodity (for example, drying grapes into raisins). In contrast, where the dehydration is a normal part of preparing the crop for trade as food (e.g., drying of hay or grains), FDA had treated the resulting material as a RAC rather than as a processed food.
            *   However, in promulgating the implementing regulations for FSMA, FDA has defined “manufacturing/processing” broadly and “farm” narrowly. As a result, numerous activities that farms normally use to prepare a food crop for trade as a RAC now transform the crop into a “processed food.” This has the effect of transforming many farm operations into food manufacturers subject to facility registration and good manufacturing practices for food.
            *   For example, FDA considers cutting, chopping, and slicing to be “manufacturing” or “processing” activities that are outside the scope of the farm definition and therefore subject to food facility registration and regulations. Such actions make sense as a transformative step for crops that are fresh produce as the term “produce” is commonly understood (for example, apples, lettuce, or carrots).
            *   However, the same activities play a different role in the preparation of crops that are not typically used as fresh produce (i.e., non-fresh-produce botanicals), these same activities are often a farm activity normally used to prepare the crop for sale as a RAC. Non-fresh-produce botanicals are normally traded in dehydrated form and packed in sacks, and as a practical matter these botanicals often require some kind of size reduction in order to facilitate dehydration, handling, and packing. For example, large roots and many barks are typically cut into smaller pieces to facilitate drying, packing, and handling. In these circumstances, the cutting, chopping or slicing is not “adding value” to the commodity or “transforming” the commodity into a new commodity; they are steps taken as a practical matter in order to prepare the crop for sale as a RAC.
            *   A similar analysis, and shift in the scope of covered products, occurs to heating and freezing steps. While it makes sense to treat such procedures as transformative steps when applied to what one would conventionally consider fresh produce commodities, the same regulatory transition becomes overinclusive when applied to, for example, initiate enzymatic fermentation. Boiling or steaming may be similarly necessary to soften the material in order to facilitate size reduction for packing (e.g., for bark and similarly tough materials). No consumable commodity exists for sale without such steps; such commodities are not sold as fresh produce and thus should not be considered transformed into processed foods.
            *   FDA should acknowledge the distinction between produce crops and non-fresh-produce crops, and must permit a much wider range of activities to remain within the farm definition when performed on non-fresh-produce crops.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   The scope of 21 C.F.R. Part 112 should be significantly narrowed to focus specifically on those crops that are, in fact, likely to be consumed by the public in fresh, unprocessed form and for which stringent food safety regulations at the farm level are therefore truly justified to protect the public health.
            *   In addition, FDA needs to acknowledge the distinction between produce crops and non-fresh-produce crops, and for practicality must permit a much wider range of activities to remain within the farm definition when performed on non-fresh-produce crops.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: As currently written, this combination of classifications causes major new regulatory costs for farm operations, significantly increasing costs to food processors and consumers, with no concomitant public benefit. Such burdens particularly accrue to smaller agricultural interests operating outside the conventional fresh produce space.

    *   Amendments to 21 C.F.R. § 190.6 would clarify the submission of NDI notifications
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. § 190.6
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   21 C.F.R. § 190.6, the specific regulation in which FDA articulates the requirements for premarket notification of a new dietary ingredient (NDI), does not include some details that are relevant to submission of an NDI notification.
            *   Specifically, 21 C.F.R. § 190.6(b) identifies requirements for information that must be included in an NDI notification to be limited to the following: “(1) The name and complete address of the manufacturer or distributor of the dietary supplement that contains a new dietary ingredient, or of the new dietary ingredient; (2) The name of the new dietary ingredient that is the subject of the premarket notification, including the Latin binomial name (including the author) of any herb or other botanical; (3) A description of the dietary supplement or dietary supplements that contain the new dietary ingredient including: (i) The level of the new dietary ingredient in the dietary supplement; and (ii) The conditions of use recommended or suggested in the labeling of the dietary supplement, or if no conditions of use are recommended or suggested in the labeling of the dietary supplement, the ordinary conditions of use of the supplement; (4) The history of use or other evidence of safety establishing that the dietary ingredient, when used under the conditions recommended or suggested in the labeling of the dietary supplement, will reasonably be expected to be safe, including any citation to published articles or other evidence that is the basis on which the distributor or manufacturer of the dietary supplement that contains the new dietary ingredient has concluded that the new dietary supplement will reasonably be expected to be safe. Any reference to published information offered in support of the notification shall be accompanied by reprints or photostatic copies of such references. If any part of the material submitted is in a foreign language, it shall be accompanied by an accurate and complete English translation; and (5) The signature of the person designated by the manufacturer or distributor of the dietary supplement that contains a new dietary ingredient.”
            *   There are no other requirements identified in 21 C.F.R. § 190.6 for any additional specific information to be included in an NDI notification.
            *   This provision does not require that an NDI notification be accompanied by a description of the NDI itself, nor, when the NDI is an herb or other botanical, identification of the part of the plant from which the ingredient is derived.
            *   However, FDA has developed a policy of expressing significant concerns in response to notifications that do not include a sufficiently precise description of the NDI or that do not identify the relevant part of the plant for botanically-derived ingredients. These concerns are still expressed where the notification provides all information currently required in an NDI notification under 21 C.F.R. § 190.6.
            *   On the issue of identification of a plant part for botanical ingredients, there is a notable contrast between the absence of a requirement for this information in 21 C.F.R. § 190.6(b) in relation to NDI notifications and the statutory language at 21 U.S.C. § 343(s)(2) that establishes that a dietary supplement that contains as an ingredient an “herb or other botanical,” as identified in 21 U.S.C. § 321(ff)(1)(C), is misbranded if the label of the product “fails to identify any part of the plant from which the ingredient is derived.”
        *   Recommendation:
            *   FDA should revise 21 C.F.R. § 190.6(b) to square the regulation with the Agency’s expectation of performance by industry when submitting an NDI notification, and to therefore establish a clear requirement for such notifications to include an accurate and sufficiently complete identification of any NDI that is the subject of the notification, including, for botanical ingredients, the relevant part of the subject plant.
            *   In addition to the two current specific gaps in 21 C.F.R. § 190.6(b) discussed above, additional revisions should be made to this regulation, both to provide greater clarity and to make the regulation more consistent with the NDI provisions of the FDCA.
            *   Toward this end, 21 C.F.R. § 190.6(b) should be amended by adding the following additional requirements for an NDI notification submission:
                *   (1) The name and complete address of the manufacturer or distributor of the new dietary ingredient or of dietary supplement(s) that contains a new dietary ingredient, that is submitting the notification.
                *   (2) The name of the new dietary ingredient that is the subject of the premarket notification, including the Latin binomial name (including the author) of any herb or other botanical;
                *   (3) The part of the plant from which the ingredient is derived if the ingredient is an herb or other botanical; a concentrate, metabolite, constituent of an herb or other botanical; or a combination of herbs or botanicals;
                *   (4) A description of the new dietary ingredient;
                *   (5) A specific description of the a dietary supplement or a general description of a range of dietary supplements that contains or will contain the NDI, including: a. the level of the NDI in the dietary supplement(s), and b. the conditions of use recommended or suggested in the labeling of the dietary supplement(s) containing the NDI, or if no conditions of use are recommended or suggested in the supplement’s labeling, the ordinary conditions of use of the supplement(s).
                *   (6) The history of use or other evidence of safety, including any citation to published articles, establishing that the dietary ingredient, when used under the conditions recommended in the labeling of the dietary supplement, will reasonably be expected to be safe which is the basis on which the manufacturer or distributor has concluded that a NDI will reasonably be expected to be safe in one or more dietary supplements.
                *   (7) The signature of a person designated by the manufacturer or distributor of the new dietary ingredient or the dietary supplement that contains a new dietary ingredient to sign the notification on its behalf.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: Uncertainties and ambiguities regarding the scope of NDI submissions have been a barrier to the introduction of new dietary ingredients into the marketplace; as such the current disconnect between regulation and practice has been a barrier to innovation in the dietary supplement marketplace.
    *   FDA should allow review of NDI submissions to be halted
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. § 190.6
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   21 C.F.R. § 190.6 sets forth the procedure for making a new dietary ingredient notification to FDA.
            *   At present, no procedure exists in this regulation to ask FDA to cease review of a submission.
            *   Such a procedure has long been permitted as part of FDA practice regarding the evaluation of Generally Recognized as Safe (GRAS) notifications. Under this procedure, the notification itself remains on file at FDA and may be released under the Freedom of Information Act with confidential proprietary and trade secret information redacted.
            *   This inconsistency and the associated data privacy concerns serve as a source of perceived hazard in the submission of NDI notifications.
            *   FDA has released new guidance outlining procedures and timelines for NDI notification submissions; unfortunately, this guidance does not delineate a withdrawal process.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   21 C.F.R. § 190.6 should be interpreted to allow a submitter to ask FDA to cease review of a submission.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: The hazards of early or overbroad disclosure of a regulatory submission are severe; these hazards are heightened when they may apply to a submission for an ingredient that could be subject to denial or delay. This disincentive toward the NDI pathway has been a barrier to the introduction of new dietary ingredients into the marketplace, and as such a barrier to private innovation with no associated public benefit.
    *   FDA should complete phased revisions to its NDI guidance
        *   Administering HHS division: FDA HFP
        *   Citation to C.F.R.: 21 C.F.R. § 190.6
        *   Matter of concern:
            *   The Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994 (DSHEA) codified 21 U.S.C. § 350(b), which sets forth the definition of and legal requirements for new dietary ingredients (NDIs). The corresponding regulation implementing this requirement is 21 C.F.R. § 190.6.
            *   In 2011, as a result of requirements established in FSMA, FDA published a draft guidance (the 2011 draft NDI guidance) discussing its interpretation of 21 U.S.C. § 350(b); this draft guidance was so inconsistent with the requirements of the law that, at the urging of Congress, FDA agreed to issue a revised draft rather than move to issue a revised and responsive final guidance.
            *   In 2016 FDA published a new draft guidance (the 2016 revised draft NDI guidance) which has also faced broad criticism for its inconsistency with statute. As introduced, the 2016 revised draft NDI guidance sought to regulate dietary ingredients on a model similar to drugs and food additives, in contravention of the intention of Congress in passing DSHEA, among other issues.
            *   FDA has recognized the incomplete and inapposite nature of the 2016 revised draft NDI guidance, and has taken the approach of revising this guidance in a phased manner, addressing individual elements through separate guidance releases on, e.g., notification procedures and timelines.
            *   This strategy, responsive to past recommendations from AHPA, provides a path to eventually resolve the myriad problems created by past FDA publications on this matter.
        *   Recommendation:
            *   FDA should continue the process of phased revisions to the 2016 revised draft NDI guidance with all available speed.
        *   Data on cost or economic impact: AHPA has no such data.
        *   Relevance to EO 14219: The 2016 revised draft NDI guidance operates in contravention of Congressional intent in the passage of DSHEA, and serves as a barrier to innovation in the dietary supplement space. It also creates burdens on regulated industry which are not matched by a similar level of public benefit.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The American Herbal Products Association (AHPA) urges FDA to streamline and clarify numerous regulations impacting the herbal products and dietary supplements industries, advocating for changes that reduce undue burdens, foster innovation, and align with Congressional intent, particularly concerning homeopathic products, labeling, cGMPs, and new dietary ingredient notifications.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** American Herbal Products Association (AHPA)
- **Type:** Trade Association
- **Role/Expertise:** National trade association and voice of the herbal products and dietary supplements industries, representing growers, importers, processors, manufacturers, and marketers, promoting responsible commerce of herbs, herbal products, dietary supplements, health and beauty products, and animal products.
- **Geographic Scope:** National
- **Stake in Issue:** Direct impact on their members' ability to manufacture, market, and distribute herbal products and dietary supplements under current and proposed FDA regulations. They advocate for regulatory changes to reduce costs, foster innovation, clarify requirements, and ensure fair enforcement for their industry.
structuredSections.corePosition: The American Herbal Products Association (AHPA) advocates for the rescission or modification of numerous FDA regulations and policies concerning conventional foods, dietary supplements, and herbal products. We assert that current regulations often impose significant costs and undue burdens on private parties, particularly small businesses, without commensurate public health benefits or clear statutory authority, thereby impeding technological innovation and economic development.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- FDA should revoke the 2022 Homeopathic Drug Guidance and return to its prior enforcement approach under Compliance Policy Guide 400.400.
- FDA should remove regulatory requirements for farmers and food companies to exchange and maintain “written assurances.”
- FDA should revise the Food Labeling Guide to allow the highlighting of ingredient and constituent names on food labels outside the Nutrition Facts or Supplement Facts label (except for nutrients with an established RDI or DRV), as long as the amount appears in the ingredient declaration or Supplement Facts.
- FDA should amend 21 C.F.R. § 101.15(c)(2) to allow foreign language representations in the name of the food without triggering full bilingual labeling, or issue clear enforcement discretion.
- FDA should revise 21 C.F.R. § 101.93(d) to require the structure/function claim disclaimer only once on a dietary supplement label or any labeling, provided a symbol links each claim to the disclaimer.
- Delete 21 C.F.R. § 101.93(g)(2)(iv)(C) and revise FDA’s Warning Letter policies to permit dietary supplement companies to cite scientific studies in labeling, including disease-related literature, so long as it's clear the product is a dietary supplement and not for disease diagnosis, treatment, cure, or prevention.
- FDA should revise the Inspections Operations Manual (IOM) to require Agency investigators to include references to the underlying cGMP regulations for each cGMP-related observation listed on Form 483s issued to conventional food and dietary supplement facilities.
- FDA should regulate food manufacturers solely based on their product labels, with firms labeling products as dietary supplements regulated under Part 111 and Part 117 Subpart B (if not overlapping), and other food products solely under Part 117.
  - If additional requirements are needed for ingredients packaged as supplements, these burdens must fall on the firm performing the packaging, not upstream vendors.
  - FDA may issue a technical correction to the preamble of Part 111, or a guidance document, to clarify this policy.
- Add specific definitions for “manufacturing,” “packaging,” “labeling,” and “holding” to 21 C.F.R. § 111.3.
  - Manufacturing: operations to make a dietary supplement for ingestion (tablet, capsule, powder, etc.).
  - Packaging: operations to place a dietary supplement into its sale container.
  - Labeling: operations to place labels on packaged dietary supplements, or to form and/or fill packages bearing such labels.
  - Holding: maintaining and storing components and bulk or retail packaged dietary supplements.
- Formalize and revise definitions for “identity,” “purity,” “strength,” and “composition” in 21 C.F.R. Part 111.
  - For "identity" of finished products, conformance should be confirmed by batch record review; if used for descriptive characteristics, adjust definitions accordingly.
  - "Strength" definition should explicitly include extract ratios, "amount per capsule/tablet," and "percent" expressions. It should only apply to dietary ingredients, not excipients.
  - "Composition" should be defined as the product formula, with ingredient levels as percents, confirmed by batch records.
  - "Purity" should be removed from the regulation; if maintained, its role must be clarified to avoid redundancy and confusion.
- Amend 21 C.F.R. § 111.205(a) to allow master manufacturing records (MMRs) to cover a range of lot or batch sizes, and to provide flexibility for MMRs to apply to either lots or batches as appropriate to facility operations.
- FDA should direct the Office of Food Chemical Safety, Dietary Supplements, and Innovation and the Office of Compliance and Enforcement to discontinue the practice of imposing manufacturing cGMP requirements under 21 CFR Part 111 on “own label” distributors until appropriate notice and comment rulemaking occurs.
- Amend 21 C.F.R. § 111.75(d)(1) to acknowledge that properly completed batch records are an accurate and practical method for confirming specifications when no current and generally available analytical method exists for chemically complex ingredients or finished product matrices.
- Amend 21 C.F.R. § 101.9(g)(4)(i) to include consideration of analytical variability for Class I nutrients (added nutrients).
- Amend 21 C.F.R. § 111.415(f) to require affixing/marking the batch, lot, or control number on the immediate container or product label of finished dietary supplements.
- FDA should develop and apply a formal policy of enforcement discretion regarding 21 CFR Part 111 (and 21 CFR Part 117 Subparts C and G) for very small firms (less than $250,000 in annual sales, 3-year rolling average, inflation-adjusted), provided they meet specific compliance conditions (local health regulations, COA review, non-Class 2a/3 botanicals).
- Revise 21 C.F.R. § 111.210(h)(3)(ii) to allow manufacturing operations with one person to use a "system" for verifying the weight or measure and addition of components, similar to infant formula cGMP.
- Significantly narrow the scope of 21 C.F.R. Part 112 (Produce Safety Rule) to focus on crops likely consumed fresh/unprocessed, and permit a wider range of activities to remain within the "farm" definition for non-fresh-produce crops.
- Revise 21 C.F.R. § 190.6(b) to establish clear requirements for NDI notifications to include accurate and complete identification of the NDI, including plant part for botanicals or their derivatives, and provide a comprehensive description of the NDI and the product(s) containing it.
- Interpret 21 C.F.R. § 190.6 to allow a submitter to ask FDA to cease review of an NDI submission, consistent with GRAS notification procedures.
- FDA should continue the process of phased revisions to the 2016 revised draft NDI guidance with all available speed.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- The 2022 Homeopathic Drug Guidance threatens enforcement against all homeopathic products, even long-marketed safe ones, imposing immense premarket approval burdens and leading to decreased competition and consumer choice.
- FSMA-implementing regulations requiring annual/biannual "written assurances" are impractical, highly burdensome (potentially over a million per firm annually), and lack commensurate public health benefit, especially for small businesses.
- FDA's interpretation of nutrient content claims unnecessarily restricts allowing ingredient/constituent names on food labels without collocated quantity declarations, even if the amount is declared elsewhere.
- The current foreign language labeling rule (21 C.F.R. § 101.15(c)(2)) is inconsistently and broadly applied, particularly to ethnic product names, requiring full bilingual labels without justification, hindering consumer understanding, and disproportionately burdening small businesses.
- 21 C.F.R. 101.93(d) requires structure/function claim disclaimers on "each panel or page," which is unnecessarily restrictive for limited label space and a source of civil litigation despite FDA's non-enforcement.
- FDA's policy allowing citations to published literature to be construed as disease claims (21 C.F.R. 101.93(g)(2)(iv)(C)) and prohibiting such literature on company websites is unsupported by DSHEA, restricts free communication of scientific information, and doesn't acknowledge the utility of disease-oriented studies for understanding permitted claims.
- FDA's internal policy of not citing specific regulations on Form 483 inspection observations creates ambiguity, inconsistency, and miscommunication, leading to regulatory uncertainty and misaligned compliance costs for regulated industry, especially small businesses.
- FDA improperly enforces 21 C.F.R. Part 111 cGMP requirements on dietary ingredient manufacturers based on downstream packaging actions by buyers, a policy that is unlawful, impractical (as ingredient manufacturers lack knowledge/control), and duplicative given Part 117 food safety requirements.
- The absence of formal definitions for "manufacturing," "packaging," "labeling," and "holding" in 21 C.F.R. Part 111 creates ambiguities in applying specific obligations, leading to unnecessary compliance and enforcement activity and impeding innovation.
- The lack of formal, clear, and consistently applicable definitions for "identity," "purity," "strength," and "composition" in 21 C.F.R. Part 111 causes compliance struggles, inconsistent enforcement, and significant costs related to developing and validating non-existent or unnecessary analytical methods, often pushing firms to "prove a negative."
- The requirement in 21 C.F.R. § 111.205(a) for a separate Master Manufacturing Record (MMR) for "each batch size" is cumbersome, impractical, and overly prescriptive, particularly for herbal products with variable yields, lot-based manufacturing, and packaging operations, creating immense recordkeeping burdens for businesses, especially small ones.
- FDA's informal practice of imposing manufacturing cGMP requirements under 21 C.F.R. Part 111 on "own label distributors" is improvised, extraregulatory, inconsistent, impractical (as distributors lack manufacturing knowledge), disruptive to contract manufacturers, and disproportionately burdens small business innovators entering the market.
- Current regulations for Class I nutrients (21 C.F.R. §§ 101.9 and 101.36) do not account for analytical variability, placing manufacturers at risk of misbranding due to testing inaccuracies and forcing them to use larger, potentially problematic, nutrient overages.
- FDA's broad definition of "produce" and narrow definition of "farm" under FSMA (21 C.F.R. Part 112/117) subjects many non-fresh, processed botanical crops and normal farm activities (e.g., cutting for drying) to disproportionate and unnecessary regulatory burdens intended for fresh produce, exceeding Congressional intent and increasing costs for farmers and consumers.
- The incompleteness of 21 C.F.R. § 190.6 regarding NDI notification requirements (e.g., lacking explicit demands for NDI description or plant part identification) creates uncertainty, leading to FDA concerns despite full compliance with current rules and acting as a barrier to innovation.
- The absence of a procedure to halt the review of NDI submissions (unlike GRAS notifications) creates data privacy concerns and a perceived hazard for submitters, disincentivizing the NDI pathway and hindering private innovation.
- The 2016 revised draft NDI guidance remains largely inconsistent with the intent of DSHEA, continues to operate as a barrier to innovation, and imposes burdens on regulated industry without adequate public benefit.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The withdrawal of the prior Homeopathic CPG 400.400 has already caused businesses to exit the market, leading to decreased competition and consumer choice in a product category consumers have relied upon for decades.
- An analysis by the Grocery Manufacturers Association indicated that the "written assurances" requirements could demand a single large firm obtain over 1.5 million documents annually, illustrating an extreme and potentially impossible compliance burden.
- FDA's inconsistent application of bilingual labeling requirements for ethnic product names on dietary supplements, contrasting with conventional foods like Italian pasta, highlights an arbitrary burden particularly on small ethnic businesses.
- Despite FDA's practical non-enforcement of the "multiple DSHEA disclaimers" rule, the existing regulation periodically triggers civil litigation against industry, imposing significant legal and relabeling costs.
- Federal inspectors have verbally communicated regulatory claims and required actions that were not documented on Form 483s and sometimes not aligned with federal regulation, leading to confusion and misaligned compliance efforts by businesses.
- The current interpretation of cGMP Part 111 that seeks to apply manufacturer responsibilities to "own label distributors" has created highly disruptive demands for contract manufacturers (who may serve hundreds or thousands of brands), forcing them to compile and support proprietary documentation for a client intermediary without direct notice or confidentiality protections. This also burdens small businesses that often start as own-label distributors.
- FDA inspectors consistently push for new, costly chemical test standards for chemically complex multi-ingredient products (e.g., botanical blends) where scientifically valid methods are rare or impossible to develop, despite a statutory prohibition against imposing standards without generally available analytical methodology. This practice can incentivize product adulteration.
- Many very small dietary supplement firms, particularly in rural areas, have been driven out of business or forced to outsource manufacturing due to compliance costs for Part 111 ($46,000+ annually), despite these regulations largely focusing on quality rather than immediate safety.
- The 21 CFR § 111.210(h)(3)(ii) requirement for two persons to verify manual weighing/addition tasks effectively prohibits single-employee dietary supplement manufacturing operations, directly impacting micro-businesses.
- FDA's broad definitions for "produce" and "manufacturing/processing" under FSMA inadvertently classify many routine farm activities for non-fresh-produce botanicals (like cutting roots for drying) as "processing," subjecting farms to burdensome food manufacturing GMPs and facility registration, beyond Congressional intent for food safety.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "The Homeopathic Drug Guidance states that “all homeopathic drug products remain subject to the premarket approval requirements” applicable to new drugs under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (FDCA) and that “there are currently no homeopathic drug products that are approved by FDA.” It further states that “any homeopathic drug product that is being marketed illegally is subject to FDA enforcement at any time.”"
- "An analysis by the Grocery Manufacturers Association (GMA) determined that the written assurances requirements found under 21 C.F.R. § 117.136 could require an individual firm with a sufficiently complex role in the supply chain to obtain in excess of a million written assurances every year."
- "AHPA is aware of circumstances in which federal inspectors have made regulatory claims verbally, including significant assertions of evidence, conduct, and necessary actions to enter compliance, that were not reflected in Form 483 and were not in alignment with federal regulation."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Head Start California is the nonprofit association supporting and representing California’s 138 Head Start providers.
*   We offer the following in response to the May 14, 2025, Request for Information regarding Head Start regulations.
*   We appreciate the important role that partnership with the Office of Head Start plays in ensuring safety, accountability, and effective implementation of Head Start services.
*   We make our recommendations in the spirit of continuous partnership and improvement, while supporting local control and reducing administrative burdens.
*   Designation Renewal System
    *   Comprehensive monitoring and oversight play a vital role in ensuring program quality.
    *   The Designation Renewal System (DRS) established pursuant to section 1304.10 – 1304.17 of the Head Start Program Performance Standards (HSPPS) plays an important role in maintaining program quality.
    *   However, certain DRS criteria are overly burdensome and inappropriately trigger an onerous review process that utilizes resources that would be better spent serving children and families:
        *   Section 1304.11(a) requires a program be subject to DRS in the event it has two or more deficiencies during its five-year grant period.
            *   This requirement does not take into account the nature, extent or severity of the deficiencies, whether and how they have been resolved, or the timing thereof.
            *   Relatively less significant issues and issues that are resolved quickly are not distinguished from broader, more severe or more systemic problems.
            *   The threshold of two deficiencies applies equally and without distinction to the smallest program in California, with one classroom serving 16 children, and to the largest program in our state serving more than 7,500 children across dozens of classrooms and multiple sites.
            *   This one-size-fits-all, cookie-cutter approach does not truly reflect the realities of program quality or child safety.
            *   The uniform threshold of deficiencies fails to acknowledge the nature of grantees with centers run by delegate agencies.
                *   A single Head Start grant may fund Head Start operations by multiple, separate delegate agencies.
                *   Under the current DRS regulations, one deficiency at each of two delegates over the course of five years forces the grantee and the remaining delegates that have zero deficiencies to go through the onerous DRS process.
                *   The result is disruption, distraction, expense, and potential denial of funds to delegates that have no deficiencies and have been providing efficient, effective, high-quality services.
            *   We recommend that the threshold of two deficiencies be increased, and be scaled to reflect the size of the program, taking into account the number of children served and the number of delegates working within a single grant.
            *   In cases where a delegate agency is found to have sufficient deficiencies to trigger a DRS review, that review should be limited to the delegate agency and not encompass all delegates funded by the grant.
        *   Section 1304.11(c) requires a program be subject to DRS based on results from the CLASS:Pre-K observation tool.
            *   We recommend that this requirement be removed.
            *   While the CLASS tool provides vital feedback that is useful in implementing continuous quality improvement, it was designed and intended to be used as a mechanism to determine professional development needs.
            *   It was not designed to be, and should not be used as, an enforcement mechanism or evaluation of a providers’ overall suitability for a Head Start grant.
            *   There are several practical issues with implementing the CLASS tool for DRS purposes:
                *   Head Start programs proudly serve students with disabilities.
                *   Many school districts supplement Head Start services with school district personnel, such as special education aides who are highly trained and instrumental to a students’ success.
                *   However, because the SPED aides are not directly employed by the Head Start program and are subject to other contracting rules, they cannot be trained on CLASS standards.
                *   Yet SPED aides and similar personnel are rated by CLASS observers.
                *   These ratings are integrated into the programs’ scores and can trigger a DRS process.
                *   CLASS observations are not limited to times that are representative of a child’s typical classroom experience and education.
                *   CLASS observations that are conducted evaluating new staff, substitutes, and volunteers who have not yet received CLASS trainings are scored and treated exactly the same way as CLASS observations of trained, permanent staff.
                *   These unrepresentative observations can also launch an unnecessary and costly DRS review.
*   Family Childcare Home Providers
    *   Changes to the HSPPS made in 2024 removed from sections 1302.23(b)(2) and (4) the ability of family childcare homes to operate with a provider and an assistant provider.
    *   Like assistant teachers, assistant providers are integral to the operations of family childcare homes.
    *   We recommend these regulations be reverted to their prior form, allowing for assistant providers.
*   Family Partnership Worker Ratios
    *   Section 1302.52(d) places a new limit on family partnership worker caseloads of 40 families per worker, unless a waiver is granted.
    *   We recommend removal of this regulation.
    *   Based on local needs, the role of an individual family service worker varies across programs, and even from site to site within programs.
    *   It is not uncommon for family partnership workers to be assigned caseloads higher than 40 in instances where families have relatively few needs; or lower caseloads when families have more intensive needs.
    *   This allows these workers to specialize in certain family circumstances and deliver services efficiently and effectively.
    *   Further, programs often blend the family partnership worker role with other roles, making a determination of the allowable relative caseload administratively burdensome, if not impossible.
*   Lead Testing
    *   Section 1302.47(b)(10) establishes new, duplicative requirements for lead testing in Head Start facilities.
    *   Facilities are already subject to state laws regarding lead testing and prevention of lead exposure; there is no evidence that additional requirements are necessary or beneficial.
    *   We recommend either removal of this regulation, or explicit deference to state law and policy.
*   Compensation and Benefits
    *   We fully and firmly believe all Head Start staff deserve fair compensation and benefits for the work they perform.
    *   The majority of our programs have made progress toward this goal in recent years.
    *   Programs need local control and flexibility to continue making progress in the manner best suited to their unique needs.
    *   Thus, we do not believe that the rules established in 1302.90(e) and (f) are necessary or helpful in working towards this goal and recommend their removal.
*   Reporting
    *   Section 1302.102(d)(1)(ii)(a) requires Head Start programs to report incidents involving children that are not served by Head Start.
    *   This requirement represents administrative overreach on the part of the Office of Head Start, which does not have authority or jurisdiction over those children.
    *   The additional reporting will create significant administrative burdens for Head Start programs and the Office of Head Start, while providing no benefit.
    *   We recommend this provision be removed.
*   Thank you for your thoughtful consideration of our comments.
*   We appreciate your engagement with the field to ensure Head Start programs are strong and have the support they need to help children and families reach their full potential.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: Head Start California, representing 138 providers, urges the Office of Head Start to revise or remove overly burdensome regulations to reduce administrative burden, ensure local control, and allow resources to be better spent serving children and families.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Head Start California
- **Type:** Advocacy Group
- **Role/Expertise:** Nonprofit association supporting and representing California’s 138 Head Start providers.
- **Geographic Scope:** State (California)
- **Stake in Issue:** Direct representative of Head Start providers in California, seeking to reduce regulatory burdens and improve operational efficiency for its members.
structuredSections.corePosition: Head Start California believes that while monitoring is vital, certain current Head Start Program Performance Standards (HSPPS) regulations are overly burdensome, duplicate existing state laws, or are misapplied, diverting resources from direct services to children and families. We advocate for revisions or removal of these regulations to support local control and ensure effective, efficient program operation.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Increase the threshold of two deficiencies for Designation Renewal System (DRS) triggers, and scale it to reflect program size (number of children served and number of delegates).
- Limit DRS reviews triggered by delegate agency deficiencies to only that delegate agency, not the entire grant and all other delegates.
- Remove the requirement that programs be subject to DRS based on CLASS:Pre-K observation tool results (Section 1304.11(c)).
- Revert regulations 1302.23(b)(2) and (4) to their prior form, allowing family childcare homes to operate with a provider and an assistant provider.
- Remove the new limit on family partnership worker caseloads of 40 families per worker (Section 1302.52(d)).
- Remove duplicative lead testing requirements (Section 1302.47(b)(10)) or include explicit deference to state law and policy.
- Remove regulations 1302.90(e) and (f) regarding compensation and benefits, as programs need local control and flexibility.
- Remove the requirement in Section 1302.102(d)(1)(ii)(a) for Head Start programs to report incidents involving children not served by Head Start.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Overly burdensome DRS criteria:**
    - The two-deficiency threshold for DRS review (Section 1304.11(a)) does not account for the nature, extent, severity, or resolution status of deficiencies.
    - This threshold is a "one-size-fits-all" approach, applying equally to the smallest and largest programs without distinction for size or complexity, leading to disproportionate burdens.
    - A single deficiency at two separate delegate agencies can trigger an onerous DRS process for the entire grantee and all other delegates, even those with zero deficiencies, causing disruption, distraction, expense, and potential loss of funds.
- **Misuse of CLASS:Pre-K observation tool for enforcement (Section 1304.11(c)):**
    - The CLASS tool was designed for professional development, not as an enforcement or suitability evaluation mechanism.
    - CLASS observations rate personnel not directly employed by Head Start, such as SPED aides, who may not be trained on CLASS standards, leading to inaccurate program scores.
    - Observations conducted on new staff, substitutes, or volunteers who have not received CLASS training are scored identically to those of trained permanent staff, leading to unrepresentative scores that can trigger costly DRS reviews.
- **Restrictions on Family Childcare Home providers:**
    - The inability for family childcare homes to operate with a provider and an assistant provider, removed in 2024, hinders operations as assistant providers are integral.
- **Inflexible Family Partnership Worker Ratios:**
    - A rigid caseload limit of 40 families per worker does not account for varying local needs or the intensity of family circumstances, preventing efficient and effective specialization.
    - Blending family partnership worker roles with other functions makes determining allowable caseloads administratively burdensome or impossible.
- **Duplicative Lead Testing Requirements:**
    - New federal lead testing requirements (Section 1302.47(b)(10)) are redundant as facilities are already subject to state laws, with no evidence of additional benefit.
- **Unnecessary Compensation and Benefits Regulations:**
    - Federal rules on compensation and benefits limit local control and flexibility, hindering programs' ability to make progress on fair compensation in a manner suited to their unique needs.
- **Administrative Overreach in Reporting Requirements:**
    - Requiring Head Start programs to report incidents involving children not served by Head Start (Section 1302.102(d)(1)(ii)(a)) represents administrative overreach, as the Office of Head Start lacks authority over those children, creating significant, benefit-less administrative burdens.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The concern regarding the "one-size-fits-all, cookie-cutter approach" to DRS deficiencies highlights how regulations disproportionately impact programs of varying sizes, comparing a program serving 16 children to one serving over 7,500 children.
- The insight that CLASS observations are flawed for enforcement purposes because they rate individuals like SPED aides who cannot be trained on CLASS standards, or new/substitute staff who haven't received training, reveals a practical disconnect between the tool's intended use and its regulatory application.
- The detailed explanation of how a single deficiency at two different delegate agencies can trigger a burdensome DRS review for an entire grant, including delegates with zero deficiencies, illustrates a significant systemic flaw that punishes high-performing entities.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "This one-size-fits-all, cookie-cutter approach does not truly reflect the realities of program quality or child safety."
- "While the CLASS tool provides vital feedback that is useful in implementing continuous quality improvement, it was designed and intended to be used as a mechanism to determine professional development needs. It was not designed to be, and should not be used as, an enforcement mechanism or evaluation of a providers’ overall suitability for a Head Start grant."
- "The additional reporting [of incidents involving children not served by Head Start] will create significant administrative burdens for Head Start programs and the Office of Head Start, while providing no benefit."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   BlueRock Therapeutics appreciates the opportunity to respond to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Request for Information (RFI) aimed at identifying opportunities to streamline the regulatory process.
*   We strongly support efforts to ensure that safe, effective, and transformative therapies reach patients as efficiently as possible.
*   As a biotechnology company advancing innovations in cell therapy, BlueRock is committed to a regulatory framework that is:
    *   Grounded in science
    *   Responsive to patient safety
    *   Adaptable to cutting-edge technologies
*   In alignment with Executive Order 14192’s goals to reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens and promote medical innovation, we offer the following recommendations for reform:

*   I. Chemistry, Manufacturing and Controls (CMC)
    *   A. Outdated Container Closure Guidance:
        *   The current FDA guidance on closure systems does not reflect the unique needs of cell and gene therapy products (ATMP).
        *   ATMPs' unique characteristics, such as sensitivity to temperature and short shelf lives, pose new challenges for container closure integrity.
        *   Many ATMPs require cryogenic storage and specialized delivery systems, which are not adequately addressed in the 1999 guidance.
        *   Recommendation: Update the 1999 guidance to include modern ATMP-specific considerations, such as cell viability, cryopreservation, and combination systems.
    *   B. Raw Material GMP Requirements for Early-Phase ATMPs:
        *   Early-stage development is hampered by stringent Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) requirements for materials not commercially available in GMP grade.
        *   Current expectations can delay development timelines and increase costs without a corresponding improvement in safety or quality.
        *   Many raw materials (RM) used in cell and gene therapies are novel or derived from academic or research sources, where GMP-grade supply is not feasible.
        *   A science- and risk-based framework would allow developers to justify the use of non-GMP materials with appropriate controls, critical to accelerating innovation while ensuring patient protection in early-phase clinical trials.
        *   These stringent requirements often result in promising candidates in development having to be cancelled due to high costs of GMP grade RMs.
        *   Recommendation: Provide additional clarity on requirements for RMs for ATMPs.
            *   Ease GMP RM requirements for certain materials to support early phase trials with proper safety controls in place.
    *   C. Genomic Stability Testing Requirements:
        *   Outdated testing requirements often rely on techniques that are time-consuming, less sensitive, or poorly suited to the complexity of modern cell therapies.
        *   Advances in next-generation sequencing and other molecular tools offer more precise and efficient ways to assess genomic integrity.
        *   The lack of clear FDA guidance on the use of these technologies creates uncertainty for developers and regulators alike.
        *   Aligning regulatory expectations with current scientific capabilities would support both innovation and safety in the development of cell-based therapies.
        *   Recommendation: Issue guidance to reflect contemporary best practices for genomic stability assessments of cell-based products.
    *   D. Misalignment between U.S. and E.U. GMP Standards:
        *   Discrepancies in air handling and other GMP requirements increase the burden for companies operating in both jurisdictions.
        *   Inconsistent standards lead to duplicative facility design, validation, and operational processes, increasing costs and complexity without improving product quality.
        *   For example, differences in requirements for Grade A/B cleanroom classifications or environmental monitoring expectations can delay global development timelines.
        *   These misalignments are particularly challenging for small or early-stage developers lacking resources to build parallel infrastructure.
        *   Greater alignment would streamline manufacturing practices, enhance regulatory predictability, and facilitate faster patient access to innovative therapies.
        *   Recommendation: Work toward harmonization with EU GMP guidance, particularly for early-phase manufacturing and sterile product handling.
    *   E. Phase-Appropriate Analytical Testing:
        *   Sponsors face ambiguity about analytical expectations at each development phase, leading to unnecessary testing burdens.
        *   Cell and gene therapy products evolve significantly during development, and imposing late-phase analytical standards too early can divert resources from critical product optimization and clinical execution.
        *   Without clear regulatory expectations, sponsors often over-test to avoid delays, increasing time and cost without improving patient safety or product understanding.
        *   A risk-based, phased approach to analytical requirements, aligned with the product’s stage of development, would promote more efficient use of resources while still ensuring safety and quality.
        *   Clear FDA guidance would also support consistency in regulatory reviews and reduce uncertainty for emerging sponsors.
        *   Recommendation: Issue clear guidance on phase-appropriate analytical development for Cell and Gene Therapies (CGTs).
    *   F. Minimal Manipulation Requirements at Clinical Sites:
        *   Current FDA guidance suggests that even minimal manipulation of a drug product (DP) at clinical sites, such as thawing, dilution, or mixing with excipients, may require adherence to full cGMP manufacturing standards and additional Quality Control (QC) release testing.
        *   Recommendation: Clarify and provide flexibility for certain forms of minimal manipulation conducted at the point of care, allowing these activities to be performed under appropriate, but not full cGMP, conditions.

*   II. Non-Clinical
    *   A. Animal Model Limitations for CGTs:
        *   Animal models often fail to accurately replicate human disease mechanisms, especially for complex or rare genetic conditions targeted by CGTs.
        *   Despite this, outdated requirements still compel sponsors to conduct animal studies that may be non-informative, delaying development and increasing costs.
        *   Recommendation: Expand FDA acceptance of validated in vitro models, such as human organoids, microphysiological systems, and other New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), to replace or reduce reliance on non-predictive animal models where appropriate.
        *   We strongly support the FDA’s April 2025 announcement to begin phasing out mandatory animal testing for monoclonal antibodies and other therapeutics.
        *   Recognizing that traditional animal studies may still be required for specific endpoints (e.g., systemic toxicity), we urge the FDA to provide clear criteria and guidance for when NAMs are sufficient, particularly in cases where animal models have limited translational value.

*   III. Clinical Development
    *   A. Placebo-Controlled Trials for CGTs:
        *   Blinding is often compromised in CGT trials because patients who receive active therapy typically experience noticeable effects within days to months, making it clear who received treatment.
        *   In some CGT trials, the scientific value of placebo arms may be diminished due to unblinding and practical limitations, making alternative designs more appropriate.
        *   This is particularly relevant when immunosuppression (IS) is required solely to mimic the treatment protocol, as administering placebo therapy with placebo IS provides no potential benefit and raises significant ethical and safety concerns.
        *   Instead, sponsors should be encouraged to demonstrate effectiveness using well-designed natural history studies or appropriate external controls.
        *   Recommendation: Ease clinical requirements for placebo-controlled CGT trials by allowing alternative designs where appropriate, especially when the risks of placebo arms outweigh their scientific value.
    *   B. Additional FDA Interaction Post Pre-IND:
        *   With complex therapies like CGTs, results from Investigational New Drug (IND)-enabling non-clinical studies often have important implications for the final clinical trial design.
        *   Sponsors would benefit from a formal opportunity to re-engage with the FDA after completing these studies, but before IND submission, to refine their clinical, CMC, and overall development strategy.
        *   Early Pre-IND meetings typically focus on broad development strategy and may occur before key study results are available.
        *   Recommendation: Create a formal opportunity for an additional FDA-sponsor interaction between Pre-IND and IND submission.
    *   C. Retinal Gene Therapy Dosing:
        *   The requirement to evaluate two dose levels in pivotal studies for gene therapies targeting retinal disorders can be scientifically and ethically problematic.
        *   In many cases, only one dose demonstrates a favorable balance of safety and efficacy in early studies, making it difficult, and potentially unethical, to administer a second dose that lacks evidence of therapeutic benefit.
        *   This is particularly concerning given the irreversible nature of many retinal gene therapies and the potential risks of re-administration.
        *   Moreover, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) has raised similar concerns, acknowledging the limited feasibility of multiple-dose studies in this context.
        *   Recommendation: Remove the requirement for two dose levels in pivotal trials for retinal gene therapies and instead allow a single well-justified dose based on preclinical and early-phase clinical data.
    *   D. Outdated Guidance on Geriatric Populations:
        *   The current FDA guidance on geriatric use, last updated in 1994, defines geriatric patients as individuals aged 65 and older and emphasizes data collection during clinical trials.
        *   It does not reflect modern advances in data science or the increasing availability and utility of post-marketing data to assess safety and efficacy in older adults.
        *   The aging U.S. population, particularly in therapeutic areas like oncology and chronic disease, makes it essential to revisit how geriatric data is collected and analyzed.
        *   Rigid reliance on clinical trial enrollment alone may limit the evidence base, especially when older adults are often underrepresented in trials.
        *   Recommendation: Issue updated guidance that revises the definition and expectations for geriatric populations and formally recognizes the value of post-marketing data, such as real-world evidence, in supporting geriatric use.
    *   E. Pharmacogenomics Guidance:
        *   The current FDA guidance on pharmacogenomic data submissions focuses primarily on drug metabolism and identifying responders for traditional small-molecule efficacy trials.
        *   While biomarkers are mentioned, the guidance does not adequately reflect advancements in precision medicine, particularly in the context of cell and gene therapies where pharmacogenomic data may inform vector selection, patient stratification, or safety risks.
        *   Innovative therapies increasingly rely on genomic insights that go beyond pharmacokinetics, including gene identification, target validation, and use of genomic data to support surrogate endpoints.
        *   Recommendation: Update the Pharmacogenomic Data Submissions guidance to address the application of pharmacogenomics to cell and gene therapies, including the full continuum from gene identification to biomarker development and surrogate endpoint justification.
            *   This would provide much-needed clarity for developers of personalized and genetically targeted therapies navigating the regulatory process.

*   IV. General Regulatory
    *   A. Regulatory Pathways for Ultra-Rare Diseases:
        *   Current regulatory requirements for cell and gene therapies targeting ultra-rare diseases (sometimes affecting only a handful of patients) still often mandate full Phase 1–3 clinical development programs.
        *   This model is economically and logistically infeasible in such settings and risks stalling potentially life-saving therapies due to rigid expectations that do not reflect scientific or practical realities.
        *   Existing tools such as adaptive trial designs, real-world evidence (RWE), and ‘n-of-1’ trial methodologies are well-suited to address the data challenges unique to ultra-rare conditions, but their use remains limited and inconsistent across review divisions.
        *   Recommendation: Expand FDA’s formal inclusion and acceptance of adaptive trial designs, RWE, and n-of-1 frameworks in the regulatory evaluation of CGT therapies for ultra-rare diseases.
    *   B. Long-Term Follow Up (LTFU) for CGTs:
        *   The current 2020 FDA guidance on long-term follow-up (LTFU) for gene therapy products provides a useful framework but lacks flexibility to tailor surveillance requirements based on product type, vector characteristics, and risk profile.
        *   Applying a one-size-fits-all approach to all CGTs can impose significant burdens on patients (who may face decade-long follow-up commitments) and on sponsors, particularly when the long-term risk is low or well-characterized.
        *   Advances in vector design, manufacturing controls, and post-marketing data have improved understanding of long-term safety risks.
        *   Recommendation: Update the Long Term Follow-Up After Administration of Human Gene Therapy Products guidance to provide a risk-based, product-specific approach to LTFU.
            *   Tailoring surveillance requirements accordingly can ease patient and sponsor burden while maintaining appropriate safety oversight.

*   BlueRock Therapeutics appreciates the HHS and FDA’s commitment to modernizing the regulatory environment to better reflect the evolving landscape of biomedical innovation.
*   Cell and gene therapies offer unprecedented potential to treat, and even cure, some of the world’s most challenging diseases.
*   We urge the agencies to prioritize science-driven, risk-based reforms that reduce unnecessary burdens, foster global regulatory alignment, and enable the efficient development of advanced therapies.
*   We welcome continued dialogue and stand ready to collaborate in shaping a regulatory system that supports both innovation and patient safety.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: BlueRock Therapeutics, a cell therapy biotechnology company, urges the FDA and HHS to modernize outdated regulations and issue new guidance across CMC, non-clinical, and clinical development to accelerate the efficient, safe, and global advancement of innovative cell and gene therapies for patients.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I am commenting on the U.S Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
*   The years of pregnancy to age three set the foundation for a baby’s development, learning and relationships.
    *   Babies rely entirely on the adults around them—parents, caregivers, and early childhood professionals—to provide safe, nurturing care.
    *   When babies or their caregivers face reduced support or program quality, babies can end up facing long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences.
    *   When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health.
*   Regulations matter.
    *   HHS, as the leading Federal agency tasked with enhancing the health and well-being of all Americans, plays a critical role in ensuring that babies, families, and the professionals who care for little ones have access to the resources, protections, and supports they need.
    *   In considering changes to regulations, HHS must preserve regulations that:
        *   Keep young children safe and healthy.
        *   Enable the adults in their lives to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
*   For example, regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings are needed to keep babies safe and developmentally on track.
*   Regulations that keep children and those who care for them healthy, like those that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care, must be maintained.
    *   This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe.
*   HHS rules reach far beyond just Medicaid and early learning, with many HHS programs laying the foundation of quality care and critical support that babies need.
*   Any changes to regulations must be:
    *   Transparent.
    *   Grounded in evidence.
    *   Focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
*   Because each regulation is different, HHS must continue to give the public—including families and early childhood professionals like me—ample time and opportunity to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes.
    *   We need a robust public process to make sure that the rules work for babies and those who care for them.
*   To keep America’s babies healthy, HHS must maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services.
*   Please uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
*   I would also like to add that I am a product of Head Start Services.
    *   I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career.
    *   I have a Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma.
    *   I have been a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for the past twenty-three years servicing the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles.
    *   It gives great pleasure to give back to my community.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An experienced early childhood education professional and Head Start alumna urges HHS to maintain and strengthen regulations that ensure the safety, health, and development of young children, advocating for transparent, evidence-based changes and robust public input.

-   **Role/Expertise:** Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma; 23 years as a vendor for the state of California Early Start system; former Head Start recipient.
-   **Geographic Scope:** Local (South Central Los Angeles, San Pedro, CA) / State (California)
-   **Stake in Issue:** As an early childhood professional directly involved in providing services to vulnerable children and a beneficiary of early childhood programs, she has a direct interest in regulations that ensure quality care and support for young children and their caregivers.

These foundational years dictate lifelong well-being, and effective regulations, grounded in evidence and developed transparently with public input, are crucial for ensuring access to quality care and services.

-   Preserve regulations that enable adults to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
    -   Specifically, maintain regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings.
    -   Maintain regulations that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care.
-   Ensure any changes to regulations are transparent, grounded in evidence, and focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
-   Provide ample time and opportunity for the public, including families and early childhood professionals, to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes through a robust public process.
-   Maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services for babies.
-   Uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.

-   Reduced support or program quality for babies and caregivers could lead to long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences for children.
-   Regulatory changes that are not transparent, evidence-based, or child-focused could negatively impact the well-being and safety of children, families, and their service providers.
-   Inadequate public involvement in the regulatory process may result in rules that do not effectively serve the needs of babies and their caregivers.
