structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   In response to the Request for Information (RFI) on ensuring lawful regulation and unleashing innovation to make American healthy again, we urge the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) to rescind certain regulations.
    *   These regulations have significant economic impact and are outdated and unnecessary for food safety.
    *   Their requirements are already addressed by the Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA) and its implementing regulations in 21 CFR Part 117.
*   We specifically urge FDA to rescind:
    *   The regulations governing Current Good Manufacturing Practices (GMPs) codified at 21 CFR Part 110.
    *   The regulations issued under FDA’s emergency permit control governing Thermally Processed Low-Acid Canned Foods Packaged in Hermetically Sealed Containers codified at 21 CFR Part 113 and Acidified Foods codified at 21 CFR Part 114.
    *   The regulations mandating Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) programs for juice products codified at 21 CFR Part 120 and seafood products codified at 21 CFR Part 123.
    *   The bottled water GMP regulations codified at 21 CFR Part 129.
*   Congress granted FDA the authority to impose comprehensive, risk-based preventive controls for human foods through FSMA, signed into law on January 4, 2011.
    *   Following FDA’s implementation of FSMA, all of the above provisions have become obsolete, duplicative, and unnecessarily burdensome on regulated industry.
    *   We respectfully request that HHS streamline its regulatory framework by rescinding these outdated requirements.
*   FDA Should Rescind its General GMP Regulations for Human Food in 21 CFR Part 110.
    *   Part 110 is duplicative of the agency’s later-promulgated preventive control requirements for human food in 21 CFR Part 117.
    *   The GMP requirements in 21 CFR Part 110 were originally promulgated in 1986, articulating standards for food manufacturers to prevent adulteration.
    *   After FSMA was enacted, FDA issued implementing regulations establishing new preventive control requirements in 21 CFR Part 117.
    *   Compliance with Part 117 is now the controlling standard for safe food production, yet Part 110 remains binding.
    *   This arrangement is burdensome and unnecessary because Part 117 modernized the GMP requirements of Part 110 and introduced new requirements for hazard analysis and risk-based preventive controls.
    *   FDA instructed the Office of the Federal Register to remove Part 110 effective September 17, 2018, but later rescinded this instruction, extending the effective date until January 27, 2020; despite the lapse of time, the regulation has not been rescinded.
    *   The agency should repeal Part 110.
*   FDA Should Rescind the Low Acid Canned Food (LACF) and Acidified Foods Regulations.
    *   FDA should rescind its LACF and acidified foods regulations in 21 CFR Parts 113 and 114, respectively, as they are unnecessarily burdensome and duplicative of the preventive control regulations in 21 CFR Part 117.
    *   FDA issued its emergency permit control regulations at 21 CFR Part 108 in 1977, relying on Section 404 of the FFDCA, which allows temporary permits to protect public health.
    *   Despite this limitation, FDA built on these emergency regulations in 1979 for thermally processed and acidified foods in 21 CFR Parts 113 and 114 to address botulinum toxin.
    *   FDA exempted entities complying with Parts 113 and 114 from obtaining emergency permits, effectively transforming a temporary emergency program into a permanent, mandatory program for LACF and acidified foods that has been in effect for over 45 years.
    *   The LACF and acidified food programs impose significant burdens on both the agency and industry.
        *   Companies must file a scheduled process before processing low-acid canned foods and acidified foods.
        *   The agency spends significant time and resources reviewing these scheduled processes.
        *   LACF regulations impose prescriptive requirements on thermal processing equipment design and construction, which may be obsolete due to technology advancements, but companies must still comply or risk rejection of their scheduled process.
        *   Changes in the scheduled process, such as using a different-sized can, require a new filing with FDA before processing.
    *   Manufacturers of acidified foods must also comply with the full requirements of the risk-based preventive controls of 21 CFR Part 117.
        *   This often forces manufacturers to navigate two sets of requirements that are frequently in tension.
        *   The complexity is evidenced by a 33-page draft guidance document attempting to clarify compliance with both regulatory regimes.
    *   This arrangement is unnecessary because FDA can rely on FSMA authorities to require preventive controls sufficient to ensure the safety of foods relying on pH or thermal processing for safety.
    *   HHS should repeal the LACF and acidified foods regulations to free manufacturers from onerous requirements while ensuring food safety under FSMA.
    *   While FSMA exempted facilities complying with LACF, seafood HACCP, and juice HACCP regulations from the hazard analysis and risk-based preventive control requirements (FFDCA § 418(j)), no such statutory authority exists for maintaining the acidified foods requirements, which supports their revocation.
    *   Even for LACF, the clear congressional intent required by recent Supreme Court precedent for regulations imposing significant burdens is absent.
*   FDA Should Rescind the Juice and Seafood HACCP Regulations.
    *   FDA issued its seafood HACCP regulations (21 CFR Part 123) in 1995 and its juice HACCP regulations (21 CFR Part 120) in 2001.
    *   These were based on general authority to prevent adulterated food (Section 402 FFDCA) and promulgate regulations (Section 701(a) FFDCA).
    *   These statutory provisions allow FDA to regulate food products but do not contemplate the detailed and prescriptive requirements found in the juice and seafood HACCP regulations.
    *   These regulations require covered entities to conduct hazard analysis, identify critical control points, establish critical control points, and establish requirements for verification and validation.
    *   Per *West Virginia v. EPA*, agencies must demonstrate "clear congressional authorization" for exercising powers in cases of "economic and political significance," which is lacking for these HACCP programs given the significant burdens they impose.
    *   Congress granted FDA comprehensive risk-based preventive controls authority through FSMA (21 U.S.C. § 350g).
    *   While FSMA exempted facilities complying with seafood and juice HACCP regulations, the FSMA framework provides sufficient statutory authority to ensure the safety of juice and seafood products without the additional requirements of these separate regulations.
    *   Eliminating these HACCP regulations would subject the industry to one set of food safety standards—those established by FSMA—rather than different programs for seafood, juice, and other FDA-regulated products.
    *   The exemption in FFDCA § 418(j) provides some congressional support but does not contain the level of statutory specificity articulated in *West Virginia v EPA*.
*   FDA Should Rescind the Bottled Water GMP Regulations.
    *   The bottled water GMP regulations (21 CFR Part 129), including prescriptive requirements for source water monitoring, testing, and use, have become unnecessary in light of FSMA.
    *   FDA cited general food adulteration provisions (Sections 402(a)(3) and (a)(4) FFDCA) and its general authority to enforce FFDCA (Section 701(a)) for these regulations.
    *   However, the prescriptive requirements, especially regarding source water, are not grounded in these FFDCA provisions.
    *   FFDCA Section 410 merely requires the standard of quality for bottled water to be as protective as EPA's, and FDA has consistently modified the standard to comply.
    *   The comprehensive risk-based preventive controls regulations in Part 117 now supersede the earlier bottled water GMP regulations and provide ample pathways for FDA to ensure bottled water safety.
    *   FSMA requires food facilities, including bottled water manufacturers, to implement comprehensive, risk-based preventive controls (Section 418(n) FFDCA).
    *   These preventive controls are more robust and better suited to ensuring bottled water safety than the outdated, one-size-fits-all mandates of Part 129.
    *   Modern requirements address hazards flexibly and science-based, tailored to specific risks, which is more effective for public health and encourages innovation.
    *   HHS should eliminate the bottled water GMPs and clarify that Part 117's risk-based preventive control measures apply to bottled water products.
*   Conclusion:
    *   For the reasons noted, we respectfully request that FDA rescind 21 CFR Parts 110, 113, 114, 120, 123, and 129 in their entirety.
    *   FDA should rely on the FSMA preventive controls regulations as the appropriate and lawful framework for ensuring food product safety.
    *   Rescinding these regulations would streamline oversight, reduce unnecessary burdens on industry, and allow FDA to focus resources on enforcing modern, science-based standards directed by Congress.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: A law firm, representing a client, urges the FDA to rescind multiple outdated and duplicative food safety regulations, including GMPs, LACF, Acidified Foods, HACCP for juice/seafood, and bottled water GMPs, asserting that the Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA) provides a sufficient and more effective regulatory framework.

- **Unnecessary Burdens on Industry:**
    - Compliance with obsolete and redundant regulations creates significant economic impact, time, and resource drains for manufacturers.
    - Companies must navigate and comply with two sets of requirements that are often in tension (e.g., acidified foods and Part 117).
    - Prescriptive requirements, such as those for thermal processing equipment design in LACF regulations, may be outdated by technological advancements but still require compliance or risk rejection.
- **Outdated and Inefficient Standards:** Regulations promulgated in the 1980s and 1990s are not as effective as modern, science-based, risk-tailored approaches allowed by FSMA.
- **FDA Overreach from Emergency Authority:** The transformation of temporary emergency permit programs (LACF/Acidified Foods) into permanent, mandatory regulations without clear ongoing congressional intent.
- **Lack of Clear Congressional Authorization:** Specific, detailed, and prescriptive regulations (like juice and seafood HACCP, bottled water GMPs) impose significant burdens without the "clear congressional authorization" required by recent Supreme Court precedent (e.g., *West Virginia v. EPA*).

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Comment Title: Scaling the Medicare GUIDE Model as a National Innovation for Chronic Disease and Dementia Prevention Through Tech-Enabled Care Navigators and Community-Based Preventive Rehabilitation
*   Summary
    *   As part of HHS’s call for public input, we offer the Medicare GUIDE Model — and our enhanced tech-enabled version — as an evidence-based deregulatory model for innovation, quality improvement, and national scaling.
    *   Since 80% of health is determined by self-management, the CMMI GUIDE model delivery and payment infrastructure aligns with the aims of the President’s “Make America Healthy Again” initiative.
        *   It offers a low-cost, scalable, technology-supported approach to upstream chronic disease prevention in addition to downstream dementia and caregiver support, all delivered in the community setting.
    *   We propose building upon the existing CMMI GUIDE Model to create a national chronic disease and frailty prevention infrastructure that:
        *   Trains and deploys a scalable workforce of human-AI and robot care navigators based in pharmacies and local businesses.
        *   Leverages AI-powered care planning and human/digital/robotic coaching to enable precision support to prevent age and lifestyle-related physical, cognitive, and emotional frailty, and to promote social well-being.
        *   Is overseen by physicians and other providers with expertise in preexisting chronic disease and lifestyle rehabilitation programs like cardiac, pulmonary, and stroke rehabilitation.
            *   These programs are proven to reverse disease progression and improve quality of life.
        *   Eliminates unnecessary regulation around licensure, documentation, and supervision, while protecting quality through outcome measurement and tech-enabled monitoring oversight.
        *   Is perfectly positioned to expand upstream from dementia care into metabolic health, frailty prevention, and multimorbidity management, consistent with national health priorities.
        *   Targets fitness, functional capacity and self-reported well-being as the nation’s primary outcome measures for health.
        *   Layers into current models of primary care as a “primary selfcare” arm.
    *   This model, already functioning through the CMMI GUIDE Model, offers a cost-saving, home-based and patient-centered alternative to overly regulated, clinic-centric care delivery.
        *   It should be scaled nationally as an HHS-endorsed quality innovation framework.
*   Responses to RFI Questions
    *   Q2. Regulations to Reconsider to Advance Chronic Disease Prevention
        *   We recommend HHS:
            *   Preserve and scale the deregulated Medicare GUIDE Model as a foundational platform for national chronic disease and frailty prevention.
            *   Enable GUIDE to cover not only dementia-related care but also upstream early cognitive impairment and those with physical frailty without dementia, moving to other high-cost conditions like CHF/COPD with an eye to moving further upstream over time.
        *   Rehabilitation physicians (physiatrists) and other providers have already demonstrated success in delivering chronic disease and frailty rehabilitation through similar team-based models like cardiac, pulmonary and stroke rehabilitation.
            *   These models offer a proven framework for behavior change and chronic disease reversal.
            *   They can be extended into the home and community at scale when supported by unlicensed but tech-enabled care navigators.
        *   This approach is evidence-based, patient-centered, and efficient, making it an ideal foundation for future national care models.
    *   Q3. Regulations That Impede Innovation or Preventive Care
        *   Current regulatory constraints often:
            *   Restrict non-licensed personnel from providing coaching or self-management support, even when based on predetermined standardized protocols and with physician oversight.
            *   Require excessive documentation for routine check-ins and coaching that creates barriers for small organizations and rural practices.
            *   Fail to reimburse or enable technology-driven community self-management support models that reduce cost and improve access.
            *   Restrict the delivery of proven chronic disease rehabilitation programs like cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation by narrowing the diagnostic criteria for participation and by limiting self-management support only to licensed staff members.
                *   We believe similar support could be rendered by low-cost and unlicensed care navigators that are supervised by doctors and pharmacists, empowered with robotic/AI/mobile technology, and focused on improving fitness, functional capacity and self-reported well-being – KEY outcome measures for chronic disease and frailty prevention.
        *   The CMMI GUIDE Model is an evidence-based team approach perfectly positioned to move from self-management support for dementia ONLY to self-management support for physical frailty and chronic disease prevention, particularly when aligned with evidence-based cardiac rehabilitation and other self-management support best practices.
            *   This could yield tremendous cost savings by preventing hospitalization, nursing home placement and overall high cost-of-care.
        *   Deregulating workforce roles, supervision rules, and documentation requirements — while retaining fitness, functional capacity and well-being outcome tracking — will create space for continued innovation.
    *   Q4. Less Burdensome Alternatives to Current HHS Approaches
        *   We propose GUIDE serve as a national template for a “Whole Health Navigation” model that:
            *   Uses a mobile-first AI-based infrastructure to deliver high-touch, low-cost care support in the community.
            *   Equips tech-enabled care navigators and AI-co-pilots to collect structured health data and deliver personalized self-management support coaching.
            *   Focuses on what matters to the patient, supported by well-being outcome measures like the PROMIS-10 and other validated “determinants” of health assessments.
            *   Replaces redundant regulation with technology-enabled oversight, continuous quality improvement, and patient outcome measurement.
        *   This model enables HHS to scale access, control cost, and reduce regulatory complexity while advancing national health goals.
*   Economic Impact Statement
    *   Our GUIDE chronic disease rehabilitation model represents an evidence-based cost-effective innovation with clear, measurable financial benefits:
        *   Hospitalization Avoidance: Upstream prevention of falls, frailty, delirium, and caregiver burnout is projected to reduce hospitalizations and emergency department visits by 20–40% in high-risk older adults, yielding per capita savings of $2,000–$4,000 annually.
        *   Delay of Nursing Home Placement: The average annual cost of nursing home care exceeds $100,000.
            *   Preventing or delaying institutionalization by 6–12 months in dementia and physically frail patients can yield Medicare and Medicaid savings of $10,000–$30,000 per individual.
        *   Dementia patients cost CMS $57,000 per year as compared with $12,000 per year for the average beneficiary, thus making dementia prevention a top priority due to above average hospital and nursing home utilization.
        *   Job Creation and Cost Reallocation: Utilizing non-licensed care navigators, supervised by medical providers and pharmacists with chronic disease rehabilitation expertise, reduces reliance on expensive clinic and specialty visits while maintaining quality and continuity out in the community.
            *   This yields labor cost efficiencies and job creation without compromising outcomes.
        *   Digital Infrastructure Savings: A mobile-first, AI-assisted platform reduces the need for duplicative and time-consuming documentation, clinic overhead, and in-person doctor’s visits.
            *   Care plans are generated from standardized assessments (e.g., PROMIS-10, Health-Related Social Needs, lifestyle screeners) and personalized by local navigators, reducing time burdens on telehealth-based physicians and improving scalability.
            *   It shifts the emphasis of care from medication prescription to self-management support prescription of lifestyle and other related determinants of health.
        *   Support for Small Businesses: Anchoring this model in community pharmacies, which already serve as trusted health access points, empowers small businesses, increases rural access, and promotes economic development — all without increasing federal regulation or infrastructure spending.
    *   These savings are both short-term (within 12 months) and cumulative over time, particularly as this approach scales across aging and chronically ill populations who are frail or pre-frail.
    *   GUIDE provides a payment and implementation structure that can support this innovation nationally without new legislation — simply through regulatory alignment and support.
*   Conclusion
    *   The GUIDE Model — as currently structured — offers an extraordinary foundation for HHS-led national health innovation.
    *   By scaling this model as a flexible, low-regulation platform for chronic disease rehabilitation and digital care navigation, HHS can:
        *   Unlock new chronic disease prevention pathways rooted in self-management support best practices derived from evidence-based models like cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation.
        *   Empower a NEW scalable national workforce of care navigators, trained in human-AI interaction and based in pharmacies and local businesses.
        *   Support innovation and job creation in rural and underserved communities through pharmacy-based, tech-enabled care.
        *   Meet the goals of deregulation while improving outcomes, lowering cost, and reducing caregiver burden.
    *   We respectfully urge HHS to formally recognize the CMS GUIDE Model as a scalable workforce development innovation and expand its reach as the national framework for preventive, tech-enabled selfcare support — a true model of government efficiency, quality improvement, and public-private partnership.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: GamePlan Medical advocates for the national expansion and deregulation of the tech-enabled Medicare GUIDE Model, leveraging AI-powered care navigators for cost-effective chronic disease and frailty prevention in community settings.

-   **Role/Expertise:** Preventive Physiatrist, National Medical Director for GamePlan Medical LLC, Participant in Medicare Innovation Center, Co-Author of Telehealth Innovation White Paper for the American Academy of PM&R, Clinical Assistant Professor of Rehabilitation Medicine at Virtua Health College of Medicine.
-   **Geographic Scope:** National
-   **Stake in Issue:** GamePlan Medical provides a tech-enabled healthcare delivery model, which they propose is an enhanced version of the Medicare GUIDE Model. They seek its national adoption and expansion, particularly for chronic disease and frailty prevention, which directly aligns with their business model and expertise.
structuredSections.corePosition: We propose building upon the existing CMMI GUIDE Model to create a national chronic disease and frailty prevention infrastructure. This model should be scaled nationally as an HHS-endorsed quality innovation framework, offering a cost-saving, home-based, and patient-centered alternative to overly regulated, clinic-centric care delivery. By leveraging tech-enabled care navigators, including human-AI and robot support, we can empower a new scalable workforce to improve health outcomes and reduce costs through self-management support.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   Preserve and scale the deregulated Medicare GUIDE Model as a foundational platform for national chronic disease and frailty prevention.
    -   Enable GUIDE to cover early cognitive impairment and physical frailty without dementia.
    -   Expand coverage to other high-cost conditions like CHF/COPD, moving further upstream over time.
-   Deregulate workforce roles, supervision rules, and documentation requirements for self-management support services, while retaining fitness, functional capacity, and well-being outcome tracking.
    -   Allow non-licensed personnel to provide coaching or self-management support based on standardized protocols and with physician/pharmacist oversight.
    -   Streamline documentation for routine check-ins and coaching to reduce barriers.
    -   Reimburse and enable technology-driven community self-management support models.
    -   Relax diagnostic criteria for proven chronic disease rehabilitation programs and allow unlicensed care navigators to provide self-management support.
-   Adopt GUIDE as a national template for a “Whole Health Navigation” model.
    -   Use a mobile-first AI-based infrastructure for high-touch, low-cost community care support.
    -   Equip tech-enabled care navigators and AI-co-pilots to collect structured health data and deliver personalized self-management coaching.
    -   Focus on patient priorities, supported by well-being outcome measures (e.g., PROMIS-10) and validated health determinants assessments.
    -   Replace redundant regulation with technology-enabled oversight, continuous quality improvement, and patient outcome measurement.
-   Formally recognize the CMS GUIDE Model as a scalable workforce development innovation.
-   Expand the GUIDE Model's reach as the national framework for preventive, tech-enabled selfcare support, fostering government efficiency, quality improvement, and public-private partnership.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   Current regulatory constraints restrict non-licensed personnel from providing coaching or self-management support, even when based on predetermined standardized protocols and with physician oversight.
-   Excessive documentation requirements for routine check-ins and coaching create significant barriers for small organizations and rural practices.
-   Existing regulations fail to adequately reimburse or enable technology-driven community self-management support models, which are crucial for reducing cost and improving access.
-   Diagnostic criteria for proven chronic disease rehabilitation programs (e.g., cardiac and pulmonary rehabilitation) are too narrow, limiting participation.
-   Self-management support within these programs is currently limited only to licensed staff members, despite the potential for low-cost, unlicensed care navigators to provide similar support when supervised and tech-enabled.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
-   **Innovative Workforce Model:** Proposing a scalable workforce of "human-AI and robot care navigators" based in community pharmacies and local businesses, overseen by physicians and pharmacists.
-   **Significant Cost Savings Projections:** Detailed economic impact statement with specific financial benefits:
    -   Projected 20–40% reduction in hospitalizations and emergency department visits for high-risk older adults, yielding $2,000–$4,000 per capita annual savings.
    -   Potential Medicare and Medicaid savings of $10,000–$30,000 per individual by preventing or delaying nursing home placement by 6–12 months.
    -   Highlighting that dementia patients cost CMS $57,000 per year compared to $12,000 for the average beneficiary, emphasizing the financial urgency of prevention.
-   **Emphasis on Self-Management:** The core premise that "80% of health is determined by self-management," positioning the model as "primary selfcare" that shifts care emphasis from medication prescription to "self-management support prescription of lifestyle and other related determinants of health."
-   **Community-Based Integration:** Advocating for anchoring the model in community pharmacies to empower small businesses, increase rural access, and promote economic development without increasing federal regulation or infrastructure spending.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
-   "Since 80% of health is determined by self-management, the CMMI GUIDE model delivery and payment infrastructure aligns fully with the aims of the President’s “Make America Healthy Again” initiative by offering a low-cost, scalable, technology-supported approach to upstream chronic disease prevention in addition to downstream dementia and caregiver support — all delivered in the community setting."
-   "Deregulating workforce roles, supervision rules, and documentation requirements — while retaining fitness, functional capacity and well-being outcome tracking — will create space for continued innovation."
-   "It shifts the emphasis of care from medication prescription to self-management support prescription of lifestyle and other related determinants of health."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The Plant Based Foods Association (PBFA) appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Request for Information: Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
    *   PBFA is the first and only trade association in the U.S. representing the plant-based food industry, an industry that generates $8 billion in retail sales across more than 20 product categories.
    *   We currently represent nearly 200 of the nation’s leading plant-based food companies.
*   PBFA shares the vision for a healthy, sustainable, and innovative food system.
    *   We agree that fostering innovation is central to improving the health of Americans.
    *   Labeling policies that impose unfair, unnecessary, and unsupported burdens on plant-based foods hinder innovation and contradict the principles of fair, transparent, and science-based regulation that the Administration has identified as central to improving public health.
*   Accordingly, PBFA urges HHS to take appropriate action to ensure that FDA withdraws the following draft guidance documents:
    *   Draft Guidance for Industry: Labeling of Plant-Based Milk Alternatives and Voluntary Nutrient Statements (FDA, February 2023)
    *   Draft Guidance for Industry: Labeling of Plant-Based Alternatives to Animal-Derived Foods (FDA, January 2025)
*   PBFA previously submitted detailed comments to the FDA on both documents and refers HHS to those filings for additional information and analysis supporting our views expressed here.

*   1. Draft Guidance for Industry: Labeling of Plant-Based Milk Alternatives and Voluntary Nutrient Statements (FDA, February 2023)
    *   The FDA’s draft guidance on labeling of plant-based milk alternatives would impose two unique labeling obligations on these products:
        *   If the product uses the term “milk” – either in its name or in a comparative claim referencing cow’s milk – and does not meet minimums for nine cherry-picked nutrients present in cow’s milk, it would be required to display a prominent front-of-pack disclaimer describing how it differs nutritionally from cow’s milk.
        *   It would be required to include in its statement of identity a description of the nature or source of the products’ characterizing or predominant ingredient(s).
    *   The draft guidance does not address any valid FDA concern.
        *   Although the FDA attempted to justify its recommendations based on alleged consumer confusion and public health risks, it offered no evidence of either.
        *   Nor would the guidance even serve to address these concerns if they existed.
        *   The approach is entirely without precedent and inconsistent with existing FDA regulation and guidance.
        *   It singles out plant-based milks for uniquely burdensome treatment, regulating them unlike any other food category, and appears designed to protect the dairy industry at the expense of its plant-based competitors.
    *   Response to Question 1: Criteria for Regulatory Repeal or Modification
        *   The FDA’s draft guidance on labeling of plant-based milk alternatives meets at least three of the criteria identified for potential regulatory repeal or modification set forth in Executive Order 14129.
        *   First, it would be unconstitutional – and would not survive a First Amendment challenge.
            *   The First Amendment “demands proof” that restrictions on plant-based food names are, at a minimum, reasonably related to an actual FDA concern.
            *   Although the FDA attempted to justify its draft guidance by claiming that consumers “do not understand the nutritional differences between milk and plant-based alternatives,” the agency’s own evidence does not support that conclusion.
                *   PBFA retained Dr. Joel Steckel, Professor of Marketing at New York University’s Stern School of Business, to review the six reports on which FDA relied.
                *   His analysis confirms that these reports are outdated, poorly designed, and provide “no scientifically valid conclusion on the subject.”
            *   The FDA also attempted to justify its draft guidance by claiming that substituting plant-based milks for cow’s milk could raise public health concerns by leading to inadequate intake of certain nutrients, but that claim is similarly unsupported.
                *   There is no reliable evidence that consumers of plant-based milks are at risk of nutrient deficiencies or that shifting toward plant-based milks presents a public health risk.
                *   In fact, only three of the nine comparative nutrients identified in the draft guidance are considered nutrients of public health concern: potassium, vitamin D, and calcium.
                    *   Cow’s milk is not a good source of potassium and is only fortified with vitamin D, as are many plant-based milks.
                    *   With regard to calcium, even the National Institutes of Health has acknowledged that the relationship between dairy intake and bone health is inconclusive and that numerous other foods provide ample sources of the nutrient.
            *   The draft guidance purports to allow plant-based milk companies to continue using the term “milk.”
                *   As the FDA stated therein: there is no legal basis on which to explicitly disallow plant-based milks from using the term “milk” because they do not purport to be, nor are they represented as cow’s milk.
                *   The FDA has long allowed standardized names of foods to be used in the names of other foods, so long as such use is not misleading.
                *   Such a prohibition would be a clear violation of the First Amendment.
                *   Instead, the FDA recommended “voluntary” disclaimers of purportedly objective factual nutrition information.
                *   Yet, the nutrient disclaimers would be tantamount to requirements, as companies that do not follow the FDA’s recommendations risk consumer class action.
                *   The nutrient disclaimers would also be disparaging, not purely factual, and would be unduly burdensome.
                *   They would function to point out to consumers nine ways in which cow’s milk might, subjectively, be more nutritious than plant-based milks and none of the ways in which plant-based milks would be more nutritious than cow’s milk.
                *   If the draft guidance is finalized, many plant-based milk companies would effectively be dissuaded from using the term “milk” on their label. For this reason, among others, the draft guidance would not withstand First Amendment scrutiny.
        *   Second, the draft guidance would be unduly burdensome as it would impose regulatory burdens on plant-based milks that would be unnecessary, inconsistent with FDA precedent, and unsupported by any consumer protection rationale.
            *   It would single out one product category for treatment that is not applied to any other, undermining both regulatory coherence and fair competition.
            *   The draft guidance recommended front-of-pack nutrient disclaimers and naming obligations that are entirely without precedent in FDA regulation.
                *   The FDA does not currently mandate any front-of-pack nutrition disclosures for any category of food.
                *   Under existing regulations, the only circumstance in which nutrient disclaimers are required (or even recommended) is when a product voluntarily makes a nutrient content claim—and even then, the required disclosures are factual and limited in scope, i.e. “See nutrition information for [exceeded nutrient] content.”
            *   By contrast, this draft guidance recommended that plant-based milks display disclaimers referencing nine specific nutrients—even though only three (calcium, vitamin D, and potassium) are considered nutrients of concern.
                *   The FDA’s own FAQ acknowledges that the recommended disclaimers would apply even for nutrients that are not under-consumed by the U.S. population, such as magnesium.
                *   These disclaimers would obligate plant-based milks to characterize their nutrient levels in a way that disparages the product relative to cow’s milk, i.e., “Contains a lower amount of ___ than milk.”
            *   The FDA is effectively treating the word “milk” – but only when used by plant-based milks – as a nutrient content claim, triggering a requirement for a nutrient disclaimer.
                *   By the logic of the draft guidance, similar disclaimers should be recommended across numerous other food categories.
                    *   For example, the FDA would need to recommend that juice drinks disclaim that they “Contain more added sugar and lower amounts of vitamins and minerals than 100% juice.”
                    *   That beef burgers disclaim they contain more cholesterol than plant-based burgers.
                    *   And that breads not made from 100% whole grain disclaim that they “Contain lower amounts of fiber and vitamins and minerals than 100% whole grain bread.”
            *   The draft guidance also invoked school nutrition standards—standards developed for a closed institutional setting, not the general marketplace—to justify a labeling regime that is wholly out of step with FDA’s approach to other food categories.
                *   These USDA criteria are tailored to the unique needs of the federal school meal programs and have no relevance to how consumers evaluate or compare plant-based products in a retail environment.
        *   Third, by singling out an innovative sector, like the plant-based industry, for unique and burdensome labeling requirements, the FDA would impede innovation across the broader food industry.
            *   This kind of targeted regulation deters investment, experimentation, and product development.
            *   In particular, the FDA’s recommendation of unsupported, misleading, and nonstandard nutrient disclaimers sends a regulatory signal that plant-based milks are inherently deficient – discouraging innovation and growth, particularly among small and emerging companies that face compliance burdens, regulatory uncertainty, and litigation risk.
    *   Response to Question 4: Alternative Approaches
        *   The existing regulatory framework governing food labeling is fully sufficient to address any legitimate concerns FDA may have regarding consumer understanding of plant-based milks.
        *   The FDA already requires macronutrients, as well as vitamins and minerals that are “nutrients of concern” to be labeled in the Nutrition Facts Panel (“NFP”).
            *   For the “nutrients of concern” at issue (potassium, vitamin D, and calcium), a product’s NFP must state the amount of nutrient, as well as the percent daily value (“DV”) – indicating to consumers both the amount of each nutrient they are recommended to consume daily and the percent of that DV they would be gaining by consuming a serving of the product.
        *   To the extent that plant-based milks compare their nutrient content to the nutrient content of cow’s milk, FDA regulations concerning “relative claims” already require them to:
            *   State the percentage or fractional difference of the nutrient compared.
            *   Make an immediately adjacent disclaimer stating the amount of that nutrient in cow’s milk.

*   2. Draft Guidance for Industry: Labeling of Plant-Based Alternatives to Animal-Derived Foods (FDA, January 2025)
    *   The FDA’s draft guidance on labeling of plant-based alternatives to animal-derived foods would incorporate one aspect of the agency’s guidance on the labeling of plant-based milk alternatives:
        *   It would impose a unique obligation on all plant-based foods to specify their specific plant source(s) in their product name.
        *   This approach takes issue with simple, clear, and consumer-friendly product names – such as “veggie burger” – that have long been used and understood without confusion.
    *   Response to Question 1: Criteria for Regulatory Repeal or Modification
        *   The FDA’s draft guidance on labeling of plant-based alternatives to animal-derived foods warrants repeal under the same three criteria.
        *   First, it would be unconstitutional because it is not grounded in any legitimate FDA concern.
            *   The FDA attempts to justify the guidance based on two claimed objectives: (a) preventing consumers from being misled into thinking plant-based products contain animal-derived ingredients, and (b) informing consumers of the specific plant source(s) of the product.
            *   But both concerns are unfounded – and even if they were valid, they are already addressed by existing regulations.
            *   Courts have consistently rejected the argument that plant-based product names mislead consumers into believing the products contain animal-derived ingredients.
                *   They have held that even the “least sophisticated” consumers are not confused and that consumers purchase plant-based products precisely because they do not contain animal ingredients.
                *   In fact, in its own draft guidance on labeling of plant-based milk alternatives, the FDA acknowledged that consumers are not misled into thinking such products contain animal-derived ingredients.
            *   As to the second claimed objective – this is already addressed by existing regulation: the requisite ingredient list discloses each ingredient in descending order by weight.
            *   Notably, the FDA did not even claim that consumers are confused about the ingredients in plant-based products.
                *   Instead, it merely suggested that consumers may want more information – a suggestion unsupported by any evidence.
                *   Even if this were true, it does not justify imposing unique and burdensome labeling obligations on an entire category of products.
        *   Second, the draft guidance would be unduly burdensome because it would impose rigid and complex naming requirements that depart from existing FDA regulations for non-standardized foods, which are intentionally flexible and emphasize simplicity.
            *   The FDA does not require specific information in the names of other types of food products – even for other alternatives to standardized foods.
                *   For example, “bread” is defined as containing wheat, yet alternatives are allowed to be labeled simply as “gluten-free bread.”
                *   “Milk chocolate” is defined as using only nutritive carbohydrate sweeteners, yet products sweetened with Aspartame or Stevia may be labeled as simply “sugar free milk chocolate.”
            *   Even “imitation” foods – which “involve literally substituting inferior ingredients” – are not required to specify their substitute ingredients in their product name.
                *   The FDA has long affirmed that plant-based foods are not “imitations” because that term suggests an inferior product cheapened by substitution of ingredients.
        *   Third, the draft guidance would disincentivize innovation.
            *   In addition to the broader chilling effect described above – where singling out an innovative sector deters investment and development – requiring manufacturers to identify specific plant sources in their product names would discourage the use of blended or multi-ingredient formulations.
            *   This would impede key areas of innovation within the sector, ultimately stifling the growth and evolution of the plant-based food industry.
    *   Response to Question 4: Alternative Approaches
        *   The draft guidance is unnecessary because existing federal law and regulation already directly address both of the FDA’s stated concerns: (a) preventing consumers from being misled into thinking plant-based products contain animal-derived ingredients, and (b) informing consumers of the specific plant sources used in those products.
        *   The Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act provides that a food is misbranded “if it purports to be or is represented as a food for which a definition and standard of identity had been prescribed, unless it conforms to such definition and standard.”
        *   In addition, FDA regulations require all foods to include an ingredients statement listing each ingredient in descending order by weight, which provides clear disclosure of plant sources.
*   PBFA welcomes the opportunity to further engage with HHS on these important issues. We encourage your office to reach out with any questions regarding these comments or if additional information would be helpful as you consider them.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The Alliance for Aging Research (Alliance) is a leading nonprofit organization dedicated to changing the narrative to achieve healthy aging and equitable access to care.
*   The Alliance strives for a culture that embraces healthy aging as a greater good and values science and investments to advance dignity, independence, and equity.
*   The Alliance appreciates the opportunity to respond to the Department’s request for regulations and Guidance that could be waived, modified, or streamlined to reduce administration burdens.
*   The Alliance addresses two topics within Medicare: Coverage with Evidence Development (CED) and a measure within the five-star rating system for secure nursing facilities.

*   Coverage with Evidence Development
    *   The Alliance recommends that HHS eliminate three “Guidances,” which constitute 25 individual regulations, as outlined in question 1 of the Request for Information (RFI).
    *   These guidances refer to or are related to the prior Administration’s “Coverage with Evidence” (CED) policy that interferes with beneficiary access to drugs and devices.
    *   The suggested changes would restore the Agency’s Advisory Opinion issued by the CMS General Counsel on January 14, 2021, which concluded that there is no statutory authority to adopt or implement a CED policy.
    *   The three Guidance documents that should be withdrawn are:
        *   Coverage with Evidence Development Guidance Document, August 7, 2024.
        *   CMS National Coverage Analysis Evidence Review Guidance Document August 7, 2024.
        *   Medicare Program; Transitional Coverage for Emerging Technologies; 89 Fed. Reg. 69724 (Aug. 12, 2024), which applies the CED policy to Medicare coverage of breakthrough medical devices through the “transitional coverage for emerging technologies (or TCET) policy.”
    *   Each of the three Guidance documents imposes a barrier to Medicare beneficiary access to drugs and devices by imposing vague, subjective, and nonworkable “clinical trial” or “registry” barriers to Medicare coverage.
    *   CMS has refused to cover certain FDA-approved drugs and devices for their on-label uses because the Agency, using vague and undefined standards not authorized by law, deems that there is not sufficient medical evidence to support a “reasonable and necessary” finding without further CMS-approved studies.
    *   Both practically and legally, the CED process does not work and simply serves as a barrier to beneficiary access to FDA-approved treatments.
    *   To the extent that a select small number of beneficiaries who participate in the clinical “trials” are able to have their use of the drugs or devices covered, it is administratively burdensome for both beneficiaries and providers to do so.
    *   Patient safety and the integrity of the Medicare program are compromised by the use of CED.
    *   In a recent article summarizing the failures of the CED program in the Journal Health Affairs entitled “Medicare’s ‘Coverage With Evidence Development’: A Barrier to Patient Access and Innovation,” Joe Grogan summarized the failure of the CED program:
        *   Since 2005, 27 medical devices or procedures have been subjected to CED.
        *   However, only four had their evidence development programs retired and their national coverage retained.
        *   CMS ceded coverage of an additional two devices or procedures to the discretion of Medicare’s regional administrative contractors.
        *   The remaining 21 items and services continue to be subject to CED, and none have preset time frames for “graduating” from the program and receiving a final coverage determination.
        *   Even amongst the products that graduated CED, the time elapsed between initiation and graduation ranged between four and 12 years.
        *   Multiple products that were amongst the first to receive CED continue to be required to generate clinical data today, almost 20 years later.
    *   Mr. Grogan also documented the administrative barriers imposed by the CED program:
        *   CED is a never-ending coverage purgatory for innovators, with more than 30 complex steps required simply to establish a program.
        *   Once CMS announces coverage of a product under CED, an organization must step in to sponsor a study to collect the evidence.
        *   This involves determining investigators, establishing a governing protocol, getting approval from both an institutional review board and CMS, preparing a database or registry, determining funding, identifying and enrolling patients, and general clinical practice.
        *   The details behind each of these steps are extensive, and mistakes can be costly.
        *   The resources required to facilitate CED can inhibit evidence development, with unclear responsibilities for costs of participation, developing data collection systems, or data sharing.
        *   This creates inconsistencies in coverage rules and access based on where a Medicare beneficiary lives, as contractors can set different rules for their regions.
    *   Given this failure, Mr. Grogan concluded that: “CMS should scrap CED altogether, choosing instead to default to coverage of on-label use for FDA-approved drugs. Where CMS is unsure of the medical necessity of an item or service, it should defer coverage to its regional administrative contractors to make claim-by-claim determinations concerning medical necessity. At minimum, CMS should refrain from placing drugs which receive FDA approval under CED…”
    *   Mr. Grogan’s conclusions are supported by the patient community, which published a report in February 2023 that came to the very same conclusions.
    *   Requiring beneficiaries to participate in clinical trials or registries is against federal law: Section 1801 of the Medicare law states that nothing in the title shall be construed to authorize any Federal officer or employee to exercise any supervision or control over the practice of medicine or the manner in which medical services are provided, or over the selection, tenure, or compensation of health service providers, or over the administration or operation of such entities.
    *   Section 1801 was included to offset criticism that Federal legislation would give Federal officials the opportunity and right to interfere in individual diagnosis and treatment, which the CED policy does.
    *   A beneficiary’s decision to not participate in a CED clinical study does not necessarily reflect unwillingness, as there are often access barriers outside a patient’s control.
    *   Agency-directed restrictions may include care setting or provider eligibility criteria or limits on CED clinical study enrollment.
    *   Post-market randomized control trial requirements (RCTs) may be unpalatable to beneficiaries and present ethical issues, as RCT study design in CED may require some Medicare beneficiaries to receive a placebo for a device, diagnostic, or prescription drug already found to be “safe and effective” by the FDA.
    *   Beneficiaries may be required to pay coinsurance for a placebo to maintain a blinded study.
    *   Some populations may experience mistrust based on historical experience or have legal concerns that create hesitancy to have personal health data collected in a clinical study.
    *   By creating barriers to patient access, denying that there are barriers, and placing the onus for shortcomings on sponsors and patients, CMS interferes with and restricts the medical autonomy of Medicare beneficiaries.
    *   Beyond the burdensome administrative requirements on both beneficiaries and providers, the CED program is illegal and threatens the integrity of the Medicare program.
    *   In the first Trump Administration, the General Counsel of the Department of Health and Human Services, Robert Charrow, issued a clear Advisory Opinion demonstrating that CMS lacked authority to implement the CED program.
    *   The Advisory Opinion, rescinded by the Biden Administration and taken off the HHS website, is explicit that there is no current legal authority for the CED program.
    *   The rescinded Advisory Opinion, which should be restored, stated:
        *   CMS has previously interpreted SSA Section 1862(a)(1)(E) as authority to make Medicare payment for items and services provided to study participants in CED clinical trials, under the theory that AHRQ “supports” this research by endorsing it.
        *   OGC re-examined this issue and concluded that this prior interpretation of “support” leads to Medicare payment that is unlawful under Section 1862, because AHRQ has not been “supporting” the clinical trials and research required as part of an NCD using CED.
        *   The term “support” as used in SSA Section 1142 is not defined, but this broad reading is fundamentally inconsistent with the regulatory definition of “support” at 42 C.F.R. § 93.221, which, while applying to research oversight under Title IX of the PHS Act, OGC now believes is the correct interpretation.
        *   Therefore, for an NCD using CED to lawfully invoke the exception at SSA Section 1862(a)(1)(E), AHRQ must “support” the study within the meaning of the definition at 42 C.F.R. § 93.221, which will involve more than merely endorsing the clinical study.
    *   For this reason, even if administrative burden and impairment of Medicare program integrity were not sufficient justification, the legal analysis similarly requires withdrawal of the three documents at this time.
    *   The 25 individual CEDs that must be repealed can be found here: https://www.cms.gov/medicare/coverage/evidence. These include:
        *   Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant for MDS
        *   Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant for Multiple Myeloma
        *   Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant for Myelofibrosis
        *   Allogeneic Hematopoietic Stem Cell Transplant for Sickle Cell Disease
        *   Amyloid PET
        *   Autologous Platelet-rich Plasma
        *   CPAP For Obstructive Sleep Apnea
        *   Cochlear Implantation
        *   Extracorporeal Photopheresis for Bronchiolitis Obliterans Syndrome Following Lung Transplant
        *   FDG PET and Other Neuroimaging Devices for Dementia
        *   Home Oxygen for COPD
        *   Implantable Pulmonary Artery Pressure Sensors for Heart Failure Management
        *   Leadless Pacemakers
        *   Monoclonal Antibodies Directed Against Amyloid for the Treatment of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD)
        *   NaF-18 PET for Bone Metastasis
        *   Off-label use of Colorectal Cancer Drugs
        *   Percutaneous Image-guided Lumbar Decompression for Lumbar Spinal Stenosis
        *   Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure (LAAC)
        *   Pharmacogenomic Testing for Warfarin Response
        *   TENS for chronic low back pain
        *   Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement
        *   Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair (TEER)
        *   Transcatheter Edge-to-Edge Repair for Tricuspid Valve Regurgitation (T-TEER)
        *   Transcatheter Tricuspid Valve Replacement (TTVR)
        *   Vagus Nerve Stimulation (VNS) for Treatment Resistant Depression (TRD)
    *   CMS released a proposed guidance in January titled, “Study Protocols That Use Real-world Data,” which seeks to make CED more predictable and clear for sponsors.
    *   The Alliance strongly opposes any future adoption of this guidance.
    *   As written, it establishes a highly structured real-world data study protocol framework for NCDs with CED, outlining elements such as fit-for-purpose study design, use of control arms, blinding where feasible, pre-specified endpoints, enrollment benchmarks, diversity requirements, and oversight mechanisms.
    *   While the research framework may appear methodologically sound, in practice it represents a significant and concerning expansion of CED.
    *   It effectively transforms CED into an ongoing federal research mandate disguised as coverage, undermining FDA’s regulatory authority and imposing open-ended data collection requirements on manufacturers.
    *   This approach goes well beyond CMS’s statutory authority under current law.
    *   Given these serious legal concerns, and all the concerns with CED more broadly, CMS should withdraw the proposed guidance in its entirety.

*   Antipsychotic Measure Within the 5-Star Rating System for Secure Nursing Facilities
    *   Comments primarily focus on general deregulatory recommendations under Executive Order 14192, “Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation.”
    *   This outlines an opportunity to eliminate the Long-Stay Antipsychotic Medication Quality Measure from the CMS Nursing Home Care Compare Five-Star Quality Rating System.
    *   To better align with best clinical practices and published provider guidelines, CMS should remove the Long-Stay Antipsychotic Medication quality measure from the Nursing Home Compare Five-Star Quality Rating System and instead modernize the Minimum Data Set (MDS) to better distinguish between appropriate and inappropriate use of antipsychotics among residents of skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) and long-term care facilities.
    *   The existing Long-Stay Antipsychotic Medication quality measure meets the following deregulatory criteria included in RFI question #3:
        *   Is confusing or unnecessarily complicated.
        *   Requires an excessive number of reports or unreasonable record keeping, or information that is not needed or used effectively.
        *   Carries excessive penalties.
        *   Is conflicting.
        *   Impedes access to or delivery of care or services.
        *   Impedes efforts to innovate.
        *   Is obsolete.
        *   Otherwise interferes with the public or private sector’s ability to address chronic health conditions or otherwise promote the health and wellbeing of Americans.
    *   CMS previously created an unscientific and punitive measure to curb the use of antipsychotics in nursing homes regardless of the appropriateness for the patient.
    *   The measure is an unsophisticated, blunt formula of the “percent of residents who received an antipsychotic medication” calculated by dividing the number of residents on a medication by the total number of residents in the SNF.
    *   Only three diagnoses are exempted from the measure: schizophrenia, Huntington’s disease, and Tourette’s syndrome.
    *   As noted in clinical guidance published by the American Psychiatric Association (APA), similar measures promulgated by the National Quality Forum (NQF) include bipolar disorder among the conditions exempted, and many stakeholders have advocated for its addition as an exemption to the CMS measure; yet CMS only permits three exempted conditions.
    *   The measure fails to distinguish between clinically appropriate and inappropriate prescribing, instead merely capturing total use of antipsychotics.
    *   The measure has led to clinically necessary treatments being withheld, causing harm to residents and burdening providers.
    *   This approach forces facilities to prioritize regulatory compliance over patient-centered care, often leading to unintended negative outcomes like the inappropriate discontinuation of medically necessary medications.
    *   While acknowledging that individuals should not be improperly medicated, there are legitimate and appropriate clinical uses of antipsychotic medications that are being suppressed due to this measure.
    *   Specific Concerns with the Existing Measure:
        *   1. Is Confusing or Unnecessarily Complicated & Requires An Excessive Number of Reports or Unreasonable Record Keeping, Or Information that is Not Needed or Used Effectively
            *   The measure and related oversight protocols impose overly complex documentation requirements that may conflict with Section 1801 of the Social Security Act.
            *   These requirements dictate that nursing homes may only use antipsychotic medications when nonpharmacological interventions are contraindicated, requiring extensive documentation to justify their use.
            *   CMS compels facilities to attempt gradual dose reduction, regardless of a patient’s medical history, clinical stability, or wishes.
            *   The result is a cycle in which residents are taken off medications they have successfully used, become destabilized, and then must be restarted on medication, often multiple times and with stops in emergency rooms and psychiatric wards along the way.
            *   This practice burdens clinicians and caregivers with excessive documentation and causes treatment disruptions, rather than supporting individualized, quality, evidence-based care.
            *   While the Revised Long-Term Care (LTC) Surveyor Guidance is directed at surveyors, the policies it instructs surveyors to enforce—such as rigid rules on PRN (as-needed) antipsychotic orders, mandatory behavioral intervention tracking, and ongoing gradual dose reduction requirements—translate directly into burdensome obligations for providers.
            *   Facilities must expend substantial resources creating and maintaining extensive documentation, not because it enhances clinical outcomes, but because it is necessary to demonstrate compliance with inflexible and untested federal standards.
            *   The Long-Stay Antipsychotic Medication quality measure duplicates existing medication review and quality assurance programs at the state level and overlaps internally with Medicare's own oversight mechanisms, such as the Plan Program Integrity Medicare Drug Integrity Contractors (PPI MEDICs).
            *   Additionally, the 917-page Revised LTC Surveyor Guidance already includes nearly 20 pages related to psychotropic medication use, including documentation of behavioral interventions, justification for medication use, and gradual dose reduction mandates, which facilities must already follow during survey and certification reviews.
            *   As a result, the use of this measure in the Five-Star Rating System introduces unnecessary and overlapping scrutiny on top of what providers are already required to demonstrate through MDS documentation and during state surveys.
        *   2. Carries Excessive Penalties and Misleads Beneficiaries and Families
            *   The measure’s heavy weighting in the Nursing Home Care Compare Five-Star Rating system can result in significant star rating downgrades for minor documentation discrepancies.
            *   It misrepresents quality of care to families evaluating long-term care facilities and unfairly penalizes facilities serving high-need populations.
            *   The outsized weighting of the Long-Stay Antipsychotic Medication quality measure over other nursing home quality measures can mislead beneficiaries and their families regarding a local nursing facility’s overall safety.
            *   On CMS’s Nursing Home Care Compare Five-Star Rating system, each facility’s reported “percentage of long-stay residents who received antipsychotic medication” is listed, along with national and state averages for comparison.
            *   No further information is provided to offer context on how to interpret results for this measure, except two general statements: “lower percentages are better” and “antipsychotic medications can be used to treat certain mental health conditions.”
            *   This reported percentage may reflect a facility’s adherence to CMS’s detailed reporting requirements but does not tell individuals and families anything about the quality of care at a facility with respect to the appropriate use of medications, as the measure only counts how many people receive an antipsychotic without any regard for medical necessity or appropriateness.
        *   3. Conflicts with Patient-Centered Care and Published Guidelines
            *   The current measure disregards and contradicts clinical practice guidelines published by the APA, which support the appropriate use of these medications in managing dementia-related agitation and psychosis, and does not reflect clinical standards used in other areas of care.
            *   The APA Practice Guideline on the Use of Antipsychotics to Treat Agitation or Psychosis in Patients with Dementia notes that while administrative data allow calculations of antipsychotic use rates, they have confounds and do not provide details about reasons for prescribing or symptom severity, thus reflecting use but not *appropriate use*.
            *   The APA guideline reflects the medical consensus that antipsychotics can be both appropriate and beneficial for certain patients when nonpharmacological interventions are ineffective or contraindicated.
            *   By contrast, CMS’s existing Long-Stay Antipsychotic Medication quality measure imposes a one-size-fits-all rigid standard, effectively discouraging any pharmacologic intervention unless non-drug alternatives are exhausted.
            *   CMS’s current framework not only contradicts expert clinical guidance but also conflicts with the agency’s own stated intent to support care tailored to a resident’s “specific, diagnosed, and documented condition.”
            *   In practice, CMS policies default to a blanket assumption that all use of antipsychotics is harmful, regardless of a particular patient’s diagnosis, clinical history, wants, or response to treatment.
        *   4. Impedes Access to or Delivery of Care or Services and Interferes in the Practice of Medicine
            *   This 2012 measure conflicts with Section 1801 of the Social Security Act, which expressly prohibits federal interference in the practice of medicine.
            *   CMS’s Revised Long-Term Care (LTC) Surveyor Guidance, which directs oversight of antipsychotic prescribing practices, underscores CMS’ interference with the practice of medicine as it includes extensive requirements for psychotropic prescribing, including strict rules for PRN (as needed) orders, behavioral intervention assessments, and gradual dose reduction mandates.
            *   These requirements effectively dictate clinical practice by requiring facilities to document extensive justifications for any use of antipsychotics, regardless of patient-specific clinical needs.
            *   The measure creates an inflexible and burdensome framework that limits clinician judgment and ultimately prohibits patients from receiving the care they need.
            *   The cumulative effect is a one-size-fits-all oversight model that lacks sensitivity to individual patient needs and clinical judgment, ultimately conflicting with the principle that CMS should not dictate medical practice.
            *   The measure often causes beneficiaries who have been stable on antipsychotic medications while living in the community to be taken off of their medications once admitted for a long-stay in a SNF; the type of care and medication a beneficiary receives should be dictated by their diagnosis and specific clinical characteristics, not the site of care where they are being treated.
    *   Solution:
        *   Eliminating the measure from public quality reporting while making several low-burden, meaningful changes to the MDS would support transparency, protect patient safety, and allow clinicians to provide individualized care consistent with the latest professional psychiatric standards.
        *   This measure, not governed by formal notice-and-comment rulemaking, could be removed through subregulatory channels, including issuing a Quality Safety & Oversight (QSO) memoranda or updates to the Nursing Home Care Compare Technical Users’ Guide.
        *   This flexible authority makes it a prime candidate for elimination under the Administration’s deregulatory agenda.
        *   Project PAUSE recommends that HHS and CMS work to change the MDS to:
            *   Expand the reasons for why gradual dose reduction has not been attempted to include a new category stating: “documented use of the drug and dose as clinically appropriate;” and
            *   Require that in cases where gradual dose reduction has not been attempted, both a physician and a pharmacist must independently document that gradual dose reduction is either clinically contraindicated or that the use of the drug and dose are clinically appropriate and beneficial.
        *   These low-burden improvements to the MDS would yield more meaningful information for oversight and facility surveyors.
        *   Expanding the list of acceptable reasons for not attempting gradual dose reduction and requiring attestation by both a physician and a pharmacist would add clinical nuance without adding significant reporting complexity.
        *   For patients stable on antipsychotic medication with a documented ongoing need and benefit from treatment, ideally providers would not need to regularly restate why gradual dose reduction has not been attempted as they are clearly contraindicated.
        *   This tailored approach could significantly reduce administrative burden and maintain program integrity while allowing facilities and surveyors to focus on the quality of care provided to skilled nursing and long-term care residents.
*   These two suggestions for reform within HHS would allow the Trump Administration to repeal nearly 30 regulations and would serve to protect patients and Medicare beneficiaries, ensuring they have access to the care they need.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The Alliance for Aging Research recommends HHS eliminate burdensome and illegal "Coverage with Evidence Development" policies and an unscientific antipsychotic medication measure in nursing home ratings, advocating for policies that prioritize patient access and appropriate care over administrative hurdles.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Alliance for Aging Research
- **Type:** Advocacy Group
- **Role/Expertise:** Leading nonprofit organization dedicated to changing the narrative to achieve healthy aging and equitable access to care; strives for a culture that embraces healthy aging and values science and investments.
- **Geographic Scope:** National
- **Stake in Issue:** Advocate for older adults, aiming to ensure beneficiaries have equitable access to necessary FDA-approved drugs, devices, and appropriate medical care under Medicare, free from unnecessary administrative and regulatory barriers.
structuredSections.corePosition: We urge HHS to eliminate current "Coverage with Evidence Development" policies, which we believe lack statutory authority and create significant, harmful barriers to Medicare beneficiary access to FDA-approved drugs and devices. Concurrently, we advocate for the removal of the Long-Stay Antipsychotic Medication quality measure from the Nursing Home Care Compare Five-Star Quality Rating System, as it is unscientific, punitive, and interferes with appropriate patient-centered care.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
*   **Eliminate all Coverage with Evidence Development (CED) policies:**
    *   Withdraw the three specific Guidance documents: "Coverage with Evidence Development Guidance Document," "CMS National Coverage Analysis Evidence Review Guidance Document," and "Medicare Program; Transitional Coverage for Emerging Technologies."
    *   Repeal all 25 individual CEDs currently in effect.
    *   Withdraw the proposed "Study Protocols That Use Real-world Data" guidance entirely.
    *   Restore the January 14, 2021 Advisory Opinion by the CMS General Counsel that concluded there is no statutory authority for CED.
    *   Default to coverage of on-label use for FDA-approved drugs and defer coverage decisions for items/services of uncertain medical necessity to regional administrative contractors for claim-by-claim determinations.
*   **Remove the Long-Stay Antipsychotic Medication Quality Measure from the CMS Nursing Home Care Compare Five-Star Quality Rating System:**
    *   Remove this measure through subregulatory channels (e.g., Quality Safety & Oversight memoranda or updates to the Nursing Home Care Compare Technical Users’ Guide).
    *   **Modernize the Minimum Data Set (MDS) to better distinguish appropriate and inappropriate use of antipsychotics:**
        *   Expand the list of reasons why gradual dose reduction has not been attempted to include a new category: "documented use of the drug and dose as clinically appropriate."
        *   Require that in cases where gradual dose reduction has not been attempted, both a physician and a pharmacist must independently document that gradual dose reduction is either clinically contraindicated or that the use of the drug and dose are clinically appropriate and beneficial.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
*   **Coverage with Evidence Development (CED) policies are unlawful and hinder access:**
    *   They lack statutory authority, as concluded by a previous CMS General Counsel Advisory Opinion.
    *   They impose vague, subjective, and nonworkable "clinical trial" or "registry" barriers that delay or deny Medicare coverage for FDA-approved drugs and devices.
    *   The CED process is administratively burdensome for beneficiaries and providers, forcing participation in trials and compromising patient safety and Medicare program integrity.
    *   It directly interferes with the practice of medicine by dictating treatment parameters, which Section 1801 of the Medicare law prohibits.
    *   The proposed "Study Protocols That Use Real-world Data" guidance would significantly expand CED, transforming it into an ongoing federal research mandate that undermines FDA authority and exceeds CMS's statutory power.
*   **The Long-Stay Antipsychotic Medication quality measure is flawed and harmful:**
    *   It is unscientific, punitive, and uses a blunt formula that simply counts antipsychotic use without distinguishing between appropriate and inappropriate prescribing.
    *   It only exempts three diagnoses (schizophrenia, Huntington’s, Tourette’s) from the measure, notably excluding bipolar disorder, which conflicts with clinical guidelines (e.g., APA, NQF).
    *   The measure leads to clinically necessary treatments being withheld, causing harm to residents (e.g., inappropriate discontinuation, destabilization, emergency room visits).
    *   It forces facilities to prioritize regulatory compliance over individualized, patient-centered care.
    *   It imposes overly complex documentation requirements, mandates gradual dose reduction regardless of clinical context, and creates unnecessary treatment disruptions.
    *   The measure carries excessive penalties due to its heavy weighting in the Five-Star rating system, leading to misleading quality ratings and unfairly penalizing facilities serving high-need populations.
    *   It duplicates existing state and federal oversight mechanisms, creating redundant and overlapping scrutiny for providers.
    *   It conflicts with patient-centered care principles and published clinical guidelines, assuming all antipsychotic use is harmful and dictating clinical practice.
    *   It causes beneficiaries who were stable on antipsychotics in the community to be taken off their medications upon admission to SNFs, demonstrating interference with the practice of medicine based on site of care rather than clinical need.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
*   The comment highlights an extensive analysis from a *Health Affairs* article by Joe Grogan, revealing that out of 27 medical devices/procedures subjected to CED since 2005, only 4 successfully graduated, with most remaining in a "never-ending coverage purgatory" for up to 20 years.
*   It points out that the CED program involves over 30 complex steps just to establish a program, leading to significant administrative barriers and resource requirements that inhibit evidence development, often with unclear cost responsibilities.
*   The comment cites specific ethical dilemmas for beneficiaries under CED, such as potentially being required to receive a placebo for an FDA-approved drug or device, and even paying coinsurance for it, along with concerns about historical mistrust and privacy of personal health data in clinical studies.
*   It brings attention to a rescinded Advisory Opinion from the Trump Administration's HHS General Counsel, Robert Charrow, which explicitly concluded that CMS lacked legal authority to implement the CED program, suggesting a fundamental legal flaw that was later suppressed.
*   Regarding the antipsychotic measure, the comment highlights that forcing gradual dose reduction, regardless of patient history or stability, results in a detrimental cycle where residents are destabilized, requiring repeated emergency room visits and restarts on medication, illustrating a clear negative unintended consequence of regulatory overreach.
*   It points out the discrepancy between CMS's antipsychotic measure, which exempts only three conditions, and clinical guidelines from the American Psychiatric Association and National Quality Forum, which include bipolar disorder, demonstrating a significant gap between regulatory standards and medical consensus.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
*   "The fact is CED is a never-ending coverage purgatory for innovators, with more than 30 complex steps required simply to establish a program."
*   "CMS should scrap CED altogether, choosing instead to default to coverage of on-label use for FDA-approved drugs."
*   "The measure has led to clinically necessary treatments being withheld, causing harm to residents and burdening providers."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Ascension appreciates the opportunity to submit comments on the Request for Information: Deregulatory Plan (AHRQ-2025-0001) (the “Deregulatory RFI”).
*   Ascension is one of the nation’s leading non-profit and Catholic health systems, with a Mission of delivering compassionate, personalized care to all with special attention to those most vulnerable.
    *   In FY2024, Ascension provided $2.1 billion in care of persons living in poverty and other community benefit programs.
    *   Across 16 states and the District of Columbia, Ascension’s network encompasses approximately 106,000 associates, 26,000 aligned providers, 105 hospitals, and 34 senior living facilities.
*   Today, the myriad of regulations that health systems must engage in have become intensively burdensome and complicated.
    *   The landscape has created a structure that is often more punitive than instructive for systems.
    *   While Ascension is deeply committed to delivering safe, high-quality care and upholding rigorous standards to protect patient well-being, excessive or duplicative regulations can hinder our ability to fulfill our mission of serving the most vulnerable populations.
