*   Evaluating the impact of a hybrid closed-loop system on acute care utilization and costs compared to standard of care therapy among patients with type 1 diabetes new to pump therapy
    *   Introduction
        *   Type 1 Diabetes (T1D) makes up approximately 5-10% of all diabetes cases, yet the cost of treating T1D in adults is significantly higher per patient than treating Type 2 Diabetes (T2D).
        *   T1D-related hospitalizations are estimated to range from $6,548 to $8,439.
        *   Two major aspects of T1D management are monitoring of blood glucose levels and achieving glycemic control.
        *   Treatment options include multiple daily injections (MDI) and continuous subcutaneous insulin infusion (CSII) via insulin pumps.
        *   Compared to MDI therapy, hybrid closed-loop systems (HCLS) improve glycemic control and may impact acute care healthcare resource utilization (HCRU) in T1D.
        *   HCLS have demonstrated improved glycemic outcomes in Medicare and Medicaid patients with T1D and T2D.
        *   Real-world data on the impact of HCLS vs MDI on acute care utilization and costs among insured patients with T1D are lacking.
    *   Objective
        *   The purpose of this study was to compare the effect of HCLS vs MDI therapy on all-cause acute care HCRU and costs among patients with T1D using U.S. real-world data.
    *   Methods
        *   This was a retrospective, observational cohort study of de-identified data from the Veradigm Network EHR linked to claims and Tandem’s HCLS data.
            *   The study period was from January 15, 2019, to December 31, 2021, with a patient selection period from January 15, 2020, to December 31, 2020.
        *   Inclusion criteria: Patients with >1 inpatient or 2 outpatient claims (at least one day apart) with a diagnosis code for T1D; receiving insulin pump or MDI therapy between January 15, 2020, to December 31, 2020; continuous enrollment with medical and pharmacy benefits 12 months pre-index and 12 months post-index.
        *   The index date was defined as the date of the earliest evidence of a HCLS (Tandem t:slim X2 with Control-IQ technology or Medtronic MiniMed 670G) or MDI therapy during the patient selection period.
        *   Exclusion criteria: During the study period: Gestational diabetes diagnoses; history of dialysis, end-stage renal disease, and/or kidney transplant; pregnancy, labor or delivery, evidence of pre-mixed insulins for patients in the MDI therapy cohort; evidence of bariatric surgery. For patients in the pump cohort, those with evidence of other/unknown pumps were excluded.
        *   The HCLS cohort was limited to patients newly initiating pump therapy.
        *   Outcomes of interest included all-cause HCRU (inpatient (IP) admission, emergency department (ED) visits) and associated costs.
        *   Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were assessed during the 12-month baseline period.
        *   All-cause IP admissions, ED visits, and associated costs were assessed during the 12-month follow-up period.
        *   Significance testing used χ2 or z-tests for categorical variables and Wilcoxon rank sum test or t-test for continuous variables. Standardized differences were assessed on baseline characteristics.
        *   Logistic regression models estimated the odds of having an IP admission or ED visit, adjusted for baseline patient demographic characteristics (age, sex, region, index month, payer), baseline hyperglycemia, diabetes complications severity index (DCSI), non-insulin diabetic medication use, and presence of baseline IP or ED (for the IP and ED models, respectively).
        *   Two-part models were used.
        *   Logistic regression models were used to examine the probability of any costs in the follow-up period. GLM with log link and gamma link distribution were used to compare groups with respect to costs.
    *   Results
        *   A total of 35,237 patients met the study criteria and were included in the analysis: HCLS (n = 7,264) and MDI (n = 27,973) cohorts.
        *   HCLS patients were younger than MDI patients (mean age 26.7 (SD=16.9) vs 33.7 (SD=17.5) years, p<0.001) and both cohorts were majority male (52.1% HCLS vs. 57% MDI).
        *   Baseline mean DCSI was slightly higher among the MDI cohort as compared to HCLS (2.5 (SD=1.6) vs. 2.2 (SD=1.8), p<0.001).
        *   Among the individual DCSI conditions, metabolic (HCLS: 50.0%; MDI: 41.4%), neuropathy (HCLS: 16.1%; MDI: 20.9%), and retinopathy/ophthalmic conditions (HCLS: 14.0%; MDI: 17.9%) were most common.
        *   In the unadjusted descriptive analyses, both HCLS and MDI resulted in reductions in HCRU: HCLS had greater reductions in all-cause inpatient admissions (-12.8% vs -3.9%, p<0.001) and all-cause ED visits (-14.5% vs -8.4%, p<0.001).
        *   Both HCLS and MDI had reductions in costs associated with IP admissions and ED visits.
        *   HCLS had lower costs pre- and post-index, with significantly greater reductions in all-cause inpatient costs (-$1,209 vs. to -$171, p<0.001), but similar rates of all-cause ED visits (-$498 vs. -$404, p=0.31).
        *   In adjusted modeling, the odds of an all-cause IP admission were greater for MDI compared to HCLS (OR=1.59, 95% CI: 1.43-1.76).
        *   The MDI cohort had a higher odds of an all-cause ED visit compared to HCLS (OR=1.44, 95% CI: 1.34-1.56).
        *   Compared to HCLS, the MDI cohort incurred $1,845 higher IP costs during the 12-month follow-up period (CR=1.63, 95% CI: 1.40-1.91).
        *   Compared to HCLS, the MDI cohort incurred $631 higher ED costs (CR=1.54, 95% CI: 1.39-1.70).
    *   Discussion
        *   In this study utilizing EHR linked to claims data of U.S. patients with T1D, use of HCLS incurred lower acute care HCRU and subsequent costs (IP, ED) than use of MDI over a 12-month follow-up period.
        *   Results from this real-world study are consistent with prior health economic modeling studies.
        *   HCLS has been shown to be more cost effective than MDI in the pediatric population.
        *   Studies have found that CSII treatment costs are offset by direct cost savings from avoidance of diabetes-related complications.
        *   Health economic modeling studies have illustrated the cost-effectiveness of the HCLS systems when compared to MDI.
        *   Our findings support the use of HCLS to reduce acute care utilization as compared to MDI therapy.
        *   Study limitations: This study used claims and EHR data, which includes limitations when used for research purposes, such as data entry errors, missing data, and coding specificity limitations. The dataset used in this analysis only included insured individuals and may not be representative of the US population.
    *   Conclusion
        *   Patients with T1D who initiate HCLS therapy were significantly less likely to experience IP and ED visits and incurred lower healthcare costs compared to patients who remain on MDI therapy.
    *   Disclosures
        *   This study was funded by Tandem Diabetes Care.
        *   Several authors are employees of Veradigm, which received funding from Tandem Diabetes Care to conduct this study, or are employees of Tandem Diabetes Care. Medical writing support was provided by Matt Salt of Veradigm.

*   Diabetes Technology Access Coalition’s Response to Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again
    *   The Diabetes Technology Access Coalition (DTAC) appreciates the opportunity to provide comments to the Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS) Request for Information (RFI) on Deregulation.
    *   Collectively, DTAC members represent millions of Americans with diabetes, health care professionals who treat them, and major manufacturers that develop diabetes therapies, equipment, and supplies.
    *   While DTAC has made strides in expanding Medicare coverage of diabetes technologies, ever evolving clinical evidence and innovation has outpaced the federal government’s bureaucracy.
    *   DTAC is pleased that HHS is interested in garnering stakeholder feedback on how to reduce regulatory burdens that will in turn improve interest in and access to critical diabetes technologies.
    *   **What regulations should we reconsider as we look to achieve some of the policy objectives outlined in Executive Order (EO) 14212, “Establishing the President's Make America Healthy Again Commission,” to focus on reversing chronic disease?**
        *   DTAC’s primary goal is to remove access barriers to a wide range of cost-effective and proven interventions, including educational resources, such as Medicare’s diabetes self-management training (DSMT) benefit, and diabetes technologies, such as continuous glucose monitors (CGMs) and insulin pumps.
        *   Improving Access to DSMT
            *   DSMT is a proven and effective intervention that teaches individuals, among other things, to administer medications and implement healthy lifestyle changes to improve diabetes management.
            *   Additionally, DSMT helps individuals set-up and use diabetes technologies, which is especially essential given the innovative advancements that have been recently made in this field, and that will be made in the coming years.
            *   DSMT has been shown to improve clinical outcomes and quality of life, while simultaneously reducing hospitalizations and healthcare spending.
            *   One study found that health service utilization and costs among newly diagnosed Medicare beneficiaries who used DSMT realized a 14 percent reduction of the chance of hospitalization, lower overall rates of hospitalizations and emergency department visits, and approximately $830 lower Medicare expenditures compared to non-DSMT users.
            *   The American Diabetes Association (ADA) considers DSMT to be “a vital component of the full treatment for diabetes,” and its 2025 Standards of Care recommends that “[a]ll individuals with diabetes should be advised to participate in developmentally and culturally appropriate diabetes self-management education and support (DSMES).”
            *   Given the proven clinical benefit of DSMT among individuals with diabetes, any unnecessary barriers for beneficiaries to access this benefit must be remedied.
            *   Accordingly, we recommend that HHS and the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) remove regulatory barriers to the DSMT benefit by:
                *   Streamlining DSMT referral orders (e.g., eliminating the requirement that the referring provider include the number of sessions, frequency, and areas of need in the referral order, per 42 CFR 410.141(b)).
                *   Providing flexibility by allowing more personalized DSMT care (e.g., removing the requirement that the majority of the initial DSMT benefit be given in a group setting per 42 CFR 410.141(c)(1)).
                *   Increasing the availability and flexibility of the limited number of DSMT hours an individual can receive per 42 CFR 410.141(c).
                *   Simplifying DSMT program accreditation process (see 42 CFR 410.144 and 42 CFR 410.145).
                *   Allowing DSMT and another essential service, medical nutrition therapy (MNT), to be delivered on the same day (see 42 CFR 410.72(b)(3)).
            *   With these changes, more Medicare beneficiaries can access critical educational interventions that allow them to learn how to manage their condition including by learning how to appropriately use diabetes technologies to best manage their condition.
        *   Improving Access to Diabetes Technologies
            *   CGMs, whether paired with or without an insulin pump, have been shown to effectively manage an individual’s type 1 or type 2 diabetes and for some individuals who suffer from severe reoccurring hypoglycemic events.
            *   All insulin pumps currently available in the United States pair with a CGM, and through the use of an algorithm can control the flow of insulin provided based on the CGM’s glucose readings.
            *   This combination of technologies, often called automated insulin delivery (AID) systems, has been shown to improve clinical benchmarks in both adults with type 1 diabetes and adults with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes.
            *   Given this evidence base, both ADA and the American Association of Clinical Endocrinology (AACE) state that CGMs, insulin pumps, and AID systems are part of the standard of care for individuals with diabetes.
            *   Individuals with diabetes uniquely experience their disease and therefore greatly benefit from individualized care as jointly determined by the individual and their health care professional.
            *   This includes ensuring that individuals with diabetes have ready access to the CGM of their choice, as CGMs can vary in their functionality and usability.
            *   Accordingly, to advance the administration’s goals of “aggressively combat[ing]” diabetes, and that agencies “ensure the availability of expanded treatment options and the flexibility for health insurance coverage to provide benefits that support beneficial lifestyle changes and disease prevention,” we urge HHS to ensure there are no impediments to the ability for individuals to select the CGM that works best for them.
            *   In part, to advance this recommendation, HHS should modify and rescind, respectively, two outdated National Coverage Determinations (NCD) issued by CMS: NCD 280.14 for insulin pumps and NCD 40.2 for CGMs.
            *   Both NCDs were last updated in the mid-2000s and no longer reflect the current clinical evidence or standards of care, creating inappropriate barriers to Medicare beneficiaries accessing life-sustaining diabetes technologies.
    *   **For more general deregulatory consideration under EO 14192, are there additional HHS regulations and/or guidance that are confusing or unnecessarily complicated; Require an excessive number of reports or unreasonable record keeping, or information that is not needed or used effectively; Impose requirements on the wrong individual or group; Impede access to or delivery of care or services, . . . Impede efforts to innovate, are obsolete; and/or Otherwise interfere with the public or private sector's ability to address chronic health conditions or otherwise promote the health and wellbeing of Americans?**
    *   **What alternative approaches could be taken to achieve or accomplish the same goal with a lesser burden? For example, are there less burdensome approaches that are used by other entities such as State governments or private companies that could be adopted by HHS to achieve its goal with less burdensome requirements? What would be the impact on costs and savings?**
        *   Despite CGMs and insulin pumps being part of the standard of care for individuals with diabetes, CMS’s coverage policies for these devices continue to be confusing, impede access to care and innovation, do not reflect current clinical evidence, impose unnecessary paperwork requirements, and generally interfere with the public or private sector’s ability to address chronic health conditions.
        *   Specifically, we wish to focus on the harms presented by two NCDs, one for insulin pumps and one for CGMs.
        *   The current NCD for insulin pumps (NCD 280.14) is unnecessarily confusing and complicated and is not based on the latest clinical evidence.
            *   NCD 280.14 has not been updated in 20 years and is significantly misaligned with the current clinical evidence and standards of care.
            *   For example, the NCD conditions insulin pump coverage on the results of a C-peptide/beta cell autoantibody test, which imposes unreasonable recordkeeping requirements on beneficiaries and providers.
            *   These tests are no longer utilized to determine insulin pump eligibility by commercial insurers, and for those individuals who had these tests performed, it was likely many years before becoming eligible for Medicare.
            *   Further, clinical evidence shows that these tests are an imperfect metric to determine whether an insulin pump would be medically appropriate for an individual with diabetes and should be abandoned in favor of more dispositive evidence that demonstrates when insulin pumps improve clinical outcomes.
            *   The current NCD also is inconsistent with commercial insurance coverage criteria for insulin pumps and misaligned with coverage for CGMs, impeding coverage of and beneficiary access to AID systems.
            *   Recognizing this, in February 2022, a group of leading diabetes clinicians, supported by DTAC, requested that CMS update NCD 280.14 to align with the current clinical evidence and standards of care. The agency – despite this request being submitted more than three years ago – has still not acted on this request.
            *   In the intervening three years, more developments have emerged that further support the reconsideration request, such as a randomized control trial (RCT) demonstrating that the use of an AID system was associated with improved clinical benchmarks compared to only using a CGM among adults with insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved AID systems for the type 2 diabetes population.
            *   Every day that CMS fails to act on this request means additional, preventable adverse events for Medicare beneficiaries who would otherwise benefit from using an insulin pump. This hinders access to a proven tool that help Americans manage one of the most common and costly chronic diseases.
        *   While CGMs are commonly considered a device for the management of diabetes, CGMs offer substantial and proven benefits to individuals who experience severe reoccurring hypoglycemic events, such as individuals who have had bariatric surgery, certain cancers, and pancreatectomies.
            *   These events can be life threatening and are relatively common following bariatric surgery, even in the absence of diabetes.
            *   However, CMS’s NCD 40.2 restricts coverage of home blood glucose monitoring, including via CGMs, to individuals with diabetes.
            *   This is despite significant clinical evidence that demonstrates that CGM use post-bariatric surgery significantly reduces the occurrence of hypoglycemic events and ADA’s recommendation that individuals use CGMs post-bariatric surgery to monitor for hypoglycemia.
            *   These developments arose within the last few years, which underscores the obsolescence of NCD 40.2, which was last updated in 2006.
            *   Given that NCD 40.2 poses dangerous restrictions to care and is misaligned with both clinical evidence and standards of care, we recommend that NCD 40.2 be rescinded and that the Durable Medical Equipment Medicare Administrative Contractors (DME MACs) update their Local Coverage Determination (LCD) for CGMs (LCD L33822) to expand coverage to populations where the clinical evidence supports CGM use.
            *   This is especially important as additional research is conducted on the efficacy of CGMs for individuals with prediabetes – a growing segment of the Medicare and general populations. Medicare must be ready to update coverage policies consistent with emerging clinical evidence.
    *   **Are there HHS regulations, guidance, or reporting requirements that are rooted in outdated technology? Can new technologies be leveraged to allow for rescinding or updating these policies? What are the cost implications?**
        *   As noted above, NCDs 280.4 and 40.2 were last updated almost 20 years ago in 2005 and 2006, respectively.
        *   Today, the antiquated coverage criteria only serve to hinder access to life-changing technologies.
        *   The innovation in diabetes technology is wide-ranging, and these NCDs do not account for undisputed clinical benefit these technologies provide.
        *   As an example, none of these NCDs incorporate coverage for the software or algorithm that serves as the “brain” of the AID system as it controls the flow of insulin provided to an individual.
        *   Without streamlined coverage criteria that allows for nimble changes to account for new technologies, like the software or algorithm of an AID system, Medicare beneficiaries could lose access to new innovative new technologies that have the potential to reduce health care costs to both the individual, the Medicare Trust Fund, and society.
        *   CGMs can significantly reduce diabetes-related adverse events such as hospitalizations and emergency department visits, decreasing overall health care spending.
            *   One study found that individuals with type 2 diabetes realized a 39.4 percent reduction in diabetes-related hospitalizations following the inception of CGM use.
            *   Another study found that the same population realized between a 32 to 57 percent reduction in acute diabetes-related hospitalizations following CGM initiation (depending on whether the individual was not taking insulin, using basal insulin, or using prandial insulin prior to CGM initiation).
            *   The savings associated with CGMs are not isolated to reduced hospitalizations, as they have also been found to reduce diabetes-related emergency room visits among the type 2 diabetes population following real-time CGM initiation.
            *   Accordingly, studies have estimated that CGM use is associated with per month, per patient (PMPP) savings of between $329 to $424.
            *   CGM coverage is predicated on NCD 40.2 and the Local Coverage Determination LCD L33822.
            *   We note that, in contrast to the NCD process, the DME MACs have consistently updated the CGM coverage criteria to ensure coverage is based on current clinical evidence.
            *   DTAC has supported a recent request for reconsideration of LCD L33822 to account for new evidence and updated Standards of Care. We ask for CMS’s support in ensuring the DME MACs timely consider and issue a proposed LCD reflecting the requested changes.
        *   Similarly, research demonstrates that insulin pump and AID system initiation reduces health care spending among both the type 1 and type 2 diabetes population.
            *   Among the type 1 diabetes population, research shows that individuals using an AID system realized significantly lower rates of all-cause inpatient admissions (-12.8 percent vs -3.9 percent) and all-cause emergency department visits (-14.5 percent vs -8.4 percent) compared to those using multiple daily insulin injections.
            *   Accordingly, AID system use was associated with lower costs, primarily due to lower rates of inpatient admissions.
            *   Specifically, administering multiple daily insulin injections was associated with significantly higher inpatient admission costs and higher emergency department costs during a 12 month follow-up period compared to AID system use.
            *   Cost savings from insulin pump use is likewise demonstrated in the type 2 diabetes population.
            *   Using real-world data, one modeling study found that among a simulated cohort of one million individuals, those with type 2 diabetes who switched from multiple daily insulin injections to a form of an AID system, Control-IQ, realized a total yearly savings of $15.1 million on non-insulin medication spending.
            *   This modeling study only assessed the avoidance of costs associated with medications; other studies have validated cost savings associated with the AID system in terms of avoiding downstream healthcare utilization.
            *   Taken together, there are significant, multifaceted cost savings available with the availability and adoption of AID systems.
        *   While CMS does not consider therapy costs in making coverage decisions, we emphasize that expanding access to critical diabetes technologies such as CGMs, insulin pumps, and AID systems, can yield significant savings to our health care system by both avoiding unnecessary health care utilization and by ensuring individuals’ diabetes is optimally managed via use of these technologies.
        *   We hope that this information further emphasizes the importance of removing barriers to coverage for CGMs and insulin pumps for populations where clinical evidence supports their use.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The Diabetes Technology Access Coalition (DTAC), representing patients, providers, and manufacturers, advocates for regulatory changes to outdated Medicare coverage policies for diabetes self-management training and advanced diabetes technologies, citing substantial clinical evidence and cost savings potential for improved patient outcomes and reduced healthcare utilization.

-   **Clinical Efficacy and Cost Savings of Diabetes Self-Management Training (DSMT):** A study found that newly diagnosed Medicare beneficiaries who used DSMT realized a 14% reduction in the chance of hospitalization, lower overall rates of hospitalizations and emergency department (ED) visits, and approximately $830 lower Medicare expenditures compared to non-DSMT users.
-   **Real-World Evidence for Hybrid Closed-Loop Systems (HCLS) vs. Multiple Daily Injections (MDI) in Type 1 Diabetes:** A study comparing HCLS to MDI therapy among 35,237 insured U.S. patients with Type 1 Diabetes found that HCLS users had significantly lower rates of all-cause inpatient (IP) admissions (-12.8% vs -3.9% for MDI) and all-cause ED visits (-14.5% vs -8.4% for MDI) compared to MDI users. The study showed HCLS led to significantly greater reductions in all-cause inpatient costs (-$1,209 vs. -$171 for MDI) and, in adjusted modeling, MDI incurred $1,845 higher inpatient costs and $631 higher ED costs compared to HCLS.
-   **Significant Cost Savings of Continuous Glucose Monitors (CGMs):** One study found that individuals with Type 2 Diabetes realized a 39.4% reduction in diabetes-related hospitalizations after initiating CGM use; another found T2D patients experienced between a 32% to 57% reduction in acute diabetes-related hospitalizations. CGM use is associated with estimated per month, per patient (PMPP) savings of between $329 to $424 due to reduced hospitalizations and ED visits.
-   **Cost Savings of Automated Insulin Delivery (AID) Systems in Type 2 Diabetes:** A modeling study estimated that among a simulated cohort of one million individuals with Type 2 Diabetes, those who switched from multiple daily insulin injections to an AID system (Control-IQ) realized a total yearly savings of $15.1 million on non-insulin medication spending.
-   **Outdated Policies Impeding Care:** CMS's NCD 40.2 restricts CGM coverage to individuals with diabetes, despite strong clinical evidence (and ADA recommendations) for its use in non-diabetic individuals experiencing severe recurrent hypoglycemia (e.g., post-bariatric surgery), where such events can be life-threatening. The fact that FDA has approved AID systems for the Type 2 Diabetes population underscores how CMS's NCDs are lagging behind current clinical advancements and evidence.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
-   "While DTAC has made strides in expanding Medicare coverage of diabetes technologies, ever evolving clinical evidence and innovation has outpaced the federal government’s bureaucracy."
-   "Every day that CMS fails to act on this request means additional, preventable adverse events for Medicare beneficiaries who would otherwise benefit from using an insulin pump."
-   "The innovation in diabetes technology is wide-ranging, and these NCDs do not account for undisputed clinical benefit these technologies provide."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   ACHP appreciates the opportunity to provide recommendations for reducing regulatory burden, improving care delivery, and unleashing innovation within the health care system.
    *   Our organization has long championed commonsense reforms that promote affordability, patient access, and market competition.
    *   We applaud the Administration’s commitment to restoring regulatory balance and advancing economic growth through the thoughtful reassessment of outdated and unnecessarily complex rules.
*   ACHP is the only national organization advancing a unique payer-provider aligned model of care that fosters competition and delivers high-quality coverage.
    *   Our member companies are nonprofit, community-based health plans that serve millions of Americans across nearly 40 states and the District of Columbia.
    *   Operating on margins of one to three percent, ACHP members remain in their markets when other carriers exit and lead the industry in driving administrative efficiency and innovation on behalf of patients.
*   With the Administration’s focus on restoring the rule of law, reversing chronic disease, and improving government efficiency, the Department has a historic opportunity to modernize outdated guidance, streamline implementation, and ensure that regulatory actions deliver value to patients.
    *   ACHP and its member companies are eager to collaborate with the MAHA Commission to make meaningful impact on the health of America’s children.
    *   In 2023, we launched the ACHP Chronic Disease Pledge, a ten-year commitment to reduce the incidence of diabetes, heart disease, and childhood obesity in communities across the country.
        *   This commitment goes beyond slogans and is rooted in on-the-ground local solutions.
    *   ACHP is leading significant research on the utilization and adoption of continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) to help improve outcomes, facilitate better behavioral decisions, and enhance quality of life for patients with diabetes.
*   As agencies across the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) work to implement Executive Orders 14219, 14212, and 14192, ACHP offers the following high-impact recommendations for immediate action.
*   High-Impact Recommendations for Regulatory Repeal and Reform under Executive Order 14219: Restoring the Rule of Law, Federalism, and Economic Growth by Reviewing Regulatory Actions
    *   Terminate the Medicare Prescription Payment Program created under the Inflation Reduction Act.
        *   While ACHP supports the goal of reducing out-of-pocket costs, the program imposes significant administrative burden on health plans with minimal value for beneficiaries.
        *   Eliminating this requirement would reduce wasteful spending and allow plans to focus resources on care delivery.
    *   Ensure consistent Part D coverage for transplant-related immunosuppressants.
        *   Under Chapter 6 of the Medicare Prescription Drug Benefit Manual (PDBM), some self-administered transplant drugs are processed under Part B with different cost-sharing rules depending on whether the transplant was Medicare-covered.
        *   This fragmented coverage structure creates member confusion and operational inefficiencies.
        *   All transplant-related drugs should be covered under Part D.
    *   Modify the 2025 Defined Standard Part D Benefit to eliminate incentives for high-rebate originator products.
        *   Current policy design encourages plans to cover high-cost originators with larger rebates, undermining the use of lower-cost alternatives and increasing total program spending.
        *   Adjusting the benefit structure would promote value-based formulary decisions.
    *   Remove restrictions against negative formulary changes during the benefit year.
        *   Section 30.3.3.1 of Chapter 6 in the PDBM prohibits plans from adjusting formularies mid-year, even when pricing, availability, or new evidence warrant changes.
        *   This restriction drives unnecessary costs for beneficiaries, plans, and the federal government.
    *   Finalize rulemaking to allow accumulator programs and clarify manufacturer coupon treatment.
        *   ACHP urges HHS to issue final regulations resolving outstanding issues in HIV+ Hepatitis Policy Institute v. HHS.
        *   Plans need certainty that manufacturer assistance does not constitute cost sharing under the Affordable Care Act (ACA).
        *   This rule would support plan design flexibility and consumer cost transparency.
*   Advancing Chronic Disease Prevention under Executive Order 14212, Establishing the President’s Make America Healthy Again Commission
    *   Eliminate the fragmented vaccine coverage framework across Medicare Parts B and D.
        *   Under Chapter 6, Section 10.14 of the PDBM, certain vaccines are reimbursed through Part B, while others are only available under Part D.
        *   This creates confusion for patients and providers and deters vaccine uptake.
        *   Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) should allow payment for all vaccines at any pharmacy or medical office and enable provider billing directly through CMS to simplify the immunization experience.
*   Reducing Red Tape under Executive Order 14192, Improving Government Efficiency and Reducing Regulatory Burdens
    *   Align timelines for drug exception requests under ACA and Medicare Part D.
        *   Section 156.122 under the ACA prohibits tolling and mandates a 72-hour review window from the time of initial request.
        *   In contrast, Part D allows timelines to begin upon receipt of a provider’s supporting statement.
        *   This inconsistency leads to confusion and unnecessary administrative pressure.
        *   Aligning the timelines would streamline the process for providers, plans, and beneficiaries.
    *   Reverse IRA guidance counting Non-Covered Plan Pay toward True Out-of-Pocket (TrOOP) Costs under Enhanced Alternative plans.
        *   Counting plan-paid amounts toward a beneficiary’s TrOOP skews cost-sharing calculations and creates compliance risks.
        *   CMS should reverse this guidance and clarify that only member-incurred costs apply.
    *   Update the Defined Standard Part D Benefit to use fixed copays instead of percentage-based coinsurance.
        *   CMS already limits copays by tier in Enhanced Alternative plans.
        *   ACHP recommends extending this to the Defined Standard Benefit to simplify cost-sharing and improve consumer understanding of prescription drug costs.
*   We welcome the opportunity to support the Department’s efforts to modernize health care regulation and advance practical reforms that improve outcomes, reduce costs, and foster market competition.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- I am 67 now, and I was only diagnosed with ADHD two years ago.
  - It was my wife who figured it out, not a doctor.
  - She read something online and said, “This sounds just like you.”
  - I brushed her off at first, thinking I had made it this far.
  - But she kept pushing, and she was right.
  - I’ve spent my whole life forgetting stuff, misplacing tools, starting five jobs around the house and finishing none.
  - I always figured I was just scatterbrained or careless.
  - Now I know it wasn’t character; it was ADHD.
- Once I got on meds, it felt like someone finally adjusted the frequency in my brain.
  - Things clicked.
  - I could follow a thought through to the end.
  - I wasn’t spinning out all the time, and I wasn’t so irritable from constantly feeling like I was one step behind everything.
  - I even started sleeping better.
    - Before, I’d lie in bed for hours, my mind jumping around like a squirrel.
    - I’d think about all the things I forgot to do, things I meant to say, bills I might’ve left unpaid.
    - That’s anxiety, which I guess I didn’t know was tied to ADHD until recently.
- But the rules around these meds just don’t make sense.
  - My pharmacy’s out of stock more than they’re not.
  - Last month, I went 12 days without my medication.
    - I started getting snappy again, couldn’t focus, and couldn’t rest.
    - My wife noticed right away.
    - I was pacing around the house at 2 a.m., couldn’t sit still.
  - I called my doctor, and they said, “Sorry, can’t do anything till the 30 days are up.”
    - This is because it’s Schedule II.
    - There are no early refills, no alternatives, and no safety net.
    - I just had to wait it out.
    - I’m 67; I’ve waited long enough.
- What bothers me most is the way it makes you feel like you’re doing something wrong.
  - I followed the steps: got a diagnosis, saw a doctor, and paid my copays.
  - But because it’s a “controlled substance,” I get treated like I’m suspicious, like I’m trying to work the system.
  - It’s humiliating; I’m not abusing anything.
  - I just want to be able to think straight and not get yelled at for forgetting something my wife asked me to pick up.
  - That shouldn’t be too much to ask.
- Look, if people are misusing these meds, maybe it’s not because they’re bad people, but because the system’s so locked down it pushes folks to desperate places.
  - If you want to prevent diversion, start by making legal treatment actually accessible.
  - Don’t punish the people who are trying to do it right.
- Don’t kill off the only way I was able to finally get diagnosed; keep telehealth.
- Reclassify these meds so we’re not sitting next to fentanyl in the DEA’s book.
- Stop treating folks like me, good, honest folks, like criminals for wanting a little peace inside their own heads.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: A 67-year-old, recently diagnosed with ADHD, implores the agency to ease restrictive Schedule II regulations on stimulant medications, advocating for continued telehealth access and an end to the stigmatizing treatment of patients experiencing medication shortages.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
-   **Name/Organization:** Anonymous
-   **Type:** Individual
-   **Role/Expertise:** 67-year-old individual diagnosed with ADHD at age 65, personally affected by challenges in accessing and refilling prescribed stimulant medication.
-   **Geographic Scope:** National (implied, as commenting on federal regulation)
-   **Stake in Issue:** Directly impacted by federal regulations governing access to ADHD medications, including their Schedule II classification and associated refill restrictions, which affect his health, well-being, and experience of care.
structuredSections.corePosition: I believe that the current overly restrictive rules governing ADHD medications, particularly their Schedule II classification, are illogical and detrimental to legitimate patients like myself. The system’s approach to preventing misuse inadvertently creates significant barriers to care, fosters a sense of suspicion and humiliation for patients, and may even drive individuals to desperate measures.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   Maintain access to telehealth services for ADHD diagnosis and treatment.
-   Reclassify ADHD medications (stimulants) to a less restrictive schedule, separating them from substances like fentanyl.
-   Stop treating patients seeking legitimate ADHD treatment as suspicious or criminal.
    -   Make legal treatment actually accessible to prevent misuse and diversion, rather than punishing compliant individuals.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   **Medication Access Barriers:**
    -   Frequent pharmacy out-of-stock issues for prescribed ADHD medications.
    -   Strict 30-day refill rules and Schedule II classification prevent early refills or access to alternatives, leading to prolonged periods without essential medication (e.g., 12 days).
    -   Lack of a safety net or flexibility for patients experiencing supply disruptions.
-   **Patient Stigmatization and Humiliation:**
    -   Feeling treated like a suspicious individual or a criminal despite following all proper diagnostic and treatment protocols.
    -   Humiliation stemming from the perception of trying to "work the system" due to the medication's controlled substance designation.
-   **Detrimental Health Impacts:**
    -   Return of severe ADHD symptoms (irritability, inability to focus, restlessness, sleep disturbances, anxiety) during medication lapses.
    -   Significant negative impact on daily functioning and quality of life when unable to access medication.
-   **Counterproductive Regulatory Framework:**
    -   Belief that the overly "locked down" system, intended to prevent misuse, actually pushes individuals to "desperate places" by making legal treatment inaccessible.
    -   Concern that current regulations punish compliant patients rather than effectively addressing diversion.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
-   Received a late ADHD diagnosis at 65 (two years prior to commenting), which was initiated by his wife based on online research, highlighting the challenges of adult diagnosis and the crucial role of informal support.
-   Described the transformative impact of medication as "someone finally adjusted the frequency in my brain," leading to improvements in focus, reduced irritability, and better sleep, while also realizing previously attributed anxiety was linked to undiagnosed ADHD.
-   Experienced a distressing 12-day lapse in medication due to pharmacy shortages and regulatory restrictions, which led to a severe return of symptoms including pacing at 2 a.m. and significant distress.
-   Shared the profound personal humiliation of feeling "like I'm suspicious" and "like I'm trying to work the system" despite following all legitimate medical procedures, simply because his medication is a controlled substance.
-   Provided an insightful perspective that medication misuse might stem from the system being "so locked down it pushes folks to desperate places," rather than inherent bad intentions, advocating for greater accessibility to legal treatment as a prevention strategy.
