structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   We are echoing the sentiments submitted by the National Child Care Association (NCCA) in response to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) invitation for stakeholders to submit ideas for deregulatory actions through Regulations.gov, docket number AHRQ-2025-0001.
    *   We submit a number of items for the Department’s consideration for rule rescission or modification of guidance.
*   NCCA supports the Administration’s goals to reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens while maintaining the integrity of protecting children in licensed childcare facilities.

*   Comments Regarding 45 C.F.R. § 98 - Background Check Implementation
    *   History
        *   There are several components that make it difficult to enforce full compliance with federal background check requirements for child care workers, as mandated by the Child Care and Development Block Grant (CCDBG) Act of 2014.
        *   We urge the Department to revise interpretations that go beyond the plain meaning of the statute authorizing background checks.
        *   Individuals with histories of child abuse, violent crimes, or sexual offenses are not permitted to work in licensed child care settings.
            *   These requirements include FBI fingerprint checks, in-state and inter-state criminal history and sex offender registry reviews, and child abuse and neglect registry searches.
        *   Unfortunately, several states, most notably California, remain out of compliance with one or more of these provisions, despite federal deadlines and technical support made available through HHS.
            *   California’s continued failure to conduct required cross-state registry checks and fully implement screening requirements undermines the integrity of the national child care safety framework.
            *   It also places children at avoidable and unacceptable risk.

*   Comment Regarding Interpretation of “Supervision” in Background Check Requirements under 45 C.F.R. § 98.43
    *   We respectfully request HHS to revise its interpretation of “supervision of provisional employees” as used in the implementation of 45 C.F.R. § 98.43, which governs background check requirements for childcare providers under the CCDBG Act.
    *   Background
        *   The CCDBG Act of 2014 and its implementing regulations require that child care staff who have not yet completed comprehensive background checks may only begin employment provisionally, under certain conditions.
            *   Specifically, if they are “supervised at all times by an individual who has received a background check.”
        *   While the statute provides necessary safeguards for children’s health and safety, the federal interpretation of “supervision” has led to operational burdens and misaligned state-level enforcement practices.
            *   Specifically, HHS has defined this term more narrowly than the statutory language passed by Congress.
            *   HHS has defined or interpreted “supervision” to mean one-on-one, line-of-sight oversight by a staff member with a comprehensive background check, effectively tethering the new provisional employee to a supervisor and undermining operational flexibility.
    *   Impact on Providers
        *   This narrow interpretation has had several detrimental consequences:
            *   Staffing Strain: Requiring a fully vetted staff member to shadow a new hire restricts classroom coverage and reduces ratio capacity, particularly in small centers and family childcare homes.
            *   Hiring Delays: Providers, especially in rural or underserved areas, are reluctant to hire needed staff when immediate supervision obligations are functionally or financially unworkable.
            *   Barrier to Entry: The rigidity of supervision standards discourages otherwise qualified individuals from entering the early childhood workforce due to administrative and logistical hurdles.
            *   Child Safety Risks: Ironically, the narrow interpretation may compromise safety by limiting the number of adults available to meet supervision ratios in classrooms, thereby increasing the risk of oversight or fatigue among cleared staff.
    *   Implications of the Chevron Decision
        *   The recent U.S. Supreme Court decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo (2024), which overturned the Chevron doctrine, has important implications for this issue.
            *   By eliminating judicial deference to agency interpretations of ambiguous statutes, the Court restored the principle that agencies must remain within the bounds of clear congressional intent.
        *   HHS’s interpretation of “supervision” under 45 C.F.R. § 98.43 appears to go beyond what the CCDBG Act itself requires.
            *   The statute permits provisional employment with supervision but does not define that term, nor does it mandate a one-size-fits-all application.
        *   In light of Loper Bright, we urge HHS to:
            *   Reexamine whether the current federal interpretation imposes unjustified burdens not supported by the statutory text.
            *   Refrain from imposing overly prescriptive definitions that limit states and providers’ ability to implement safe and effective supervision practices.
            *   Affirm that states may adopt reasonable, risk-based interpretations of supervision, consistent with health and safety and operational feasibility.
    *   Recommended Revision
        *   We recommend that HHS issue revised guidance or initiate formal rulemaking to adopt a more functional definition of supervision, such as:
            *   “Supervision means on-site oversight by a cleared staff member who is physically present, readily accessible, and responsible for monitoring the activities of a provisionally employed individual through appropriate methods consistent with the child care setting, including visual checks, classroom presence, or proximity-based observation.”
        *   This language allows for safe, structured oversight of new staff while enabling providers to maintain staff-child ratios and preserve operational flexibility.
        *   It mirrors the practical application already in use in many states for substitute teachers and classroom aides.

*   Comment Regarding Unlawful Restriction on Provisional Child Care Employment Under the CCDBG Act in 45 C.F.R. § 98.43(d)(4) as interpreted by HHS in light of the United States Supreme Court decision Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. ___ (2024).
    *   HHS is currently requiring that child care providers wait until state and federal background checks in the state of employment are completed and cleared before permitting a “prospective staff member” to begin employment, in a supervised, provisional capacity.
    *   This policy is not only inconsistent with the statute, but it now stands in direct violation of the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo.
    *   I. The Plain Text of the Statute Permits Provisional Employment Upon Submission of Background Check Requests
        *   Under the CCDBG Act of 2014, codified at 42 U.S.C. § 9858f(h)(1)(C), Congress made clear that: “A child care staff member may begin work for a child care provider after the staff member has submitted a request for a criminal background check… and while awaiting the results… provided that such individual is supervised at all times by an individual who has received a qualifying result.”
        *   Congress in their wisdom recognized that child safety is multifaceted, and it essential for providers to be in ratio to ensure the physical safety and protection of children.
        *   Foreseeing situations where employees fail to show to work or quit unexpectedly, the statutory language plainly permits supervised provisional employment once a background check application has been submitted—not after it is completed or returned.
        *   Congress considered and rejected the idea of delaying employment until clearance was issued.
        *   Instead, it balanced child safety with the operational realities of childcare programs by allowing supervised employment during the processing period.
    *   II. HHS’s Implementation Adds Unauthorized Conditions
        *   Despite this clear directive, the Department’s implementation of 45 C.F.R. § 98.43(d)(4)—and subsequent agency guidance—has created a de facto requirement that no employment may begin until background checks are fully returned.
        *   In many states, this has been interpreted and enforced to mean:
            *   Staff may not be scheduled or onboarded in any capacity.
            *   Staff may not have any contact with children, even under supervision.
            *   Supervision must occur with line-of-sight or one-to-one monitoring.
            *   Providers cannot count supervised provisional staff toward ratios.
        *   These additional restrictions are nowhere found in the statute, nor is it reasonably derived from its plain meaning.
        *   It imposes a requirement Congress deliberately did not adopt.
    *   III. The Loper Bright Decision Invalidates Chevron Deference for This Rule
        *   In Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, 603 U.S. ___ (2024), the Supreme Court overturned the Chevron doctrine, holding that: “Courts may not defer to an agency interpretation that goes beyond the bounds of statutory text. Courts must exercise independent judgment in determining whether an agency has acted within its lawful authority.”
        *   In light of this decision, HHS may no longer rely on regulatory interpretations or guidance that conflict with or extend beyond the clear language of the CCDBG statute.
        *   When the statute allows provisional employment after submission of a background check, HHS has no authority to require providers to wait for completed results as a precondition of employment.
        *   By imposing requirements more burdensome than those authorized by Congress, the Department exceeds its statutory authority and runs afoul of Loper Bright and the Administrative Procedure Act (APA).
    *   IV. Real-World Implications for Providers and Families
        *   The unlawful policy has real-world consequences:
            *   Providers cannot hire when needed, exacerbating already critical workforce shortages.
            *   Enrollment is capped, leaving families without care and preventing them from going to work in many instances.
            *   New employees are deterred from entering the field due to unnecessary onboarding delays.
            *   Low-income and rural providers suffer most, as they have fewer staffing reserves to absorb delays.
        *   In short, the Department’s unlawful policy is harming the very system CCDBG is meant to strengthen.
    *   We respectfully request that HHS take the following actions:
        *   1. Rescind any guidance, regulation, or enforcement action that prohibits provisional employment after a background check application is submitted.
        *   2. Issue updated guidance to all states, affirming that supervised employment is permissible immediately upon submission of the background check request, consistent with 42 U.S.C. § 9858f(h)(1)(C).
        *   3. Affirm the Department’s commitment to operating within statutory authority, particularly in the post-Loper Bright legal environment.
    *   The Department’s current practice is inconsistent with federal law and judicial precedent.
    *   If not corrected, it will continue to restrict provider staffing, reduce childcare access, and increase regulatory liability.
    *   HHS must act swiftly to bring its background check policy back into alignment with the statute and the rule of law.

*   Comment Regarding Challenges Obtaining Child Abuse Registry Checks Under the CCDBG Act in 45 C.F.R. § 98.43(d)(4) as interpreted by HHS.
    *   As of January 2024, approximately 37 states, plus the District of Columbia, American Samoa, Guam, and Puerto Rico, maintain statutory “central registries”—statewide databases for reporting and investigating child abuse and neglect cases.
    *   When focusing specifically on the ability to conduct out-of-state child abuse and neglect registry checks—a key requirement under the 2014 CCDBG reauthorization—recent federal surveys show that:
        *   35 states and territories have implemented out-of-state child abuse and neglect registry checks.
        *   Roughly 37 states (out of 50) have central registries by law.
        *   35 states currently conduct cross-state registry checks under CCDBG requirements.
    *   In the CCDBG statutory text, it specifically outlines a 45-day window by which states must make a determination of whether a prospective employee has received a satisfactory background check, including the child abuse registry check.
    *   We strongly urge the HHS to interpret this 45-day rule to deem an employee to have a satisfactory comprehensive background check at the 45-day mark if the prospective employee has submitted all background checks regardless of whether the state has responded to the child abuse registry request.
    *   Using Texas as an example, the Texas Health and Human Services Commission (TTHHS) currently requires child care providers to wait 45 days before declaring a background check complete when another state fails to respond to a request for a child abuse and neglect registry check (also known as the Child Straight” component).
    *   The National Child Care Association (NCCA) raises the following key concerns with this policy:
        *   1. Disproportionate Impact on Providers and Families
            *   This rigid 45-day delay punishes providers and applicants for delays caused by other states.
            *   It creates staffing shortages and hiring delays, particularly in high-need or rural areas.
            *   Families experience delays in access to child care, affecting workforce participation and stability.
        *   2. Inconsistent with Federal Flexibility
            *   Federal CCDBG guidance permits states to document good-faith efforts when other states do not respond.
            *   States like TTHHS’s strict 45-day policy exceeds federal requirements and lacks flexibility.
        *   3. Operational Challenges and Misaligned Incentives
            *   Delays harm provider operations while failing to enhance safety, as other background check components (e.g., FBI, state criminal) are typically completed.
            *   The current policy shifts systemic inter-state issues onto local providers instead of addressing them through interstate cooperation or federal escalation.
        *   4. Recommended Policy Adjustments
            *   NCCA urges HHS to instruct all states the following:
                *   Allow completion of checks at the 45-day expiration after documented good-faith attempts when states don’t respond.
                *   Permit supervised provisional employment while registry responses are pending.
                *   Collaborate with the Office of Child Care to escalate issues with persistently non-responsive states.
            *   This policy change would protect children while ensuring timely hiring, operational viability, and improved access to care—key goals under the CCDBG Act.

*   Comment Regarding 45 C.F.R. § 98.33(a)(4) — Public Posting of Child Care Provider Inspection Reports
    *   We respectfully request that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) rescind or revise 45 C.F.R. § 98.33(a)(4), which mandates that state Lead Agencies publicly post inspection and monitoring reports for all eligible and licensed childcare providers.
    *   While the goal of transparency is important, this rule has had unintended consequences that undermine the long-term stability of the childcare provider network.
        *   Specifically, providers are reporting that inspection reports posted on public-facing consumer education websites are increasingly used by insurance companies and legal entities as a basis for denying liability insurance or raising premiums.
            *   This occurs even in cases where violations are minor, one-time, or fully corrected.
            *   In some cases, the very presence of a citation—regardless of severity or resolution—triggers adverse insurance decisions.
    *   This practice has become a barrier to sustaining childcare operations, especially for small providers or those serving high-need communities.
        *   The loss of or cost-prohibitive increase in liability insurance coverage makes it difficult or impossible for providers to obtain liability insurance to protect both business owners and the children in their care.
        *   Furthermore, the increase in cost, which has been in the triple digits for some providers over the past five years, is being passed on to families making childcare cost prohibitive expensive for some families.
        *   In other cases, providers are ceasing operations altogether, directly undermining access to care for working families.
    *   In light of these concerns, we urge HHS to either:
        *   Rescind the requirement in 45 C.F.R. § 98.33(a)(4), or
        *   Amend the regulation to include the following:
            *   1. Require states to allow each posted inspection report to include a provider’s written response or explanation, giving context to the findings and any corrective action taken.
            *   2. Require states to offer summarized or tiered reporting formats that reduce the risk of misinterpretation by non-regulatory third parties such as insurance companies.
            *   3. Clarify through guidance or rulemaking that these reports are intended solely for family consumer awareness—not for use by insurers to assess provider risk or eligibility.
    *   This proposed revision strikes a balance between transparency and fairness.
        *   While public access to inspection results supports parental awareness, the current one-sided presentation exposes providers—especially small, community-based operations—to reputational and financial harm.
        *   A required provider response ensures due process and more accurate public understanding, while preserving oversight goals without collapsing the fragile childcare insurance market.
    *   Without such a revision, the industry is at risk of the following:
        *   1. Chilling Effects on Child Care Supply: Providers report that publicly accessible inspection reports—particularly those reflecting minor, corrected, or first-time violations—are being used by commercial liability insurers to deny coverage, restrict eligibility, or significantly raise premiums.
        *   2. Risk of Market Contraction: The increasing difficulty in securing affordable liability insurance is driving some providers to exit the market or operate at reduced capacity, exacerbating the existing national shortage of childcare options.
        *   3. Misuse of Context-Free Citations: In the absence of context or provider explanation, posted reports can create a misleading or incomplete public record. Insurers and families alike may misinterpret the seriousness or resolution status of a cited issue, further harming providers’ reputations and viability.
    *   (b) Alternative Implementation
        *   If rescission is not adopted, the regulation shall be amended to include the following safeguard:
            *   “The Lead Agency shall ensure that any posted inspection report includes, alongside the citation or violation, a written response from the provider. This response shall be posted in equal prominence and may include:
                *   Factual clarification or correction,
                *   Description of corrective actions taken,
                *   Explanation of any mitigating or contributing circumstances.”
    *   (c) Limitation on Insurer Use
        *   HHS is further encouraged to issue non-binding guidance discouraging insurers from relying solely on publicly posted inspection reports—absent a formal adjudication or finding of gross negligence—as a basis for denying or limiting liability coverage.
    *   Rationale: This provision strikes a balance between transparency and fairness. While public access to inspection results supports parental awareness, the current one-sided presentation exposes providers—especially small, community-based operations—to reputational and financial harm. A required provider response ensures due process and more accurate public understanding, while preserving oversight goals without collapsing the fragile child care insurance market.

*   Comment Regarding Payment Based on Enrollment Versus Attendance the 2024 Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) Final Rule in 45 C.F.R. § 98
    *   We recommend that DHS revise the rule in 45 C.F.R. § 98 regarding paying providers based on enrollment versus attendance to require that states may not repurpose or redirect any current funds used to serve children in order to meet the enrollment-based payment requirement outlined in the recent rule.
    *   The rule requiring states to pay child care providers based on enrollment rather than attendance is part of the 2024 Child Care and Development Fund (CCDF) Final Rule, issued by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
        *   This rule was published in the Federal Register on March 1, 2024, and became effective on April 30, 2024.
    *   Under this rule, states and territories are mandated to implement payment practices that align with those commonly used in the private-pay market.
        *   Specifically, child care providers must be paid prospectively (i.e., in advance) and based on the child’s authorized enrollment rather than actual attendance.
        *   This change aims to provide a more stable and predictable funding stream for providers, thereby improving the financial stability of child care operations and increasing access to care for families.
    *   The shift to enrollment-based payments is intended to reduce administrative burdens on providers and ensure they receive consistent payments, regardless of fluctuations in daily attendance.
        *   This approach supports the goal of enhancing the quality and accessibility of child care services for families participating in the CCDF program.
    *   This clarification is critical to ensure that existing funding streams dedicated to direct services for children are not reduced or compromised in the implementation of the new policy.
        *   Without this safeguard, there is a risk that states could reallocate resources away from services in an effort to comply with the rule, ultimately undermining the goal of improving access and quality of care.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: Ellen Reynolds, CEO of True North Strategies, supporting the National Child Care Association, urges HHS to revise child care background check and public inspection report regulations to alleviate undue burdens on providers, align with statutory intent and the *Loper Bright* Supreme Court decision, and ensure stable funding for child care services without compromising child safety or access.

  - This practice becomes a barrier to sustaining childcare operations, forcing cost increases onto families or leading providers to cease operations.
  - The absence of context or provider explanations in posted reports creates a misleading public record, harming providers' reputations and viability.
- Risk that states might repurpose or redirect existing funding streams dedicated to direct child services to comply with the new enrollment-based payment rule for providers, thereby undermining the goal of improving access and quality of care.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   QHP Capital, L.P. ("QHP") appreciates the opportunity to provide comments in response to the Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation to Make Americans Healthy Again.
*   The current HHS Administration announced the largest deregulatory effort in history, seeking public input on how to dramatically deregulate across the entire healthcare industry.
    *   HHS is looking to identify opportunities to produce cost savings, increase efficiency, and stimulate health and economic innovation through deregulation.
    *   The RFI specifically asks for identification of US regulations and guidance that should be modified or repealed, along with associated costs.
*   QHP supports HHS's intent to reduce regulatory burdens and advance America’s healthcare sector, allowing providers and caretakers to focus on preventing and treating chronic diseases rather than paperwork.
*   As a strategic capital investment firm in the healthcare and life science sectors, QHP is particularly interested in addressing impediments to innovation and access.
    *   QHP Capital (formerly NovaQuest Private Equity) and its founders have over 40 years’ experience operating and investing greater than $10 Billion in growing biopharma and other life science sector companies.
    *   QHP is responding to this RFI because:
        *   The companies QHP invests in are part of the regulated industry, providing decades of insight into regulatory issues and opportunities that serve neither the public nor industry.
        *   QHP's current investment portfolio employs over 2,000 people, conducted over 2,250 clinical trials, approved over 25 therapeutics, and served over 4 million patients in the last six years.
        *   QHP has created over 1,300 jobs by partnering with U.S.-based life science/biopharma services companies that have served overlooked patients (rare, orphan, niche).
        *   QHP is uniquely positioned and qualified to offer real-time industry insights to advance the current HHS mandate.
    *   QHP's investment criteria align with Federal Register goals, focusing on tech-enabled life sciences and pharma service companies that help reduce total cost of care, fulfill unmet medical needs, diminish unnecessary procedures, improve efficiency, and elevate patient quality of life.
*   QHP has identified several areas where FDA guidance and HHS policy could be revised or modified to address the Administration’s concerns.

*   I. Efforts to Improve Agency Efficiency
    *   a. Meeting timelines
        *   i. Requirement and authority
            *   FDA’s timelines are set forth in its Guidance for Industry: Formal Meetings Between the FDA and Sponsors or Applicants of PDUFA Products, last revised in September 2023.
        *   ii. Summary of requirements and Issues Posed
            *   FDA has specific timelines and procedures for requesting and conducting formal meetings with sponsors, typically scheduled 30 to 75 days after a meeting request.
            *   Requesters must submit meeting packages 30 to 50 days before the scheduled meeting, with failure to adhere leading to cancellation or rescheduling.
            *   FDA issues official meeting minutes, which are not transcripts but contain FDA’s discussion summary and final word, within 30 calendar days after the meeting.
            *   Meeting minutes may include a "post-meeting discussion" section reflecting internal FDA conclusions.
            *   While meeting timeframes are transparent, some timelines are burdensome.
            *   Every day a company waits for meeting minutes delays research and development, costing industry money.
            *   Companies, potential investors, or partners often wait for official meeting minutes before proceeding due to potential interpretive differences between the company and FDA.
            *   These delays impede private enterprise and entrepreneurship.
        *   iii. Proposed Action – modification
            *   Given new technologies, waiting 30 days for meeting minutes is excessive.
            *   FDA should introduce artificial intelligence (AI) into its process for developing meeting minutes to track, summarize, and provide an initial version for FDA staff review.
            *   FDA’s new Elsa platform appears to be partially suited for this task.
            *   FDA could also use AI to summarize meeting packages, reducing the need for them to be submitted so far in advance (e.g., 47 days for Type C meetings).
            *   Reliance on AI would reduce the burden on FDA staff, allow policy updates, speed up access to medicines, and reduce time to market, assisting industry in addressing chronic health issues.
        *   iv. Cost & Savings
            *   Delays from FDA’s meeting processes significantly affect a drug’s development program and a company’s return on investment.
            *   The lag time between meeting requests and minutes stalls product development, as sponsors cannot move forward without FDA feedback.
            *   Companies often struggle to raise money during this period, as investors prefer to see FDA’s feedback in writing.
            *   For Type B meetings (505(b)(1) applications), the cumulative delay across ten typical meetings can be 34 months.
            *   Adopting new technologies could truncate this delay by up to six months.
            *   Reducing delays speeds access to therapies and increases investment value, as every two years of delay results in a 40 percent loss of net present value on return on investment.
    *   b. PREA (Pediatric Research Equity Act)
        *   i. Requirements and authority
            *   PREA is governed by 21 U.S.C. § 355c and implemented by several guidance documents, including Guidance for Industry: Pediatric Drug Development: Regulatory Considerations – Complying with PREA and Qualifying for Pediatric Exclusivity Under the BPCA and Guidance for Industry: Clarification of Orphan Designation of Drugs and Biologics for Pediatric Subpopulations of Common Diseases, both published in 2023.
        *   ii. Summary of Requirements and Issues Posed
            *   PREA requires sponsors to include pediatric assessments in certain marketing applications, covering new active ingredients, indications, dosage forms, dosing regimens, or routes of administration.
            *   Assessments must include safety and efficacy data for relevant pediatric subpopulations to support dosing and administration.
            *   These assessments are onerous, and recruiting pediatric patients for studies is challenging.
            *   Sponsors can obtain a waiver or deferral, but a full waiver is only available if studies are impossible/impracticable, the drug is ineffective/unsafe in all pediatric groups, or it offers no meaningful benefit and is unlikely to be used substantially in pediatric patients.
            *   Demonstrating "impossible or highly impracticable" to FDA is difficult, and specific guidelines are lacking, leading to a lack of transparency in Agency decision-making.
            *   FDA's recent guidance (2023) states that PREA studies are no longer eligible for pediatric exclusivity, a change from past practice where FDA issued Written Requests for PREA-required studies that qualified for exclusivity.
            *   In July 2018, FDA issued guidance announcing that pediatric subpopulations would no longer be designated as orphan drugs to avoid PREA requirements, closing a "loophole" that allowed PREA exemption for non-rare diseases.
            *   No new pediatric-subpopulation designations have been granted since 2018.
        *   iii. Proposed action – partial repeal of guidances, exercise of discretion
            *   FDA’s implementation of PREA requirements meets criteria for modification/repeal, including being inconsistent with underlying statutory authority, imposing significant costs not outweighed by benefits, harming national interest by impeding R&D, unduly burdening small businesses, impeding access to care, and impeding innovation.
            *   While PREA is statutory and cannot be repealed, FDA’s interpretation of the statute can be refined to better incentivize pediatric development.
            *   FDA’s policy that PREA studies are ineligible for pediatric exclusivity and that pediatric subpopulations are ineligible for orphan drug designation should be targeted for deregulation, as these policies are not in the plain language of the PREA statute.
            *   These interpretations strip away incentives under the pediatric exclusivity and orphan drug designation programs.
            *   The resources dedicated to PREA could be better used for sponsor-chosen research, development, and innovation.
            *   The administration should request FDA repeal, at least partially, its guidance documents pertaining to PREA implementation.
            *   FDA should be more willing to revisit agreed-upon PREA obligations even after approval and launch, especially when they become practically or ethically infeasible.
            *   Instead of just publishing lists of non-compliant companies, FDA should exercise discretion to waive impractical or unethical studies post-approval.
            *   FDA could permit the use of real-world evidence and/or retrospective studies to meet PREA requirements instead of mandating new studies.
            *   Current PREA commitments can disincentivize development of products for smaller markets due to economic hardship destroying potential return on investment.
            *   If "impracticability" included economic hardship, it would incentivize development of products in rare, orphan, or niche markets, benefiting underserved patients.
            *   FDA should exercise its discretion under PREA to require pediatric studies when necessary but remain flexible to avoid being a barrier to innovation when obligations are not practical.
            *   Clarity on FDA's decision-making guidelines would also encourage innovation and prevent early demise of innovative treatment options.
        *   iv. Costs & Savings
            *   Pediatric studies under PREA can cost $12 million to $40 million, with 60% of costs required upfront.
            *   These studies take years to complete, largely due to enrollment difficulties, and often remain uncompleted.
            *   Sponsors invest millions in PREA studies, only to have prices undercut by generics that immediately add pediatric labeling updates from the reference product without incurring costs.
            *   The value of pediatric research is eroded as soon as generic drugs enter the market.

*   II. Manufacturing
    *   a. Nitrosamines
        *   i. Requirements and authority
            *   Nitrosamines are discussed only in guidance, specifically FDA’s Guidance for Industry: Control of Nitrosamine Impurities in Human Drugs (September 2024).
        *   ii. Summary of Requirements and Issues Posed
            *   The guidance recommends steps for manufacturers and applicants to detect and prevent unacceptable levels of nitrosamine impurities in drug products.
            *   Nitrosamine impurities are probable or possible human carcinogens, requiring a risk assessment strategy for their potential presence.
            *   The guidance recommends a three-step mitigation strategy and actions to reduce/prevent impurities.
            *   The guidance applies the same standard regardless of drug use frequency, treating a single-use drug the same as a daily-use drug.
            *   This conflicts with FDA’s existing approach for drugs intended for less than a lifetime, M7(R2) Assessment and Control of DNA Reactive (Mutagenic) Impurities in Pharmaceuticals to Limit Potential Carcinogenic Risk.
            *   The differing approach for nitrosamines is scientifically unsupported and imposes significant costs on manufacturers.
            *   The guidance lacks instructions for calculating acceptable intake limits, leading to Complete Response Letters for pending applications.
        *   iii. Proposed Action – Revise guidance
            *   FDA should not repeal the nitrosamine guidance due to safety concerns but should update it.
            *   The guidance should comport with M7(R2) and adopt a different approach for drugs intended for less than lifetime use.
            *   FDA should also revise the guidance to provide clear instructions for calculating acceptable intake limits.
        *   iv. Costs & savings
            *   Due to the newness of FDA’s nitrosamine approach, data on costs and savings from revisions is not yet available.

*   III. Incentives for innovation
    *   a. 505(b)(2) exclusivity incentives
        *   i. Requirements and authority
            *   The 505(b)(2) pathway was adopted under section 505(b) of the federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (“FDC Act”) or 21 U.S.C. § 355(b)(2).
            *   Implementing regulations on exclusivity are at 21 C.F.R. § 314.108.
        *   ii. Summary of requirements:
            *   Section 505(b)(2) provides an abbreviated pathway for drugs where investigations were not conducted by or for the applicant, and the applicant has no right of reference.
            *   Applications can rely on published literature or FDA’s findings of safety/effectiveness for another drug product.
            *   While attractive due to fewer required full studies, the 505(b)(2) pathway offers few incentives to offset R&D costs and patent litigation.
            *   Unlike a 505(b)(1) NDA (often eligible for five years of exclusivity and patent term restoration), 505(b)(2) NDAs typically only qualify for three years of clinical study exclusivity.
            *   This exclusivity is limited to the studies conducted, meaning the 505(b)(2) NDA remains subject to competition even with exclusivity.
            *   Properly incentivized, the 505(b)(2) pathway could encourage competition and drug price reduction.
            *   Unlike generic ANDAs that must closely formulate competitive products, potentially infringing more RLD patents, 505(b)(2) developers can more easily overcome formulation patents and enter the market sooner, leading to price competition.
            *   Development of 505(b)(2) products is generally more expensive than ANDA products, requiring further innovation beyond the RLD.
            *   Without proper incentives, investment in 505(b)(2) products is less attractive.
            *   Market exclusivity for first-filer ANDAs under the Hatch-Waxman Act significantly increased competition, and similar exclusivities for the 505(b)(2) pathway (not limited to clinical study) could also increase price competition.
        *   iii. Proposed Action – modification of regulations
            *   While no regulation can be repealed to grant new exclusivity, FDA could adopt additional incentives to make the 505(b)(2) pathway more attractive, encouraging innovation and competitiveness.
            *   This would align with the RFI's objectives to improve innovation and access to care.
            *   FDA could incentivize 505(b)(2) NDA development by allotting priority review, allowing for potential approval four months earlier than standard review.
            *   FDA should also incentivize innovation by adopting an additional period of exclusivity for 505(b)(2) NDAs that can demonstrate a product’s ability to compete with the RLD, by revising 21 C.F.R. § 314.108.
        *   iv. Costs and savings
            *   The Hatch-Waxman Act created a "gold rush" in the generics industry, leading to competitive products that saved Americans $2.9 trillion in ten years (2013-2023).
            *   In 1983, only 35% of top-selling branded drugs with expired patents had generic competition, and 13% of prescriptions were for generics. By 2012, 84% of US prescriptions were generics, with spending growing by $8 billion.
            *   Creating additional incentives for competition would further reduce costs and increase access to medicines.
    *   b. TE code assignment (Therapeutic Equivalence)
        *   i. Requirements and authority
            *   FDA defines therapeutic equivalence in regulations at 21 C.F.R. § 314.3, and further explains it in Guidance for Industry: Evaluation of Therapeutic Equivalence (Draft, July 2022), and the Approved Drug Products With Therapeutic Equivalence Evaluations (“Orange Book”) Preface.
        *   ii. Summary of requirements
            *   FDA assigns therapeutic equivalence codes for multisource prescription drug products approved under section 505 of the FDC Act, as detailed in the Orange Book and accompanying guidance.
            *   TE codes are used by states and other entities to determine product substitutability for their Reference Listed Drug (RLD).
            *   Availability of lower-cost therapeutically equivalent drugs saves consumers money, so swift TE code assignment promotes access to care.
            *   FDA automatically assigns TE codes to generic drugs approved under section 505(j) but not routinely to drugs approved under the 505(b)(2) pathway.
            *   A new statutory provision mandates FDA assignment of TE codes within 180 days for certain 505(b)(2)s (those differing from the listed drug only by an inactive ingredient not permitted under 21 C.F.R. § 314.94(a)(9)(iii) or (iv)).
            *   Sponsors of other 505(b)(2) NDAs must petition FDA for TE code assignment post-approval, but FDA frequently fails to respond to such petitions.
            *   As a result, even approved, therapeutically equivalent drugs may not be automatically substitutable for years, costing consumers money and/or impeding sponsor returns on investment.
            *   Sponsors of therapeutically equivalent 505(b)(2) NDAs may also unnecessarily pay user fees from which they would otherwise be exempt under the Prescription Drug User Fee Act, which exempts pharmaceutically equivalent drugs listed in the Orange Book.
            *   A TE code is necessary for this exemption, so fees continue until FDA responds to a citizen petition.
        *   iii. Proposed action – Revise guidance, Orange Book Preface, and regulation
            *   To encourage access and promote health, FDA should revise the definition of “therapeutic equivalence” to treat closely-related dosage forms as therapeutically equivalent.
            *   Currently, “therapeutic equivalents” are “pharmaceutical equivalents for which bioequivalence has been demonstrated,” and “pharmaceutical equivalents” are “drug products in identical dosage forms and route(s) of administration that contain identical amounts of the identical active drug ingredient.”
            *   Revising this definition would allow greater substitution of 505(b)(2) NDAs for listed drugs and simplify TE code assignment.
            *   Another revision is to amend the guidance Evaluation of Therapeutic Equivalence, the Orange Book Preface, and FDA policy to establish more efficient TE determinations for 505(b)(2) NDAs.
            *   While Congress mandated a 180-day timeline for certain 505(b)(2) NDAs, HHS and FDA should impose a 180-day deadline on responses to all citizen petitions requesting TE determinations.
            *   Alternatively, they should create another process for timely TE code assignment to 505(b)(2) NDAs upon request.
        *   iv. Costs and savings
            *   Currently, there is insufficient information to provide cost estimates for the proposed change.

*   IV. Transparency
    *   a. Drug pricing
        *   v. Requirements and authority
            *   Neither HHS nor FDA have regulations or guidance concerning pricing transparency; individual state laws control.
        *   vi. Summary of requirements
            *   State-level price transparency legislation is common but highly variable in terms of reported drugs, data collection level (aggregate or individual), and data publication/analysis.
            *   The lack of a unifying federal program forces sponsors to comply with over 20 different and often confusing state requirements, with more expected.
            *   This increases costs for industry, which are then passed on to patients.
            *   Current transparency requirements do not mandate disclosure of negotiated prices with pharmaceutical “middle-men,” including wholesalers/distributors, group purchasing organizations (GPOs), and pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs).
            *   Transparency of discounts, rebates, and chargebacks from manufacturers to patients would undermine unfair price increases.
            *   Transparency of “marketing fees,” “wholesaler fees,” and other fee-for-service models between commercial participants would prevent abuse and ultimate cost passing to consumers.
        *   vii. Proposed action – federal preemption
            *   HHS can and should preempt state transparency initiatives by imposing a federal transparency requirement.
            *   This action would be consistent with Executive Order 14221, Making America Healthy Again by Empowering Patients with Clear, Accurate, and Actionable Healthcare Pricing Information.
            *   Transparency should extend beyond Wholesale Acquisition Cost (WAC) to include discounts, rebates, and chargebacks as drugs move through commercial channels.
            *   Transparency of fee-for-service models in commercial channels would prevent abuse that increases drug costs.
        *   viii. Costs and savings
            *   Precise figures are challenging due to varied state requirements, but harmonization would lead to significant cost savings, especially for small entities (the majority of the pharmaceutical industry).
            *   Small companies pay disproportionately higher middlemen fees.
            *   QHP has observed a 12% spread in distributor fees: a $100 million business might incur 18% of revenue in middlemen fees, while a $1 billion company incurs 7%.
            *   Such fees drive up prices for customers and insurance companies.
            *   Widespread transparency from a federal rule would reduce costs by allowing payers to pressure distributors, wholesalers, and other middlemen to equalize fees, preventing overwhelming impacts on small entities.

*   V. Data Requirements
    *   a. Clinicaltrials.gov
        *   i. Requirements and authority
            *   Clinicaltrials.gov is mandated by the Public Health Service Act at 42 U.S.C. 282(j) and implemented by 42 CFR Part 11.
        *   ii. Summary of Requirements
            *   Regulations require clinical trial information submission to NIH and public availability at ClinicalTrials.gov.
            *   Clinicaltrials.gov is difficult to navigate and often incomplete, hindering identification of recruiting studies.
            *   Lack of patient engagement and enrollment adds years and significant costs to studies.
        *   iii. Proposed Action – Revise clinicaltrials.gov
            *   Clinicaltrials.gov could be an excellent repository for physicians and patients to find studies, but it requires an overhaul that no entity has an economic incentive to undertake.
            *   HHS should intervene to reform the site, making it more user-friendly to effectively link patients and physicians to enrolling studies.
            *   The site should be a reliable repository for all clinical studies where treating physicians or patients can effectively search for open, enrolling trials.
            *   Data on participating sites and physicians is often outdated, making it unreliable for finding active trials in specific geographic areas.
            *   Reorganizing Clinicaltrials.gov by therapeutic and indication area, aligning with healthcare diagnoses, would expedite clinical development (possibly by months or years) and reduce clinical study costs.
        *   iv. Costs & savings
            *   Reducing hurdles to patient enrollment would undoubtedly reduce industry costs for clinical trial recruitment, but quantifying those savings is challenging.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: QHP Capital, a healthcare and life science investment firm, strongly advocates for targeted deregulation and policy revisions by HHS and FDA to boost efficiency, incentivize innovation, reduce drug costs, and improve patient access by leveraging new technologies and promoting market competition.

structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   **Improve Agency Efficiency (FDA Meeting Timelines):**
    -   FDA should introduce artificial intelligence (AI) into its process for developing meeting minutes to track, summarize, and provide initial versions for review, reducing the 30-day waiting period.
    -   FDA should use AI to summarize meeting packages, reducing the need for them to be submitted so far in advance (e.g., 47 days for Type C meetings).
-   **Reform Pediatric Research Equity Act (PREA) Implementation:**
    -   HHS should request FDA repeal, at least partially, its guidance documents pertaining to PREA implementation, specifically:
        -   Reversing the policy that PREA studies are ineligible for pediatric exclusivity.
        -   Reversing the policy that pediatric subpopulations are ineligible for orphan drug designation.
    -   FDA should be more willing to revisit and waive agreed-upon PREA obligations post-approval if they become practically or ethically infeasible.
    -   FDA should permit the usage of real-world evidence and/or retrospective studies to meet PREA requirements rather than mandating new studies.
    -   FDA should define "impracticability" to include the economic hardship a product faces in sustaining PREA commitments, incentivizing development for rare, orphan, or small markets.
    -   FDA should provide clear guidelines for decision-making regarding PREA waivers and flexibility.
-   **Revise Nitrosamine Manufacturing Guidance:**
    -   FDA should update the Guidance for Industry: Control of Nitrosamine Impurities in Human Drugs to align with the M7(R2) guidance, taking a different approach for drugs intended for less than lifetime use.
    -   FDA should revise the guidance to provide clear instructions for calculating acceptable intake limits.
-   **Enhance 505(b)(2) Exclusivity Incentives:**
    -   FDA should adopt additional incentives for the 505(b)(2) pathway to encourage innovation and competitiveness.
    -   FDA should allot priority review for 505(b)(2) NDAs.
    -   FDA should adopt an additional period of exclusivity for 505(b)(2) NDAs that demonstrate a product’s ability to compete with the Reference Listed Drug (RLD), by revising 21 C.F.R. § 314.108.
-   **Streamline Therapeutic Equivalence (TE) Code Assignment:**
    -   FDA should revise the definition of “therapeutic equivalence” to treat closely-related dosage forms as therapeutically equivalent, allowing for greater substitution of 505(b)(2) NDAs.
    -   HHS and FDA should amend the Guidance Evaluation of Therapeutic Equivalence, the Orange Book Preface, and FDA policy to establish more efficient TE determinations for 505(b)(2) NDAs.
    -   HHS and FDA should impose a 180-day deadline on responses to all citizen petitions requesting TE determinations, or create another process for timely assignment of TE codes to 505(b)(2) NDAs upon request.
-   **Implement Federal Drug Price Transparency:**
    -   HHS should preempt disparate state transparency initiatives by imposing a single, unifying federal transparency requirement.
    -   This federal transparency should extend beyond Wholesale Acquisition Cost (WAC) to include discounts, rebates, and chargebacks as drugs move through commercial channels.
    -   Transparency of fee-for-service models in commercial channels should be required to prevent abuse that increases drug costs.
-   **Overhaul Clinicaltrials.gov:**
    -   HHS should intervene to reform Clinicaltrials.gov to create a more user-friendly website that effectively links patients and their physicians to enrolling studies.
    -   The site should be reorganized by therapeutic and indication area, aligning with healthcare diagnoses, to expedite clinical development.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   **FDA Meeting Delays:** The 30-day waiting period for official meeting minutes is excessive, causing significant delays in drug development and impacting a company's return on investment, particularly as companies and investors often wait for written feedback before proceeding.
-   **Burdensome PREA Requirements:** Pediatric studies under PREA are onerous, expensive ($12-$40 million per study, 60% upfront), difficult to enroll patients for, and often remain uncompleted, with their value eroded by generics that benefit from the research without cost.
-   **Lack of PREA Incentives:** FDA's recent policy changes, making PREA studies ineligible for pediatric exclusivity and restricting orphan drug designation for pediatric subpopulations, strip away crucial incentives for pediatric drug development.
-   **Lack of Transparency in PREA Waivers:** FDA's decision-making process for granting PREA waivers (e.g., for "impossible or highly impracticable" studies) lacks specific guidelines and transparency.
-   **Inconsistent Nitrosamine Standards:** FDA's guidance on nitrosamine impurities holds manufacturers to the same standard regardless of drug frequency of use, conflicting with existing risk assessment approaches (like M7(R2)) for drugs intended for less than lifetime use, leading to significant costs.
-   **Lack of Nitrosamine Calculation Guidance:** The nitrosamine guidance fails to provide instructions for calculating acceptable intake limits, resulting in delays and "Complete Response Letters" for pending applications.
-   **Limited 505(b)(2) Incentives:** The 505(b)(2) pathway, despite its potential for abbreviated approval, offers insufficient incentives (typically only three years of limited clinical study exclusivity) to offset R&D costs and patent litigation, making it less attractive than it could be for fostering competition and reducing drug prices.
-   **Inefficient TE Code Assignment:** FDA's failure to routinely assign therapeutic equivalence codes to 505(b)(2) drugs and its frequent unresponsiveness to citizen petitions for TE code assignment delay market entry of lower-cost alternatives, costing consumers and imposing unnecessary user fees on sponsors.
-   **Fragmented Drug Pricing Transparency:** A patchwork of over 20 differing state-level drug price transparency laws creates confusion, unnecessary complexity, and increased costs for the industry, which are passed on to patients.
-   **Lack of Middleman Transparency:** Current transparency requirements do not disclose negotiated prices, discounts, rebates, chargebacks, or "marketing fees" paid to pharmaceutical "middle-men" (wholesalers, GPOs, PBMs), allowing these entities to unfairly increase drug prices, disproportionately affecting smaller companies.
-   **Dysfunctional Clinicaltrials.gov:** The Clinicaltrials.gov website is difficult to navigate, often incomplete, and has outdated information on participating sites and physicians, hindering patient and physician efforts to identify and enroll in recruiting studies, adding years and significant costs to clinical trials.

-   "QHP has seen a 12 percent spread between distributor fees with large companies seeing significantly more favorable rates. For example, a $100 million business might incur fees to middlemen of 18 percent of revenue while a $1 billion company would incur 7 percent."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
-   As an early childhood advocate and Head Start employee for over 26 years, I appreciate the opportunity to offer information in response to the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS’s) recent Request for Information (RFI) on “Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.”
-   Prenatal-to-five programs like Head Start/Early Head Start provide locally controlled, community-driven services to families in every state.
-   The regulations and standards that HHS creates for the early care and learning field are critical to continued service to families and accountability for taxpayer-funded programs.
    -   They provide important guidance to the state- and community-based organizations that are entrusted with carrying out critical services.
    -   They promote program consistency, quality, accountability, and continuous improvement.
-   While every Head Start program is designed to meet the needs of their own community, performance standards provide the guidance necessary to ensure that we are both accountable for federal dollars and providing the essential services necessary to most effectively support children and families.
-   I strongly caution HHS against broad removal of accountability measures with the following key considerations:
    -   Ensuring Success in All States and Communities:
        -   In early childhood services, accountability measures from HHS uphold key pillars like program quality, child safety, and workforce supports.
        -   These ensure that the taxpayer-funded programs that yield positive outcomes can be replicated in all types of communities – rural, urban, exurban, suburban, and tribal.
        -   HHS’s standards are a critical tool for ensuring consistently positive outcomes across the U.S.’s vast range of geographies.
    -   Honoring Parent Choice:
        -   Local Systems of Care:
            -   Communities across the country have shaped their early care and learning and maternal health landscapes to be responsive to the needs of parents in their local community.
            -   Standards and accountability measures from HHS provide a key framework from which communities can operate to implement services that are consistent in quality and unique in the specific services, delivery methods, and curriculum they offer in response to parent input.
            -   I urge HHS to uphold standards as essential frameworks that communities build and innovate from.
            -   These standards allow parents the opportunity to take advantage of community services with the confidence that HHS is holding programs accountable on quality and safety.
        -   Family Leadership:
            -   In order to preserve parents’ rights to choose the best education for their child starting in the earliest years, I strongly urge HHS to maintain a robust public comment process on regulations pertaining to maternal health and child and family services.
                -   This will allow families to engage with HHS to create the types of early care and learning opportunities that will best align with their personal views on the type of early childhood education they want their child to receive.
            -   I strongly urge HHS to uphold the integrity of family leadership and feedback loop opportunities that are embedded into the structures of child and family services, including Head Start Parent Policy Councils and Head Start and Child Care Development Block Grant and Maternal, Infant, Early Childhood Home Visiting program community needs assessments.
            -   These opportunities to inform accountability measures and policies play a critical role in uncovering and promoting parent choice in early care and learning and maternal health services.
    -   Preserve Accountability for Public Funds:
        -   Through its standards, HHS supports state- and community-based entities in remaining accountable to their communities and to the federal government by requiring public disclosure around the use of federal funds.
        -   This is a critical function of regulations that I urge HHS to maintain, as it re-enforces principles that child and family serving services consider core to their mission: transparency, fiscal integrity, and accountability to families.

*   I am commenting on the U.S Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
*   The years of pregnancy to age three set the foundation for a baby’s development, learning and relationships.
    *   Babies rely entirely on the adults around them—parents, caregivers, and early childhood professionals—to provide safe, nurturing care.
    *   When babies or their caregivers face reduced support or program quality, babies can end up facing long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences.
    *   When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health.
*   Regulations matter.
    *   HHS, as the leading Federal agency tasked with enhancing the health and well-being of all Americans, plays a critical role in ensuring that babies, families, and the professionals who care for little ones have access to the resources, protections, and supports they need.
    *   In considering changes to regulations, HHS must preserve regulations that:
        *   Keep young children safe and healthy.
        *   Enable the adults in their lives to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
*   For example, regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings are needed to keep babies safe and developmentally on track.
*   Regulations that keep children and those who care for them healthy, like those that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care, must be maintained.
    *   This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe.
*   HHS rules reach far beyond just Medicaid and early learning, with many HHS programs laying the foundation of quality care and critical support that babies need.
*   Any changes to regulations must be:
    *   Transparent.
    *   Grounded in evidence.
    *   Focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
*   Because each regulation is different, HHS must continue to give the public—including families and early childhood professionals like me—ample time and opportunity to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes.
    *   We need a robust public process to make sure that the rules work for babies and those who care for them.
*   To keep America’s babies healthy, HHS must maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services.
*   Please uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
*   I would also like to add that I am a product of Head Start Services.
    *   I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career.
    *   I have a Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma.
    *   I have been a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for the past twenty-three years servicing the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles.
    *   It gives great pleasure to give back to my community.
