        *   MA plans often invoke the Medicare Part B date of service rule, 42 CFR § 414.510(a), such that the date of service is the date of specimen collection, not the date when the test is performed.
        *   If a healthcare practitioner does not obtain prior authorization prior to ordering the test or before the date the sample is collected, the lab will attempt to obtain prior authorization when it receives the order.
        *   However, this frequently results in a denial as the DOS has passed by the time the request is submitted, resulting in issues with the appeals process and creating unnecessary burden for all parties involved.
        *   CMS can address the misuse of the date of service for laboratory tests as a reason to deny coverage by updating existing policies.
        *   Providing clarity and guardrails around the use of the date of service will remove this administrative burden for patients, providers, and payers.
        *   Quest recommends that CMS prohibit MAOs from denying a prior authorization request on the basis that the request was submitted after the DOS of the lab test, which is the date of specimen collection.
        *   CMS should amend 42 C.F.R. § 422.122, Prior Authorization Requirements, to add a subsection “(d): Date of Service: 1. In the case of a clinical diagnostic laboratory test that requires prior authorization, an Medicare Advantage (MA) organization must accept a prior authorization request from the provider who ordered the test or the clinical laboratory that furnished the test at any time before a timely claim for reimbursement is submitted. 2. An MA organization may not deny a request for prior authorization or a request for an organization determination for a clinical diagnostic laboratory test because the request was made after the date of service of the test.”
        *   Furthermore, CMS should amend 42 C.F.R. § 414.510 to read: “The date of service for either a clinical laboratory test or the technical component of physician pathology service determines which provider should bill for the service and is as follows…” to clarify the purpose of the definition and clearly state that the lab date of service is not intended to be used to deny appropriate coverage or restrict beneficiary access to appropriate services.
    *   III. Organization Determination Requirement
        *   Clinical laboratories face significant challenges related to organization determination (OD) requirements and the prior authorization process within Medicare Advantage (MA) plans.
        *   Ordering providers are not obtaining ODs when ordering non-covered laboratory testing.
        *   In most cases, it is impractical for a laboratory to seek an OD on an MA enrollee's behalf after receiving a test order from the enrollee's physician but prior to performing the test.
        *   Oftentimes, the laboratory does not receive an order until either after the date of service (i.e. the date the patient's blood was drawn in the physician’s office) or at the time of service (if the patient has their blood drawn at a lab’s patient service center); a laboratory cannot delay testing to seek an OD on behalf of an enrollee due to specimen integrity issues and testing turnaround time requirements.
        *   Moreover, an MAO has up to 14 days after receiving a request to respond to standard ODs, and CMS regulations permit only an enrollee or a physician to request an expedited OD.
        *   It is not possible for a laboratory to hold up a specimen for up to two weeks while awaiting a response from the MAO regarding an OD request.
        *   Laboratories have been put in the untenable position of providing laboratory services to MAO enrollees without receiving reimbursement for the services their ordering providers have determined are medically necessary.
        *   While the CY 2026 Policy and Technical Changes to the Medicare Advantage Program Proposed Rule (CMS-4208-P) attempted to clarify appeal rights and made it clear that regulatory appeal rights do not apply to the denial of a claim when there is no further financial liability, and thus an enrollee cannot be held financially responsible, it did not clarify the plan's responsibility to pay for plan-directed care (CMS did not address these issues in the final rule).
        *   It is illogical that a laboratory to whom a referral is made – and that furnished the ordered service as requested by the ordering physician – should be held financially liable.
        *   Rather, the referral is a “favorable determination made on behalf of the MAO and a laboratory should be paid for the service.
        *   Plan-directed care is when a contracted provider furnishes a service or refers an MA enrollee for a service that the enrollee reasonably believes is a service covered by the plan.
        *   It occurs not only when a contracted provider (i.e., ordering physician) refers an enrollee to a non-contracted provider, but also when a contracted provider refers an enrollee for a service without securing an OD on behalf of the enrollee in advance of rendering the service.
        *   For laboratories, as contracted providers with MAOs, notice and appeal rights do not apply.
        *   Participating providers that have not explicitly agreed to assume the cost of non-covered services under their agreement with an MAO should be granted the same rights as non-participating providers with respect to the appeal and review process.
        *   Quest Diagnostics urges CMS to improve and clarify the OD process requirements so that laboratories are also protected from undue financial liability as MAO enrollees are in the regulations.
        *   CMS should further provide that unless the MAO has contracted with the provider to assume financial responsibility, the MAO should be financially responsible for plan-directed care.
        *   In addition, we believe the referral for the laboratory service from a participating ordering practitioner should be considered a favorable OD, regardless of whether the lab is participating, and an MAO should pay a laboratory for these services.
        *   Most importantly, MA beneficiaries should have the same rights as traditional Medicare beneficiaries to elect to receive laboratory testing without the delay or administrative burden of first receiving an OD.
        *   It is unreasonable to place additional requirements on MA beneficiaries regarding access to non-covered testing.
        *   Giving an MA beneficiary the right to elect to move forward with testing without exercising their right to an OD does not impact the patient’s appeal or other rights.
        *   In addition, the OD process not only delays testing, but it results in waste and time delay as it often requires a return visit to the physician or patient service center for an additional specimen collection.
        *   Finally, there is little value to the MA beneficiary in waiting for the MA plan to issue the unfavorable OD when the lab knows at the time of the service that the information provided by the ordering provider is not sufficient based on Medicare coverage policies.
    *   IV. National Correct Coding Initiative
        *   Duplicative and conflicting coding guidance from the National Correct Coding Initiative (NCCI) Medicare Policy Manual and the American Medical Association (AMA) leads to compliance issues and denials for clinical laboratories.
        *   Coding guidance currently provided in the Medicare NCCI Policy Manual is inconsistent with the AMA Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) code set for laboratory services.
        *   This discrepancy places an immense burden on laboratories, as they must use the AMA HIPAA-compliant code set and AMA guidance.
        *   Laboratories must code claims correctly to avoid false claims liability, and reimbursement for medically necessary services provided to Medicare beneficiaries should be tied to correct coding, not to coding inconsistent with AMA CPT guidance.
        *   It is imperative that NCCI manuals and other established NCCI methodologies not include information that contradicts AMA CPT coding structure or guidance.
        *   To address these duplicative and conflicting Medicare requirements, Quest Diagnostics recommends that CMS make the following changes to the NCCI Medicare Policy Manual:
            *   (1) In Chapter X: Pathology/Laboratory Services, Introduction, Section A, CMS should remove the quoted paragraph in its entirety: “If a laboratory procedure produces multiple reportable test results, only a single HCPCS/CPT code shall be reported for the procedure. If there is no HCPCS/CPT code that describes the procedure, the laboratory shall report a miscellaneous or unlisted procedure code with a single unit of service.” [Ch. X, X-4.]
            *   (2) CMS should delete the Molecular Pathology section [Ch. X, Section, F.8] in its entirety.
            *   (3) CMS should delete the Medically Unlikely Edits (MUE) section [Ch. X, Section M.15] in its entirety.
            *   (4) In the General Coding Policies [Chapter 1, page I-22]4 CMS should modify the quoted language “CMS may adopt NCCI edits that are not consistent with CPT Assistant” to “CMS shall not adopt NCCI edits that are not consistent with CPT instructions and guidance, including CPT Assistant.”
    *   VI. Appeal Timeline Discrepancy
        *   Medicare includes a 120-day deadline for stakeholders to file a redetermination request, while MA has only a 65-day deadline for a first level appeal.
        *   While the truncated MA timeline impacts all denied claims, it disproportionately affects claims denied due to burdensome medical documentation requests.
        *   Obtaining frequently duplicative medical documentation can involve extensive time and multiple communications between the laboratory and the ordering provider to assemble and submit the documentation to the payer’s specifications.
        *   This process frequently takes longer than 65 days, and the short timeframe prohibits providers and MA enrollees from continuing through the appeals process if this first deadline is not met.
        *   Quest Diagnostics recommends that CMS require MA plans to accept appeals filed within 120 days, which aligns with traditional Medicare rules.
    *   VII. Remote Review
        *   Quest was encouraged by the 2023 announcement that CMS would continue to exercise enforcement discretion to permit pathologists and other lab personnel to review digital laboratory data, digital results and digital images (“digital materials”) remotely, without obtaining a separate Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments (CLIA) certificate for the remote testing site, provided that the designated primary site or home base has such a certificate (using the address of the primary site) and the work being performed at the remote testing site falls within the specialties/subspecialties under the primary site’s certificate.
        *   In line with ACLA, Quest urges CMS to make permanent policy changes to formalize the current “enforcement discretion” and ensure that review of all patient-specific digital laboratory information — including histopathology and cytology images — is permissible at a remote testing location that operates under a primary site CLIA certificate.
        *   Such practices remain subject to CLIA, but they are understood to be conducted under the oversight of the laboratory that holds the primary site CLIA certificate.
        *   In contrast, review of physical slides — or other specimens — should continue to be performed at a laboratory that holds its own CLIA certificate (unless subject to a different exception under sections 493.43(b) and 493.55(b)).
        *   The transport and analysis of physical slides presents different risks than review of digital laboratory information and requires more direct control by a CLIA-certified laboratory.
        *   To allow for review of images at a remote testing site, an exception from the requirement for each lab to hold its own CLIA certificate should be added to 42 CFR §§ 493.43(b) and 493.55(b) as follows:
            *   “(4) Laboratories, from which a board-certified pathologist or other laboratory professional accesses the designated primary site system using a secure remote access protocol to retrieve, review, and analyze patient specific digital laboratory information.”
        *   To effectuate these changes for remote analysis of digital lab information, conforming edits to the regulations are required.
        *   Per ACLA, we propose defining the term “digital laboratory information” and amending the definition of “laboratory” at 42 CFR § 493.2 as follows:
            *   “Digital laboratory information:
                *   (1) means any of the following:
                    *   (A) a digital image derived from a glass slide; or
                    *   (B) data or digital images including, but not limited to, flow cytometry plots; cytogenetic karyograms; chromatographic, mass spectrometric, clinical chemistry, immunological, and hematologic data; electropherograms; gel images; and genetic expression, array, and sequencing data; and
                *   (2) is patient-specific when it is accompanied by information that can be used to identify the individual from whose specimen the information was derived.
            *   Laboratory means a facility for the biological, microbiological, serological, chemical, immunohematological, hematological, biophysical, cytological, pathological, or other examination of materials derived from the human body, including patient-specific digital laboratory information, for the purpose of providing information for the diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of any disease or impairment of, or the assessment of the health of, human beings...”
        *   This change to the definition of “laboratory” is necessary because digital laboratory information may not otherwise meet the definition of “materials derived from the human body.”
        *   Moreover, the “patient-specific” modifier is important because only examination of patient-specific digital laboratory information should be subject to regulation under CLIA.
        *   Entities analyzing only deidentified information for the purpose of supporting a clinical laboratory’s examination of a patient specimen, such as third parties that receive deidentified genetic variant information, should not be regulated as clinical laboratories under CLIA.
        *   Finally, to allow for remote review of cytology slides, the standard for cytology should be revised so that slide review may not be required to be done on the premises of the laboratory certified to conduct testing in the subspeciality of cytology (the transmitting laboratory) and that performed the technologic preparation of the slides but may be reviewed by a laboratory certified to conduct testing in the subspeciality of cytology that was provided with properly prepared and transmitted digital images of the slides by the transmitting laboratory.
        *   This could be achieved with minor revisions to 42 CFR § 1274(a) to read as follows:
            *   “(a) Cytology slides: All cytology slides must be prepared on the premises of a laboratory certified to conduct testing in the subspecialty of cytology.”
*   4. What alternative approaches could be taken to achieve or accomplish the same goal with a lesser burden? For example, are there less burdensome approaches that are used by other entities such as State governments or private companies that could be adopted by HHS to achieve its goal with less burdensome requirements? What would be the impact on costs and savings?
    *   I. Enforce Current Medicare Advantage Requirements
        *   CMS can decrease administrative burdens on healthcare providers by addressing the multitude of administrative barriers routinely deployed by MA plans.
        *   Currently, providers who serve MA enrollees must jump through multiple hoops throughout the claims filing process and appeals pathway to obtain a similar coverage rate as traditional Medicare for most claims.
        *   CMS should enforce the regulation that requires MA plans to comply with National Coverage Determinations (NCDs), Local Coverage Determinations (LCDs), and general coverage and benefit conditions included in traditional Medicare laws and regulations.
        *   Coverage policies must be consistent with coverage criteria and support the requirements for appropriate medical necessity determinations as provided in 42 CFR § 422.101.
        *   Quest Diagnostics recommends that CMS focus on ensuring that claims are properly adjudicated by MA plans, which would decrease administrative burden on providers and MA plans.
        *   Another area of concern that requires attention is the trend by MA plans, or laboratory benefit managers (LBMs) on behalf of MA plans, of adopting and implementing internal coverage criteria not “publicly accessible” and not based on “current evidence” in widely used treatment guidelines or clinical literature as required by § 422.101(b)(6).
        *   Quest Diagnostics urges CMS to require MA organizations or their contracted laboratory benefit managers to include a publicly accessible list of payable diagnosis codes to increase transparency and efficiency in the system.
        *   Additionally, Quest Diagnostics joins other stakeholders in calling for CMS to establish a streamlined mechanism for providers to report systemic issues with MA plans.
        *   Specifically, we recommend that CMS create a provider-specific electronic form to report systemic MA violations to CMS.
        *   CMS should ensure that this mechanism will allow providers to report hundreds or even thousands of claims denied for similar reasons from a single MA plan in a single batch, without requiring that each claim be submitted individually.
        *   Further, CMS should establish a clear process to allow providers to escalate patterns of suspected violations and to resolve disputes between providers and MA organizations.
        *   To ensure that MA tactics are not preventing beneficiaries from accessing clinically necessary testing and resulting in denials of reimbursement for appropriate services, it is crucial that CMS is prepared to receive and handle reports of MA plans that routinely employ aggressive internal coverage criteria and so-called “utilization management” tactics.
    *   II. Local Coverage Determination Process Transparency
        *   While requirements under the 21st Century Cures Act improved the transparency of the submission process for a local coverage determination (LCD), Quest Diagnostics remains concerned about the extensive timeline from requesting an LCD to final determination, the inability to determine when a requested LCD might be developed, and a lack of clarity about where an LCD stands in the queue.
        *   According to ACLA, laboratories report that after an LCD request has been “accepted” by a Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC), it can take years for the MAC to issue a final decision.
        *   During this time, MACs are unable to provide any updates to the applicants or to the public, until a draft policy is released and/or the MAC schedules public meetings to discuss policy development.
        *   Complicating the matter, LCD requests are not necessarily considered in the order they are submitted – a MAC can prioritize a request for a specific LCD, such as one it believes will impact larger numbers of Medicare beneficiaries, over an earlier request.
        *   To increase transparency and accountability, Quest Diagnostics recommends that CMS instruct MACs to make publicly available a dashboard of LCD requests that are under consideration, along with the submission date.
        *   This would be similar to the NCD Dashboard, which is maintained and distributed by CMS.
        *   Ideally, the LCD dashboard would display when a policy is actively under review as opposed to waiting in the queue after being accepted.
        *   Publicly sharing the topics in the waitlist will help stakeholders avoid request duplication and will help applicants understand where their applications fall in the queue based on the application date.
        *   Providing this information publicly will also allow Medicare beneficiaries and policy makers to understand the true length of time for coverage of novel services.
*   5. Are there HHS regulations, guidance, or reporting requirements that are rooted in outdated technology? Can new technologies be leveraged to allow for rescinding or updating these policies? What are the cost implications?
    *   I. E-Signature Policies for Laboratory Testing
        *   Due to the inability of an ordering provider to include an electronic signature on a Health Level Seven (HL7) electronic test order, laboratories and ordering providers frequently face an increased administrative burden to obtain and provide the patient’s medical record to Medicare or another payor to demonstrate that the ordering provider intended to order the test for the patient.
        *   Currently, there are no means for a laboratory to obtain an electronic signature through an HL7 electronic test order.
        *   A laboratory cannot include a signature on an order in an X12 275 health care attachment because a clinical laboratory order does not contain a signature field.
        *   Electronic Health Records (EHRs) and Laboratory Information Systems (LISs) do not support the HL7 Clinical Documentation Architecture (CDA) to exchange orders and results; they predominantly use HL7v2, which is a “transactional” standard that has been used for many years that can handle the data necessary to support high-volume clinical laboratory ordering and resulting.
        *   CDA, on the other hand, is a document-based standard, suitable for messaging a final laboratory result, but not suitable for the high-volume transactional exchange necessary for clinical laboratory orders.
        *   An HL7v2 message used to communicate a laboratory order includes data that identifies the ordering practitioner, and it is possible to determine if that ordering practitioner was authorized to place the order.
        *   This type of process has been in place for more than a decade without concerns raised about the validity of such electronic orders, or clinicians’ intent to submit such orders.
        *   Quest Diagnostics recommends that CMS work with the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy and Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ASTP/ONC) to establish standards for electronic signatures for laboratory tests, making clear that an electronic signature on an order submitted through a certified electronic health record (EHR) is a signed laboratory order and is evidence of the physician’s intent to order to the test.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: Quest Diagnostics, a leading diagnostic information services provider, urges HHS to implement broad regulatory reforms to reduce administrative burdens, improve reimbursement clarity, and leverage technology to enhance patient access and chronic disease prevention through laboratory testing.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Quest Diagnostics
- **Type:** Organization
- **Role/Expertise:** World’s leading provider of diagnostic information services; serves one in three adult Americans and about half of U.S. physicians and hospitals annually; operates over 7,400 patient access points; diagnostic testing accounts for 2-3% of healthcare spending but drives up to 70% of healthcare decisions.
- **Geographic Scope:** National (United States)
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly affected by federal regulations governing clinical laboratory testing, reimbursement policies (e.g., PAMA), medical documentation, prior authorization, and the adoption of new technologies in healthcare diagnostics. Their operational efficiency and financial viability are tied to these regulations.
structuredSections.corePosition: Quest Diagnostics supports HHS's goals to deregulate, alleviate administrative burdens, and reduce inefficiencies to foster innovation and improve public health. We believe that reforming regulations related to laboratory testing, such as Medicare reimbursement, prior authorization, and technological integration, is critical to ensuring patient access to care and enabling more effective chronic disease management.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- **Medicare Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (PAMA)**:
    - CMS should maintain current CLFS rates in 2026, holding off on scheduled reductions of up to 15 percent.
    - CMS should change the next PAMA data collection period from January 1 – June 30, 2019, to January 1 – June 30, 2025.
    - CMS should conduct an aggressive education campaign to ensure all laboratories (physician office, hospital outreach, independent) understand their PAMA reporting obligations.
- **Medical Documentation**:
    - CMS should clarify that a Test Requisition Form (TRF) is a valid form of medical documentation, sufficient to determine medical necessity.
    - CMS should update the Program Integrity Manual (Pub. No. 100-08, Ch. 3, Sec. 3.3.2.1) to reflect TRF sufficiency.
    - CMS should communicate this update to Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs) and Medicare Advantage (MA) plans.
- **ICD-10 Guidelines for Clinical Laboratory Tests**:
    - CMS and CDC National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS) should modify ICD-10-CM Official Guidelines for Coding and Reporting to remove “Excludes Notes” (Section I.A.12).
    - Alternatively, agencies should clarify that Excludes Notes cannot be the sole basis for claims denial, requiring payers to obtain information from the ordering provider before denial.
- **Expanding Access and Frequency of Lab Screening Tests**:
    - CMS should modernize Medicare policy to allow for more flexible, clinically guided access to screening lab tests, deferring to licensed healthcare practitioners' medical decision-making.
    - HHS should align lab screening test coverage and utilization policies within its programs to support prevention, early detection, and equitable access.
- **CMS Universal Foundation Initiative**:
    - CMS should evaluate adding a quality measure of appropriate low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) testing to its Universal Foundation initiative.
- **Lab Results to Empower Patient Choice**:
    - HHS should encourage the development and delivery of digital tools, including AI, that support laboratories in providing clear, evidence-based education with test results.
    - HHS, in coordination with OIG, should explore safe harbors, exceptions, or regulatory clarification to allow laboratories to share clinically relevant decision support and technology enhancements with patients and providers, recognizing these as care delivery, not inducement.
- **Prior Authorization**:
    - CMS should clarify and enforce the rule that MA plans cannot restrict prior authorization requests solely to ordering providers, allowing enrollees, their representatives, and any provider (including labs) to initiate requests.
- **Date of Service Policy**:
    - CMS should prohibit MAOs from denying a prior authorization request for a lab test because it was submitted after the date of specimen collection.
    - CMS should amend 42 C.F.R. § 422.122 to state that MA organizations must accept prior authorization requests from ordering providers or clinical labs anytime before a timely claim is submitted, and cannot deny based on request submission after the date of service.
    - CMS should amend 42 C.F.R. § 414.510 to clarify that the date of service for lab tests is for billing purposes and not to deny coverage or restrict beneficiary access.
- **Organization Determination Requirement**:
    - CMS should improve and clarify OD process requirements to protect laboratories from undue financial liability.
    - Unless an MAO has contracted for a provider to assume financial responsibility, the MAO should be financially responsible for "plan-directed care."
    - A referral for a laboratory service from a participating ordering practitioner should be considered a favorable OD, regardless of the lab's participation status, and the MAO should pay the laboratory.
    - MA beneficiaries should have the same rights as traditional Medicare beneficiaries to elect to receive laboratory testing without the delay or administrative burden of first receiving an OD.
- **National Correct Coding Initiative (NCCI)**:
    - CMS should remove the quoted paragraph in Chapter X: Pathology/Laboratory Services, Introduction, Section A, regarding single HCPCS/CPT codes for multiple reportable results.
    - CMS should delete the Molecular Pathology section [Ch. X, Section, F.8] and the Medically Unlikely Edits (MUE) section [Ch. X, Section M.15] in their entirety.
    - CMS should modify the language in General Coding Policies [Chapter 1, page I-22] to state that NCCI edits shall not be inconsistent with CPT instructions and guidance, including CPT Assistant.
- **Appeal Timeline Discrepancy**:
    - CMS should require MA plans to accept appeals filed within 120 days, aligning with traditional Medicare rules.
- **Remote Review**:
    - CMS should make permanent policy changes to formalize enforcement discretion, allowing remote review of all patient-specific digital laboratory information (including histopathology and cytology images) under a primary site CLIA certificate.
    - Add an exception to 42 CFR §§ 493.43(b) and 493.55(b) for labs accessing primary site systems via secure remote access for digital information review.
    - Define "digital laboratory information" and amend the definition of "laboratory" at 42 CFR § 493.2 to include patient-specific digital laboratory information.
    - Revise 42 CFR § 1274(a) for cytology to allow digital slide review by a certified lab, even if not on the premises of the transmitting lab.
- **Enforce Current Medicare Advantage Requirements**:
    - CMS should enforce regulations requiring MA plans to comply with National Coverage Determinations (NCDs), Local Coverage Determinations (LCDs), and traditional Medicare coverage/benefit conditions.
    - CMS should require MA organizations or their contracted laboratory benefit managers to include a publicly accessible list of payable diagnosis codes.
    - CMS should establish a streamlined mechanism (e.g., provider-specific electronic form) for providers to report systemic MA violations, allowing batch reporting of similar denials and a clear escalation process.
- **Local Coverage Determination Process Transparency**:
    - CMS should instruct MACs to make publicly available a dashboard of LCD requests under consideration, including submission dates, similar to the NCD Dashboard.
    - The dashboard should ideally show when a policy is actively under review vs. waiting in the queue.
- **E-Signature Policies for Laboratory Testing**:
    - CMS should work with ASTP/ONC to establish standards for electronic signatures for laboratory tests.
    - Clarify that an electronic signature on an order submitted through a certified EHR is a signed laboratory order and evidence of physician's intent.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **PAMA Implementation Flaws**: The current implementation of PAMA has resulted in significant cuts to laboratory reimbursements and CLFS rates that do not reflect commercial market rates.
    - Flaws include overrepresentation of independent labs in data, underreporting by hospital/physician labs, lack of reporting penalties, use of pre-pandemic rates, year-over-year cuts up to 15%, no challenge mechanism for CLFS rates, and failure to reflect payments in light of ACOs/delegation/sequestration.
- **Burdensome Medical Documentation**: Clinical laboratories face significant administrative burden due to varied and demanding medical documentation requirements from payers, including refusal to accept test requisition forms (TRFs) as valid documentation.
- **ICD-10 Excludes Notes Misuse**: ICD-10 coding guidelines, specifically "Excludes Notes," are being used by payers as a basis for front-end claims denials for medically necessary services, imposing administrative burden and leading to non-payment for labs.
- **Restrictive Lab Screening Test Coverage**: Current Medicare policy for lab screening tests is too narrow in scope, frequency, and eligibility criteria, not reflecting modern clinical practice or the needs of an aging population, hindering early detection and prevention of chronic diseases.
- **Limitations on Leveraging Technology**: Current policies, particularly Anti-Kickback Statute safe harbors and Stark Law exceptions, limit the ability of labs to pair test results with advanced technology like AI and clinical decision support tools for patient and provider empowerment.
- **Prior Authorization Barriers**: Many MAOs prevent labs from submitting prior authorization requests for services they perform, leading to denials for already-performed, medically necessary tests and shifting financial burden to the lab, not the ordering clinician.
- **Date of Service Policy Misuse**: The CMS "date of service" policy for lab tests (date specimen collected) is misused by MA plans to deny prior authorization requests if submitted after the specimen collection date, causing denials and administrative burden when labs receive orders after the DOS has passed.
- **Impractical Organization Determination (OD) Requirements**: Labs find it impractical to seek ODs for non-covered lab testing due to specimen integrity issues, turnaround time requirements, and the 14-day MAO response time, often leading to services being performed without reimbursement.
    - MAO beneficiaries do not have the same rights as traditional Medicare beneficiaries to elect non-covered testing without delay or administrative burden of an OD.
- **Conflicting NCCI Coding Guidance**: Duplicative and inconsistent coding guidance between the NCCI Medicare Policy Manual and AMA CPT code set creates compliance issues and claims denials for clinical laboratories, forcing them to navigate contradictory rules.
- **Truncated MA Appeal Timelines**: The 65-day deadline for first-level appeals in MA plans is shorter than traditional Medicare's 120 days, disproportionately affecting claims requiring extensive medical documentation and preventing providers from completing the appeals process.
- **Lack of LCD Process Transparency**: The process for Local Coverage Determinations (LCDs) is extensive, taking years from request to final determination, with no public updates on status or queue position, hindering transparency and accountability.
- **Outdated E-Signature Policies**: The inability to include electronic signatures on HL7 electronic test orders creates administrative burden for labs and ordering providers, requiring additional medical record submissions to prove intent to order.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- Quest Diagnostics highlights that diagnostic testing, while accounting for only 2-3% of healthcare spending, drives up to 70% of healthcare decisions, underscoring its disproportionate impact.
- The comment details the systemic nature of PAMA's flaws, noting that Congress has intervened five times to delay payment cuts and six times to delay data reporting, and a D.C. Circuit Court ruled CMS's definition of "applicable laboratory" as arbitrary and capricious, indicating widespread recognition of the issue.
- They provide powerful statistics on the impact of LDL-C testing, stating that over 200 studies involving more than 2 million patients confirm LDL-C levels can cause atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, and project CVD costs to triple from $400 billion to $1.3 trillion between 2020 and 2050.
- Quest acknowledges and seeks to formalize CMS's existing "enforcement discretion" that currently permits remote review of digital laboratory data, results, and images under a primary CLIA certificate, demonstrating an existing workaround they want codified into permanent policy.
- The comment strongly argues for MA beneficiaries to have the same rights as traditional Medicare beneficiaries to elect to receive laboratory testing without the administrative burden or delays of Organization Determinations (ODs), emphasizing equity and patient access.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "Diagnostic testing accounts for only two to three percent of healthcare spending yet drives up to 70 percent of healthcare decisions."
- "It is illogical that a laboratory to whom a referral is made – and that furnished the ordered service as requested by the ordering physician – should be held financially liable."
- "MA beneficiaries should have the same rights as traditional Medicare beneficiaries to elect to receive laboratory testing without the delay or administrative burden of first receiving an OD."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I am commenting on the U.S Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
*   The years of pregnancy to age three set the foundation for a baby’s development, learning and relationships.
    *   Babies rely entirely on the adults around them—parents, caregivers, and early childhood professionals—to provide safe, nurturing care.
    *   When babies or their caregivers face reduced support or program quality, babies can end up facing long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences.
    *   When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health.
*   Regulations matter.
    *   HHS, as the leading Federal agency tasked with enhancing the health and well-being of all Americans, plays a critical role in ensuring that babies, families, and the professionals who care for little ones have access to the resources, protections, and supports they need.
    *   In considering changes to regulations, HHS must preserve regulations that:
        *   Keep young children safe and healthy.
        *   Enable the adults in their lives to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
*   For example, regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings are needed to keep babies safe and developmentally on track.
*   Regulations that keep children and those who care for them healthy, like those that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care, must be maintained.
    *   This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe.
*   HHS rules reach far beyond just Medicaid and early learning, with many HHS programs laying the foundation of quality care and critical support that babies need.
*   Any changes to regulations must be:
    *   Transparent.
    *   Grounded in evidence.
    *   Focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
*   Because each regulation is different, HHS must continue to give the public—including families and early childhood professionals like me—ample time and opportunity to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes.
    *   We need a robust public process to make sure that the rules work for babies and those who care for them.
*   To keep America’s babies healthy, HHS must maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services.
*   Please uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
*   I would also like to add that I am a product of Head Start Services.
    *   I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career.
    *   I have a Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma.
    *   I have been a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for the past twenty-three years servicing the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles.
    *   It gives great pleasure to give back to my community.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An experienced early childhood education professional and Head Start alumna urges HHS to maintain and strengthen regulations that ensure the safety, health, and development of young children, advocating for transparent, evidence-based changes and robust public input.

-   **Name/Organization:** Elizabeth Villanueva
-   **Type:** Individual
-   **Role/Expertise:** Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma; 23 years as a vendor for the state of California Early Start system; former Head Start recipient.
-   **Geographic Scope:** Local (South Central Los Angeles, San Pedro, CA) / State (California)
-   **Stake in Issue:** As an early childhood professional directly involved in providing services to vulnerable children and a beneficiary of early childhood programs, she has a direct interest in regulations that ensure quality care and support for young children and their caregivers.
structuredSections.corePosition: I strongly believe that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) must preserve and uphold regulations that safeguard the health, safety, and development of young children from pregnancy to age three. These foundational years dictate lifelong well-being, and effective regulations, grounded in evidence and developed transparently with public input, are crucial for ensuring access to quality care and services.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
-   Preserve regulations that keep young children safe and healthy.
-   Preserve regulations that enable adults to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
    -   Specifically, maintain regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings.
    -   Maintain regulations that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care.
-   Ensure any changes to regulations are transparent, grounded in evidence, and focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
-   Provide ample time and opportunity for the public, including families and early childhood professionals, to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes through a robust public process.
-   Maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services for babies.
-   Uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
-   Reduced support or program quality for babies and caregivers could lead to long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences for children.
-   Regulatory changes that are not transparent, evidence-based, or child-focused could negatively impact the well-being and safety of children, families, and their service providers.
-   Inadequate public involvement in the regulatory process may result in rules that do not effectively serve the needs of babies and their caregivers.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
-   Personal testimony as a "product of Head Start Services," attributing her education and career advantages to the program.
-   Extensive professional experience as a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for 23 years, specifically servicing "the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles."
-   Expresses deep personal satisfaction and commitment to her work, stating "It gives great pleasure to give back to my community."

-   "When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health."
-   "This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe."
-   "I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- The American Association of Christian Schools (AACS) provides comments on the Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation to Make America Healthy Again (AHRQ-2025-0001).
  - AACS is a national organization with over 700 member schools, employing more than 13,000 teachers and staff, and serving approximately 118,000 students nationwide.
  - We appreciate the opportunity to provide input regarding regulations that we believe should be rescinded or replaced.

- 1. Department of Health and Human Services “Improving Child Care Access, Affordability, and Stability in the Child Care and Development Fund” Rule (45 CFR Part 98, RIN 0970-AD02)
  - We recommend that the 2024 rule be repealed or replaced with one that complies with Congressional intent and statutory requirements while ensuring parental choice and participation in faith-based programs.
  - Background:
    - Faith-based child care providers, operated by churches, synagogues, or other religious organizations, are a vital component of the CCDF’s mixed-delivery system, serving a significant portion of the approximately 1.3 million children who receive CCDF subsidies monthly.
    - They are particularly important in underserved or rural areas where they may be the primary or only option, often integrating religious teachings and values as part of their mission.
    - Under the Child Care and Development Block Grant Act of 2014 (42 U.S.C. 9857 et seq.), parents have the right to choose providers, including faith-based ones, through certificates.
    - Certificates are considered indirect federal financial assistance because funds flow through parents’ choices, not directly to providers, which preserves faith-based providers’ First Amendment rights by allowing them to participate without federal restrictions on religious activities.
    - In contrast, grants or contracts involve direct federal financial assistance, subjecting providers to federal regulations like 45 CFR Part 87, which requires explicitly religious activities to be separated in time or location and participation to be voluntary.
    - For inherently religious faith-based providers, these requirements conflict with their mission, leading some to opt out of direct funding to maintain religious autonomy.
    - The February 2024 CCDF final rule (89 FR 15366, effective April 30, 2024) mandates that states and territories use “some” grants or contracts for direct child care services to address supply shortages, especially for underserved populations.
      - Specifically, 45 CFR 98.30(b)(1) states: “Lead Agencies shall use some grants or contracts for direct child care services to increase the supply of quality child care for children described in paragraph (a)(3) of this section.”
      - HHS justifies this by arguing that grants and contracts stabilize providers by guaranteeing payments, encouraging participation, and addressing supply gaps where certificates are insufficient.
    - This mandate applies to all states and territories (except Tribal Lead Agencies) and requires reallocating CCDF funds from certificates to grants or contracts, necessitating significant restructuring for approximately 43 states that predominantly or exclusively use certificates.
  - Inconsistent with Statutory Text:
    - The 2014 reauthorization explicitly states that nothing in the act shall be construed “(1) to favor or promote the use of grants and contracts for the receipt of child care services. . . over the use of child care certificates; or (2) to disfavor or discourage the use of such certificates for the purchase of child care services, including those services provided by private or nonprofit entities, such as faith-based providers” (42 USC 9858o(b)).
    - The 2024 rule, by removing language to ensure parental certificates and requiring grant funding without parental certificate options for underserved populations, de facto violates this statutory prohibition.
  - Impact on Faith-Based Providers: The shift to grants or contracts poses unique challenges due to legal and operational implications of direct federal financial assistance.
    - Direct vs. Indirect Assistance:
      - Certificates: Faith-based providers receive funds indirectly, aligning with Supreme Court precedents (e.g., Zelman v. Simmons-Harris, 2002) that uphold indirect aid to religious organizations as constitutional, allowing full integration of religious content.
      - Grants or Contracts: These are direct agreements making providers recipients of direct federal financial assistance, requiring them under 45 CFR 87.3 to ensure CCDF-funded services are free of “explicitly religious activities” and that participation is voluntary, which is incompatible with pervasively religious programs.
    - Potential Withdrawal:
      - Many faith-based providers prioritize their religious mission and First Amendment protections over participation in programs imposing secular requirements.
      - A 2021 analysis noted some faith-based providers withdrew from direct funding (e.g., Head Start grants) due to concerns about losing religious character or hiring autonomy.
      - The 2024 rule’s mandate for grants or contracts could lead faith-based providers to decline participation, as a church-based provider integrating Bible study might find it impractical to separate religious activities.
      - Historical precedent in the 1990s saw some faith-based organizations exit federal programs after Charitable Choice provisions clarified direct funding rules, citing conflicts with religious autonomy; a similar dynamic is feared.
    - Scale of Impact:
      - A 2021 Bipartisan Policy Center report estimated 15% of working parents use faith-based providers, often serving low-income families eligible for CCDF.
      - If even a portion withdraws, it could reduce the supply of CCDF-eligible providers, particularly in areas with few alternatives, undermining the regulation’s goal for underserved populations.
  - Consequences for Access to Child Care: The potential withdrawal of faith-based providers undermines the regulation’s goal of increasing child care supply and could exacerbate access challenges for low-income families.
    - Reduced Provider Pool:
      - If faith-based providers opt out, states may struggle to meet supply increase requirements, potentially leaving families with no CCDF-eligible options in rural areas where faith-based centers are primary providers.
      - The 2024 rule assumes grants and contracts will attract providers through stable payments, but this may not apply to faith-based providers prioritizing religious autonomy.
    - Impact on Families:
      - Families relying on faith-based providers may lose access to subsidized care, forcing choices between unsubsidized care, non-faith-based providers, or foregoing employment/education, contradicting the CCDBG Act’s emphasis on parental choice and family economic stability.
    - Regional Disparities:
      - The impact will vary by state, with those highly reliant on faith-based providers (e.g., Alabama, Georgia) facing greater supply reductions, as FY 2022–2024 CCDF plans show southern states often report faith-based providers as key partners.
  - For these reasons, we request that the 2024 rule be repealed or replaced with one that complies with Congressional intent and statutory requirements while ensuring parental choice and participation in faith-based programs.

- 2. Nine Agency “Partnerships with Faith-Based and Neighborhood Organizations,” Rule (45 CFR Part 87, RIN 0991-AC13)
  - We recommend that the 2023 Nine Agency Rule be rescinded and replaced with the 2020 rule from President Trump’s first term.
  - Background:
    - In 2023, nine federal agencies issued a final rule modifying regulations for faith-based organizations partnering with agencies to provide services, in response to former President Biden’s Executive Order 14015, which aimed to undo Executive Order 13831 and subsequent 2020 regulations.
    - The requirements of the 2023 rule unnecessarily burden faith-based service providers, pressuring them to alter their religious practices or identity to offer services and impeding fair competition with secular organizations.
  - Burden to America’s Faith-Based Religious Service Organizations:
    - The 2023 rule includes a notice-and-referral requirement (88 Fed. Reg. 2399) that mandates faith-based providers inform beneficiaries that if they object to the provider’s religious nature, the provider must make reasonable efforts to refer them to an alternative.
      - This requirement burdens faith-based providers with extra work detracting from their mission.
      - It also encourages religious discrimination against providers by beneficiaries, essentially targeting them due to their religious nature.
      - The requirement to provide alternative options applies only to faith-based organizations, unfairly singling them out.
    - Additionally, the rule alters language for recipients of “indirect financial assistance,” now stating that faith-based providers receiving such assistance cannot require beneficiaries to attend religious activities that are part of the program.
      - Beneficiaries must also have a secular option to religious providers to ensure a “genuine and private” decision.
      - This implies that a religious organization’s right to partner in service programs depends on a nearby secular group offering the same service, which is questioned by Supreme Court cases such as Trinity Lutheran Church v. Comer (2017), Fulton v. City of Philadelphia (2021), and Carson v. Makin (2022).
  - Inconsistent with Statutory Law and the U.S. Constitution:
    - The 2023 rule eliminates references to “religious exercise” and the requirement that agencies will not disqualify a faith-based organization based on its religious motivation for providing services.
    - Instead, the rule states agencies cannot discriminate based on religious affiliation or for reasons that would “disfavor a similarly situated secular organization such as one that has the same capacity to effectively provide services” (88 Fed. Reg. 2402).
    - Rather than offering clarification for religious accommodations, this change will effectively gut religious nondiscrimination and accommodation protections for faith-based organizations by ignoring free exercise rights and viewing religious organizations’ conduct identically to secular ones.
    - The rule also eliminates language from the 2020 regulations that clarified which laws require a religious accommodation (e.g., First Amendment, Religious Freedom Restoration Act, Weldon Amendment, other conscience protection laws).
      - This opens the door for arbitrary and capricious decisions regarding religious accommodation requests, rather than decisions based on legal and careful analysis of religious nondiscrimination laws.
    - Finally, the 2023 rule limits the scope of the Title VII religious exemption, claiming it merely allows religious organizations “to hire only people of a particular religion in the absence of any inconsistent statutes” (88 Fed. Reg. 2402).
      - The rule further states that the Title VII exemption “does not permit such organizations to discriminate against workers on the basis of another protected classification, even when an employer takes such action for sincere reasons related to its religious tenets (such as those that might amount to discrimination on the basis of employees’ sex)” (Id.).
      - The rule also removed language from the 2020 Rule that affirmed the rights of a religious organization to make employment decisions based on its religious tenets.
      - However, the Title VII religious exemption clearly protects religious organizations’ rights to make employment decisions based on religious tenets, and even in *Bostock v. Clayton County* (2020), the Supreme Court recognized the applicability of Title VII’s religious organization exemption, the First Amendment’s exception, and RFRA protection in appropriate cases.
      - This indicates Title VII’s religious organization exemption should serve as a valid defense to a sex discrimination claim, protecting the rights of religious organizations to make employment decisions based on religious tenets.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The American Association of Christian Schools urges the federal government to repeal recent regulations that disproportionately burden faith-based organizations, arguing they undermine parental choice, restrict religious freedom, and reduce access to essential services by forcing providers to compromise their core mission.

structuredSections.corePosition: We advocate for the repeal or replacement of recent federal regulations that we believe undermine parental choice, restrict the religious autonomy of faith-based service providers, and create unnecessary burdens that could reduce access to essential services for families. structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Regarding the 2024 CCDF Rule:**
  - The mandate for states to use "some" grants or contracts for direct child care services violates statutory prohibitions against disfavoring certificates to favor grants and contracts, contradicting Congressional intent.
  - This shift imposes "direct federal financial assistance" requirements on faith-based providers, forcing them to choose between participating in CCDF programs and maintaining their religious mission by separating religious activities from services.
  - Potential withdrawal of faith-based providers from grant/contract programs could significantly reduce the supply of CCDF-eligible child care, especially in underserved or rural areas where they are often the primary option.
  - Reduces parental choice by limiting access to preferred faith-based providers for families who rely on subsidized care, potentially forcing them into misaligned options or exacerbating economic instability.
  - Creates regional disparities, disproportionately affecting states with high reliance on faith-based providers.
- **Regarding the 2023 Nine Agency Rule:**
  - Imposes a notice-and-referral requirement on faith-based providers, burdening them with extra work and encouraging religious discrimination against them by beneficiaries.
  - Alters rules for "indirect financial assistance" by requiring secular options for beneficiaries and prohibiting required participation in religious activities, implying religious organizations’ rights depend on the availability of secular alternatives.
  - Eliminates references to "religious exercise" and weakens protections against discrimination based on religious motivation, effectively "gutting" religious nondiscrimination and accommodation protections.
  - Removes specific legal references (e.g., RFRA, Weldon Amendment) for religious accommodations, opening the door for arbitrary denials of accommodation requests.
  - Limits the scope of the Title VII religious exemption, misinterpreting its protections for religious organizations' employment decisions based on religious tenets, contrary to Supreme Court precedent (e.g., Bostock v. Clayton County).
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- Historical precedent demonstrates that faith-based organizations have previously withdrawn from direct federal funding programs (e.g., Head Start grants in the 1990s after Charitable Choice provisions) due to concerns about maintaining religious character and hiring autonomy, suggesting a similar outcome is likely with the 2024 CCDF rule.
- The argument that requiring a secular option for beneficiaries receiving indirect financial assistance is inconsistent with Supreme Court precedents, specifically citing *Trinity Lutheran Church v. Comer* (2017), *Fulton v. City of Philadelphia* (2021), and *Carson v. Makin* (2022).
- The assertion that the 2023 Nine Agency rule, by eliminating references to "religious exercise" and changing non-discrimination language, will "effectively gut religious nondiscrimination and accommodation protections for faith-based organizations."
- A detailed legal analysis of the 2023 rule's misinterpretation and limitation of the Title VII religious exemption, emphasizing that the Supreme Court's *Bostock v. Clayton County* (2020) decision recognized the continued applicability of this exemption.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "The mandate that states deliver “some” of the funds as grants and contracts and the restructuring of state programs necessitated by the regulation is a de facto violation of the statutory prohibition against disfavoring certificates to favor grants and contracts."
- "This requirement not only burdens the faith-based providers with extra work that detracts from their mission of service and faith, but it also encourages religious discrimination against the providers by the beneficiaries, essentially targeting these providers because of their religious nature."
- "To ignore a religious organization’s free exercise rights and merely view such organizations’ conduct in the same light as secular organizations’ is to ignore the very foundational principles of liberty and free exercise of religion on which our country was founded and our Constitution protects."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The Natural Products Association (NPA), the leading trade association for the natural products industry, is submitting comments in response to the Request for Information (RFI) regarding Docket ID AHRQ-2025-0001.
*   NPA requests that the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) clarify, via its regulations and guidance, that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has exclusive oversight over the labeling, quality, and safety of dietary supplements under the Federal Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act (FD&C Act) (21 U.S.C. 301 et seq).
    *   NPA further requests that HHS clarify that any state prohibitions on the labeling, marketing, and sale of these products are expressly and impliedly preempted by federal law.
*   Consistent with the RFI's intent, this change will contribute to better promoting the health and well-being of Americans by eliminating conflicting state regulations that currently impede consumer access to lawful, safe dietary supplement products subject to comprehensive FDA oversight.

*   DSHEA-FD&C Act
    *   The Dietary Supplement Health and Education Act of 1994 (DSHEA) amended the FD&C Act, creating a comprehensive framework for FDA regulation of vitamins, minerals, botanicals, and other dietary supplement products.
    *   DSHEA defined "dietary supplement," authorized nutritional support statements (structure/function claims), created safety standards, established when products are adulterated or misbranded, and authorized FDA to promulgate good manufacturing practices.
    *   In its findings, Congress determined that "dietary supplements are safe within a broad range of intake, and safety problems with the supplements are relatively rare."
    *   Congress also found that "a rational federal framework must be established to supersede the current ad hoc, patchwork regulatory policy on dietary supplements."
    *   To make a structure/function claim under 21 U.S.C. § 343(r), manufacturers must:
        *   Have substantiation that the statement is truthful and not misleading.
        *   The statement must contain a prominent disclaimer in boldface type that FDA has not evaluated the statement and the "product is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease."
    *   The FD&C Act preempts labeling requirements for structure/function claims that are not identical to the federal requirements (e.g., Ferrari v. Vitamin Shoppe Industries LLC, No. 22-1332 (1st Cir. 2023); Greenberg v. Target Corp., No. 19-16699 (9th Cir. 2021)).

*   Federal preemption of state law
    *   The U.S. Supreme Court recognizes that federal law can preempt state law either expressly or impliedly.
    *   Congress may expressly preempt state law by stating so.
    *   In the absence of express pre-emptive language, Congress' intent to preempt all state law in a particular area may be inferred where the federal regulation scheme is sufficiently comprehensive ("field preemption"), leaving no room for supplementary state regulation.
    *   Preemption is also inferred where the federal interest is so dominant that the federal system is assumed to preclude enforcement of state laws on the same subject.
    *   Courts also recognize preemption of state laws that conflict with federal law.

*   State bills restricting access to dietary supplements
    *   A growing number of state legislatures (e.g., Massachusetts, New York, California) have recently introduced bills to restrict minors’ access to dietary supplement products marketed for weight loss and muscle building.
    *   In 2024 alone, over a dozen states considered creating state-level regulatory schemes for dietary supplements.
    *   Special interest groups supporting these proposals consistently attempt to link products with significant safety portfolios, such as creatine, as directly causing eating disorders.
    *   In April 2024, a New York law (NY Gen. Bus. Law § 391-oo) took effect, establishing restrictions on the sale of OTC diet pills and dietary supplements for weight loss or muscle building to people under 18.
    *   In determining whether a product is covered by this legislation, state courts are directed to consider factors including, but not limited to:
        *   Whether the product contains:
            *   An ingredient approved by FDA for weight loss or muscle building;
            *   A steroid; or
            *   Creatine, green tea extract, raspberry ketone, garcinia cambogia, green coffee bean extract.
        *   Whether the product’s labeling or marketing bears statements or images that express or imply that the product will help:
            *   Modify, maintain, or reduce body weight, fat, appetite, overall metabolism, or the process by which nutrients are metabolized; or
            *   Maintain or increase muscle or strength.
        *   Whether the product or its ingredients are otherwise represented for the purpose of achieving weight loss or building muscle.
    *   Courts are also directed to consider whether the retailer has categorized the dietary supplement for weight loss or muscle building by:
        *   Placing signs, categorizing, or tagging the supplement with the described statements;
        *   Grouping the supplements with other weight loss or muscle-building products in a display, advertisement, webpage, or area of the store; or
        *   Otherwise representing that the product is for weight loss or muscle building.

*   Preemption argument
    *   NPA requests that HHS clarify through its regulations and guidance that NY Gen. Bus. Law § 391-oo and similar bills are expressly preempted under federal law.
    *   New York’s law restricts consumer access to dietary supplements based on structure/function claims (weight loss or muscle building statements).
    *   The state labeling regulations applicable to dietary supplement products are not identical to federal requirements for structure/function claims and are therefore preempted by federal law.
    *   The New York law constitutes a de facto ban on structure/claims authorized under DSHEA and FDA regulations (21 CFR 101.93, 65 Fed. Reg. 1000).
    *   Assuming arguendo that NY Gen. Bus. Law § 391-oo does not expressly regulate structure/function claims, the federal regulation scheme for dietary supplements is sufficiently comprehensive to infer that Congress left no room for supplementary state regulation ("field preemption").
    *   DSHEA comprehensively governs the labeling, manufacturing, sale, and safety of dietary supplement products.
    *   Congress intended exclusive federal regulation, as shown by its finding that "a rational federal framework must be established to supersede the current ad hoc, patchwork regulatory policy on dietary supplements."
    *   State-led restrictions on the sale of dietary supplement products directly conflict with Congress' intent and findings in passing DSHEA and are therefore preempted by federal law.

*   Conclusion
    *   In summary, NPA respectfully requests that HHS clarify (via its regulations and guidance) that FDA has exclusive oversight over the labeling, quality, and safety of dietary supplements under the FD&C Act.
    *   NPA also requests clarification that any state prohibitions on the labeling, marketing, and sale of these products are expressly and impliedly preempted by federal law.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The Natural Products Association urges HHS to clarify that federal law, specifically the FD&C Act and DSHEA, exclusively governs dietary supplement labeling, quality, and safety, thereby preempting all conflicting state-level regulations.
