structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   The National Indian Head Start Directors Association (NIHSDA) submits this comment letter in response to the Request for Information (RFI) titled “Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.”
    *   While NIHSDA has not identified any regulations implementing the Head Start Act that meet the RFI's criteria, we submit this letter to ask for partnership from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to seek amendments to provisions of the Head Start Act that are overly burdensome on American Indian/Alaska Native (AI/AN) Head Start programs.
    *   We also aim to work together to improve the administration of AI/AN Head Start for the benefit of Native children and families.
    *   NIHSDA extends gratitude to HHS and Secretary Kennedy for fighting to preserve funding levels for Head Start in the President’s Fiscal Year (FY) 2026 Budget Request, and for making protecting Tribal funding and Tribal sovereignty a priority.
    *   As the Administration continues its work to improve federal government efficiency, NIHSDA offers suggestions to improve the AI/AN Head Start program and to support Tribes’ sovereign authority to provide tailored, quality early childhood services.
*   Allow Tribes To Certify Their Own AI/AN Head Start Teachers and Staff
    *   The Head Start Act requires Head Start teachers to have a baccalaureate degree in early childhood education (42 U.S.C. § 9843a(a)(2)(A)).
    *   The Act requires Head Start teaching assistants to have a Child Development Associate (CDA) credential in early childhood education or be enrolled in a program leading to a CDA credential or associate or baccalaureate degree (Id. § 9843a(a)(2)(B)(ii)).
    *   AI/AN Head Start programs have great difficulty in recruiting and retaining teachers and teaching assistants that possess the required qualifications.
        *   Potential employees are often not aware of the CDA credential prior to seeking employment with Head Start, making it rare for job applicants to already have a CDA.
        *   The CDA process often begins only after the program hires the employee.
        *   Finding mentors and other support staff that are easily accessible to Tribal communities as part of the CDA process is difficult for many programs.
        *   Many Indian reservations do not possess institutions of higher learning where potential employees can obtain an associate or baccalaureate degree in early childhood education.
        *   Many reservations are located in extremely rural areas, making distance learning institutions inaccessible for rurally located Tribal communities.
    *   Head Start employees who obtain a degree are able to seek employment with the local school system or other early childhood programs for a higher paying wage.
        *   Due to inadequate funding levels, AI/AN Head Start programs are unable to compete with the wages that other schools and early childhood education programs can offer to employees.
        *   When Head Start teachers leave for higher wages with fewer requirements in other programs, it creates perpetual vacancies within the Head Start program.
    *   The Head Start Act of 2007 does not recognize Tribally awarded teaching certifications for satisfying the degree requirements for Head Start staff.
        *   Empowering Tribes to certify their own teachers supports Tribal sovereignty and self-determination by restoring to them the power to control key aspects of their educational programs and ensuring they can address their own priorities and goals.
        *   Allowing Tribes to set their own certification standards will also improve recruitment and retention of local educators who are familiar with and committed to the community.
        *   This concurrently honors the critical roles that Indigenous knowledge and cultural practices play in the health and development of Native children.
        *   This can be particularly important in remote or underserved areas where recruiting staff that meet the Head Start qualifications can be challenging.
    *   The Office of Head Start currently has authority to offer conditional and time-limited waivers of minimum credential requirements for Head Start center-based preschool classroom teachers (42 U.S.C. § 9843a(a)(4)(B)).
        *   To qualify for a waiver, programs must provide evidence they unsuccessfully attempted to recruit an individual with at least an associate degree in early childhood education.
        *   Programs must also provide evidence the individual for whom a waiver is requested is enrolled in a program that grants a qualifying associate or higher degree in a reasonable time (not to exceed 3 years).
        *   The individual must have a current CDA or equivalent (or be awaiting its award).
        *   The need to request waivers for teacher degree requirements presents several issues:
            *   Extensive documentation and evidence.
            *   Approval delays that affect immediate staffing needs.
            *   A lack of consistency in the approval process.
            *   The 3-year time limitation of the waiver is often not enough time when the teacher is working full-time, raising a family, and subsistence harvesting.
            *   Our experience is that the process does not acknowledge or value Indigenous knowledge, which is crucial in culturally relevant teaching environments.
            *   There is no waiver authority for infant and toddler center-based teachers in Early Head Start.
    *   Therefore, we urge HHS to work with NIHSDA to seek an amendment to the Head Start Act to recognize Tribally awarded certifications of AI/AN Head Start teachers.
*   Exempt AI/AN Head Start Programs from the 20% Non-Federal Match Requirement
    *   The Head Start Act provides that federal financial assistance provided to a grantee shall not exceed 80% of the approved costs, but HHS may approve a waiver if it furthers the Head Start program's purpose (42 U.S.C. § 9835(b)).
    *   The requirement for AI/AN Head Start programs to contribute a 20% non-federal share of their grant funding is particularly challenging for many Tribal communities, especially those without gaming revenue.
        *   These communities often experience high poverty rates, limited economic opportunities, and historical underfunding, making it difficult to generate necessary financial resources.
        *   The financial strain of starting and maintaining a Head Start program, combined with unanticipated cost increases (e.g., inflation or natural disasters), further exacerbates the challenge.
        *   AI/AN Head Start programs are often located in remote or economically depressed areas, making it harder to raise funds or secure in-kind contributions.
    *   The potential closure of Tribal Head Start programs due to an inability to meet the non-federal share requirement would have devastating effects on Tribal communities.
        *   These programs are often the sole means by which Tribal children can learn and preserve their Native languages and cultures.
        *   The loss of these programs would not only disrupt early childhood education but would also erode cultural identity.
        *   The federal government’s trust and treaty obligations to support the education and well-being of Tribal Nations further highlight the need to reassess this requirement for AI/AN Head Start programs.
    *   The Head Start Act provides the Office of Head Start with the authority to waive the 20% match requirement after considering factors such as:
        *   The lack of resources available in the community that may prevent the agency from providing all or a portion of the non-Federal contribution.
        *   The impact of the cost the agency may incur in initial years.
        *   The impact of an unanticipated increase in costs.
        *   Whether the agency is located in a community adversely affected by a major disaster.
        *   The impact on the community that would result if the agency ceased to carry out such program.
    *   The current waiver process for the non-federal share requirement, while designed to provide relief, is complex and resource-intensive.
        *   Programs must submit extensive documentation to justify their need, including detailed financial statements and evidence of efforts to secure non-federal funds.
        *   This process introduces uncertainty, as there is no guarantee of approval, which can lead to financial instability and difficulty in planning and budgeting.
        *   Even when waivers are granted, they often provide only temporary relief and do not address the underlying issue of inadequate funding and the unique challenges faced by Tribal communities.
    *   To address these challenges, AI/AN Head Start programs should be categorically exempt from the 20% non-federal share requirement.
        *   This exemption would alleviate the financial burden on Tribal communities, ensuring the stability and continuity of these essential programs.
        *   A precedent for such an exemption exists within the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), which recently eliminated the non-federal share requirement for Tribal child support programs, citing that the match requirement limited growth, caused disruptions, and created instability.
        *   Applying the same logic to AI/AN Head Start programs, removing the non-federal share requirement would allow them to focus on delivering high-quality, culturally appropriate early childhood education without an added threat of financial instability or program closure.
        *   This change would also honor the federal government’s treaty and trust obligations to provide education to Tribal children and would recognize the unique economic and cultural circumstances of Tribal Nations.
*   Conduct Tribal Consultation on Proposed Reforms to Head Start
    *   The ACF Congressional Justification accompanying the President’s FY 2026 Budget Request states that the President’s Budget Request “proposes a set of reform principles to modernize the Head Start program for the 21st century.”
        *   These reforms aim to increase parental choice; improve health, education, and employment outcomes; promote parental engagement; and enhance efficiency by reducing prescriptive requirements and streamlining federal oversight to increase state and local flexibility.
        *   The Justification does not provide additional detail as to what these reform principles are.
    *   We urge HHS to immediately provide detailed information about these proposed reforms to Tribal Nations in the form of a Dear Tribal Leader Letter and conduct Tribal consultation on these proposed reforms.
        *   AI/AN Head Start facilitates our exercise of Tribal sovereignty and tailored service delivery to meet local needs.
        *   It empowers our Tribal government to develop and implement culturally grounded, community-specific curricula and programs.
        *   Any proposed reforms that impact AI/AN Head Start must respect Tribal sovereignty and maintain the direct transfer of funds from the federal government to AI/AN Head Start agencies without state involvement.
        *   Tribal consultation is essential to ensure that any proposed reforms respect the unique needs and sovereignty of Tribal Nations.
    *   Indeed, the Head Start Act enshrines HHS’s Tribal consultation duty into statute.
        *   HHS is required to conduct Tribal consultation annually to ensure that the needs of Indian children are met and to provide training and technical assistance to AI/AN Head Start programs (42 U.S.C. § 9835(l)(4)).
        *   The Head Start Act also requires HHS to “consult with Indian tribes, including Alaska Natives, experts in Indian, including Alaska Native, early childhood education and development, linguists, and the National Indian Head Start Directors Association on the review and promulgation of [program performance] standards” (Id. § 9836a(a)(2)(D)).
        *   With regular Tribal consultation on changes and improvements to AI/AN Head Start, HHS can ensure that its policy priorities align with the unique needs of Tribal communities.
*   Continue to Protect Funding for AI/AN Head Start (Including Seeking Increases)
    *   NIHSDA extends sincerest appreciation for efforts to ensure that Head Start was not eliminated and maintained level funding in the President’s FY 2026 Budget Request.
    *   However, AI/AN Head Start programs already receive insufficient funding to provide quality services to their communities.
        *   Due to inflation and other economic factors, level funding at approximately $12.3 billion for Head Start will not reach as far as it did in FY 2025.
        *   The ACF Congressional Justification itself states that Head Start is expected to fund 21,789 fewer slots for children and 7,591 fewer Head Start staff.
    *   AI/AN Head Start programs cannot afford to stretch existing funds even further than they already do.
    *   Failure to increase appropriations for Head Start would further exacerbate the poor health and related economic outcomes that already plague many Tribal communities.
        *   All AI/AN Head Start programs offer services to promote early childhood and family health, including services related to nutrition, behavioral health, safety, and well-being.
        *   Some of these services are the only accessible services of their kind in a Tribal community.
    *   We urge consideration of the impacts of level funding for AI/AN Head Start on our community’s health and economic outcomes as HHS continues to make funding requests to Congress in FY 2026 and beyond.
    *   AI/AN Head Start programs are not only in need of level funding, but increased funding, including, at minimum, a 3.2% cost of living adjustment for AI/AN Head Start allocations.
*   Conclusion
    *   In furtherance and recognition of our unique government-to-government relationship with the United States, we are again requesting partnership to improve the administration of AI/AN Head Start by aggressively seeking statutory exemptions to burdensome requirements, conducting Tribal consultation on proposed reforms to Head Start, and seeking increased appropriations for Head Start in FY 2026 and beyond.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The National Indian Head Start Directors Association urges HHS to amend the Head Start Act to allow Tribal teacher certification, exempt AI/AN programs from the 20% non-federal match, ensure comprehensive Tribal consultation on reforms, and increase funding to protect vital early childhood services rooted in Tribal sovereignty for Native children.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** National Indian Head Start Directors Association (NIHSDA)
- **Type:** Advocacy Group
- **Role/Expertise:** Represents directors of American Indian/Alaska Native (AI/AN) Head Start programs, advocating for policies that support Tribal sovereignty and effective early childhood education for Native children.
- **Geographic Scope:** National, representing AI/AN Head Start programs across the United States.
- **Stake in Issue:** Directly represents and supports AI/AN Head Start programs, which are critically impacted by federal regulations, funding levels, and policy decisions related to staff qualifications, financial requirements, and overall program administration.
structuredSections.corePosition: We ask the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to partner with us to seek amendments to the Head Start Act that address provisions overly burdensome on American Indian/Alaska Native (AI/AN) Head Start programs. Our fundamental stance is that these changes, along with robust Tribal consultation and increased appropriations, are essential to improve the administration of AI/AN Head Start and support Tribes’ sovereign authority to provide tailored, quality early childhood services to Native children and families.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Seek an amendment to the Head Start Act to recognize Tribally awarded certifications of AI/AN Head Start teachers.
  - This would support Tribal sovereignty and self-determination by allowing Tribes to control key aspects of their educational programs and address their priorities.
  - It would improve recruitment and retention of local educators familiar with and committed to the community.
  - It would honor Indigenous knowledge and cultural practices crucial for Native children's development.
  - This addresses current issues where programs struggle to recruit staff with federal degree requirements, finding mentors for CDA, or accessing higher education in rural areas.
  - It also resolves issues with the current conditional waiver process, which is burdensome, delayed, inconsistent, too short (3 years), and undervalues Indigenous knowledge.
- Categorically exempt AI/AN Head Start programs from the 20% non-federal match requirement.
  - This would alleviate the significant financial burden on many Tribal communities, especially those without gaming revenue, which often face high poverty and limited economic opportunities.
  - It would ensure the stability and continuity of these essential programs, which are frequently the sole means for Tribal children to learn and preserve Native languages and cultures.
  - This would honor the federal government’s trust and treaty obligations.
  - It would eliminate the complex, resource-intensive, and uncertain current waiver process, mirroring a precedent set by ACF for Tribal child support programs.
- Immediately provide detailed information about proposed Head Start reforms to Tribal Nations via a Dear Tribal Leader Letter and conduct Tribal consultation on these reforms.
  - This is essential to ensure any proposed reforms respect Tribal sovereignty and maintain the direct transfer of funds from the federal government to AI/AN Head Start agencies without state involvement.
  - It fulfills the statutory requirement for annual Tribal consultation (42 U.S.C. § 9835(l)(4)) and consultation on performance standards (Id. § 9836a(a)(2)(D)).
- Continue to protect funding for AI/AN Head Start and seek increased appropriations.
  - Advocate for, at minimum, a 3.2% cost of living adjustment (COLA) for AI/AN Head Start allocations.
  - This is critical because AI/AN Head Start programs already receive insufficient funding, and level funding combined with inflation will lead to fewer funded slots and staff, exacerbating poor health and economic outcomes in Tribal communities.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Teacher Recruitment and Retention Challenges:**
  - Significant difficulty recruiting and retaining staff who possess the federally required baccalaureate degrees for teachers or CDA credentials for assistants.
  - Potential employees often lack awareness of the CDA credential, requiring programs to initiate the process after hiring.
  - Scarcity of accessible mentors and support staff for CDA training in rural Tribal communities.
  - Lack of local higher learning institutions on many reservations makes obtaining required degrees challenging, and distance learning is often inaccessible.
  - Inability to compete with higher wages offered by local school systems or other early childhood programs, leading to perpetual staff vacancies in Head Start programs.
- **Lack of Recognition for Tribally Awarded Certifications:**
  - The Head Start Act does not recognize Tribally awarded teaching certifications, which undermines Tribal sovereignty and limits control over their own educational programs.
- **Burdensome and Ineffective Teacher Qualification Waiver Process:**
  - The current waiver process for teacher degree requirements is extensive, requires significant documentation, causes approval delays, and lacks consistency.
  - The 3-year time limit for waivers is often insufficient for teachers balancing full-time work, family responsibilities, and subsistence harvesting.
  - The waiver process fails to acknowledge or value Indigenous knowledge, which is crucial for culturally relevant teaching environments.
  - There is no waiver authority for infant and toddler center-based teachers in Early Head Start.
- **Financial Strain from 20% Non-Federal Match Requirement:**
  - The 20% non-federal share requirement is a major financial burden for many Tribal communities, especially those without gaming revenue, due to high poverty, limited economic opportunities, and historical underfunding.
  - Unanticipated cost increases (e.g., inflation, natural disasters) further exacerbate the difficulty of meeting this requirement.
  - Inability to raise funds or secure in-kind contributions in remote or economically depressed Tribal areas.
  - The potential closure of programs due to inability to meet this match would be devastating, as these programs are often the sole means for Tribal children to learn and preserve Native languages and cultures, eroding cultural identity.
- **Ineffective Non-Federal Match Waiver Process:**
  - The current waiver process for the 20% match is complex and resource-intensive, requiring extensive financial documentation and evidence of fundraising efforts.
  - The uncertainty of approval creates financial instability and planning difficulties, and even when granted, waivers often provide only temporary relief without addressing underlying systemic issues.
- **Lack of Transparency and Consultation on Proposed Head Start Reforms:**
  - The Administration's proposed "reform principles to modernize the Head Start program" for FY 2026 lack detailed information.
  - Failure to immediately provide these details and conduct thorough Tribal consultation disregards Tribal sovereignty and the unique needs of AI/AN Head Start programs, raising concerns that reforms might negatively impact direct federal-to-AI/AN funding or culturally grounded curricula.
- **Insufficient and Stagnant Funding Levels:**
  - AI/AN Head Start programs already receive inadequate funding to provide quality services.
  - Level funding for FY 2026 (approximately $12.3 billion) will not stretch as far as in FY 2025 due to inflation and economic factors, leading to an estimated 21,789 fewer slots for children and 7,591 fewer staff.
  - Inability to stretch existing funds further will exacerbate poor health and economic outcomes in many Tribal communities, where Head Start often provides the only accessible services related to nutrition, behavioral health, safety, and well-being.
structuredSections.notableExperiences:
- The practical challenges faced by AI/AN Head Start programs in recruiting and retaining staff, including the common scenario where potential employees are not aware of the Child Development Associate (CDA) credential until hired, and the subsequent difficulties in finding accessible mentors and support staff for CDA training in rural Tribal communities.
- The insight that current federal requirements, such as the 3-year time limit for teacher qualification waivers, do not align with the realities of Indigenous life, where individuals often balance full-time work, raising a family, and subsistence harvesting, making degree attainment within such strict timelines challenging.
- The observation that the federal waiver process for teacher qualifications often fails to acknowledge or value Indigenous knowledge, despite its crucial role in culturally relevant teaching environments.
- A compelling illustration of the critical role of AI/AN Head Start programs as often the "sole means" for Tribal children to learn and preserve their Native languages and cultures, underscoring the devastating impact that program closures due to financial burdens like the 20% non-federal match requirement would have on cultural identity.
- The strategic insight that a precedent for categorical exemption from the non-federal share requirement exists within the Administration for Children and Families (ACF), which eliminated it for Tribal child support programs, citing that the match limited growth, caused disruptions, and created instability—providing a strong justification for a similar exemption for AI/AN Head Start.
structuredSections.keyQuotations:
- "To expect that programs can recruit and hire someone with an existing CDA is not possible. It is very rare that a job applicant already has a CDA. It is only after the program hires the employee that the CDA process can begin."
- "Our experience is that the process does not acknowledge or value Indigenous knowledge, which is crucial in culturally relevant teaching environments."
- "The potential closure of Tribal Head Start programs due to an inability to meet the non-federal share requirement would have devastating effects on Tribal communities. These programs are often the sole means by which Tribal children can learn and preserve their Native languages and cultures. The loss of these programs would not only disrupt early childhood education but would also erode cultural identity."

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Letter from Licensed Child Care Association of Oklahoma Inc. (LCA)
    *   Re: Public Comment on Deregulation and HHS Deregulatory RFI Pursuant to Executive Orders 14192 and 14219.
    *   Submitted in response to the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) invitation for stakeholders to submit deregulatory ideas through Regulations.gov, docket number AHRQ-2025-0001.
    *   We, on behalf of the Licensed Child Care Association of Oklahoma (LCA)'s members, appreciate the opportunity to provide input on HHS's comprehensive deregulatory effort.
    *   LCA supports and appreciates the Administration’s goals to reduce unnecessary regulatory burdens while maintaining the integrity of protecting children in licensed childcare facilities.
    *   We submit the following for the Department’s consideration for rule rescission or modification of guidance.
*   Subject: Eliminate Access to CCDBG Funds for Federally Funded Head Start Grantees
*   Summary Recommendation
    *   We urge HHS to adopt a clear and firm policy that Head Start programs may only be funded through Head Start appropriations and must not be permitted to access Child Care and Development Block Grant (CCDBG) funds.
    *   Doing so will end a harmful and anticompetitive practice that undermines the viability of private child care small businesses and exacerbates inequity in the early childhood education sector.
*   Regulation/Practice at Issue
    *   Under current practice, some Head Start grantees are allowed to "braid" or "layer" their federal Head Start funds with CCDBG subsidies.
    *   This means they receive two sources of federal funding to serve the same child during overlapping hours when the Head Start program funds a full-day program.
    *   This model of dual funding effectively allows federally operated programs to function with vastly more resources than private child care businesses.
        *   This creates crushing competition that non-Head Start providers cannot survive.
    *   Private child care businesses are typically ineligible to become Head Start grantees and are not offered equitable partnership opportunities.
    *   As a result, these federally funded programs dominate the market, absorb the available workforce, and drive closures among private providers.
        *   Private providers are subject to the same (or greater) regulatory burdens but receive only a single stream of limited funding.
*   Executive Order 14219 Criteria Met
    *   This policy meets multiple criteria for repeal under Executive Order 14219:
        *   (v) It imposes significant costs on private parties (licensed child care businesses) that are not outweighed by public benefits.
            *   It inflates funding to already heavily subsidized programs while destabilizing the rest of the industry.
        *   (vii) It imposes undue burdens on small businesses and impedes entrepreneurship in the child care sector.
            *   93% of providers are women small business owners.
        *   (iv) It raises issues of economic significance not clearly authorized by statute.
            *   While Head Start and CCDBG are each authorized under distinct federal laws, nothing in statute compels or authorizes their funding to be combined for overlapping care of the same child.
*   Recommended Deregulatory Action
    *   HHS should immediately issue a regulation or guidance that:
        *   Prohibits Head Start grantees, programs, and collaborative contracted programs from receiving CCDBG subsidies for the same children they are serving under Head Start grant awards.
    *   This deregulatory action would:
        *   Ensure that each program serves its intended audience without duplication.
        *   Restore fair competition in the early education market.
        *   Prevent misuse of taxpayer funds through redundant funding streams.
        *   Protect private-sector child care providers from artificial government-created market disadvantages.
*   Impact and Cost Savings
    *   This deregulatory change would yield substantial benefits:
        *   Stabilize the private child care market, especially in rural and underserved areas where small businesses are struggling to compete with federal programs.
        *   Increase access to CCDBG subsidies for families using private providers, rather than concentrating funds in already fully funded Head Start programs.
        *   Enhance transparency and accountability in federal funding.
        *   Restore fair market conditions for the child care sector, which is composed largely of women and minority-owned businesses.
        *   Reduce duplication of services, streamlining oversight and administrative costs for both CCDBG and Head Start oversight agencies.
*   Alternative Approaches Considered
    *   No alternative approach achieves the same outcome as a clear prohibition.
    *   While some have advocated for "blending and braiding" with accountability measures, in practice this has led to selective partnerships, opaque decision-making, and further exclusion of private providers.
    *   A full separation of funding streams is the only way to restore market balance and respect the original statutory purposes of each program.
    *   In Oklahoma, Head Start grantees have secured massive amounts of ad buy space on billboards in metro markets advertising:
        *   "$4000 sign on bonus"
        *   Pay rates of "$22 per hour"
        *   "Free Child Care"
    *   This is while non-Head Start grantees in this market cannot come close to paying that rate in the market, offer sign on bonusses of even $50, or certainly not Free Child Care or even buy ad space on premium billboards.
*   Conclusion
    *   If HHS and the Administration are serious about deregulation, supporting small business, and eliminating duplicative government spending, the clearest path forward is to end the dual-funding of Head Start and CCDBG for the same services.
    *   Allow Head Start to be funded through Head Start funds.
    *   Reserve CCDBG funds for working families who choose licensed private providers.
    *   This change will lift a crushing regulatory and financial barrier from thousands of American small businesses, allowing them to thrive and expand access to child care where it is most needed.
    *   More importantly, it gives parents the choice in providers that they overwhelmingly seek.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   As a physician-scientist and board-certified pathologist in Wisconsin, I urge you to refrain from any broad deregulatory actions and to reinstate the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Advisory Committee (CLIAC).
*   I am a health professional educator, and I teach my students that regulations are important to keep our patients safe, protect healthcare workers, and hold our institutions accountable.
*   Many of our current regulations have arisen out of tragic situations that harmed patients.
    *   This includes the so-called "Pap mills" that led to the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Act of 1988 (CLIA88).
        *   In "Pap mills," laboratories offered cervical cancer screening as a loss-leader to bring in other business.
        *   This led to low compensation for cytologists (then known as cytotechnologists), pressure to screen patient samples without the appropriate time and attention, and other negligent practices.
        *   These practices led to missed cancer cases in patients who had been up-to-date on their cancer screenings [1,2].
    *   We cannot afford to repeat these mistakes.
*   More recently, the biotechnology company Theranos exploited limited oversight of the laboratory developed test process to market and deliver poorly-performing tests [3].
*   The FDA's case studies from 2015 give a broad range of examples of laboratory developed tests that show a variety of problems.
    *   These problems include high false positives, high false negatives, and a lack of clinical utility [4].
*   It is distressing to find that some of the laboratory developed tests highlighted in those case studies are still in use today.
    *   This includes tests that may have significant adverse impacts but are directly marketed to the public through telehealth/concierge medicine services.
*   On one specific point, I ask that you keep the current CLIA credential requirements for laboratory staff, and particularly directorship requirements for high complexity laboratories.
    *   Oversight by a director with the appropriate board certification establishes a minimum level of oversight that is necessary to provide safe and high-quality results for all high complexity clinical testing.
*   CLIAC should be reinstated to provide the appropriate transparency and expert oversight for regulatory decisions that affect the medical laboratory.
    *   The public benefits from open discussion among experts when decisions are being made that affect their health, including laboratory testing.
*   References
    *   1. Bogdanich W. Lax Laboratories: The Pap Test Misses Much Cervical Cancer Through Labs’ Errors --- Cut-Rate “Pap Mills” Process Slides Using Screeners With Incentives to Rush --- Misplaced Sense of Security? The Wall Street Journal. November 2, 1987. Accessed October 19, 2018.
    *   2. Davey DD, Austin RM, Birdsong G, Zaleski S. The impact of the Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendments of 1988 on cytopathology practice: a 25th anniversary review. Journal of the American Society of Cytopathology. 2014;3(4):188-198. doi:10.1016/j.jasc.2014.04.004
    *   3. An outdated loophole is letting faulty lab tests hit the market. Nat Med. 2022;28(2):215-215. doi:10.1038/s41591-022-01729-y
    *   4. Food and Drug Administration. The Public Health Evidence for FDA Oversight of Laboratory Developed Tests: 20 Case Studies. November 16, 2015. Accessed February 26, 2025. https://wayback.archive-it.org/7993/20171115144712/https://www.fda.gov/downloads/AboutFDA/ReportsManualsForms/Reports/UCM472777.pdf

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I am commenting on the U.S Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make American Healthy Again.
*   The years of pregnancy to age three set the foundation for a baby’s development, learning and relationships.
    *   Babies rely entirely on the adults around them—parents, caregivers, and early childhood professionals—to provide safe, nurturing care.
    *   When babies or their caregivers face reduced support or program quality, babies can end up facing long-term emotional, physical, and developmental consequences.
    *   When the rules are created with babies in mind, we can set up an entire generation for lifelong health.
*   Regulations matter.
    *   HHS, as the leading Federal agency tasked with enhancing the health and well-being of all Americans, plays a critical role in ensuring that babies, families, and the professionals who care for little ones have access to the resources, protections, and supports they need.
    *   In considering changes to regulations, HHS must preserve regulations that:
        *   Keep young children safe and healthy.
        *   Enable the adults in their lives to give babies and toddlers the care they need for healthy growth and development.
*   For example, regulations that set child-to-provider ratios and provider education in Early Head Start and child care settings are needed to keep babies safe and developmentally on track.
*   Regulations that keep children and those who care for them healthy, like those that help parents and babies access pediatric screenings, early intervention services, and other types of care, must be maintained.
    *   This is how we prevent chronic conditions and keep babies on a healthy track—by making sure we keep in place the rules that keep them cared for, healthy, and safe.
*   HHS rules reach far beyond just Medicaid and early learning, with many HHS programs laying the foundation of quality care and critical support that babies need.
*   Any changes to regulations must be:
    *   Transparent.
    *   Grounded in evidence.
    *   Focused on the well-being and safety of children, families, and those who serve them.
*   Because each regulation is different, HHS must continue to give the public—including families and early childhood professionals like me—ample time and opportunity to weigh in on any proposed regulatory changes.
    *   We need a robust public process to make sure that the rules work for babies and those who care for them.
*   To keep America’s babies healthy, HHS must maintain the standards that safeguard basic quality and access to services.
*   Please uphold the regulatory framework that ensures babies and toddlers have the strongest start in life.
*   I would also like to add that I am a product of Head Start Services.
    *   I truly believe that Head Start services gave me an advantage in my education and my career.
    *   I have a Master Degree in Early Childhood Education with a specialization in Trauma.
    *   I have been a vendor for the state of California Early Start system for the past twenty-three years servicing the most vulnerable children in South Central Los Angeles.
    *   It gives great pleasure to give back to my community.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: An experienced early childhood education professional and Head Start alumna urges HHS to maintain and strengthen regulations that ensure the safety, health, and development of young children, advocating for transparent, evidence-based changes and robust public input.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   Submitted via www.regulations.gov on July 14, 2025.
*   The Association for Dressings and Sauces (ADS) is the international trade association representing manufacturers of salad dressings, mayonnaise, condiment sauces, and their suppliers.
*   ADS submits comments regarding the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Request for Information (RFI) to identify and eliminate outdated or unnecessary regulations, announced May 14, 2025.
*   ADS supports HHS’s efforts to eliminate unnecessary and burdensome regulations and appreciates the opportunity to submit comments.
*   ADS believes the Acidified Foods regulations (21 Code of Federal Regulations Part 114 and section 108.25, and any necessary corresponding changes) should be rescinded because:
    *   It is redundant with 21 CFR Part 117 and its significant costs are not outweighed by public health benefits.
    *   It lacks transparency and a sound scientific approach.
    *   It is not enforced consistently, which increases burden and impedes private enterprise and entrepreneurship.

*   21 CFR Part 114 is Redundant with 21 CFR Part 117 and Costs Do Not Outweigh Public Health Benefits
    *   FDA promulgated specific requirements surrounding the manufacture of “acidified foods” in 1979, set forth in 21 CFR Part 114, Acidified Foods, and in 21 CFR 108.25.
    *   At the time, FDA’s general food manufacturing authorities and requirements were limited, and the agency concluded that manufacturing acidified foods required controls to help prevent risks (namely Clostridium botulinum).
    *   In 2011, Congress passed the Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA), which overhauled and significantly expanded FDA’s food safety authorities.
    *   One foundational pillar of FSMA is 21 CFR Part 117, Current Good Manufacturing Practice, Hazard Analysis, and Risk-Based Preventive Controls for Human Food (PCHF regulation).
    *   21 CFR Part 117 subpart C requires food facilities to have a food safety plan for each product that includes a written analysis of biological, chemical, and physical hazards, and written risk-based preventive controls.
    *   The principles used in this process are similar to those used in HACCP schemes.
    *   Every food facility in the US must comply with 21 CFR Part 117 for every food it produces, including acidified foods.
    *   This means the acidified food regulations, established more than 30 years before FSMA, are now entirely redundant.
    *   The PCHF regulation requires food manufacturers to control for hazards during production, including microbiological hazards such as Clostridium botulinum.
    *   If the agency rescinded Part 114, the microbiological hazard from acidified products could be handled solely under the PCHF rule.
    *   Manufacturers could then simplify the development of their food safety plans and focus on food safety concerns.
    *   21 CFR 108.25(c) requires acidified foods manufacturers to register their production facilities and to file the processes with FDA.
    *   These registration and filing requirements do not advance food safety and are burdensome and redundant.
    *   There would be no loss in oversight if the emergency permit requirements of facility registration and filing of processes under section 108.25 were rescinded.
    *   All food facilities must register with FDA already, and FDA investigators would have full access to the food safety plans during an inspection or investigation.
    *   Eliminating facility registration and process filing requirements for acidified foods would lessen the burden on industry and allow for more focus on developing and implementing food safety plans rather than dealing with two rules that cover the same risk.
    *   At a minimum, 21 CFR 108.25(c) should be removed as the registration and filing requirements do not advance food safety and are burdensome.
    *   The acidified food framework imposes significant costs upon industry that are not outweighed by public benefits.
        *   The cost required to register a facility and file a process (including challenge studies and labor costs) per formulation ranges from $20,000 to $40,000 if an outside process authority is used.
        *   There is inconsistency among process authorities and FDA investigators regarding how to determine whether a food is an acidified food subject to these requirements.
        *   Lead times for new product introductions are also increased.
        *   In the dressing and sauce industry, a new product not considered an acidified food takes one-third of the time for that of an acidified food.

*   Interpretation of 21 CFR Part 114 Lacks Transparency and Sound Scientific Approach
    *   FSMA promotes the use of scientific risk analysis to develop preventive controls to produce safe food.
    *   21 CFR Part 117 allows food companies to focus their efforts on potential risks for the specific product being produced.
    *   These risks and preventive controls are outlined in the food safety plan required by 21 CFR Part 117, which is transparent and required to be based on a sound scientific approach.
    *   21 CFR Part 114 is neither transparent nor based on a sound scientific approach.
    *   ADS and its member companies have met with FDA to seek clarity on specific terms used in the definition of “acidified food,” including “small amount” of low acid ingredient and “significant shift in pH.”
    *   One member was told by an FDA official to send formulations to them for a case-by-case determination of whether a product was acidified.
        *   This type of determination leads to a lack of clarity, inconsistency, and unpredictable regulatory approaches.
    *   David Bresnahan of Bresnahan Thermal Processing Consultancy shared a similar experience in a letter to the editor to Food Safety News regarding the recommendation to rescind 21 CFR Part 114.
        *   At a food safety-related conference, Mr. Bresnahan noted that an FDA presenter was asked how a limit for one of the acid versus acidified decision criteria was arrived at.
        *   According to the letter, the FDA presenter’s response was, “We had to draw a line in the sand somewhere.”
        *   This type of “decision criteria” does not align with FSMA food safety principles or other food safety schemes and is not grounded in science.
    *   Sound science is a key tenet of 21 CFR Part 117 and allows industry to partner with the agency on keeping foods safe through the development of a food safety plan.
    *   The same is not true of 21 CFR Part 114, which has not moved beyond the science of 1979.
    *   Recent research provides sound science-based data about buffer capacity (BC) and the influence that ingredient addition will have on the final product pH in an acid environment.
        *   This information helps answer ongoing questions pertaining to “small amounts of low-acid food” and “significant pH shift,” which have been major stumbling blocks in interpreting the Acidified Foods regulation.
    *   In 2022, ADS recommended that the agency publish a “Letter to Industry,” Compliance Policy Guide (CPG), or guidance explaining the role of buffer capacity in defining whether a product is or is not an acidified food.
        *   The agency did not move forward with any type of guidance to address buffer capacity or to recognize this science-based approach.
    *   This lack of transparency is not efficient for the agency, as it leads to confusion and arbitrary decisions.
    *   If the Acidified Foods regulation were rescinded, FDA could focus its efforts on food safety and the food safety plans established by companies under Part 117.
    *   They too would only need to focus their efforts on one rule covering the same risk.
    *   The food safety plans required by 21 CFR Part 117, which require a scientific risk analysis approach and related preventive controls, are sound science as the cornerstone to prevent foodborne illness and not “lines drawn in the sand” in the absence of such an approach.

*   Enforcement of 21 CFR Part 114 Is Inconsistent
    *   Given that the interpretation of 21 CFR Part 114 lacks transparency and a sound scientific approach, enforcement is inconsistent.
    *   This inconsistency is causing confusion and frustration for industry and FDA, increasing costs for all.
    *   Over the years, ADS members have expressed frustration with the inconsistent classification of products as an acidified food and the change of classification depending on a particular interaction with the agency.
    *   In 2024, ADS solicited members’ input on their experiences with state and federal investigators/inspectors raising questions about the status of members’ products as acidified foods.
        *   The input indicated that this issue was commonly raised in inspections of facilities that make dressings and sauces.
        *   Inspectors/investigators have taken widely varying and inconsistent approaches to determining whether ADS members’ dressings and sauces are acidified foods.
        *   ADS member companies have also seen variation in investigators’/inspectors’ approaches in acidified food classification in inspections of facilities owned by the same company across different regions.
        *   Several members were aware of investigators/inspectors relying on draft guidance that FDA had rescinded.
        *   Others report that investigators/inspectors applied criteria similar to or stricter than the criteria articulated in the rescinded guidance.
        *   The feedback indicated this was a significant area of concern for the dressing and sauce sector and highlights the need for a clear, consistent, and science-based approach for evaluating dressings and sauces.
    *   The proper classification of food as an acidified food product is an ongoing challenge.
    *   Evaluating whether a food is an acidified food historically involves the advice of experienced process authorities or other knowledgeable individuals.
    *   Expert guidance is important because the definition of “acidified foods” includes two inherently subjective concepts: (1) “small amounts of low-acid food(s)” and (2) “pH that does not significantly differ from that of the predominant acid or acid food.”
    *   There is ongoing debate among manufacturers, academia, food processing authorities, inspectors, and regulatory bodies with interpreting the Acidified Foods regulation correctly, given these ambiguous and often subjective concepts.
    *   There are direct regulatory implications based on that determination.
    *   This confusion is not necessary. Part 117 requires the control of hazards for all foods and does not necessitate classification of foods into a particular category.

*   In conclusion, ADS believes that 21 CFR Part 114 and 21 CFR 108.25 should be rescinded. At a minimum, consideration should be given to rescind 21 CFR 108.25(c).
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The Association for Dressings & Sauces, an international trade association, advocates for the repeal of the Acidified Foods regulations (21 CFR Part 114 and 108.25), arguing they are redundant, costly, unscientific, and inconsistently enforced, thereby hindering innovation and burdening the industry without enhancing public health.

    -   The separate facility registration and process filing requirements under 21 CFR 108.25(c) are unnecessary, as all food facilities already register with FDA and FDA has access to food safety plans under Part 117.
-   **Significant financial burden without public health benefits:**
    -   Costs to register a facility and file a process (including challenge studies and labor) range from $20,000 to $40,000 per formulation.

-   **Increased lead times and hindered innovation:** Acidified food products take three times longer to introduce to market compared to non-acidified foods, slowing innovation and entrepreneurship.
-   **Lack of transparency and sound scientific approach:**

submitter: National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   On behalf of the National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals (NABIP), formerly NAHU, we appreciate the opportunity to provide comments in response to the Department of Health and Human Services’ request for information regarding federal regulations that may be outdated, overly burdensome, or in need of reform.
    *   NABIP represents thousands of licensed health insurance professionals who assist individuals, families, and employers in accessing health coverage and navigating the healthcare system.
    *   We are committed to a regulatory framework that better promotes the health and well-being of the American people.
    *   These suggestions are a compilation of ideas from NABIP members who actively serve beneficiaries in the Medicare and ACA marketplaces, as well as small and large group markets.

*   ACA Marketplace
    *   Three-Way Call Requirement for Coverage Changes in the Federally-facilitated Marketplace (FFM)
        *   Impact of Mandate:
            *   The lack of robust identity verification in the FFM has led to a surge in unauthorized coverage changes and fraudulent plan switching.
            *   Bad actors—often overseas call centers or private firms—have exploited these gaps at scale, in some cases altering millions of enrollments.
            *   Consumers often discover these changes only when seeking care, resulting in denied claims, unexpected costs, and disrupted treatment.
            *   Ethical agents and brokers are also affected, losing commissions and client trust when their enrollments are overridden.
            *   The temporary solution of the three-way call requirement for coverage changes is a clunky and time-consuming process for consumers and agents and brokers alike.
            *   Without a secure authentication system, the integrity of the Marketplace is compromised, and CMS’s enforcement resources are overwhelmed.
        *   Proposed Solution: We support the widespread recommendation that CMS implement multiple-factor authentication (MFA) within the FFM to prevent the majority of unauthorized coverage changes that are occurring within the Federal Exchange.
        *   Outcome of Proposed Solution: Replacing the three-way call requirement with multi-factor authentication within the Direct Enrollment (DE) and Enhanced Direct Enrollment (EDE) platforms would most efficiently and effectively address this issue, protect consumers, maintain the integrity of the FFM, decrease the resources required from CMS, and decrease the time expected of consumers and agents to institute security.
    *   Consumer Consent Documentation 10-year Requirement (45 CFR 155.220)
        *   Impact of Regulation and Justification for Reform:
            *   The current 10-year documentation retention requirement places an undue financial and administrative burden on independent agents and brokers, particularly small businesses.
            *   Many agents manage large client bases, and maintaining consent records for a decade requires costly long-term cloud storage solutions and added administrative oversight.
        *   Proposed Solution: Reduce the required retention period to 3-5 years.
            *   Most agency audits occur on documentation going back this length of time.
            *   This aligns with practical needs without compromising compliance integrity.
        *   Outcome of Deregulation: This change would alleviate unnecessary burdens on small businesses and agents, reduce compliance costs, and still protect consumers appropriately.

*   Group/Employer Market
    *   Statutory Requirement: Gag Clause Prohibition Compliance Attestation
        *   Impact:
            *   While NABIP supports the intent of the gag clause prohibition, the current enforcement framework lacks the clarity and reach needed to ensure plan sponsors have full access to their own claims data.
            *   Many service provider contracts still include non-disclosure clauses that restrict employer-sponsored plans from using their data to negotiate rates, evaluate networks, or improve plan design.
            *   Plan sponsors also face systemic barriers to obtaining provider taxpayer identification numbers (TINs), which are critical for transparency and fraud prevention.
            *   Access to prescription drug data remains inconsistent, particularly when managed by separate vendors or carved-out PBAs.
            *   In addition, some third-party administrators (TPAs) and pharmacy benefit managers (PBMs) employ non-contractual tactics that effectively impose gag clauses—such as long delays in fulfilling data requests, excessive fees, or supplying unusable formats like scanned PDFs.
            *   These practices undermine the law’s intent while maintaining surface-level compliance.
        *   Proposed Solution: NABIP urges the Departments (Treasury, HHS, and DOL) to:
            *   Explicitly define provider TINs and prescription drug claims data as components of de-identified claims data required to be accessible to plan sponsors.
            *   Prohibit non-contractual practices that restrict data access through indirect means.
            *   Shift primary compliance responsibility from plan sponsors to service providers.
            *   Require that all claims data be shared in real-time, machine-readable formats.
            *   Establish enforceable financial penalties for service providers that impose undue restrictions or delays.
        *   Outcome: These improvements would ensure meaningful access to critical data, enabling plan sponsors to meet fiduciary obligations, detect fraud, improve plan efficiency, and better serve enrollees.
            *   True transparency depends on both regulatory intent and practical enforceability.

*   Medicare
    *   Regulation & CFR Citation: Call Recordings - Requirement to Store for 10 years (42 CFR Part 422)
        *   Impact of Regulation and Justification for Reform:
            *   This requirement imposes a significant financial and operational burden on independent agents and brokers.
            *   Digital call recordings are often large and expensive to store in the cloud, especially for small businesses.
            *   The rule also creates potential privacy risks for beneficiaries whose personal data is retained for extended periods.
        *   Proposed Solution: Reduce the required retention period to 3 years.
            *   The vast majority of CTMs are submitted within 2 years and carriers typically request data of up to 3 years, if they request.
            *   This aligns with practical needs and modern data security practices without compromising compliance integrity.
        *   Outcome of Deregulation: This change would alleviate unnecessary burdens on small businesses and agents, reduce compliance costs, and still protect consumer data appropriately.
    *   Regulation & CFR Citation: Disclaimer Requirement Within First 60 Seconds of Call (42 CFR Part 422)
        *   Impact of Regulation and Justification for Reform:
            *   NABIP members find this requirement disruptive, especially during the early part of a call when agents are typically orienting the conversation or responding to beneficiary inquiries.
            *   The disclaimer interrupts the flow and confuses beneficiaries.
        *   Proposed Solution:
            *   The disclaimer should only be required for unsolicited calls, and not for those placed by existing clients or initiated by the beneficiary.
            *   It should be treated similarly to a privacy notice—delivered once annually—and presented at a contextually appropriate time in the conversation.
            *   NABIP also recommends a revision of the disclaimer language to eliminate the need for agents to list every plan option available.
            *   Instead, a simplified statement indicating which plans the agent represents in the area should suffice.
        *   Outcome of Deregulation: Streamlines conversations, reduces confusion, and respects beneficiaries' need to understand the purpose of the interaction before regulatory language is introduced.
    *   Regulation & CFR Citation: Scope of Appointment 48-Hour Rule (42 CFR § 422.2264(c)(1) and § 423.2264(c)(1))
        *   Impact of Regulation and Justification for Reform:
            *   The 48-hour requirement can hinder timely assistance for beneficiaries facing urgent needs.
            *   While beneficiaries often do not expect to require immediate enrollment help, appointments frequently reveal pressing issues -- especially near the end of the month -- that necessitate swift action.
            *   This rule may therefore lead to delays in securing coverage.
        *   Proposed Solution: NABIP recommends incorporating a safe harbor within the scope-of-appointment form, where a beneficiary can opt out of the 48-hour requirement.
            *   This would preserve consumer protection while enabling more timely service.
        *   Outcome of Deregulation: Balances timely care access with meaningful consent, giving flexibility to both consumers and agents in urgent scenarios.
    *   Regulation & CFR Citation: Late Enrollment Penalties for Federal Retirees and Veterans (42 CFR § 406.27)
        *   Impact of Regulation as It Currently Stands: Many federal retirees and veterans have credible coverage but are penalized due to a lack of clarity in eligibility exceptions.
            *   This results in financial harm and confusion.
        *   Proposed Solution: Create a permanent SEP and exempt these populations from LEPs when they can demonstrate continuous, credible coverage through federal or military sources.
        *   Outcome: Protects vulnerable populations and ensures fair treatment of those who have served or worked in public service.

*   To better promote the health and well-being of the American people, we ask the Department to review opportunities to minimize disruption to beneficiaries during the upcoming Annual Enrollment Period (AEP).
    *   Ahead of last year's AEP and now this year's, carriers have been determining ways to steer beneficiaries towards preferred plans by removing products from electronic enrollment platforms and restrict to just telephonic or Medicare.gov channels, limiting beneficiary choices.
    *   Additionally, carriers eliminated agent commissions after AEP had already begun last year and they have already made these decisions for both initial enrollments and renewal enrollments ahead of this year’s AEP.
    *   Both developments will prevent millions of Medicare beneficiaries from receiving the help of agents to navigate a complex, overly confusing system and set of decisions.
    *   We ask CMS to require carriers to prohibit changes to:
        *   Which plans are displayed on electronic enrollment platforms.
        *   Posted commissions after October 1, coinciding when plans are finalized and released ahead of AEP.

*   We thank you for your consideration of these recommendations.
    *   NABIP welcomes the opportunity to collaborate further and can facilitate direct conversations with impacted members who are willing to share additional insight.
    *   We are confident that these suggested changes would modernize compliance, reduce administrative burdens, and improve consumer outcomes.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The National Association of Benefits and Insurance Professionals (NABIP) urges HHS to reform regulations across ACA, employer, and Medicare markets to reduce administrative burdens on agents and brokers, enhance consumer protection, and ensure greater transparency and access to care.
