structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   I am a scholar at the Ethics and Public Policy Center (EPPC), a member of EPPC’s Administrative State Accountability Project (ASAP), and a former attorney in the U.S. Department of Justice’s (DOJ) Civil Rights Division.
*   I write to offer public comment in response to the Department of Health and Human Services’ (HHS) “Request for Information (RFI): Ensuring Lawful Regulation and Unleashing Innovation To Make America Healthy Again.”
    *   This RFI concerns HHS’s efforts to “implement the President’s Deregulatory Initiatives, including Department of Government Efficiency Deregulatory Agenda, and to better promote the health and well-being of the American people.”
    *   HHS seeks input on how to "dramatically deregulate" and welcomes submissions explaining how regulations, guidance, paperwork requirements, and other regulatory obligations can be repealed.
*   The RFI is an excellent fit for ASAP’s mission.
    *   EPPC’s HHS Accountability Project, now ASAP, was launched in February 2021 in response to the Biden Department of Health and Human Services’ hostility to good medicine and the rights of conscience.
    *   Our project is part of EPPC’s broader effort to advocate for laws and public policies that reflect "the truth of the human person."
*   We are grateful for efforts by HHS and the Trump administration to stop and reverse harmful and unlawful Biden regulatory actions.
    *   We bring to your attention publications summarizing egregious Biden administration actions in our focus areas.
    *   We outline regulatory actions requiring attention, directing to our public comments and other documents describing problems.
*   We hope this comment helps equip HHS to implement President Trump’s policy priorities and uphold the rule of law.
    *   In many instances, this may involve rescinding regulations, in whole or in part.
    *   Where Biden administration actions have been challenged in court, the Trump administration should consider conceding that challenged regulations are unlawful.
*   We thank HHS for this invitation to submit a public comment on our work on behalf of the American people, promoting human flourishing and the rule of law.

*   I. We encourage HHS to review ASAP publications that document the Biden administration’s illegal actions.
    *   It may be helpful for HHS to refer to ASAP scholars’ publications documenting the Biden administration’s illegal actions.
    *   A. EPPC’s website and the attached appendix collect ASAP scholars’ public comments and commentary on regulatory proposals.
        *   The most comprehensive collection of ASAP’s comments on Biden administration regulations is on EPPC’s webpage, “EPPC Engagement on Agency Actions.”
            *   This site collects ASAP scholars’ public comments, Executive Order 12866 meetings with government officials, and related commentary on regulatory proposals.
            *   The website is organized chronologically, with most recent proposals at the top.
        *   Attached is an appendix prepared by ASAP listing agency actions (regulations and memoranda) recommended for review.
            *   This appendix is organized by federal agency.
            *   It includes an “issue key” indicating the reason for concern (LIFE = Right to Life/Abortion, RL = Religious Liberty/Conscience Rights, SOGI = Sexual Orientation and/or Gender Identity).
            *   Where relevant, links to EPPC comments and comments from other groups are provided.
        *   ASAP has continued to submit public comments since President Trump took office.
            *   These comments generally highlight aspects of Biden administration proposals contrary to the President’s stated policy goals and executive orders, including commitment to the rule of law and reigning in the administrative state.
    *   B. ASAP scholars’ amicus brief in Tennessee v. Becerra provides an overview of the Biden administration’s unlawful efforts to promote abortion.
        *   Aside from public comments, ASAP scholars have submitted amicus briefs and published articles collecting and describing examples of unlawful regulations.
        *   In April 2024, ASAP scholars Eric Kniffin and Rachel N. Morrison submitted an amicus brief in support of Tennessee v. Becerra, a pending lawsuit in the Sixth Circuit Court of Appeals.
            *   This lawsuit challenges HHS’s attempt to rescind Tennessee’s Title X funding solely because the state would not counsel and refer for abortions illegal under state law.
            *   Title X is a federal program funding state and private health care organizations offering voluntary family planning services.
            *   Congress explicitly prohibited Title X funds from being used "in programs where abortion is a method of family planning" (42 U.S.C. §300a-6).
            *   In March 2022, HHS awarded Tennessee a five-year grant of Title X funds.
        *   Our amicus brief noted that the Supreme Court in Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization returned the issue of abortion “to the people and their elected representatives.”
            *   Instead of listening to the American people, President Biden “committed to doing everything in his power” to “protect access” to abortion.
            *   The brief described the following Biden administration actions, deemed worthy of HHS’s attention:
                *   Turning Title X into an abortion counseling and referral mandate (Id. at 7-10).
                *   Turning taxpayer dollars into abortion funds (Id. at 10-14).
                *   Turning hospital emergency rooms into abortion clinics (Id. at 14-16).
                *   Turning pharmacies into abortion drug dispensaries (Id. at 24-27).
                *   Turning HIPAA’s privacy protections into a shield against laws regulating abortion (Id. at 28-32).
    *   C. ASAP director Rachel N. Morrison’s article provides an overview of the Biden administration’s efforts to promote gender ideology.
        *   In January 2024, Rachel N. Morrison published an article in The Federalist outlining “How Democrats set the stage in 2023 for an LGBT onslaught in 2024.”
            *   This article addresses many different regulations poised to be finalized in the last year of the administration, including:
                *   HHS rule that would unlawfully prohibit discrimination based on gender dysphoria.
                *   HHS rule that called “non-affirming” foster parents abusive.
        *   Some of these agency actions are described in more detail below.
        *   These overviews may help HHS staff and leadership understand the scope and pattern of unlawful conduct by the Biden administration on issues central to EPPC’s Administrative State Accountability Project.

*   II. EPPC’s Administrative State Accountability Project submits that the following Biden-era regulations are especially harmful to the common good and in need of rescission.
    *   We draw HHS’s attention to the following actions by the Biden administration, which we believe are particularly detrimental to the common good.
        *   These regulations are organized chronologically by finalization date in the Federal Register.
    *   As requested, we provide detailed reasons for rescission, drawing upon our public comments and commentary.
    *   We encourage the administration to consider whether these arguments also provide grounds to concede in court that these regulations are unlawful.
    *   We indicate where we are aware of ongoing litigation for each rule.
    *   A. HHS should rescind Ensuring Access to Equitable, Affordable, Client-Centered, Quality Family Planning Services, 86 Fed. Reg. 56144 (Oct. 7, 2021).
        *   On April 15, 2021, HHS proposed a rule to repeal Trump administration Title X regulations and readopt most 2000 Title X regulations with additional requirements, including abortion counseling and referrals.
        *   On May 17, 2021, our project submitted a public comment opposing the proposed rule on several grounds:
            *   The proposed rule runs afoul of Title X’s abortion prohibition and federal conscience protections.
            *   It does not support Title X’s purposes.
            *   It undermines Title X project accountability and transparency.
            *   It provides a flawed analysis of the impact of the 2019 Rule and the projected impact of the proposed regulations.
        *   We urged the department to withdraw the proposed rule.
        *   On October 7, 2021, HHS published its final rule.
            *   The 2021 rule rescinded physical and financial separation requirements and largely readopted Clinton-era regulations with additional requirements, such as “advancing health equity through the Title X program.”
            *   The new rule also requires Title X providers to make abortion referrals upon request, jeopardizing conscience rights of providers who object to abortion as a method of family planning.
        *   These regulations are contrary to Title X’s express terms and federal conscience protections.
        *   The Biden HHS’s pro-abortion extremism is contrary to the Supreme Court’s direction in Dobbs, which stated that abortion policy should be determined by elected representatives, not "deep state bureaucrats."
        *   We urge HHS to rescind these regulations.
    *   B. HHS should rescind Safeguarding the Rights of Conscience as Protected by Federal Statutes, 89 Fed. Reg. 2078 (Jan. 11, 2024).
        *   On January 5, 2023, HHS issued a proposed rule to rescind conscience regulations promulgated under President Trump in 2019.
        *   On March 3, 2023, we filed our public comment opposing HHS’s proposed rule.
            *   We noted that while HHS claimed its proposed rule would “safeguard rights of conscience,” “strengthen conscience and religious nondiscrimination,” and “prevent discrimination,” the proposed rule told a very different story.
            *   Among many points, we pointed out HHS failed to establish a need for the rule.
            *   Our comment argued it would be arbitrary and capricious for HHS to excise provisions from the 2019 Rule that provided needed clarity, even as HHS claimed its new rule was needed to reduce “confusion.”
            *   We took issue with HHS’s claim that new rules were needed to reflect a “balance” Congress allegedly struck in conscience protection laws, demonstrating these laws say nothing about such a “balance.”
            *   We also asked HHS to acknowledge that conscience protection laws apply to sterilizing “gender transition” procedures.
            *   “In short,” we said, “HHS’s proposed rule—coupled with the Biden-Becerra HHS’s abysmal track record on protecting conscience and religious freedom rights—undercuts the Department’s assertions that it takes these rights seriously.”
        *   HHS’s January 9, 2024, final rule made some good changes from its 2023 proposal, clarifying terms and confirming OCR would receive complaints about alleged violations of federal conscience protection statutes.
            *   However, HHS doubled down on its claim of authority to “balance” conscience rights with Biden administration policy priorities, especially abortion.
            *   The final rule mentioned “balance” thirty-six times, even while HHS acknowledged that “the text of the conscience statutes themselves generally does not contain balancing tests.”
            *   The final rule also mentioned fourteen times that HHS would apply these laws on a “case-by-basis,” an approach not legally required and which deprives covered entities of guidance, especially given HHS’s opaque and unlawful “balancing” approach.
        *   On the whole, we believe HHS’s 2024 conscience regulations were unnecessary, make conscience protection laws harder to understand and follow, and illegally introduced “balancing” standards not found in the laws HHS has authority to enforce.
        *   For all these reasons, and additional reasons in our public comment, we ask HHS to rescind the 2024 conscience regulations and reinstitute the 2019 final rule.
    *   C. HHS should rescind HIPAA Privacy Rule To Support Reproductive Health Care Privacy, 89 Fed. Reg. 32976 (April 26, 2024).
        *   On April 17, 2023, HHS issued a proposed rule to change the longstanding HIPAA Privacy Rule to create new rules applicable only to protected health information (PHI) tangentially related to “reproductive health care.”
        *   On June 16, 2023, our project submitted a public comment opposing the proposed rule on several grounds:
            *   First, the Department failed to establish a need for the Proposed Rule; its conjectures and reliance on reaction pieces after Dobbs do not establish current rule confusion.
            *   Second, even if the current rule caused “confusion,” the Proposed Rule makes it worse by introducing critical terms that are poorly defined or undefined.
            *   Third, the Proposed Rule will create more confusion by greatly complicating the decision-making process for covered entities deciding whether to use or disclose PHI.
        *   We also expressed concern that the Privacy Rule would chill health care professionals from cooperating with legal and legitimate state activities stemming from their traditional police powers (promoting public health, morals, safety, and general well-being).
        *   On February 28, 2024, we met with federal officials to reiterate serious concerns.
        *   On April 26, 2024, HHS issued its final rule.
            *   HHS narrowed the rule in response to public comments.
            *   HHS added a new “presumption” provision: if a covered entity is asked for “reproductive health care”-related PHI regarding a procedure performed by another person, that entity must presume the procedure was performed legally and must refuse to release the PHI unless convinced otherwise.
        *   We share concerns raised by Roger Severino (former colleague at EPPC, former head of HHS’ Office of Civil Rights) that HHS’s rule puts health care providers “in an impossible situation.”
            *   The vague rule makes providers choose between risking contempt for refusing a lawful subpoena for PHI or risking a finding by HHS of HIPAA Privacy Rule violation.
            *   Severino rightly noted the final rule also makes it substantially harder for law enforcement to investigate unlawful activity.
        *   As we predicted, after the rule was finalized, several lawsuits were filed by states and private entities against HHS’s new HIPAA privacy rule.
            *   One was filed in Texas by a family physician; the district court issued a preliminary injunction last December.
            *   The following month, over a dozen states sued, recognizing the HIPAA rule interferes with their ability to carry out legitimate law enforcement investigations.
            *   The States’ motion for preliminary injunction, filed in February, attached EPPC’s public comment on the HIPAA proposed rule as an exhibit.
        *   HHS should rescind the 2024 HIPAA Privacy Rule in total.
            *   HHS did not demonstrate any need for this rulemaking.
            *   It is arbitrary and capricious for HHS to create separate rules only for PHI tangentially related to reproductive health care.
            *   The rule is vague and appears designed to intimidate covered entities out of cooperating with legitimate law enforcement activities related to advancing important interests recognized by the Supreme Court in Dobbs.
            *   We urge HHS to prioritize rescinding this rule and to concede its illegality in court.
    *   D. IHS should rescind Removal of Outdated Regulations, 89 Fed. Reg. 34144 (April 30, 2024).
        *   On January 8, 2024, HHS’s Indian Health Service (IHS) issued a proposed rule to eliminate regulations preventing IHS funds from paying for any abortion except those necessary to save the life of the mother.
            *   IHS claimed these regulations were outdated and conflicted with the Hyde Amendment.
            *   The proposed regulations did not merely attempt to authorize payments for abortions in cases of rape or incest; they proposed to eliminate all abortion regulations, including record keeping requirements. No rationale was given for removing all regulations.
        *   Consistent with its 2022 circular (issued days after Dobbs), IHS claimed federal law preempted state law and that IHS thus had legal grounds to require its health care facilities to perform abortions even where such procedures were illegal under state law.
            *   While some IHS facilities are on Native American reservations, many are not and should therefore be subject to state law.
        *   On March 8, 2024, our project filed a public comment opposing the rule:
            *   The Hyde Amendment merely permits federal funding for limited abortions; it does not mandate IHS fund abortion.
            *   Further, the Hyde Amendment does not support removing regulations on definitions, ectopic pregnancy, recordkeeping, and confidentiality, making the IHS’s proposal arbitrary and capricious.
            *   IHS fails to address the federalism impacts that could preempt state laws protecting unborn children and adequately consider alternatives.
            *   IHS should withdraw its proposed rule and maintain all current regulations.
        *   Our project encouraged withdrawal and recommended various alternatives.
        *   On April 18, 2024, our project met with officials from the Executive Office of the President to reiterate concerns via an EO 12866 Meeting.
        *   On April 30, 2024, HHS IHS issued its final rule, ignoring public comments that pointed out misinterpretation of the Hyde Amendment.
            *   Although IHS offered no other justification than claims about the Hyde Amendment, it stated that “comments about the substance and application of the Hyde Amendment itself are outside of the scope of this rulemaking,” a remark repeated four times.
        *   The IHS 2024 rule was arbitrary and capricious, does not satisfy the APA’s requirement for reasoned decision making, violates states’ rights to advance policy interests recognized by Dobbs, and violates the federal Hyde Amendment.
            *   There was nothing “outdated” about the previous regulations.
            *   We urge IHS to rescind the 2024 rule and reinstate previously operative regulations for abortion in IHS facilities.
    *   E. ACF should rescind Designated Placement Requirements Under Titles IV–E and IV–B for LGBTQI+ Children, 89 Fed. Reg. 34818 (April 30, 2024).
        *   On September 28, 2023, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services Administration for Children and Families (ACF) proposed a rule titled, “Safe and Appropriate Foster Care Placement Requirements for Titles IV–E and IV–B,” requiring foster care providers to “affirm” a child’s “LGBTQI+ identity.”
        *   On November 27, 2023, our project submitted a public comment opposing the proposed rule.
            *   Our comment agreed all children in foster care should receive “safe and proper” care, including LGBTQI+ children.
            *   However, we argued this rule’s special rules for “LGBTQI+ children” were premised on two incorrect and harmful assumptions:
                *   Not “affirming” a child’s self-proclaimed LGBTQI+ identity is unsafe and abuse.
                *   Foster care providers who hold traditional beliefs (religious or otherwise) about marriage, sexuality, and gender are unable to provide LGBTQI+ children with safe and loving homes.
            *   We argued these premises are false, harmful to children, and would undermine religious freedom and parental rights beyond foster care.
            *   Our comment urged HHS to withdraw and abandon its harmful proposed rule.
        *   On April 30, 2024, ACF issued its final rule.
            *   The final rule doubled down on HHS’s spurious claims that LGBTQI+ kids face particular harms and risks and are “especially vulnerable.”
            *   It claimed “significant body of evidence” demonstrates a connection between suicide risk in LGBTQI+ children and caregiver conduct/treatment toward their sexual orientation or gender identity.
            *   ACF also claimed research shows support from families/caregivers related to sexual orientation/gender identity is highly predictive of mental health and wellbeing.
        *   Weeks later, Joseph Figliolia and Leor Sapir of the Manhattan Institute published an article debunking the final rule’s bad science.
            *   We agree with their conclusion that ACF’s final rule reflected the Biden administration’s flawed, ideologically-driven effort “to use federal policy to cajole foster families and agencies into affirming a child’s mistaken gender identity, entrenching the idea that failing to do so constitutes abuse.”
            *   The policy will compound challenges for vulnerable children.
            *   HHS’s recent report on care for children with gender dysphoria (cited below) affirms the Manhattan Institute’s analysis.
        *   Not only does the ACF rule reflect bad science, it has also been found unlawful.
            *   In March 2025, a federal district court found in favor of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, holding ACF lacked statutory authority to issue its mandate.
        *   For all these reasons, we urge ACF to rescind its 2024 foster care rule.
    *   F. HHS should rescind the Health and Human Services Grants Regulation, 89 Fed. Reg 36684 (May 3, 2024).
        *   On July 13, 2023, HHS issued a proposal to rewrite sex discrimination provisions in over a dozen laws undergirding federal grant programs.
            *   HHS proposed applying these provisions as if they also prohibit discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity.
        *   On September 11, 2023, EPPC scholars submitted a public comment opposing the proposed rule.
            *   Our comment argued the proposed rule offers inadequate protections for religious liberty.
            *   Social services programs created by these statutes depend substantially on religious organizations, many of whom cannot comply with HHS’s reinterpreted grant terms without violating religious convictions.
            *   Yet, the proposed rule offers no religious exemptions or accommodations, only allowing grant recipients to voice concerns for “prompt” consideration by HHS.
        *   As we explained in our comment:
            *   The Proposed Rule contradicts long-standing scientific understandings of human biology, thereby endangering public health.
            *   The Proposed Rule turns back the clock on girls’ and women’s rights, tramples parental rights, harms children’s interests, dismantles sex-based protections, and violates religious freedom and conscience rights of grantees and religious institutions.
            *   While the Department claims to “take[] seriously its obligations to comply with Federal religious freedom laws, including the First Amendment and RFRA,” the proposed religious exemption process is inadequate.
            *   The Proposed Rule inverts civil rights law and should be withdrawn and abandoned.
        *   EPPC scholars urged HHS to withdraw the proposal.
        *   On April 1, 2024, one project scholar met with government officials in the Executive Office of the President to reiterate concerns and urge abandonment of the unlawful proposal.
            *   I argued HHS’s interpretation of Bostock was implausible:
                *   The Supreme Court did not, as HHS claims, conclude Title VII bars discrimination on the basis of gender identity.
                *   Moreover, the Supreme Court explicitly denied its interpretation of Title VII applied to other statutes—not to Title IX and not to the thirteen statutes listed in the proposed rule.
                *   HHS has no mandate from Congress and no duty under Bostock to redefine what discrimination on the basis of sex means under these laws.
            *   The EO 12866 comment also noted that while HHS claims to “take[] seriously its obligations to comply with Federal religious freedom laws, including the First Amendment and RFRA,” the proposed religious exemption process is inadequate.
            *   We again urged OIRA and HHS to reverse course, acknowledge fundamental problems, and abandon this attempt to rewrite over a dozen federal statutes.
        *   On May 3, 2024, HHS issued its final rule, cementing its proposal to redefine “sex discrimination” based on an expansive Bostock interpretation.
            *   Although the rule dramatically expanded covered entities’ nondiscrimination obligations under HHS grant programs, HHS denied imposing new obligations.
            *   Instead, HHS claimed this was “merely an interpretive rule” and denied imposing costs or having Federalism implications.
            *   The final rule also reflected Biden administration hostility toward religious liberty.
            *   Instead of forthrightly addressing RFRA obligations, HHS created a process (identical to its 2024 ACA Section 1557 regulations) to allow recipients to raise concerns that final rules, as applied, violated RFRA rights.
            *   We pointed out this process appeared calculated to help HHS avoid accountability in court with drawn-out, ill-defined promises to consider religious liberty concerns.
            *   HHS attempted to justify this approach by making indefensible claims about its inability to make simple judgments about how RFRA applies to easily foreseeable situations.
        *   A Louisiana school board filed suit against the HHS Grants final rule in January 2025, alleging the Biden administration’s gender-identity mandate was unlawful and did not qualify as a “housekeeping” rule.
        *   HHS should abandon its illegal attempt to unilaterally change nondiscrimination requirements in HHS grants.
        *   It should rescind the 2024 grants rule and concede in court that this rule is unlawful.
    *   G. HHS should rescind Nondiscrimination in Health Programs and Activities, 89 Fed. Reg. 37522 (May 6, 2024).
        *   On August 8, 2022, HHS issued a proposed rule claiming authority under Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act to impose a radical transgender mandate on the American health care system.
        *   On October 3, 2022, our project filed a public comment opposing HHS’s proposed mandate.
            *   The comment argued the proposed rule would radically remake American healthcare by replacing science-based medicine with ideology-driven mandates.
            *   As proposed, the Rule is arbitrary and capricious, exceeds statutory authority, and is unlawful and unconstitutional.
            *   Primary proposed changes are unsupported by substantial evidence.
            *   The Proposed Rule contradicts long-standing scientific understandings of human biology, thereby endangering public health.
            *   The Proposed Rule turns back the clock on girls’ and women’s rights, tramples parental rights, harms children’s interests, dismantles sex-based patient protections, and violates religious freedom and conscience rights of medical professionals, hospitals, and religious institutions.
            *   The Proposed Rule inverts civil rights law and should be withdrawn and abandoned.
        *   We noted proposed regulations would trample conscience and religious freedom rights of medical professionals and threaten rights of providers and insurers to decline to assist or pay for elective abortions.
        *   We followed up in February 2024, meeting with Executive Office of the President officials to reiterate concerns.
            *   We noted that, as with conscience regulations, the executive branch was abusing the regulatory process to advance radical policy goals not shared by Congress or the American people.
            *   We argued: HHS’s rule would harm children and negatively impact healthcare and access to care. The rule also has massive implications for conscience and religious freedom rights, which HHS continues to set aside.
            *   Given flagrant legal problems and HHS’s prior concession in legal challenges to its 2016 Section 1557 rule, we are confident this proposal awaits a similar fate, leading to extensive litigation and plaintiff victories.
        *   On May 6, 2024, HHS issued its final rule under Section 1557.
            *   The final rule repeated the 2016 rule’s broad definition of discrimination “on the basis of sex,” even though the rule failed to define “sex.” The regulation contained 42 definitions, but "sex" was not one.
            *   This came on the heels of the Biden administration’s Title IX final rule, which similarly found it “not necessary” to define sex or sex discrimination.
            *   The final rule also renewed the declaration from the 2016 rule that claimed it is unlawful sex discrimination to “have or implement a categorical coverage exclusion or limitation for all health services related to gender transition.”
            *   The rule made conflicting and confusing claims about abortion. HHS said “nothing in this rule requires the provision of… abortion,” but also maintained Section 1557 prohibited discrimination on the basis of “termination of pregnancy.” HHS failed to resolve this tension.
            *   HHS maintained in the final rule that Section 1557 did not incorporate Title IX as a whole, but only its prohibition on sex discrimination.
                *   We believe this is incorrect and that it was arbitrary and capricious for HHS to declare itself not bound by Title IX’s religious exemption, 20 U.S.C. § 1681(a)(3), and its abortion neutrality provision, 20 U.S.C. § 1688.
            *   HHS attempted to justify its “gender transition” mandate by claiming these procedures are supported by a “robust consensus.”
                *   However, as HHS recognized in its recent report, these claims are false.
                *   On May 1, 2025, HHS issued its report, Treatment for Pediatric Gender Dysphoria: Review of Evidence and Best Practices.
                *   The report’s “umbrella review” determined that “the overall quality of evidence concerning the effects of any intervention on psychological outcomes, quality of life, regret, or long-term health, is very low.”
                *   The report also details ethical concerns raised by allowing minors to consent to irreversible procedures under false pretenses, especially given the “unfavorable” risk/benefit profile of medical interventions.
        *   Given the administration’s commitment to sound science, fighting gender ideology, and protecting religious liberty, and in light of HHS’s recent report, we strongly recommend HHS rescind the 2024 Section 1557 final rule.
    *   H. HHS should rescind portions of Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability in Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance, 89 Fed. Reg. 40066 (May 9, 2024).
        *   On September 13, 2023, HHS issued a proposed rule to clarify discrimination against individuals with disabilities under section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and, by extension, the Americans with Disabilities Act.
        *   Our public comment, submitted in November 2023, applauded HHS for efforts to better protect dignity of disabled persons in medical treatment, proposals believed formulated during the first Trump administration.
        *   However, we criticized the Proposed Rule’s claim that people with gender dysphoria qualify for protections under Section 504.
            *   We argued this claim did not withstand scrutiny and reliance on Williams v. Kincaid, 45 F.4th 759 (4th Cir. 2022) was unwarranted.
            *   We emphasized enormous religious liberty problems expanding Section 504 to include gender dysphoria as a disability would create.
            *   We urged HHS to drop this effort and reiterated concerns in a meeting with White House officials under Executive Order 12866.
        *   Unfortunately, in its May 2024 final rule, HHS persisted in its claim that gender dysphoria counts as a disability under Section 504, even admitting Congress explicitly excluded “gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments” from the Section 504 definition of disability.
            *   This aspect of the final rule directly contradicts 42 U.S.C. § 12211.
            *   Months after the final rule, a coalition of 17 states filed a lawsuit against HHS challenging this aspect of the disability rule. A Louisiana school district filed a second lawsuit.
        *   Last month, on April 11, HHS issued a clarification “document” “out of an abundance of caution” to “clarify and emphasize” that gender discrimination is not a protected disability under federal disability discrimination requirements.
            *   As revealed in the clarification document, the Trump HHS is taking the position that the discussion about gender dysphoria in the Biden rule’s preamble “does not have the force or effect of law” and “is not, and never was, enforceable.”
        *   We are grateful HHS recently took this step.
        *   We urge the administration to take whatever steps prudent to rescind or otherwise nullify the “gender dysphoria” aspect of the 2024 disability rule and resolve litigation against HHS over this rule.

*   CONCLUSION
    *   We thank HHS for this invitation to submit public comment and for its dedication to the rule of law.
    *   We encourage HHS to rescind the agency actions identified above and for the administration to take whatever steps it deems necessary to protect the American people from regulatory overreach.
structuredSections.oneLineSummary: The Ethics and Public Policy Center, through its Administrative State Accountability Project, urges HHS to rescind numerous Biden-era regulations promoting abortion and gender ideology, arguing they are unlawful, arbitrary, harmful to public health and religious liberty, and undermine the rule of law.
structuredSections.commenterProfile:
- **Name/Organization:** Ethics and Public Policy Center (EPPC)
- **Type:** Advocacy Group
- **Role/Expertise:** Scholar at EPPC and member of EPPC’s Administrative State Accountability Project (ASAP); former attorney in the U.S. Department of Justice’s Civil Rights Division. EPPC and ASAP advocate for laws and public policies that reflect "the truth of the human person" and aim to rein in the administrative state.
- **Geographic Scope:** National
- **Stake in Issue:** An organization deeply invested in federal health and human services policy, particularly regarding abortion, conscience rights, religious liberty, and gender identity, actively opposing what it views as unlawful and ideologically-driven regulations from the previous administration.
structuredSections.corePosition: We are grateful for efforts to stop and reverse harmful and unlawful Biden regulatory actions, which we believe are particularly detrimental to the common good. We hope this comment helps equip HHS to implement President Trump’s policy priorities and uphold the rule of law, protecting the American people from regulatory overreach. This will often involve rescinding regulations or conceding their illegality in court.
structuredSections.keyRecommendations:
- Review ASAP publications that document the Biden administration’s illegal actions.
- Rescind specific Biden-era regulations deemed especially harmful to the common good, including:
  - "Ensuring Access to Equitable, Affordable, Client-Centered, Quality Family Planning Services" (Title X rule, Oct. 7, 2021).
  - "Safeguarding the Rights of Conscience as Protected by Federal Statutes" (Jan. 11, 2024).
  - "HIPAA Privacy Rule To Support Reproductive Health Care Privacy" (April 26, 2024).
  - "Removal of Outdated Regulations" (IHS abortion rule, April 30, 2024).
  - "Designated Placement Requirements Under Titles IV–E and IV–B for LGBTQI+ Children" (ACF foster care rule, April 30, 2024).
  - "Health and Human Services Grants Regulation" (May 3, 2024).
  - "Nondiscrimination in Health Programs and Activities" (ACA Section 1557 rule, May 6, 2024).
  - Nullify or rescind the "gender dysphoria" aspect of "Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability in Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance" (May 9, 2024).
- Consider conceding in court that challenged Biden administration regulations are unlawful.
- Take all necessary steps to protect the American people from regulatory overreach.
structuredSections.mainConcerns:
- **Violation of Federal Law and Congressional Intent:**
  - Biden administration regulations are contrary to the express terms of federal statutes like Title X, which prohibits funding for abortion as family planning.
  - New conscience protection rules unlawfully introduce "balancing" standards not found in federal conscience protection laws, making them harder to follow.
  - Interpretation of Bostock by HHS as applying to over a dozen other federal statutes, contrary to Supreme Court's explicit denial that its interpretation of Title VII applied to other statutes.
  - Illegal attempt to include "gender dysphoria" as a disability under Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act, directly contradicting 42 U.S.C. § 12211.
  - Misinterpretation and misconstruction of the Hyde Amendment by IHS to remove all abortion regulations and record-keeping requirements, without reasoned justification.
- **Undermining Conscience and Religious Freedom:**
  - Requiring Title X providers to make abortion referrals jeopardizes conscience rights.
  - The 2024 conscience regulations undercut the department's assertions of taking conscience and religious freedom seriously.
  - HHS grants rule offers inadequate religious exemptions and accommodations for religious organizations, effectively forcing them to violate religious convictions.
  - Section 1557 mandate tramples conscience and religious freedom rights of medical professionals and threatens rights of providers/insurers to decline to assist or pay for elective abortions.
- **Promotion of Ideology Over Sound Science and Public Health:**
  - Regulations promoting "gender ideology" (e.g., foster care, Section 1557) are based on "bad science" and ideologically-driven efforts, contradicting "long-standing scientific understandings of human biology."
  - ACF’s foster care rule is premised on incorrect and harmful assumptions that not "affirming" a child’s LGBTQI+ identity is abuse and that traditional-belief foster parents cannot provide safe homes.
  - HHS's own 2025 report on pediatric gender dysphoria found "very low" quality of evidence concerning the effects of interventions and raised ethical concerns about irreversible procedures for minors.
  - Proposed rules endanger public health and invert civil rights law.
- **Undermining State Authority and Law Enforcement:**
  - The HIPAA Privacy Rule on reproductive health appears designed to intimidate healthcare providers from cooperating with legitimate state law enforcement activities related to abortion regulations, making investigations substantially harder.
  - IHS rule claimed federal law preempted state law on abortion, even for facilities not on reservations, violating states’ rights recognized in Dobbs.
- **Arbitrary, Capricious, and Unnecessary Rulemaking:**
  - Lack of demonstrated need for rules, reliance on "self-serving conjectures" rather than evidence (e.g., HIPAA Privacy Rule).
  - Introduction of vague or undefined terms that create more confusion rather than clarity.
  - Failure to provide reasoned decision-making or address federalism impacts (e.g., IHS rule, where HHS claimed comments on Hyde Amendment substance were "irrelevant").
  - Creation of a drawn-out, ill-defined process for religious exemptions designed to avoid accountability in court.
- **Negative Impact on Healthcare and Vulnerable Populations:**
  - The Section 1557 rule would "radically remake American healthcare" and "harm children."
  - Foster care rules will "compound the challenges facing some of the nation’s most vulnerable children" by reducing the pool of available foster families.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
- FDA should repeal the antiquated 1996 design control requirement for Class I software.
  - Design controls, a part of the good manufacturing practice (GMP) requirements promulgated in 1996, are still requiring all Class I devices that are "automated with computer software" to comply with traditional medical device quality requirements (21 CFR 820.30(a)(2)(i)).
  - This requirement was written before apps and smartphones existed.
  - It is not always necessary for low-risk modern day software-based devices.
  - In light of E.O. 14192, FDA should repeal 21 CFR 820.30(a)(2)(i).
  - This repeal would ensure that Class I software devices are not subject by default to GMP design controls without consideration of the software's intended use and associated risks.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
-   The following items in HHS guidance documents require an excessive number of reports or unreasonable record keeping, request information that is not needed or used effectively, or impede efforts to innovate.
    -   **NIH Grants Policy Statement 2.3.7.2 Requirements for Submitting Unsolicited Applications Requesting $500,000 or More in Direct Costs:**
        -   Current NIH policy for most grant types requires applicants requesting $500,000 or more of direct cost funding in any one year of a proposed project to obtain approval from NIH at least six weeks before grant submission.
        -   The $500,000 limit with advance notice was first established in 2001 (NOT-OD-02-004) and has not been changed since.
        -   Since the threshold is intended to ensure that large, expensive projects are scientifically aligned with the specific interests and priorities of the relevant Institute or Center, it is recommended that NIH periodically set the threshold to a percentile of the size distribution of awards, for example the 60th percentile award size for the prior 3 years, to reduce onerous administrative burdens on both the applicant and NIH at the proposal stage.
    -   **NIH Grants Policy Statement 4.1.15 Human Subjects Protections:**
        -   Eliminate the regulation that requires principal investigators of some large projects to seek approval from the federal sponsor before beginning research with human subjects.
        -   Such approval by the federal sponsor is redundant to the original research approval from a local institutional review board (ethics board) that the PI must obtain and causes unwarranted delays in starting research activities.
    -   **NIH Grants Policy Statement 8.1 Changes in Project and Budget:**
        -   Extend to more grants the NIH policy that allows grantees to automatically carryover surplus funds from one year of a project to the next year.
        -   This policy currently applies to regular research grants, but not to larger, more complex grants, which could also benefit from the time and cost savings it provides.
    -   **NIH Grants Policy Statement 13 Modular Applications and Awards:**
        -   In 1998 NIH policy began allowing applicants requesting $250,000 or less in direct costs per year in a new proposal to use a simplified ‘modular’ budget format.
        -   It is recommended that NIH increase the ceiling amount for modular budgets defined in the NIHGPS to $500,000, significantly extending a budgetary format that is less administratively burdensome for applicants, reviewers, and NIH administrators.
    -   **General Application Guide For NIH and Other PHS Agencies G.220 - R&R Other Project Information Form:**
        -   Current NIH instructions for new grants’ ‘facilities and resources’ section are vague and open-ended, instructing applicants to “describe how the scientific environment in which the research will be done contributes to the probability of success (e.g., institutional support, physical resources, and intellectual rapport). In describing the scientific environment in which the work will be done, discuss ways in which the proposed studies will benefit from features of the scientific environment.”
        -   It is recommended that NIH more closely align instructions with that found in the NSF PAPPG Chapter II.2.g. Facilities, Equipment and Other Resources language to “describe only those resources that are directly applicable” to the proposed project.
    -   **NOT-OD-25-110 (5/7/2025):**
        -   Reinstate the authority of recipient organizations to approve first time ‘no cost extensions’ (automatic carryover of surplus funds at the end of a project) for selected projects.
        -   NIH notice suspended this authority indefinitely, requiring all requests for no-cost extensions to be submitted to and approved by NIH.
        -   This rollback of a prior deregulatory policy causes burdensome paperwork and delays in completing projects.

structuredSections.detailedContent:
*   On May 14, 2025, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) issued a Request for Information (RFI) seeking input on how it can dramatically deregulate across all areas it touches.
    *   Input on how regulations, guidance, paperwork requirements, or other regulatory obligations can be repealed was cited as in scope.
    *   A significant number of FDA regulations either stifle or are overly burdensome to the consumer healthcare industry.
*   The Consumer Healthcare Products Association (CHPA), founded in 1881, is the national trade association representing leading manufacturers and marketers of consumer healthcare products, including over-the-counter (OTC) medicines, OTC medical devices, and dietary supplements.
    *   For over 144 years, CHPA has advocated for the consumer healthcare products industry.
    *   CHPA members provide safe, effective, and affordable therapies for common ailments and diseases.
    *   From this perspective, CHPA offers recommendations to foster innovation in self-care products, benefiting consumers.

*   Issue 1: Unique Device Identification (UDI) Regulation (21 CFR Parts 801 and 830) and Guidance
    *   FDA Center: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) Center for Devices and Radiological Health (CDRH)
    *   Anticipated impact of revising, removing, or sunsetting the regulation, guidance, or policy: High
    *   Regulated Product Category(ies): Select Class I, Class II, and Unclassified medical devices with OTC marketing status (used by a lay person without a prescription).
    *   Proposed Action:
        *   Exempt Unclassified and Class II medical devices that meet the definition of "consumer health product" from requirements for submissions to the Global UDI Database (GUDID).
        *   Permit use of the universal product code (UPC) and/or QR code to satisfy the UDI requirement for all devices that meet the definition of consumer health product.
    *   Existing Regulation(s), Guidance(s), or Alternative Approaches: Unique Device Identification: Policy Regarding Compliance Dates for Class I and Unclassified Devices, Direct Marking, and Global Unique Device Identification Database Requirements for Certain Devices (Guidance for Industry and Food and Drug Administration Staff); 21 CFR § 801.40(d).
    *   Additional Background Information
        *   The UDI system was created for nationwide active post-market surveillance of medical devices, relying on stakeholder engagement for data input into a database for signal detection and predictions.
        *   This framework aims to track medical devices through the healthcare system by incorporating national healthcare databases like electronic patient records.
        *   A 2024 GAO report found that a decade after the UDI rule, progress to leverage UDI for active post-market surveillance has been very limited due to low stakeholder engagement and high program costs.
        *   For OTC medical devices used outside the healthcare system, UDI system effectiveness is even more diminished.
        *   Most OTC medical devices are purchased in retail channels and used by the general public outside healthcare settings, so their uses are not captured in electronic health records (e-HRs) or CMS reimbursement systems.
        *   The UDI regulation permits UPC codes for Class I devices, capturing UDI information through retail point-of-sale scans.
        *   In 2024, the consumer products industry decided to adopt QR codes in lieu of UPC codes, which will minimize UDI information capture in retail and eventually render UPC barcodes on OTC medical devices obsolete in retail.
        *   FDA currently exercises enforcement discretion on GUDID submission requirements for Class I "consumer health products" (510(k)-exempt Class I devices sold OTC that do not fall into specific excluded categories).
        *   CHPA proposes extending this enforcement discretion to Unclassified and Class II OTC medical devices meeting the "consumer health product" definition.
        *   Requiring manufacturers to enter UDI data for Unclassified and Class II OTC medical devices that are consumer health products into GUDID is an unnecessary burden for devices intended for sale without a prescription or healthcare professional assistance.
        *   OTC medical device manufacturers use GS1 identifiers, product names, barcodes, and lot codes for product retrieval; UDI is not used for OTC medical device recalls.
        *   Existing tracking systems can be used for product tracking and safety data collection.
        *   CHPA also requests extending the 21 CFR § 801.40(d) provision allowing UPC codes to serve as UDI for Class I devices to Class II and Unclassified devices meeting the "consumer health product" definition.
        *   Given the industry transition, FDA should recognize QR codes as an alternative to UPC codes for UDI requirements for all devices defined as consumer health products.
        *   CHPA requests UDI deregulation for OTC medical devices based on the following criteria:
            *   Applicability: Class I, Class II, and Unclassified medical devices sold in retail establishments without prescription from healthcare providers that meet the definition of consumer health product under the Final UDI Guidance.
            *   Expand compliance policy in FDA’s Final UDI Guidance regarding GUDID submission requirements for certain Class I devices considered “consumer health products” to also cover Unclassified and Class II devices that meet the definition of consumer health product under the Final UDI Guidance.
            *   Permit UPC code to serve as UDI for not only Class I devices, but also Class II and Unclassified devices that meet the definition of consumer health product.
            *   Permit use of QR code in lieu of UPC code to satisfy the UDI requirement for all devices that meet the definition of consumer health product.

*   Issue 2: Label Review Process for Applications for FDA Approval to Market a New Drug (21 CFR 314)
    *   FDA Center: FDA CDER Office of Nonprescription Drug Products (ONPD)
    *   Anticipated impact of revising, removing, or sunsetting the regulation, guidance, or policy: High
    *   Regulated Product Category(ies): OTC drugs sold under an approved new drug application (NDA) or abbreviated new drug application (ANDA).
    *   Proposed Action: FDA staff should align internally on all requested changes to labeling during each cycle of the review process and convey this information as a single request to the sponsor no less than 14 calendar days before the FDA issues an approval letter.
    *   Existing Regulation(s), Guidance(s), or Alternative Approaches that Address Issue Proposed for Deregulation: None.
    *   Additional Background Information
        *   During the review process for approved labeling for an OTC marketed under an NDA, FDA ONPD staff often request updated labels on a rolling-basis instead of in a single request.
        *   This lack of a coordinated request forces sponsors to complete multiple production runs for the same label, often with only slight differences, and with updated labels expected in days or hours. This is burdensome due to staffing and printing costs.

*   Issue 3: Use of Representative Labeling During Review Process for Applications for FDA Approval to Market a New Drug (21 CFR 314) is Not Permitted.
    *   FDA Center: FDA CDER ONPD
    *   Anticipated impact of revising, removing, or sunsetting the regulation, guidance, or policy: High
    *   Regulated Product Category(ies): OTC drugs sold under an NDA or ANDA.
    *   Proposed Action: Sponsors should be permitted to use representative labeling for OTC drugs marketed under an approved NDA or ANDA during the review process; representative labeling should be used during the review and approval process. Industry will submit all labels as final printed labeling of all shelf keeping units (SKUs) should it be required post-approval.
    *   Existing Regulation(s), Guidance(s), or Alternative Approaches that Address Issue Proposed for Deregulation: None.
    *   Additional Background Information
        *   CHPA defines representative labeling (RL) as a PDF rendering of a label or set of labeling that can illustrate changes to existing product labeling or for new labeling, serving as an "RL template" for a "product family" (all SKUs with the same National Drug Code (NDC) product code but different package sizes).
        *   CHPA previously suggested FDA pilot a program to streamline the label change process, but no pilot was attempted, nor formal guidance issued.
        *   CHPA strongly recommends allowing sponsors to use representative labels during the review period and for approval, to establish that required edits have been made to all remaining labeling prior to marketing.
        *   RL could be used to illustrate FDA-requested or sponsor-initiated label changes without requiring submission of every package size (SKU) within the product family.
        *   The current FDA process requires pre-approval for nearly all label changes, no matter how minor.
        *   Rare instances where FDA has allowed RL create uncertainty among sponsors, demonstrating the process is feasible but inconsistently applied.
        *   Establishing a formal RL process would create consistency across the industry.
        *   Significant burden arises if an NDA or ANDA has multiple SKUs (e.g., one OTC drug has over 60 labels needing updates for last-minute changes).
        *   Sponsors could certify that the RL language reflects changes for all SKUs, as they already certify data accuracy on FDA form 356h (willfully false statements are criminal offenses).
        *   FDA would be able to review all labels post-approval, with sponsors submitting final printed labeling (FPL).
        *   The current requirement to submit all draft labels for multiple SKUs during review is overly burdensome and wastes resources (time, staff, financial).

*   Issue 4: FDA Can Reduce Regulatory Burden for the Agency and Industry by Adhering to Regulation and Its Existing Guidance on “Changes to an Approved NDA or ANDA” for Minor Labeling Changes.
    *   Government Agency: FDA CDER ONPD
    *   Anticipated impact of revising, removing, or sunsetting the regulation, guidance, or policy: High
    *   Regulated Product Category(ies): OTC drugs sold under an NDA or ANDA.
    *   Proposed Action: FDA CDER ONPD staff adhere to existing regulation and Agency guidance for minor labeling changes that can be made via a sponsor’s annual report according to existing regulations.
    *   Additional Background Information
        *   There is regulatory inconsistency in CDER’s process for minor label changes across OTC NDAs, ANDAs, and OTC monographs.
        *   ONPD has expanded its internal definition of major or moderate label changes for OTC NDA products, requiring prior approval supplements (PAS) even for changes without safety concerns.
        *   These same types of changes for ANDAs or OTC monograph drugs do not require prior approval, creating unnecessary workload for FDA and sponsors.
        *   CHPA’s interpretation of existing regulation (21 CFR 204.66(d)(3)) and FDA guidance ("Changes to an Approved NDA or ANDA," April 2024) would allow certain commercial-based label changes to be classified as minor.
        *   Examples of routine commercial-based label changes: new trade dress, promotional coupons, changes/additions to coupons, other commercial offers, and regulatory changes to net contents statements.
        *   Changes to graphics (colors, logos) are unlikely to affect drug identity, strength, quality, purity, or potency, and are typically "editorial" (21 CFR § 314.70(d)(2)(x)), provided they align with requirements like color contrast (21 CFR § 201.66(d)(3)).
        *   These changes could be reviewed in electronic drug listings or described in the applicant’s next Annual Report (21 CFR § 314.70(d)).
        *   ONPD currently requires all net content changes to an OTC NDA to be submitted as PAS, despite FDA guidance noting minor changes like "A change in the number of units… or labeled amount… of nonsterile solid dosage form in a multiple-unit container" are permitted via annual report as having "minimal potential to have an adverse effect" on drug safety or effectiveness.
        *   Requiring prior approval for net quantity changes causes needless delays for consumers and is inconsistent with policies for prescription, ANDA, and OTC monograph drugs.
        *   The practice of requiring prior approval for every label change or attachment for NDA-regulated OTC drugs creates significant delays for industry.
        *   FDA can reduce its workload and review burden by adhering to regulations/guidance allowing minor label changes to be reported in annual reports.
        *   This would provide consumers faster access to OTC products and innovation without increasing public health risk.

*   Issue 5: OTC Drugs Should Be Exempt from Drug Volume Reporting Requirements.
    *   FDA Center: FDA CDER Drug Shortage Staff
    *   Anticipated impact of revising, removing, or sunsetting the regulation, guidance, or policy: High
    *   Regulated Product Category(ies): OTC drugs.
    *   Proposed Action: Exempt all OTC drugs from drug volume reporting requirements.
    *   Existing Regulation(s), Existing Guidance(s), or Alternative Approaches: Reports submitted to FDA online or via email and use of the CDER Direct NextGen Portal.
    *   Additional Background Information
        *   Drug volume reporting (DVR) requirements, under the CARES Act of 2020, apply to anyone registered with FDA under section 510 of the FD&C Act for human or animal drugs, including repackers and relabelers.
        *   This information aims to provide FDA visibility into the drug supply chain and assist in preventing drug shortages (e.g., during the Coronavirus pandemic).
        *   FDA should require reporting only for prescription drugs essential to public health, not for OTC drugs, which span a wide range of therapeutic categories.
        *   DVR imposes a significant administrative burden on pharmaceutical companies through detailed data collection, verification, and submission, consuming human and financial resources that could be diverted from R&D, especially for smaller companies.

        *   Several existing tools address drug shortages, such as a publicly available online portal or email for consumers/stakeholders/HCPs to report potential shortages.
        *   Manufacturers must comply with mandatory reporting requirements for drugs marketed under approved applications, providing essential shortage information.
        *   Manufacturers and applicants can use the CDER Direct NextGen Portal to report shortages, supply interruptions, recalls, and increased product demand. These existing options should be leveraged to reduce DVR redundancy.

*   Issue 10: FDA’s Guidance on Format and Content of Over-the-Counter Monograph Order Requests (OMORs) is Overly Burdensome in Its Data Requirements for Well-established OTC Drug Ingredients.
    *   FDA Center: FDA CDER ONPD.
    *   Anticipated impact of revising, removing, or sunsetting the regulation, guidance, or policy: High.
    *   Regulated Product Category(ies): OTC drugs marketed under an FDA administrative order (i.e., OTC monograph).
    *   Proposed Action: FDA must adopt standards and expectations consistent with historical principles of Generally Recognized as Safe and Effective (GRASE) and the intent of the OTC Monograph User Fee Act (OMUFA), rather than the NDA paradigm, which is overly burdensome.
    *   Existing Regulation(s), Existing Guidance(s), or Alternative Approaches that Address Issue Proposed for Deregulation: Historical principles of GRASE.
    *   Additional Background Information
        *   FDA released a draft guidance "Over-the-Counter Monograph Order Requests (OMORs): Format and Content" on April 13, 2023.
        *   Several recommendations in the OMORs guidance are contrary to established GRASE principles for OTC monograph drugs and align more with new drug application (NDA) requirements.
        *   Finalizing this guidance and imposing its detailed information requirements would significantly burden the OTC industry.
        *   CHPA reiterates concerns primarily on data submission principles and data types FDA should consider when reviewing an OMOR:
            *   Submission of complete data sets for GRASE ingredients should not be required; for ingredients deemed GRASE in existing final orders, complete data summaries (e.g., literature, postmarketing experience) are unnecessary. Requestors should not need to re-submit data supporting GRASE status if already determined for Category III (TFM) or Category I (ANPR) ingredients.
            *   Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Controls (CMC) data should not need to be submitted in an OMOR; this information has not historically been included in OTC monographs, is generally confidential, and is available to FDA on request or during inspection.
            *   The focus of an OMOR should be on the active ingredient, not the drug product; OTC monographs do not include formulation or manufacturing information and do not mandate specific excipients, allowing manufacturers flexibility (codified in 21 CFR 330.1(e)).
            *   Certification for all evidence related to GRASE status should only be required when ingredients have not been recognized as GRASE; a complete summary should not be requested when the ingredient is GRASE, and previously submitted data for Cat III (TFM) or Cat I (ANPR) ingredients should not be required.
            *   Requests for extensive data in various modules (e.g., Module 3: Quality Data; Module 4: Nonclinical Study Reports) should only apply to very specific situations, such as an OMOR for a new ingredient GRASE determination; pre-submission meetings could identify additional data needs. Nonclinical summaries should only be requested for ingredients not deemed GRASE in a final order or for OMORs relying on nonclinical studies as supporting evidence.
            *   FDA should not disregard data from published literature due to lack of case level detail, nor exclude data from older studies simply because methodology has evolved; data from published peer-reviewed literature has always been acceptable for GRASE determination, and such reports seldom contain NDA-level detail.
